articles.title: Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries
articles.text:
Oil can help achieve SDG 7

Globally, over 666 million people do not have access to electricity. If those without electricity were a country, they would be the third most populous on earth. There is no shortage of ‘how-to guidance’ on addressing this human tragedy. Much of it comes from the UN, in tracking progress on Sustainable Development Goal 7 (SDG 7), which aims to achieve universal access to electricity by 2030. Such advice is framed, however, almost exclusively, in the language of solar and wind power, grid access, storage and financing. Most reports omit any role for hydrocarbons in closing the electricity access gap. The opposite is the case. Hydrocarbons are predominantly referred to in such documents in terms of how they can be phased out and removed. Two goals are pursued simultaneously: universal electricity access while restricting electricity generation by certain fuels. With just four years remaining to achieve the goal of universal energy access, perhaps it is time to acknowledge a fact borne out by realities. Never, in human history, have a group as large as 666 million people achieved access to electricity in a four-year time frame by generating electricity through a restricted number of energy sources. The scale is unprecedented. The timeframe is unprecedented. The policies aimed at achieving it, with two seemingly contradictory goals, are unprecedented. Furthermore, there is no historical example of hundreds of millions of people gaining access to electricity without hydrocarbons. Large jumps in access have always come through a mix of fuels and technologies. Texts and progress reports on SDG 7 never suggest oil can play a positive or practical role in closing the electricity access gap. While statistically oil constitutes a small percentage of global electricity generation, roughly 3%, in the bid to achieve universal access, no fuel should be dismissed. There are specific circumstances when oil is appropriate for electricity generation. Three points illustrate this. The first is remote settlements, or those with no grid connection. In such cases, bringing in generators and fuel is simpler than building new lines or facilities. This is why island nations often generate a high proportion of their electricity from oil. For example, the EU country with the highest proportion of electricity generated by oil is Cyprus. The majority of those without electricity live in remote areas, 84% of the 666 million live in rural areas. These are predominantly low-income regions, often in fragile security situations and with weak infrastructure. In such cases, diesel-powered generators can be the right solution. Secondly, diesel-powered generation often has low upfront costs and simple deployment. This avoids the need for large loans that, for example, some well-designed solar mini grids at community scale may require. As climate financing from developed countries has not come close to the levels developing countries require, short-term bridge solutions, like diesel-powered generators, may become more necessary to improve electricity access. The third case when oil plays a crucial role in electricity generation is in terms of emergency backup generation. Diesel generators are known as the ‘default workhorse’ backup generators for critical infrastructure, airports, emergency operation centres, defense facilities, data centres, hospitals and much more.This is because of how promptly they can start operations, their ability to function well in harsh weather conditions and their capacity to sustain power supply for long periods. Many authorities and emergency planners pre-stock diesel generators as part of continuity and civil protection plans.This is not restricted to developing countries. One large survey has found that about 85% of backup generators in commercial buildings and critical facilities in the US run on diesel, and another report suggests that the share worldwide is over 60%.An illuminating example of this is the backup generator system in the largest hospital in Vienna, the Allgemeine Krankenhaus. If the public grid were to fail, within just 15 seconds, a diesel-powered emergency generator would take over the hospital’s power supply, ensuring critical, life-saving equipment keeps functioning. This diesel emergency power plant can maintain power for the entire hospital for 48 hours of autonomous operation and, with shed loading, this can be extended further.These points underscore the fact that there are circumstances when oil powered electricity is an appropriate option. Given that electricity demand is expected to increase by a massive 85% by 2050, perhaps an expanded role of oil in meeting this demand should be considered. In the 1990s, oil constituted around 10% of total electricity generation globally. With technological innovation improving its environmental credentials, oil’s role in future electricity generation cannot be discounted. This important role for oil in electricity generation depends on a secure and stable supply of crude oil, and this is fundamental to all OPEC’s actions and activities. Oil should not be dismissed, nor should any energy source, as the SDG 7 2030 deadline for universal access to electricity looms ever nearer.

articles.title: With Echoes of 1974, a Decisive Victory for the Democratic Party | PIMCO
articles.text:
Libby Cantrill

11/4/2026

| 8 min read

Share via Email

Share via Linkedin

Share via Twitter

In what some are calling a “blunami,” a “bluelash,” and “a red wipeout,” Democrats have won both the House and the Senate in a historically decisive victory.
Two specific indicators had been pointing to a blue wave: 1) the Generic Congressional Ballot, where Democrats were preferred over Republicans by +9 points on average nationwide, and 2) the enthusiasm gap, in which Democrats were more enthusiastic than Republicans about voting by +10 points. Both of those metrics – which have been two statistically significant indicators in other waves (and were not present in 2022) – suggested a 2006-style blue wave, when Democrats took control of both chambers, winning the House by 31 and the Senate by 6 seats.
However, yesterday’s election looks more like 1974 than 2006. Democrats ended up winning by 13 points nationwide, much like in 1974, when voters, tired of Watergate and presidential overreach and angry about inflation and Vietnam, ushered in one of the largest Democratic freshman classes in the House and the Senate as a rejection of Nixon-style politics. This was followed by several years of legislative efforts toward passing “good government” reforms and trying to constrain the executive branch – something we could see in 2027.

The two G’s and two H’s

The two G’s and the two H’s – gas, groceries, housing, and healthcare – are top of mind issues for voters in 2026, as they have been since COVID. Exit polls indicate affordability had a lot to do with last night’s outcome, but there were other issues, including concerns over presidential overreach – particularly as they relate to immigration (in Texas, 65% of voters said Trump had gone too far with immigration).
This was also coupled with a rejection of the general incivility in our politics as well as a response to the Supreme Court’s decision on Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act.
We also note that voters in the U.S. date politicians (and political parties), they do not marry them. Last night was a testament to this. Many of the gains that Trump was able to make in 2024 – with Hispanic voters, young men, and broadly Independents, in particular – were erased last night. Importantly, in our days of thermostatic politics, these folks can swing back, something Democrats would be wise to keep in mind.

Expect a more moderate Democratic majority in both chambers

Something that may be lost in the immediate aftermath, but is pertinent for markets in particular, is that Democrats won by winning in deep Republican states (South Carolina is a Trump +18 state) and House districts. Expect these “majority makers” to avoid cultural lightning rod issues and lean into affordability and oversight; and for deficit hawks, we should expect a renewed “Blue Dog” coalition – the group of moderate Democrats focused on fiscal responsibility.
Additionally, it appears that moderate Democrats did substantially better than progressive candidates in swing states that will be key to 2028. This was the case in Ohio, where the Democratic gubernatorial candidate (Amy Acton) outpaced the more progressive Senate candidate (Sherrod Brown) by 3 points, as well as in Michigan, with Jocelyn Benson outperforming Abdul El-Sayed by 4 points.

Candidate quality really matters

Another lesson from last night, in which Democrats overcame what looked like a nearly impossible Senate map – having to win in deep double-digit Trump territory in order to have a shot at taking back the Senate – is the importance of candidate quality. Many of the candidates recruited by Democrats for the Senate, including Annie Andrews, Roy Cooper, and James Talarico, were not running on the national Democratic platform, but very local ones.
Also, in addition to some strong Democratic candidates, there are Republicans who are wondering how those results would have looked if President Trump had not put his finger on the scale with many of the candidates (e.g., Ken Paxton in Texas, Darline Graham in South Carolina, as well as candidates in North Carolina and Georgia).
In true wave elections, some weird things happen, and last night was no exception. Indeed, Democrats are winning in places they did not know were competitive – in Nevada’s House District 2, for instance, Democrats won for the first time ever (the district was created 40 years ago). In Kansas, of course, a state that has not elected a Democratic senator since 1932, Adam Hamilton easily beat incumbent Republican Senator Roger Marshall.

Where do we stand as of now?

The House: Recall that Democrats needed to win +3 seats to get to the 218 votes to win a simple majority. While many House races have not yet been called as of this writing on Wednesday, it looks like Democrats are on track to win the House by +40 to +45 seats, bringing them to nearly 260 seats. Depending on how the remaining seats are called, this could be the largest Democratic House majority since 2008.
The Senate: Democrats needed to hold onto their current seats and win +4 seats in the Senate, and as of this writing, Democrats have won +7 Senate seats, including South Carolina, North Carolina, Texas, Kansas, Maine, Ohio, and Iowa. But they are also leading in both Mississippi and Alaska, which, if they win, would bring the Democratic majority to 56-44, the biggest majority since 2008.
The governors’ races: The Democratic sweep extended to the gubernatorial races, and while some have not yet been called, it appears that Democrats will take a majority of the governors’ mansions (trending at 28 of the 50 as of this writing). Importantly, this is where the risk lies to the AI trade, not from the federal government.

What about data centers?

The biggest risk to the AI infrastructure buildout is at the state level, and while votes are still being counted, it appears that all of the 45+ data center ballot initiatives that restrict data centers – from Ohio to Nevada to Kansas – have passed, and by large majorities in most cases.
Importantly, many of the newly elected Democratic governors ran on platforms of a statewide moratorium, including in many of the areas with the largest potential buildout that could be the most vulnerable to a pause, including Texas, Georgia, Ohio, and Iowa. What is more is several state legislatures flipped to pure Democratic control, including Arizona, Michigan, Wisconsin, Minnesota, and Nevada – some of which are also likely to take up the issue of codifying data center restrictions.
The conventional wisdom seems to be that the data center rhetoric is merely election-year rhetoric, but we would disagree. We think because the politics around data centers are just so bad – people have a more favorable view of nuclear reactors than they do data centers – and importantly a deep distrust of big tech, this issue has staying power politically. And as with many things, politics often leads policy. We think these new governors will be hard-pressed to not follow through and impose at least some restrictions on data centers, if not outright moratoriums. At the very least, we would expect more restrictions at both the state and local levels and a higher cost of doing business for hyperscalers in particular. A slower buildout could put downward pressure on growth, inflation, and rates.

What does the Democratic sweep mean for national policy?

Remember, even with a blockbuster night, there are still constraints on Democrats in terms of what they can get done. President Trump is still in the White House with veto authority; it takes two-thirds of both chambers to overturn a veto; and Democrats, even with 56 votes in the Senate, would still need at least 4 Republicans to work with to overcome a filibuster in the first place (the filibuster is not going anywhere).
Issues of possible compromise: While there will be a lot of investigations (e.g., tech, Wall Street, defense contractors, and health insurance), there are some areas of possible compromise between Democrats and President Trump, who of course was formerly a Democrat. Those include drug pricing and housing, as well as some black swans such as Social Security reform and immigration. We could possibly see something on AI safety, but we would put lower odds on that. Again, the data center issue is likely to be more at the state level.
Spending: We continue to believe the deficit is a loser from elections in Washington – regardless of how those elections may turn out. Democrats will want to spend more on healthcare – many ran on restoring the Obamacare subsidies and reversing the Medicaid cuts – while Trump will want to (need to) spend more on the Pentagon. We think there is a scenario where the upcoming 2027 debt ceiling is not a volatility event at all as Democrats and Trump are able to find common ground on more spending. Of course, there is another scenario where each overplays their hand, and we see significant volatility into the debt ceiling’s so-called X date, which is mid to late 2027. Regardless, we think deficits will stay elevated above 6%.
Veto-proof issues: There are several issues that could pass both the House and the Senate by a veto-proof majority – 290 in the House and 67 in the Senate – which could include a rescission of Canadian tariffs, a rebuke of the Iran war (this would have to be done through some funding constraint of the Pentagon), and a mandatory imposition of Russian sanctions (that prevents Trump from having any sort of “waiver” authority).
Reconciliation: Recall, there is a Senate procedural process that allows for certain legislation to pass with only 50 votes in the Senate, not the typical 60. We could see Democrats use this to repeal tax credits for tech, for instance, or to increase the debt ceiling, thereby daring Trump to veto it. It is too early to say exactly how this will play out, but I would expect Democrats to lean into this procedural tool.
No or very few confirmations: The biggest difference between a split Congress and a Democratic sweep is the ability for a Democratic Senate to block all judicial and federal nominees; this includes Fed governors, meaning any concern about Fed independence should be finally put to rest. This also means we could see several departures in the lame duck; remember that Defense Secretary Donald Rumsfeld resigned the day after the 2006 elections.
Peak Trump: We said at the beginning of this year that 2025 was likely “peak Trump” as the first year often is for other presidents who enjoy a congressional majority. We think 2027 and 2028 will see Trump’s power much more diminished (as was the case for Biden after the midterms), although it is important to keep in mind that Trump still enjoys broad authorities around foreign policy (Iran escalation still seems a possibility), as well as export controls, sanctions, immigration enforcement, and tariffs, an area we could still see him lean into despite pushback from Congress.

What about 2028?

It is way too early to talk about 2028, but certainly, the large majorities in both chambers will make it more difficult for Republicans to win back Congress, particularly the Senate. But one lesson from 2024 to 2026 is that many voters – almost a simple majority of voters identify as Independents – are renting, not owning, their politicians and their parties. While there are certainly large cushions to insulate Democrats in both chambers, there is of course a risk that Democrats overinterpret these results as an endorsement, rather than what they seem to be more of – a protest.
With that said, we do think last night means that we will see not only a (crowded) open primary for Democrats, but likely one for Republicans as well, as Vice President JD Vance is likely to have to compete for the Republican nomination, rather than be coronated.

Bottom line

Last night will go down in history as one of the largest midterm waves – similar to 1974 and 2006 for Democrats and 2010 for Republicans – but what we have also seen in our thermostatic politics is that things can change in the next election, so it is wise not to draw too many conclusions from last night, although the odds that Democrats hold Congress in 2028 have gone up because of their large cushion.
The immediate market reaction to the election has generally been favorable, with both equity markets and bond markets rallying. For the bond market in particular, an independent Federal Reserve, political focus on affordability, and potentially slower technology investment and AI capital expenditure could shift recent headwinds into tailwinds.
There will be a lot more to chew on over the next few weeks and months, but here are some open questions for both parties: For Republicans, how do they try to recreate the Trump coalition of 2024, including with young people and Hispanics? And for Democrats, do they learn the lesson from this election that at its core, the U.S. is a centrist country with moderates outperforming progressives, or do they pivot too far left, and fail to build on their gains from last night?

articles.title: From “brain drain” to “brain gain”: The case for global skill partnerships in healthcare
articles.text:
Published on
Let's Talk Development

From “brain drain” to “brain gain”: The case for global skill partnerships in healthcare

Limon Bade Rodriguez

Pablo Acosta

November 06, 2026

This page in:

English

English

When designed well, Global Skill Partnerships can transform a global health worker shortage into a development opportunity. | © Shutterstock.com

The world faces a shortfall of approximately 15 million health workers. Yet in lower-income countries, many people who could fill these jobs lack the training that would make them competitive at home or abroad. Global Skill Partnerships (GSPs) were designed to close this gap. They finance training in the worker's home country, then place graduates either in domestic jobs (the "home" track) or in safe, orderly, and legal jobs abroad (the "abroad" track). When they work, everyone gains. Sending and receiving countries strengthen their health workforces, workers build skills while their families benefit from higher incomes.
Building on an earlier blog introducing GSPs, this post draws on a review of existing programs, labor mobility schemes in Asia and the Pacific, and frameworks including the World Health Organization (WHO) Global Code of Practice and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations' (ASEAN) mutual recognition agreements. It assesses what the evidence says about GSPs' effectiveness in delivering quality jobs at home and abroad, and what policymakers should consider before adopting the model in the health sector.

Key insights from the analysis:
1. From “brain drain” to “brain gain.” Emigration of skilled workers is a valid concern, especially in Africa and small island developing states. However, evidence points to potential “brain gain” through at least three mechanisms. GSPs reduce “brain drain” by design. Under the Philippines-Germany GSP, as of April 2025, more than 300 nurses had been trained or were in training, with almost 200 working or planning to work in the Philippines through the “home” track. Prospects for working abroad raise expected returns to health professional education, spurring investment in training in origin countries, particularly by the private sector. In the Philippines, migration incentives were associated with nine additional nurses licensed domestically for every nurse who migrated to the United States. Diasporas further support worker pipelines at home; the German-Kosovar diaspora invested in Heimerer Medical College in Kosovo, with majority of the graduates working domestically.

The Philippines-Germany Nursing GSP’s “home” track mitigates “brain drain”

"Abroad" track (Germany)

Source: Rodriguez, Limon, Galsim, Gian, Lao, Mary Katherine, and Dempster, Helen. 2025. Hundreds of Nurses Trained Through Philippines-Germany Global Skill Partnership. London: Center for Global Development.

Note: Number of nurses on the “home” track (Philippines) and “abroad” track (Germany) as of March 2025.

2. Skill recognition reduces “brain waste.” Early in Germany’s labor mobility program in healthcare, known as the Triple Win, nurses from sending countries waited up to two years for full accreditation, working below their qualifications at lower salaries. The GSP model sought to address this issue by requiring language training and credentials to be completed before departure, so participants arrive already recognized as fully qualified nurses, with access to higher salaries—compared to nurses whose qualifications are not fully recognized in destination countries—, professional development, and pathways to family reunification and residency. Canada’s recognition of nursing qualifications from Aga Khan University in Pakistan offers another model GSPs could adapt.

3. Co-investment delivers proportional benefits. The 2026 amendments to the WHO Global Code of Practice on the International Recruitment of Health Personnel encourage co-investments in health systems for mutual benefit, aside from expanding the Code’s scope to include care workers. In the Philippines-Germany GSP, German employers finance not only the training, migration, and accreditation costs, but also modern equipment, curriculum upgrades, and scholarships in partner nursing schools. This also illustrates how employer financing and private capital can help expand the skill systems needed for jobs at home and abroad. The World Bank’s aged care GSPs - linking Colombia, Ecuador, and Dominican Republic with Spain, and Kenya with Canada - similarly co-invest in healthcare education and training systems in origin countries. The key principle: GSPs must respond to origin countries’ health and employment priorities to build political support.

4. Language training and integration are essential. The Philippines-Germany GSP provides advanced language training, and the fact that nurses on the "abroad" track stay with the same employer despite no employment bond suggests these investments support retention. Japan's programs facilitating nursing and caregiving from Indonesia, the Philippines, and Vietnam, including Japanese language training—supported by the Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA) through online portals, mobile apps, and migrant worker consultation services—point in the right direction.

5. South-South and intra-regional GSPs are growing. The scale of the global health worker shortage makes South-South and intra-regional GSPs just as important as traditional South-North programs. In the Pacific, labor mobility in aged care from Solomon Islands to Niue and in nursing from Papua New Guinea to Fiji are potential starting points; South Asia presents similar opportunities as Sri Lanka's working-age population peaks. Strengthening Papua New Guinea’s capacity to train nurses, for instance, could help meet demand both domestically and in neighboring Pacific countries. These programs can build on existing frameworks like ASEAN's mutual recognition agreements and Aga Khan University's nursing campuses in Kenya, Tanzania, and Uganda. The World Bank, the Asian Development Bank, and bilateral donors including the Belgian Development Agency are paying increasing attention to this model.

Policy recommendations
To deliver on their promise, GSPs in the healthcare sector need to:

Foster human capital accumulation in both origin and destination countries by creating enabling conditions for public and private investment in education and training

Ensure mutual benefit by linking GSPs to origin and destination countries’ health, education, and employment priorities, building political support through clear and tangible public benefits

Reduce “brain waste” by embedding skill recognition before international labor mobility begins, not after a multi-year waiting period upon arrival

Invest in integration through language training, housing support, and community engagement from the outset and in reintegration of returnees through employment assistance and social protection.

When designed well, GSPs can transform a global health worker shortage into a development opportunity. For origin countries, they mean higher-quality training, greater availability of qualified health workers, stronger health systems, increased remittances, and diaspora investment. For destination countries, they mean a reliable, qualified, and integrated workforce.

The authors acknowledge Edson Araujo, Manjula Luthria, and Thomas Walker for their valuable feedback and Wonjun Jung for his research assistance.

articles.title: Market update - November 6th 2026 | CoinShares
articles.text: Bitcoin, the AI sell-off and October payrolls Bitcoin had initially taken the Democratic sweep relatively calmly, which is perhaps unsurprising given markets had been rehearsing the outcome for weeks. The more disruptive move came yesterday, when the AI trade finally wobbled hard enough to drag almost everything else with it. The Nasdaq fell 5.5%, the Nasdaq 100 6.4% and semiconductors 12%, while Bitcoin fell just over 5%. More than US$1B of leveraged crypto positions were liquidated in the process. The weakness was particularly acute among Bitcoin miners that have increasingly repositioned themselves as AI and data-centre plays, with several falling by double digits. Highlighting that this looks less like a crypto-specific deterioration and more like Bitcoin becoming collateral damage in a broader de-risking of the technology trade.The election itself still looks more relevant for the pace of crypto reform rather than specifically for Bitcoin’s medium-term direction. The CLARITY Act now faces a harder path, while Democratic control gives the party greater influence over committee agendas, appointments and investigations into Trump-linked crypto ventures. But The CLARITY Act is also becoming less important than it once was. The GENIUS Act is already law, while the SEC and CFTC have continued to provide regulatory pathways within their existing powers. Congress is therefore no longer the only route to progress. The CLARITY Act would still provide more durable statutory certainty, particularly for Ethereum, DeFi and token issuers, but its absence no longer amounts to regulatory paralysis.The consequences should vary considerably across the market. Bitcoin is relatively insulated because its regulatory status is already well established. US exchanges, token issuers and businesses dependent on new permissions have more at stake. Established, compliant operators could even benefit if political scrutiny falls disproportionately on weaker competitors. Among listed crypto equities, miners remain more complicated. Their existing power and data-centre infrastructure makes them attractive to AI hyperscalers, but that same exposure now leaves them vulnerable when the AI trade itself comes under pressure.Oil has also fallen sharply as hopes for progress in US-Iran talks have improved, taking some pressure off inflation expectations. That looked supportive for rates yesterday, especially as the equity sell-off drove demand into Treasuries and pulled expectations for a December hike lower. The relief did not last long. Today’s October payroll report came in at 165,000, massively above the roughly 65,000 consensus, while unemployment edged down to 4.1%. Professional and business services, healthcare and transportation all added jobs. The labour market is clearly stronger than the market had assumed.The latest payrolls data reinforces the Fed’s hawkish stanceThat is an awkward result for Bitcoin with yesterday’s tech rout briefly giving markets reason to think the Fed might be able to soften its stance, particularly with oil falling and financial conditions tightening through equities. Today’s payroll beat pushes back in the opposite direction. With inflation still elevated, a labour market adding 165,000 jobs gives the Fed considerably less reason to worry about growth and more room to focus on price stability. Bitcoin remains highly sensitive to precisely this sort of repricing in short-term rate expectations.For crypto policy, the election result is not game over, there was bipartisan support for The CLARITY Act before the vote, and stablecoins still provide a useful additional source of demand for US Treasuries at a time when fiscal pressures remain uncomfortable. The administration also retains substantial executive authority. Less legislative freedom does not necessarily mean less policy influence, and a frustrated president may lean more heavily on foreign policy and executive action, hardly a recipe for lower market volatility.So the picture is more complicated than it looked immediately after the election. Political uncertainty has fallen, oil is moving in the right direction and regulatory progress can continue without The CLARITY Act. Against that, yesterday’s AI sell-off exposed how intertwined crypto has become with the broader technology and data-centre trade, while today’s payroll number has restored some of the hawkish macro pressure. For Bitcoin, real yields, dollar liquidity and ETP flows still matter more than the composition of Congress. The election changes the political backdrop, but the Fed still holds the more important cards.SourcesUS Bureau of Labor Statistics, Employment Situation, October 2026, released 6 Nov 2026CoinDesk, AI-led technology and crypto sell-off, 5-6 Nov 2026Federal Reserve / CME FedWatch, December rate expectations, 5-6 Nov 2026US Bureau of Labor Statistics, JOLTS, September 2026S&P Global, US PMI, October 2026

articles.title: Take Two: Central banks on hold - BNP Paribas Asset Management - United States
articles.text:
What do you need to know?

The Federal Reserve decided to keep interest rates on hold at 3.75%-4% by a vote of 10-2, with two of the 12-member committee favouring a 25-basis-point rise. The Fed stated that while inflation remains high, “the accumulation of more information” is first needed to guide its return to the 2% goal – though expectations of a further rate hike by year end remain strong. Meanwhile, an advance estimate for US GDP growth in the third quarter showed expansion at an annualised 3.4%, up from Q2’s 2.2% and above expectations of 3.2%.

Around the world

The European Central Bank voted to keep interest rates steady last week, despite annual inflation accelerating to 3.8% in September, a three-year high. The ECB noted that rising energy prices are likely to drive up inflation and lower growth within the region. The eurozone economy grew 0.4% on a quarterly basis in Q3, a slowdown from Q2’s 0.6%, according to official data released after the ECB meeting. Elsewhere, the Bank of Japan kept rates unchanged at 1.25% and said underlying inflation had reached its 2% target, the first time since the goal was set in 2013.

Figure in focus: 37%

Foreign direct investment increased by 37% globally in the first half of 2026, compared to the average half-year level in 2025, according to the United Nations’ Trade and Development arm. The rise was largely driven by developed economies which saw investment flows rise by more than 70% in the first half of 2026. However, overall activity weakened, with the number of new projects falling by 15% and international project finance deals declining by 11%. The slowdown in activity reflects global uncertainty over geopolitical tensions, energy prices and supply chain disruptions, the UN said.

Chart of the week

About a third of US and Europe-listed companies had released their third quarter earnings as of last week. Things are going well. In the US, earnings have risen by 37%, though a big contributor to that growth is the technology sector. Excluding technology stocks, the earnings growth rate is a still good 17%. In Europe, earnings are up 25%. Investors also look at how much better or worse the results are compared to what was expected. So far, earnings have surpassed expectations by 3%-4%, in line with historical averages.

Words of wisdom: Big Bang

The deregulation of the London Stock Exchange, referred to as the Big Bang, marked its 40th anniversary last week.On 27 October 1986,the open outcry trading floor was replaced by electronic order books, and fixed broker commissions were abolished, leading to a sudden surge in trading volumes and lower costs for investors. This transformed London into a leading global financial centre. As investment from the US and Asia flowed into London, the Big Bang caused a ripple effect across Europe with the region accelerating the pace of modernising its own trading models.

What’s coming up?

On Tuesday, the Reserve Bank of Australia convenes to set interest rates. Wednesday sees the eurozone release a flash estimate for October’s inflation rate. Several final Purchasing Managers’ Indices for October are issued on Wednesday covering the eurozone, China, UK, and the US. The Bank of England meets to set interest rates on Thursday. On Friday, the US releases its latest jobs data.

Greg Hall: Hey, everybody, welcome to another episode of Accrued Interest, PIMCO's podcast dedicated to serving financial advisors, their clients and the wealth management community. As usual, I'm your host, Greg Hall. I lead our wealth management business here in the United States. And today we are going to talk about the election. I am so fortunate to be joined in the room by Libby Cantrill.
Libby is our head of public policy. Libby has lived and breathed the midterm elections, what, for months.
Libby Cantrill: I'm here to talk about it, though. I have survived.
Greg Hall: Yeah, that's true. So we're recording this Thursday afternoon. Libby has been nonstop watching the results, interpreting them, helping our investment committee interpret what's going on and what the implications might be for markets and for policy going forward. And we, of course, appreciate this. You've been spending a lot of time with our clients, helping them do the same thing.
So, Libby, thanks for carving out a few minutes here to talk to us on the podcast.
Libby Cantrill: Always happy to be on the pod.
Greg Hall: All right. I'm so excited to get into this because I really want to hear your take on this stuff. Why don't... let's just start with a level set. In your words, in your analysis, what happened? And we'll talk about some of the, you know, the things underneath the surface that you think are interesting, and the results themselves.
Libby Cantrill: Yeah. I mean, this was, you know, a generational, you know, rejection of, referendum on, rebuke of the administration. You know, as you know, the midterm elections are always a referendum on the party in power. So Democrat, Republican, oftentimes the party in power loses seats. And that was our expectation. We were looking at some two kind of wonky indicators: the generic congressional ballot, the sort of preference of one party over another among voters.
Democrats were leading that by about ten points. And then also the enthusiasm gap. You know, how excited is one group of voters over another? Democrats were leading that by 11 points. The reason why I focus on those indicators is because they have been suggesting waves in other wave elections. For instance, in 2022, when everyone was talking about the red wave,
those indicators were not in wave territory. So these were suggesting that we would see a very good night for Democrats and a bad night for Republicans. But what ended up unfolding was really the sort of blue... blue-sami, or the blue-back, or however you want to talk about it.
Greg Hall: The blue-nami. The...
Libby Cantrill: The blue-nami, or "nami"? Yes. My fatigue is showing here. It was just a, you know, a Republican wipeout. And what you saw is that Democrats were competitive in places that they didn't even know that they were going to be competitive in, right? They won House seats that they've actually never won before. House congressional districts that were created, you know, 40 years ago, that had been long held by, or only held by, Republicans.
And then, of...
Greg Hall: Of course, one of the late-night guys that I pick up on YouTube, usually the morning after, because I can't stay up until midnight or 12:30 anymore. I'm not that cool. He joked that the last time Kansas sent a Democrat to Congress was before they sent Dorothy to Oz.
Libby Cantrill: I mean, 1932. It is. Yeah, that is. Yeah. And the same thing, you're seeing this in the South, right? The fact that Democrats were even competitive in places like South Carolina and Mississippi. And now, in South Carolina's case, they have won that seat. They probably will win in Mississippi as well. So again, I think we were expecting a good-to-great night.
What, you know, for Democrats, it's kind of a great-to-fantastic night. I think there are a couple of observations that are worth noting for investors, because I do think, and, you know, we've seen this before, where a party wins a mandate and then they over-interpret that mandate. And I think what we saw on Tuesday night was really just indicative of what we've really seen over the last few cycles, which is sort of this thermostatic nature of politics.
We kind of, you know, you kind of go, you get too cold, and then so you go, you know, you turn up the thermostat, and then you get too hot, and then you go cold again. It's kind of the same way with the left, right and left. And so we saw independents breaking for Democrats disproportionately. They're mad about affordability, they're mad about the Iran war. We can talk about those things. We saw young people, again, breaking for Democrats. We saw Hispanics breaking for Democrats. These are... these three cohorts had really helped to get President Trump elected, and now, of course, helped with this blue-nami or what have you. But, and this is a big but, you know, these folks are still shopping, right?
They are, you know, we're renting politicians in this country. We do not own them. We are dating them, we do not marry them. And I think they are going to be looking at these companies, you know, using their subpoena authority, you know, requiring them to come to Capitol Hill, and just making them more kind of headline risk around technology companies, and then also potentially investors. So I think there's maybe a little bit more reputational risk, more headline risk now, with the Democratic sweep, than maybe was sort of priced in.
But again, that's a little bit more sizzle than steak, if you will. Makes for sort of sexy headlines. Doesn't actually really do anything, right? It maybe sets up the platform for what Democrats want to run on in 2028, but outside of that, doesn't have any sort of real near-term policy implications. The near-term policy implications is that, again, at the state level.
And what we were watching were many of these governor races, where there is a lot of compute that has been planned to be built in terms of data centers. So you have some of them permitted, but a lot of them just sort of in the hopper, kind of planned but not permitted. The construction has not begun on them, and what have you. And those, I do think, are... were vulnerable going into Tuesday night. But now, if you've looked at how these governor races have turned out, they're pretty vulnerable. And the reason is because...
Greg Hall: So talk about the governors for a second, just because I, you know, we didn't spend time on it at the outset. But, I mean, equally surprising, in many cases, of what we saw.
Libby Cantrill: Yeah, I mean, this, you know, the Democratic sort of tidal wave did not discriminate, right? It did not discriminate between the House, the Senate or the governor's mansion. And I think what you saw was a lot of governors' races that were close flip, but then you saw some that weren't really necessarily close also flip. And Texas, I think, is an example.
Sure. And Texas, of course, is very relevant to this, because there's just so many existing data centers in Texas, and there are a lot that are planned. So Texas was what we were looking at. One of the states, Ohio, I mean, I would argue that sort of ground zero for this debate is, you actually... Ohio, I think, had 10 or 15 measures directly on the ballot that were all anti-data center, all easily passed.
You also have now a Democratic governor-elect who has run on a platform of a conditional moratorium in Ohio. Ohio, sort of the second most, you know, state that has the most planned compute kind of in the works. And then Georgia is also another state with a lot of kind of planned compute. And that also flipped to Keisha Lance Bottoms, who also ran on a platform of a moratorium.
I think they're all sort of... I mean, there's nuance around what they mean by a moratorium. Does that apply to just new projects? Will they actually follow through on the moratorium? I think they will. And I don't mean to be the Debbie Downer here, but I just hear a lot of folks on the sell side, in particular on television, who are saying, oh, this is just election-year rhetoric. Maybe, but this is such a politically toxic issue that I think we should... it's sort of misplaced, this optimism that you don't have some politician sort of follow through on the rhetoric and actually impose, if not more restrictions around the edges, a full-on moratorium. And I do think that's the easiest thing for a lot of these governors to do: use executive authority, a little bit like what Kathy Hochul did here.
Right. And it wasn't super politically... popular among sort of industry, but it was politically popular. She just rode to, you know, to reelection very easily here.
Greg Hall: She just made a blanket prohibition, right?
Libby Cantrill: Like, she basically just said, hey, we're going to press pause on all of this. Now, New York has not been kind of ground zero for a lot of this data center buildout. So in terms of actually affecting a lot of the projects, it was pretty minimal. But what she said was like, hey, I'm going to try to get in front of the state legislature, which was going to go for an even more draconian prohibition, and more permanent, and I'm going to get in front of it.
I'm going to press pause. I'm going to work with the state legislature to kind of come up together with some guidelines for what these data centers need to adhere to in order to invest. And that is the nature of what I think this prohibition could look like, if you see one in Ohio or Georgia or Texas, where it would be pressing the pause button, not the stop button.
And I think that is a distinction with a difference. It's worth, you know, reinforcing that. But it does mean, in the short term, that you could see a meaningful slowdown in, you know, some of this CapEx buildout. Not sure, if you just look at the GDP growth estimates, that they're really factoring that. And as you know, we've had sort of active debates around this, around kind of how important are the politics on this.
I just think on this particular issue, it is tapping into a lot of voter discontent, affordability, you know, the sort of this David and Goliath setup, and then also real suspicion around Big Tech.
Greg Hall: Yeah. It's... I don't know what the analog would be. You probably have thought about this, you know, whether it's fracking or nuclear or, you know, because it... Yeah, it doesn't feel like a one-sided issue. Again, I don't... I live in New York City. I don't think they're going to build a data center on my block. It would probably be difficult and expensive, but...
Libby Cantrill: Pretty expensive, I think, at the very least.
Yeah.
Greg Hall: But I think, you know, in these kind of, like, semi-rural, exurban spots, it's economically... it can, obviously, it adds a lot of jobs. It can be valuable to the local economy, the local tax base. But then there's the environmental impacts and power impacts, the water impacts and all that stuff. And, you know...
Libby Cantrill: And the interesting thing... Sorry to interrupt you. I think the interesting thing is that It does add a lot of jobs on a... and I'm not trying to be endorsing one view or another, but I think this is part of the... why this politically has more problems than people think, is because those jobs, yes, it absolutely helps the local economy, the, you know, the deli and the, you know, however, whatever. That... All of that sort of the surrounding...
Greg Hall: temporary housing, those... Construction and...
Libby Cantrill: Yeah, exactly. Yeah, absolutely. But, you know, those jobs are relatively short-lived. They're construction jobs, they're HVAC jobs or what have you. And what a lot of these towns are finding is that they don't have the labor. And so they're having to bring folks from out of town into town. And that has its own kind of political implications.
This is not like the GM plant, right? That's then built, and then your, like, sister works at the GM plant, your father-in-law works at the plant. This isn't like the sort of local, kind of community-oriented place. This is a place that is... a lot of folks are coming from out of town. They're building that. Yes, there's some generating some local activity, and then they're leaving.
Now, of course, you said, you know, the taxes, the property taxes in particular, are very attractive to a lot of these mayors and what have you. But to the voters, they're not necessarily. And, you know, I think it all means is that just there's going to be more friction in this buildout. It's going to cost a lot more.
So even if these moratoriums don't come to pass, these governors are going to put some pretty high price concessions or requirements in place. Obviously, tax incentives are just going to be completely rolled back. But then what are they going to demand from these hyperscalers and data center developers to build locally? You know, we've obviously invested in some of these data centers, you know, Project Beignet in particular, in Louisiana.
I think Meta did do a nice job of some of making sure that, A, it was a community that really wanted these data centers, and also that there were some very clear benefits to the populace in terms of teacher salaries and what have you. So it's not to say this is impossible, and that, you know, they don't have some practice doing it.
But I do think that just the bar to build all of this, because of the politics... Again, politics leads policy. Policy is downstream from politics. And the politics of this are just so bad. The nuclear stuff is so interesting, because if you look at the surveys, this is more unpopular than a nuclear reactor. So you're like, you'd rather have a... a nuclear reactor in your backyard than a data center? The voters are saying yes.
Greg Hall: I mean, I'm not sure it's what I would do.
Libby Cantrill: But, and there is a... there's obviously some emotional... I mean, this is sort of a reflexive kind of emotional issue, and it's kind of captured the imagination. I mean, maybe the Keystone pipeline was a little bit like this, but this was... it was nothing... It was much more kind of localized, and it wasn't as broad-based. But I, talking to our energy analyst, you know, John Devir, who's head of credit research, I mean, he sort of has likened this.
He's like, yeah. And that was, you know, that had a lot of... the politics led the policy on that one. And the policy were, obviously, that, you know, we had to stop the building of Keystone. So...
Greg Hall: Well... Look, it's... I think for those of us who live in the city, right, like, it's eye-opening. My mom lives in Potomac, Maryland. And of course, Loudoun County is right across the river, and sort of ground zero for some of this stuff. And that gave me a real sense of just the pitched community resistance. And I've been fortunate enough to have gone to a number of kind of community meetings and civic meetings and smaller towns over the course of, you know, not always living in New York City.
And these are passionate and engaged. It's actually... it's a wonderful testament to the power of the civic fabric.
Libby Cantrill: Again, like David and Goliath. I mean, my dad's family is from Kansas and they own farmland, and there's a data center developer that wants to go in there. And it is just... to see the resistance in rural Kansas.
Greg Hall: Yeah.
Libby Cantrill: I mean, it's really been pretty striking.
Greg Hall: All right. Well, it'll be obviously, it'll be fascinating to see how that plays out. The, you know, one of the things that we've been, you know, just mentioning to advisors as often as we can is that, you know, for markets, it's not necessarily always just the direction of how something works fundamentally, but it's what's priced in, of course, the expectations. And with stocks having, you know, sort of resided at peak valuations, peak, you know, P/E, depending on how you measure it, for a little bit of time now, it's probably not surprising to sort of see some violent adjustments to valuations in the marketplace as they sort of digest the uncertainty that's been injected into this trade. And we'll just have to see where it goes from here, and do what we always do, which is adjust to the facts as they develop.
Libby Cantrill: Absolutely. And just make sure that we are being as selective, and always with our fiduciary hat on, which, of course, is the hat that we always wear.
Greg Hall: And with your advice, I'm sure our investment committee will be well steered through these churning waters. All right, Libby, we've gone for 45 minutes.
Libby Cantrill: Sorry about that.
Greg Hall: No, No,
Libby Cantrill: never short of... You know, no one has ever accused me of being...
Greg Hall: We haven't even talked about…
Libby Cantrill: 2028.
Greg Hall: We haven't...
Libby Cantrill: It's too early. That's kind of the, you know, the headline.
Greg Hall: When should we talk to you again? When are we going to know more?
Libby Cantrill: I mean, I always enjoy talking to you, Greg, but I think probably next summer is really when you're going to really start seeing... You'll see people declare probably, you know, maybe in the next month, but next summer we should have a good sense of what the field looks like. And then we may even be having some debates, and I apologize.
And, you know, for those people who are not signed up to Washington Watch, they can sign up if they want to, because I will be writing, most likely, about some of those debates, because we probably... I mean, it's going to be an open primary on the left, but probably on the right too, it looks like. I think this is one of the read-throughs for 2028, is that, you know, JD Vance is not going to be coronated. It probably will be a competitive and likely crowded primary on the right too.
Greg Hall: Okay, lot to unpack here. One, Washington Watch is Libby's newsletter that she sends out. And if you're interested in being on that newsletter, you can contact your PIMCO representative, and we can get you on that list. It's a terrific read. I read it every time it comes out. Secondly, we're not waiting until summer to talk to you again, so you can just put that out of your head. We will be speaking at some time or, you know, earlier in the year. I'm sure something will happen, between now and then. And then, you know, it's funny, because when you said debates, I thought, surely she must mean internal debates at PIMCO about the direction of things. And you mean full...
Libby Cantrill: I mean full-on, like, primary debates. And we remember the Trump debates with 17 people on the stage, and Little Marco, and all of that. So, yeah, I mean, I really, you know, this is going to, I think, probably good for democracy, maybe bad for headline risk and maybe some volatility for markets. But I think good for democracy on both sides.
Greg Hall: Everybody enjoy your six or seven months off then. And then get the popcorn for next summer. With that, thank you for being with us, as always. Thank you, everybody, for listening. Please do, if you enjoyed today's podcast, if you want to learn more, you can visit us at PIMCO.com in the US, or your local PIMCO website
in another country, if you happen to be listening to us overseas. At PIMCO.com, if you identify yourself as a financial advisor, you'll be taken to Advisor Forum. That's your one-stop shop for anything you need from PIMCO to digest the news and its implications as quickly and efficiently as possible, and get back out there, spending time with your clients and helping them navigate these volatile markets.
Please also do us the tremendous favor of pressing like and subscribe if you're listening to this on Spotify, if you're listening to this on Apple Podcasts. It just helps us know that you're there, and we can continue to devote time, effort and attention to bringing you the best quality content that we can. Good luck out there, and we'll talk to you soon.

From This Episode

After a blue wave swept the 2026 midterms, PIMCO Head of Public Policy Libby Cantrill checks in on what drove the results and what comes next. She explains why the swing to the left was part protest vote and part gravity finally taking hold, as affordability concerns brought the realities of a two-speed economy to the ballot box. It was a historic victory for Democratics, but one that carries risk for the party if they overplay their hand. Tune in to hear how the new political landscape could shape fiscal policy, debt and spending levels, the AI buildout, and your clients’ portfolios.

articles.title: AOR Update: The Big Picture Beats Politics | Franklin Templeton
articles.text:
Election Day has markets watching how divided Washington will be over the coming two years. A Democratic House is the consensus outcome, and markets increasingly expect Democrats to win the Senate as well. What remains unknown is the size of each potential majority, which will determine whether the next two years bring gridlock and brinkmanship, or a bipartisan spending deal. Regardless of the result, we believe above-trend economic growth, powerful earnings delivery and a historically strong post-midterm window could support a more durable rally for equities in the year ahead.

A Low Bar for House Democrats

History suggests there is a low bar for Democrats to retake the House of Representatives. The president’s party has lost House seats in 18 of the 20 midterms since World War II, and both exceptions came when the president’s approval rating was in the 60% range. Today looks very different than those exceptions, with President Trump’s approval rating sitting in the mid-to-high 30s, Republicans holding only a slim House majority and current polling favoring the Democrats. Prediction markets have largely priced this in with the odds that Republicans lose the House at roughly 90%.

The Senate is a closer contest, but momentum has shifted toward Democrats. Prediction markets now give them roughly a 65% chance of winning control, which would require a net gain of four seats. A Democratic sweep of Congress is no longer an unlikely scenario, which shifts the focus to the margin in each chamber.

Margins Matter More Than the Majority

Speaker Johnson’s tenure has shown how hard it is to run the House with a majority of fewer than five seats, and the Senate has recently offered a similar lesson. With a 50-50 split early in the Biden administration, Senators Joe Manchin and Kyrsten Sinema often held the deciding votes and used them to reshape major Democratic priorities.

When the margin is that thin, a few members can block legislation, extract concessions or stall the legislative agenda entirely. If the midterms leave either chamber with a similarly slim majority, it would likely bring gridlock and brinkmanship over government funding, a higher risk of shutdowns and little new fiscal legislation.

The Case for a Grand Bargain

If Democrats win both chambers with workable margins, a grand bargain between congressional Democrats and the White House could emerge. Democrats could back higher defense spending in exchange for fully restoring social programs. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act included more than US$1 trillion in cuts to Medicaid and SNAP over 10 years, and Democrats want to reverse them.

The lesson from the first Trump administration, when Democrats won the House in the 2018 midterms, could be a useful case study for what lies ahead. The two parties went on to pass the Bipartisan Budget Act of 2019, which raised both defense and nondefense spending caps and led the Congressional Budget Office to raise its 10-year deficit projection by US$1.7 trillion.

A deal is far from certain, however, as both sides would need to sell a compromise to their bases with 2028 in view, and any agreement would likely follow a stretch of grandstanding. A deal, if enacted, could lift nominal growth and benefit defense contractors, Medicaid-exposed health care providers and consumer businesses serving lower-income households. The trade-off is a larger deficit, which could keep upward pressure on long-term yields and strengthen the case for the Fed to move further into restrictive territory.

History Favors Investors After the Vote

Whatever the outcome, policy effects will likely show up only at the margin: modest tailwinds or headwinds for certain sectors rather than major changes for the broad index. For the S&P 500 Index, the most important thing has historically been simply getting past the midterms.

Since 1950, the S&P 500 has gained an average of 15.1% in the 12 months after the midterm election, which has tended to act as a clearing event. Every one of those 19 periods produced a positive return (see chart below). Stocks have typically benefited as election uncertainty dissipates, divided government limits big policy surprises and the post-midterm window overlaps with the third year of the presidential term, which historically has been the strongest stretch of the four-year cycle. Although past performance doesn’t guarantee future results, this seasonal tailwind is hard to ignore.

Exhibit 1: Post-US Midterm Election Stock Market Performance

The Economy Is the Stronger Signal

Beyond the calendar, an even bigger reason for optimism comes from a robust economy that is gaining momentum. US gross domestic product grew at a 3.4% annualized pace in the third quarter, accelerating from 2.2% in the second quarter. Business investment led the way as the artificial intelligence buildout continues and steady consumer spending provided additional support. Our Recession Dashboard tells a similarly resilient story. Eleven of its 12 indicators are flashing expansionary green, with no changes in October, a reading that implies recession odds of only 15% over the next 12 months.

Exhibit 2: US Recession Dashboard

Data as of October 31, 2026. Sources: BLS, Federal Reserve, Census Bureau, ISM, BEA, American Chemistry Council, American Trucking Association, Conference Board, Bloomberg, CME Group, FactSet and Macrobond. The US Recession Dashboard was created in January 2016. References to the signals it would have sent in the years prior to January 2016 are based on how the underlying data was reflected in the component indicators at the time.

That economic momentum is showing up even more forcefully in corporate profits. S&P 500 earnings are on track for 30% year-over-year growth in the third quarter, which would mark a third consecutive quarter above 25%. Just as notable, estimates for both 2026 and 2027 continue to climb, bucking the typical tendency for forward estimates to drift lower over time. Rising earnings are what ultimately drive stock prices in the long run.

Exhibit 3: EPS Earnings Robust

EPS Earnings Robust

Sources: FactSet, S&P. Past performance is not a guarantee of future results. Investors cannot invest directly in an index and unmanaged index returns do not reflect any fees, expenses or sales charges.

Big Picture > Politics

Putting it all together, prediction markets are decisively pricing a divided government scenario given the low bar in the House. However, history suggests that the size of the majorities will matter more for markets than which party wins control. A narrow Congressional majority would likely bring gridlock and brinkmanship, offering little new fiscal support while periodic shutdown scares add volatility. A Democratic sweep with healthy margins could yield a grand bargain that funds both parties’ priorities and adds a modest fiscal boost. That said, neither outcome changes the bigger picture with markets entering what has historically been a strong post-midterm period. Beyond that seasonal tailwind, we believe above-trend economic and earnings growth will overwhelm any election-related volatility to drive stocks forward in the year ahead. 6 November 2026
Daily Navigator

Download Report

Key highlights
USD holds steady despite sharp equity sell-off: The USD index (DXY) was little changed on Thursday as concerns over tighter AI regulation and slower data-centre investment following the Democrats’ landslide victory at the US mid-term elections weighed on US equities. The Nasdaq fell 5.5% and S&P 500 declined 4.4%, boosting demand for US government bonds and pushing yields lower. Weekly jobless claims fell to 189,000, matching a 57-year low, while Q3 productivity rose 3.6% annualised. Fed officials Hammack and Barkin highlighted persistent inflation risks. However, markets reduced the probability of a December Fed hike to around 66%, from 80% a week ago. DXY support is at 100.95, with today’s US employment report the next catalyst.
JPY gains on safe-haven demand and hawkish BoJ minutes: USD/JPY fell 0.5% to 157.70. The BoJ’s September minutes showed support for further rate increases, with some members open to faster tightening if inflation accelerates. Governor Ueda’s IMF speech later today (US time) will be watched for guidance ahead of December’s policy meeting. Investors will also monitor Japan GPIF’s upcoming quarterly report for potential shifts towards domestic government bond investments. USD/JPY support is at 157.00.
AUD faces near-term pressure despite interest-rate advantage: AUD/USD fell 1.1% to 0.6931. The US equity sell-off outweighed earlier support from surging gold prices, a softer USD and Australia’s firm trade surplus. The Nasdaq slump and copper’s decline to a three-month low on AI-spending concerns weighed on the risk-sensitive AUD. Tuesday’s cautious RBA hike also weighed on sentiment, while speculative AUD shorts stood at 128,315 contracts as of 27 October. Australia’s policy rate remains 85bps above the top of the Fed funds target range. We expect AUD/USD to consolidate near term, while retaining our bullish 3M and 12M forecasts of 0.72 and 0.74 respectively.

articles.title: Money Markets Committee and UK Money Markets Code
articles.text:
Money Markets Committee and UK Money Markets Code

The Bank of England chairs the Money Markets Committee, which has endorsed the voluntary UK Money Markets Code setting out best practice for participants in the deposit, repo and securities lending markets.

In this section

Fair and Effective Markets
Foreign currency reserves
Market intelligence
Bank of England Market Operations Guide
Settlement and collateral management
SONIA interest rate benchmark
Transition from LIBOR to risk-free rates

On this pageMoney Markets CommitteeUK Money Markets Code CommitteeSecurities Lending CommitteeMoney Markets Liaison Committee and Securities Lending and Repo CommitteeUK Money Markets Code

Money Markets Committee
The Money Markets Committee (MMC) is a senior-level forum for market participants and the relevant UK public authorities to discuss issues concerning the UK unsecured deposits and funding market, the securities lending market and the repo market.
The MMC is chaired by the Bank of England.
The committee meets quarterly and also has two permanent sub-committees: the UK Money Markets Code Sub-Committee and the Securities Lending Committee.
Objectives of the Money Markets Committee

To discuss important domestic and global market or structural developments affecting the UK money, repo and securities lending markets.
Where appropriate, to propose responses to any issues identified.
To aid understanding and enhance monitoring of the functioning of the UK money markets.
To endorse and facilitate continuing market-wide adoption of the UK Money Markets Code, a voluntary code of good practice for the money and securities financing markets.
To identify and address any high-level issues concerning contingency planning in the UK money markets and payment systems, having regard to international developments.

Increasing diversity in our committees
The UK Money Markets Code includes an expectation that market participants will promote the development of a diverse and inclusive within their money market teams. This includes working to create a diverse pipeline of potential future Committee members.
We also aim for diversity within the Money Markets Committee and its Sub-committees, in order that they can best represent the people of the United Kingdom. Diverse membership means that these Committees benefit from diversity of thought, which bring different viewpoints and help to ensure well-informed decision-making.
We work with members from the Money Markets Committee to diversify its membership. As part of this, we provide opportunities for members to bring observers to Committee meetings, in order that these observers can gain a better understanding of the Committee, and to help identify potential future diverse candidates.
You can find out more about ‘Meeting Varied People’ – our initiative to increase the diversity of the market contacts that we engage with – on the Market intelligence page.

Minutes of the Money Markets Committee meetings

Final report of the MMC discussion group: Wholesale Market Response to the extended RTGS Outage simulated in SIMEX16 (PDF 0.1MB) Opens in a new window

UK Money Markets Code Committee
The project to update and revise the former codes for non-foreign exchange market products in the UK market led by a sub-committee of the Money Markets Committee. The UK Money Markets Code Sub-Committee is a permanent sub-committee of the MMC, and is co-chaired by, and made up of, senior market participants. The sub-committee meets regularly to ensure that the code remains relevant and up to date as markets evolve.

Terms of reference for the UK Money Markets Code Sub-Committee
UK Money Markets Code Committee current membership list (PDF 0.1MB) Opens in a new window

UK Money Markets Code Committee minutes

Letter to Signatories of Statement of Commitment to UK Money Markets Code (PDF 0.1MB) Opens in a new window

Securities Lending Committee
The Securities Lending Committee (SLC) is a sub-committee of the Money Markets Committee. The SLC is chaired by a market participant. It is a forum for market participants and the relevant UK public authorities to meet to discuss issues concerning the UK securities lending market, including all collateral activities.
Objectives of the Securities Lending Committee

To discuss important domestic and global market or structural developments affecting the UK securities lending market.
To discuss legal, regulatory, trading, settlement, infrastructure, tax, disclosure and other related developments in this market.
Where appropriate, it will propose responses to these issues.
To aid the understanding and enhance the monitoring of the functioning of this market.

Working Group on Settlement Efficiency
The Bank of England Securities Lending Committee has established a Working Group to examine the issue of settlement failure in the UK securities lending market. It provides a senior-level forum for market participants to meet to identify root causes for settlement issues in the UK securities lending market and suggest best practices.
The Working Group will examine drivers and impact of fails and determine potential solutions to settlement failure in the UK securities lending market. Part of this work will be to advocate best practice in the securities lending market.
Membership of the group will reflect a diverse group of market participants with relevant expertise, perspective and knowledge. It is chaired by Tim McLeod (Blackrock, Inc.). The Bank of England will participate as Ex-Officio members and provide administrative support.
Please note that views and outputs of the Working Group do not constitute guidance or legal advice from, and are not necessarily endorsed by, the Bank of England (including the Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA)).
Securities Lending Committee Settlement Efficiency Report - June 2024 Opens in a new window

Securities Lending Committee terms of reference (PDF 0.1MB) Opens in a new window
Securities Lending Committee Membership List (PDF 0.1MB) Opens in a new window

Securities Lending Committee minutes

Money Markets Liaison Committee and Securities Lending and Repo Committee
The Money Markets Committee was formed in March 2017 to replace previous markets committees, the Money Markets Liaison Committee (MMLC) and Securities Lending and Repo Committee (SLRC).
Please see the National Archives for historic MMLC and SLRC minutes.
The National Archives Opens in a new window
UK Money Markets Code
The UK Money Markets Code is a voluntary code written by market participants. It incorporates revised relevant sections of the Non-Investment Products (NIPs) Code, and also a revision and update of the Gilt Repo Code and Securities Borrowing and Lending Code.
The UK Money Markets Code was published on 26 April 2017.

The UK Money Markets Code
The UK Money Markets Code: explanatory notes

Voluntary codes of best practice can help to establish the basis on which financial markets function, ensuring trust between participants. This in turn creates an environment so that a fair, effective and transparent market can flourish and in which, by adhering to such codes, high standards of behaviour can be assured.
The code sets out such standards and the best practice expected from participants in the deposit, repo and securities lending markets in the UK. It supersedes previous guidance for participants in these markets provided by the NIPs Code, the Gilt Repo Code and the Securities Borrowing and Lending Code. By bringing these together it will more clearly establish the framework for transacting in UK money markets. The code is endorsed by the Money Markets Committee and will be updated regularly.
The Money Markets Committee has also established a Public Register of Institutions who have signed a Statement of Commitment or a Statement of Support to the Code. The purpose of the Register is to further restore trust in financial markets by making it easier to see which institutions have taken the important step of committing to the principles set out in the Code.
UK Money Markets Code: Public Register
The UK Money Markets Code Committee and the Association of Corporate Treasurers have produced this guide to promote and encourage wider adherence to the Code among the Corporate sector.

UK Money Markets Code: A guide for corporates (PDF 0.4MB) Opens in a new window

The UK Money Markets Code, along with the FX Global Code and the Global Precious Metals Code, replaces the Non-Investment Products Code.
