articles.title: Types of Financial System Vulnerabilities and Risks
articles.text:
Financial Stability

What Is Financial StabilityTypes of Financial System Vulnerabilities and Risks Monitoring Risk Across the Financial System Proactive Monitoring of Markets and InstitutionsFinancial Stability and Stress Testing

Types of Financial System Vulnerabilities and Risks

Related Content

Financial Stability Report

Monetary Policy Report

Financial Stability Monitoring (PDF)

Mapping heat in the U.S. financial system

Federal Reserve staff regularly and systematically assess a standard set of vulnerabilities as part of their periodic review of financial stability. These assessments generally are provided to the Board and Federal Open Market Committee four times per year. Using a range of data sources as well as insights gained from discussions and engagement with domestic and foreign counterparts, staff regularly monitor vulnerabilities in four areas:

1. Elevated valuation pressures are signaled by asset prices that are high relative to economic fundamentals or historical norms and are often driven by an increased willingness of investors to take on risk. As such, elevated valuation pressures imply a greater possibility of outsized drops in asset prices.

2. Excessive borrowing by businesses and households leaves them vulnerable to distress if their incomes decline or the assets they own fall in value. In the event of such shocks, businesses and households with high debt burdens may need to cut back spending sharply, affecting the overall level of economic activity. Moreover, when businesses and households cannot make payments on their loans, financial institutions and investors incur losses.

3. Excessive leverage within the financial sector increases the risk that financial institutions will not have the sufficient capacity to absorb losses when hit by adverse shocks. In those situations, institutions will be forced to cut back lending, sell their assets, or, in extreme cases, shut down. Such responses can substantially impair credit access for households and businesses.

4. Elevated funding risks can occur when financial institutions raise funds from the public with a commitment to return investor money on short notice, but those institutions then invest much of the funds in illiquid assets that are hard to sell quickly or in assets that have a long maturity. This liquidity and maturity transformation can create an incentive for investors to withdraw funds quickly in adverse situations, commonly referred to as a “run.” Facing a run, financial institutions may need to sell assets quickly at “fire sale” prices, thereby incurring substantial losses and potentially even becoming insolvent.

These vulnerability assessments inform internal Federal Reserve discussions concerning both supervision and regulatory policies and monetary policy. Two times a year, the Federal Reserve publishes its Financial Stability Report summarizing its current assessment of these vulnerabilities, the salient risks to the financial system originating in the United States and abroad, and how they might interact. A shorter summary of current vulnerabilities is included in the twice-yearly Monetary Policy Report to Congress. They also inform Federal Reserve interactions with broader monitoring efforts, such as those by the Financial Stability Oversight Council and the Financial Stability Board.

Asset Valuations and Risk Appetite

Asset valuations are the prices of assets after accounting for economic fundamentals, such as future expected cash flows and interest rates. Valuations that are high relative to history or to economic fundamentals constitute a vulnerability because the unwinding of high prices can be destabilizing in the financial system and economy. Moreover, stretched asset valuations may be an indicator of a broader buildup in risk appetite leading to investors taking on higher levels of risk, or new risks that are not fully understood.

This dynamic can be more concerning when (1) the assets are widely held and the values are supported by excessive borrowing, (2) the maturity of the asset is significantly longer than the maturity of the liability financing that asset, or (3) there is a lack of publicly available information about the asset.

However, it is very difficult to judge whether an asset price is overvalued relative to fundamentals. As a result, analysis typically considers a range of possible valuation metrics, as well as developments in areas where asset prices are rising especially rapidly, the size and pace of inflows to an asset class, or the implications of unusually low or high levels of volatility in certain markets.

Borrowing by Businesses and Households

Excessive borrowing by businesses and households leaves them vulnerable if their incomes decline or the assets they own fall in value. In the event of such shocks, businesses and households with high debt burdens may need to cut back spending sharply, affecting the overall level of economic activity. A default can significantly limit their ability to obtain credit in the future. Moreover, when businesses and households cannot make payments on their loans, financial institutions and investors incur losses.

Leverage in the Financial System

Highly leveraged financial system intermediaries—those with significantly more debt than equity—can amplify the effect of negative shocks in the financial system and broad economy. For example, if highly leveraged institutions collectively respond to a negative shock in the economy (e.g., a sharp decline in house prices) by tightening lending standards and shrinking their balance sheets more than called for by the shock itself, perhaps because outsized credit losses threaten their solvency, the resulting contraction in credit will aggravate the decline in economic activity resulting from the shock.

Sufficiently large losses for highly leveraged institutions, especially if those institutions have a significant share of short-term funding, can lead to “fire sales,” where assets are unloaded quickly at extremely low prices. These fire sales then reduce the value of similar assets held by other financial institutions, potentially leading to a negative feedback loop.

The Federal Reserve monitors leverage in the banking sector with the help of an extensive data collection program. This includes the data collected in support of the Dodd-Frank Act stress tests for large banking institutions, the quarterly Reports of Condition and Income for all banks, and the Consumer Credit report. Additionally, periodic surveys of nonbank providers of leverage, such as the Senior Credit Officer Opinion Survey, as well as collaboration and data sharing among all the financial regulatory agencies offer valuable insights on nonbank financial leverage.

Funding Risks and Maturity Transformation by the Financial System

One key benefit provided by the financial system is to aggregate short-maturity liabilities so that they can be used to fund long-maturity assets. This function has historically occurred primarily in the traditional banking system or other depository institutions, which use deposits from consumers as part of the financing to provide multiyear auto or mortgage loans. In recent decades, nonbank financial institutions have grown substantially. For example, mutual funds offer their investors the convenience of daily withdrawals even though they invest in longer-term debt instruments.

However, as seen during the 2007–09 financial crisis and the outbreak of COVID-19 in March 2020, the mismatch between long-term assets and short-term funding creates systemic vulnerabilities that can threaten the functioning of financial markets and the broader economy. This manifests when a large fraction of those investors withdraw their funding suddenly in response to an increase in risk aversion after a negative shock.

Deposit insurance provides some protection against this vulnerability within the traditional banking system. However, firms that use short-term liabilities such as repurchase agreements (or “repos”) or commercial paper, and the financial institutions that invest in them, like money market mutual funds, are also prone to run risk. Indeed, money market mutual funds came under considerable pressure during both the 2007–09 financial crisis and the pandemic in 2020. For this reason, the Federal Reserve actively monitors—as best it can, given available data and measurement—both liquidity risk and the degree of maturity transformation in the financial system.

articles.title: Sustainability as a driver of long-term investment outcomes - BNP Paribas Asset Management - United States
articles.text:
How can investors navigate a world reshaped by environmental pressures, technological disruption and geopolitical uncertainty? For BNP Paribas Asset Management, sustainability is central to answering that question.

Jane Ambachtsheer, Chief Sustainability Officer, discusses BNPP AM’s updated Global Sustainability Strategy, which sets out its priorities through to 2030. Building on the recent merger with AXA Investment Managers, the strategy embeds sustainability expertise across asset classes, using ESG research, due diligence and stewardship to achieve better-informed investment decisions.

Jane explains how integrating sustainability considerations with financial analysis can help investors identify material risks and opportunities, while recognising that clients have different objectives and preferences. From net zero alignment and carbon footprint reduction to positive contributions towards the UN Sustainable Development Goals, the approach aims to deliver tailored solutions and better client outcomes. “Our underlying ambition is to connect sustainable investment practices with long-term returns to help clients navigate a rapidly changing world.”

Listen to the full Talking Heads podcast for insights into solutions across many asset classes can help investors achieve their sustainability ambitions.

You can also listen and subscribe to Talking Heads on YouTube, Spotify, or wherever you normally get your podcasts.

XXX

Read the transcript

Andrew Craig: Hello and welcome to this week’s BNP Paribas Asset Management Talking Heads podcast. Every week, Talking Heads will bring you in-depth insights and analysis through the lens of sustainability on the topics that really matter to investors. In this episode, we’ll be discussing our new revised edition of the Global Sustainability Strategy. This provides the framework for action on the environmental, social and governance considerations that are embedded in our investment processes and are grounded in the conviction that traditional financial analysis alone is insufficient to capture all the risks and opportunities in today’s global economy.

I’m Andy Craig, Co-Head of the Investment Insights Centre, and I’m joined today by Jane Ambachtsheer, Chief Sustainability Officer at BNP Paribas Asset Management. Welcome, Jane. Thank you for joining me today.

Jane Ambachtsheer: Thanks, Andy. It’s a pleasure to be here.

AC: Can you explain why we need [a] Global Sustainability Strategy?

JA: Well, sustainability, is a core part of how we invest and how we operate as an entity, so it’s important to have a strategy which really articulates how we go about doing that and what our objectives are.

Our previous sustainability strategy took us to 2026, so it was time for us to launch our new one, which we’ve recently done, which takes us out to 2030. The other important component of our new strategy is that it reflects our new entity having evolved and completed the integration of AXA Investment Managers, which now results in BNP Paribas Asset Management being one of the world’s 10 largest investors, with over €1.7 trillion in AUM (assets under management) across liquid and alternative asset classes and a local presence in 35 countries.

So given our new size and scale, it was also certainly time for an evolved approach to our global sustainability strategy.

AC: How does the sustainability strategy fit with the new corporate strategy for the combined entity? What are the key components and how has it evolved?

JA: When we launched at the beginning of 2026 ‘AMplify 2030’, the overall strategy for the new entity, we identified sustainability as one of the core enablers of how we’ll achieve that strategy. That then opened the door for us to publish this new specialised strategy really focused on sustainability.

As a long-term investor, we believe our client outcomes and real economy outcomes are closely connected. Resilient companies, well-functioning markets and sustainable economic growth are really fundamental to the long-term returns our clients seek.

Our strategy sets out our forward-looking priorities and milestones through [to] 2030 and is organised around the pillars of how we achieve that. So, a focus on the future and identifying system level risks around how we do ESG research and due diligence stewardship. Our approach around articulating responsible business conduct expectations which can lead to different exclusions. Our approach to sustainable products and solutions and also around leading by example – our approach to our own culture, sustainability education and the corporate responsibility practices that we’re adopting for our own entity.

AC: How does this new strategy enable us to deliver the best outcomes for our clients?

JA: That’s at the core of everything we do. Our strategy is built for clients, informed by our clients’ expectations and what we believe best practice to be in the global market.

The first [thing] is around making sure we’re helping our clients navigate a changing world. We know that the world is being reshaped by a number of powerful forces:

Environmental pressures: reshaping industries, supply chains, capital allocation, presenting both risks and opportunities

Technology and innovation: creating new technologies, disrupting business models, creating different opportunities

Demographic shifts: transforming labour markets, changes to inequality around the world, consumption patterns and ageing

Geopolitical developments: influencing trade, energy security, energy systems, our approach to climate in nature and access to resources around the world in this changing geopolitical framework.

These megatrends are inter-connected and we try and take a forward-looking lens to help our clients navigate them through understanding the risks and the opportunities that they present. So that’s the broader macro perspective.

We also believe that by integrating ESG considerations alongside financial analysis from a bottom-up asset class perspective, we can have better insights and make better decisions on behalf of our clients.

So sustainability is not a separate investment decision. It’s an important component of informed decision-making from an asset class basis. One of the new evolutions in terms of our overall framework is that we now embed sustainability expertise across the different asset classes.

We have a central team which I lead, which is really responsible for driving the overall strategy and ambition, with our global leadership team overseeing stewardship, supporting our clients, supporting our overall external commitments and reporting stewardship and CSR (corporate social responsibility).

Then we have a number of sustainability experts embedded across the organisation within the different asset classes, reporting up to the different CIOs to make sure we have best quality ESG data, tools, research capabilities embedded into our investment decisions.

That takes me to this final point – the fact that the strategy is built for clients. We have clients from all around the world. They have different objectives, regulatory environments and sustainability preferences. To be able to cater to those different clients, we offer a range of investment approaches and have the opportunity to build structured, custom[ised] sustainability portfolios for our clients.

We have clients optimising around their own preferences or the preferences of their beneficiaries, whether that’s measuring a positive contribution to some of the specific sustainable development goals, achieving certain net zero alignment outcomes, measuring and achieving a certain carbon footprint reduction target.

Different clients have different preferences. A big part of our strategy and our new size and scale is that we have the ability to bring the firm in terms of helping our clients to achieve the best outcomes for them, tapping into the resources across BNP Paribas Asset Management, but also often working in partnership with our colleagues and the broader resources across BNP Paribas Group.

AC: Of course, there are implications for us, BNP Paribas Asset Management as a firm and our own practices. Can you talk us through those?

JA: At the end of the day, we’re a people business. Our people, the intellectual capital that they bring, their relationships with clients, are the greatest opportunity for embedding sustainability into who we are, how we deliver investment outcomes and how we’re operating as an entity.

So we have a strong focus on integrating sustainability into our culture and our own corporate practices. This is one of the unique differentiators for the way we’re approaching sustainability as an organisation.

In terms of our own corporate reporting, we seek to meet and exceed the standards and expectations we’re setting for the companies we’re investing in. That’s really important to our credibility as an asset manager – to live up to those expectations where we’re asking others to do the same.

We have a strong focus on sustainability education and we’ve developed different training pathways for different portions of our population, depending on their existing levels of expertise and focus areas – whether it’s investment teams or legal teams or client-facing teams – to make sure they have the right opportunities around internal training, but also the opportunity to pursue external certifications or training programmes.

We also have a strong focus on being active in the communities where we’re operating –volunteering, philanthropy and developing partnerships with organisations in different communities. Also our annual Community Impact Week, where we have a volunteering fair that we set up around our offices around the world, which is really a chance to engage in some of those organisations, but also to further enhance our internal community, give employees an opportunity to spend time together and spend time giving back.

So there’s a rich ecosystem of things we’re doing internally around creating awareness, providing educational opportunities and volunteering engagement opportunities for colleagues across the different offices around the world in BNP Paribas Asset Management.

AC: Can you talk [to] us about the key upcoming milestones and how you’ll be measuring success as we go forward?

JA: The first and most important measure of success is that we’re able to deliver the outcomes that our clients are engaging us to deliver. That’s front and centre for what we’re doing around our overall sustainability strategy.

But we will also continue to provide our annual sustainability report, which includes progress across all of the different six pillars of our sustainability strategy, including stewardship, which is an area of significant interest for many of our clients. We’re happy to be able to continue to evolve the level of detail around our different approaches for stewardship, be it statistics across the whole platform, a rich range of different examples of company engagement, as well as public policy advocacy.

Later this year, we’ll also be updating our new Net Zero commitment as a combined entity. That’s something we’ve committed to publish and we’ll be sharing in the coming months. We’ll also be introducing our new progress monitor in our next annual report, where we share a number of key indicators that [we] will be measuring and reporting on every year.

We view communication on sustainability as an ongoing opportunity, both at a portfolio and at a firm level, and it’s something that we’ll continue to share updates on with clients as we go.

AC: Jane, thank you. We’ll be looking forward to joining you to talk about those updates as the months go by. Thank you very much for joining me today.

JA: Thanks so much for having me. It was a pleasure to be here.

AC: That’s it for this week’s episode of Talking Heads. If you’d like to learn more about our Global Sustainability Strategy, please reach out to your BNP Paribas Asset Management contact or check out Viewpoint, our website for investment insights, at viewpoint.bnpparibas-am.com. Viewpoint brings you commentary and analysis in a variety of formats, from investment outlooks to asset allocation videos and podcasts to help investors make better informed decisions.

You’ve been listening to the BNP Paribas Asset Management Talking Heads podcast with me, Andy Craig and Jane Ambachtsheer, Chief Sustainability Officer at BNP Paribas Asset Management.

Please do join us again next time. Until then, take care.

articles.title: Protecting Our Clients Against Potentially Fraudulent Activity
articles.text:
Protecting Our Clients Against Potentially Fraudulent Activity

Protecting Our Clients Against Potentially Fraudulent Activity
Across the industry, we are seeing an increase in bad actors impersonating and misusing corporate brands to get access to personal information and funds from unsuspecting individuals. These activities may involve individuals acting as company representatives and may include fake websites, social media inquiries, or communications that closely resemble official channels.
Please read the below for important reminders that can help protect you from potentially fraudulent activity.
We strongly caution against providing personal data or transferring funds in response to unsolicited requests. For your safety, always verify the authenticity of communications claiming to be from Lazard by contacting us through our official website or known contact points.
Specifically, Lazard will never engage in the following activities:

If you believe that you have fallen victim to fraud, please contact your bank immediately. Additionally, you should report the incident to law enforcement in your jurisdiction as soon as possible.

articles.title: A Democratic Sweep: Oversight, Investigations, And Potential For Compromise
articles.text:
A Democratic Sweep: Oversight, Investigations, And Potential For Compromise

Democrats have swept both the House and Senate, reshaping Washington’s
balance of power. While early polling had pointed toward a more divided
government, with Democrats gaining control of at least one chamber, the
broader sweep now gives the party more policy leverage heading into 2027.

November 2026

Democrats Take Both Chambers
Democrats have swept both the House and Senate, reshaping Washington’s balance of power. While early polling had pointed toward a more divided government, with Democrats gaining control of at least one chamber, the broader sweep now gives the party more policy leverage heading into 2027.
The central dynamic of a Democratic Congress will likely involve more oversight hearings and investigations. Democrats may pursue legislation signaling party priorities, though such bills are likely to face frequent presidential vetoes. We believe investors could see increased political scrutiny of certain sectors and companies, slower confirmation votes, and fewer significant legislative changes. Budget standoffs and potential government shutdowns are likely, though there may be room for limited bipartisan compromises on spending deals.
Where the Tailwinds May Blow
A Democratic Congress could restore support to solar and wind power, slowing the fossil-fuel momentum of the prior two years. Healthcare segments could also benefit, particularly hospitals, life sciences tools, the Affordable Care Act (ACA), and Medicaid, as Democrats would likely push to restore funding for the National Institutes of Health and ACA-related programs.
Where the Headwinds May Lie
A Democratic Congress is likely to agree to modest defense spending increases in exchange for funding Democratic priorities, though we believe any supplemental funds tied to the Iran conflict could face tougher scrutiny. Cryptocurrency and unconstrained artificial intelligence (AI) and data center expansion could face additional policy headwinds, as Democrats plan to expand oversight of AI development and deployment through a new House Select Committee. Healthcare may offer the most potential for compromise between a Democratic Congress and the administration, especially on pharmaceutical pricing controls, which would be challenging for the sector.

AI Regulation Moves to the States
We think states may take the lead on AI regulation, as there have been no federal guidelines or legislation, and a lack of votes for federal pre-emption, similar to the role California has historically played in driving national fuel efficiency standards. Key states to watch for potential impact on the AI buildout include Texas, Georgia, Ohio, and Pennsylvania. Governors’ races, utility commissions, and state legislatures in those states could shape regulatory approvals, grid costs, and tax incentives.
Tariffs and Trade: A Consistent Path
Trump administration tariffs look likely to continue, with Section 301 reinforcing tariff levels, alongside continued support for U.S. manufacturing reshoring through tax incentives and industrial policy. Democratic legislation in the new Congress may signal the party’s stance on any future tariff adjustments. Democrats appear supportive of protecting key manufacturing sectors while reducing tariffs on certain consumer goods to address affordability concerns.
The Fiscal Backdrop
Fiscal pressures are likely to remain a central focus in 2027. Despite market concerns, there is little chance of fiscal consolidation after the midterms, while at least one government shutdown, potentially paired with another debt-ceiling standoff, is likely. The split dynamic of a Democratic Congress and a Republican administration means budget pressures and shutdown risk persist even under new leadership.
Looking Ahead
In our view, the midterm results can offer signals on where policy is headed, with more consequential changes and an unusually broad range of outcomes in play for the 2028 presidential election. For investors, a Democratic sweep has notable sectoral implications, as renewable energy and healthcare gain ground, while defense, crypto, and unconstrained AI expansion face new challenges. Tariffs and executive actions are difficult to reverse, and the reshoring momentum behind U.S. manufacturing looks likely to continue regardless of the outcome.

articles.title: SAA Market Strategy | NDR | Investment Research
articles.text:
Strategic Asset Allocation Market Strategy
NDR’s cross‑asset strategic allocation applies decades of quantitative research to guide investors over long‑term horizons.

NDR’s cross-asset strategic asset allocation service leverages NDR’s quantitative methodology and forty-five years of market analysis to help investors navigate a long-term investment horizon. Underpinned by NDR’s 10-year LTCMA analysis, the SAA team provides positioning optimized to a 3-5 year investment horizon across two distribution channels: Financial Advisor model portfolios (six risk-mapped models from Very Conservative to Very Aggressive) and Institutional policy portfolios (optimized relative to policy benchmarks within a tracking error budget). Grounded by a robust, academically supported, methodology and simulation, the service provides long-term coverage of individual asset classes, relative positioning between TAA and SAA portfolios, dynamic allocation bands, and opportunities for consultative advice including investment committee participation (dependent on service level). Institutional portfolios provide explicit active positioning relative to policy with full risk attribution — mirroring how pensions, endowments, foundations, and other institutional investors, manage capital.

Public Equities (global, regional & style boxes)

Portfolio Implementation & Analytics

Implementable positioning with dynamic allocation bands and rebalancing triggers. Investment tools: regime analysis, risk analysis, macro insights, and chart library.

Advanced Forecasting & Engagement

Monte Carlo simulations (10,000 paths) linking allocation choices to probability of meeting return targets. In‑person or virtual strategist discussions on positioning and rebalancing.

Customization & Outsourced Solutions

Abstract: Service fees continue to proliferate in a wide range of markets, from retail to payments, generating questions about their impact on consumer choice, competition, and fairness. This paper explores how sensitivity to such fees varies across consumers, use cases, and competitive settings, and whether it is affected by consumer learning. I am able to conduct this in-depth empirical analysis thanks to a uniquely detailed, high-frequency panel data set on surcharged ATM cash withdrawals. Results show that average elasticity estimates mask substantial heterogeneity in consumer sensitivity to service fees. I explore ways in which market and behavioral mechanisms can help explain this heterogeneity. Finally, I investigate whether consumers strategically adjust their behavior in response to service fees.

How Wuxi AppTec Stayed Sanction-Proof

Tom Hancock

Gavekal Technologies: Briefing | 2 Nov 2026

China’s two “Wuxi” biotech firms—AppTec and Biologics—are key partners for the US pharmaceutical industry, as contract developers and manufacturers of hundreds of thousands of chemical compounds. They combine near cutting-edge technology with unmatched process knowledge, strong supply chain control, and robust intellectual-property protection. Washington lawmakers are increasingly uneasy about rising American reliance on the Wuxi firms. But their efforts to curb Wuxi’s access to the US market have been blocked, thanks to strong lobbying by the US pharma and biotech industries, which see collaboration with Chinese contract drug research firms as essential to their own success.Also in this issue of China Tech Brief:

Key trade routes have been severely disrupted—especially for the oil and gas exporters who depend on the Strait of Hormuz—and energy costs have spiked. Unlike in previous energy shocks, Persian Gulf oil and gas exporters face the largest growth downgrades, while the effects were more contained in middle-income countries. Conflict has compounded humanitarian needs and existing vulnerabilities in fragile settings. In many economies, higher interest rates and increased uncertainty are delaying investment decisions and increased social protection needs are putting pressure on already strained fiscal resources. Against this near-term background, this report examines how artificial intelligence (AI) will reshape labor markets and productivity across the region in the longer term. Wide differences in capacity and readiness will prevent the region from capturing the full potential of AI. Weak private sector dynamism and inadequate innovation ecosystems remain binding constraints. Three mutually reinforcing gaps—in localization, usage, and foundational human and physical capital—need to be addressed simultaneously. Advances in leading economies, such as Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, can create opportunities for regional collaboration and generate shared gains across the region.PublicationEurope and Central Asia Economic Update, October 2026: Making AI Work: Jobs, Firms, and Productivity (Washington, DC: World Bank, 2026-10-06) World BankAmid higher prices for imported energy, heightened uncertainty, and weaker economic expansion in the European Union, growth in Europe and Central Asia (ECA) has slowed further in 2026, with a gradual but uneven recovery expected through 2028. Against this difficult backdrop, artificial intelligence (AI) could help offset declining productivity. Yet AI's transformative potential exceeds the region's capacity to absorb it. About one in five workers in ECA holds a job exposed to AI, but fewer than one in ten firms use AI, roughly half the share in the EU. Many of the digital foundations for AI are already in place, but the region faces shortages of computing capacity and weaknesses in data readiness. Governments can help by expanding access to affordable computers, strengthening skills, and investing in data as a public good. Confusing adoption and adaptation with innovation may lead governments to invest in building national models at unnecessary cost. The main risk over the next decade is too little adoption and adaptation of AI across the region, not too much.PublicationThe Global Findex Database 2025: Connectivity and Financial Inclusion in the Digital Economy (Washington, DC: World Bank, 2025-07-16) Klapper, Leora; Singer, Dorothe; Starita, Laura; Norris, AlexandraThe Global Findex 2025 reveals how mobile technology is equipping more adults around the world to own and use financial accounts to save formally, access credit, make and receive digital payments, and pursue opportunities. Including the inaugural Global Findex Digital Connectivity Tracker, this fifth edition of Global Findex presents new insights on the interactions among mobile phone ownership, internet use, and financial inclusion.

The Global Findex is the world’s most comprehensive database on digital and financial inclusion. It is also the only global source of comparable demand-side data, allowing cross-country analysis of how adults access and use mobile phones, the internet, and financial accounts to reach digital information and resources, save, borrow, make payments, and manage their financial health. Data for the Global Findex 2025 were collected from nationally representative surveys of about 145,000 adults in 141 economies. The latest edition follows the 2011, 2014, 2017, and 2021 editions and includes new series measuring mobile phone ownership and internet use, digital safety, and frequency of transactions using financial services.

The Global Findex 2025 is an indispensable resource for policy makers in the fields of digital connectivity and financial inclusion, as well as for practitioners, researchers, and development professionals.PublicationGlobal Economic Prospects, June 2026 (Washington, DC: World Bank, 2026-06-11) World BankThe global economy is facing a major shock as the Middle East conflict drives sharp energy price increases. Global growth is projected to slow to 2.5 percent in 2026, with emerging market and developing economies (EMDEs) facing the weakest per capita income growth since the pandemic. The effects across EMDE regions differ based on direct impact of the conflict, energy exposure, and policy buffers. Risks to the outlook remain skewed to the downside and include escalating hostilities, further commodity market disruptions, and additional geopolitical strains, while broader adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) offers some upside. Policy action is critical: globally to safeguard energy and food security and advance the energy transition, and domestically to control inflation, strengthen fiscal sustainability, and support job creation through investment in physical, human, and digital capital. Compounding pressures from the energy shock, rising debt is driving up sovereign borrowing costs for EMDEs, particularly for those most indebted, underscoring the need for stronger revenue mobilization and improved debt management. Commodity-exporting EMDEs can improve their fiscal resilience by using credible fiscal rules, maintaining well-governed sovereign wealth funds, and diversifying revenue sources to better manage commodity price cycles.PublicationIntegration: World-Class Trade Logistics Along the Trans-Caspian Transport Corridor (Washington, DC: World Bank, 2026-09-28) Alam, Muneeza Mehmood; Blancas, Luis C.The Trans-Caspian Transport Corridor (TCTC), also known as the Middle Corridor, is a developing network of rail freight, maritime shipping, and cargo handling connections linking markets in East Asia, Central Asia, the South Caucasus, Türkiye, and the rest of Europe. Considering the TCTC’s unique length and multimodal, multipurpose nature; the large number of host and terminus countries that comprise it; and the significant economic opportunity that the integration of these markets represents, transforming the TCTC into an efficient economic corridor is among the world’s most consequential—and complex—challenges in global trade logistics today.

Integration: World-Class Trade Logistics Along the Trans-Caspian Transport Corridor provides an in-depth assessment of the TCTC’s value proposition; its current status and performance gaps; the magnitude of the economic impacts that can be expected from addressing these gaps; and both the investments and the reimagined, transformational solutions that are needed to attain these improvements. The report makes the case that transforming the TCTC into an economic corridor will take more than investments in infrastructure; it will require integration-driven approaches to trade facilitation, logistics service delivery, and cross-border collaboration. What is at stake is the opportunity to more closely integrate the nations of Eurasia through trade and investment; to boost the economic and job creation performance of TCTC host countries; to facilitate the delivery of more efficient and more cost-competitive logistics services to a diverse range of shippers; and to make Eurasian trade more resilient to market and nonmarket disruptions.

Global experience in corridor building, including from the TCTC host and terminus countries themselves, and these countries’ own plans and aspirations suggest that this momentous opportunity in intercontinental logistics is achievable—with fit-for-purpose measures that can be sustained over time. Through its structured narrative, the report seeks to contribute to the multi-country, multi-stakeholder task of enabling world-class trade logistics in the TCTC.

articles.title: DPRK Fake Interview Playbook: How Hackers Targeted Binance
articles.text:
Summary
Binance disclosed that a DPRK fake employment scheme was behind its $6 billion hack: Attackers used a fabricated job opportunity and a series of fake interviews to target a Binance employee, turning a seemingly routine recruitment process into the entry point for the largest crypto theft in history.
Smaller attacks may have helped DPRK hackers perfect their playbook: Chainalysis has attributed more than $14.3 million in losses over the past 18 months to similar DPRK-linked fake interview schemes. Our analysis suggests these earlier compromises allowed North Korean actors to refine their methods on small targets before deploying them against higher-value targets.
The attack is part of DPRK’s wider illicit employment ecosystem: Fake interview schemes are just one component of North Korea’s lucrative ecosystem, which includes fraudulent IT employment schemes and crypto laundering. Chainalysis tracks these evolving tactics and the crypto infrastructure underpinning them.
Binance’s $6.4 billion theft by North Korean actors started with an all-too-common tactic for DPRK’s hacking teams: employment fraud.Chainalysis investigators have followed this strategy for years. It takes many forms; in the Binance case, DPRK workers lured their targets into applying for a phony job and infected their computer with malware. But in other instances the attackers are themselves the applicants, either working under false pretenses to generate money for the regime, infecting corporate systems, or both.Each instance can leave an on-chain footprint. Over the past 18 months, Chainalysis has attributed more than $14.3 million in losses to similar DPRK-linked fake interview and malware schemes. These schemes have spanned a wide range of targets, from individual crypto holders and private wallets to organizations, protocols, and DAOs. Binance is now the latest in this string of cases.“We’ve identified dozens of other job interview compromises that have led to wallet compromises” at the individual level, said Tom McLouth, our senior intelligence analyst. While losses in these earlier incidents ranged from tens of thousands to millions, the greater significance may lie in what they taught the attackers.Across successive compromises, DPRK actors were “perfecting and evolving their methodology,” McLouth explained, refining their approach and potentially building the capabilities needed to target increasingly valuable victims. “That’s how you end up with the biggest heist in history.”Seen in this context, the Binance attack may represent the culmination of months, or even years, of preparation and practice.How a fake interview opened the door to BinanceOn Tuesday, Binance released its initial findings into DPRK’s multi-stage attack against the exchange.The attack began in September with an engineer receiving an invitation to a job interview. Binance revealed how attackers spent weeks building trust with a Binance employee, first approaching the employee through a legitimate job platform with a job opportunity. After two rounds of interviews with a fictitious company, the Binance employee was asked to download an interview assignment that contained malicious code. This gave the attackers their initial foothold. From there, they deployed malware and exploited access to an internal AI tool to move deeper into Binance’s system.While the scale of the breach was unprecedented, this method of entry was not. ​​As Chainalysis Senior Manager of Global Services Alec Zebrick discussed this week, DPRK actors have repeatedly used what he calls “contagious interviews” to target employees with privileged access, exploiting their credentials and permissions to infiltrate organizations’ internal systems. This makes employees with access to sensitive infrastructure particularly valuable targets for these operations.DPRK malware embeds itself in target systemsThe Binance attack shows how a fake interview can provide an entry point into a major organization. Working with our partners, we’ve seen how attackers have cultivated this approach.We have observed multiple cases in which victims had wallet private keys stolen from cloud storage following a malicious interview. In some cases, victims reported that the seed phrases had never been downloaded to the infected device, suggesting the attackers’ access extended beyond local files, potentially through compromised cloud credentials or browser sessions.This is consistent with Microsoft’s reporting that DPRK malware searches infected systems for cryptocurrency seed phrases and password-manager artifacts. The credentials attackers collect early in an operation can open access to connected accounts well beyond the infected device. In the Binance attack, that same basic playbook (using a fake interview to gain an initial foothold) ultimately enabled the attackers to move deeper into the exchange’s infrastructure.Inside DPRK’s lucrative illicit employment ecosystemThe Binance attack is just one example of DPRK’s highly lucrative illicit employment ecosystem.The DPRK uses a range of social engineering tactics, including other fake recruitment schemes as well as fraudulent IT employment to infiltrate companies.Chainalysis has tracked several other ways DPRK actors are evolving and deploying these techniques. One emerging threat is the use of public blockchains to conceal malware instructions, a tactic we term Blockchain Dead Drops (BDDs). Our research has identified a fivefold surge in these blockchain-assisted cyberattacks over the past year, a surge driven by nation-state actors and the potential use of open-weight AI models.Our research indicates that North Korean actors began using these tactics, known variously as “Etherhiding” in early 2025 to maintain a link between the victim-computers compromised in their fake job interview schemes, and the malware command-and-control (C2) infrastructure. They do this because blockchain transactions are more resilient places to stage C2 infrastructure than relying on centralized or law enforcement-responsive hosting they can seize.One DPRK technique that our on-chain analysis uncovered adds redundancy by spreading the C2 communication across two blockchains (TRON and Aptos) to direct infected devices to a third, BSC. The attacker embeds pointers on TRON and Aptos that point to a transaction on BSC. If the infected machine can’t get what it needs from querying TRON, it turns to Aptos as a backup. Either way, it ends up where it needs to be, on BSC, where the payload is stored.More recently DPRK has employed a tactic referred to as null receiver, where the same C2 communication instruction is embedded in a specially crafted address which is not actually controlled by anyone and is not designed to control any cryptocurrency assets. The address itself can be decoded into an instruction that is read by infected machines.DPRK’s IT workers fraudulently embed in companiesOn the other side of DPRK’s employment fraud playbook is its large-scale IT worker scheme. In this, North Korean operatives pose as legitimate job applicants to secure employment at companies around the world, earning salaries and potentially gain access to sensitive systems, while generating revenue for the state.The United Nations estimates the DPRK’s IT worker ecosystem generates upwards of $600 million in annual revenue for the regime. This shadow workforce often intersects with crypto directly. In many cases the IT workers have attempted to embed themselves in crypto companies. But they also use crypto to launder their illicit proceeds. Last month, we outlined a network of Russian and DPRK nationals who were sanctioned by the U.S. for their role in DPRK-run IT worker schemes.Chainalysis closely tracks the inclusion of crypto addresses in sanctions designations targeting DPRK IT worker schemes, as well as open-source information on this threat.The DPRK IT workers themselves are usually deployed overseas where they use different obfuscation techniques such as VPNs and stolen identity documents to gain employment at companies across the world. Once hired, these workers often request payment in stablecoins.We’ve uncovered such on-chain activity, including in one case when wallets received regular payments indicative of salary payments.Once their salaries are paid, DPRK IT workers transfer the crypto to intermediaries such as the Russian and DPRK nationals mentioned above.How Chainalysis follows the moneyThe Binance case illustrates how North Korea continues to develop, test and refine a multi-pronged cybercrime playbook.The same actors can exploit recruitment platforms, compromise corporate infrastructure, infiltrate legitimate businesses and use cryptocurrency to move the resulting proceeds. As their methods evolve, organizations must look beyond conventional cybersecurity controls and consider the financial infrastructure that enables these operations.Chainalysis closely monitors how DPRK actors use cryptocurrency to generate revenue, move and consolidate funds, and launder illicit proceeds.Blockchain intelligence is critical to that effort. When combined with traditional cybersecurity measures and threat intelligence, blockchain analysis can help organizations and investigators identify and freeze stolen funds, map DPRK’s expanding financial networks, and uncover procurement and payment patterns that can support sanctions investigations and enforcement.The Binance investigation remains ongoing and we expect the stolen funds to continue moving in the coming days. Chainalysis is committed to supporting Binance and the wider industry as we trace the stolen funds, disrupt further laundering, and work to mitigate additional losses.FAQsHow did North Korean hackers steal $6.4 billion from Binance?The attack began with a fake job opportunity targeting a Binance employee. After building trust through multiple rounds of interviews with a fictitious company, attackers sent the employee a malicious coding assignment that infected their computer and gave them an initial foothold in Binance’s systems. They then deployed malware and exploited access to an internal AI tool to move deeper into the exchange’s infrastructure.What are DPRK fake interview schemes?DPRK fake interview schemes use fraudulent recruitment processes to compromise job candidates’ computers and gain access to sensitive systems or cryptocurrency wallets. Attackers may pose as recruiters or hiring managers, conduct seemingly legitimate interviews, and use malicious coding assignments or other downloads to deliver malware. Chainalysis refers to these operations as “contagious interviews.”Have North Korean hackers used fake interviews in other crypto attacks?Yes. Over the past 18 months, Chainalysis has attributed more than $14.3 million in losses to similar DPRK-linked fake interview and malware schemes. Targets have included individual crypto holders, private wallets, organizations, protocols, and DAOs. These earlier attacks may have helped DPRK actors refine their methods before pursuing larger targets.How do fake job interviews help DPRK hackers infiltrate organizations?Fake interviews can give attackers access to an employee’s device, credentials, and permissions. Employees with privileged access to sensitive infrastructure are particularly valuable targets because compromising their accounts can provide a path into an organization’s internal systems.What is a DPRK illicit IT worker scheme?North Korean operatives pose as legitimate job applicants, often using stolen identities and other obfuscation techniques, to secure remote employment at companies around the world. They earn salaries that generate revenue for the regime and may gain access to sensitive corporate systems. The United Nations estimates this ecosystem generates more than $600 million annually for North Korea.How does North Korea use cryptocurrency in its cybercrime operations?DPRK-linked actors use cryptocurrency both to receive proceeds from illicit employment and to move and launder funds from cyberattacks. IT workers may receive salaries in stablecoins before transferring funds to intermediaries. Hackers also exploit public blockchains to conceal malware instructions and maintain command-and-control infrastructure.How does Chainalysis help track DPRK-linked cybercrime?Chainalysis analyzes blockchain activity to identify how DPRK-linked actors receive, move, consolidate, and launder illicit funds. This intelligence can help investigators and organizations trace stolen cryptocurrency, identify intermediary networks, support sanctions investigations, and work to freeze funds where possible. There is only one Goldman Sachs.Discover CareersWORKING AT GSStudentsLife at GSBenefitsFeatured OfficesOpen RolesExchanges John Waldron on GDP Growth, AI, and the M&A Outlook Nov 4, 2026ShareGoldman Sachs President and COO John Waldron says clients have a cautiously optimistic outlook and the surge in M&A is a sign of that confidence. In the Exchanges podcast, he also discusses opportunities in asset and wealth management and how AI can help the firm serve clients better.
Subscribe: Spotify / Apple Podcasts / YouTube
Download TranscriptKey takeaways:

The momentum in M&A should continue: Corporate M&A could rise 30% to 35% in 2026, supported by strong pipelines for dealmaking and companies pursuing both scale and sharper strategic focus.

Investors are optimistic about economic growth in the US and Asia: While economic expansion in Europe is more muted, Waldron says the environment there is constructive and may be better than “the narrative suggests.”

Recent acquisitions and AI are an important part of the firm’s strategy: Waldron says targeted acquisitions are building strength and capabilities in asset management, and discusses AI use at the firm

Transcript:
Allison Nathan: Markets are navigating an unusual mix of resilient growth, shifting rate expectations, and rapid technological change. Against that backdrop, how is Goldman Sachs reading the moment and positioning the firm for what comes next? I'm Allison Nathan, and this is Goldman Sachs Exchanges. Today, I'm joined by John Waldron, President and Chief Operating Officer of Goldman Sachs.
We'll discuss the current sentiment among business leaders and investors, the outlook for markets and the economy, and where Goldman Sachs sees its next avenues for growth. John, welcome back to Exchanges.
John Waldron: Thank you, Allison. Good to be here.
Allison Nathan: John, let's just start with a quick gut check. There's so much going on in the world, and markets, as you well know, have been increasingly volatile. You spend much of your time with our corporate and investing clients. How would you describe the mood among business leaders and investors today compared to, say, a year ago?
John Waldron: I think still, generally speaking, optimistic. Maybe a little more cautious at the margin versus where it would have been six, 12 months ago.
Inflation is higher, and that feeds through a lot of businesses. So particularly for CEOs running large multinational corporations, inflation is a real challenge. I think geopolitics continues to be a challenge. It hasn't necessarily gotten any better, maybe a little bit worse, particularly when you think about the Iran situation.
And so I think more caution around the impact of the geopolitics on inflation and then obviously on rates. So, the environment we're in today versus where we would've been six, 12 months ago is we have higher inflation, we have higher rates. And so the cost of capital in the economy is higher. The cost of doing business from an inflation standpoint is higher.
Fortunately, nominal growth is very good, so most companies are seeing pretty strong end demand, and we still have very strong earnings. So, I'm still on the side of optimism when I think about our clients and what they're feeling. A little bit more caution and a little bit more concern in the full in the 2027 planning. I think more of a concern about the continuous impact of higher prices, whether it's in inflation terms or in cost of capital terms.
Allison Nathan: When you speak to CEOs and boards, what's really driving their decisions right now? Is it that more challenging financing environment? Obviously, you just discussed the geopolitical situation may be a little bit worse. There's regulatory uncertainty as well. Is that beginning to weigh on their risk appetite, or what are you observing in terms of their decision-making?
John Waldron: I think, first of all, we've had an extraordinary capital-raising year, so that tells you that companies are ... Obviously, AI is in the frame and everybody thinks it's all AI.
So, there's a lot of capital raising going on in the economy. People are building and growing and stands to reason the US economy is going to have nominal growth of north of 6%. So, there's plenty of good things going on, and people are investing and spending accordingly.
And the consumer is still very resilient. So I think whether it's the consumer end markets or the wholesale end markets, the enterprise end markets, markets are strong. Obviously, it's not all the same all over the world, but I think particularly in the United States, demand is very good. So companies see that.
They're investing into that. I do think there's a big bias for scale. So, we see that in M&A business, where there's been a lot more corporate M&A of scale. The bias is the larger companies are attracting more capital. They're generating better returns on that capital. They're being treated better in the marketplace.
There's more of an ability to spend into the AI theme and thesis and actually get the value for the compute that is obviously very expensive. And so I think that theme continues to play forward, and I think we will see more M&A on the forward from a corporate standpoint, which is generally speaking, a pretty good indicator of CEO confidence.
CEOs are not going to do M&A transactions if they're not feeling confident in their own business.
Allison Nathan: Let me ask a couple follow-ups to that. As you said, the economic resilience, it's actually been pretty striking. But the market has become more volatile. It may be pricing a little bit more uncertainty.
How is the firm viewing the economic outlook ahead?
John Waldron: We're constructive. As I said, nominal growth in the US looks like it's going to be north of 6%. We obviously are running with hotter inflation, so real growth is in the twos, let's say. And I think our, you would know as well as I do, I think our forecast is kind of 2.5% real growth plus minus.
That's pretty strong. It could get to 3% if things break in a certain way. We obviously think as a firm inflation will start to migrate down, and that could be quite helpful. So I'd say we're generally pretty constructive on the US economy. I've been spending a lot of time in Asia.
The Asia economies are very strong. China obviously it's almost a tale of two cities. It's kind of a weak domestic economy, but very strong innovation economy and a lot of export growth. But generally speaking, growth in the US and Asia, very strong. Growth in Europe, more muted. A little better than I think the narrative suggests.
People are very down on Europe. That's actually a little bit better than would be the narrative. But I'd say generally speaking, Europe is underperforming from a growth standpoint. But generally speaking, the environment's pretty constructive.
Allison Nathan: Do you sense a difference in sentiment in Asia? Versus Europe relative to the US.
John Waldron: For sure. The sentiment in Europe is not good. I think the combination of politics, geopolitics, lack of energy security, the war in Ukraine, the war in Iran, probably having a disproportionate impact on the European economies. I think the China export machine has been pretty pernicious for the European economy, particularly in places like autos where they're really feeling that excess supply coming into their marketplace at lower prices.
And so I think the sentiment in Europe is generally speaking not very good. I always feel like I have to give people a hug when I'm visiting European clients. I don't think it's as bad as they feel it, but they certainly feel it in a negative way. When you get to Asia, there's more buoyancy and more optimism.
I'll take a market like Japan, where I was a few weeks ago. Japan has had a long run of relatively muted growth, but all of a sudden, Japan's having a real moment where there is more growth, there is more loan demand. There's a little bit of a yield curve to work with now. There's more of an asset management push to unlock a bunch of those lazy deposits.
So, Japan all of a sudden has much more positive sentiment. And so, there are plenty of places in the world where the sentiment is quite strong. Europe, I would say, has the worst sentiment among those markets.
Allison Nathan: And a lot of political turbulence as well. You already started talking about actual activity versus sentiment. We think about where we are in the M&A cycle. There have been some starts and stops. It feels like there's more positive momentum now. Do you see that continuing?
John Waldron: I do. We're going to see corporate M&A up 30%, 35% this year. So that's a pretty healthy growth factor on what was already a pretty strong base.
Should be a record year in M&A this year. And we look at our backlogs and our pipelines are very strong. With all that volume still coming through the marketplace, we still see a lot of appetite on the forward. And so you can feel pretty positive momentum. And it's back to what I said earlier.
I think the bias for scale is real. And these transactions, it's an interesting marketplace to me because typically in M&A, you'll have a theme, scale or maybe de-merging, and no scale or lack of scale or less scale. We actually have scale arguments going on at the same time as we have fit and focus arguments going on.
So we see a lot of spins, a lot of carve-outs. So, companies are getting bigger and stronger in the places where they see growth and where they think they can win, and they're getting out of the businesses or getting smaller in the businesses where they don't see those dynamics in play and selling them to private equity firms or spinning them out to the public markets and finding ways to get out of those businesses.
And so that, that is driving kind of an offensive and defensive part of the M&A cycle. And I think that continues. I think the marketplace rewards companies that are large and growing and predominantly positioned in their areas of focus. But companies are being rewarded for getting out of businesses where those factors aren't in place and the market is really rewarding that type of activity.
Allison Nathan: With all of that in mind, John, where does the firm stand on its key priorities? Where do you see the most compelling growth opportunities over the next several years?
John Waldron: I think financing is still an enormous opportunity in the world. There's an enormous need for capital. Obviously, the AI build is front and center. There's a lot of infrastructure that needs to get built in the world. There are still decarbonization opportunities in the world. So, there's a lot of capital that's going to need to be sourced to finance this activity.
And frankly, I look at governments as becoming a little less relevant at the margin because they're pretty levered. We came out of COVID and the governments were the engine of fiscal stimulus to bring us back from the COVID challenges. And so governments have levered up, and now the private sector, I think is going to have to be a bigger engine of that capital formation.
So, we're pretty optimistic about the opportunity to raise a lot of capital in the coming years, and Goldman Sachs sits at the center of a lot of that capital formation. So I'm very bullish on that opportunity set. I'm quite bullish on Asia. I think there's going to be a lot of economic growth. I think there's going to be a lot more opportunity.
Ad again, we've got a very nice business there, and we've put a lot of investment on the ground in the important markets in Asia. And so I see a lot of opportunity across the marketplace in Asia. And then I'd get back to asset and wealth management as big opportunities, certainly for Goldman Sachs, but I think for many firms.
There's obviously an enormous amount of wealth creation that has occurred over the last five, 10 years and I think will continue to occur. And that wealth creation needs to be asset managed. People need access to good products and solutions to manage their wealth accordingly, and firms like Goldman Sachs are exceptionally well positioned to do that.
Allison Nathan: We've already talked about AI a few times in this conversation. It's really impossible not to talk about it, given the pervasiveness of the technology. We're incorporating it in our core strategy at Goldman Sachs. Talk to us a little bit about how we're using the technology, the impact it's making.
John Waldron: Yeah. AI is having a huge impact on our firm and I'm very encouraged about the progress we've made at Goldman Sachs. We basically have a four-pronged strategy.
The first of which is literacy and adoption. So we want to get our employees as literate as possible and as comfortable using the tools as possible. So we've really done a lot of work putting tools out for our employees to use and then teaching them how to think about using them and putting a lot of training out, and I think we've done well in that first pillar.
The second is really around software development and software development life cycle, which is probably where we've seen the early wins in terms of efficiency and productivity. If you talk to the coders at Goldman Sachs, they would wax on about how valuable tools like it have been to Goldman Sachs in terms of driving a lot of coding efficiency and productivity across the whole life cycle.
And we think that will continue to accelerate. And that has a huge impact on Goldman Sachs because we write a lot of code in this firm, either because we're trying to deal with deferred maintenance on older systems or because we're trying to build new systems, new capabilities, new tools for our clients.
The third area is what I would put in the broad bucket of re-engineering the firm, which is automation. So we're not a manufacturing organization, we're a human capital organization, we're a services company. If we were a manufacturing company, we'd be talking about getting some robots on the floor.
We're using a lot of digital agents to start automating a lot of the processes that run across our organization. I call them the interstate highways, so they run across state lines, and they need to be automated because they've really not been automated in any real way over time.
They're much more human-centric processes. So, there's a big opportunity for us to unlock and make the firm more resilient, more scalable. Not really just about taking cost out, but frankly about building a stronger foundation from which we can grow.
And then the fourth area is really around tools for clients. Can we use the Goldman Sachs data, which is extensive and now in a much cleaner shape than it would've been five, 10 years ago plus our human capital, our judgment, our experience, plus the technology of LLMs and digital agents, and can we package all that together and can we give our clients better advice faster?
And that I'm very excited about. I think we're just on the beginning stages of coming up with some tools that we can bring to our clients in an environment that is the Goldman Sachs environment, coupled with our human intelligence. I think those two things married together can be quite powerful, and I think we're going to make a lot of progress.
So, we're putting a lot more tools out there. We're building a lot more use cases. We're working with a lot of partners, LLMs and hyperscalers and other compute providers, to make sure that we have the capacity to do what we want to do. And I'm very encouraged about the progress, and I think 2027 is going to be a much bigger year for Goldman Sachs and our deployment of AI than 2026 was, which was also quite a good start for us.
Allison Nathan: So, a lot going on and a lot to look forward to on the AI front. Let me just get back to the growth front for a moment. The firm has recently made a series of targeted acquisitions: Industry Ventures, Innovator, NEOS Investments, and LCN Capital Partners. What's the strategic thinking behind these specialized acquisitions? Why now? And how do you approach integrating several unique platforms simultaneously?
John Waldron: So, we have one of the top five asset managers in the world. We are very scaled. We're north of $4 trillion of assets on our platform, and we've long believed that global broad and deep is an important thought process around running a scaled asset manager.
So, we want to have the capabilities in all the important asset classes. We want to be very deep with our expertise, and we want to obviously be very global in our approach. When you think about it that way, there are places where we are either not big enough or we don't really have the capabilities that we want to have, and we could, of course, go about setting our course on building those capabilities, but there are acquisitions you can make to make that go faster and to really fill in those gaps in an important way.
So, the gaps would be either around solutions, asset classes where we want to be stronger and better, or distribution. So, I'll give you a good example. We actually did a partnership with T. Rowe Price. It wasn't an acquisition. We just formed essentially a partnership together with them. T. Rowe Price has one of the largest and best retirement platforms in the United States.
Goldman Sachs doesn't have that. We're not very likely to build a retirement platform from scratch anytime soon. But we can partner with T. Rowe Price and have access to their retirement platform, and we can marry their expertise and our expertise in public markets and in private markets to design products and solutions that fit the retirement savers in America.
And so we're going about doing that, whether it's model portfolios, private credit, interval fund structures, multi-asset public-private structures. We're starting to really work on some pretty interesting solutions that serve their retirement customers and clients and also serve the broader wealth channel.
Industry Ventures is a venture capital platform embedded in the Silicon Valley ecosystem, very synergistic for Goldman Sachs, phenomenal track record of raising capital and deploying capital and venture capital transactions up and down the ecosystem. We've done transactions in leasing net lease platform which is LCN, Innovator and NEOS are ETF platforms.
So in each area, we're building strength and capabilities where we otherwise were small and not as strong as we want to be, or we don't have the distribution heft that we would like to have. And so we're finding places to know, fill in those gaps. And then your integration question is a really important question.
So we have not done that many acquisitions in our history at Goldman Sachs. This firm has been relatively organically built. We are now building the capability to integrate acquisitions and find ways to build playbooks and be more systematic about how we acquire something and make it fit into our company.
And I think we're getting better at it. Every transaction we do, we get a little bit sharper. And we're trying to build something that we can repeat. So yes, each transaction has its own elements. The most important thing is culture. We have to make sure that when we buy companies or assets and people, that we think the cultural fit will be strong, and we can actually bring those people into our firm, and they can feel like they're part of Goldman Sachs, and they've always been part of Goldman Sachs.
And so, we spend a lot of time on the early part of the diligence process thinking about that, and then we get to the integration part. We work hard at making sure those cultural integrations are strong. And I think so far we've done a very good job in these recent acquisitions, and I'm encouraged about our opportunity to do more of those.
Allison Nathan: Let's expand on that culture point. It is so important. We often say that culture is the defining asset of Goldman Sachs. Our people are our defining asset. How do you preserve what's distinctive about the firm's culture as we grow, as we diversify and bring in a new generation of talent, some of which may be AI agents?
John Waldron: Yeah. Listen, culture is the most important thing at Goldman Sachs. We are a human capital organization. We're going to be a human capital organization. Yes, we're going to deploy digital agents, but we're still going to be a human capital organization. We rely on that talent to really propel the firm forward, and talent on its own, not working collaboratively together, is not going to get it done.
We have to bring that talent together and have that talent really want to work as a cohesive unit. That's really all about One Goldman Sachs. One Goldman Sachs has been successful because we've been able to take the talent that we have and get it to work together to be even more powerful than any individual talent would've been.
And so I think for us, to me, culture is about narrating the words. What does it mean? When we say collaborative, what does it mean? Let's bring it to life. So, I think both in terms of the actual narration, the examples of the words that you want to use, showing people what it means, celebrating those victories when you see it in action.
Helping people understand when you see things that are not core to the culture happening in the firm, how we get rid of that, how we stop that, how we change that. I think teaching people how to embrace AI and use AI and make it a core part of what makes the firm special and unique, and how it can be in the service of clients, is going to be really important for us.
So yes, having digital agents will be part of the firm. They've got to be in the name and service of clients, or in the name of service of making the firm more resilient and scalable so we can serve our clients better, and I think that'll be the way we narrate and work hard on that aspect of the culture.
Allison Nathan: I think that's a good note to end on. But I do have a final question, which is: What advice would you give to someone starting their career in finance today, and has that advice changed given that the nature of work itself is changing?
John Waldron: Yeah. I think intellectual curiosity, to me, is pretty important. It's always been important. Right now, it may be even more important. Now the good news with all these tools that we have in LLM modeling capability is you can learn a lot quickly. And I think when you come into a firm like ours, being intellectually curious and being willing to learn is going to serve you very well.
We can give you a lot of information, the technology can amplify that, and your willingness to absorb all that and be willing to take some risks and learn things that you don't otherwise really know well. Work on your weaknesses, get a little smarter in areas where you haven't had that same kind of background in your development.
I think all those areas are really important. So that's what I say to young people coming into the firm is be very open-minded. Be a sponge and just learn, because we're going to show you and offer you an enormous amount of information and perspective and experience and judgment that you can learn over time, and that's going to be the most important thing.
Allison Nathan: I mean, it's never been a better moment, I think, for young people to embrace that experience and learn.
John Waldron: I agree. I mean, I think there's a lot of concern on college campuses. I see it in the eyes of young students when I go to those campuses, that they're worried about can they get a job?
Is this world going to be hospitable for them? I'm much more optimistic. I think particularly if you're willing to learn and you show that desire to stretch your mind, this is an extraordinary time. We need a lot of talent at Goldman Sachs. We need to onboard young talent, young energy.
They're going to be very facile with the tools. I think it's going to be an extraordinary period for young talent in our firm and in the economy more broadly.
Allison Nathan: Thanks so much for sharing your insights, John. Always a pleasure.
John Waldron: Nice to be here. Thank you.
Allison Nathan: This episode of Goldman Sachs Exchanges was recorded on Tuesday, November 3rd, 2026.
If you enjoyed the show, we'll hope you subscribe to Apple Podcasts, Spotify, or wherever you get your podcasts, and leave us a rating and comment. I'm Allison Nathan. Thanks for listening.

Weekly Market DirectionsENFR

Summary

Global central banks are striving to balance economic growth and inflation expectations driven by factors such as the war in the Middle East and AI capex. Accordingly, the Fed and the ECB kept policy rates unchanged as they await the effects of previous tightening to show up in the data.

The Fed, the ECB and the Bank of Japan (BOJ) kept rates on hold at their October policy meetings.This decision to wait allows the Fed and the ECB to assess additional data before acting in December. Uncertainty over their future policy decisions remains high, as central banks would like to tame price pressures without crippling economic activity.

Major central banks, including the Fed, ECB and BOJ, kept their benchmark rates unchanged last week. The Fed seems to be assessing the effects of its rate hike in September and believes financial conditions are tighter today than they were previously. However, Chair Warsh was categorical in saying that conditions are not tight, the economy is strong and inflation is “too high”. We think the Fed is buying time and has left the door open for a hike in December this year, although it declined to provide any forward guidance. We also think that one of the reasons the US economy is staying strong is AI and related investment. In the long term, this should improve productivity across the economy, but in the short term all that heavy spending is creating strong demand for AI products and infrastructure, which may be pushing up inflation. The ECB also kept rates steady and believes financial conditions have tightened. Higher energy prices, along with the risk of second-round effects from energy prices and wage pressures, both of which are contained for now, will drive the bank’s decisions in December and next year.

This week at a glance

US equities fell amid weak corporate earnings, as markets appeared to question companies’ massive spending on artificial intelligence. By contrast, European stocks gained. In fixed income, the appeal of bonds as safe havens increased in this environment, and yields fell. Markets also digested the latest policy decisions from central banks. Meanwhile, gold prices declined. Overall, investors are now looking ahead to the outcome of the US mid-term elections.

The chart shows the price of gold.Diversification does not guarantee a profit or protect against a loss.

Amundi Investment Institute Macro Focus

AmericasDomestic demand offsets trade headwindsUS GDP grew by 3.4% QoQ in Q3, above the 3.2% consensus, confirming an economy on solid footing. Consumer spending and strong AI-related investment drove domestic demand, with capex also strengthening beyond technology, despite a large drag from net exports. Further growth remains likely, albeit at a slower pace, as current spending contributions may prove hard to sustain. Elevated energy prices and low savings could weigh on consumption heading into 2027.EuropeUnderlying growth remains modestEurozone GDP rose by 0.4% QoQ in Q3, beating expectations, but the preliminary reading was flattered by volatile Irish data. Excluding Ireland, growth was 0.2%, pointing to a moderate underlying pace despite the energy shock. German business confidence rose for a sixth month, led by manufacturing, while services sentiment weakened. October surveys suggest modest growth ahead, although elevated energy prices and tighter financial conditions leave risks tilted to the downside. AsiaMixed data from JapanJapan's industrial production rebounded by 2.2% mom in September, led by vehicles and machinery, pointing to firmer factory activity. Retail sales, however, fell by 0.7%, signaling softer household demand. AI-related exports and business investment remain supportive, but high energy costs weigh on consumers and firms, leaving the recovery uneven.
