articles.title: Take Two: Central banks on hold - BNP Paribas Asset Management - Corporate English
articles.text:
What do you need to know?

The Federal Reserve decided to keep interest rates on hold at 3.75%-4% by a vote of 10-2, with two of the 12-member committee favouring a 25-basis-point rise. The Fed stated that while inflation remains high, “the accumulation of more information” is first needed to guide its return to the 2% goal – though expectations of a further rate hike by year end remain strong. Meanwhile, an advance estimate for US GDP growth in the third quarter showed expansion at an annualised 3.4%, up from Q2’s 2.2% and above expectations of 3.2%.

Around the world

The European Central Bank voted to keep interest rates steady last week, despite annual inflation accelerating to 3.8% in September, a three-year high. The ECB noted that rising energy prices are likely to drive up inflation and lower growth within the region. The eurozone economy grew 0.4% on a quarterly basis in Q3, a slowdown from Q2’s 0.6%, according to official data released after the ECB meeting. Elsewhere, the Bank of Japan kept rates unchanged at 1.25% and said underlying inflation had reached its 2% target, the first time since the goal was set in 2013.

Figure in focus: 37%

Foreign direct investment increased by 37% globally in the first half of 2026, compared to the average half-year level in 2025, according to the United Nations’ Trade and Development arm. The rise was largely driven by developed economies which saw investment flows rise by more than 70% in the first half of 2026. However, overall activity weakened, with the number of new projects falling by 15% and international project finance deals declining by 11%. The slowdown in activity reflects global uncertainty over geopolitical tensions, energy prices and supply chain disruptions, the UN said.

Chart of the week

About a third of US and Europe-listed companies had released their third quarter earnings as of last week. Things are going well. In the US, earnings have risen by 37%, though a big contributor to that growth is the technology sector. Excluding technology stocks, the earnings growth rate is a still good 17%. In Europe, earnings are up 25%. Investors also look at how much better or worse the results are compared to what was expected. So far, earnings have surpassed expectations by 3%-4%, in line with historical averages.

Words of wisdom: Big Bang

The deregulation of the London Stock Exchange, referred to as the Big Bang, marked its 40th anniversary last week.On 27 October 1986,the open outcry trading floor was replaced by electronic order books, and fixed broker commissions were abolished, leading to a sudden surge in trading volumes and lower costs for investors. This transformed London into a leading global financial centre. As investment from the US and Asia flowed into London, the Big Bang caused a ripple effect across Europe with the region accelerating the pace of modernising its own trading models.

What’s coming up?

On Tuesday, the Reserve Bank of Australia convenes to set interest rates. Wednesday sees the eurozone release a flash estimate for October’s inflation rate. Several final Purchasing Managers’ Indices for October are issued on Wednesday covering the eurozone, China, UK, and the US. The Bank of England meets to set interest rates on Thursday. On Friday, the US releases its latest jobs data.

articles.title: Euro Tax Flash from KPMG's EU Tax Centre: 04 November 2026
articles.text:
Go back to the Euro Tax Flash homepage.

KPMG feedback on the European Commission Tax Omnibus proposal

At a glance: KPMG member firms in the EU have submitted feedbackopens in a new tab on the European Commission’s Tax Omnibus proposal, broadly welcoming its simplification measures while identifying areas where further changes or clarifications may needed.Taxpayer impact: The Tax Omnibus could reduce tax-related costs and compliance burdens for businesses operating across the EU, although the extent of these benefits will depend on the outcome of Council negotiations.

European Commission – Tax Omnibus – Direct taxation – Withholding taxes – Parent-Subsidiary Directive – Interest and Royalties Directive - ATAD – CFC rules – Interest limitation – R&D tax incentives – Merger Directive – Tax dispute resolution

Background

On September 10, 2026, the European Commission (EC) launched a public consultation on its Tax Omnibus proposalopens in a new tab, inviting interested parties to submit comments by November 5, 2026.The consultation follows the publication, on June 24, 2026, of the Commission’s Tax Omnibus proposal, which forms part of its broader agenda to simplify the EU direct tax framework, reduce administrative and compliance burdens and support the competitiveness of the EU internal market.The proposal would amend several key EU direct tax Directives, including the Anti-Tax Avoidance Directive (ATAD), the Parent-Subsidiary Directive (PSD), the Interest and Royalties Directive (IRD), the Merger Directive and the Directive on Tax Dispute Resolution Mechanisms (DRM). Key measures include:removing withholding taxes on qualifying intra-EU dividends, interest and royalties and introducing a simplified procedure for accessing withholding tax relief;introducing a carve-out from EU Controlled Foreign Company (CFC) rules for groups within the scope of Pillar Two;further harmonizing the ATAD interest limitation rules, including by making certain currently optional relief provisions mandatory and introducing additional carve-outs;introducing a common minimum standard for R&D tax incentives;extending the Merger Directive to certain cross-border conversions; andamending the DRM with the aim of facilitating access to dispute resolution procedures and strengthening taxpayers’ procedural rights.KPMG member firms1 in the EU have submitted feedbackopens in a new tab on the Commission’s Tax Omnibus proposal. The submission builds on recommendations made by KPMG member firms in response to the Commission’s earlier call for evidence and provides comments on the specific measures included in the Tax Omnibus proposal.The proposal is currently being discussed by Member States in the Council, with a political commitment to reach agreement by the end of 2027. As amendments to EU direct tax legislation require unanimous agreement, the final scope and timing of the package will depend on the outcome of those negotiations.For more information on the Tax Omnibus proposal and KPMG’s earlier recommendations, please refer to Euro Tax Flash Issue 582 and Issue 577.

KPMG feedback

We welcome the ambition of the Tax Omnibus proposal and its focus on simplifying the EU direct tax framework, reducing compliance burdens and supporting the competitiveness of the EU internal market.In particular, we welcome the proposed removal of withholding tax barriers on intra-EU payments, the CFC carve-out for groups subject to Pillar Two, targeted changes to the ATAD interest limitation rules and the proposed common minimum standard for R&D tax incentives and we believe that they send the right signal to enhance the EU's attractiveness as a place to invest.In the submission, we acknowledge Member States’ concerns regarding the potential budgetary impact of certain measures but consider that the potential short-term revenue impact should be weighed against the longer-term benefits of reducing barriers to cross-border investment, lowering compliance costs and supporting the competitiveness of the EU internal market.As Council discussions progress, we encourage Member States to preserve the overall ambition of the Commission’s proposals and to ensure that additional anti-abuse safeguards or conditions do not significantly reduce the practical benefits of the proposed simplification measures.In our submission, we also highlight areas where further changes or clarification could help ensure that the proposals deliver meaningful simplification in practice. Key observations with respect to the different Tax Omnibus building blocks include:Withholding tax relief for intra-EU paymentsWe welcome the proposed removal of withholding taxes on qualifying intra-EU dividends, interest and royalties and the move to a common and simplified relief procedure based on self-assessment, which could reduce compliance costs and cash-flow constraints for businesses. We also welcome the proposed extension of the dividend withholding tax exemption to EU pension funds and suggest considering similar treatment for certain investment funds and other entities that are tax-exempt for genuine public-policy reasons. We consider that the current participation thresholds create an arbitrary distinction between economically comparable investments, rather than serve as an effective anti-abuse filter. Potential abuse can instead be addressed through existing anti-abuse rules and targeted ex-post controls.The submission therefore stresses that any notification, documentation, anti-abuse or ex-post review requirements should be clear and administrable and operate within appropriate deadlines. We also recommend greater clarity on the proposed safeguard for interest and royalty payments to recipients in zero-tax jurisdictions, including a common EU approach to identifying the jurisdictions concerned and clarification of its application where the income is effectively taxed elsewhere in the ownership chain.CFC rules and overlaps with Pillar TwoWe welcome the proposed carve-out from EU CFC rules for groups within the scope of Pillar Two as an important step towards reducing overlapping anti-avoidance rules and associated compliance obligations. We also suggest considering whether similar simplification could be extended to the ATAD anti-hybrid mismatch rules. The submission notes, however, that the proposed carve-out includes specific limitations for groups headquartered in jurisdictions operating a qualified Side-by-Side regime and calls for these provisions to be clarified to avoid uncertainty and differences in implementation across Member States. At the same time, we consider that the existing flexibility for Member States to apply either Model A or Model B under the ATAD CFC rules should be retained.GAARWith respect to the proposed extension of the ATAD General Anti-Abuse Rule (GAAR) to Pillar Two Top-up Taxes, we recommend taking into account the ongoing OECD work on Pillar Two integrity measures to ensure that the two sets of rules are compatible and do not overlap.ATAD interest limitation rulesWe support the proposed changes to the interest limitation rules, including making the 30 percent EBITDA threshold, the indexed EUR 3 million de minimis threshold, the group escape clause and the carry-forward of non-deductible interest mandatory across Member States. We also welcome the proposed additional carve-outs, including for qualifying third-party debt and significant reductions in EBITDA. However, the conditions attached to the third-party debt carve-out could limit its practical benefit, particularly where groups borrow externally through centralized treasury functions. We also suggest reconsidering the proposed removal of Alternative Investment Funds from the carve-out for financial undertakings.R&D tax incentivesWe welcome the proposed introduction of a common minimum standard for R&D tax incentives, while allowing Member States to maintain or introduce more favorable domestic incentives. We note, however, that the proposed allowance may provide limited benefit to loss-making businesses, including early-stage innovative companies, where domestic rules restrict the use of tax losses. We therefore suggest considering additional mechanisms, including the possibility of allowing losses generated by the R&D allowance to be surrendered in exchange for cash tax credits. We also recommend considering whether the EU State aid framework should be updated to facilitate incentives that qualify for favorable treatment under the Pillar Two Substance-based Tax Incentive Safe Harbour.Cross-border reorganizationsWe welcome the proposed alignment of the Merger Directive with developments in EU company law, including the extension of tax neutrality to cross-border conversions. We consider that further attention should be given to the treatment of carry-forward losses and other tax attributes, particularly where losses could remain trapped in the departure jurisdiction or be lost following a reorganization. The submission also calls for further guidance on divisions by separation and the interaction between cross-border conversions and EU exit taxation rules.Dispute resolution proceduresWe welcome the proposed clarifications to the scope of the Directive on Tax Dispute Resolution Mechanisms, including changes that would make it easier for taxpayers to access the procedures and reduce the risk of complaints being rejected on procedural grounds. We note, however, that taxpayers may continue to incur late-payment interest even where double taxation is ultimately eliminated and that differences between Member States in the treatment of penalties may affect access to the procedure. The submission also calls for greater clarity where a complaint is accepted by one Member State but rejected by another.

ETC Comment:

Following the release of the Tax Omnibus proposal end of June, Member States subsequently submitted initial questions and comments to the European Commission. In addition, several discussions covering the individual elements of the package have been held at Council level (in the so-called Antici Group composed of foreign affairs ambassadors with tax experts contributing to the discussion where appropriate).The public comments from Member States, dated July 27opens in a new tab and July 31opens in a new tab, indicate that several elements of the proposal remain under debate based on a number of concerns that can be grouped as follows:Sovereignty: Several Member States consider in their comments that parts of the package go beyond administrative simplification and amount to substantive harmonization of direct tax policy (e.g., through the proposed introduction of anti-derogation clause). This is particularly relevant in relation to ATAD, which was originally designed as a minimum standard and currently allows Member States to apply stricter domestic anti-avoidance rules.Budgetary concerns: According to the comments from some Member States, the proposed withholding tax changes, amendments to the interest limitation rules and the common R&D allowance could all have potentially significant budgetary effects. Some countries have therefore requested country-by-country impact assessments from the EC, or have commissioned local assessments, rather than relying only on EU-wide estimates of compliance savings and economic benefits.Tax avoidance concerns: According to some Member States’ comments, simplification should not weaken enforcement or existing anti-abuse protections. This concern arises, for example, in relation to the removal of ex-ante WHT relief controls, proposed new carve outs from the interest limitation rules, and the suggested exclusion of Pillar Two groups from the EU CFC rules.It will therefore be important for stakeholders to engage with the process to ensure the final rules are workable in practice and achieve their intended objectives without being diluted during the Council negotiations.This is similarly true for the public consultation on the Directive on Administrative Cooperation (DAC) recast proposal, which is being conducted by the EC in parallel and that closes on December 1, 2026 – see E-News Issue 237 for more details.

Should you have any queries, please do not hesitate to contact KPMG’s EU Tax Centre or, as appropriate, your local KPMG tax advisor.

articles.title: Market Watch
articles.text:
04 November 2026
Market Watch

Download Report

Blue Wave: Democrats sweep the US midterms

Summary
Event: The Democrats gained control of the House of Representatives and the Senate at the US midterm elections that took place this week.
Our View: With the US government now no longer under unified control of the Republicans, gridlock has returned to Washington. We believe investors should not overreact to these results and should stay invested.
In equities, investors should continue to diversify their equity exposure into more defensive sectors. As we transition to mid-cycle for the equity markets, we expect stocks to continue to deliver positive returns in the 8-10% range per annum, a downshift from the torrid pace of gains in the earlier part of the cycle.
In bonds, income remains attractive given recent spread widening. We favour non-hyperscaler investment grade corporate bonds at the three to seven-year part of the curve. We continue to expect the US dollar to remain range-bound in the near term, as we expect two more rate hikes from the Fed, but as this mini rate hike cycle ends in the second quarter of 2027, the USD index (DXY) is likely to depreciate towards 98.5 as markets start to anticipate a Fed rate cut in the second half of next year.
Oil is likely to rebound in the short-term on heightened geopolitical risk, but as supply chains adapt to the current situation and Congress exercises oversight on defense spending, WTI prices are likely to drift towards our 12-month target of USD 80 per barrel.

Democrats made solid gains across the Senate, House of Representatives and State Governors
Results reported as at 7:45PM Singapore Time

Source: The Wall Street Journal, Standard Chartered

Major implications of Democrat control of Congress
1. Fiscal expansionary policies may slow. Democrats are now in position to block any new tax cuts or spending plans from the Trump administration. At the same time, any fiscal policies proposed by Democrats may also face Trump’s veto. Hence the fiscal trajectory of the US will likely remain stuck over the next two years. As we get into the second half of 2027, the US debt ceiling will once again loom, and gridlock could potentially bring back government shutdowns. However, as they have always done in the past, compromise will ultimately prevail, in our opinion.
2. Trump remains in control of foreign policy. With the midterms now out of the way, could Trump decide to re-start combat operations with Iran? We believe there is a risk that US and Israel – now that both countries’ have concluded important elections – will once again be tempted to restart combat operations to force an end to the conflict. However, the duration of any renewed hostilities may be limited by Congress next year as the Democrats will likely withhold funding forfurther military operations. In the near-term, oil prices may experience renewed volatility before stabilising at a lower level next year. The introduction of new tariffs on trading partners may prove harder with Democratoversight.
3. AI data centre moratoriums could grow, though model development regulatory changes would be harder to pass. While the headlines have focused on the House and Senate results, one important development has also occurred at the gubernatorial level. Notably, Democrats have won the governor races in Texas and Georgia, two big data centre states. As data centre build out permits are largely decided at the local state level, this will have important ramifications for build out plans next year. However, any Democratic proposals to regulate AI model developments would need to be signed off by President Trump, who continues to wield veto power on any such proposals.

Asset class strategy
Equities: Remain invested and continue to diversify. While investors initially overreacted, President Trump’s relatively conciliatory response has provided some welcome relief, helping markets recover strongly from their pre-market lows. Hence, we recommend investors avoid overreacting, remain invested and continue to diversify their equity exposure across sectors and regions. A few themes stand out from the early pre-market reaction to the mid-term elections. On the positive side, defensive stocks continue to fare well, while themes favoured by Democrats are also outperforming. Clean energy is a notable beneficiary, with solar stocks among the biggest winners.

Policy uncertainty and a change in the innovation cycle is consistent with our view of a mid-cycle transition, where equity returns moderate but remain positive

today. Affordability-related themes are also rallying, including companies that could benefit from potential tariff rollbacks. Medicaid-related stocks are also moving higher on expectations that potential policy changes could provide a tailwind for the healthcare sector.
On the negative side, semiconductor weakness continues amid concerns around potential data centre moratoriums. Our AI capex estimates remain conservative relative to consensus, but with a potential reset in expectations around data centre spending, investors should remain selective. After downgrading semiconductors last month, we have maintained a conservative stance on the industry, with a lower recommended allocation compared to September.
While we believe the mid-term election outcome is not a complete surprise to markets, particularly given pre-election polling and the recent weakness in both the S&P 500 and Nasdaq, the overnight correction highlights how complacent investors had become, with the VIX initially surging more than 10% in pre-market trading, although down from intra-day highs after President Trump’s comments.
As we have highlighted in our recent notes on the transition to mid-cycle, this phase is typically characterised by greater political headwinds. The mid-term election outcome reinforces the trend. The experience of 2015-2017, highlighted in the second table, offers a useful historical parallel. Despite the knee-jerk reaction, investors should not overreact based on one day’s moves. While we had trimmed equities to a core allocation last week, we continue to expect equities to deliver mid-to-high single-digit returns per annum during the mid-cycle, even amid political headwinds, supported by steady underlying earnings growth in both 2027 and 2028.
So, what should investors do to navigate the next few months before the newly elected representatives are sworn in and take control of the House and Senate? As we have been highlighting in recent notes, equity markets should still deliver positive returns, albeit at a more moderate pace. Hence, we recommend staying invested but diversification remains key to navigating the next phase of the cycle.
FX: DXY near-term support at 100.7, 12-month target at 98.5. A Democratic sweep potentially removes the legislative runway for further tariff escalation and for fiscal expansion, the two structural pillars of US exceptionalism that have anchored dollar demand in 2026. Reduced fiscal impulse compresses the growth and yield differential that has kept the US dollar well-bid all year. Additionally, potential Democratic restrictions on AI and data centre investment could weigh on US equity outperformance, which is likely to act as a secondary dollar-negative channel.
However, despite historical readings supporting a near-term DXY headwind from a Democratic sweep, the magnitude will

likely be modest and short-lived unless compounded by a weaker than expected non-farm payrolls report on Friday. We see the Fed narrative, not the election, as the dominant medium-term driver. Near-term we see USD index (DXY) support at 100.7, and retain our 12-month target at 98.5.
Fixed Income: Still attractive all-in yields; prefer investment grade corporates at three-to-seven year tenors to earn income and manage interest rate risk. The US Treasury bond market reaction appears to reflect a moderation in expectations of future economic growth after the election results. Yields at the intermediate end of the curve dropped the most, while the 30-year US yield moderated more modestly. We continue to expect two more Fed rate hikes between now and H1 2027 as still sticky inflation and the robust economy support further tightening.
In the past few weeks, the US Treasury yield curve has broadly shifted downwards, after our opportunistic call to go long 10-year Treasuries at the end of September. We are of the view the ultra-long end downshift in yields is overdone (given the still challenging US fiscal trajectory) and would recommend investors who had earlier taken long duration exposures at the 20 to 30-year parts of the curve reduce their positions now. We continue to believe the 3 to 7-year part of the curve offers the most optimal balance of income and interest rate risk, particularly via investment corporate bonds.
Within corporate credit, we expect a potentially slower pace of AI data centre buildouts could marginally improve market technicals, as hyperscaler and tech sector bond issuance may slow (and reduce “crowding out” of other bond issuances). Conversely, from a credit perspective, we believe this dynamic may also make the data centre focused deals less viable, and would be cautious on some of this sector’s lower quality names. Meanwhile, less AI capex dependent issuers continue to offer solid credit profiles amidst the still strong economy. High yield corporate spreads have widened in recent weeks but dispersion within the complex is wide, with BBs and Bs credit spreads staying relatively resilient, while CCCs have widened to distressed levels. For income-focused investors, we would recommend staying within the crossover range of between BBB-BB.
Commodities: As noted in the opening section, we believe there is a higher near-term risk of a restart of combat operations in Iran given the conclusion of the midterm elections. Given that, we believe there is a risk that oil prices could see a short-term spike, despite recent diplomatic overtures from Iran. However, for 2027 we continue to expect oil to stabilise at lower levels, as we think the Mideast situation should de-escalate given Democratic oversight of the defense budget, and the likely re-configuration of oil supply chains. On the margin, we are also closely monitoring regulatory developments in the US shale oil industry as the Democrats may seek to introduce new regulations on the sector. On gold, we view the recent change in control in the Congress as only having a marginal impact and thus stay Overweight. USD strength is a headwind (which is more dependent on Fed policy), but gold’s sensitivity to real yields has eased amid continued central bank buying, led by China, and resilient investor demand
— Jonathan Liang, CFA, CIO, Fixed Income & FX

Opinion
Commercialising frontier discoveries: what separates the winners from the others?
Since 2010, explorers have found 140 billion boe in frontier basins. More than half of those discoveries remain sub-commercial. What separates the fields that generate value from those that stall is not just what lies underground. It is the commercial conditions in place at discovery and the speed at which operators move.

Two discoveries account for a disproportionate share of everything frontier exploration has produced since 2010. That concentration tells the story of frontier exploration more plainly than any aggregate figure: transformational rewards for very few, and a much harder road for everyone else.
Scale can come from a single giant or from a cluster. But while size helps, the broader record of frontier discoveries shows that it is not the defining variable.
The full report provides field-by-field analysis, operator comparisons and a fast-track framework for understanding what separates frontier discoveries that generate value from those that stall. Fill in the form to download the full report, or read on for a preview of some of the key themes explored.
1. The divide between oil and gas
By volume, the picture is stronger, with oil accounting for most of the value. Size helps. Larger discoveries are more likely to be commercial than smaller finds. But size is not the defining variable.
The real divide is between oil and gas. The problem is rarely geology. It is a monetisation trap. Oil has a buyer and a price on day one. Gas has neither until markets, pipelines and fiscal terms line up, often in places where none previously existed.
What separates the gas discoveries that become commercial from those that remain stranded? Find out more in the full report.
2. Time is the real competitor
The range of time from discovery to final investment decision varies significantly. After FID, development timelines become more predictable.
That consistency after sanction points to where the real competition is. Value is won or lost before the development is committed, not during execution. The gap between the fastest and slowest outcomes comes from the pre-FID period.
What determines how quickly a frontier discovery can move from discovery to sanction? Download the full report to explore the analysis.
3. What the fast projects share
The quickest projects share five conditions: a committed market at discovery, existing infrastructure available to reuse, dominant or sole operatorship, a deliberately simple first phase, and an operator built to move quickly.
Each case follows a different path, but the underlying logic is the same: commercial conditions are resolved early, scope is kept manageable and the operator moves without waiting for certainty it cannot have.
Explore the conditions shared by the fastest-moving frontier projects, and the operators putting them into practice, in the full report.
4. What it means for capital allocation
For ministers, the message is that projects can move quickly when the right conditions are in place. For investors, the lesson is to focus on the commercial conditions as much as the rocks.
Frontier exploration still delivers transformational value. But the broader record makes clear that discovery is the starting point, not the outcome.
What separates frontier discoveries that create value from those that stall? Download the full report for the field-by-field analysis, operator comparisons and fast-track framework.

The NDR Daily Trading Sentiment Composite remains in neutral territory, reflecting the market’s tug-of-war between concerns over elevated oil prices, persistent inflation, and slowing job growth, and optimism surrounding strong corporate earnings, AI-driven productivity gains, and resilient economic growth.

Although sentiment briefly fell into pessimistic territory on September 18 with a reading of 30.0 before rebounding to neutral, that low would rank as the second-highest sentiment trough preceding a midterm year-end rally since 1982, well above the historical median low of 15.4 (table above).
Historically, midterm years have often produced year-end rallies as investor anxiety surrounding potential shifts in Congressional control reaches extreme levels, but the current sentiment backdrop is less supportive than in past cycles. articles.title: What really drove post-pandemic inflation? | Brookings
articles.text:

Podcast
What really drove post-pandemic inflation?

Listen on

Spotify

Pod.link

More

Brookings Podcast on Economic Activity

Brookings Podcast on Economic Activity

Hosts:
Janice C. Eberly and

Janice C. Eberly

Nonresident Senior Fellow
- Economic Studies

Jón Steinsson

Jón Steinsson

Nonresident Senior Fellow
- Economic Studies

Interviewer:
Louise Sheiner

Louise Sheiner

The Robert S. Kerr Senior Fellow
- Economic Studies,

Policy Director
- The Hutchins Center on Fiscal and Monetary Policy

Guests:
Domenico Giannone and

Domenico Giannone

Bloomberg Distinguished Professor of Economics and Statistics
- Johns Hopkins University

Giorgio Primiceri

Giorgio Primiceri

Professor of Economics
- Northwestern University

November 5, 2026

Unexpectedly strong demand, rather than supply shocks, was the dominant driver of post-COVID pandemic inflation in both the U.S. and the euro area, which followed nearly the same path about six months later.
Pent-up demand, expansionary fiscal policy, and an unusually accommodative monetary stance helped offset the supply shocks and support the recovery, at the cost of higher inflation.
Real-time data understated the strength of the recovery, which likely helped make the surge look supply-driven at the time.

20 min read

Bluesky Streamline Icon: https://streamlinehq.comBluesky

Post-COVID pandemic inflation is often blamed on broken supply chains and energy shocks. A new BPEA paper argues that unexpectedly strong demand was the dominant driver of the surge in both the U.S. and the euro area. On this episode of the Brookings Podcast on Economic Activity, Louise Sheiner talks to the paper’s authors, Domenico Giannone of Johns Hopkins University and Giorgio Primiceri of Northwestern University, about what drove the surge and what it means for policy.

Related Content

Demand-driven inflation

Monetary Policy

Demand-driven inflation

Domenico Giannone, Giorgio Primiceri

September 23, 2026

Listen to the Brookings Podcast on Economic Activity on Apple, Spotify, YouTube, or wherever you like to get podcasts.
Learn about other Brookings podcasts from the Brookings Podcast Network.
Sign up for the podcasts newsletter for occasional updates on featured episodes and new shows.
Send feedback email to podcasts@Brookings.edu.

Transcript

[music]
EBERLY: Welcome to season nine of the Brookings Podcast on Economic Activity. I’m Jan Eberly, the James R. and Helen D. Russell Professor of Finance at Northwestern University. And this season, we’ll be listening to discussions about papers from the fall 2026 Brookings Papers on Economic Activity conference, hosted by Brookings in September.
STEINSSON: And I’m Jón Steinsson, Marek Professor of Public Policy and Economics at the University of California, Berkeley. We are the co-editors of the Brookings Papers on Economic Activity, a semi-annual conference and journal that pairs rigorous research with real-time policy analysis to address the most urgent economic challenges of the day.
EBERLY: Once again, we have a great lineup of timely topics, energy markets, inflation, migration’s effects on labor and housing markets, financing AI, and more. Over the course of this season, we’ll hear a lot more about the conference papers and importantly, how decision-makers should be thinking about the topics they explore.
This episode takes on one of the most debated economic questions of the last few years: What actually caused the post-pandemic surge in inflation? Louise Sheiner, policy director for the Hutchins Center on Fiscal and Monetary Policy at Brookings, speaks with Domenico Giannoni of Johns Hopkins University and Giorgio Primiceri of Northwestern on their new paper, “Demand-Driven Inflation.”
STEINSSON: This debate has really been quite heated, which is perhaps not surprising given that there were so many unusual things going on during those years. On the supply side, there were supply chain disruptions, a substantial fall in labor supply, and large increases in energy prices associated with Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.
But then on the demand side, there was huge fiscal stimulus, and monetary policy was, at least until the spring of 2022 quite unresponsive.
EBERLY: Given all of that, it’s quite striking that inflation in the U.S. and Europe followed almost identical paths, just offset by about six months.
STEINSSON: Yes, that suggests that the cause of inflation must be something that was not special to the United States, but quite a few of the main proposed explanations affect both economies.
Now, Giannoni and Primiceri argue that the primary driver of inflation was demand, and what’s driving this conclusion is really to a large extent, monetary policy. Monetary policy was much more accommodative than one would have expected it to be given how the Fed and ECB had conducted monetary policy prior to this episode.
Here, the authors are making a subtle point. Whether inflation counts as demand-driven or supply-driven depends critically on the counterfactual one has in mind. If that counterfactual involves monetary policy responding aggressively to changes in inflation, then the conclusion is that the lack of a response of the Fed and ECB in 2021 was what caused inflation.
EBERLY: So, with that intro, let’s turn it over to Louise and the authors.
[3:16]
SHEINER: Thank you, Jan. Thank you, Jon. And welcome, Domenico.
GIANNONE: Nice to be here.
SHEINER: And welcome, Giorgio.
PRIMICERI: It’s great to be here. Thank you.
[3:24]
SHEINER: Okay. Giorgio, let’s start with you. So, the conventional story about post-COVID inflation is that it was mostly about broken supply chains and energy shocks. You argue that’s largely wrong. What’s the real driver?
[3:37]
PRIMICERI: So, we think that the main driver was actually demand, Louise, and this is true both in the United States and in the, in the Euro area. And to be more precise, our results suggest that approximately two-thirds of the surge in inflation after COVID was due to a boom in demand.
And there were three main contributing factors for this boom in demand. The first was private demand. So, the reopening of the economy after the restrictions of the pandemic, released some private pent-up demand. You know, after being at home for a while, people went out and decided to spend a little bit more than what they would have done otherwise, and probably very understandably so.
The second factor was fiscal policy, which was very supportive of incomes and spending during and after the pandemic. And it might be useful to give some numbers here. In the United States, government deficit relative to GDP increased by approximately nine percentage points. And in the Euro area, this number was seven percentage points, so almost equally large.
The type of fiscal intervention was a little bit different because in the U.S. It took the form mostly of direct transfers to households, stimulus checks essentially. While in Europe, they were mostly energy and employment subsidies, but the size of the fiscal intervention was comparable.
And the third factor that contributed to the boom in demand was monetary policy, which was unusually accommodative, both in the Euro area and in the United States. And just some numbers here are useful. Again, the timing is quite revealing because the Federal Reserve first raised interest rates in March of 2022 when the latest reading on CPI inflation was 7.9%.
The ECB first increased interest rates in July of the same year, when inflation in the Euro area was 8.9%. Okay? So, this is to say that monetary policy was clearly fairly accommodative in the sense that central banks have responded less aggressively than they would have normally done in the pre-pandemic period.
[6:16]
GIANNONE: So, let me also add that we are not claiming supply problems didn’t matter. They did. What our estimates say is that supply shocks alone would have produced less inflation and a weaker economy. And coming back to the conventional story, some of the development usually classified as supply problems, such as higher energy prices, shipping costs, and delivery delays, also reflected booming global demand.
So, supply constraint mattered, but exceptionally strong demand and accommodation by policy was the main force that turned those constraints into broad-based inflation.
[7:01]
SHEINER: Yeah, I thought that was so interesting to think about. So, people heard about stories about how the ports couldn’t keep up, and it seemed, seemed like it was a supply constraint.
And some of these measures of supply constraints were about like, how busy were the ports? But a big shock in demand where demand has just increased can create that supply constraint. Right? And so, like, what do you call it? And you’re gonna say, well, that was demand that created that supply constraint. Is that, is that the right way to think about it?
[7:24]
GIANNONE: Exactly. Exactly. And, you know, bottlenecks tell you where the congestion is, not necessarily what caused it. So, as you were saying, if a port is congested because dock workers aren’t available, that’s a supply shock., But if it is congested because households are ordering far more good than usual, the underlying cause is demand, even though what we see is a supply chain problem.
So, during the recovery, shipping costs, delivery times, commodity prices, energy prices, they all reflected limited capacity and also very strong spending. Of course, if we treat them all as movement in the supply shocks, then we overstate the role of supply.
[8:16]
SHEINER: Makes a lot of sense. Okay, Giorgio, so the U.S. and the European inflation were almost exactly the same, just the timing was different. They were offset about six months. So, you compare this— these two episodes, you compared the U.S. and Europe, and what did that comparison teach you about what was driving the inflation?
[8:35]
PRIMICERI: So, that was very striking to us, the similarities between the two the two regions. And as you said, the only difference was that inflation peaked a few months later in Europe relative to the United States.
And this similarity is not just about headline inflation. It is about many subcomponents of inflation. For example, goods inflation behaved similarly, services inflation behaved similarly, and perhaps more surprisingly, energy inflation behaved very similarly in the U.S. and the euro area.
The case of energy is actually very interesting because in Europe, the much larger increase was in the price of gas, electricity, and heating. This was not particularly surprising. Europe was indeed more exposed to the energy shock due to the Russian invasion of Ukraine. In the U.S. instead, the the larger increase was in the price of gasoline and other transportation fuels, which increased a lot more than in Europe.
But once we put these two components of energy prices together into a single energy price index, it turns out that the differences cancel out, and this aggregate energy price index of inflation behaves very similarly in the two countries.
And we have mentioned before that the similarities are wider than this. The two economies also shared a a broader demand and policy environment. You know, fiscal policy was expansionary, monetary policy was accommodative, private demand boomed because of pent-up demand.
So, to answer your question more directly about what this comparison has taught us, uh, I don’t think it has necessarily taught us what the drivers were, but more that we would expect the drivers to be similar.
[10:32]
SHEINER: Yeah. It’s interesting because I definitely had this view, because it was what I read about, was that certainly in Europe, you know, the inflation was energy driven. And that’s what policymakers were talking about. So, why do so many central bankers believe that?
[10:49]
GIANNONE: I think the main reason is because based on what they saw at the time, that explanation was plausible. So, because in real time that explanation was plausible, the economy looked weaker at the time than it was. Policymakers were seeing high inflation alongside apparently weak activity. And that combination looked like a supply problem. The initial GDP estimates were later revised upward. So, today, with the hindsight, we see stronger activity and realize demand had a stronger role.
Part of why the picture was so hard to read is that this episode was unprecedented. In last year Brookings Papers, Stock and Watson showed that in the United States, the COVID recession was the shortest on record. With the mindset shaped by previous recession, it was natural to expect a slower recovery and hard to recognize how quickly the economy was coming back. And on top of this, the supply problems made the front-page news throughout COVID.
[11:59]
PRIMICERI: I’d like to add a third reason to what Domenico just said, which I think is important, and maybe also a little bit more controversial than what Domenico mentioned, which is that after the very severe economic downturn of 2020, policymakers were probably a little bit worried about withdrawing support too early, understandably so, probably.
And so, interpreting inflation as supply-driven and likely to be transitory, I think made this greater tolerance of inflation appear less risky and more viable. And, you know, to be clear, I do not mean in any way to criticize policymakers. I think given the information available at the time, the risks that they were facing, allowing inflation to run temporarily higher to accelerate the recovery, you know, might have been a perfectly reasonable choice, if not the optimal one.
[12:57]
SHEINER: Okay, great. I was gonna ask, Domenico, I’m just gonna go back, because you said something that I think is very much part of the paper that we haven’t discussed a lot yet, which is part of how you know the difference between a supply shock and a demand shock. And you said that during the episode, GDP at first looked quite weak, and so that looks like a supply shock, but it turns out it was actually quite strong, and that’s w-what looks like a demand shock.
Is that, is that the right way to think about it and how you could tell the difference between the two?
[13:26]
GIANNONE: Yes. Yes, absolutely. So, at the time, so we were observing a weak economy and inflation, which is indicative of supply problems. While today, with the hindsight, now we see that the economy was stronger. So, the economy was strong and inflation was strong, putting more in the direction of of demand.
Basically, our model is working on based on this intuition, and we have a formal model that make predictions and look at forecast errors in this prediction. And when you see co-movement into output and prices, it interpreted as a positive co-movement as demand, negative co-movement as supply.
And our model is run with the data of today, so with the hindsight, we can realize its demand. In real time, it was not that clear.
[14:23]
PRIMICERI: So, we now know that this was the fastest recovery in post-war history. In real time, this might have not been entirely clear.
[14:33]
SHEINER: Yeah. I mean, that’s fair. We know a lot of people get criticism now as if they should have known it at the time. But of course, there was a lot of uncertainty.
Okay, so let’s go back. So so, using your model you decided it was demand. But when you talk about demand, you say how you classify whether or not it was a demand shock or a supply shock actually depends on how aggressively the Fed and the ECB were fighting inflation. Can you explain that?
[15:02]
PRIMICERI: Yes. This is actually a very important part of the paper. The short answer to your question is that demand and supply shocks themselves are not observed. What we observe is the effect of the shocks on some economic variables like prices and production and income and consumption and these things.
And as it is well known, the effect of shocks on economic variables depend on the conduct of monetary policy. So, I’m gonna give you a concrete example. Let’s imagine that the economy is hit by an adverse energy supply shock. If the central bank responds aggressively by raising interest rates and compressing demand, then the shock is probably gonna produce not much inflation, but a more severe recession.
Vice versa, if the central bank decides to look through the shock, the same shock will produce more inflation and a smaller decline in output. So, the originating shock is the same in this example, but the inflation that we observe as a consequence of the shock is different depending on the conduct of monetary policy.
And we can now extrapolate from this example, and perhaps it’s easier to understand why any decomposition of an historical episode is going to depend necessarily on the monetary policy regime in place.
So, to see why this matters, mine was just an example so far, but to see why this matters in practice, consider how monetary policy was conducted before the pandemic by both the Fed and the European Central Bank. So, for many years, both central banks had established a pattern of responding quite forcefully to inflationary pressures, whether those pressures originated on the demand side or the supply side.
But during the pandemic, their response was more accommodative than usual. They accepted more inflation in order to support a faster recovery.
And again, I mentioned this before, that choice might have been justified, but it did change how supply shocks showed up in the data. So, they likely produced more inflation than usual and less economic weakness than in a pre-pandemic regime.
So, the point here of the paper is, or one of the points of the paper is that part of the inflation that is commonly attributed to supply shocks also reflects the accommodative stance of monetary policy in response to these shocks, which was unusual.
[17:51]
SHEINER: So, just to clarify, if there’s a supply shock and in normal times that would have led to less output, and in this time the monetary authorities decided to support demand, and have more inflation and more output, then that becomes a demand shock.
[18:08]
PRIMICERI: Then it doesn’t necessarily become a demand shock, but its effect, it’s amplified by the chosen demand policy.
[18:18]
SHEINER: Right. So, in your classification, that’s one piece of the demand shock, that monetary policy being more accommodative. So, you do break down demand into monetary policy, fiscal policy, and, like, other forces like pent-up demand, as you said. For the U.S. and Europe, which of these matter the most? Whether they’re about the same or how do, how do they compare?
[18:38]
GIANNONE: So, Louise, they all mattered and at different times. So first, monetary policy. So, it turned accommodative in 2021 as rates stayed low while inflation rose. And this is where the two economies look almost identical. The contribution was similar in the United States and the euro area, and more pronounced during the run-up of inflation. As Giorgio was saying at the beginning, both central banks raised rates when inflation was already high.
Second, fiscal policy. In the United States, it was very strong immediately. In Europe, it was similar in size, but the contribution was more spread over time.
Third, pent-up demand and other private spending. That mattered more for the United States, especially during the reopening as the fiscal push faded. In Europe, the contribution of pent-up demand and private spending was less important, and during the reopening, we still had some important fiscal policy shocks bringing up inflation.
[19:55]
SHEINER: Super interesting. Okay. So, what is the one thing you’d want policymakers to take away from your research?
[20:03]
PRIMICERI: So, I would say that one central lesson for policy here is that the inflationary effects, as we just mentioned, of a shock, they do depend on the conduct of monetary policy because policy helps determine, you know, how much of a certain shock is gonna appear in prices and how much is gonna appear in economic activity.
And to be sure, this is a familiar result in monetary theory. It’s not new. The role of the paper is to show just how important this has been in this particular episode in history.
So, take my usual example: supply shocks. The usual recommendation for policy is that policy should look through them, as central banks like to say, especially, you know, when those shocks are expected to be transitory.
The key point here is that being transitory is not an intrinsic property of the shock. So, some supply shocks may be expected to be transitory simply because in the past, central banks have reacted to them in a way that has prevented them from becoming persistent. And if policy suddenly switches, it suddenly becomes more tolerant of inflation and starts looking through supply shocks more than they would normally do, then that shock might lose this transitoriness property that allowed people to look through them in the first place.
If I may add something, this has a concrete counterpart. Right? Because this is not just a theoretical point, that this is exactly the problem that the Fed and ECB are facing now, with the war with Iran. There are disruptions in energy markets. Oil prices are increasing. Inflation never really went back to the 2% target. Demand is still fairly strong, so central banks might need to raise interest rates even more than they have already done in order to prevent this initial energy shock from spreading to other prices and becoming more persistent.
[22:13]
SHEINER: Domenico, you have anything to add?
[22:14]
GIANNONE: Yes. My takeaway is about measurement. COVID reminded us that measuring the economy in real time is difficult and taught us that it becomes harder when there is so much variation and uncertainty.
As we document in the paper, the early data understated the strength of the recovery. And with a clearer picture, policy might have responded differently, and inflation might have been lower.
Something similar had happened in the 1970s. And indeed, policymakers are putting renewed effort into this. The Fed has just launched the five task forces to advance the conduct of monetary policy, and one of them is exactly about the quality and timeliness of data that inform policy decisions.
SHEINER: Yeah. We’re all looking forward to hearing the results of those working groups. So, this has been a really super interesting conversation, and I’ve learned so much. Thank you so much, Giorgio, and thank you so much, Domenico.
PRIMICERI: Thank you, Louise.
GIANNONE: Thank you.
[music]
STEINSSON: Once again, I’m Jón Steinsson.
EBERLY: And I’m Jan Eberly.
STEINSSON: And this has been the Brookings Podcast on Economic Activity. Thanks to our guests for this great conversation.
EBERLY: As always, you can find the full papers and the Brookings Papers on Economic Activity conference proceedings on our website at Brookings dot edu slash BPEA.

articles.title: Binance Hack: Tracing the $6.4 Billion Theft to North Korea - Chainalysis
articles.text:
Key takeaways
Around 4:20 p.m. ET on October 29, 2026, funds began leaving Binance hot wallets across multiple blockchains. Unauthorized transfers totaled approximately $6.4 billion, the largest theft in crypto history.
Chainalysis attributes the hack to TraderTraitor, a North Korean cybercrime group. Stolen Binance funds commingled on-chain with funds from last month’s Bitget theft, which was attributed to North Korea.
Freezes began by 5:14 p.m. ET. About $2.8 billion has been frozen as of 11:30 a.m. ET on November 3, 2026.
The attacker swapped $325 million in stablecoins for $285 million in ETH over nearly 20 minutes to stay ahead of freezes.
Laundering shows signs of automation: thousands of transactions, with many addresses first receiving exactly 1 TRX.
How did the Binance hack happen?Chainalysis investigators assess the $6.4 billion hack of Binance — the largest in the history of crypto, and one of the single-largest financial crimes of all time — to be the work of North Korean cybercrime group TraderTraitor. This group has repeatedly targeted the cryptocurrency industry, exchanges, DeFi protocols, and investors to raise funds for the regime.We base our intelligence assessment on on-chain activity observed in the hours following the hack.From the beginning: Around 4:20 p.m. Eastern Time on October 29, funds began leaving Binance hot wallets across multiple blockchains. On Ethereum, the attacker used an operational wallet funded through Tornado Cash to submit valid signed authorizations that allowed a Binance hot wallet to run attacker-deployed code. The attacker then called that wallet to sweep its assets into attacker-controlled addresses, while other affected Binance wallets appeared to send funds through ordinary signed transfers. Across the affected blockchains, the unauthorized transfers totaled approximately $6.4 billion USD.At this point the attacker was in a race against the clock. While billions of dollars in crypto under their control were denominated in unfreezable cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin and Ethereum, billions more were held in stablecoins like USDT and USDC that can be frozen. It was only a matter of time before the issuers of those stablecoins would freeze those funds — in coordination with law enforcement and industry partners such as Chainalysis.Freezing funds takes time. The attacker attempted to stay ahead of that process by quickly moving $500 million of stablecoins into a wallet whose job it was to swap out those freezable assets to non-freezable assets. Over nearly 20 minutes it swapped $325 million in stablecoins into $285 million in ETH. Ten minutes later, the exploiter sent the remaining $175 million in stablecoins to stopover wallets, likely trying to move faster than a blacklist or freeze. But the industry caught up with them more quickly than they expected: by 5:14 p.m. Eastern, the freezes started.Across multiple blockchains, Chainalysis investigators, law enforcement, stablecoin issuers, and other industry participants raced to freeze stolen funds before the attacker could convert them into assets beyond issuers’ control. Much of this work happened independently, with organizations acting in parallel. Chainalysis proactively shared investigative leads with industry partners to help identify and freeze stolen funds. Approximately $2.8 billion has been frozen so far. While that does not diminish the scale of the crypto theft, the response shows an industry increasingly able to act quickly, both independently and together.Commingled funds strengthen the link to TraderTraitorSeveral laundering patterns initially suggested that TraderTraitor was responsible for the Binance theft. The strongest evidence emerged when Chainalysis investigators observed, in real time, funds stolen from Binance commingling with funds stolen in last month’s Bitget exploit, which had been attributed to North Korean actors. That direct on-chain link strengthened our assessment that TraderTraitor carried out the Binance hack and we announced it on October 30, 12:30 a.m. Eastern Time.Laundering patterns suggest automationAs Chainalysis investigators continue to trace funds stolen from Binance, we are observing laundering patterns we have not seen before. Thousands of transactions in a short period suggest that the attackers are using automation to obscure the trail of funds. Rather than simply moving funds onward, they repeatedly circulate them among addresses, often sending funds back to addresses involved earlier in the sequence.Many addresses follow a consistent pattern: they receive exactly 1 TRX, then receive additional funds, then forward funds to other addresses. This repeated sequence suggests a programmatic process for moving and redistributing the stolen cryptocurrency.The investigation continues The investigation remains ongoing and we expect the stolen funds to continue moving in the coming days. Chainalysis is committed to supporting Binance and the wider industry as we trace the stolen funds, disrupt further laundering, and work to mitigate additional losses.Crypto exchanges remain attractive targets for hackers because they hold substantial funds, regardless of where they operate. While this security incident is unprecedented in scale, cyber-attacks on exchanges are not new. Every cryptocurrency exchange should remain vigilant and prepared to respond quickly when an attack occurs.Chainalysis customers can use our solutions to identify exposure to addresses linked to this incident. We will continue to monitor the flow of funds and update labels as new information emerges. To learn how Chainalysis can help your organization identify exposure and trace funds, contact our team.FAQsWhat happened to Binance?On October 29, 2026, starting around 4:20 p.m. ET, an attacker moved approximately $6.4 billion out of Binance hot wallets across multiple blockchains. Who hacked Binance?Chainalysis attributes the hack to TraderTraitor, a North Korean cybercrime group that targets exchanges, DeFi protocols and investors to raise funds for the regime. Funds stolen from Binance commingled on-chain with funds stolen from Bitget last month, a theft attributed to North Korea.How much was stolen in the Binance hack?Approximately $6.4 billion across multiple blockchains.How much of the stolen crypto has been frozen?About $2.8 billion as of 11:30 a.m. ET on November 3, 2026. Stablecoin issuers began freezing funds by 5:14 p.m. ET on October 29, working with law enforcement and industry partners such as Chainalysis.Is the Binance hack the largest crypto hack ever?Yes. At approximately $6.4 billion, it is the largest cryptocurrency theft in history.How can compliance teams check exposure to the Binance hack?Chainalysis customers can identify exposure to addresses linked to this incident in KYT and Address Screening. articles.title: Beyond buyouts: How infrastructure debt is broadening the opportunity set in private credit | Macquarie Groups
articles.text:
Perspectives
Beyond buyouts: How infrastructure debt is broadening the opportunity set in private credit

Link copied to clipboard

Private credit's growth has largely been portrayed as a direct lending story, but infrastructure debt is rapidly broadening the opportunity set beyond traditional sponsor-backed lending.
Focused on the build-out of physical assets, infrastructure debt offers investors access to a $US150 trillion capex supercycle1 supported by long-term structural demand drivers.
One of the fastest-expanding segments of private credit, infrastructure debt carries unique risk-return characteristics, demanding a combination of deep operational infrastructure experience and credit expertise from investors to succeed.
Macquarie Asset Management has been investing in infrastructure debt for more than 20 years, completing more than 300 transactions to become one of the world’s largest infrastructure debt managers.2

3 November 2026
Global infrastructure investment is forecast to reach $US150 trillion between 2024 and 2050 - in real terms, double what was spent over the previous 20 years.1
This capex supercycle is driven by a series of powerful structural demand drivers as populations and economies outgrow the power grids, water systems and transport networks that were designed for a less populous and digital world. It also reflects a shift in national priorities: energy security, technological leadership and supply chain resilience now sit high on government agendas and are increasingly treated as strategic imperatives.
With fiscal capacity constrained and the capital requirement likely to outpace what banks and public balance sheets can supply, infrastructure debt can help close the gap. Already one of private credit's fastest-expanding segments, it can offer prescribed, cycle-resilient income and portfolio diversification. Unlike many traditional forms of private credit, infrastructure debt is frequently secured by essential assets whose cash flows are linked to the ongoing provision of critical services.
While the scale of the opportunity is indisputable, the challenge for investors is understanding how to access it.
Investor snapshot

0
%

expect to raise their infrastructure debt allocations this year, ahead of direct lending (39 per cent) and asset-based lending (35 per cent)

0
%

expect infrastructure debt to offer the best risk-adjusted returns over the next three years

Source: Benefit Street Partners3

Image source: CVE

Extending the private credit universe
Private credit is often associated with direct lending, typically loans to businesses backed by private equity sponsors. While infrastructure debt offers many of the same characteristics - direct relationships, bespoke structures, negotiated protections - it finances a different opportunity set: essential infrastructure assets that underpin economies and communities.
Evolving from a market dominated by banks before many retrenched following the 2008 global financial crisis, infrastructure debt now spans long-dated, investment-grade project finance through to higher-yielding, sub-investment-grade credit.4 It offers investors exposure to multiple global, structural thematics across digitalisation, decarbonisation, deglobalisation and demographics.
While the opportunity set is diverse, the assets financed by infrastructure debt all benefit from a consistent set of economic characteristics. These are sometimes summarised by acronym HALOID: hard assets, low obsolescence and inelastic demand.

HA
Hard Assets
Deliver essential societal economic services

LO
Low Obsolescence
High barriers to entry and long cycle relevance

ID
Inelastic Demand
Benefit from long-term demand drivers

Managing risk in the era of build-outs
While HALOID assets can offer highly resilient cash flows, they are not automatically low risk. As opportunities widen across the risk spectrum, seniority in the capital structure alone is no longer sufficient protection.
Successful execution depends on operational infrastructure experience and credit expertise working together. Lenders require a deep understanding of how an asset will develop, what could go wrong and what remedies and controls are available if it does. Knowledge of contractor and construction markets, power pricing, supply chains, operating costs, asset utilisation, and technological and regulatory change must sit alongside a proven track record in structuring, documentation, capital structure analysis and workout experience.
The benefits of this combined expertise go beyond efficient execution: they determine the quality of assets that can be accessed and enable investors to identify opportunities long before they reach a wider, more competitive market.

The Macquarie Asset Management toolkit
At Macquarie Asset Management (MAM), our approach is defined by three core capabilities: asset expertise, structuring discipline, and origination.
Asset expertise
We are a leading global asset manager, with more than 30 years of experience managing infrastructure assets.5 Our investments underpin economies, communities and households around the world, and are relied on by more than 310 million people every day.6 This operational expertise has been central to our ability to successfully complete more than 300 infrastructure debt transactions across 31 countries, making us one of the largest infrastructure debt managers globally.7
Four different assets, four different drivers, and yet each respond to the same underlying pressure: capacity that needs to be built faster than the public sector alone can finance it.

CVE

€350 million financing
Supported a French solar platform with more than 1 GW of capacity in operation and under construction with the continued build-out of its portfolio and simplification of its capital structure.8

Nexamp

$US350 million facility
Supported the construction of a 6 GW pipeline of US utility-scale solar and battery storage projects, backing supply as demand for electricity continues to outpace it.9

Eurofiber

€125 million senior loan
Part of a ~€2.2 billion refinancing, supporting the expansion of Eurofiber’s 77,500 km fibre network and data centres across the Netherlands, Belgium, Luxembourg, France and Germany, serving hyperscale and enterprise customers directly.10

UK housing

£1.45 billion+ debt facilities
Provided to UK local authorities and housing associations since 2015, including financing linked to energy efficiency improvements across more than 1,100 homes, as public bodies look to deleverage and modernise ageing stock.11

Image source: Cottsway Housing Association

Structuring discipline
Two data centres can carry very different credit risk despite benefiting from the same AI tailwinds, depending on power access, tenant commitments and location. MAM’s underwriting framework, refined across our long track-record and multiple credit cycles, is what allows us to differentiate between them. Our investments are structured around seniority, equity cushions, covenants and step-in rights, rather than assuming a strong investment thematic is protection enough.
Origination
As one of the world's largest infrastructure managers, MAM combines deep asset expertise with a global infrastructure platform spanning equity and debt investing. Our $US242 billion infrastructure equity platform works alongside our $US161 billion Credit & Insurance business, providing differentiated access to infrastructure financing opportunities globally.

Across our infrastructure debt track record, more than 95 per cent of transactions have been sourced bilaterally or through club deals, rather than through syndication.12 That combination enables us to surface bilateral and proprietary financing opportunities that would not otherwise reach the market, with us often acting as lead or sole lender. It also gives clients one point of access to both equity and debt capital, which can enhance sourcing, diligence and structuring capabilities, rather than working with each capability separately.

The next phase of private credit will finance build-outs as well as buyouts. Differentiated origination, deep asset expertise and structuring discipline are what set MAM apart in capturing that opportunity.”

Tom van Rijsewijk

It is also about identifying investments with resilient downside characteristics and contractual cash flows. It requires the operational judgement to know which assets will perform and the credit discipline to structure around what could go wrong.
With over 20 years and more than 300 transactions across 31 countries, MAM brings both.13 As the infrastructure capex supercycle accelerates, we're well placed to help investors build considered exposure to it.
