articles.title: The institutional form of independent central banks: from history to contemporary challenges - speech by Andrew Bailey
articles.text:
The institutional form of independent central banks: from history to contemporary challenges - speech by Andrew Bailey

Given at LSE TRIUM Anniversary Conference

Published on
04 September 2026

In his speech Governor Andrew Bailey argues that the foundation of independent central banks rests on more than technocratic expertise alone and elaborates on the long intellectual and historical tradition of their accountability. He contends that central banks exist to protect public goods, namely stable money and a resilient financial system, by insulating key decisions from short term political pressures while remaining accountable within a democratic framework.

Speech
I would like to reflect on independent central banks as institutions, and how their authority is grounded and is challenged.
On 3rd September 1780 (246 years ago yesterday) a 23 year old aide to George Washington wrote that: “the Bank of England unites public authority and faith with private credit and hence we see what a vast fabric of paper credit is raised on a visionary basis.” That 23 year old was Alexander Hamilton.footnote [1]
The meaning of central bank independence is not just a technical point about monetary policy or financial stability, or just a point about the design of public institutions. It is about the relationship between societies and the institutions they create to serve them. This brings to mind Douglass North's definition of institutions as the rules of the game in a society or, more formally, the humanly devised constraints that shape human interaction.footnote [2]
Institutions are not just organisations. They are durable arrangements through which societies solve collective problems. To do this, they must embody understandings about how authority should be exercised, how conflicts should be managed, and how common interests should be protected.
Independent central banks are among the most distinctive institutions modern societies have created. They exercise important powers. Their decisions influence borrowing costs, saving decisions, employment prospects, investment plans and the broad stability of the financial system. Their powers, and how they are used, are always the subject of debate, and that's fair enough given the importance.
Now, there are critics of these arrangements. Some critics argue that central banks disproportionately reflect the interests of financial markets and financial institutions. In a similar, but distinct, spirit others argue that central banks are too detached from the preferences of citizens. These criticisms often differ in their origins and motivation, but they converge on a common question. Why should an unelected institution possess such significant authority?
My purpose today is not just to defend central bank independence, though you can be assured I am happy to do that robustly. Rather, it is to reflect on the deeper intellectual traditions from which it has emerged and to consider what those traditions can tell us about the challenges we face.
When economists explain central bank independence, they often begin with questions about the credibility of policy regimes and their time consistency. These arguments are important. They explain why in many countries independence emerged because governments at crucial times had demonstrated incentives to pursue short-term monetary policies that ultimately undermined economic stability, and to undercook financial stability outside more immediate proximity to a financial crisis.
But they do not fully answer a more fundamental question: why should society trust an institution that operates with a degree of independence from day-to-day political control? To answer that question, it is useful to look further back.
One important tradition begins with the French philosopher Montesquieu.footnote [3] Writing in the eighteenth century, Montesquieu was preoccupied with the problem of concentrated power. His great concern was how societies could prevent authority (in that case royal authority) from becoming arbitrary. His answer was that power should be moderated through institutions that stood between rulers and citizens.
Parliaments, courts of law and other intermediary bodies performed this role. They constrained power, not simply through legal rules but because they possessed recognised standing within society. They had identities, traditions and sources of legitimacy independent of those they were intended to restrain. For Montesquieu, these roots mattered. Institutions could not simply be invented and expected to command authority. They required legitimacy that grew over time.
At first sight, modern central banks appear rather different. A central bank derives its authority primarily from legislation. Its independence is granted through statute. It does not rest upon inherited privilege, social rank, or customary authority. Modern central banks are deliberately designed to be technocratic institutions. And yet, the questions Montesquieu asked remain relevant. His central concern was how societies create institutions capable of constraining the exercise of power for the common good. In that sense, the challenge he identified remains with us.
A second intellectual tradition is also relevant. This tradition emerged from English political thought in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, and from debates about sovereignty, money and commerce. As David Hume put it, in the seventeenth century commerce, for the first time, became a “reason of state”.footnote [4]
Thomas Hobbes provided one starting point in this development.footnote [5] In the world of Hobbes, the authority to determine the value of money belonged to the sovereign. Just as the sovereign commanded armies and administered justice, so too the sovereign controlled the monetary system of the day, such as it was. Given this overriding concern with political order and stability, for Hobbes dividing authority over money risked dividing authority itself.
But this view was challenged. John Locke argued against the idea that governments should be able to alter the value of money according to political convenience.footnote [6] During the monetary controversies of the 1690s, Locke insisted that arbitrary changes in the value of money damaged trust, disrupted commerce and undermined the public faith upon which economic exchange depended.
This marked a significant intellectual shift. Money was no longer seen just as an instrument of sovereign authority. It became something that served a broader public purpose. Its stability mattered not merely because government or the Sovereign desired it, but because society required it.
David Hume developed this argument further.footnote [7] Hume observed that commerce had become central to the prosperity and strength of nations. Economic life was no longer peripheral to statecraft. It had become one of its defining concerns. Stable money and reliable credit systems became essential foundations for expanding commerce. They enabled people to transact, invest, save and plan with confidence.
In this tradition, monetary stability became a public good. It is from this intellectual lineage that modern central banking most directly emerged. The founding of the Bank of England in 1694 illustrated this evolution, reflecting two powerful forces.footnote [8]
The first was the rapid expansion of trade and commerce. As markets became more sophisticated and more interconnected, the need for a stable and reliable monetary and financial framework grew.
The second was the necessity of financing war. In 1694, England's conflict with France created urgent demands for finance. The arrangement that established the Bank of England enabled private capital to be mobilised in support of public objectives.
One of the interesting points in The Spirit of the Laws is that Montesquieu linked England's financial credibility to its constitutional arrangements (comparing it to France). In England, public credit was not merely a matter of financial technique; it depended on institutions capable of generating public trust. This interpretation is entirely consistent with the quote from Alexander Hamilton.
But the opposite view is also powerful, as set out by John Pocock and summarised by Istvan Hont:-
“The understanding of commerce and commercial society in late seventeenth century England was most advanced by just those thinkers who saw the political health of the English nation as jeopardised by the pervasive corruption that resulted from the intrusion of the demands of the war economy into the sphere of domestic politics.” There was a growing awareness of the distractions which the new of kind of war finance, the running of a huge public debt, might cause to the balance of the English constitution. A political and military regime financed by the public debt implied a danger of the rising in influence of a financier class, which could exercise power without enjoying a proper and legitimate place in the politics of the country.footnote [9]
One way to describe the importance of the growth of commercial societies is to show how they led to the emergence of some of the most profound issues of political economy, namely:

The rise of nation states as economic and commercial agents in their own right;
The need for a properly constituted system of sovereign power to settle internal and external disputes;
The demand for state finance;
The role of justice in economic distribution;
The growth of elaborate divisions among economic interests;
Greater complexity and opacity in the workings of economies; and
The development of tools for authorities to modify the workings of markets, and the risk of a variety of motives for doing so.footnote [10]

These issues remain at the heart of economic policymaking today. The early Bank of England was an important part of the development of commerce. It is however important to recognise that the original Bank of England looked very different from the institution we know today. It was not conceived as an independent guardian of monetary stability. It emerged from a partnership between government and a relatively small and concentrated group of financially sophisticated investors. And, unlike the modern institution, the early Bank was not removed from politics.footnote [11]
The origins of the Bank align as much with Mancur Olson's later analysis of organised interest groups as with any modern idea of an independent public institution.footnote [12] My point is not to criticise those origins. They reflected the realities of the time. But they do remind us that central banking did not emerge fully formed. It evolved gradually as understandings of money, credit, commerce and public authority evolved. Nonetheless, the big themes we wrestle with today were beginning to emerge at that time.
The modern central bank is therefore the product of a long historical process. On one hand lies the Montesquieu tradition, concerned with limiting arbitrary power through institutional checks. On the other lies the tradition of Locke and Hume, concerned with establishing money and credit as public goods upon which society depends.
Modern central banks bring these traditions together. Their essential purpose is to safeguard the stability of money including the resilience of the financial system. These are not interests that belong exclusively to any group. They are public goods from which society as a whole benefits.
The important distinction between the public interest and the public good, as set out by Brian Barry, is important in this respect.footnote [13] Individual citizens naturally have different preferences, priorities, and interests. Democracies exist in part to sort out those competing claims. But some goods are valuable to the public as a whole precisely because they are universally shared.
Monetary and financial stability is one such good. Whatever our views on taxation, spending, regulation or public services, we all operate within a common monetary and financial framework. The value of money is something upon which every household and every business rely. To be effective in the sense of trust and legitimacy in society, support for such a public good should come from the plurality of society rather than any single member group.
This does not mean that monetary policy and financial stability are devoid of distributional effects. Interest rates affect borrowers and savers differently. Financial stability policies can affect sectors and institutions in different ways. Public policy inevitably has consequences that are not distributed uniformly.
But recognising those consequences should not obscure the broader purpose that these policies serve. The objective is not to favour one group over another. It is to preserve the monetary and financial conditions that make sustained prosperity possible.
In that sense, central bank independence represents a modern adaptation of Montesquieu's thinking. The institution exists not to accumulate or counter arbitrary power but to protect the value of money from short-term pressures that could damage the public interest. But this arrangement also creates an enduring challenge.
Unlike the institutions that Montesquieu had in mind, central banks do not possess deep social roots of their own. Indeed, they must be careful not to become identified with any single interest group. A central bank that became closely aligned with particular sectors or political movements would undermine the very rationale for its independence, and therefore its legitimacy
As John Dunn has argued, this gets us to the issue of the constitutional theory of how power can be institutionalised and thus be implemented effectively in practice. This is the critical relationship between “the constitutional order of power and the pragmatic determination of economic policy”. It’s the modern version of the problem Montesquieu identified and sought to solve. As Dunn notes, constitutional order can appear very settled and continuous, whereas economic policy can appear anything but at times. Writing in the mid 1980s, Dunn argued that a constitutional order which rendered the benign conduct of economic policy more likely than not had not yet been constructed. Solving this challenge has been critical for the legitimacy of modern central banks.footnote [14]
So where does legitimacy come from? The answer, I believe, is now straightforward. Modern independent central banks are not independent of democratic government in the important sense that their authority originates in legislation or the like enacted by elected representatives. In the Bank of England’s case, Parliament defines the objectives, establishes the powers, and retains the authority to amend the framework within which we operate. This role is critical.
This brings me to the contemporary challenge. Across many countries we have witnessed growing scepticism towards public institutions generally. In the case of central banks, as I mentioned earlier, some critics argue they are too close to financial interests and that they stand in the way of popular preferences.
This challenge is not new, but some aspects of it are sharply set out at present, particularly in the area of financial regulation. The argument goes that central bank policies affect the distribution of returns, wealth and welfare directly, which pulls economic interests back into the picture. This concern applies more to financial stability policy than to monetary policy, though monetary policy is not immune from it. One version of the criticism is that the central bank remains too close to financial interests. A central bank's usual response is that the public good of stable money substantially outweighs any distributional effects. But this response can return the argument to Olson's thinking, since the financial world does contain well organised and concentrated interests.
The irony is that central banks can, and today do, face an opposite accusation from the financial interests themselves, who argue that regulation has gone too far. So, criticism arrives simultaneously from two directions that contradict each other.
The fact that criticism can come simultaneously from opposing directions does not prove that central banks are correct. On their own, two perceived wrongs don’t make a right. But it does underline that independence often requires making decisions that do not align with the private interests of any constituency or group, and that at times resisting pressure from the concentrated interests that Mancur Olson identified is part of the task of protecting a public good like the value of money.
A second challenge comes from populist political movements. As Jan-Werner Müller has argued, populism often rests on the claim that a particular political movement alone represents the authentic will of the people.footnote [15] Put thus, the public interest is something that a single ideology can capture and deliver directly. This effectively collapses Barry's distinction between the public interest and the public good.
Any institution seen to get in the way becomes an unrepresentative elite standing between the people and their will, and thus an obstacle to popular sovereignty. This is a serious challenge. We have developed systems of government (in the broadest sense of this term) in which legitimacy rests in the plurality of society, not in the preferences of any single group within it. Courts of law, universities, regulatory bodies and central banks all derive authority through forms of democratic delegation set within a framework of that plural society.footnote [16] Maintaining the trust that goes with that delegation matters deeply.
Central banks cannot take legitimacy for granted. They must explain their decisions clearly. They must engage openly with the public. They must remain accountable to elected representatives for their statutory objectives. In our case that means the Treasury Select Committee of the House of Commons. Through this engagement and accountability, we must demonstrate how our actions serve the public good, in its traditional meaning.
Let me conclude. Institutions that exercise significant authority should expect scrutiny. Such scrutiny is a sign of democratic health. But we should also recognise what is at stake.
Sustained economic prosperity depends upon confidence in the future. Households must be able to spend and save. Businesses must be able to produce and invest. Financial markets must be able to allocate capital efficiently. All of these activities rely upon confidence that the value of money will remain stable including that the financial system will remain resilient.
Those conditions cannot be created overnight. They depend upon institutions that are trusted, durable and credible. Central bank independence does not mean detachment from democracy. It means insulation from short-term political pressures within a democratic framework. Its legitimacy derives from a parliamentary delegation and accountability goes with that independence. It is the basis on which independence legitimately rests.
In our own time, as in previous generations, the challenge is therefore not to weaken that foundation but to strengthen it: through accountability, through transparency, through public engagement and through an unwavering commitment to the public good of sound money that independent central banks exist to serve.
Thank you.

articles.title: Sustainability as a driver of long-term investment outcomes - BNP Paribas Asset Management - Corporate English
articles.text:
How can investors navigate a world reshaped by environmental pressures, technological disruption and geopolitical uncertainty? For BNP Paribas Asset Management, sustainability is central to answering that question.

Jane Ambachtsheer, Chief Sustainability Officer, discusses BNPP AM’s updated Global Sustainability Strategy, which sets out its priorities through to 2030. Building on the recent merger with AXA Investment Managers, the strategy embeds sustainability expertise across asset classes, using ESG research, due diligence and stewardship to achieve better-informed investment decisions.

Jane explains how integrating sustainability considerations with financial analysis can help investors identify material risks and opportunities, while recognising that clients have different objectives and preferences. From net zero alignment and carbon footprint reduction to positive contributions towards the UN Sustainable Development Goals, the approach aims to deliver tailored solutions and better client outcomes. “Our underlying ambition is to connect sustainable investment practices with long-term returns to help clients navigate a rapidly changing world.”

Listen to the full Talking Heads podcast for insights into solutions across many asset classes can help investors achieve their sustainability ambitions.

You can also listen and subscribe to Talking Heads on YouTube, Spotify, or wherever you normally get your podcasts.

XXX

Read the transcript

Andrew Craig: Hello and welcome to this week’s BNP Paribas Asset Management Talking Heads podcast. Every week, Talking Heads will bring you in-depth insights and analysis through the lens of sustainability on the topics that really matter to investors. In this episode, we’ll be discussing our new revised edition of the Global Sustainability Strategy. This provides the framework for action on the environmental, social and governance considerations that are embedded in our investment processes and are grounded in the conviction that traditional financial analysis alone is insufficient to capture all the risks and opportunities in today’s global economy.

I’m Andy Craig, Co-Head of the Investment Insights Centre, and I’m joined today by Jane Ambachtsheer, Chief Sustainability Officer at BNP Paribas Asset Management. Welcome, Jane. Thank you for joining me today.

Jane Ambachtsheer: Thanks, Andy. It’s a pleasure to be here.

AC: Can you explain why we need [a] Global Sustainability Strategy?

JA: Well, sustainability, is a core part of how we invest and how we operate as an entity, so it’s important to have a strategy which really articulates how we go about doing that and what our objectives are.

Our previous sustainability strategy took us to 2026, so it was time for us to launch our new one, which we’ve recently done, which takes us out to 2030. The other important component of our new strategy is that it reflects our new entity having evolved and completed the integration of AXA Investment Managers, which now results in BNP Paribas Asset Management being one of the world’s 10 largest investors, with over €1.7 trillion in AUM (assets under management) across liquid and alternative asset classes and a local presence in 35 countries.

So given our new size and scale, it was also certainly time for an evolved approach to our global sustainability strategy.

AC: How does the sustainability strategy fit with the new corporate strategy for the combined entity? What are the key components and how has it evolved?

JA: When we launched at the beginning of 2026 ‘AMplify 2030’, the overall strategy for the new entity, we identified sustainability as one of the core enablers of how we’ll achieve that strategy. That then opened the door for us to publish this new specialised strategy really focused on sustainability.

As a long-term investor, we believe our client outcomes and real economy outcomes are closely connected. Resilient companies, well-functioning markets and sustainable economic growth are really fundamental to the long-term returns our clients seek.

Our strategy sets out our forward-looking priorities and milestones through [to] 2030 and is organised around the pillars of how we achieve that. So, a focus on the future and identifying system level risks around how we do ESG research and due diligence stewardship. Our approach around articulating responsible business conduct expectations which can lead to different exclusions. Our approach to sustainable products and solutions and also around leading by example – our approach to our own culture, sustainability education and the corporate responsibility practices that we’re adopting for our own entity.

AC: How does this new strategy enable us to deliver the best outcomes for our clients?

JA: That’s at the core of everything we do. Our strategy is built for clients, informed by our clients’ expectations and what we believe best practice to be in the global market.

The first [thing] is around making sure we’re helping our clients navigate a changing world. We know that the world is being reshaped by a number of powerful forces:

Environmental pressures: reshaping industries, supply chains, capital allocation, presenting both risks and opportunities

Technology and innovation: creating new technologies, disrupting business models, creating different opportunities

Demographic shifts: transforming labour markets, changes to inequality around the world, consumption patterns and ageing

Geopolitical developments: influencing trade, energy security, energy systems, our approach to climate in nature and access to resources around the world in this changing geopolitical framework.

These megatrends are inter-connected and we try and take a forward-looking lens to help our clients navigate them through understanding the risks and the opportunities that they present. So that’s the broader macro perspective.

We also believe that by integrating ESG considerations alongside financial analysis from a bottom-up asset class perspective, we can have better insights and make better decisions on behalf of our clients.

So sustainability is not a separate investment decision. It’s an important component of informed decision-making from an asset class basis. One of the new evolutions in terms of our overall framework is that we now embed sustainability expertise across the different asset classes.

We have a central team which I lead, which is really responsible for driving the overall strategy and ambition, with our global leadership team overseeing stewardship, supporting our clients, supporting our overall external commitments and reporting stewardship and CSR (corporate social responsibility).

Then we have a number of sustainability experts embedded across the organisation within the different asset classes, reporting up to the different CIOs to make sure we have best quality ESG data, tools, research capabilities embedded into our investment decisions.

That takes me to this final point – the fact that the strategy is built for clients. We have clients from all around the world. They have different objectives, regulatory environments and sustainability preferences. To be able to cater to those different clients, we offer a range of investment approaches and have the opportunity to build structured, custom[ised] sustainability portfolios for our clients.

We have clients optimising around their own preferences or the preferences of their beneficiaries, whether that’s measuring a positive contribution to some of the specific sustainable development goals, achieving certain net zero alignment outcomes, measuring and achieving a certain carbon footprint reduction target.

Different clients have different preferences. A big part of our strategy and our new size and scale is that we have the ability to bring the firm in terms of helping our clients to achieve the best outcomes for them, tapping into the resources across BNP Paribas Asset Management, but also often working in partnership with our colleagues and the broader resources across BNP Paribas Group.

AC: Of course, there are implications for us, BNP Paribas Asset Management as a firm and our own practices. Can you talk us through those?

JA: At the end of the day, we’re a people business. Our people, the intellectual capital that they bring, their relationships with clients, are the greatest opportunity for embedding sustainability into who we are, how we deliver investment outcomes and how we’re operating as an entity.

So we have a strong focus on integrating sustainability into our culture and our own corporate practices. This is one of the unique differentiators for the way we’re approaching sustainability as an organisation.

In terms of our own corporate reporting, we seek to meet and exceed the standards and expectations we’re setting for the companies we’re investing in. That’s really important to our credibility as an asset manager – to live up to those expectations where we’re asking others to do the same.

We have a strong focus on sustainability education and we’ve developed different training pathways for different portions of our population, depending on their existing levels of expertise and focus areas – whether it’s investment teams or legal teams or client-facing teams – to make sure they have the right opportunities around internal training, but also the opportunity to pursue external certifications or training programmes.

We also have a strong focus on being active in the communities where we’re operating –volunteering, philanthropy and developing partnerships with organisations in different communities. Also our annual Community Impact Week, where we have a volunteering fair that we set up around our offices around the world, which is really a chance to engage in some of those organisations, but also to further enhance our internal community, give employees an opportunity to spend time together and spend time giving back.

So there’s a rich ecosystem of things we’re doing internally around creating awareness, providing educational opportunities and volunteering engagement opportunities for colleagues across the different offices around the world in BNP Paribas Asset Management.

AC: Can you talk [to] us about the key upcoming milestones and how you’ll be measuring success as we go forward?

JA: The first and most important measure of success is that we’re able to deliver the outcomes that our clients are engaging us to deliver. That’s front and centre for what we’re doing around our overall sustainability strategy.

But we will also continue to provide our annual sustainability report, which includes progress across all of the different six pillars of our sustainability strategy, including stewardship, which is an area of significant interest for many of our clients. We’re happy to be able to continue to evolve the level of detail around our different approaches for stewardship, be it statistics across the whole platform, a rich range of different examples of company engagement, as well as public policy advocacy.

Later this year, we’ll also be updating our new Net Zero commitment as a combined entity. That’s something we’ve committed to publish and we’ll be sharing in the coming months. We’ll also be introducing our new progress monitor in our next annual report, where we share a number of key indicators that [we] will be measuring and reporting on every year.

We view communication on sustainability as an ongoing opportunity, both at a portfolio and at a firm level, and it’s something that we’ll continue to share updates on with clients as we go.

AC: Jane, thank you. We’ll be looking forward to joining you to talk about those updates as the months go by. Thank you very much for joining me today.

JA: Thanks so much for having me. It was a pleasure to be here.

AC: That’s it for this week’s episode of Talking Heads. If you’d like to learn more about our Global Sustainability Strategy, please reach out to your BNP Paribas Asset Management contact or check out Viewpoint, our website for investment insights, at viewpoint.bnpparibas-am.com. Viewpoint brings you commentary and analysis in a variety of formats, from investment outlooks to asset allocation videos and podcasts to help investors make better informed decisions.

You’ve been listening to the BNP Paribas Asset Management Talking Heads podcast with me, Andy Craig and Jane Ambachtsheer, Chief Sustainability Officer at BNP Paribas Asset Management.

Please do join us again next time. Until then, take care.

articles.title: Monthly Market Views: The tech divide, rising bond yields and China’s industrial renaissance - BNP Paribas Asset Management - United States
articles.text:
Key points

Technology market volatility

Bond yields’ structural drivers

China as an AI disruptor

Equity markets: The tech and non-tech divide

Equity markets have diverged into two different worlds: tech and non-tech, with correspondingly different interactions with global bond yields. Over the summer, the oil price was the key driver of bond yields. Rising oil prices and bond yields led – as expected – to declines in non-tech equities. Tech equities, however, were largely impervious as the positive earnings outlook mattered more.

The recent sell-off in tech stocks, however, has led investors to seek safety in government bonds, driving yields lower even as oil prices rise. Defensive (non-tech) equities have also benefited from the lower yields and inflows from investors looking for perceived safe havens.

What happens next will depend on whether tech market volatility subsides. Investors have been disappointed by the earnings of some tech stocks. Given the high expectations implicit in the strong gains for tech indices year to date, there may be little room for further disappointment.

Government bonds: Many moving parts

Government bond yields have increased significantly this year, worsening financial conditions and sparking worries about debt sustainability. While no second-round effects are yet visible, the unanticipated inflation acceleration is certainly a key variable behind bond yields.

Another important variable is major central banks’ monetary policy U-turns. For example, market-based expectations initially indicated the Fed would cut interest rates in 2026. Instead, the Fed hiked rates and current market expectations suggest another two hikes over the next 12 months.

However, this is just one side of the story. There are structural factors as well; in particular, the oversupply of long-term bonds resulting not only from governments’ need to fund their spending, but also from changing demand. The government bond market has transitioned from being driven by price-insensitive investors with seemingly infinitely elastic balance sheets, to highly price-sensitive investors with constrained balance sheets. Therefore, the expected interest rate peak, government bond risk premiums and the shape of the yield curve have become once more an integral part of fixed income allocation decisions.

An industrial renaissance in progress

The artificial intelligence buildout is generating a capital investment cycle of an historic scale, reshaping industrial supply chains, power infrastructure, manufacturing geography, and sovereign economic strategies across both developed and emerging markets. Surging financing and extensive order backlogs confirm the structural nature of this wave, anchored primarily by the US and China.

However, this industrial renaissance is highly uneven and bottlenecks are shifting. US-led AI capital expenditure is driving the growth disparities; non-AI driven-economies are facing slower expansion. Moreover, China’s investment and production-biased policies are adding pressure to traditional manufacturing sectors.

Simultaneously, as a byproduct of its own tech competition drive, China could emerge as a disruptor within the AI trade. Operationally, power availability and grid interconnection timelines are increasingly outweighing core tech infrastructure, land, and labour as the primary deployment constraints.

Consequently, development is shifting toward behind-the-meter and off-grid facilities –connected directly to solar, batteries, or power plants – to accelerate energisation and reduce grid dependence. These trends will likely lead to divergent investment outcomes in 2027 and beyond.

Implementation ideas

Flexibility within euro credit

The euro credit market remains resilient, supported by strong fundamentals, despite geopolitical tensions and elevated energy prices. While investment grade spreads remain relatively tight, high yield spreads have widened in recent weeks. This has restored some value in the higher-yielding segments of the market, but it also calls for greater selectivity.

With the third-quarter reporting season now under way, company results will be key to confirm the strength of corporate balance sheets. Overall, conditions remain supportive with elevated all-in yields and an attractive income. Tactical duration positioning could potentially be beneficial, particularly given the market has already priced in expectations of future European Central Bank interest rate hikes. An agile, flexible approach could help investors capitalise on opportunities across the euro credit spectrum, including high yield and subordinated debt, while mitigating idiosyncratic risks.

Inflation and rates fluctuation protection

Geopolitical tensions are sustaining high levels of inflation uncertainty, particularly due to volatile energy prices, while financial conditions remain restrictive. The distinctly hawkish turn by various central banks means short-dated inflation-linked bonds look attractive, given their near-term growth potential and inflationary risks. Given that multiple interest rate hikes are already embedded in market pricing, both inflation indexation – bonds where the principal is linked to inflation – and the potential returns investors can earn from holding the bond offer potential attractive opportunities through year-end. Short-duration strategies can potentially help protect against the risk of higher inflation as they are less sensitive to interest rates compared with all-maturities strategies.

Environmental solutions enabling AI development

The artificial intelligence revolution is not just about investing in semiconductors and technology. Behind the rapid growth of AI is a significant build-out of critical enabling infrastructure, particularly power and water. Rising data centre demand requires more electricity generation, stronger and smarter grids, transformers, battery storage, energy efficient cooling, and reliable water infrastructure. Meeting this growing demand while supporting the transition towards a lower-carbon power system will require significant investment in environmental solutions. We believe this creates a broad, multi-year potential investment opportunity in the providers that enable the continued expansion of AI.

articles.title: Daily: Chip rout tests AI investment case
articles.text:
Talk to a UBS Financial AdvisorFrom the studioVideo:The AI sell-off and US midterms: Live at the UBS Disruptive Tech Summit (6 mins)Video: Allocating Assets | Adding FX carry, hedging oil risks, managing volatility(6 mins)Video: CIO Monthly | Mark Haefele on AI earnings, energy prices, interest rates (4 mins)Thought of the dayWhat happened?
US technology stocks led broader markets lower on Thursday, as the post-election relief rally reversed and investors reassessed the implications of the Democratic gains, especially at the state level, for AI infrastructure and data centers. The Nasdaq 100 and S&P 500 fell by around 6.4% and 4.4%, respectively.Semiconductor and AI infrastructure companies were at the center of the decline, including Qualcomm, which fell sharply after its profit outlook disappointed investors. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell 12.3%, extending its drawdown since June to around 38.3%.Pressure extended into Friday, with North Asia's tech-heavy indices leading declines. Japan's Nikkei 225 and South Korea's Kospi closed 6% lower, and Taiwan's benchmark index shed 4.5%. Major European stock indices all stand roughly 1% lower at the time of writing.The sharp risk-off move followed an initial post-election rally, when the removal of political uncertainty and the prospect of policy gridlock were seen as supportive for stocks. Investors now appear to be focusing more closely on how greater congressional oversight and changes in state governments might affect electricity consumption, water use, permitting, and development costs for data centers.Oil and geopolitical developments remained a secondary source of volatility, with Brent crude rebounding to around USD 100 per barrel before coming down to around USD 98 at the time of writing. US Treasuries and perceived safe havens have gained since the market close on Tuesday. The yield on 10-year US Treasuries has fallen by 12 basis points to near 4.84%, while gold is holding near USD 4,070/oz.What do we think?
In our view, the decline reflects uncertainty about the cost and pace of the data center buildout rather than a sudden deterioration in the outlook. It also appears to represent a de-risking event rather than a material change in fundamentals.Further technology volatility would not be surprising. The sector has delivered strong gains in recent years, leaving valuations, expectations, and investor positioning elevated in parts of the market. Investors are hence moving from rewarding spending commitments to demanding clearer evidence of monetization, capacity utilization, potential returns, and the ability to raise capital. The sensitivity of AI-linked stocks to company guidance, regulatory developments, and changes in risk appetite has increased.Greater congressional oversight may indeed increase scrutiny of data center construction and AI regulation. However, except in the event of a widespread AI security issue, we believe broad federal restrictions would likely face legislative and presidential constraints.And while political opposition at a state and local level may delay, relocate, or raise the cost of data center projects, it is unlikely to change underlying demand. Proposed US capacity of around 400 gigawatts already far exceeds our buildout assumption of roughly 90 gigawatts by 2030. We therefore see regulation as potentially redistributing and extending the investment cycle rather than derailing it, with power access, permitting, financing, and execution increasingly separating leaders from laggards.Underlying AI-related demand also remains strong. Recent earnings have shown accelerating cloud revenue and growing advance orders for computing capacity. Recent reports point to significant chip backlogs among Chinese buyers. We forecast aggregate AI capital spending of USD 1.0tr in 2026, USD 1.4tr in 2027, and USD 1.5tr in 2028.For the sell-off to signal a lasting downturn in the AI investment cycle, we think we would need to see evidence that AI-related revenue growth is slowing, cloud utilization is weakening, or lower AI costs are failing to generate sufficient new usage to absorb expanding capacity. We would also reassess the outlook if advances in algorithmic efficiency sharply reduced compute requirements, larger investments failed to produce commensurate gains in AI capabilities, or tighter financial conditions constrained spending by the largest technology platforms and frontier labs.How do we invest?
We see potential for gains in broad equity indices over the next six to 12 months and believe the sell-off looks overdone, given our base case for only modest changes to the outlook for the pace, timing, and cost of data center deployment. We believe the AI investment cycle remains intact, corporate earnings growth is resilient, and a positive global cyclical backdrop should support equities.Nevertheless, we acknowledge that investors may need more certainty about the data center policy environment before volatility fully abates, and we could see a period of market indigestion following the election results. This reinforces the importance of diversification and disciplined portfolio construction.Investors should decide in advance how they would respond to further market swings rather than making allocation decisions during periods of stress. This could include identifying target weights for equities, technology, fixed income, and alternative assets, then addressing allocation gaps progressively as markets move. Structured strategies may enable investors to respond in a disciplined way.Manage concentration risks. Although broad indices were down sharply on Thursday, volatility was even more elevated at the individual stock level. To prepare for potentially greater differentiation within the technology sector in the weeks and months ahead, investors should review portfolios and progressively reduce excessive single-stock concentration relative to technology and broad market benchmarks.Within AI, we prefer diversification over concentrated exposure to individual companies experiencing bottlenecks. We favor financially strong platform and application companies that can monetize growing AI adoption, together with infrastructure businesses that have durable pricing power, strong competitive positions, and access to capital. We are more selective toward highly valued companies whose investment case depends heavily on a single component, capacity constraint, customer, or stage of the data center buildout. Diversified exposure across foundry, compute, networking, power, and other enabling technologies can provide participation in structural growth while reducing dependence on any one bottleneck.Rebalance across sectors and regions. We reduced our sector preferences for US IT and US communication services to Neutral in February. Investors whose US tech exposure has risen materially in recent years and now stands in excess of benchmark weights should consider using opportunities to rebalance toward other sectors. Within equities, our preferred sectors include industrials, health care, and financials. Regionally, we have a relative preference for the Eurozone, emerging markets, and Asia ex-Japan.Build a strong core portfolio. To prepare for possible further equity market volatility ahead, investors with significant bond underweights should prepare for opportunities to rebuild allocations: We see attractive diversification and income potential in fixed income, particularly in high-quality bonds with short- to medium-term maturities and in emerging market bonds. Allocations to alternatives and commodities can also provide investors with exposure to a broader, differentiated range of return drivers beyond traditional asset classes.

6 November 2026
Weekly Market View

Download Report

Increasing signsof a bottom
Democrats’ thumping win in the US mid-term elections has three key implications: i) policy gridlock is back in Washington, likely stalling fiscal expansion and new tariffs; ii) the chance of a prolonged Middle East conflict is curtailed, lowering oil prices and inflation expectations; and iii) the pace of AI data-centre buildout is at risk, curbing AI-linked bond supply.
For portfolios, the election reinforces our mid-cycle playbook: remaining broadly balanced across assets, while looking for tactical opportunities.
As the S&P500 volatility index (VIX) surpasses 25, we see rising signs of equity market bottoming. We add an opportunistic idea on the US IT sector, while using volatility to earn income through structured strategies.
In bonds, we prefer the 3-7-year part of the Developed Market bond yield curve and BBB-to-BB-rated corporate bonds to earn attractive income as AI supply eases. In FX, we position for a modestly weaker USD over 6-12 months via our allocation to ex-US assets.

What are the equity market implications of the US mid-term elections?

Does emerging US jobs data alter your view on Fed rates and US bond yields?

What is your outlook for GBP after this week’s BoE meeting?

Democrats’ emphatic win in the US elections should curtail President Trump’s powers to prolong the Iran conflict

Editorial

Increasing signs of a bottom

Strategy summary: Democrats’ thumping win in the US mid-term elections has three key implications: i) policy gridlock is back in Washington, likely stalling fiscal expansion and new tariffs; ii) the chance of a prolonged Middle East conflict is curtailed, lowering oil prices and inflation expectations; and iii) the pace of AI data-centre buildout is at risk, curbing AI-linked bond supply. Higher corporate and wealth taxes are a long-term risk if Democrats win the 2028 presidential elections.
For portfolios, the election reinforces our mid-cycle playbook already in place: remaining broadly balanced across assets, while looking for tactical opportunities. As the S&P500 volatility index (VIX) surpasses 25, we see rising signs of equity market bottoming. We add an opportunistic idea on the US IT sector (see page 4), while using elevated volatility to earn income through structured strategies. In bonds, we prefer the 3-7-year part of the Developed Market bond yield curve and BBB-to-BB-rated corporate bonds to earn attractive income as AI supply eases. In FX, we position for a modestly weaker USD over 6-12 months by allocating to ex-US assets.
Policy implications: Oil fell 12% over the past week as Democrats captured the US Senate and House. The party also flipped governorships in five states – Georgia, Iowa, Nevada, Ohio and Texas – securing a majority of governorships among 50 US states for the first time since 2010. Vice President Vance and Republican leaders attributed the defeat to the Iran conflict, making it harder for President Trump to sustain it. Democrat control of the defence budget from next year further constrains conflict escalation. Despite near-term escalation risks, we see the geopolitical risk premium in oil prices fading, with oil easing towards USD 80/bbl over 6-12 months. Oil-driven disinflation should allow central banks to adopt less aggressive policies.
Adding tactical exposure to US IT sector: Semiconductors slumped this week amid concerns over data-centre moratoria, while beneficiaries of Democrat policies include defensives, affordability-related stocks, tariff rollback beneficiaries and the healthcare sector. We use the volatility to add tactical exposure to the US IT sector. As we enter mid-cycle dynamics, equities
.

should return 8-10% annually. The 2015–2017 mid-cycle offers a useful comparison: with an opposition Congress, S&P 500 returns slowed to 8.3%, but remained positive. Diversification across sectors and regions remains a priority amid the rotation.
Prefer belly of the bond curve: Government bonds rallied on expectations of slower growth. We still expect two more Fed hikes by H1 2027, given sticky near-term inflation and a robust economy. However, cheaper oil should lower inflation towards the Fed’s 2% target next year, allowing rate cuts in H2 2027. Ultra-long yields remain elevated due to fiscal challenges. Bonds, particularly those from non-hyperscaler investment-grade corporates, offer attractive income. The 3-7-year segment – the belly of the yield curve – offers the best balance of income and sensitivity to interest-rate changes.
Credit to benefit from restrained AI supply: Since states control data centre regulations, Democrat wins in governorship races in leading data centre states, such as Texas and Georgia, means growth in this segment is likely to be restricted. Slower data-centre construction could improve credit supply-demand conditions due to reduced issuance by hyperscalers. However, some data-centre-focused deals could become less viable, warranting caution towards lower-quality issuers. High-yield credit spreads have widened, but BB- and B-rated bonds have held up, while CCC-rated debt has reached distressed levels. We prefer the BBB–BB range, spanning the boundary between investment-grade and high-yield debt, for income.
A modest headwind for the USD, tailwind for gold: The dollar should remain range-bound near term before weakening modestly over 6-12 months. Democrat control of the Congress limits tariff escalation, fiscal expansion and rapid AI buildout, three pillars of US exceptionalism supporting the USD through 2026. Disinflation should also encourage a less aggressive Fed stance, removing another source of USD support. Near-term support for the USD index (DXY) remains at 100.7. A weaker-than-expected payrolls report tonight could accelerate the USD’s decline, and vice versa. A softer dollar and sustained central-bank buying, led by China, remain supportive of gold.
— Rajat Bhattacharya

The weekly macro balance sheet

Our weekly net assessment: On balance, we see the past week’s data and policy as negative for risk assets in the near-term
(+) factors: Robust US manufacturing and job openings; Potential easing of geopolitical tensions after Democratic wave in US elections(-)factors: Weak China PMIs; BOE, RBA hike; a recalibration of AI trade

Top client questions

What are the equity market implications of the US mid-term election results?

Our view: The US mid-term election outcome adds political headwinds but does not alter our outlook for positive equity returns. Investors should maintain a Core allocation to global equities and continue to diversify their equity exposure across regions and sectors. We initiate an opportunistic idea on the US information technology (IT) sector, moving our opportunistic idea positioning from a defensive tilt to a more balanced positioning. Higher volatility also presents opportunities to use structured strategies for equity exposure.
Rationale: The Democrats’ victory in both chambers of Congress has supported the outperformance of themes aligned with their policy priorities, with clean energy stocks, including solar companies, among the notable beneficiaries. Affordability-related themes have also benefited, including companies that could gain from potential tariff rollbacks. Medicaid-related stocks have also risen on hopes that healthcare will gain from policy changes.
Meanwhile, semiconductor stocks remain under pressure amid concerns about potential moratoriums on data centres. Our AI capital expenditure (capex) estimates remain conservative relative to consensus, but with a potential reset in expectations around data centre spending, investors should remain selective.
We initiate an opportunistic idea on the US IT sector after a significant 17% correction this quarter. Historically, this has been followed by strong positive returns over the next few quarters (see table). Semiconductors, about 40% of US IT, appears oversold after correcting more than 30% since we closed our opportunistic idea a month ago. Earnings growth for US IT continues to be solid, with volume driven growth in semiconductors, AI monetisation opportunities, ongoing cloud growth and resilient services revenue.
As we highlighted in our November 2026 Global Market Outlook, the transition to mid-cycle is typically characterised by greater political headwinds. The mid-term election outcome reinforces this trend. The mid-cycle experience of 2015-17 offers a useful historical parallel for returns that moderate, but remain positive. Although we trimmed global equities to a Core allocation last week, we continue to expect equities to deliver mid-to-high single-digit returns per annum during the mid-cycle, even amid political headwinds, supported by steady earnings growth in both 2027 and 2028.
Stay invested and diversify, with Overweight allocations to the US and AxJ, which offer the strongest earnings growth. Sector diversification is key as we expect market leadership to broaden. We are Overweight the US IT, US healthcare, US financial, US materials, Europe ex-UK financial and Japan financial sectors.
— Fook Hien Yap, Senior Investment Strategist

Policy uncertainty and a change in the innovation cycle is consistent with our view of a mid-cycle transition, where equity returns moderate but remain positive
Comparison of recent equity bull markets

US IT sector has historically seen positive returns the next few quarters after a sharp quarterly decline
US information technology sector performance

Source: FactSet, Bloomberg, Standard Chartered

Top client questions (cont’d)

What are the key takeaways from Q3 2026 US earnings?

Our view: Q3 US earnings remain robust, but more modest earnings beats reinforce our view that equity markets are entering a mid-cycle phase. We remain Overweight US equities, but recommend investors to maintain diversified sector exposure as returns moderate and market leadership broadens.
Rationale: As of 30 October, 82% of S&P500 companies that had reported had beaten earnings estimates. However, aggregate earnings were just 4.5% above expectations, a smaller beat than in recent quarters. Still, Q3 US earnings growth remains robust at 31.6% y/y, supporting expected full-year growth of 36.1% in 2026 and 16.4% in 2027 for the S&P500. The slower pace of upgrades suggests the bull market is maturing as investors focus on the sustainability of earnings growth. This raises the hurdle for positive share price reactions and makes selectivity more essential. For Big Tech, capex commitments remain high, while free cash flow is under pressure and expected to remain negative. Financing risks weigh on sentiment, particularly for companies with weaker balance sheets. We remain Overweight US equities, given the strong earnings growth, but we expect elevated volatility and modest returns. We prefer quality exposure within technology while maintaining diversified exposure across US financials, healthcare and materials.
— Ryan Goh, Investment Strategist

S&P500 Q3 2026 earnings surprises have been smaller than in previous quarters
S&P500 aggregate quarterly earnings surprise relative to consensus estimates (%)

Source: LSEG I/B/E/S, Standard Chartered

What to expect from Japanese banks’ upcoming results?

Our view: We expect Japanese banks’ earnings growth to continue over the medium term, supported by higher domestic net interest income (NII) and resilient fee income. We remain positive on the sector, favouring banks with strong deposit franchises and scope to increase shareholder returns. Investors will focus on whether full-year guidance upgrades and buybacks exceed expectations.
Rationale: The BoJ’s September rate hike to 1.25% took effect late in the quarter, so its benefit should be more visible from the December quarter as loans reprice. We expect three further BoJ rate hikes by June 2027, supporting further NII expansion. We will also look for signs that stronger corporate investment is driving faster loan growth and higher financing and advisory fees.
We prefer to place more weight on guidance upgrades driven by recurring lending and fee income than on those driven by gains on equity disposals. Continued reductions in cross-shareholdings could free up capital for additional buybacks, providing a further boost to return on equity (ROE). Key risks: faster-than-expected deposit rate repricing, rising credit costs and bond portfolio losses.
— Robin Xie, CFA, Senior Investment Strategist

Japanese banks’ earnings expectations have risen
TOPIX Banks Index consensus EPS estimates for 2026-28 (JPY)

Source: Bloomberg, Standard Chartered

Top client questions (cont’d)

What are the fundamental reasons behind your India equity upgrade? Which sectors offer favourable risk-reward?

Our View: Indian equities offer an increasingly attractive risk-reward profile. With India’s valuation premium to Emerging Markets (EMs) narrowing, foreign ownership near decade lows, Underweight EM positioning and a stabilising Indian rupee (INR), conditions are increasingly supportive of Indian equity outperformance vs. the broader AxJ region.
Rationale: We have upgraded Indian equities to Overweight within our AxJ equities allocation. While Indian markets have witnessed USD 32bn of foreign investor outflows in 2026 year-to-date, strong domestic institutional investor inflows of USD 74bn have more than offset foreign selling. These outflows and the Indian equity market’s underperformance vs. global peers reflect broader EM allocation shifts towards AI, rather than weakening Indian fundamentals. Capital has gravitated towards markets such as the US, Taiwan and South Korea, which offer direct exposure to AI beneficiaries. However, we expect market leadership to broaden, as the rapid AI buildout is increasingly debt-funded, and US mid-term election results raise uncertainty. We prefer to diversify and we see investors reallocating towards structurally strong growth markets such as India, which offer non-AI driven growth.
The RBI’s measures have supported INR stability, but underlying USD demand remains elevated. Lower oil prices would improve external balances, but the INR is likely to follow a path of gradual, controlled depreciation rather than a quick downward move. On valuation to its own historical average, the Nifty 50 one-year forward P/E is trading 18% below its long-term average while ROE at 14.7% is above historical averages. With India now marginally Underweight in large EM portfolios compared to the c.2% average Overweight historically, the case for a recovery in foreign flows is strengthening.
India’s earnings growth remains intact. The Nifty 50 clocked Q1 FY27 and Q2 FY27 profit-after-tax growth of c.20% y/y (ex-oil marketing companies). Large-caps offer greater earnings visibility and downside protection, while stronger growth in small- and mid-caps warrants a selective approach given elevated valuations.
India’s growth outlook remains supported by a strengthening investment cycle, manufacturing momentum, supply chain diversification, resilient consumption and healthy corporate and banking balance sheets. Importantly, earnings growth remains robust and broad-based across the financial, metals, telecom, automobiles and other domestic sectors, with Nifty 50 earnings growth expectations of c.14-15% over 2027 vis a vis AxJ’s technology driven earnings growth of 29% in 2027.
— Shaily Gang, Chief Investment Strategist, India

Top client questions (cont’d)

Does the emerging US job market data alter your view of the Fed’s rate path and government bond yields?

Our view: We do not expect the recent and incoming US job market data to alter our outlook unless there are significant deviations from the US economy’s current trajectory.
Rationale: The US economy continues to exhibit resilience, with the latest Job Openings and Labour Turnover Survey data showing job openings surprising to the upside at 7.5mn. Initial jobless claims remain near three-month lows. There is little evidence of a material slowdown in labour demand. Inflation is expected to trend lower through H2 2027, but the disinflationary impulse remains a medium-term story and is unlikely to manifest meaningfully in the near term.
The market is now pricing in two additional 25bps hikes by H1 2027 (down from three previously), in line with our view. These two rate hikes are largely priced into the US government bond yield curve. We estimate 2- and 10-year US government bond yields to range between 4.5-4.75% and 5-5.25%, respectively, over the next three months. Our twelve-month forecast for 2- and 10-year US government bond yields are 4.25-4.5% and 4.75-5%, respectively, The2-year yield is already trading within our expected range and would only move materially higher if a significantly stronger-than-expected payrolls print led markets to price in a third hike. With two hikes baked in, long-run disinflation expectations intact and an uncertain fiscal outlook, the longer end of the yield curve is expected to be less sensitive to a single payrolls release.
— Ray Heung, Senior Investment Strategist

We expect 2- and 10-year US government bond yields to range between 4.5-4.75% and 5-5.25%, respectively, over the next three months
US 2- and 10-year government bond yields and expected range

Source: Bloomberg, Standard Chartered

What is your outlook for the GBP following the BoE’s rate hike this week? Do you see any impact on EUR/GBP?

Our view: The BoE rate hike supports the GBP, but upside remains limited. We remain constructive on EUR/GBP, expecting a rebound towards 0.8450.
Rationale: The BoE hiked by 25bps to 4% as expected. The GBP was little changed, despite hawkish inflation guidance. With markets pricing only around 50bps of additional BoE tightening over the next 12 months, we see the GBP remaining vulnerable. In contrast, the ECB held its deposit rate at 2.50% in October but signalled readiness to tighten if inflation remains elevated. We expect Euro area inflation to rise further, keeping the ECB’s tightening bias alive. This suggests EUR/GBP has fallen too far relative to interest rate differentials.
Germany’s planned increase in federal debt issuance should support Euro area growth, while Moody’s decision not to downgrade France has removed an important EUR tail risk. Meanwhile, tighter UK fiscal policy is likely to weigh on domestic growth and business investment. We expect EUR/GBP to recover towards 0.8450.
— Vincent Tan, Senior Investment Strategist— Iris Yuen, Investment Strategist

Top client questions (cont’d)

Why is the AUD underperforming despite the RBA hike?

Our view: The AUD has lagged because markets had largely priced in the RBA’s November rate hike to 4.85%, and the bank gave investors less reason to expect another. Equity weakness also weighed on the currency. We remain bullish on AUD/USD and would add on pullbacks. Australia’s interest rate advantage and a sustained recovery in risk sentiment should support a move towards 0.72 in three months and 0.74 in 12 months.
Rationale: Ahead of the 3 November RBA rate decision, market pricing implied an 88% chance of a 25bps hike, leaving little scope for an upside surprise. What changed after the announcement was the pricing of the next hike. The RBA dropped its reference to further rate increases, and three members preferred a rate hold. Markets scaled back the odds of rates reaching 5.10% next year to around 30%, thus weighing on the AUD.
The AUD is sensitive to swings in global risk appetite, especially the US tech sell-off spread to global equities, triggering margin calls and weighing on the currency. An equity recovery would ease that pressure. Even after the two 25bps Fed hikes we expect by mid-2027, Australia would retain a 35bps rate advantage over the top of the Fed’s target range, supporting a gradual AUD recovery.
— Vincent Tan, Senior Investment Strategist— Iris Yuen, Investment Strategist

articles.title: Custody+ and the Future of Market Intelligence
articles.text:

Technology & InnovationCustody+ and the Future of Market IntelligenceArticle • November 05, 2026Amit AgarwalGlobal Head of CustodyInvestor Services, CitiThe custody model is evolving. So are client expectations.Accelerated settlement cycles, continuous trading models, digital assets and AI are reshaping the post-trade landscape. Clients increasingly need faster access to information, greater transparency and more flexibility in how they consume custody services.That's the vision behind Custody+, Citi's next-generation custody platform. Moving beyond a traditional one-size-fits-all model, Custody+ provides a modular framework that allows clients to tailor custody solutions to their needs while leveraging the scale, resiliency and reach of Citi's global network.Eliminating friction starts with modern infrastructure and intelligent insights.At the core of Custody+ is Citi's patented Single Event Processing (SEP) technology for real-time asset servicing. By processing more than 80% of events only once across Citi's global and domestic custody layers, SEP significantly reduces operational touchpoints and accelerates the delivery of critical information.The results are tangible. In the U.S., SEP has reduced processing times for voluntary corporate actions by up to 92%, with 96% of events now processed in less than two hours. Combined with Citi's proprietary custody network of 62 branches, clients gain faster access to information, more time to make decisions and greater flexibility to redeploy capital.Custody+ is also applying AI to eliminate longstanding inefficiencies. There is only one Goldman Sachs.Discover CareersWORKING AT GSStudentsLife at GSBenefitsFeatured OfficesOpen RolesReal Estate & HousingThe Outlook for US Housing in 2027 amid Rising Mortgage RatesOct 30, 2026Share Mortgage rates have risen to such a degree this year that affordability challenges are outweighing the impact of the longstanding US housing shortage. An expected decline in mortgage rates next year is likely to fuel a rebound in housing activity by the second half of 2027. Existing home sales are likely to slip in 2027 as many homeowners face the prospect of paying much higher borrowing costs if they move to another home. Home prices are likely to keep growing in the year ahead, but at an “anemic” rate of less than 1%. Rising mortgage rates are likely to outweigh a longstanding housing shortage in the US next year, leading to a drop in both the sales of existing homes and the construction of new ones, according to Goldman Sachs Research.
“In 2027, we expect the headwind from affordability to increasingly dominate, weighing further on activity,” economists Ronnie Walker and David Mericle write in a report.
They project that existing home sales will total just 3.9 million in 2027, modestly below their forecast of 4 million for 2026 but 26% below 2019 levels. Against the backdrop of slower home sales, they forecast another year of “anemic” home price growth: 0.8% December-over-December in 2027 after 1.1% in 2026 and 1.2% in 2025.

Borrowing costs are a key component of housing affordability. This year’s jump in mortgage rates—in response to the Iran War, higher oil prices, and the prospect of rate hikes by the Federal Reserve—has reduced incentives for homeowners to sell. More than 95% of mortgage borrowers have interest rates below current market rates, and 65% have rates two percentage points below market rates, creating a “lock-in” effect that is slowing sales. In order to purchase a new home, such homebuyers would need to prepay their current mortgage and take out a new mortgage at a higher rate.
“The combination of mortgage borrowers refinancing at low rates en masse in 2020 and 2021 and the high current level of mortgage rates has created a significant financial cost to moving,” Walker and Mericle write.
Rates for 30-year mortgages in the US have climbed to 7.32% (as of October 22). Goldman Sachs Research’s credit strategists expect mortgage rates to decline in 2027 but remain elevated at 6.4%. Even if that decline is realized, affordability will remain at historically poor levels.
When is US housing market activity likely to improve?

Beyond next year, Goldman Sachs Research expects existing home sales to gradually edge higher, reflecting the natural decay of the lock-in effect that comes from, for example, borrowers paying down their mortgages.
The renewed popularity of adjustable-rate mortgages in the post-pandemic period could theoretically accelerate this process as well. As rates on such mortgages reset, they tend to erode the impact of the lock-in effect, as seen in other countries where adjustable-rate mortgages are more prevalent. But that impact is likely to be modest in the US, especially over the next couple of years. Adjustable-rate mortgages represent less than 10% of all outstanding mortgages in the US, and only a small share of them will begin to reset in the coming years.
Housing activity as measured by residential fixed investment (RFI)—a component of gross domestic product that includes new home construction—is likely to begin recovering by next summer after an expected decline in the months ahead.
After posting an estimated 3.1% annualized increase in this year’s third quarter, RFI is forecast to contract by 2.5%, 4%, and 1% annualized in the three quarters that follow, respectively. Thereafter, our researchers expect activity to rebound to a 1-2% growth pace starting in the second half of next year, reflecting the impact of declining mortgage rates. If rates remain at current levels instead, that would lower their RFI growth forecasts by one to two percentage points through the end of 2027.

How higher mortgage rates are forecast to impact US homebuilding in 2027

The longstanding housing shortage has kept single-family homebuilding resistant to higher interest rates. Single-family starts have averaged 3% higher than above 2019 levels despite mortgage rates that are three-and-a-half percentage points higher today. This year, however, they have declined by 3% compared with last year, and the slippage is likely to continue. Goldman Sachs Research expects single-family starts to total 0.87 million in 2027 compared to an estimated 0.90 million in 2026.
Our economists point to the increase in the available supply of housing, as well as the corresponding compression of margins for homebuilders back to pre-pandemic levels. The elevated pace of homebuilding in recent years has eased historically tight supply-and-demand balances. When the available supply of housing improves, it tends to increase homebuilders’ sensitivity to affordability constraints. Prior analysis by Goldman Sachs Research shows that the higher the vacancy rate was the year before, the more sensitive housing starts are to mortgage rate increases.
The combination of still-solid supply growth and slightly weaker demand should push the homeowner vacancy rate higher in the months ahead, from 1.2% in this year’s second quarter to 1.4% by the fourth quarter of 2027.
Housing demand is being buoyed by domestic demographic trends that remain supportive, along with real income growth that is likely to accelerate next year, and “build-to-rent” housing, which typically involves a partnership between single-family rental companies and homebuilders to construct rental homes. But on the negative side, survey-based measures of purchase intentions have declined in recent months. Our economists also expect that reduced immigration will continue to weigh on household formation.
“We expect housing demand to remain tepid,” Walker and Mericle write.
