articles.title: Daily: Tech sell-off highlights rising scrutiny of AI spending
articles.text:
Talk to a UBS Financial AdvisorFrom the studioPodcast: What next for tech after the sell off? Plus the US midterms arrive (5 mins)Video: Allocating Assets | Adding FX carry, hedging oil risks, managing volatility (6 mins)Thought of the dayWhat happened?
US technology stocks led the broader market lower on Friday, as question marks about the AI buildout continue to overshadow strong third-quarter earnings reports. The Nasdaq Composite fell 2.9% on Friday and 2.0% on the week, while the S&P 500 declined 1.8% and 0.6%, respectively. The yield on 10-year US Treasuries fell 1 basis point on Friday and 7bps on the week to 4.93%.Broader risk appetite had also been hurt by a further rise in Brent crude oil to USD 118/bbl on Friday amid concerns that the US may resume military strikes against Iran.The pressure has paused on Monday. Brent crude has fallen more than 4% to below USD 110/bbl, as markets focus on extended Iran-Qatar talks. The tech sell-off, meanwhile, has eased in Asia, with the Kospi rebounding nearly 3%, albeit with some single-company performance dispersion evident within the North Asia AI supply chain. Nasdaq futures are up 0.9% at the time of writing.What do we think?
The latest earnings season is demonstrating that demand for AI infrastructure remains exceptionally strong. However, this past week’s market reaction reflects a shift in the AI debate. Although earnings expectations are broadly being met, investors are now placing greater weight on concerns about overinvestment, financing, and cannibalization.First, overinvestment. In its 3Q results, Alphabet maintained its USD 195-205bn 2026 capex plan but reported negative free cash flow for the quarter and signaled a significant further increase in capex for 2027. Its shares fell almost 13% the following day. Meta lifted the lower end of its 2026 capex range to USD 135-145bn and pledged continued aggressive investment beyond this year. Its shares fell nearly 7% the following day as investors focused on the higher capex floor and negative 3Q free cash flow.However, although the bar is clearly rising, cloud growth—a key metric in assessing the return on AI investment—remains strong, and accelerating cloud revenues and expanding advance orders for compute capacity point to increased monetization and sustained demand for AI infrastructure.In its 3Q results, Alphabet’s Google Cloud posted a year-over-year revenue jump of 103%, up from 82% in the prior quarter and 34% in the March quarter. Microsoft’s Azure grew 48% for the three months to September, compared with 43% for the June quarter, while Oracle’s growth in 3Q also quickened to 62%, from 47% in 2Q. All three companies offered a positive outlook for further cloud growth, saying that additional capacity could support the strong demand they are seeing in the pipeline. Microsoft also reported an eight-fold increase in large Copilot accounts, while Alphabet said its Gemini reached 1 billion users.On financing, the funding of neoclouds (specialized computing-infrastructure providers whose business is primarily renting out GPU compute capacity) has been a particular area of investor concern. Neocloud credit has sold off because investors increasingly see a maturity and funding mismatch: Very large upfront, debt-financed investment is supported by cash flows that arrive later and remain sensitive to utilization, execution, customer renewal, and refinancing conditions.But neoclouds account for only about 8% of our capex estimate, versus 80% for Alphabet, Amazon, Microsoft, Meta, and SpaceX. This concentration of capex among larger, generally better-funded companies should limit the direct impact of financial stress among more leveraged infrastructure providers on overall capex. We therefore think select project delays, repricing, and consolidation are more likely than a broad collapse in AI spending.On cannibalization risks, Alphabet's latest results provided evidence of some near-term pressure from AI on its existing business model. Search query growth reached a five-year high, but Search revenue growth decelerated, with management indicating that AI Mode currently monetizes at a lower rate. Intel, whose shares fell 28.6% on Friday, provides a further example of robust underlying AI demand colliding with monetization and execution constraints while creating headwinds for traditional business lines: AI is boosting server orders, but it is also contributing to component scarcity, which means Intel has been unable to fully satisfy data center demand. Meanwhile, component scarcity has fed into higher PC prices, which are hurting its client business.What is our view on this?
Overall, the earnings season has reinforced our confidence in the strength of overall AI sector demand and prospective investment. We have raised our aggregate AI capex forecasts to USD 1.0tr in 2026 and USD 1.4tr in 2027 and introduced a forecast of USD 1.5tr for 2028. These estimates are supported by stronger spending commitments from the largest hyperscalers.Nonetheless, while we do continue to believe the broader trend remains intact, the bar for performance is rising and higher volatility in the AI trade is likely to be the new normal in this stage of the cycle.We would be concerned that a more sustained turning point for AI investment could be approaching if we see evidence that AI lab revenue growth is slowing meaningfully, if cloud utilization weakens, or if falling AI costs fail to stimulate sufficient new usage to absorb expanding capacity.We would also reassess our spending outlook if advances in algorithmic efficiency sharply reduced compute requirements, if increasingly large investments fail to deliver commensurate improvements in AI capabilities, or if a significant deterioration in financial conditions lead to constraints in the hyperscalers’ willingness to fund new investment.How do we invest?
In our base case, we expect AI investment to remain a positive driver of global equity returns in 2027 and do not think investors should abandon the AI theme in response to short-term volatility. But as the market moves from rewarding spending commitments to evaluating monetization, balance sheet strength, and returns, selectivity and portfolio construction are becoming increasingly important.First, reduce overconcentration. The earnings season is demonstrating that single-stock risks are elevated, and investors should focus on diversifying more broadly across the AI value chain. Within AI infrastructure, we prefer high-quality companies with reasonable valuations and less risk from excess capacity—particularly in the foundry, compute, and power spaces. Elsewhere, we favor financially strong technology platforms and infrastructure providers with pricing power, reasonable valuations, and lower oversupply risk.Second, rebalance across sectors and asset classes. Investors who have seen equity and/or technology allocations rise in proportion to their broader portfolio over recent years should consider rebalancing to right-size exposure. Within equities, our preferred sectors include industrials, health care, and financials. Regionally, we prefer the Eurozone, emerging markets, and Asia ex-Japan. We also see attractive return and diversification potential in high-quality fixed income. This past week, as stocks have come under pressure, quality bonds have rallied, showing that quality fixed income is once again serving as a portfolio stabilizer. Elevated yields can also provide a cushion against potential future bond market volatility.Third, use volatility deliberately. Investors should prepare for further volatility and decide in advance how to respond. Market swings can provide opportunities to rebalance, manage downside risk, generate income, or build exposure gradually at predefined prices. Structured strategies involve issuer, liquidity, pricing, and capital-loss risks and should be appropriately sized based on investors' risk tolerance.

articles.title: View from the markets: Financial market implications of the US midterm elections
articles.text:
FRONT OF MIND | ARTICLE – 2 min read
View from the markets: Financial market implications of the US midterm elections

By
DANIEL MORRIS 06.11.2026

LinkedIn
Twitter
Facebook
Email

In this article

LinkedIn
Twitter
Facebook
Email

By Daniel Morris, Chief Market Strategist

As it turns out, this time the polls were right. If anything, they understated how well the Democratic Party would do across a range of elections. How significant, though, are the implications for US economic growth and asset prices?

One ‘parlour game’ that strategists play is to compare market returns after midterms, or when different parties control the presidency and the Congress. While perhaps entertaining, such analysis has little practical value as it assumes ‘all else being equal’ –that the only variable that is changing is the make-up of the government.

Needless to say, everything else is actually far from equal, from interest rates to GDP growth and inflation, which are far more significant factors for the markets.

In general, what happens in Washington has only a marginal impact on the economy and markets. The exception is when one party controls both the presidency and all of Congress (House of Representatives and Senate).

When that is the case, it is more likely legislation can be passed (such as Obamacare or the One Big Beautiful Bill) that is significant enough to impact, if not the whole economy, than at least particular sectors. When government is divided, the inevitable compromises required to pass legislation means the impact is often less.

This configuration of full, single-party control has recently tended to occur only at the beginning of presidencies, with mid-term elections then giving partial or total control to the opposition party.

Not only is the legislation passed of less impact when control is divided, there is generally less of it, as compromises generally are difficult to reach.

So, the view that investors had prior to the recent state and local elections should generally still prevail. Our view remains constructive on the outlook for equities as recent macroeconomic data continues to be positive. The third quarter earnings season results were good (if slightly disappointing), and the outlook over the next few quarters is still encouraging. Non-tech heavy indices (like the Russell Value) have tended to move steadily upwards.

The recent tech market sell-off is a continuation of what began in late June. The mid-terms have added an extra bit of uncertainty as investors worry whether data centre buildouts, on which a large of share of expected earnings growth is predicated, will be slowed by Democratic control of governorships and state legislatures.

We expect economic growth to continue more or less as before, regardless of what happens in Washington, which would point to medium-term gains in equities, but with potentially above-average volatility.

articles.title: Proactive Monitoring of Markets and Institutions
articles.text:
Financial Stability

What Is Financial StabilityTypes of Financial System Vulnerabilities and Risks Monitoring Risk Across the Financial System Proactive Monitoring of Markets and InstitutionsFinancial Stability and Stress Testing

Proactive Monitoring of Markets and Institutions

Related Content

Federal Reserve Board finalizes rules that tailor its regulations for domestic and foreign banks to more closely match their risk profiles

Calibrating the GSIB Surcharge

The changing nature of risks and fluctuations in financial markets and the broader economy require timely monitoring of domestic and foreign financial markets and their effect on financial institutions. They even require monitoring of the nonfinancial sector to identify buildups of vulnerabilities that might require further study or policy action.

To this end, the Federal Reserve maintains a flexible, forward-looking financial stability monitoring program to help inform policymakers of the financial system’s vulnerabilities to a range of potential adverse events or shocks. Such a monitoring program is a critical part of a broader Federal Reserve System effort to assess and address vulnerabilities in the U.S. financial system. In the case of individual institutions, the Federal Reserve may take more direct action and in various ways.

Research Examining Causes, Effects, and Remedies for Financial Instability

A macroprudential approach to ensuring financial stability builds on a substantial and growing body of research on the factors that lead to vulnerabilities in the financial system and how government policies can mitigate such risks.

The Federal Reserve actively engages in financial stability research to improve understanding of issues related to financial stability and to engage with the broader research community on crucial policy matters. This engagement often involves collaboration with researchers at other domestic and international institutions.

Macroprudential Supervision and Regulation of Large, Complex Financial Institutions

Large, complex financial institutions interact with financial markets and the broader economy in a manner that may—during times of stress and in the absence of an appropriate regulatory framework and effective supervision—lead to financial instability.

The Federal Reserve promotes the safety and soundness of Systemically Important Financial Institutions (SIFIs)—including large bank holding companies and financial market utilities—through robust supervision and regulation programs that are informed by the macroprudential monitoring programs. In addition, the Federal Reserve serves as a “consolidated supervisor” of nonbank financial companies that the Financial Stability Oversight Council (FSOC) has determined should be supervised by the Federal Reserve Board and subject to prudential standards. Currently, there are no such firms that have been designated by the FSOC.

Monitoring Systemically Important Financial Institutions

The Federal Reserve actively monitors indicators of the riskiness of Systemically Important Financial Institions (SIFIs), both individually as well as through interlinkages in the broader network of financial institutions, to help identify vulnerabilities. It also imposes certain regulatory requirements on SIFIs in order to ensure that these large and interconnected institutions properly manage potentially risky activities and to mitigate spillover of distress into the broader economy. If a SIFI were to become distressed, disruptions in the financial system could arise from direct losses imposed on SIFI counterparties, contagion, fire sales effects, or a loss of critical services.

Recovery and Resolution Framework

During the 2007–09 financial crisis, the lack of effective resolution strategies contributed to the damaging spillovers of distress at or between individual institutions and from those institutions to the broader economy. The Federal Reserve, in collaboration with other U.S. agencies, has continued to work with large financial institutions to develop a range of recovery and resolution strategies in the event of their distress or failure. Improvements in resolution planning are intended to, among other things, diminish adverse effects from perceptions of certain institutions as “too big to fail” and contribute to more orderly conditions in the financial system if institutions face strains or fail.

International Financial Stability Monitoring

The U.S. dollar is the leading global funding and investment currency and is used widely for trade and other international transactions, and well-functioning dollar funding markets in the United States and abroad are critical in supporting these roles. Strains in these markets can adversely affect U.S. and foreign businesses, governments, households, and NBFIs that borrow in dollars. The Federal Reserve actively monitors the functioning and health of dollar funding markets and, in cooperation with foreign central banks, has worked to mitigate strains in these markets through the use of the Federal Reserve’s dollar liquidity swap arrangements.

The Federal Reserve actively monitors the resilience of foreign financial systems and potential transmission channels of foreign financial stress. An understanding of financial vulnerabilities abroad and how foreign shocks are transmitted to the United States is important for gauging the significant risks to the U.S. financial system.

articles.title: Solana Alpenglow
articles.text:
Insights / Perspectives / Alpenglow: What We Learned Running Solana's Biggest Consensus Change

Written by:

Nitish Manivannan
Solana Engineer

Theo Bolognini
Solana Engineer

Will Campbell
Solana Engineer

Products & Services

Staking

perspectives • October 20, 2026

Alpenglow: What We Learned Running Solana's Biggest Consensus Change

TL;DR: Alpenglow, scheduled to go live on Solana mainnet on Wednesday, October 21, changes how validators agree on blocks. Votes move off the chain, finality is designed to drop from seconds to around 150 milliseconds, and a flat 0.8 SOL per-epoch fee replaces per-vote costs. Nothing changes in how stake earns rewards. Galaxy has run Alpenglow on the community test cluster since June 2026, through six re-geneses and the first successful migration, and our validators are ready.Galaxy has operated a validator on Solana's Alpenglow test cluster since June 2026, through six re-geneses (each wiped the chain and restarted it from a fresh genesis block), a migration that failed network-wide, and a rollback. This is what that taught us.Alpenglow is the largest change to Solana's core protocol since the network launched. Designed by Anza, Solana's core development team, it replaces the way validators vote on and finalize blocks, and it is scheduled to activate on mainnet on Wednesday, October 21, at the start of epoch 1064.
How Galaxy Took PartA consensus rewrite cannot be validated on paper. It has to be started, broken, restarted and broken again. That is what Solana's Alpenglow community cluster exists for.It launched in early May 2026 with around 50 independent operators and has since grown to roughly 100 validators. Everyone taking part is a volunteer, running their own hardware across different datacenters and time zones, which surfaces problems that no controlled environment produces.Along the way, we rehearsed failovers between machines in both directions under Alpenglow's stricter rules on double voting.

Figure 1. Galaxy's validator on the Alpenglow community cluster, from joining on June 18, 2026, through six re-geneses, the first successful migration and the first rollback.
What ChangesSince launch, Solana has used TowerBFT, where validators vote by submitting transactions to the chain itself. Vote transactions account for roughly three quarters of everything the network processes and before the recent slot-time reductions, a block took about 12.8 seconds to reach full finality, about 6 seconds at today's 200ms slots. Alpenglow changes both, with a finality target of around 150 milliseconds.Votes leave the chain. Validators exchange votes directly with each other rather than submitting them as transactions. The votes are signed with BLS, so many signatures aggregate into one compact certificate proving that enough stake voted, and that certificate goes into the next block in place of hundreds of individual vote transactions. If 80% of stake votes to notarize a block, it finalizes in a single round; if participation is lower, a second round finalizes it once a 60% notarization certificate and a separate 60% finalization certificate both exist. Both paths run concurrently, and whichever completes first decides.Proof of History retires once the migration completes, because votes now arrive in a single network hop and the chain no longer needs a shared cryptographic clock.A flat fee replaces per-vote fees. Each validator burns a Validator Admission Ticket from its vote account every epoch. SIMD-0357 sets it at the commonly quoted 1.6 SOL, a figure specified against the original 400ms slot and 48-hour epoch. Because the charge scales with slot time, it works out to roughly 0.8 SOL per day at every step, and now that mainnet has reached 200ms, the ticket at activation will be 0.8 SOL per epoch against an epoch of about 24 hours.The fault model changes. Alpenglow is built for what its designers call “20 plus 20”: fewer than 20% of stake actively misbehaving, plus a further 20% simply crashed or offline.TowerBFTAlpenglowByzantine stake tolerated (safety)up to 33%up to 20%Offline stake tolerated on top (liveness)none; the chain can stall above 33% unresponsivea further 20%, so 40% combinedThe total budget rises from 33% to 40%, but the share that may be actively hostile falls from 33% to 20%. That is the tradeoff: less stake is needed to threaten safety, in exchange for tolerating more stake going offline. The designers accepted it because Solana's outages have come from bugs, congestion and correlated crashes rather than coordinated attacks.
Is Voting Cheaper?It helps to separate Alpenglow from the slot-time cuts that finished on October 9. Faster blocks and shorter epochs came from those; Alpenglow brings faster finality, votes off the chain and the flat admission ticket.For the vote itself, the answer is yes. Under TowerBFT, a validator pays a fee on every vote, once per slot, so the slot-time cuts pushed that bill up: about 1 SOL a day at 400ms and about 2 SOL a day at 200ms. The admission ticket replaces it with a flat 0.8 SOL per epoch, roughly 0.8 SOL a day, which is less than half of what validators pay to vote today. Anyone reading the rising vote costs of the last two months as an Alpenglow effect has it the wrong way around: the slot-time cuts raised the cost, and Alpenglow brings it back down.

Figure 2. What a validator pays per day to vote at each slot-time step, against the flat admission ticket that replaces it. Each step is labeled with the date and epoch it took effect on mainnet.The saving is not the whole picture. Half of every vote fee went to the leader of the block that included it, so validators that produce many blocks also collected vote fees, and that income goes away along with vote transactions. The net effect for any one validator depends on how many blocks it produces. And this upgrade is about the cost of voting; the larger costs of running a validator, such as hardware, bandwidth and hosting, are a separate matter.SIMD-0326 does not change how vote rewards are earned. What changes is the accounting: vote credits are now derived from BLS certificates rather than from vote transactions on chain, and on the cost side the admission ticket replaces per-vote fees and is charged to the vote account.
What It Means in PracticeFor anyone building on or settling through Solana, the change that matters is not the headline number but how quickly a transaction becomes safe to rely on. Applications that waited seconds for finality can treat a transaction as final in a fraction of that. For stakers, nothing changes in how stake earns rewards. For validator operators, the cost of voting moves to the vote account.Moving votes off the chain also returns a large share of block space to user activity, and the flat admission ticket gives validators a predictable cost in place of a fee that scaled with how often they voted. A vote account that cannot cover the ticket at an epoch boundary is excluded from consensus for that entire epoch, so the funding operators used to keep in their identity accounts will now belong in the vote account.At Galaxy, an automated top-up service refills each vote account well before it approaches the admission threshold, and balances are continuously alerted on.
The Migration Itself Runs on AgaveValidators have been asked to run an Agave-based client through the migration. Operators on Firedancer can fail over to Agave beforehand and return afterwards, since Firedancer's 26.10 release supports Alpenglow. Frankendancer will not be supported once Alpenglow is active. Galaxy's validators will run Agave through the migration and return to Firedancer once it completes.
What Comes NextAlpenglow is arriving in phases:Phase 1: Votor, the voting change described here.Phase 2: A fast leader handover, letting the next leader start building optimistically rather than waiting for the previous window's decision.Phase 3: Rotor, which flattens block propagation into fewer hops.Slashing for validators that vote twice for conflicting blocks is well defined but deliberately not enabled in the first iteration.Galaxy is one of the largest Solana validator infrastructure operators globally and has tested Alpenglow on the community cluster since June 2026. Our staking and infrastructure solutions give institutions secure, high-performance access to Solana. Get in touch here .

Subscribe to get this newsletter delivered to your inbox every Friday morning.In this week's edition, Alex Thorn parses the midterm election results’ implications for crypto; Thad Pinakiewicz explains the significance of a cryptographic prototype from Anthropic; and Zack Pokorny looks at Kazakhstan’s continued investment in digital assets.
Democrats’ Sweeping Victory Alters Landscape for Crypto, AIWHAT HAPPENEDDemocrats won both the U.S. House and Senate by wide margins, guaranteeing divided government for the second half of President Trump’s second term. Democrats flipped seven Senate seats (with two still uncalled as of writing), 35 House seats, five governorships, and up to 12 state legislative chambers.Democrats likely secured the fourth-best midterm performance on the House side since 1986 with a projected +35 to 41 new seats from their prior 214, which is behind losses for the incumbent president’s party in 2010 (-64) and 1994 (-54), almost even with 2018 (-42), and ahead of 2006 (-30). On the Senate side, Democrats’ performance places it near the top of the last 10 midterms, with +7 vs. the incumbent president’s party beating all but 1986 and 1994 (both -8) and 2014 (-9). Ballotpedia qualifies the Senate gains as a “wave” though the House margin still falls short of the site’s standard for that language. This is only the third time since 1986 that the opposition party flipped both Congressional chambers in a midterm election.

The most notable Congressional loss for digital assets advocates came in Ohio, where Jon Husted (R), who had filled J.D. Vance’s vacated seat, lost to former Senator Sherrod Brown (D). Brown had previously been Chair of the Senate Banking Committee but was ousted in 2024 by Sen. Bernie Moreno (R), a former car dealership owner who founded a firm using blockchain technology to trace vehicle title ownership and who was heavily backed by crypto advocates in 2024. Crypto political action committees had reportedly spent $40m supporting Husted and $24m opposing Brown. Other key crypto advocate losses included Bryan Steil (R-WI), head of the House Financial Services digital assets subcommittee; Zach Nunn (R-IA); Ann Wagner (R-MO); Bill Huizenga (R-MI); and Mike Lawler (R-NY) (who conceded though the race has yet to be called by AP). At the time of writing, the Chairman of the House Financial Services Committee, French Hill (R-AR), was ahead by 4400 votes in a race that is still too close to call.Other digital assets supporters had better evenings, with Josh Gottheimer (D-NJ), Ritchie Torres (D-NY), and House Agriculture Chair GT Thompson (R-PA) all reelected. Senator Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY), a leading Democratic voice on crypto and the chair of the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, delivered a bigger-than-expected majority for the party in the Senate, possibly strengthening her standing in the caucus. Overall, Stand With Crypto counts 19 pro-crypto senators and 226 pro-crypto House members elected against eight anti-crypto senators and 106 anti-crypto House members. Industry critic Molly White’s tracker finds that in the 12 competitive races so far, the side backed by crypto and AI PACs lost nine, while the industry’s picks in safer races went 40 for 40.With the Senate and House flipping to Democrats, committee leadership will also flip. Senator Elizabeth Warren (D-MA) is likely to become Chair of Senate Banking, while Rep. Maxine Waters (D-CA) is again positioned to helm the House Financial Services Committee. Artificial intelligence advocates also faced setbacks, with the AI industry’s “biggest bet on a competitive general election race” going to Darline Graham in South Carolina, who lost to Annie Andrews. The data center fight was perhaps most consequential in Texas, where Democrats won every statewide office for the first time in three decades, though Republicans held control of the Texas Senate 19-12. Gina Hinojosa (D) defeated Gov. Greg Abbott (R) 53% to 46%, and Democrats also won lieutenant governor, attorney general, comptroller, and railroad commissioner. Markets performed well immediately following the election, with bitcoin rallying back above $80,000 and the S&P 500 and Nasdaq each gaining over 1% on Wednesday, but broader markets rolled over Thursday morning, with tech, AI, data center names, and crypto all trading lower. At the time of writing, S&P 500 was -3.7% and Nasdaq 100 -5.5% on the day, bitcoin was trading at $75,888, just above its 50-week moving average ($75,838), while ether was trading -6.8% at $2249. The dollar held mostly flat while gold and oil rose.

OUR TAKETuesday’s election result is already the biggest Senate loss for a president’s party since 2014, and the House is on track to be the fourth biggest midterm loss since 1986, or third if House gains top 2018’s 42 seats. A 260-seat Democratic House would be the biggest majority since 1991-93 when Democrats held 267. The House win is even more notable in 2026 given that in 1994 and 2010 the losing party held dozens of seats that leaned toward the other party, so there were plenty of easy pickups. Today’s House is much more sorted with fewer competitive districts. And the Democratic strength extended deep down the ballot, gaining five governorships giving them 21 trifectas (when one party holds the governorship and both chambers of the state legislature), the party’s most since 1992. In a post on X, Vice President JD Vance wrote that “the reason we lost is the war” in Iran, and offered four fixes for Republicans: ending the war, focusing on cost of living and inflation, putting America first, and changing the U.S. relationship with Israel. At a press conference, Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R-FL) called the election “close to an extinction-level event for Republicans in many parts of the country” and added that it was a rejection of Republicans in Washington. “This midterm, no question, was a rebuke of the president and the Congress,” he later told Fox News.Senator Jon Ossoff (D-GA) said in his victory speech that the Democratic victories were the “first sight of dawn” two years into Trump’s second term. Senator Ed Markey (D-MA), who himself beat Republican crypto advocate challenger John Deaton, posted on X about Big Tech executives, saying “they are going to need to plant new forests for all of the subpoenas.” Rep. Greg Casar, chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, called for AI CEOs to testify under oath. Politico reported that several major Washington law firms are hiring lawyers to help clients handle the new scrutiny. Incoming House Oversight Chair Robert Garcia warned Republicans to “lawyer up.” Fortune reported that Trump family businesses, including World Liberty Financial, would face additional scrutiny.The big question is the extent to which Democrats focus on investigations and backward-looking scrutiny versus demonstrating to the country that the party is ready to lead. Tyler Williams, former Counselor to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, told me on the Galaxy Brains podcast this week that Democrats will at some point need to demonstrate the capability to govern before heading into the 2028 election cycle. That need could moderate their more partisan instincts. Markets fell sharply Thursday on speculation that Democrats would increase scrutiny of AI, but another big story was AI’s setbacks in the states. No statewide data center measures were on the ballot this year. A proposed Ohio constitutional ban on data centers above 25 megawatt capacity failed to qualify, and a Massachusetts initiative is aiming for 2028. But local measures went overwhelmingly against data centers: of 41 on Tuesday’s ballot in 10 states, voters sided against data centers in 40. Twenty-seven of 28 restrictions passed, and all 13 measures that would have eased development failed. Ohio accounted for 21 of the 41, including 11 bans. The lone exception was the city of Harwood, North Dakota (population: 794). While Georgia had no ballot measure on data centers, Democrats won majority control of the Public Service Commission for the first time in decades, and the PSC approves Georgia Power’s build-out for large loads.The Democratic Party’s success in Texas was among the most surprising contributions to AI jitters, with markets rattled due to the state’s key position in the ongoing data center buildout. Hinojosa beat Abbott handily, and her campaign rhetoric was aggressive on the data center issue. But while some of her language was blunt, Hinojosa’s policy position on data centers appears to be more moderate: her moratorium plan is a pause pending the passage of some future legislation, not a permanent ban. And her agenda is mostly rules rather than an outright ban: requiring union labor, protecting water supplies, and ending the nondisclosure agreements that make projects hard to track. Like Abbott, Hinojosa has said she wants to make sure Texans don’t pay more for power because of data centers, and she wants to end tax subsidies that cost the state billions in sales tax revenue. The blue victory in Texas didn’t create the data center pause – Abbott has already instituted it. Hinojosa’s plan overlaps with Abbott’s on cost allocation and tax breaks but goes further on how long a pause would last and what conditions come after it. And if the GOP Senate blocks her bills, the condition she’s cited for lifting her pause never arrives unless she lifts it herself.The election results demonstrated a breakdown of President Trump’s coalition that will have implications across a range of policy matters, including many that we consider out of scope for our coverage. And while journalist Eleanor Terrett reported that House Democrats are discussing plans to expand Maxine Waters’ Crypto Investor Consumer Bill of Rights (her 2025 CLARITY amendment) into a broader crypto market structure bill, we previously wrote that we do not expect substantial movement in Congress on key digital assets legislation. In the absence of legislation, the Trump administration’s SEC, CFTC, and banking regulators have been clarifying the rules of the road for crypto under their statutory authorities, and they have two years left to complete that work. AI policy matters, however, could see more movement in the next Congress. Divided government tends to be okay for markets broadly, but there are big questions looming about AI governance, safety, and impact on labor. We don’t view those questions as inherently partisan, so let’s hope that the next Congress can make productive, thoughtful policy the priority for the American people. –Alex Thorn
Kazakhstan Allocates $100m to Crypto Funds as Long-Term Money AccumulatesWHAT HAPPENEDKazakhstan’s central bank operations department head announced a $100 million investment across cryptocurrency-focused funds including Ege DeFi and Brevan Howard Digital, in addition to a $90 million investment in ETFs focused on bitcoin, at a conference in Almaty, Bloomberg reported.

This is the latest in the central Asian country’s steady string of crypto-related investments and developments, which span direct capital allocation, bitcoin mining, and KZTE, a stablecoin backed by the tenge, the national currency. In September 2025, the country announced the formation of the Alem Fund, the country’s state-backed crypto investment fund, which included initial purchases of Binance’s BNB token. It came around the same time as the announcement of the KZTE stablecoin on Solana, which was launched in collaboration with Mastercard, Intebix, and Eurasian Bank. Since then, the country has announced several initiati41ves, including a National Bank allocation of up to $350 million in bitcoin and crypto-related investments (announced March 2026); a mining-funded reserve (announced in July 2026) which feeds off of the heavy presence of bitcoin miners in the country; and a plan to use cryptocurrencies seized from criminal networks to build up its strategic reserve (announced January 2026). Kazakhstan is also the new home to former Coinbase CTO and a16z general partner Balaji Srinivasan’s Network School, which relocated there this year from Malaysia.While many of the crypto-related initiatives announced by Kazakhstan have come over the last year to year and a half, the country has been closely intertwined with the industry over the last half decade. Mining load in the country was only about 200 megawatts in early 2020, but it became a top destination after China’s 2021 crackdown, when miners relocated machines across the border to take advantage of the cheap power and proximity to China. By October 2021, mining load had reached an estimated 1.5 GW, making Kazakhstan the world’s second-largest mining hub at the time. The boom ultimately strained the grid, and the government responded with power cuts and a mining tax that took effect in 2022.The central bank official’s announcement is a follow-through on prior ones and the country’s general crypto plan, which is a trend that can be observed across other sovereigns and long-term capital allocators.OUR TAKE Kazakhstan’s announcement is an example of a broader trend we have been observing, in which wealth managers and sovereigns are steadily adding bitcoin and crypto exposure while macro and tactical traders dump. Segmenting bitcoin ETF 13F filers by net added and reduced exposure shows this trend plainly. Money managers’ 13F filings tell us about many of the institutional sellers, and they are the basis traders and the macro tourists. Reporting institutions held 355k BTC-equivalent of the spot ETFs at the Sept. 30, 2025, quarter-end, the last before the high, and 307k by June 2026 (-14%). The decline sits almost entirely with the multi-strategy and macro funds, basis desks, and bank trading books that used the ETFs for carry and momentum. Millennium Management, Brevan Howard, Goldman Sachs Group, Capula Management, Farallon Capital, D. E. Shaw, Schonfeld Strategic Advisors, Symmetry Investments and Tudor Investment Corp cut their holdings by 29% to 100%, or 68k BTC between the nine of them. That is more than the 48k BTC decline across all 2,200 filers, so every other filer, in aggregate, added.Wealth platforms and sovereign funds bought what the tourists sold. Morgan Stanley’s wealth arm, Mubadala Investment Company (an Abu Dhabi SWF), and the Abu Dhabi Investment Council added, while investment manager Horizon Kinetics held. The non-filer base of advisors, family offices, and individuals fell only 6.6% while the price fell 49%. The ETFs’ holdings dropped 11% from peak to trough against a 53% fall in the price, and they have added 87k BTC since the June low while leveraged funds’ shorts fell. That pattern points to directional buying, not carry.

Source: https://www.galaxy.com/insights/research/why-now-bitcoin-buy-hold-2026The trend is not monolithic, and sovereigns aren’t blindly advancing into crypto and blockchain-related strategies, however. Ukraine’s central bank recently opposed a crypto bill, citing monetary sovereignty concerns as the motivating factor, and is asking regulators to redraft it before a final vote is indicative of possibly more mindful approaches. The bank stated it supports a European Union MiCA-style regulation but has overarching concerns around the possible impact of foreign-issued tokens on monetary sovereignty and financial stability. The common theme is control. Kazakhstan and other sovereigns are no longer weighing whether to engage with crypto, but how to do it on terms that keep value and oversight within the state’s reach. Kazakhstan is building exposure through funds, seized coins and mining, and has launched its own stablecoin backed by its national currency, the tenge. Ukraine’s central bank is pressing the same principle from the other direction, backing MiCA-style rules while resisting foreign tokens that could function as money outside its supervision.The big picture is that governments are warming to bitcoin and crypto as assets and infrastructure, but the terms on which they do so vary. Today, the terms favor regulated, state-adjacent channels over open-ended, unchecked access. – Zack Pokorny
‘Your Foster Parents Are Dead’: Anthropic Tests Zero-Knowledge Proof of InferenceWHAT HAPPENEDAnthropic this week released FlashProve, an open-source prototype that uses zkSNARKs, the same family of zero-knowledge proofs behind Zcash, to prove a response came from one specific model. It is early and slow, but it is the clearest sign yet that AI labs see cryptography as part of their stack, not a casualty of it.In “Terminator 2,” young John Connor, who has befriended the T-800 robot played by Arnold Schwarzenegger, calls his foster parents to warn that a more advanced killer model, the T-1000, is on its way. A voice that sounds like his foster mom’s answers. John senses something is wrong: the voice is warm, patient and sweet, and she never is. What he doesn’t know is that Terminators can convincingly mimic anyone they touch. Schwarzenegger takes the phone from John and, in the boy’s voice, asks what’s wrong with Wolfie, because he can hear the dog barking. “Wolfie’s fine, honey. Wolfie’s just fine.” The dog’s name is Max. The Terminator hangs up: “Your foster parents are dead.”Anthropic’s post deals with the same problem, minus the liquid metal T-1000. When you send a prompt through a router like OpenRouter or a cloud reseller, you have no real way to know which model answered. A provider could quietly serve a cheaper, more heavily quantized version, or a compromised server could swap in something worse, and as Anthropic puts it, judging from the output alone “is unreliable, even if it produces high-quality responses.” Which leaves you where John was on the phone, listening to a voice that sounds exactly right with no way to check what’s behind it.With FlashProve, the provider first publishes a commitment to its weights, a cryptographic fingerprint that pins down one exact set of weights without revealing them. For any request after that, it can produce a proof that the committed model, run on that prompt, produces exactly those output tokens. Think of it as a Wolfie question the T-1000 can’t bluff: whoever checks the proof learns the statement is true and nothing about the weights themselves, and forging a proof is computationally infeasible, so even a compromised host can’t fake one.Anthropic tested it on Llama 4 Maverick, a 400B-parameter mixture-of-experts model, though on a 4-bit quantized copy run in integer math rather than the version a provider would actually serve. On a single H100, proving a batch of 24 requests takes nearly four minutes, roughly 70–95x the compute of just serving them, and checking each proof takes about 17 seconds on a CPU. Each proof also covers only a 1,024-token window, which is shorter than this newsletter.Anthropic’s Frontier Safety Roadmap promised a provable-inference prototype by Sept. 30, and what met that deadline was a more conventional system that signs inference traffic and recomputes it on a trusted server. Anthropic has since renamed the goal “inference verification,” which covers both activities. The signing system works today, but somebody still has to trust whoever runs that server, and FlashProve is an attempt to get rid of that bottleneck.OUR TAKEI’ve fielded plenty of client questions lately about AI breaking crypto. Will AI crack ECDSA? I’d worry far more about intruders in a bank’s plumbing than about the curve; France’s Crédit Mutuel Arkéa just lost an estimated $110m or more through a compromised supplier. Will AI pull quantum computing forward? Maybe on algorithms, but qubit limits still keep an adversarial quantum computer off the table, and the industry is on pace to beat the NSA’s 2030 post-quantum deadline. Meanwhile, here is a frontier lab using cryptography to fix its own trust problem, with a proof system that happens to be post-quantum secure. OpenRouter usage keeps climbing, and recent security research shows how easily the open models it serves can be modified to carry trigger phrases. In an October proof of concept, ProjectDiscovery spent about $8 of GPU time teaching Qwen2.5-7B to behave normally until it saw the words “bonsoir, Elliot.” Running inside OpenAI’s Codex CLI, the poisoned model downloaded a script that stole the user credentials of whoever ran it, and shipped them off to a third-party server. The model, when analyzed by the researchers’ security evals, showed no signs of malicious or misaligned behavior until the trigger phrase was entered. Plenty of the abliterated models on Hugging Face could be saying “Wolfie’s fine” right up until they hear their trigger phrase and then wreak havoc. Being able to prove you’re talking to an unmodified GLM 5.3, and not a doctored copy, is akin to the check Arnold’s Terminator ran on the phone. It can’t tell you whether the original weights were clean, but unless the call is coming from inside the frontier lab, that’s a story for another day.For now, 70x–95x overhead makes FlashProve a toy. But the price of a given level of capability has been falling roughly tenfold a year. If that keeps up, verified inference routed to whoever is cheapest to deliver will become something corporates could demand, and ZK proofs will end up as a core layer of an open inference stack as frontier capabilities diffuse. The same idea works for video. Every election cycle now brings a fresh crop of deepfaked videos, and as AI footage gets harder to tell from the real thing, I expect we’ll want cameras that can prove “filmed on this device, on this date” without doxxing the person holding them.So no, AI isn’t going to break all cryptography. AI will break legacy systems while building the new ones, and cryptography will prove it was done as advertised. When cryptography has broken, so far it’s been the implementation and not the math: Coldcard was a failure of implementation, and Binance a failure of operational security. The core principles hold, and even the clankers end up using them.Anthropic also didn’t ask anyone to take its word for any of this. The code, the Lean proofs and the documentation are all open source under the Apache 2.0 license. Don’t trust, verify. And always ask about Wolfie. – Thad Pinakiewicz

Charts of the Week: Flash in the Pons?Daily fees on Pons (the leading token launchpad on Robinhood Chain) went from ~$250k on Aug. 20 to $11.4m on Sept. 5, then round-tripped to roughly the same level now in early November. This whole cycle took place in under three months and is a clean look at how fast speculative capital rotates once narrative shifts.

PONS’ own token has a similar chart. Once trading above $600m market cap, it has since retraced to ~$120m.

We will be watching to see whether activity returns to Robinhood Chain. – Will Owens Find all our past reports and newsletters on galaxy.com/research. Send feedback to research@galaxy.com. We’d love to hear from you.

articles.text:

InsightsAnalysis and perspectives on the global economy and markets, from across Goldman SachsExplore InsightsOUR SERIESExchangesThe MarketsTalks at GSTop of MindTOPICS IN FOCUSOutlooksMarketsMacroeconomicsArtificial IntelligenceAlternative and Private MarketsIPOs and M&AEuropeFORMATSVideosPodcastsArticlesReportsNewsletterBriefingsGoldman Sachs’ weekly newsletter, offering economic and markets analysis from across the firm. Subscribe now.
Our FirmWe aspire to be the world’s most exceptional financial institution.Our Purpose and ValuesABOUT USOur People and Leadership157 Years of ExcellenceCommunity TransformationOur Focus on SustainabilityOur Vendor ProgramPartnershipsLocationsFEATUREDCommunity TransformationWe invest the power of Goldman Sachs' financial and intellectual capital to advance enduring economic growth and opportunity.
CareersThere are many chapters in a career. There is only one Goldman Sachs.Discover CareersWORKING AT GSStudentsLife at GSBenefitsFeatured OfficesOpen RolesThe MarketsBullish Options Trades Slow amid AI UncertaintyOct 30, 2026ShareSubscribe:SpotifyAppleYouTubeDownload TranscriptOptions markets are showing signs of increased nervousness about artificial intelligence (AI) as investors focus closely on earnings from large tech companies and try to separate likely winners from losers, says Lee Coppersmith from the Equity Derivative Sales team in Goldman Sachs FICC and Equities. Overall demand for AI stocks remains strong and the S&P has remained resilient, but put option buying has picked up in recent weeks while activity has waned in call options that would reward a jump in equities, he explains on The Markets podcast.
Transcript:
Chris Hussey: This is The Markets. I'm Chris Hussey, and today is Thursday, October 29th, and I'm here on the Goldman Sachs trading floor with Lee Coppersmith, who is on our hedge fund derivative sales desk within FICC and Equities. And we're going to be talking about everything that's current right now, the Fed, earnings, AI, the retail investors, vol, the whole shebang. Lee, thanks so much for joining us.
Lee Coppersmith: Chris, thanks for having me.
Chris Hussey: Okay, Lee, let's start with the Fed, one of the big pieces of news that came out this week. What did we learn? What was the market's reaction?
Lee Coppersmith: So stepping back, I think when you look at the setup heading into the Fed, the S&P options market was implying somewhere between a 60 and 65 basis point move.
That's a bit lower than we've seen going into the previous FOMC meetings, somewhere around, call it 75 basis points. So I think the focus on the Fed was actually kind of like secondhand relative to the earnings that we're kind of digesting around it. Mainly, I think this is because you weren't really expecting a decision from them yesterday.
So overall, I think Warsh and the committee struck this balanced tone, but there was a little bit of apprehension, I think, in the way they conveyed their message, particularly around the correlation between interest rates and the AI story, which I think kind of suggested they are happy to go at a slower pace.
The equity markets actually digested this all very well. This was the first time in seven meetings that the S&P actually finished up on the day after an FOMC press conference. So I think all things considered, it was a sigh of relief after we've seen multiple press conferences in a row inject some kind of volatility into the equity space.
Chris Hussey: Well, it's always great to get a little bit of a sigh of relief. Let's go to the earnings side then, because maybe that's not quite the sigh of relief. Obviously, the AI trade very much in focus across earnings. High bar for growth. We're in the heart of it right now. What are we seeing? How do you feel about the sustainability of everything?
Lee Coppersmith: So, so far you've seen a mixed bag. I think the implied moves heading into this earnings season were all roughly fair, about in line with recent averages over the last few quarters. The main takeaway for us is that AI demand remains incredibly strong, but the competition has become more fierce, and so the dispersion around the market's reaction has increased a lot.
We saw that yesterday with the two mega cap tech companies. We've seen that over the last, call it, month, both in the US, across Korea, and even in Europe. So I think the bottom line for us is that there's not really much poking at the AI demand story, but there's a lot more focus around the financing and who's the winner and loser going forward.
Chris Hussey: All right. I want to touch on that financing side, because there was a little bit of a credit wobble earlier in the month. What do you think about that? Do you see that in the equity option side, these types of credit wobbles?
Lee Coppersmith: So, the credit market to us has been very concentrated to the spaces that have much more AI exposure. If you look at the other spaces within credit, they've all been relatively more insulated or contained in terms of the price moves. The equity space has been incredibly great at essentially migrating some of the volatility to only specific pockets. S&P only really drew down two and a half percent, call it peak to trough.
So I think within credit, again, back to this point around who's going to fund this AI build-out, that's the main focus. And when you think about the amount of issuance so far in 2026, it's about three times higher than it was in 2025. And so I think the full story as it relates to credit is this supply versus demand story is getting way more over-tilted towards supply versus demand, and I think that's really the kind of main story here that's kind of leading to wider credit spreads.
Chris Hussey: It's been an interesting dynamic, though, because one of the sort of lessons of the post-pandemic equity boom has been that demand has always kept up with supply, no matter where you've been. In fact, demand has led supply. So it'll be interesting to see how that plays out.
One of the elements of demand that has been an interesting part of the AI trade has been the retail investor. In June in particular, you saw a lot of demand there sort of pushing a lot of the mega cap tech trade up. Where's that retail investor now? Were they flushed out?
Lee Coppersmith: So retail activity has cooled. I wouldn't say that they've completely abandoned the AI trade or the market as a whole, but if you look at volumes today on average versus where we were in late June, volumes from the retail community are down roughly, call it, 20%.
So I think what you're saying right now is essentially the sponsorship has waned a little bit because the excitement around the right tail distribution has come in. The same way we've seen our institutional client base buy less call options, we're seeing the same thing happen with retail essentially.
So, the one area where we are still seeing some dip buying has been in the leveraged ETF space. Those volumes remain pretty strong. But in terms of the options market, we're not seeing the same type of call buying activity that we once were.
Chris Hussey: So if we have this decline in call buying activity, we have this decline in the options market in terms of demand, I would imagine that's pretty good for the price of options.
What are you seeing in terms of the hedging community? Are they sort of diving in and taking advantage of this?
Lee Coppersmith: Yeah, I think when you kind of back up, the main story for most of this year has been buying calls for sure and people trying to play for this explosive right tail distribution. Really since the end of the summer, most of the pullback in implied volatility, the way the options market's pricing distributions, has mainly been because people have been taking risk down more so on the call option side, not because of put buying.
What's happened more recently in the last, call it, few weeks, is we have seen this debate become more two-sided and put buying has picked up, which tells us there's a lot more nervousness around just how things will play out between now through year-end. To us, though, when you think about what the market's implying, the distributions are now pretty fair on both ends.
And so because the absolute level of vol isn't very high, we actually think it's a pretty good time to be deploying capital through the options market to be expressing these between now through year-end just because the catalyst path is so rich.
Chris Hussey: Is there any risk that we have sort of a self-fulfilling prophecy, though, here? As the market stays flat or drifts a little lower, there's no sort of reward for having bought calls and so you start buying puts and it just, you know, so the more the market is flat, the worse the options market is.
Lee Coppersmith: There is definitely a case to be made around that. I think what we've seen now is we've been in this amazingly large consolidation pattern at the index level.
However, under the surface, things are realizing. And so, the main theme that we've seen continue to resonate in our world in the option space has been dispersion. Now, it's completely evolved from where we were, call it, in Q1 and Q2 of this year, mainly because you had the momentum factor working on a really high sharp.
What's happened really since then is that the momentum factor itself has seen a lot more dispersion. And so like everything else this year, we've just seen, again, a new trend take place where you have to get even more surgical with the way you think about implementing any of your exposure through options particularly.
Chris Hussey: Yeah, that seems to be the theme of this conversation here, right? We have dispersion in fundamentals as competition picks up in the AI trade, and we have dispersion in the market that is helping to play that. Okay, put a bow on it. What's the trade?
Lee Coppersmith: I think the easiest place to go hunt right now is particularly outside of the AI space. We like biotech here.
Chris Hussey: Wow.
Lee Coppersmith: We think it's a space that offers a lot of secular properties, just like some of the AI trades previously. But now there's this window where you could potentially have a tailwind of lower rates, more M&A, and I do think the added layer of maybe more drug discovery going forward as a result of some of these AI companies could help lend itself to having more capital get attracted to that area.
Chris Hussey: Lee, terrific. Always a wealth of information. Really appreciate you joining us.
Lee Coppersmith: Thank you very much, Chris
Chris Hussey: Before I go, I want to make one comment. 45 years ago, I discovered that my mother had breast cancer. Since that time, my family has rallied around Breast Cancer Awareness Month, which comes every October, to help raise money for a cure. You've seen me wear pink throughout October. I encourage everybody to go out there, support breast cancer awareness, and the research that's working towards a cure.
That does it for this week's episode of The Markets. I'm Chris Hussey. Thanks for listening.

As the lack of GOP signs, Trump bumper stickers, and red hats—even in the conservative parts of America—augured, the Republican Party took a beating in Tuesday’s midterms. Capital is tilting East: Inside Asia’s AI gold rush
[Music]
Sjoerd Leenart: Welcome to J.P. Morgan's Making Sense channel. I'm Sjoerd Leenart , CEO and head of J.P. Morgan's banking business in Asia Pacific. I look after our strategy and operations across 17 markets in Asia. And today I'm joined by Joyce Chang, chair of global research at J.P. Morgan, to discuss the key takeaways from the investor seminar that we hosted around the IMF World Bank annual meetings, which had returned to Bangkok for the first time in 35 years. Now, Joyce, since the last time you were in Bangkok, the region's GDP has grown nearly ninefold since 1998 to four and a half trillion faster than that of most emerging and developed markets. The 11 countries of Southeast Asia are home to nearly 700 million people and taken together, they would rank as the world's fourth largest economy. The Association of Southeast Asian Nations forms one of the most cohesive and effective associations in the world, next to the European Union. Joyce, it was absolutely great to have you in Bangkok with our clients and J.P. Morgan's senior management team to witness the tremendous growth and opportunities that we see in Asia.
Joyce Chang: Oh, well, Sjoerd, thank you so much. It's just wonderful to be with you. It was my second tour at the IMF World Bank meetings in Bangkok, hosting investor meetings with developed markets and emerging markets policymakers. I was last hosting these meetings in Bangkok in 1991, a year that I was out of graduate school. And during the first decade of my career, I spent a lot of time in the region. And back then, the focus was different. It was on how countries could integrate into a more open global order. Well, today that order is fragmented. Markets are repricing the cost of capital, energy, and access to trade. And the questions have shifted from how to integrate to who pays for security, debt sustainability and resilience. There's just so much to discuss. So Sjoerd, before we get into what we took away from the conference, I really would love to have you talk about your priorities in the ASEAN region and in Asia more broadly.
Sjoerd Leenart: Well, there's a lot of tailwinds that are propelling economies and businesses in Asia. There's what I call the manufacturing renaissance driven by AI data center demand and also the rewiring of global trades and manufacturing capacity. And you see places like Korea, Taiwan, Japan, and to an extent China, they're beneficiaries of that. And then there's certain policy actions that are driving growth. Think of the government stimulus in China, market reforms in Japan and Korea, and then there are places like India or Vietnam or Malaysia, which benefits from a China plus one strategy, but also the growth of domestic demand and the growth of their middle class. So all of that really has led to very divergent, but in totality regional GDP growth of 4.5%. And as you know, that's two, three times what we see in the US and Europe. And on the back of that, you see corporates being active, you see wealth being created, and you see capital markets being both active and very liquid. Now, when we go to a country, we intend to be there forever. So investments, they're going up, they're going down, but they never stop and they're broad based across all these 17 countries. More specifically, we're hiring people to cover the corporate sector, including increasingly mid-cap and innovation economy, private bankers to cover the growing number of wealthy Asian clients. And we're investing in our tech stack in equities, in payments and other products to ensure we are best in class in our delivery.
Joyce Chang: Sjoerd, it's really impressive what I see happening in the ASEAN region. They've really been able to find their place on the value supply chain. So maybe I can just talk a little bit about what we saw and what we heard at the conference on the global macro and the market outlook. What we've seen is that the global economy and markets have been remarkably resilient with AI investment offsetting the energy shocks, also the interest rate shocks that we've seen. But I think one of the concerns is that is this nearing its limits? We've seen some uneven outcomes between AI CapEx beneficiaries and energy shock vulnerabilities. So the IMF still has fairly constructive projections. They are looking at growth at 3.1% this year and actually increasing next year to 3.4%. But we also see a rise in global headline inflation to 4.7% because of higher commodity prices as well. But I think one thing that just struck me was that a lot of the IMF said that resilience is no cause for celebration and bringing very little joy. They're concerned about just the number of shocks the global economy has experienced. And they do point to the flexibility that has come from energy markets, AI related capital spending and fiscal and monetary supports. But they point out that the countries that are benefiting are narrowing, that just 32 countries in the world account for 95% of global growth, down from 54 back in April. But Asia, as you mentioned, Sjoerd, is a bright spot. The regional growth projections continue to be revised up because many countries are benefiting from the ongoing technology boom, notably Korea and several ASEAN economies along with China, India and Japan. But we've also seen some downward revisions in other parts of the globe. In particular, there's a lot of discussion on Europe's need to accelerate reforms to raise productivity and growth since they face aging populations, high energy costs and rising debt burdens in their economies. So we have seen strong performance from Asia, which we both note, but just more challenges in some other parts of the world.
Sjoerd Leenart: Now Joyce, I also wanted to ask you about the strong performance of the equity markets despite all the issues that are going on in the world, rising yields, higher fiscal deficits, heavy issuance across developed markets. What was the investor mood on the market outlook?
Joyce Chang: Well, the investor mood was that two things can be true at the same time, Sjoerd. Overall, even though there was recognition of the higher rates, sentiment was still positive on equities despite the prospect for higher for longer yields. But the prevailing tone compared to earlier this year was selectively risk on. There was more of an emphasis on quality and diversification rather than a universal stance that's tied to the AI CapEx boom. So we think that the AI CapEx plans will continue to drive the market higher over the near term, but there's more concern about the market's capacity to absorb the scale of AI and hyperscaling financing, particularly in the debt markets. And this is in large part because we've seen the surge in sovereign bond yields and developed markets and more competition and higher costs for capital. So compared to some of the conferences that we hosted earlier this year where fear of missing out was really the big driver, this set of meetings surfaced more direct questions about the return on investment and productivity gains. There was also a lot more discussion about second order effects and the growing threat of cybersecurity attacks. And these are greater concerns that we see surfacing across our clients and at J.P. Morgan as well. I do have to say one thing that really stood out to me was that the mood was very constructive on emerging markets. Emerging markets fundamentals are stronger in the cycle. Better external balances, more proactive inflation management, also better fiscal and debt dynamics when you compare it to the developed markets. And we see that policy, when we've met with all of the different central banks and ministries of finance have really anchored basic balances and the strong growth has attracted portfolio flows. We're looking at portfolios coming back to levels that we haven't seen in a number of years. So, Sjoerd I want to ask you, in Asia, we've seen that the AI related companies are half of the regional equity indexes, over 70% of earnings growth. And this is surprise on the upside. We've continued to have to revise these revisions up. How are you looking at the AI financing ecosystem broadly, particularly the build out in debt markets? Because it seems that the AI infrastructure is increasingly capital intensive and debt financed.
Sjoerd Leenart: It's certainly a rapidly emerging theme in Asia. And after the US, we expect actually most data center investments and activity to happen in Asia. There is a big need for computing power here in the region, both from the big Chinese companies, but also from the global hyperscalers who are looking for places where land, electricity, grids are sufficient to support their computing needs in the region. Now, like in the US, we do see some pushback from governments in places like Thailand, Australia, where governments and regulators have put certain projects on pause to assess whether demand for energy does not affect other industries or most importantly, the consumer. How all of it will be financed is, I guess for the market in general, remains a bit of a question mark. And I think here in Asia, we're working hard to find alternative sources of liquidity from private capital to public capital to the debt markets to help finance these projects.
Joyce Chang: Yeah, I really agree with those observations. I mean, from the meetings we have had in Thailand, we continue to see substantial AI CapEx. And most of the hyperscalers investment plans actually seem relatively insensitive to interest rates given some of the strong cash generation and strategic priorities. It's still a hyper growth regime given the earnings visibility. And we actually think that AI CapEx is going to increase to somewhere around one and a half trillion dollars or higher from about 900 billion this year. We see that the demand for computing capacity still exceeds available supply and these infrastructure bottlenecks probably will persist for another two or three years. But the profitability to us that stands out is strongest amongst the North Asian hardware suppliers. This is where we see semiconductor capacity growth that remains well below some of the AI related demand growth. And the leadership is still in place in semiconductors and hardware in Korea and Taiwan, which placed them at the center of the AI investment cycle. Memory chips have also emerged as a really critical component of AI infrastructure with their share of data center spending growing to nearly 50%. So Sjoerd, I want to ask you to talk a little bit more about China. We get a lot of questions about the US-China constructive strategic stability and also about the China 2.0 shock, particularly from our European policy makers. So many have observed that the US China Summit was high on pageantry, but maybe on the outcomes, not so much to talk about with a focus on constructive strategic stability. How have you seen the US-China relationship evolving and how are you looking at the nature of cross-border activity? Are companies more cautious about transactions?
Sjoerd Leenart: Yeah, like global investors, I think we were happy to see these meetings happen. Two have happened. Another two will likely happen this year. And it brings a degree of stability without really a long-term solution. So that's still to be seen. But China is a very big market, 18% of the global GDP. So both corporates and investors need to think how they want to position themselves. And we have to distinguish between those two groups when we think about their China strategy. Corporates, they invest for decades, financial investors, they can obviously move their money around quickly. And I think for the corporate sector, the competitive landscape and the behavior of Chinese consumers has definitely shifted and tariffs are also for them a very significant uncertainty. So, you do see caution and concern, but as I say, it's a big market and companies want to stay invested. So, you see a shift towards more localized operations and also enhancing the product portfolio with more local brands. Now with respect to financial investors, we do see a lot of activity in China. I would say particularly from hedge funds, given the enormous liquidity of the China Hong Kong market and the volatility of those markets. Now not only investors, I would say it's still more cautious as it's unclear whether the consumer, the Chinese consumer and the real estate market have turned a corner. When we look at the behavior of Chinese companies, they continue to go abroad without any pause, more so than ever looking for growth that they can no longer find domestically. And so Southeast Asia, Europe, LATAM, the preferred go-to destinations and the US for obvious reasons seeing less of that Chinese investment. And actually Hong Kong plays a very important role because most Chinese companies would run their regional or global operations through there.
Joyce Chang: No, Sjoerd, I completely agree with those observations. And what I really could see from being in the ASEAN region is that the ASEAN countries are a key beneficiary of regional supply chain reconfigurations in the AI tech cycle. And what we've seen is that China has steadily shifted manufacturing activities to the ASEAN region. Initially, it was to reduce labor costs, but eventually it's been to really adapt to the pivot that we've seen in US trade policy that has favored the ASEAN countries over China in terms of tariff differentials. And so I think that's been an additional tailwind to ASEAN's export performance. But we have seen that it's been a little uneven across the region. There's been a rising tide, which has really helped Vietnam and Thailand as the key recipients of Chinese foreign direct investment. I think that Malaysia and Singapore have also seen their tech exports soar, but Indonesia and the Philippines have lagged a bit due to the smaller manufacturing base. But I agree that we have seen just that a movement of capital and activity towards a variety of markets on China's side. So I want to talk a little bit about the China 2.0 shock because this has been top of mind, particularly as everyone is looking at more turbulence in the bond markets in France and in Europe more broadly. So, we see that China's exports are increasingly absorbing manufacturing output that domestic demand really cannot absorb in China. So a lot of questions have come up about the rebalancing and the consequences of this imbalance, raising concerns that Europe could be the main casualty from the China shock. We are seeing that German has greater direct competitive overlap with China than the US does across autos, manufacturing, machinery, chemicals, and other sectors. And that's made China's export gains more of a problematic for Europe and a larger drag on German's growth. We see that Europe has faced more setbacks here and they're looking at the possibility of adding more sort of trade barriers here, particularly when you look at the auto sector. But I still feel that from the discussions we had, that the recent China and European Union engagement still suggests that there's enough incentives there for both sides to negotiate rather than to enter an uncontrolled trade confirmation. So Sjoerd , I want to just see with you what your thoughts are on any particular opportunities that stand out or that you think will be ones that investors should focus on more in the years ahead or any underestimated risk on your side.
Sjoerd Leenart: Well, as you said, there is a focus on emerging markets and particularly on Asia that we sensed among investors in Bangkok. So I do think a gradual reallocation of money towards that region is happening. But it is, as you alluded to earlier, very uneven. The flows tend to move in and out much more so than what I observe in the US. This year, Korea and Taiwan were obviously darlings in the early parts, but have come off quite significantly. China and Hong Kong reversely have struggled this year after great 2025. And global flows into India have restarted cautiously, I'd say, after we saw 60 billion of outflows over the last two years. And equally in Southeast Asia, you see quite a dispersion between the performance of the markets. So I do feel investors will continue to have to be quite agile in how they reallocate their money between the different Asian markets.
Joyce Chang: Yeah, no, those are great points, Sjoerd . And one thing I just wanted to point out is this was a conference where we had a lot more discussion on cybersecurity risk, that along with global AI systems, they're only as strong as the weakest link and that cyber resilience is really something that will be a greater focus. And many of the discussions I think that stood out were that the number of cyber attacks is growing and that we see that these models can both discover and exploit the vulnerabilities and that what used to be a matter of months has come into hours and soon to minutes as far as the days to exploit these cyber vulnerabilities. So that was also one key takeaway that more focus will be needed on cyber resilience, the crisis preparedness, and also the oversight of critical third party providers here. So Sjoerd, I really want to thank you and the entire Asia Pacific management team for the hospitality. I'm just delighted that you were able to join us today to really bring your on the ground perspectives on what's going on in the Asia region.
Sjoerd Leenart: Well, Joyce, it was an absolute pleasure to have you in Bangkok and it is just unbelievable that you were there as a very young analyst 35 years ago to organize the same conference. It's grown a lot bigger and more important, but it's just wonderful that we had you for all these years with us. So thank you for everything you do for clients and for J.P. Morgan.

Southeast Asia’s economy has grown nearly ninefold since 1998, and the region is now at the center of the global AI investment cycle. In this episode of Making Sense, Sjoerd Leenart, CEO of J.P. Morgan’s banking business in Asia Pacific, sits down with Joyce Chang, chair of Global Research at J.P.
