articles.title: Daily: AI delivers despite volatility
articles.text:
Talk to a UBS Financial AdvisorFrom the studioVideo: CIO Monthly | Mark Haefele on AI earnings, energy prices, interest rates (4 mins)Video: Why China's equity markets have lagged (6 mins)Thought of the dayNasdaq futures are pointing 1.2% lower ahead of the US market open on Thursday, after Alphabet shares fell almost 10% in after-hours trading on Wednesday and Samsung Electronics slid over 4% following their respective results. Alphabet’s September-quarter sales from most of its core businesses came in below market expectations, while Samsung’s chip operations missed estimates and capital expenditure expanded. The South Korean company also delayed the details of a new shareholder return plan until the end of January.But Alphabet’s cloud revenue growth accelerated, and Samsung’s record quarterly profits were nearly nine times higher than a year ago. Microsoft’s Azure Cloud also exceeded expectations, while Oracle beat estimates on both its top and bottom lines.The market reaction to the latest set of tech results underscores the elevated expectations going into the reporting season and a sharpening investor focus on AI monetization. Amazon’s results due later today are another catalyst to watch.Without commenting on individual companies, we think recent tech results reinforce our view that AI fundamentals remain robust overall and support our constructive outlook on the AI trade.The acceleration in cloud growth demonstrates hyperscalers’ ability to generate returns on their AI investment. With investors increasingly demanding evidence on AI monetization, the acceleration in cloud revenue growth is one of the key highlights in recent results. Alphabet’s Google Cloud posted a year-over-year revenue jump of 103%, up from 82% in the prior quarter, and 34% in the March quarter. Microsoft’s Azure grew 48% for the three months to September, compared with 43% for the June quarter, while Oracle’s growth also quickened to 62%, from 47%. All three companies offered a positive outlook for further cloud growth, saying that additional capacity could support the strong demand they are seeing in the pipeline.Monetization of AI products also showed encouraging trends. While cloud growth is a key metric in assessing the return on AI investment, there are increasing signs of monetization across AI products as well. Microsoft reported an eight-fold increase in large Copilot accounts, while Alphabet said its Gemini reached 1 billion users. A leading AI lab recently reported that compute costs are now less than 60% of its revenues, and that AI spending from its large enterprise customers only account for less than 1% of their total expenses.Robust capex should continue to support the compute complex amid robust demand. Microsoft reduced its 2026 capex guidance slightly, from USD 175bn to USD 170bn, but stated that investment will accelerate in the coming year. Alongside Meta’s recent equity raise and Alphabet’s signal of significant capex increase in 2027, we believe the robust growth in overall AI capex should continue to benefit quality semiconductor and hardware names, driving the industry’s earnings growth. While funding pressures and execution risks at specialized AI cloud providers warrant caution, rising GPU rental prices point to still robust demand for AI compute capacity amid supply constraints.So, we think AI remains a key growth engine for markets, and we continue to see opportunities in hyperscalers as well as high-quality semiconductor and hardware companies. Investors, however, should manage overly concentrated positions by considering exposure to more defensive areas of tech and diversifying across sectors and regions. Those willing and able to tolerate associated risks can use structured strategies with capital preservation or yield generating features to manage potential volatility.

articles.title: What the Democratic sweep means for markets
articles.text:
Investment Talks

Elections

Geopolitics

Politics

US

Fiscal policy

5 November, 2026

14 minutes

What the Democratic sweep means for markets

EDM

Investment TalksENFR

What the Democratic sweep means for markets

14 minutes

EDM

Investment TalksENFR

Summary

Increased constraints on President Trump, but not a policy reversal: Congress will have greater oversight of foreign policy, funding and appointments, while President Trump retains significant executive authority. This points to more political gridlock, which may constrain policy activism but not fully restore discipline.At the macro level, less fiscal stimulus and greater regulatory scrutiny: increased congressional oversight should limit the scope for further fiscal stimulus. However, this is unlikely to deliver meaningful deficit reduction. Markets would distinguish reduced legislative uncertainty from a genuine improvement in the fiscal trajectory. Greater regulatory scrutiny, particularly of AI and Big Tech, could also slow investment in selected areas, even though more careful consideration of capex and regulatory oversight on AI security may now be welcome.Iran and AI are the two key policy fault lines. Congress may push to reduce funding for the Iran war and challenge tariffs, potentially easing pressure on oil prices and inflation. At the same time, greater scrutiny of AI, Big Tech and data-centre development could weigh on technology investment and valuations.The market reaction points to relief and rotation. The market reaction reflects lower political uncertainty, with bonds benefitting, the dollar weakening and equity leadership broadening beyond US technology. AI, data centres and defence face greater policy risk, but the underlying investment themes remain intact.Investment implications: not a game changer, seek broader diversification in equities. The result is mildly positive for global fixed income, as it could lead to lower inflationary pressure. In US bonds, we continue to favour intermediate maturities. In equities, the election result favours diversification into non-US equities and non-tech sectors.

How is the market reacting to the election result?

The initial market reaction suggests that the blue wave was broader than expected, but not fundamentally surprising. The early sell-off quickly reversed as investors looked beyond the scale of the shift and focused on the removal of a major source of uncertainty. The immediate message is relief – not enthusiasm for the outcome itself.This is not a classic risk-on move. Government bonds are rallying, the dollar is weakening and precious metals are rising. With expectations for the next Fed meeting broadly unchanged, lower yields appear to reflect less risk of an additional fiscal impulse, incremental Treasury supply and term-premium pressure – rather than hopes of easier monetary policy. Gold and silver are benefiting from lower yields and a softer dollar, while retaining value as hedges against future political and institutional confrontation. Acceptance of the result and a less confrontational foreign-policy tone have also reduced immediate tail risks, helping oil retreat.Equity dispersion shows where policy concerns remain. In the US, materials, financials, health care and consumer staples are leading, while technology is participating less fully and energy and industrials are lagging. AI and data-centre names are pricing concerns over tighter permitting constraints, while defence is exposed to greater budget uncertainty. Neither theme is collapsing, however, suggesting that the market is repricing targeted policy rather than a rupture in the earnings regime. The broader rotation is equally revealing. Small caps are outperforming large-cap technology, while European equities and cyclical sectors are benefiting from lower yields and a narrowing US policy premium. This looks like a broadening away from concentrated US growth and pre-election policy winners toward assets benefiting from lower yields, reduced policy exceptionalism and a broader global opportunity set – not a rejection of US risk assets.Options markets went into the vote priced for movement but positioned for relief. Elevated volatility, along with call demand and risk reversals, pointed to a constructive post-election bias. The softer volatility curve and equity rebound suggest uncertainty is clearing to the upside.

Markets price less uncertainty, tighter fiscal constraints, and stronger oversight – not a policy revolution.

The implied message is clear: markets price less uncertainty, tighter fiscal constraints, and stronger oversight – not a policy revolution. Markets today are pricing greater political clarity, but policy risks persist. Reduced legislative optionality does not eliminate execution discretion. The remaining risk is that legislative constraint becomes confrontation through budgets, the debt ceiling, investigations or restrictions on AI investment. For now, clarity and upside optionality are outweighing policy anxiety.

What is the likely election impact on domestic policy?

The Democrats’ message during the election was aimed at Big Tech, AI, and alleged corruption in the administration. Therefore, pushback against the AI data centre buildout should be expected, as well as greater scrutiny of Big Tech. In addition, there are likely to be investigations into President Trump and his administration around his business interests and conflicts of interest; therefore, expect a lot more domestic political noise. Furthermore, as the Senate also confirms Supreme Court justices, Democrats can now block judicial nominations.Importantly, in the Republican and Democratic parties the succession battle now begins. Both parties have big questions to answer over their political positions. The Democrats will see an internal battle playing out between the progressive and more centrist wings, while in the Republican Party MAGA and what it stands for will be questioned.

How do you see foreign policy changing following the election result?

The election results increase pressure on President Trump to de-escalate tensions with Iran, but also the risk of unpredictability.

Since the Democrats won the Senate by a larger margin than expected, they will be able to exercise greater oversight of President Trump’s foreign policy agenda. There will be more scrutiny and therefore more uncertainty. However, a weaker president does not necessarily mean a less assertive foreign policy. President Trump retains executive authority and can still push through his goals on foreign policy and tariffs. Further, since he is now significantly constrained at home, he will likely become more interventionist.In particular, the most immediate impact will likely be on Iran given that the cost of the war for US consumers has been a key issue in this election. While another round of escalation and US/Israeli attacks on Iran are widely expected in the short term, the election results increase the pressure on President Trump to de-escalate over the medium term also because Congress has greater oversight of funding. President Trump’s interests are now also likely to clash with those of Republicans seeking to succeed him. Nevertheless, the election outcome does not change the political realities in the region, and the likelihood of a return to the pre-war status quo remains low. The US has heavily built out its military presence in the Middle East and US and Iranian demands for a compromise remain far apart.Ukraine will likely benefit from more support and pushback against President Trump’s overtures to President Putin, as the Democrats will likely push for increased assistance and better security guarantees. Similarly, for Europe, the election results likely mean more sympathetic voices in Congress and more support for legislation to ensure that US troops remain in Europe. The election result also improves the outlook for US commitment to NATO. The next key piece of legislation to watch is the National Defense Authorization Act, due towards the end of the year, as it outlines US foreign policy priorities and authorises related funding. Nevertheless, there remains fatigue on all sides regarding US involvement in ‘foreign’ conflicts and the desire to reduce defence commitments. Finally, no major change should be expected in US policy towards China, although the results will likely increase support for US allies in South and East Asia.

What are the implications for the US economy?

The Democratic emphasis on redistribution, healthcare support, and benefits for lower-income households could support consumption at the margin.

The Democratic priorities would likely centre on redistribution rather than austerity, with a focus on healthcare. This would include efforts to reinstate the enhanced Affordable Care Act subsidies that expired at the end of 2025, reverse Medicaid cuts, and expand coverage. The emphasis on redistribution, healthcare support, and benefits for lower-income households could support consumption at the margin, but it would not necessarily materially boost it. The impact on inflation should be limited unless the Democrats secure the reintroduction of Obamacare-related subsidies, which we consider unlikely. As far as investments are concerned, a Democratic sweep should make tighter regulation more likely, probably focusing on areas such as consumer protection, labour impacts, environmental costs, energy consumption, and local permitting. Across the broader economy, given the geopolitical priorities of the current administration, we would expect continued emphasis on innovation, competitiveness, and faster infrastructure buildout in the race for AI dominance.In general, several measures cannot be adopted unilaterally. President Trump has already declared that he will exercise his veto power whenever he deems it necessary, and overriding such a veto would require a two-thirds majority in both chambers, which is clearly out of reach. That said, the new political landscape will create greater checks on presidential power. A Democratic Congress will create more friction for the administration, especially around judicial, regulatory, and Federal Reserve appointments. While the fiscal stance may become more neutral or possibly restrictive next year as stimulus fades, we do not envisage a credible path to a large-scale debt-stabilisation programme. Significant deficits would remain the backdrop, with the Congressional Budget Office baseline pointing to deficits of at least 5.6% of GDP over 2026–36.

What can we expect for markets?

At the margins, the result is mildly positive for global fixed income and mildly negative for AI stocks. Non-tech and international markets may benefit.

Looking ahead there are two major questions that may push markets in opposite directions.Will Congress look to reduce financing for the Iran war and roll back tariffs? If so, this could reduce inflation pressure by pushing oil prices lower and reducing taxes on imported goods. Will Congress want to regulate AI and slow the building of data centres? This could be a direct threat to the revenue growth of tech companies and drive stock prices lower across the sector.On fixed income, the election result is not a game changer, but at the margin can be seen as slightly positive. In the US, we keep a close to neutral stance on duration. We favour intermediate maturities, while we remain more cautious on the long end of the curve, where fiscal credibility and term premium remain key considerations.In equity sectors, AI/Tech names are under scrutiny, but a lot will depend on how much the Democratic Party can change the status quo. More broadly, the AI race is increasingly about execution, not just innovation. Eneregy availablity, infrastructure bottonecks and social accepance – all of which can be shaped by state and federal regulation – may determine the pace and geography of future AI investments. This calls for greater diverisication across the AI value chain, including power infrastructure, grid investment, compute and enabling technologies tied to AI applications. Investors may also seek rotation outside the tech sector and, geographically, beyond the US towards the rest of the world. Some data centre projects may be delayed, but it remains hard to imagine a regime change given the structural investment and the competition with China.With regard to the dollar, looking at past mid-term elections (12 episodes since 1978), the dollar has tended to weaken, with the effect building over the first 6 months, with the weakness looking more persistent in the sweep case and then fading back to flat over a 12-month horizon. Within G10 foreign exchange, the Swiss franc, New Zealand dollar and euro have been the main beneficiaries of dollar weakness at the six-month horizon. Meanwhile, the Japanese yen, Norwegian krone and Swedish krona show little directional bias, and their historical upside in our sample is small.

What the Democratic sweep means for markets

articles.title: No bank too big to fail, and none too small to resolve − speech by Ruth Smith
articles.text:
No bank too big to fail, and none too small to resolve − speech by Ruth Smith

Given at The Florence School of Banking & Finance Resolution Academy, European University Institute

Published on
23 September 2026

Ruth Smith discusses the Bank’s approach to managing small and medium-sized firm failure within the UK’s resolution framework. She emphasises the evolution of the resolution toolkit to ensure the regime remains robust for small and medium-sized firms, and reflects on the importance of transparency, proportionality and optionality.

Speech
Good evening, everybody. It’s a pleasure to have had the opportunity to listen to many of you over the course of today’s insightful presentations and discussions on banking resolution. Thank you to the European University Institute and Florence School of Banking and Finance for inviting me to speak today.    
Resolution is in many ways a team sport, and events like the Bank Resolution Academy are a real opportunity to learn from one another, understand the parts we each play, and look at what we can learn from a different viewpoint.    
Following on from today’s sessions on resolving medium-sized banks and the tools available to us in a resolution, I hope to provide a UK perspective on how the Bank of England prepares for resolving small to medium-sized firms.    
As you know, in the UK we have resolution regimes for banks and CCPs.  Today I am focusing on banks and will discuss what we mean in the UK when we talk about small to medium-sized firms and our approach to resolution planning for this large and varied group. I will also cover the lessons learned from the resolution of Silicon Valley Bank UK in 2023, and the new mechanisms we have added to our toolkit to improve optionality in a resolution while still seeking to lessen the burden on firms.    
Despite our recent experience of carrying out a resolution, and the improvements we have made as a result of that, there is still plenty of work to do when we consider resolution of smaller firms.   
The UK banking sector   
The UK has a diverse banking system, comprising some of the world’s large globally systemic banks right down to banks who have balance sheets in the tens of millions. This diversity requires flexibility in how our colleagues in the supervisory arm of the Bank of England, the PRA, apply their regulatory focus and equally needs us as the separate but collaborative Bank of England UK Resolution Authority, to tailor our approaches accordingly. Like any successful team, we each have distinct roles, but we are working towards the same objective of a safe and sound financial system.   
The UK remains a competitive and dynamic marketplace with multiple firms engaging in our pre-application process each year via the New Bank Start-up Unit, and the international presence remains strong, with firms of all sizes having UK subsidiaries and branches. Within the sector we see firms successfully entering, embedding their business, adapting to the demands of the marketplace, and in some cases exiting. This breadth of presence requires us, as the UK’s Resolution Authority, to be ready for those firm exits with a flexible and proportionate approach. Perhaps most importantly, we must be aligned to not only our teammates in the PRA, but where those subsidiaries and branches are part of a wider global group, to our resolution colleagues in overseas jurisdictions such as those here today.   
In practice then, what does this diversity of banking sector and tailoring our approach mean for UK resolution planning?     
We think about our banks in three broad groups,footnote [1] the first of which generally comprises our largest banks, where we plan for bail-in.    
We then have what we describe as mid-tier banks, typically with balance sheets in the £25-40 billion range, where firms can be set either a transfer or a bail-in as the preferred resolution strategy. For the firms currently in this range, we generally set a preferred resolution strategy which involves transferring these firms in resolution to a private sector purchaser, or, in the absence of a purchaser, temporarily to a Bank of England owned bridge bank – pending a further sale.    
Following an update to our policy on how much loss absorbing capacity firms must hold, or “MREL policy”, last year,footnote [2] unlike bail-in firms, transfer firms are not required to maintain MREL above minimum capital requirements. However, both bail-in and transfer firms are subject to the Resolvability Assessment Framework, or RAF. The RAF is our framework to assess UK financial firms’ resolvability and depending on the value of deposits held, some of these banks are also required to publicly disclose their own resolution self-assessment.    
In most cases, unless a firm with assets of less than £25 billion were viewed as posing a risk to financial stability, these smaller banks are then assumed to enter liquidation as a means of resolving their business if they are unable to either recover or complete a solvent wind-down. These are the firms we would use the Bank Insolvency Procedure or BIP for and do not hold additional MREL above minimum capital requirements or maintain additional capabilities to prepare for their failure.  BIP involves a rapid pay-out of depositors by the UK deposit guarantee scheme.footnote [3]  
As always there is judgement in setting a preferred resolution strategy, it is not solely based on a firm’s size and as such a transfer strategy can nevertheless be set in circumstances where the Bank assesses that a firm below the £25 billion mark would pose an unacceptable risk if it were to enter modified insolvency.    
Since the 2007-2008 global financial crisis the focus for resolution has rightly been on the largest, most systemic banks, those described as ‘too big to fail’. For these firms, the necessary team may well be large and international, and involve each person playing their role to produce the desired outcome of a smooth resolution.  And, as we look forward at an ever more interconnected system, operationally speaking, for not only our largest firms but smaller banks too, and join this together with our experiences of a small bank failure, we find ourselves working with the same teammates, and asking the same questions about stability and confidence in the wider sector as well as the impact of that failure on the bank’s customers. With this experience still relatively fresh in our minds it is this I want to speak about in depth.   
Our approach to small firms    
For our smallest banks, those typically defined as having less than £25 billion total assets, the plan for the majority of them should they fail is theoretically straightforward. Where a firm experiences severe stress which it is unable to recover from, the simplest solution is a director led solvent wind-down, allowing the firm to exit the market in an orderly manner while remaining a going concern. This enables the firm to stay in control of its own exit, minimising disruption to customers, creditors, and the wider market.    
Not all solvent wind-downs require active involvement from the resolution authority.  The PRA leads the assessment of whether a firm can continue to meet its obligations and execute an orderly exit from the market.  Where there are concerns about the firm’s ability to complete the wind-down solvently, the Bank, as resolution authority, works closely with the PRA to understand what alternative actions may be required, such as a BIP, should the firm’s plans prove no longer credible.    
Across all our work, the close relationship we have with the PRA is one of the most important aspects of our resolution framework. They are a teammate that we cannot be successful without.   
In the situation where a firm enters solvent wind-down, both authorities must be satisfied throughout that the firm’s wind down plan is credible, that it has sufficient resources to meet its obligations to depositors and creditors, and that allowing the firm to continue with their solvent wind-down plan aligns with our respective statutory objectives.  For a smaller firm, where a solvent wind-down ceases to be credible, insolvency may be the only remaining option.    
A BIP is a modified insolvency process. While the BIP shares many of the features of a standard insolvency process, it is specifically modified for deposit takers such as banks and building societies.    
Unlike an ordinary corporate liquidation, a BIP has a key objective of protecting covered depositors, which is done in two possible ways: payout or transfer. A BIP payout involves the insolvency practitioner or bank liquidator winding up the bank, whilst the Financial Services Compensation Scheme, the FSCS, carries out a rapid payout of deposits to the eligible depositors.    
Authorities in the UK have worked to significantly improve the speed and effectiveness of this payout process, learning from our European counterparts, to help ensure that protected depositors can regain access to their funds as quickly as possible. This speed of payout is important in maintaining public confidence in the efficacy of the resolution regime, and in the stability of the wider financial system.   
The second option is a BIP transfer, which involves the transfer by an appointed insolvency practitioner of the firm’s covered deposit book to another firm, with the insolvency practitioner winding up the remainder of the firm. For many of our smaller firms, the BIP provides a credible and proportionate resolution strategy.    
 So far so good and, hopefully, relatively straightforward and with minimal disruption.    
The boundary between BIP and transfer    
However, the small bank sector in the UK is highly diverse, innovative, and faces heavy competition. These characteristics have resulted in many of these smaller firms developing specialised business models which serve key customer groups, sectors, or communities that may not be well served elsewhere in the market or not be able to quickly and easily transfer their banking services to an alternative provider.   
The BIP is ultimately a liquidation procedure, and while it ensures covered depositors benefit from FSCS protection and payout, it is not designed to maintain the continuity of banking services.    
As such, customers of the failed firm may lose access to their existing banking relationships, payments may be disrupted, and those with uncovered deposits may need to wait for distributions through the insolvency procedure. For some smaller firms’ business models this may be acceptable, but for other firms, particularly where customers rely on continued access to banking services to operate on a daily basis, the impact can be significant and potentially outside the risk appetite of the collective authorities.    
This means that the picture in the UK is nuanced, requiring our assessments of whether a BIP would meet our statutory special resolution objectivesfootnote [4] to consider not only the size of a balance sheet, but also the nature of the customers it serves and the services it provides. As the Resolution Authority we need both a clear game plan and the ability to adapt it in real time.    
Lessons learned from SVB UK    
For the Bank, our experience with Silicon Valley Bank UK in March 2023 provides a powerful illustration of why flexibility in resolution planning is so important.    
At the time, SVB UK was a relatively small institution, with a balance sheet of around £12 billion and a preferred resolution strategy of BIP. Following the failure of its US parent and intervention by the FDIC, the Bank announced on Friday 10 March that, in the absence of further information, it intended to place SVB UK into insolvency.    
Based on what was known at that point, insolvency appeared to be the option that best met the public interest and the resolution objectives.   
As the situation developed over the weekend, however, it became clear that many customers relied on SVB UK not just for deposits, but for critical banking and payment services. At the same time, we needed to be cognisant of public confidence in the system against the backdrop of several other small bank failures in the US.   
We therefore kept multiple options open over the weekend, including insolvency. HSBC emerged as the credible bidder able to complete a transaction before markets opened on Monday while ensuring continuity of critical services, and with close liaison with FDIC throughout, and consultation with the PRA, FCA and HM Treasury, we concluded that a private sector transfer would better meet the special resolution objectives than a BIP.   
Unlike a BIP, the transfer provided protection for all depositors, not just those within the covered limits, ensured continuity of banking services, and most importantly protected and enhanced public confidence in the stability of the wider UK financial system in a way that did not incur costs on public funds.     
For me, this evidences that a preferred resolution strategy provides a vital starting point in contingency planning, but authorities need the flexibility, operational readiness and judgement to adapt quickly when executing a resolution as circumstances change in real-time. In the case of SVB UK, that flexibility was critical to achieving a better outcome for customers, for financial stability, and for the public interest.   
With this in mind, I want to speak to three key takeaways from this, our most recent experience of a bank resolution - transparency, optionality and international cooperation.     
Transparency   
First, SVB UK underlined the importance of a transparent resolution regime and communicating clearly and openly with markets, and authorities. The UK’s resolution framework relies not only on the Bank’s powers as resolution authority, but also on firms, investors, and other market participants understanding how these powers are used in practice, so that they can react accordingly.    
During the resolution weekend for SVB UK, both regulatory and finance ministry authorities worked together to consider multiple strategies in parallel. While this demonstrated the flexibility of the UK's framework, it also reinforced the value of ensuring there was common understanding about how different resolution options would be executed in a live event - between authorities, potential buyers, and the firm itself. Success depended on everyone understanding their role and how the wider team would operate under pressure.   
To bolster this shared understanding, in April we published the Bank’s operational guide to transfer resolution. The guide explains how the Bank would use its transfer powers in practice, whether the transfer involves selling the failed firm to a private sector purchaser, or placing it into a temporary bridge bank owned by the Bank of England.    
It aims to provide greater transparency around the key stages of a transfer, including preparatory work for both us and the firm, buyer engagement, transaction execution, and the information needed to support an accelerated sale process.    
By setting out these operational arrangements publicly and in advance of a future stress, the guide explains that transfer is not simply a theoretical power, but a credible and operationally deliverable resolution strategy. It helps firms better understand what may be expected of them, including the importance of maintaining the information and capabilities needed to support a rapid transfer if required.  It provides transparency to all potential stakeholders within a transfer, including prospective buyers, on how the bidding process would run for a transfer, improving the quality of bids, the competitiveness of an auction, and the smoothness of running the process overall.  
We applied the same learnings on transparency and communications to the Bank’s updated operational guide to bail-in resolution.  As firms grow, they face different resolution expectations. The guide provides greater clarity on how the Bank would execute a bail-in, giving firms, investors and other stakeholders a clearer understanding of the practical steps involved. In doing so, it supports preparedness, reduces uncertainty and reinforces the credibility of the UK's resolution framework across the full spectrum of firms.   
Optionality   
Moving on then to consider the optionality that our resolution framework gives us when planning for a firm failure. While the existing regime gave us an effective and flexible set of options that we were able to use to resolve SVB UK smoothly over a weekend, since 2023 we have continued to work very closely with our colleagues in HMT, our finance ministry, to introduce a new choice in our toolkit in the form of the recapitalisation payment mechanism.    
Introduced via the Bank Resolution (Recapitalisation) Act 2025, this tool is intended to cover associated losses or recapitalisation needs in a transfer via a new industry-funded safety net.    
Simply put, assuming the failing firm meets the public interest test, the recapitalisation mechanism allows us to cover certain costs associated with transferring a firm in resolution up front, be that to a private purchaser or a bridge bank, and then recover these from the industry via the financial services compensation scheme levy ex-post. This minimises the risk to public funds while providing options to use stabilisation powers to resolve a smaller firm when in the public interest.  We were fortunate that in the case of SVB UK the write-down of the regulatory capital was sufficient to enable us to transfer the firm to an interested and credible buyer – but this will not always be the case.  
Use of the mechanism may include recapitalisation of a firm during transfer due to a capital shortfall or potentially providing funds to the purchaser upfront and possibly in the form of guarantees to address any material concerns raised during the bidding process.    
For example, we recognise that the circumstances around a failing firm are often uncertain and extremely fast moving, resulting in limited time for due diligence to be conducted by interested buyers and introducing significant barriers which must be navigated to ensure a successful transfer.    
The new mechanism also gives us the space to be more proportionate in terms of what we require from small and medium-sized firms prior to a resolution. As I have noted, transfer firms are no longer required to hold MREL, in part due to the industry-funded safety net that this new mechanism provides.   
This flexibility represents a big step forward in strengthening our resolution toolkit. However, as always, we need to balance the needs of the failing firm with those of the wider financial system – recognising that any funds used to support the transfer are ultimately repaid by the wider industry.    
Importantly, it is not a replacement for BIP – an insolvency procedure is still a viable option for many firms and dependent on the scenario, may still be the right approach to take when considering our resolution objectives. While the use of the recapitalisation payment mechanism will always be situation specific, in all cases, the Bank will seek to use any funds in the most efficient and effective way possible, and the Act will not be used inappropriately to protect creditors from losses.    
This addition to the Bank’s resolution toolkit recognises that the UK runs a non-zero failure regime, and therefore it is important for firms to be allowed to grow but also be allowed to fail and exit the market smoothly – regardless of their size. It places a portion of that accountability back onto industry, not taxpayers, and ensures the Bank as Resolution authority has more options available to it and is ready for multiple failure scenarios without excessive burden on our smaller firms.   
International cooperation and coordination   
Third and finally, SVB UK underlined the importance of close coordination between authorities, particularly where a failing firm forms part of a wider international banking group.    
Effective resolution of cross-border firms requires more than financial resources and legal powers. It also depends on strong cooperation between home and host authorities, shared understanding of the firm's operational dependencies, and a common objective of maintaining critical services for customers. Like any team, it is helpful to train together before a match, and cross-jurisdictional exercises that allow us to practice and understand how we best work together are an important part of preparing for firm failure before the moment of stress arrives.    
While SVB UK involved close coordination between the UK and US authorities, the same principles would apply to firms operating across other jurisdictions.    
As banking groups become international, maintaining these relationships and coordination channels is an essential part of ensuring that resolution strategies remain credible and operationally deliverable.    
Conclusion   
What does the evolution of our framework mean in reality then? For me, it demonstrates that within the UK resolution regime, we have a robust toolkit that gives us confidence in having options to resolve small, medium and large firms.  
But looking ahead, I can still see areas of the banking sector where we could do more, particularly when it comes to small and medium-sized firms, to better prepare ourselves as authorities and prepare firms, in “peacetime”. I have spoken about how flexible options allow us to execute a resolution in more than one way for any given firm, in order to prioritise better outcomes for depositors while still protecting the public purse and wider financial stability.  
We often envisage using these options when presented with new information that challenges our original game plan during a resolution. However, I consider that we can do more to ensure we are always ready, by working with supervisors and firms to use their existing data and regulatory reporting to identify where they may be on the boundary of a BIP or transfer strategy in advance.   
As trailed in our update to the MREL policy last year, we are reviewing the indicative threshold of 40,000 to 80,000 transactional accounts as an intervention point for when a transfer strategy may need to be set for a firm under £25 billion in total assets. In part, this review is taking into account that the recapitalisation payment mechanism gives us more optionality for firms that do not hold MREL, and that consumer banking behaviour has changed since the threshold’s original implementation, making it less in step with the judgements we have to make when setting preferred resolution strategies.   
However, by removing the burden of MREL for such firms, we still need to ensure that we can execute a transfer effectively.  As part of this review, we are working with the PRA to ensure our resolution planning and reporting policies reflect these recent developments. This includes considering the information we require BIP firms to report on regularly. Are we asking the right questions? Is there existing data that firms already have through recovery and solvent exit planning that would better support our shared readiness for resolution planning as a BIP or in preparation for a transfer strategy in the future?  
With a more established resolution regime we must ask ourselves these kinds of questions to ensure we are continually improving and evolving our approach to firm resolution across the sector. I expect that we will publish our updated approach in early 2027 and look forward to hearing industry views in due course.   
A firm’s resolvability journey is never done, and as such our job as resolution authority isn’t either. No single authority can deliver resolution alone; it remains, at its core, a team effort and we will all need to remain live to an evolving sector to ensure our capabilities and policies are in step with the firms we regulate. The world rarely stays still and advances in technology, how firms operate and where the next risk may arise from is a horizon that we must keep at the front of our mind when considering barriers to an orderly resolution. Firms are a part of our team in a resolution, and I hope by continuing to work closely with one another, we can maintain readiness through a proportionate and effective resolution regime.   
I would like to thank Mala Gopalakrishnan, Kat Hind and Amanda Tennant for their help in preparing these remarks. I would also like to thank Geoff Davies, Charlotte Gerken and Dave Ramsden for their helpful comments.

articles.title: A future in another city? How migration costs shape young people's college choices: Guest post by Merve Demirel
articles.text:
Published on
Development Impact

A future in another city? How migration costs shape young people's college choices: Guest post by Merve Demirel

Development Impact Guest Blogger

November 05, 2026

This page in:

English

English

This is the first in this year’s series of posts by PhD students on the job market.
A central puzzle in economics is how massive income disparities over space can persist. If the gains from migrating are so large, why do people stay in places with fewer opportunities? Economists often infer that there must be costs that prevent them from leaving. Some of these costs, such as the monetary cost of transport, can be observed and counted. But estimates of these costs are usually not high enough to explain why people don’t move, suggesting other costs may matter more.
Other costs—feeling unsafe, lonely or unhappy away from home—can be harder to observe and quantify. As a result, we know less about their importance in shaping migration decisions, and whether people anticipate them accurately. This matters for policy design: if people stay put because of excessive fears of what they will experience if they migrate, then information could help alleviate these fears, and a contact who has already moved may be the best person to provide it. But if their beliefs about the costs of migration reflect true conditions at the destinations, policy that aims to encourage migration may instead need to make life away from home safer and easier.
To understand the expected costs of migration, and whether expectations change through contact with a migrant peer, in my job market paper I ran two experiments with 1,682 high-school students in two districts of Maharashtra, India, together home to more than seven million people. I followed them through their final year of school as they made their first major migration decision, and one of the most consequential of their lives: where to attend college.
My first experiment, a choice experiment, reveals that migration costs are large, rise sharply with distance, and are tied to students’ expectations about safety, happiness and loneliness away from home. My second experiment evaluates a mentoring program that connects high-school students with college students who had left home to study, showing that such a contact can raise applications to colleges elsewhere in students’ own district from 18 to 23 percent, but not to the major education hubs farther away, where mentors study.
What does educational migration offer?
Students in my study come from 52 schools, which are broadly similar to public schools in the two districts. They are preparing to apply to college, and interested in learning more about their options. Many can continue studying at home, but looking further away, beyond their district can expand the number of programs they could typically qualify for by tenfold. Many of the most selective programs are in the state’s major education hubs, such as Pune and Mumbai, which also offer better-paid jobs.
Students understand the potential returns to migration. More than half expect studying away to lead to jobs paying higher salaries after graduation, even after accounting for living costs. Yet the majority still prefer to study near home, even among those who expect to earn more elsewhere. This points to migration costs high enough to outweigh those gains.
Experiment one: how large are migration costs?
The magnitude of the salary gains that students would be willing to give up to avoid migration reveals the value of the perceived costs of migration in monetary terms. The first experiment therefore presents students with pairs of hypothetical colleges and asks which they would choose if admitted to both. The colleges’ locations and their graduates’ expected earnings vary experimentally, and tuition and living expenses stay fixed within the student’s budget. Since the survey also served as the application to the mentoring program, and responses were used to match students with mentors, students had an incentive to answer truthfully.
On average, students are indifferent between colleges at home and away only if migrating more than doubles their expected salary, with women requiring about three times as much as men. The required increase rises with distance: students see moving to a nearby city within their district and moving to major educational hubs several hours away as substantially different choices (Figure 1).

To unpack these costs, I also asked students what they expect life to be like in each destination. Away from home, they expect to feel less safe and less happy. They also anticipate lower parental approval, weaker ties with family, fewer friends, and greater difficulty managing daily life. Women are particularly concerned about safety, parental approval, and what others would think.
Experiment two: can connections to a migrant peer decrease expected migration costs?
How well-informed these fears are is unclear. Students have few sources of information about colleges and student life elsewhere. Nearly 30 percent know no one to ask for college advice, and half have no relatives or friends in other destinations. Those who do know someone in a city expect to be happier and safer in that city, but they may differ in other ways from those who do not, so this pattern cannot tell us how providing a connection would change beliefs and choices. That is the question the second experiment asks.
For this experiment, I developed a phone-based peer mentorship program to help students make more informed college choices. I randomly offered half of the students a place in the program, which ran throughout the academic year.
Each student was matched with a same-gender college student who had left home to study in Pune or Mumbai, two of the most common destinations for those who move outside of the district, where possible in the field and the city that the student was most interested in. They spoke about college choice and applications, but also about other aspects of moving to that city: housing, transport, safety, budgeting, making friends, and what daily life in a new city could look like.
Students offered mentorship became more likely to apply to study away from home, by four percentage points from a control mean of 34 percent, and to move away, by three points from 22 percent. A pre-specified index of educational migration that combines overall progress in higher education with migration rose by 0.16 standard deviations.
However, the induced applications and moves stayed within the home district, where migration costs were smaller to begin with (Figure 2). There was no corresponding increase toward the more distant hubs, where the mentors study.

The effects were driven by men, whose applications away from home rose by ten percentage points. Women’s did not change, which may not be surprising given the much larger migration costs they expect.
Beliefs at the end of the experiment follow the same pattern: mentorship lowered what men expected it would cost to live in the nearest city. It did not improve students’ expectations about life in the more distant cities. Among women, those expectations became, if anything, less favorable.
What this means for policy
Migrating for education could help reduce spatial inequality and ensure that students access the best educational opportunities. But the two experiments show us that migration costs are a major obstacle to these moves. Light-touch interventions providing information on living costs, or scholarships, may be effective for the short moves, where migration costs are small.
Moving farther to large cities is different. It is where the potential gains are largest, with access to more selective programs and better-paid jobs. But students expect much larger practical, social and emotional costs when moving far. Talking to a peer who had left home to study neither improved those expectations nor made a distant move more attractive.
A natural response to large migration costs is to bring education closer to students, for example by expanding colleges in smaller towns. But to the extent that good jobs require migration after graduation, investing only in local education may leave students in places with fewer opportunities. If policy instead aims to connect students to educational opportunities farther from home, this might mean lowering migration costs at the destination, such as providing safe housing, practical help with moving, or support that continues after arrival.
Merve Demirel is a PhD student at the Institute for International Economic Studies, Stockholm University.

Dear Merve - fascinating findings, resonating very much with our own from observed migration patterns in Tanzania elaborated on in this co-authored VoxDev blog (https://voxdev.org/topic/migration-urbanisation/proximity-over-pay-why-small-towns-attract-migrants). Linking the findings to the more widely observed migration patterns across towns and cities (many more rural residents moving to towns than to cities despite larger gains from moving to cities than to towns), we also find how the costs of migration (not just transport costs as you highlight) continue to trump the gains from agglomeration. As you, we also believe it draws attention to the role of towns and the importance of supporting towns (including through educational institutions/university towns) in fostering development and poverty reduction, especially also as smaller urban entities may suffice to capture the available economies of agglomeration in low and middle income settings. articles.title: Mercado Bitcoin Hack: $10M in Stolen Funds Frozen by Chainalysis
articles.text:
Early this morning Mercado Bitcoin, Brazil’s largest crypto exchange, suffered a security incident that resulted in approximately $49 million in stolen funds. As a Chainalysis customer, Mercado Bitcoin alerted our team in the early hours of the incident. We immediately mobilised our global team of investigators to lead the blockchain intelligence response, working closely with Mercado Bitcoin, law enforcement, and industry partners to help freeze nearly $10 million in stolen funds.Chainalysis analysts from three continents logged into our digital war room to discuss the flow of funds and coordinate a response plan.Our team focused on three immediate priorities:
Identify, trace, and label stolen assets, establishing the initial movement of funds and making relevant intelligence available through Chainalysis products.
Identify opportunities for intervention, prioritising assets that could potentially be frozen or otherwise secured.
Coordinate action with external partners, rapidly disseminating actionable intelligence to law enforcement, stablecoin issuers, and other relevant organisations.
How the attack happenedIn the early hours of November 2 an attacker began moving assets held across 17 blockchains, working in waves to drain an estimated $49 million in various cryptocurrencies. The largest tranches came from Bitcoin and Ethereum, but assets on smaller blockchains, like Base, Tron, and Polygon, were also swept.How Chainalysis responded to the hackThe first few hours of any hack are the most important for investigators. In that window of opportunity they can help freeze some assets, like centrally-issued stablecoins, before the attackers are able to convert them into harder-to-disrupt cryptocurrencies, like BTC and ETH.For that reason, Chainalysis investigators worked from Hour 0 researching what assets had been taken, which of those assets could be frozen, and who outside the company needed to know it.At 2:30 am Eastern Time a Mercado Bitcoin director phoned our in-country solutions expert with the news: the exchange had been hacked. He shared with our expert a list of the unauthorized transactions, and our investigator began mapping it out.Within 30 minutes we made contact with law enforcement to relay freezable addresses. Before long we were also in communication with stablecoin issuers, helping them understand opportunities to disrupt the theft. By the time morning had arrived we had helped lock down $4 million in stolen stablecoins. Over the coming hours our work led to $9 million in total freezes.Over the course of this hack we communicated directly with Paxos, Anchorage Digital, Ripple, Circle, and Tether, working together with law enforcement to shut down stolen stablecoins issued by them.For example, our investigators identified stolen funds held in USDT and rapidly traced them to addresses where the assets could potentially be frozen. Using our established relationships with Tether and law enforcement, we escalated the relevant addresses and supporting intelligence, enabling Tether to take action and freeze over $4 million in stolen funds.This was not simply a case of tracing assets on the blockchain. It required our investigators to identify an opportunity for intervention, understand which organisations could act, and rapidly coordinate the necessary response.”What happens nextOur involvement doesn’t stop with the initial freezes. We’re continuing to trace the remaining funds, monitor their movement, and identify further opportunities for intervention.The funds will keep moving and labeling addresses tied to the theft helps keep that activity visible. By sharing relevant intelligence with partners positioned to act, we can help the wider ecosystem recognize stolen funds and respond as they move. The ten-year Treasury rose above 5% in September 2026, a level it has reached only once since 2007, briefly in October 2023.¹ With upward pressure on the yield curve, the spread between institutional real estate yields and the ten-year is about a fifth of its long-run average. Similarly, the all-sector NCREIF index yield is approximately 90 basis points less than Baa-rated corporate bonds, which historically yielded a little less than real estate, not more.² The Treasury is a real benchmark again.

Our view is that real estate offers a selective set of opportunities despite elevated benchmark rates, and we believe that as market conditions change, more attractive opportunities are likely to emerge. We see opportunities today where current income or income growth pays for the excess risk over the ten-year Treasury. Where it does not yet, the conditions that would need to change are specific, which we describe in subsequent sections.

The question for each type of real estate is simple: is the investor paid for the risk?

articles.title: IFRS 9: expect scrutiny to continue
articles.text:
Strengthening banks’ resilience to geopolitical risks and macro-financial uncertainties is one of the ECB’s two leading supervisory prioritiesopens in a new tab for 2026-28, with prudent risk-taking and sound credit standards identified as a core goal.Earlier this year, we highlighted the ECB’s concerns over inconsistencies in banks’ application of IFRS 9. For example, the ECB has argued that banks’ use of overlays is insufficiently risk-sensitive and has found deficiencies in their capture of forward-looking risks, and varying approaches to staging and provisioning under the expected credit loss (ECL) framework.Since then, rapid evolutions in the global risk landscape – including rising geopolitical tensions, exceptional climate risks, and the AI boom – have driven a renewed supervisory focus on IFRS 9 and provisioning practices.Conversations with a wide range of banking clients across the SSM suggest that some of the most notable variations in banks’ interpretation and implementation of IFRS 9 include:

Around half of banks have not yet fully integrated Climate and Environmental (C&E) risks into their ECL models for different reasons. Progress on physical C&E risks is more advanced than for transition risks, and there is a significant range of approaches including the use of climate scenarios in modelling, in-model adjustments, and data-driven overlays.

Geopolitical risks account for a large share of post-model adjustments, often impacting staging decisions and estimates of ECL. Approaches to governance for overlays vary across banks, and there is room for improvement in some cases when it comes to transparency or justifiability.

Only around half of banks use the ECB’s preferred measure of a three-fold increase in the probability of default (PD) as a backstop for moving assets from Stage 1 (performing) to Stage 2 (underperforming). A significant increase in credit risk (SICR), typically comparing PD at reference date with PD at origination, is the main driver of Stage 2 transition.

Around half of banks plan to recalibrate their IFRS 9 frameworks within the next two years in response to emerging risks, the changing macro picture, or simplification initiatives.

Given the leeway that Advanced IRB banks have to model key drivers of their credit risk capital requirements - including probability of default (PD), loss given default (LGD) and exposure at default (EAD) – some variation in provisioning practices is unavoidable.However, it is inevitable for the ECB to be concerned when wide variations in IFRS 9 implementation lead to unjustifiable uneven impacts on banks’ balance sheets. In our view, banks should therefore:

Expect the ECB to keep asking questions about IFRS 9 sound implementation and bank specific practice.

Monitor ECB commentary and publications on best practice, as they evolve.

Prepare, where practice is not closely aligned with ECB expectations, for additional scrutiny by joint supervisory teams.

There is an inherent tension between IFRS 9’s accounting goal of producing true and fair financial statements, and the ECB’s prudential goal of strengthening institutional and systemic stability. Banks would be well advised to actively monitor and respond to evolving supervisory thinking in this crucial area.

articles.title: The importance of public engagement in maintaining trust in banknotes - Speech by Victoria Cleland
articles.text:
The importance of public engagement in maintaining trust in banknotes - Speech by Victoria Cleland

Speech at the Intergraf Currency & Identity Conference, Denmark

Published on
15 October 2026

Maintaining trust in banknotes is crucial to their continued demand and relevance. This requires more than robust security features and resilient infrastructure. Victoria Cleland explores how communications and public engagement can help build and maintain confidence and trust in cash.

Speech
Trust is essential to everything the Bank of England (the Bank) does. It underpins all our activities, from setting Bank Rate to operating payment settlement systems and much in between. And banknotes are among the most visible manifestations of that trust.
The Bank is the second oldest central bank in the world and issuing banknotes (originally promissory notes) was one of its earliest functions. Historically, confidence in banknotes was linked to their convertibility into gold. You can still see the words ‘I promise to pay the bearer on demand’ on our banknotes. While the nature of that promise has evolved over time and our notes are now indirectly backed by UK government bonds,footnote [1] the principle remains the same: banknotes derive their value from trust, and that trust must be maintained.
Every time someone accepts a banknote, they trust that it is authentic and worth the value stated. They have to be confident that it can be used again in the future: whether to spend it, save it or bank it. Without that trust, a banknote is simply an object, albeit with a beautiful design. With it, households spend, businesses trade and economies function.
Central banks play a crucial role in maintaining this trust in banknotes. We do so by ensuring banknotes are available, that the cash industry remains effective, resilient and sustainable, and that banknotes remain a secure method of payment.
Communicating openly with businesses and the public so that they can recognise and easily authenticate banknotes is also an essential part of maintaining this security. The Bank has engaged extensively with the UK public on the imagery for our next series of banknotes to ensure our banknotes remain recognisable as national symbols. This culminated in last week’s announcement that the Atlantic puffin, barn owl, buff-tailed bumblebee and European hedgehog will feature as the central imagery on our next series of banknotes.
I will now dive deeper into the Bank’s work to ensure this essential trust in our banknotes through availability, secure design and public engagement.
Ensuring trust through availability
The public need to trust that banknotes will be available when required. The Bank does not, and cannot, do this in isolation. Just as a beehive depends on its community of different bees performing complementary roles, maintaining trust in banknotes requires organisations across the cash ecosystem to work together.
Central banks, printers, cash centre operators, cash-in-transit companies, financial institutions and retailers are all important members of this ecosystem. They all play crucial and complementary roles in ensuring that the public can continue to access and use banknotes so that cash remains a trusted source of payments. At the Banknote Conference earlier this year,footnote [2] I spoke about the importance of preserving choice in payments and the role of cash in preserving choice. Ensuring that choice remains requires the whole industry to work together like an efficient beehive.
For the Bank, this includes issuing banknotes to meet public demand. The use of cash for transactions has declined over recent years, accounting for 8% of all transactions in the UK in 2025, down from 45% a decade earlier.footnote [3] But according to our research, cash is still the preferred payment method for one in seven people and, is used at least once a week by almost a quarter of the public. It is essential for some people and is seen as an important contingency by many.
And the value of Bank of England notes in circulation has continued to increase, reaching £91.5 billion at the end of February 2026. This demonstrates the enduring importance of cash to our economy and our society.
We are committed to meet the demand for our banknotes and to ensure that the right banknotes are available, in the right places at the right time. It is important to us that people and businesses who want to use cash can continue to do so. We do this by monitoring payment trends and a range of economic factors to inform demand forecasts and contingency requirements, and to help us decide how many banknotes we need our printer De La Rue to produce.
Authorities and industry must work closely together to ensure the cash cycle as a whole remains effective, resilient and sustainable. The wholesale cash distribution market is the underlying “plumbing” that gets cash to where it is needed, via cash centres through to ATMs and retailers. Last year, the Bank took on a new role to supervise firms in the wholesale cash industry who operate cash centres and their backing FIs.footnote [4] In addition, the Financial Conduct Authority has powers to protect retail access to cash for consumers. Together, these regimes will help ensure that cash will be available and accessible.
Ensuring trust through design
Another key component of trust in banknotes is counterfeit resilience: the public and businesses must be confident that the banknotes they receive are genuine. We do this by incorporating sophisticated security features into the design: these need to be both hard to counterfeit and easy to authenticate. For trust in the security of banknotes to endure, it is important that central banks change the design from time to time to incorporate the latest security features. This requires suppliers and manufacturers to innovate and invest in developing new technology and more resilient features. To maintain trust in banknotes, it is essential that this innovation continues.
When you picture a puffin, you may think of its distinct colouring including its bright orange beak. Did you know their beaks glow under UV light, just like our banknotes? These markings and photoluminescence are not purely about aesthetic appeal but also serve a functional purpose in helping puffins lure prey, deter predators and attract mates. Similarly, at the Bank, we need to design banknotes that are not only attractive but also designed with function, particularly security, at their heart.
Our next series of banknotes (Series H) is currently being designed. The driver, as with any new series, is to further enhance counterfeit resilience. And following public consultation, the new notes will celebrate UK wildlife. Images of wildlife will also support resilience, enabling us to incorporate intuitive movements into the security features which are engaging and easy for the public to recognise and distinguish.
Trust also stems from our notes being accessible to all. We are continuing to invest in banknote accessibility, running research on how people with disabilities use cash today and including tactile features to help people with visual impairments differentiate between denominations.
Ensuring trust through communication and engagement
Trust in banknotes is founded on availability and effective design, but sustaining it requires engagement – with businesses, law enforcement and the public. Even the most sophisticated security feature is only effective if people know how to use it to verify a banknote. And so public engagement and communication are a pivotal part of our anticounterfeiting strategy.
The Bank provides free educational materials, such as booklets and posters to help businesses and the public to authenticate banknotes. We also provide online training and run a free Banknote Checking Scheme to help businesses keep a watchful eye out for counterfeits: a vigilance one could compare to the barn owl which will feature on our next series. This Scheme has grown considerably, now covering over 50,000 business locations.
Recently, we have supplemented this by launching a communications campaign aimed at businesses. This campaign shows business owners talking about their own experiences and how using best practice banknote checking has enhanced their trust in banknotes. We also engage closely with law enforcement, including the National Crime Agency and local police forces, to help them investigate and prosecute potential counterfeiters.
Incorporating images that resonate strongly with the public and which they can easily recognise is also a key part of banknote authentication and maintaining trust. So last year, we launched a two-stage process to engage the public in the choice of imagery for the next series of banknotes.
In July 2025, we announced that we would introduce a new series of banknotes with even more robust security features. A new series necessitates changes to the imagery, so we launched a consultation asking the UK public which theme they wanted to see featured in the design. The Bank has been celebrating historic figures on our banknotes since 1970. However there are many ways to represent the UK so we wanted to hear the views of the public, the users of our banknotes.
Around 60% of respondents chose nature as one of the themes they wanted to see featured with many nominating specific native animals. And this March, we announced that in the light of feedback from the consultation, images of UK wildlife would feature on the next series of our banknotes. We worked closely with a panel of wildlife experts to create a shortlist of native UK animals and in June we launched a second consultation asking the public to help us choose which of the shortlisted animals to feature as the central imagery on the next series. We were delighted by the scale of the response, with almost half a million people participating.
The Bank’s overarching objective is to increase counterfeit resilience through secure design, and for this to be effective, it is also important that the new series represents the UK and resonates with the users. After all, banknotes are not just a means of payment, but also a shared symbol of national identity. This helps to promote trust and security, as familiar imagery which resonates with the public will mean they look more closely at their banknotes.
The importance of awareness and familiarity is not new. In 1797, when the Bank rushed to issue new £1 and £2 banknotes following gold shortages, counterfeiting surged as counterfeiters took advantage of people’s unfamiliarity with new banknotes. The lesson remains relevant today: when introducing a new series, issuers must bring the public along on the journey to ensure they can recognise and authenticate the notes.
To do this successfully and inclusively, central banks need to engage people through different methods including the platforms they use every day. To help publicise our most recent consultation, the Bank used an integrated communication strategy which included press, social media, engagement with schools and visiting local communities around the UK. We also collaborated with influencers to help us reach young people and audiences who may not have engaged with the Bank’s work in the past.
We opened the consultation with a launch event at the Wildfowl and Wetlands Trust (WWT) London Wetland Centre to celebrate the shortlisted animals and give journalists an opportunity to ask questions – both to me and the wildlife Expert Panel who helped us develop the shortlist of animals. This provided an engaging backdrop to create content about wildlife to help raise awareness and encourage participation in the consultation.
To sustain momentum, we produced a variety of engaging and accessible content with the aim to appeal to different audience groups and help convey our broader message. This included factsheets on each of the animals and educational posts showing how banknotes have evolved over time, as well as some more fun posts.
Alongside the formal consultation, we also visited schools and ran a design challenge for children across the country to give young people a voice in shaping our next generation of banknotes. And we held a number of in-person Youth and Citizens’ panels in communities including Llandudno and Devon. These were a great opportunity for the Bank to learn directly from people about the role that cash continues to play in society as well as their views on the shortlisted wildlife.
Conclusion
Trust in banknotes begins with secure design but only endures if banknotes are available and recognised. Keeping banknotes trusted and relevant requires innovation and strong collaboration across the whole of the cash industry. And this must be coupled with communication and engagement to enable businesses and the public to understand, recognise and trust the banknotes they use.
Our recent consultation gave people a voice, helping them connect with the banknotes they use and have a meaningful say about their future design. There will now be a quieter period in our communications about the next series, while our design work continues in the background, with security at its heart. Like the hedgehog emerging after its winter retreat, we will return when we are ready to unveil the first denomination.
I would like to thank Elijah Lee, Zahra Damji, Nick McLaren, Ellen Caswell, Stuart Cooper, Lauren Murphy, Kiran Keer, Millie Rettie and Lisa Young.

articles.text:

Mark Thomton
