News Release
Permitting reform is likely move for Democratic controlled US Congress
Bipartisan BAAJA paves way for fast-tracked energy permitting

04 November 2026
6 minute read

Email
Share by email

With Democrats capturing the House of Representatives and Senate in the US mid-term elections, permitting reform could be a top agenda for advancing power growth and reducing energy costs in the US, according to Wood Mackenzie analysis. The elections came amid rising energy costs driven by the conflict in Iran, which drove peak diesel and jet fuel prices in the US roughly 2.5 times higher than pre-war forecasts. Prices should ease as the conflict subsides, though the hardest-hit products will still be 30% above pre-war forecasts in 2027.
Congress has three policy levers to address energy affordability, each with very different odds:

Permitting reform: Bipartisan interest makes it, in Wood Mackenzie’s view, the likeliest route to faster gas, transmission and wind approvals. Nuclear, CCUS, and upstream get an incremental boost.
Subsidies for renewable energy: Democrats have proposed several expansions, but a presidential veto makes new credits unlikely.
Large-load cost rules: Federal mandates face legal and political resistance, so states will set cost allocation policy for data centers.

A Democratic Congress does not guarantee legislative success under a Republican White House. President Trump retains veto authority, and executive agencies can dilute the impact of any legislation that does pass. But permitting reform has a path that other Democratic priorities do not. The midterm results point to a sentiment shift in the US. The cost of energy has emerged as a check on the president's agenda, creating common ground for both parties on affordability.
With rapid development in data centers and power infrastructure, the US will see load growth lifted 3% from 2026 to 2035, driving wholesale power prices up 46% in Wood Mackenzie’s base case over the same time period and making affordability a likely key driver for permitting goals.
"While we see the likelihood for permitting reform, how policy is legislated and implemented remains a risk to the US economy," said David Brown, Director, global integrated energy research for Wood Mackenzie. "Entrenched partisanship could fuel policy stagnation and regulatory confusion."
Most likely option — Permitting reform
Supported by key Senate architects and a coalition of clean energy developers, oil and gas producers, mining operators and trade unions, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) could speed up infrastructure approvals.
Key initiatives include:

Mandates that environmental impact analyses under the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) are fully completed within two years
Prevents federal agencies from revoking permits
Limits litigation to a 150-day window after project environmental approvals are issued
Mandates a 9-month timeline for evaluating water quality dredge and fill permits required for new gas pipelines

Permitting reform matters most for front-of-the-meter gas-fired power, which is typically located away from gas supply basins and requires new pipelines to support Wood Mackenzie's forecast of 166 GW of net new natural gas-fired capacity from 2026 to 2035. Permitting reform would also remove regulatory delays for short laterals, pipeline interconnections, and compressor upgrades that are necessary for behind-the-meter (BTM) power. Wood Mackenzie reports BTM gas demand is approaching 6 billion cubic feet per day (bcfd), about 6% of US domestic gas demand excluding LNG and piped supply.
"Without reform, midstream bottlenecks are likely to return, stifling upstream investment and pushing regional gas and power prices higher, most acutely in the power-hungry Northeast," said Siddhant Warrier, research analyst, North American power for Wood Mackenzie. "Prolonged pipeline delays would also slow data center development, a high priority for both parties."
High-voltage transmission speeds up — but who pays is in question
With congestion costs exceeding $10 billion a year and high-voltage completions in the 2020s running at under half the 2010s rate, the need for faster grid buildout is urgent. BAAJA addresses the permitting side of that challenge, mandating one-year NEPA assessments, protecting against permit revocation, and limiting post-approval litigation to a 150-day window. The next legislative frontier will be inter-zonal cost allocation: who pays for a line that crosses multiple utility territories and benefits multiple states.
Wind: new legislation will help clear the permitting backlog
The Restoring Renewable Energy Parity Act would require the Defense Department to sign mitigation agreements for pending wind, solar and transmission projects and overturn executive actions targeting renewables. But wind carries added risk: the President has targeted it directly, and the federal government controls offshore leasing.
"The wind industry's best bet for permitting reform is to be included in a national bill across multiple technologies and to have Congress monitor implementation," said Warrier.
States step up as federal policy outlook remains uncertain
Should federal energy policy stall under divided government, state-level energy policies and market rules will take on even more importance. States hold broad statutory authority over retail electricity, utility regulation, and siting, cementing their independence from federal gridlock.
The midterm gubernatorial results highlight this dynamic. In Texas, the election of Gina Hinojosa as Governor marks a significant shift in data center policy. The incoming regulatory environment could increase execution risk for developers with longer permitting and community approval timelines if Hinojosa's platform becomes law in the January 2027 legislative session.
Texas will remain a leading market for data center investment given its renewable resources, natural gas infrastructure and regulatory autonomy from FERC, but the new Governor will push for new constraints on speed to power in the Lone Star State.
Supply chain: executive order adds new uncertainty
An August executive order restricting bulk-power equipment from 24 countries, including China, adds a further layer of complexity. Implementation rules due in late December will clarify exposure for grid-connected data centers. New restrictive policies under the order could exacerbate existing supply chain deficits, 18% for power transformers and 14% for substation transformers.
Can a sentiment shift solve big problems in the US?
"While we see the potential and likelihood for advancing permitting reform, there is a wider concern over how policy is created, managed, and implemented in the US," said Brown.
Brown noted that economic headwinds could create divergence, with Congress focusing on affordability issues and the Executive branch pursuing foreign policy agendas that create policy confusion and stagnation. Veto power from the White House could derail significant advancements as well.
"The US has had moments of bipartisanship when it needed them most. Twenty years ago, Democrats took Congress amid an unpopular US-led war in the Middle East, resulting in deep partisan gridlock," Brown continued. "But the Energy Independence and Security Act of 2007 raised Corporate Average Fuel Economy (CAFE) standards, set lighting and appliance efficiency standards and expanded renewable fuels with bipartisan support. A similar effort is needed now to build affordable energy at home and for the US to keep global leadership in AI."

articles.title: Why generals need economists to win long wars
articles.text:
Blog Name

RealTime Economics

Why generals need economists to win long wars

Elina Ribakova (PIIE)

Date
October 30, 2026 1:15 PM

Photo Credit: Hans Lucas via Reuters

XLinkedInBlueskyEmailShare

Body
The US National Defense Strategy(link is external) published by the Trump administration in January 2026 reassures allies that the European component of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) "dwarfs Russia in economic scale, population, and, thus, latent military power." Non-US NATO GDP is $26 trillion compared to Russia's $2 trillion. Their economic clout is not even close. But this comparison is misleading. At purchasing power parity, which reflects the purchasing ability of different currencies, Russia's military spending is almost the same as that of the European Union and the United Kingdom(link is external).
On the other hand, Russia's economy(link is external) itself is more than 10 times the size of Ukraine's. Yet four and a half years into an invasion Moscow expected to finish in three days, Ukraine is still fighting back.
In a different part of the world, Iran's economy(link is external) is barely 1 percent the size of the United States' economy. Yet over the eight months of war, Tehran has tied down US forces, burned through half to two-thirds of US missile defense interceptors that will take at least five years to rebuild(link is external), and is still holding global energy markets hostage, while driving up US inflation. Composite measures such as the Composite Index of National Capability(link is external) narrow the gaps, but they measure potential, not mobilization.
What explains this imbalance between the size of an economy and its ability to wage war?
If countries seek to convert economic power into military success(link is external), economists and the military need to cooperate more closely. Indeed, economists' contributions grow in importance as wars settle into long wars, wars of attrition, or asymmetric conflicts. In such cases, economic management must be part of military strategy, not just a backdrop.
Of course, economists cannot replace the military's ability to deploy armed forces(link is external). Nor can economists replace bargaining: Wars still end at the negotiating table(link is external). But converting economic power into military power determines how long each side can hold out and how much each side can afford to lose, thus setting the stage for negotiations.
A proposed new research agenda on the economics of war
This blog post presents a brief overview of the current literature on the economics of war(link is external)—much of it outdated and siloed in the different disciplines of economics, international relations, and political science—and maps out a research agenda, highlighting what work has been done and what still needs to be done rather than attempting to resolve central questions. Four building blocks—generating resources, converting resources into military capabilities, denying resources to an adversary, and staying in power—can help us understand how economic size becomes sustained fighting power, where that conversion breaks down, and what economists and military specialists need to understand together.
For example, nationwide mobilization requires paying for production, finding cost-effective ways to wage war, mobilizing the right number and type of people, adopting new technologies faster than the adversary, and denying the other party resources through economic warfare. These imperatives raise economic issues as much as military ones.
The post Cold-War record indicates that economists and generals rarely work together, except in rare cases like Finland, Singapore, and increasingly Russia and Ukraine.The absence of a large-scale war between industrial states in recent history has erased wartime economic expertise from institutions on both sides. Defense studies have recently begun to take an interest in the economics of mobilization(link is external), and the economics profession should refresh its own frameworks for the economics of war.
Historians of past wars—including Paul Kennedy(link is external), Mark Harrison, and Stephen Broadberry in their comparative volumes on the First(link is external) and Second(link is external) World Wars, and Alan Milward(link is external) in the postwar period—have shown that productive capacity shapes outcomes over the long run. Recent work has advanced individual topics. Economists Jonathan Federle, Dominic Rohner, and Moritz Schularick find that windfall revenue gains raise a country's odds of winning(link is external), enabling them to increase military spending. Political scientist Rosella Cappella Zielinski explains how states choose to pay for wars(link is external). Economists Jeffrey J. Schott of PIIE; Edward Fishman(link is external), author of Chokepoints; and the historian Nicholas Mulder(link is external) trace the rise of sanctions as a tool of modern war. Mark Harrison now distills lessons for defense industrial policy(link is external), among them that costs matter in long wars and autarky is a costly delusion, and Phillips Payson O'Brien, strategic historian, argues, controversially, that wars are won by full-spectrum powers(link is external) able to sustain them. The field even has its own journal Defence and Peace Economics(link is external). The recent wars suggest that it is time to bring it back to the mainstream.
The four building blocks that can help us understand the importance of economics as it relates to war are as follows:
1. Generating resources: Mobilizing funding and labor, and related trade-offs
War finance depends on the speed and credibility of mobilizing capital and the trade-offs between taxation, debt, money creation, and, increasingly, reliance on external financing. The core choices are how much to finance through taxes versus debt, with which instruments, particularly which taxes, and which nominal or inflation-indexed bonds.
The economist John Maynard Keynes's volume How to Pay for the War(link is external), written nearly a century ago for an economy constrained by supply rather than demand, remains an important part of the debate on rearmament. Central banks make up the financial rear: keeping payment systems running, banks liquid and solvent, and monetary policy predictable. Central banks not only help avoid a financial crisis but also help preserve confidence that the state still governs and will survive the war.
External support has increasingly become an important but still understudied input. We can also think of the absorptive capacity of countries receiving such support as the multiplier: Ukraine converts allied aid(link is external) into fighting power, while the $145 billion(link is external) the United States spent rebuilding Afghanistan over 20 years did not prevent its government's collapse. Labor mobilization also requires trade-offs—between the war front and the home front. Ukraine lost roughly a quarter of its effective labor force during Russia's 2022 invasion. Yet wage flexibility, remote work, and hiring women and older workers kept the decline in job-matching efficiency to about 15 percent(link is external). In Israel, prolonged call-up of reservists and exclusion of Palestinian workers are weighing on the economy(link is external).
2. Converting resources: Technological adaptation and innovation
Choosing where to focus military production is a critical economic choice. Over the past few decades, the United States and Germany have tended to invest more in highly sophisticated and expensive materiel that takes years, if not decades, to produce. Ukraine and Iran are at the opposite side of the spectrum. Ukraine has been forced to mobilize production rapidly because of shortages of manpower and financial resources, and Iran by decades of isolation.
But these scarcities can serve as an advantage: Existing large corporates in the United States and Germany have a history of government contracts for specific types of capital-intensive, bespoke, highly sophisticated military equipment. These companies want to protect their status, so when cheap drones are suddenly needed, it is hard for new companies to enter the market. By contrast, in Ukraine and Iran, there are few incumbents to resist shifting away from capital-intensive military industry.
Russia lags Ukraine in innovation, though it is closing that gap and is also more successful at scaling production, mostly of older, proven technology. Ukraine's ability to expand its industrial base across more than 180 European partnerships should help it achieve scale as well. Finally, recent wars have reversed the traditional defense research and development model: After decades of lower post–Cold War spending, civilian technology is now pulled into military use rather than the other way around.
3. Denying resources: Economic warfare
Denying the adversary its capacity to convert economic power into military advantage is the flip side of building your own. Economic warfare cannot win wars by itself but can make an important contribution. Sanctions are one instrument of economic warfare(link is external) alongside blockades, strategic bombing, and long-range strikes on oil refineries(link is external) and shipping lanes. Coalition size, costs borne by the sanctioning country, adaptation, and enforcement are the main constraints. US Senate hearings with experts(link is external) and companies(link is external) revealed a pressure point: More than 40 percent of 2,500 components in Russian weapons used in Ukraine came from four American suppliers(link is external). Meanwhile, Iran's disruption of the Strait of Hormuz shows how a much smaller economy can wage asymmetric warfare, imposing steep, far-reaching costs on a much richer adversary.
4. Constraints: Staying in power
Narratives directed at the domestic or international community can reduce the cost of every other input. Credibility with bond markets, the public, and allied militaries—whose supply chains can assist a smaller state—keeps finance and materiel flowing and people at work. Government can also use its ability to shape narrative to suppress statistics or shape how people understand wars being waged. Leaders' choices are constrained(link is external) by the need to keep the support of those who can keep them in power, even when doing so comes at the expense of the wider public. As political scientist Stephen Biddle and defense analyst and researcher Robert Zirkle explain, what secures the cooperation of elites is not always what is best for the economy, and coup-proofing(link is external)—organizing the military to keep a country's ruler safe from overthrow, rather than for maximum efficiency—and patronage impose deadweight loss on converting economic power into military power. Political scientists Abramo Fimo Kenneth Organski(link is external) and Jacek Kugler demonstrate how relative political capacity(link is external) measures how much a government can use its potential. Political scientist Randall L. Schweller(link is external) shows why fragmented states fail to do enough to counter an external threat because internal disagreements prevent them from building defenses or forming effective alliances.
After the Iran-Iraq war, Iran's Revolutionary Guards understood the need to control resources to continue to militarize; Iranian economists are often left to manage the consequences, and the best are often pushed out of government. Venezuela shows how a regime can survive while an important economic resource, in this case the oil industry, decays. It offered no resistance to an intervention by a foreign power, namely the United States. Regime survival and national capability are different things(link is external).
As the United States and Europe commit trillions of dollars to increasing their military capabilities, they cannot rely on aggregate GDP, or even defense spending as a share of GDP, to deter or win protracted conflicts. They must measure what that spending actually delivers: using purchasing power parity to compare resources, and tracing how funding, including allied support, becomes production, deployable capabilities, and battlefield effects. That work requires economists and military specialists to build a common framework.

Data Disclosure

This publication does not include a replication package.

articles.title: Depleted inventories leave oil markets exposed to further supply disruptions
articles.text:
Published on
Data Blog

Depleted inventories leave oil markets exposed to further supply disruptions

Paolo Agnolucci

Nikita Makarenko

Kaltrina Temaj

November 05, 2026

This page in:

English

English

Global oil inventories declined by about 2.4 million barrels per day between March and September 2026, reducing the market's buffer against future supply disruptions. / Image: Shutterstock

This blog post is part of a special series based on the October 2026 Commodity Markets Outlook, a report published by the World Bank Group. This series features concise summaries of commodity-specific sections extracted from the report. Explore the full report here.

Front-month Brent crude futures climbed above $115 per barrel (bbl) in late October, then eased to nearly $95/bbl in the first week of November as renewed near-term active conflict in the Middle East appeared less likely. After the Islamic Republic of Iran and the United States failed to reach a follow-on agreement to their June memorandum of understanding, Brent fluctuated between $75/bbl and $100/bbl and then stayed above $100/bbl in September and October. Oil product markets also tightened sharply. The European diesel premium over Brent averaged about $91/bbl in September, a record high, and U.S. retail diesel prices averaged nearly $6.20 per gallon in October.

Made with Flourish • Create a chart

Middle Eastern crude exports have rebounded, yet the declines in global supply and demand remain historically large. By early October, Middle Eastern oil exports were near 2025 levels, supported by ship-to-ship transfers, untracked shipments, and pipelines bypassing the Strait of Hormuz. Refinery damage delayed the recovery in refined-product exports, including diesel. Global output fell about 9 million barrels per day (mb/d) (8.5 percent) year-on-year in 2026Q2 and 7 mb/d in Q3, largely in Saudi Arabia and Iraq. Gains in six major producers—including Brazil, Kazakhstan, and the United States—offset just 18 percent of gross losses. Supply is projected to fall 5.5 mb/d (5.2 percent) in 2026, the steepest annual decline in over four decades apart from 2020. Consumption fell 5.0 mb/d (4.8 percent year-on-year) in 2026Q2 and 3.7 mb/d (3.4 percent) in Q3, mainly in emerging market and developing economies (EMDEs). China contributed about 35 percent of the decline in EMDE oil consumption, partly as electric vehicles displaced oil. Global demand is projected to shrink 2.6 mb/d (2.5 percent) for the year, a decline surpassed only in 1980 and 2020.

Made with Flourish • Create a chart

Lower inventories have left oil markets more exposed to further supply disruptions. As supply losses outpaced the decline in demand, the implied market deficit widened to 2.9 mb/d in 2026Q2 before easing in Q3. Observed global inventories declined at an average rate of about 2.4 mb/d from March to September, dropping from near the top of their 2021–25 range at the year’s start to near the bottom by end-September. Although stocks totaled about 7.8 billion barrels, much of the oil was in transit, needed for operations, or otherwise not readily available. OECD government stocks reached their lowest level in over three decades; U.S. strategic reserves remained at their lowest since 1982. In early October, International Energy Agency members agreed to accelerate the release of 100 million barrels of emergency stocks through January 2027, initially prioritizing diesel.

Made with Flourish • Create a chart

Oil prices are projected to ease gradually as supply rebounds and the market shifts into surplus. Brent is forecast to average nearly $100/bbl in 2026Q4 and $91/bbl for 2026 as a whole, before falling to $79/bbl in 2027 and $70/bbl in 2028. This outlook assumes a sustained recovery in Middle Eastern crude shipments, a return of Gulf refinery throughput to pre-conflict levels by 2027Q2, and a rebound in Russian crude output. Consumption is expected to recover in 2027 but remain about 0.5 mb/d below 2025 levels. Global supply would return to about 106 mb/d in 2027, near its 2025 level. The market would enter surplus conditions in 2027Q2, enabling inventories to recover about 80 percent of their 2026 drawdown by end-2027.

Made with Flourish • Create a chart

Near-term risks to oil prices remain tilted to the upside. Renewed hostilities could reverse the recent recovery in shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, while attacks on Gulf pipelines, Red Sea shipping, or Russian oil infrastructure could exacerbate shortages of crude oil and refined products. With inventories already depleted, even modest additional supply losses could trigger sharp price increases. In an adverse scenario in which Gulf production falls by about 5 mb/d in the first half of 2027 and Russian exports remain constrained, Brent would average $105/bbl in 2027—about 33 percent above the baseline forecast. A more restrictive OPEC+ production policy poses an additional upside risk. Downside risks become more prominent later in the forecast horizon: a durable resolution of the conflict, stronger-than-expected growth in supply from countries outside of OPEC+, and faster adoption of electric vehicles could put downward pressure on prices.

articles.text:
Annual outlook 2026: Investing in tomorrow

In our PERSPECTIVES 2026 publication, we look to the year ahead across our ten key investment themes, identifying opportunities and risks on the horizon.

Get in touch

Click here to activate this content.

Investing in tomorrow – Opportunities and risks

The global economy is in constant flux. Trade flows are shifting, regions are gaining or losing influence, and new technologies are also reshaping the economic map. 2025 has been challenging in some respects, but many local equity indices did deliver very good performance. Given the positive macro environment, we expect 2026 to be another constructive year, albeit with continuing market volatility. Although we anticipate a reduction in some uncertainties, it will definitely not be a time for complacency – especially as global trade relations are far from settled. The continued rise of artificial intelligence (AI) may open up new growth opportunities, which should encourage companies to increase their investment activity, potentially giving fresh impetus to both private and public consumption.

The US administration’s tariffs agenda appears to have now been largely implemented. While the disorientation that followed the declaration of “Liberation Day” in early April still lingers globally and domestically, most US trading partners have managed to significantly reduce initial steep tariff hikes through renegotiation. Overall, markets seem to have priced in the effects of the new environment, with overall tariffs still considerably higher than in January 2025 when the current administration began its tenure.

US growth is likely to be supported by the continuation and introduction of extensive tax relief measures, as well as increased spending on security and defence under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. The three interest rate cuts expected from the Federal Reserve by the end of 2026 and planned deregulation in the banking sector should also further improve the investment and consumption environment. What makes these government stimuli remarkable is that they come at a time when the US economy is not in recession but is already growing robustly. The US also appears to be close to full employment. Despite the long-term risks such an environment may pose – including inflationary pressures and rising public debt – we expect fiscal and monetary measures to deliver noticeable economic support in 2026.

We also anticipate that policy will deliver a cyclical impulse in Europe, for example due to Germany’s EUR500bn special fund. Planned investments, particularly in infrastructure and climate neutrality, could trigger a short-term upswing. To achieve sustainably higher growth, however, improving domestic economic flexibility remains crucial to foster entrepreneurial initiatives and create an investment climate that enhances productivity. In my view, urgent action is still needed here.

We maintain a broadly constructive outlook for equity markets in 2026. This will be partly due to strong demand for new AI-based applications, which should continue to drive substantial corporate investment flows. Beneficiaries will not only include US “Big Tech” but also a wide range of sectors – construction (thanks to new data centres), utilities (via higher electricity demand) and industrial and basic materials along the supply chain. Our earnings growth forecasts for companies across all major regions are therefore firmly in double-digit territory.

As outlined in our annual outlook themes, investors should also consider potential risks in equity markets. In the area of highly energy-intensive AI applications, for instance, a global power shortage could dampen investor expectations for progress. Not every stock will be a winner in 2026, and short-term corrections at index level remain possible.

Investors should therefore continue to act with discipline. This means focusing on fundamentals rather than chasing perceived trends, while utilising the broad spectrum of investment opportunities. Diversification remains key. Alongside equities, corporate bonds may be attractive – depending on your risk appetite, both investment-grade and high-yield segments. Gold and some non-traditional investments, such as in private equity or infrastructure, also merit consideration. We explore these in detail in the “Alternative Investments” section of this annual outlook.

Overall, we expect a dynamic year for capital markets in 2026 with numerous compelling opportunities. The central question will be whether constructive forecasts can hold up amid a backdrop of economic and geopolitical challenges. Further disruptions to global trade flows or a renewed escalation of tariff tensions could, for example, temporarily pressure corporate earnings and increase market volatility.

In a complex and uncertain environment, investors would therefore be well advised to actively manage risks. This will enable them to respond to market developments in line with their personal investment strategy. Staying invested with a defined strategic asset allocation will be key, as attempts to perfectly time market entry and exit points can often result in missing the best-performing days and weeks.

I hope you find our annual outlook insightful and full of stimulating ideas for your portfolio. We are always available to review and discuss these ideas and look forward to hearing from you.

Christian Nolting

Global CIO

Start a conversation with us

We’d like to learn more about your ambitions for the future and how can support your investment needs – both day-to-day and for the long term.

Theme #1
Value at risk – Crises and conflicts

Geopolitics, inflation, sovereign debt, tariffs: many risk factors likely to persist in 2026.

Earnings expectations: disappointments could trigger volatility.

AI: more of a structural boom than a bubble.

Theme #2
Politics – Cooperation!

Trade tensions between the US and China set to continue in 2026.

Pragmatism may prevent escalation temporarily.

US midterm elections in November to dominate the domestic US agenda.

Theme #3
Economy – The art of intelligence

Global economy set for robust growth overall in 2026.

US growth still ahead of Europe’s. Outlook for China subdued.

AI to drive structural growth, with monetary and fiscal policy as additional drivers.

Theme #4
Policy – Intervention!

Trend toward greater state intervention expected to continue.

State-directed economic policy in China and the US – but also in Europe.

This can often cause more harm than good: risk of missteps remains.

Theme #5
Dollar – The empire strikes back

USD stability maintained, including against the EUR.

JPY may appreciate slightly against the USD.

PBoC appears intent on keeping the USD/CNY stable.

Theme #6
Bonds – Playing with fire

Normalisation of the US yield curve likely to persist.

10-year Bunds and Treasuries to offer positive real returns.

Pay attention to the quality and size of corporate issuers.

Theme #7
Equities – Discipline beats drama

High corporate earnings expected worldwide.

Spectrum of interesting investment opportunities likely to widen.

Market corrections possible at any time – investment discipline remains essential.

Theme #8
Commodities – Fiercely contested

Chinese quasi-monopoly on rare earths; search for substitutes should intensify.

Oil prices expected to stabilise at low levels.

Gold has further upside potential.

Theme #9
Alternatives – Evolution and resilience

New regulatory frameworks simplify access to alternative investments.

Alternatives provide additional opportunities for portfolio diversification.

Infrastructure investments remain an obvious focus.

Theme #10
Investment strategy – Beyond the benchmark

Diversification and active risk management remain core elements.

Beyond traditional liquid markets, alternative investments may also be appropriate.

Investors should adapt their strategy dynamically to changing conditions.

articles.title: The Global Economy’s Tenuous Balance: Resilience Amid Uncertainty
articles.text:
Skip to main content
Global Markets and EconomyThe Global Economy’s Tenuous Balance: Resilience Amid UncertaintyGlobal Economics Outlook & StrategyArticle • October 30, 2026ResearchKEY TAKEAWAYSGlobal growth remains resilient with GDP expected to grow 2.7% this year and 2.8% next year despite geopolitical tensions fiscal concerns and uncertainty surrounding AIInflation risks have intensified driven by higher energy prices and supply-chain pressures prompting many central banks to adopt a more hawkish stanceAI remains a major global growth driver but financial excesses weakening political support and rising cyber risks represent important challenges to the sustainability of the investment boomA new Citi Research report from a team led by Global Chief Economist Nathan Sheets explores the global economy’s remarkable resilience despite mounting challenges, from the sustainability of the artificial intelligence (AI) boom to geopolitical tensions. The number of such challenges in growing. The U.S.-Iran conflict has pushed Brent crude to $115 a barrel, close to this year’s high. Concerns about the AI boom have intensified, while renewed worries over French fiscal performance have added to broader sovereign debt pressures. Consumer and business confidence indicators remain subdued, with households particularly pessimistic.Yet despite notable and apparently increasing headwinds, we now expect global gross domestic product (GDP) growth of 2.7% this year, slightly stronger than last month’s forecast and broadly in line with our expectations at the start of the year. Developed markets are performing somewhat better than we anticipated in December, largely because of continued U.S. strength. Meanwhile, emerging markets remain slightly softer overall, as stronger growth in Asia is nearly offset by weaker outcomes in the Middle East and Africa. We expect global growth to climb to 2.8% next year.Recent Purchasing Managers’ Index (PMI) readings reinforce this picture. Global manufacturing activity has continued to strengthen, supported by the electronics sector and AI-related investment. Sharply rising U.S. investment has boosted production and technology exports across other regions, especially in Asia. Economies with significant exposure to AI, including Taiwan and South Korea, have posted strong growth despite their vulnerability to higher oil prices.The services sector has also remained resilient. After weakening during the early phase of the U.S.-Iran conflict, the global services PMI has rebounded. Labor markets remain firm, hiring has held up, and consumption continues to grow. Despite consumers’ caution, spending hasn’t materially slowed. Citi’s global Surprise Index similarly suggests that economic data continue to exceed expectations, while China has improved modestly and euro-area data have moderated.The key takeaway is that it will likely require a substantially larger shock to derail global growth. For now, businesses continue to adapt effectively to changing conditions, helping sustain expansion despite mounting risks.Inflation, however, has become a more significant concern. Since February, oil prices have risen roughly 60%, while jet fuel prices are up 100% and diesel prices 110%. As a result, we expect global headline inflation to reach 3.4% this year, compared with 2.8% last year, before easing to 3.0% next year provided that oil prices moderate.Core inflation pressures have also intensified. Higher transportation costs and disruptions to supply chains — particularly in aluminum, petrochemicals and fertilizers — are gradually feeding through to consumer prices. We now expect core inflation this year to be at least 0.5 percentage point higher than we projected in February for economies including Brazil, Australia, South Korea, the euro area and Thailand. Central banks are increasingly moving toward tighter policy stances.A notable consequence of this environment has been rising sovereign bond yields. Since the U.S.-Iran conflict began, 10-year yields have increased by 175 basis points (bp) in France, more than 100 bp in both the U.S. and the UK, and 75 bp in Japan, Germany and Canada. Several emerging markets have also experienced rising yields, including the Philippines, Indonesia and India.We attribute these moves partly to growing competition for global savings. U.S. Treasury issuance is likely to remain at $2 trillion or more annually, financing needs elsewhere are substantial, and AI investment is emerging as another major consumer of capital. Global AI-related capital expenditures are projected to exceed $3.5 trillion by 2030. At the same time, investors are demanding greater compensation for geopolitical uncertainty, fiscal risks, inflation volatility and governance concerns, contributing to higher term and risk premiums. We also see oil-market volatility as playing a role.France remains a particular source of concern. Even under relatively favorable assumptions, rising interest costs are likely to keep budget deficits near 4% of GDP, while government debt approaches 120% of GDP. Political uncertainty ahead of next spring’s presidential election has further undermined confidence. Encouragingly, pressures have largely remained contained, though Belgium and Italy have shown some sensitivity to French developments, and we continue to monitor potential spillovers to the UK.On AI, we remain constructive. We view the current investment cycle as being driven by businesses seeking productivity gains and competitive advantage. For many firms, AI investment has become an imperative for survival. We expect this spending wave to persist well into the next decade, with meaningful productivity benefits beginning to emerge over the next two to three years.That said, three risks warrant close attention. First, financial disruptions remain possible. As with the internet boom of the late 1990s, a transformative technology can generate bubbles, mispricing and failures. However, investors today appear highly alert to these risks, and periodic corrections may be reducing the likelihood of a broader speculative bubble.Second, political support for AI appears to be weakening, particularly in the U.S. Concerns about electricity demand, power-grid capacity and job displacement have become increasingly prominent, raising the possibility of more-restrictive policies toward data-center construction and AI deployment.Third, cyber risks are increasing alongside AI capabilities. More sophisticated cyberattacks or failures involving advanced AI systems could have significant economic and political consequences, potentially triggering stricter regulation.Against this backdrop of resilient growth and elevated inflation, central banks have pivoted toward tighter policy. Across 27 major central banks, we now expect 16 to raise rates this year, six to remain on hold, and only five to ease policy. This marks a sharp departure from expectations earlier in the year, and we note that in contrast to the period after the pandemic, central banks have generally refused to “look through” the supply shock.Looking ahead, we see a more mixed picture, with monetary policy remaining heavily dependent on oil prices and the trajectory of the U.S.-Iran conflict. We expect additional tightening from the Federal Reserve, European Central Bank, Bank of England, and Bank of Japan, although the outlook for 2027 appears more balanced. For now, central banks remain focused on preventing inflation from becoming entrenched, even as growth continues to prove more resilient than many expected.Our new report, Global Economic Outlook & Strategy: The Global Economy’s Tenuous Balance — Resilience Amid Uncertainty, also offers region-by-region economic discussions. articles.title: You saved for retirement. Now comes the hard part
articles.text:
Better Vantage podcast

You saved for retirement. Now comes the hard part

November 04, 2026

Video length: 21 minutes 27 seconds

Read the transcript

Rebecca Choo Quan: Imagine you have spent decades saving for retirement and the big day has finally come, but the paychecks have stopped, and the hard part begins: turning your wealth into income. Welcome to season three of Better Vantage by Vanguard, a podcast series hosted by Custom Content from WSJ and Vanguard. I'm Rebecca Choo Quan of Vanguard's Investment Strategy Group sitting in today for Christine Kashkari of WSJ Custom Content. And with me is co-host and our resident expert, Joe Davis, global chief economist at Vanguard. Joe, in season one, we asked, is America even ready to retire? But today we're going to ask how do we actually do it? Joining us to help answer that question are Kelly Hahn, Vanguard's head of retirement research, and Garrett Harbron, Vanguard's head of advised wealth management strategies. Kelly, Garrett, thanks so much for spending time with us today.
Garrett Harbron: Thanks, Rebecca. Good to be here.
Kelly Hahn: Thanks for having us.
Joe Davis: As my mom likes to remind me. I'm no spring chicken, right. So, retirement income is increasingly important. It's important to my parents as well. And there's times it's like I don't know where to go, what information to trust. And I'm greedy here for our listeners, like I want actionable items, right? And so I think what I'm really excited - Kelly and Garrett, giving their expertise. They're going to turn that conceptual idea into reality for us.
Rebecca: Yeah, you need to get your advice right here and right now. So, we are going to start with a little bit of a lightning round and just ask a few quick-fire questions that we will then dig into later in the podcast. So, why don't we start with the first one? There's this so-called 4% rule. Is that useful or outdated? Garrett?
Garrett: Surprisingly useful.
Joe: Really, how about so how about annuities? Good, bad, indifferent?
Garrett: It depends.
Kelly: It depends.
Joe: Oh man, you sound like an economist here. It depends…
Kelly: Retirement income is such a hard problem to solve. How many years have people been retiring, and we're still dealing with this challenge because it's so complicated?
Rebecca: We promise not to just say it depends. We'll get some accurate answers. What's the biggest retirement myth you'd like to eliminate?
Kelly: Well, RMD isn't the only thing you can withdraw from.
Rebecca: RMD--required minimum distributions. Garrett?
Garrett: Your account balance is not what determines whether you retire successfully.
Joe: All right. Whoa. I shouldn’t be looking at my account balance? Not the most important thing?
Garrett: Not the most important thing.
Joe: All right, we're going to come back to that.
Garrett: Absolutely.
Rebecca: Biggest misconception retirees have about spending in retirement?
Garrett: It's easy.
Rebecca: I find spending to be very easy.
Kelly: That they don't want to spend because of all of the worries and anxiety they have about uncertainties. I mean, that's certainly the case with my mom. She's a widow, and I think her biggest worry is that she's going to be a burden to her kids, me and my sisters. So, she's very, very frugal and intentionally so. So, we're trying to work with her is you do have some capacity to spend and how do we get you more comfortable utilizing the wealth. So, I feel like a lot of people feel they can't spend their money.
Rebecca: What's one thing a new retiree should do on their very first day of retirement?
Kelly: Consolidate accounts.
Garrett: Decide what you want your retirement to look like.
Joe: All right, all right, so there's a lot to unpack here, right? A lot to unpack here. Where do you want to go? We want to go to the mindset shift.
Rebecca: Let's talk about that. I mean, interestingly, so Kelly as head of retirement research, looks at millions of participant accounts in 401(k) plans and millions of investors in America in their 401(k) plans. So, it's sort of the average Joe account, not your account, Joe. So, maybe she can tell us a little bit about how the average American worker is thinking about retirement income.
Kelly: So, I want to ask you a question. Since we're being interviewed, I'm going to flip the tables. How many people in America, the average Americans, are doing what economists think they should do? Smooth consumption into retirement. It's not a trick question, Joe. What do you think?
Joe: Can I say it depends? No, 40%.
Kelly: 40%. No, that is a high number. Only one in 10 average Americans in retirement are consistently taking money out from their wealth. And for the most part, the vast majority, they're hoarding or holding on to their wealth because of all the anxieties and worries they have about what retirement may look like.
Joe: Can you say that again? Just one in 10?
Kelly: One in 10. Yeah, one in 10. About half, they're tapping their retirement wealth when they need it, like a piggy bank. Where about 40%, they're not taking any money out until they get to RMDH, which is really shocking when you think about it. It could be 10 years of not spending money. People are intentionally being frugal, just like my mom. It gives her joy of knowing that she's saving up her wealth in case something happens. Long term care or healthcare.
Rebecca: Peace of mind. That’s got a value.
Garrett: Peace of mind absolutely has value, right. And, and I think that's one of the important things to keep in mind when we're talking about retirement spending. One of the reasons we say a lot that it depends is because we can do the math. We can tell people like from a quantitative standpoint, here is what the ideal is. But I haven't come across an algorithm or a formula yet that captures peace of mind. And I think we have to really remember that peace of mind has its value. We may not be able to calculate it, but that doesn't mean that someone who trades optimal tax strategy for a little bit more peace of mind is making a bad decision.
Kelly: It's really the balance of how much you can generate today versus how much you may need in the future for peace of mind. So, I think retirees really need to think about both. But right now, it's very much overweight to: what's going to happen to me. I don't want to spend the money in case something major or or something dire may happen.
Joe: You mentioned Social Security. You mentioned RMD. Like, that's where I need help here. How do I start breaking through?
Garrett: Yeah, I think that is where creating a retirement plan, a spending plan, really has a lot of value. So, people need to ask themselves, what do I want my retirement to look like? What do I want to do? What hobbies do I want to engage in? What kind of travel might I want to do? And create a budget for it and compare that budget to their assets and their spending plan to see if it's sustainable.
And if you can do that, then that accomplishes a number of things. It helps you spend. It almost gives you permission to spend in a way because you've planned for it. It gives you the peace of mind that yes, this spending plan is sustainable, and perhaps most importantly, it gives you the permission to live the retirement that you want to live.
Rebecca: So, Kelly, you have actually done a lot of research about one of the biggest misconceptions people have. RMD's tell us what RMD is and what are people misthinking about them.
Kelly: RMD stands for required minimum distribution. It literally means it's the minimum amount that you need to take out from your tax deferred portfolios like 401(k)s and IRAs. And many people think that they need to start taking out money when RMD starts, which can be 73 or 75 depending on their birth year. But when in fact, people can actually start taking out money sooner as early as 59-1/2. And they also think it's a recommendation by the government that how much they can safely draw down. It's really not. It's a way to tax the money that has not been taxed yet. So, what we recommend is that RMD should always be the floor. It's part of the retirement income planning. But that should not be the only strategy.
Joe: Is that a big one?
Kelly: That's a big one. That's a really big one. About four and 10 are taking Social Security right as they retire, let's say 63 or 64, and then they wait another full decade to take money out when RMD starts. But the tricky part with RMD is because you're backloading everything, people may actually pay more in taxes in aggregate, lifetime taxes, that potentially a retiree may be paying, by delaying consumption.*
Joe: Well, you've underspent and then you paid more in taxes.
Kelly: Exactly.
Joe: How is this not more well known?
Kelly: This is why we're doing the podcast!
Garrett: Just to add on to what Kelly was saying, you know, waiting to take RMD's for a lot of people is about the worst thing you can do from a tax standpoint, right? Because once you get into that RMD phase, you are forced to take money out year after year after year. It's a required minimum distribution, right? And so, no matter what the rest of your tax picture looks like, once you start taking those RMDs, it can change that tax picture significantly, right? So, one of the big things that people run into is Social Security is taxable depending on what your other income looks like. So, it can be 0%, 50% or 85% taxable. Someone who has is not used to having their Social Security taxed because they have relatively low income, probably because they haven't been taking money from their retirement accounts, can suddenly find their Social Security is being taxed at that 85%.
Kelly: And Medicare surcharge.
Garrett: And Medicare surcharge. Exactly.
Rebecca: Okay, Garrett, let's go back to something we talked about in the lightning round--the 4% rule. Is that now passe?
Garrett: No, it's not passe at all. But let's talk about what the 4% rule is and isn't. The 4% rule says that you in your first year of retirement, you spend 4% of your beginning account balance and then you spend that amount in dollars adjusted for inflation each year after that. Now a lot of people think that the 4% rule means you take 4% of your portfolio balance each year in retirement, and that's not what this is.
Rebecca: That's what I thought it was.
Joe: That's a big difference.
Garrett: That's a different rule. That's the percentage of portfolio rule.
Kelly: So, I have very mixed feelings about the 4% rule. You know, I think giving people general guidance is a good thing because right now, as we see in the data itself, people are not utilizing their wealth and we hear from our clients over and over, I don't need any more educational materials, don't teach me, just tell me what I should do. Right? So, I think 4% rule, something that they can follow easily is a good one. So, they can actually act on it. But because of the sequence of withdrawal, I find it difficult to recommend something that's going to be static if you don't come back and update your financial planning when things like market downturn may happen.
Garrett: Well, so you said two really important things there, right?
Kelly: So, I think I said many more.
Garrett: Fair. Two things that I'm going to reply to. One of the things that our research has found is that just a little bit of flexibility with your spending from year to year based on market returns can dramatically increase the lifetime of a portfolio.
Joe: So, take like a three-year moving average or something like that to smooth out the ups and downs.
Garrett: Or just put a put a ceiling and floor above and below your spending.
Kelly: Like a guardrail.
Garrett: If you do what we call dynamic spending, which is you go into your spending plan saying, okay, I'm going to adjust my spending with market returns, but I'm not going to increase my budget by any more than 5% a year and I'm not going to decrease my budget by any more than 2 1/2% per year. That approach gets you a lot of the portfolio longevity benefits of a percentage of portfolio rule without all of the volatility.
Rebecca: But how do you deal with unexpected shocks? I mean, in retirement, you have could have a big, most often, healthcare shock. So, you might have the best laid plans for a floor and a ceiling and then something big happens and you need in-home care that's not covered by Medicare or something like that.
Kelly: That's why I think it's really important at the outset to think about your goals in two buckets. What could I afford today knowing that there's likelihood that I may have adverse health events? So, the number that you may use to generate income today may be somewhat lower in order to have the liquidity that you may need.
Joe: So, you would put that on the spreadsheet--$100,000 or some number for long term care.
Kelly: You carve that out so that you have both peace of mind, if something happens, and then today being able to have that permission to spend and enjoy retirement.
Joe: My wife and I just did this with long-term care. We don't know actually what number that's going to be, but psychologically, I know once since the economist in me saying I'm just doing mental accounting, I just bucketed it. But Kelly, I'm trying to channel you and Garrett, I'm saying that that's actually gave us, we just did this. It gave us a lot of comfort knowing that we don't know if we'll ever need it or someone in our family will need it, but we have dedicated funds that are just there for that, right? I actually labeled it on my Vanguard account, long-term care account.
Kelly: And surprisingly, a lot of people are going to need long-term care about one in two. I mean, the severity may vary. And I think women are more likely is we're lucky that we're going to have a longer and healthcare and long-term care issues.
Joe: What's a framework to help me get at some loose number for that sort of called sidecar for long-term care.
Garrett: So, coming up with an exact number is difficult. Because there are a lot of variables going into it. Where you live, your family history, these are all things that play into this number. That varies widely depending on where people live, the cost of long-term care varies greatly across different parts of the country. But probably the biggest indicator of what your long-term care costs are, or your spouses long-term care costs are going to be, is looking back at your parents and your grandparents and seeing what kind of long-term care they required and how long they lived.
Rebecca: It’s expensive so it’s really something you need to put a lot of thought up front into.
Joe: What's your thoughts on annuities? And you sounded like an economist and saying: it depends.
Garrett: I'm going to go back to it depends, Joe.
Joe: Help break that down for me. okay, who is the strongest use case for it and what type of annuity, if you can go that far, where it's viable knowing that it's not for all.
Garrett: Annuities are best used when there is a gap between what we call essential expenses, right? Housing, food, utilities - the things that you can't cut back on. And you're guaranteed income. So, when we talk about guaranteed income, we're talking about social security, pensions, that sort of thing. When that gap exists and there is real longevity risk involved, right? So, if you look at your account balance and your spending needs and you say, you know what, I only need to withdraw 2% of my portfolio per year, you really don't have any meaningful longevity risk, right? But if you have what meaningful longevity risk and you have that gap between essential expenses and you're guaranteed income, that's where annuities become extremely valuable because annuities can plug that gap and give you guaranteed income that you can't outlive and is not dependent on what the market does. And that's exactly what you want when it comes to covering those essential expenses. You're turning assets into income, right? That's all you're doing, right? You're giving the insurance company assets and in return, they're giving you a stream of income for the rest of your life.
Joe: Usually it's like a percentage of the portfolio.
Garrett: Yeah, usually just a piece of it.
Kelly: Also, the biggest annuity that everybody has is Social Security.
Joe: Supplemental Social Security. Now what's the retirement income 2O1 version, the more advanced version? What's the next layer of potential help.
Rebecca: Or maybe even things coming over the next decade.
Garrett: So, I think one of the biggest things is tax planning, right? It's one thing to figure out what your retirement plan is and what your spending plan is, but taxes can make a big difference over a period of 30 years. Like even small differences, you know, we talk a lot about the power of compounding of interest and things like that. We tend to forget that applies in retirement too. I think one of the biggest things people overlook are Roth conversions. We talk about them a lot, but I don't know that they actually get done nearly as often as they should be.
Rebecca: Can you just explain what happens in a Roth conversion?
Garrett: So, Roth conversion, you've got your traditional 401(k), your traditional IRA, the money that you take out of that, it goes in tax free, but the money you take out gets taxed at fully as income when you take it out, right? Not only that, but when you pass it on to your heirs, they have to pay income tax when they draw down on it as well. Roth IRA, you pay tax on the money that goes in, but neither you nor your heirs ever pay income tax on the withdrawals.
Another difference between a traditional IRA and a Roth IRA is Roth IRAs do not have any RMDs. So, there's never a minimum drawdown that you have to take out of that account. So, what a Roth conversion does is you take money out of your traditional IRA or 4O1(k), pay the income tax on it, put it into a Roth vehicle IRA. And incidentally this has to be done directly. You can't withdraw it and then redeposit it, right. And then that money from that point on grows tax free. Retirement, especially the early years of retirement, are a really good time to do that because you're not working anymore. So, you're out of the highest income years of your life, right? You may or may not be collecting Social Security at that point, depending on whether you've decided to delay claiming or not. But because of that, they tend to be some of the lowest income years in retirement and since they are low income, that means lower income tax. So, that is an ideal time to do Roth conversions and the tax savings from a Roth conversion, especially done early, can be really, really powerful depending on balances and things like that. We've seen real cases in our advice offer where clients saved a quarter of a million dollars in income taxes over their lifetime by doing a Roth conversion.
Joe: So, it sounds like the first day I retire, I'm doing a Roth conversion. But it sounds like that's a good place to start.
Garrett: Yeah, make sure you talk to someone like an advisor or an accountant, someone who knows what they're doing, right? Because every dollar you don't pay in tax is another dollar you have to spend and to give to family to give to causes you care about.
Kelly: So, I think for me, like one thing, if you were asking me where is 2.0 for retirement income would be just like we've automated savings for people. I would love to automate generating income so we could give people permission to spend and safety.
Rebecca: So, automation might actually help you both get over the mindset and also control some of the risks.
Joe: So, how does every listener here, what is the one thing when they turn off this episode that they say you want to help their loved ones, to help themselves, if you haven't done it already?
Kelly: People need to take stock of their situation. As I mentioned before, consolidation of accounts is so critical. People retire with three or four different accounts, 401(k)s, and IRAs. When you have things scattered all over, you don't know how much you can generate. So, I mean, you ask for one thing, but I'm going to give you two or three things. Social Security, know how much you're going to get, make sure your balance sheet is consolidated so you have a holistic view, and then think about the life you want and can you afford it. I think those three things, people will get 90% of what they need to do, they can tackle that.
Garrett: I think the biggest single thing that people can do is really sit down and think about what is this money for. And that’s why I think a retirement plan is so important because it can bring that clarity and almost give permission for people to spend knowing that a) they’ve identified all of their goals and b) those goals are appropriately funded.
Rebecca: Yeah, that's I think that's actually a great place to leave the conversation. I hope we all retire with more confidence.
Joe: It sounds like this is just going to be topic we could keep coming back to. Thank you Garrett, Kelly amazing insights, gave me, gave us some action items, too. A lot to do. Thank you.
Rebecca: Date night with spreadsheets. Well, thank you so much, Kelly and Garrett. It's been great to have you here. And that's it for today's episode. Next time we will examine whether the portfolio that worked for the past decade is the right one for the next ten. So, stay tuned. Join us for that conversation and all of our future episodes.
Christine Kashkari: If you enjoyed this episode and found it helpful, subscribe and share.

*Source for time stamp 8:00 – 8:12: Dickson, Joel, Marcos Dinerstein, Aaron Goodman, Fiona Greig, Kelly Hahn, Min Kim, Zachary Rayfield, and Nicky Zhang, "From Retirement Savings to a Retirement Paycheck," Vanguard, 2026. $25,000 figure calculated from Vanguard Financial Advice Model simulations, using life expectancy assumptions from Society of Actuaries mortality tables, and steady state capital market and inflation assumptions from 10,000 Vanguard Capital Markets Model paths as of February 26, 2026

All annuities are subject to risk, including the possible loss of the money you invest. Investments in bond portfolios are subject to interest rate, credit, and inflation risk. Product guarantees are subject to the claims-paying ability of the issuing insurance company.

Read more

In this episode of Better Vantage, Kelly Hahn, Vanguard’s head of retirement research, and Garrett Harbron, Vanguard's head of advised wealth management strategies, reveal that only one in 10 Americans consistently withdraw from their retirement accounts, while about 40% wait until required minimum distributions force them to tap their wealth.
This reluctance to spend stems from anxiety about healthcare costs and longevity, but it often leads to unnecessary tax burdens and diminished quality of life. By waiting to tap retirement wealth until required minimum distributions begin at age 73 or 75, retirees may pay significantly more in aggregate lifetime taxes than if they had drawn down funds strategically in their early retirement years.1
Hahn and Harbron argue that creating a spending plan can act as a strong incentive to spend in retirement and minimize taxes. The plan should account for both essential expenses and discretionary goals, with dedicated reserves for healthcare uncertainties that one in two Americans will eventually face.
The path forward requires three essential steps: consolidate accounts for a holistic view, understand your Social Security timeline, and define the retirement lifestyle you want to afford. The goal is not simply preserving wealth but converting it into the experiences and security that make retirement meaningful.
