articles.title: Market update - October 30th 2026 | CoinShares
articles.text: Bitcoin held its ground through a Fed hold and a nervous pre-election weekBitcoin spent most of the week consolidating with admirable discipline, quickly recovering a brief dip below US$77k on Thursday. Investors are positioned defensively, the premium traders pay to hold leveraged bets on rising prices has shrunk, and there is little appetite to chase risk ahead of the US elections. Yet despite that rather flat surface, Bitcoin has held up better than much of the broader crypto market and many more volatile assets. It does not feel like a market suddenly overcome with optimism, more one becoming increasingly selective about where it is prepared to take risk.A hold, not an all-clearRates were left unchanged at 3.75% to 4.00%, which surprised nobody, while Fed Chair Kevin Warsh was less hawkish than many had feared.¹ His view was that September’s hike is beginning to have an effect, financial conditions have tightened and the Committee can now afford the luxury of waiting for more evidence. He was careful not to imply that tightening is over, but equally avoided commentary that would have sent short-dated yields sharply higher. The relief therefore came less from any sense that the Fed is finished than from the absence of any signal that it intends to go beyond the further hike already pencilled in for this year. The official statement still described inflation as elevated and economic activity as expanding at a strong pace.¹The data behind that caution are not encouraging. September CPI, published earlier in the month, ran at 3.7% year-on-year,² and last Friday’s flash PMI offered little consolation. The composite remained firmly expansionary, while selling-price inflation accelerated to its fastest pace since August 2022.³ The Fed is therefore stuck with a particularly awkward combination: growth that refuses to roll over politely and inflation that refuses to disappear on cue.Alphabet’s earnings have added another wrinkle.⁴ Revenue was not the problem. The concern is that markets have become rather less willing than they were a few months ago to reward anything wearing an AI badge, and the bar for a convincing earnings beat has risen sharply. Disappointment is being punished accordingly. Bitcoin has been caught in some of that volatility, but has again behaved with rather more composure than many of its neighbours.Wall Street moves onto crypto railsOne development this week deserves rather more attention than it has received. trade[XYZ] and ICE, the owner of the New York Stock Exchange, plan to bring 24/7 perpetual futures (futures contracts with no expiry date that trade around the clock) to US investors, built on Hyperliquid, a blockchain-based trading venue. The launch remains subject to CFTC approval.⁵ For Hyperliquid, this is a significant endorsement. It suggests the technology is beginning to move beyond crypto-native experimentation and into the architecture of regulated traditional markets, precisely the sort of crossover we have expected as tokenisation (issuing conventional assets on a blockchain) and 24/7 trading mature.Elections and oilPolymarket implies a 93% probability that Democrats take the House and a 68% probability that they also take the Senate.⁶ Divided government may initially be read as negative for crypto, but we would be wary of pushing that conclusion too far. Stablecoin and digital asset policy has become increasingly bipartisan. Stablecoins, digital dollars backed largely by short-dated US Treasuries, are also a new source of demand for government debt, and that appeal is unlikely to disappear simply because Congress changes colour.Israel’s election has produced no clear majority,⁷ while renewed Middle East tensions continue to push energy prices higher. If that persists, the consequences are fairly mechanical: higher oil, firmer inflation expectations and a Fed with even less room to soften. It remains one of the cleaner channels through which geopolitics can still feed directly into Bitcoin.Waiting, without a tantrumSo the market waits. For the elections, for the next inflation print, for the Fed, and perhaps for somebody else to blink first geopolitically. Bitcoin is not breaking higher, but neither has it been willing to break lower despite tighter policy expectations, volatile equities and elevated geopolitical risk. In a market this uncertain, its refusal to have a tantrum is probably the most constructive signal on offer.SourcesFederal Reserve, FOMC statement and Chair Warsh press conference transcript (preliminary), 28 Oct 2026US Bureau of Labor Statistics, Consumer Price Index, September 2026, released 14 Oct 2026S&P Global, Flash US PMI, October 2026, released 23 Oct 2026Alphabet, Q3 2026 earnings release, 28 Oct 2026trade[XYZ], announcement of planned US perpetual futures market with ICE, 29 Oct 2026Polymarket, US 2026 midterm election markets, accessed 29 Oct 2026Associated Press, Israeli election results and coalition outlook, 27–28 Oct 2026

articles.title: Inference Market (and Micro) Structure
articles.text:
Insights / Perspectives / When Intelligence Commoditizes, Compute Becomes the Trade

Written by:

Vikram Singh
Investor

Topics

AI

Cryptocurrency

perspectives • August 11, 2026

When Intelligence Commoditizes, Compute Becomes the Trade

TLDRIntelligence is commoditizing through open-source models. Open source models are almost at parity with the frontier and usage is up 350× since January 2025. Since serving inference for open-source models is permissionless, a competitive market for inference is emerging.The inference “market structure” is somewhat like a trading venue. There are buyers of tokens (Cursor, Lovable, enterprises), a marketplace (OpenRouter), and sellers of tokens (Fireworks, Baseten, Together AI) quoting a one-sided order book on a model’s tokens.Inference providers are like market makers: they quote continuously, hold inventory in the form of compute, earn a spread, and vie for token flow. The marketplace is like an exchange: OpenRouter earns a “matching” fee (5.5% take rate) with potentially room to charge the “market makers” for token flow PFOF.GPU-hours are the homogenous input into producing every token and serve as the layer for transferring risk for inference token production. Compute futures emerge as a mechanism to manage the 130% volatility of GPU-hours and to protect inference provider’s COGSA few trends are playing out in real time:Intelligence is commoditizing and democratizing rapidly. Since GPT-4, no frontier model has held the lead for more than 100 days. New models are shipping every 41 days . Open source models are catching up to the best frontier lab models within months vs years. This changes frontier labs economics substantially since they only have 4 months to amortize training capex before spend migrates towards open source models.

Source: Epoch AI's ECI benchmark data[2] (CC-BY, credit Epoch AI)

Source: Epoch AI's benchmark data[3] (CC-BY, credit Epoch AI)
Jevons’ Paradox is playing out in real time. Cost savings achieved by switching from frontier models to open-source models are being reinvested into more token spend. Thus, token consumption compounds even if budgets stay flat. This is evidenced through OpenRouter routing 125× more tokens last week than it did in January 2025 with 75% of volume being open source models vs 27% earlier.

Source: OpenRouter datasets API, as of Jul 22 2026
The proliferation of open source models is leading to higher short-to-medium term GPU rentals. Utilization and rental prices have shot up across the Ornn H100 index after the recent open source model releases

Source: OpenRouter’s weekly rankings , Ornn’s H100 SXM index.
Venture investment in inference providers, GPU rental marketplaces, and routing platforms has heated up intensely over the last three months.

With token flows migrating to open-source models, token buyers growing more price-conscious, and inference being permissionless, a competitive market for serving inference is emerging. Competitive markets tend to develop mature market structures. The inference serving stack roughly resembles a trading venue and a deeper exploration reveals some interesting intricacies.
Inference Market StructureThere are three core participants in the inference trading analogy: Buyers of Tokens, Sellers of Tokens, and a Marketplace.

Source: https://openrouter.ai/docs/faq), (https://sacra.com/c/fireworks-ai/)
Customers/Buyers of TokensConsumers chatting with ChatGPT, engineers running Cursor, apps like Lovable and Harvey serving models behind their own features, agent fleets doing background research, and enterprises wiring LLM APIs into production workflows – all are buyers of tokens. These users are split across a distribution of token-price elasticity:15% are highly elastic. For e.g., Developer experimentation25% medium elasticity. For e.g., Consumer chat40% low elasticity. For e.g., Enterprise SaaS5% price inelastic. For e.g., Real-time response needs

Source: arXiv 2603.21690
Normalizing for the model used, elasticity is somewhat a function of who waits on the inference response. Human-facing demand is inelastic while agent-originated batch demand is elastic. For example, identical tokens cost half as much if you accept a 24-hour batch window instead of a synchronous reply.The aggregate numbers overstate how sticky demand is: a 10% price cut buys only a 0.5–0.7% bump in usage, but that average blends enterprises that will pay almost anything for mission-critical work with hobbyists and dev pipelines that flock to whatever is cheapest. Closed models serve the trusted high-cost work and open models absorb the cheap high-volume flow.As such, the average token is not elastic, but the marginal token is very elastic. Most of the volume already flowing today is bought by a person waiting on the answer: a chat reply, a Cursor completion. That buyer barely notices price and nobody switches models mid-conversation to save cents. However, the next phase of token-demand is bought by software: agent loops, batch research jobs, CI pipelines. Thus, the marginal token satisfies an objective function that maximizes quality while minimizing cost and one in which times plays a lesser role. OpenRouter already optimizes for this future demand as its default router splits a model’s traffic across providers weighted by 1/price² . Thus, a provider that halves its quote roughly quadruples its share of the flow. And since over 70% of routed tokens already come from CLIs and agents, almost all incremental token demand is likely elastic demand.
Inference Providers/Sellers of TokensThese are your sellers of tokens (Fireworks, Baseten, Together AI, and so forth). They burn GPU-hours to produce tokens and quote their token prices on the marketplace. Inference providers can differ on several price-based and performance-based axes. We will discuss them more in depth in the microstructure section.
Marketplace/ExchangeThis platform connects token buyers with inference providers and charges a fee for offering that service. For tokens, the clearest example here is OpenRouter.However, the token marketplace differs from a trading venue in that it’s not two-sided. You can buy tokens from an inference provider but you cannot sell them back to the provider or to any third party. This is inherent to the nature of the token which is manufactured on demand and consumed on delivery, which leaves nothing behind to warehouse or resell. A financial product that structurally cannot have a bid-side has limited avenues for price discovery.So, what does the absence of price discovery look like in practice?Below is OpenRouter's live provider board for DeepSeek V4 Pro. One open model, eighteen sellers, quoted simultaneously:

Three things stand out:Firstly, token quotes cluster at an administered anchor. At the bottom of the board sit five providers (Weights & Biases, Together, Fireworks, Baseten, and Parasail) quote the exact same price: $1.74/$3.48. The same pattern holds on every flagship open model. On Kimi K2.6, seven hosts quote exactly $0.95/$4.00 (including Moonshot itself):

And on GLM-5.2, six hosts quote exactly $1.400 (including Z.ai) while six more run promotional discounts off that same administered price.

Interestingly, the first-party prices are not always the floor. DeepSeek posts the cheapest V4 Pro endpoint, but on K2.6, GLM-5.2, and V4 Flash, third parties undercut the anchor.Secondly, prices can range highly and delivery quality remains questionable. In the DeepSeek example, the quotes span from $0.435 to $1.74 (a 4x gap) across 17 providers. Disclosures around quantization are self-reported and often incomplete (3/5 hosts at the same price list don’t list their quantization). Thus, a cheap quote can be confused for a degraded model vs. an efficient provider for new entrants.Thirdly, mechanisms for price convergence do not exist in token-land. Since the order book is one-sided and secondary marketplaces don’t exist tokens cannot be resold and there are no venues for arbitrage.Thus, tokens themselves are not tradeable today but exploring the microstructure for all parties in a token transaction reveals a two-sided marketplace somewhere else.
Inference Market MicrostructureBy microstructure, we mean the mechanics of the token transaction itself: what instrument each participant actually holds, how their margins are constructed, and what risks sit on their “books.”

BuyersMargin=Value created from token use-Token CostBuyers operate on a value-based business model. They ingest tokens and output a product of some value. Thus to maximize their margins, they must optimize for lower token costs. They are beginning to do this by:Efficient model routing: Coinbase has saved 90% of their dollar spend on tokens by routing prompts to OSS models , holding AI costs flat while growing token usage exponentially. Lindy cut 100% of its traffic over to DeepSeek and saved millions. Cognition and Factory already offer model routing within their harness and Cursor launched their own router yesterday to offer users 60% costs savings. This suggests, OSS models are capturing “token flow” from the frontier labs for non high-value tasks.Restructuring workloads: Batch jobs price cost half the live price , and caching helps cut costs by 60-80% for repeated prompts. For instance, Sail Research looks to solve for longer-running background agents and claims up to 12× more tokens per dollar for work that can wait minutes instead of milliseconds.Professionalizing procurement: Routing policies, model-mix budgets, and substitution playbooks are emerging as COGS management tools. Cloud spend experienced a similar transformation when AWS bills got big enough and FinOps teams emerged to manage spend. Token spend is undergoing a similar transformation
ExchangeAn exchange’s margin looks like:Margin=Spread+Fees+Axuillary SourcesFor token marketplaces like OpenRouter, the spread is non-existent since there is no markup — provider prices are passed through at list. However, OpenRouter charges a 5.5% fee when you buy credits – $1B in GPV accrues $55M in net revenue.The 5.5% is a convenience fee. OpenRouter offers model aggregation (sign up for one account, use 400+ models), easier billing, failover guarantees, strong UI/UX, and most recently it introduced intelligent model selection through openrouter/auto (similar to the model router Coinbase built internally). One of the core premise of using OpenRouter is because as a user you get all capacity available. Fallback is a big value proposition. Even if an app or company builds internal routing or aggregation themselves, providers would prioritize flow from OpenRouter.Since aggregators/marketplaces own the end user experience, they can extract those rents from both sides of the table – not only the buyers. As such, OpenRouter may charge a tax on the inference providers as well and charge them a share of their margins for providing them token flow – similar to how Robinhood charges Citadel for order flow.That said, switching costs for OpenRouter are high but not insurmountable. $10M of token spend involves a $550k rent to OpenRouter. An exchange charging 550bps per trade while taking on zero risk sounds a bit egregious and preserving such high margins while taking no principal risk may be difficult. It is not farcical to imagine loss-leading competitors arising but they will have to compete on UX.That said, there are ways for the exchange to preserve its take. Token quality is invisible at the point of purchase and OpenRouter is the intermediated trusted party between the buyers and sellers that records quantization, uptime, latency, throughput, and data usage policies across every inference provider. It can charge rent for that trust and for verification similar to how a ratings agency does.
Inference ProvidersInference providers like Baseten, Fireworks, and Together AI own or rent GPUs and run model inference on them. Most inference providers can only run open-source models, while Anthropic and OpenAI inference can only be provided by the labs themselves and Infra-as-a-Service partners such as Amazon Bedrock and Google Vertex.The margins for an inference provider look like:PNL=Proceeds from tokens sold-Cost to produce tokensA market maker quotes prices continuously, carries inventory, and earns a spread between what its inventory costs and what market orders pay. Similarly, an inference provider quotes prices for tokens they produce, holds token-production inventory in the form of GPU-hours, and earns the spread between what it costs for them to “make” a token and what the market pays for them.

Different inference providers also carry different “grades” of tokens. The same model can differ across providers on the non-price axes:Quantization (FP8 vs FP4 vs INT8): Fewer bits per weight is cheaper and faster to serve, at some cost to model quality. Time to first token (TTFT): How long before the reply starts. Important for human-facing chatTokens per second (TPS): How fast the reply streams. Important for agentic workloads.Uptime: Provider blackout during urgent requests can be quite detrimentalFor an inference provider, revenue is flow × price, and flow on a marketplace goes to the most competitive quote (sorted by 1/price² on OpenRouter). Defending margin at a competitive quote thus requires the lowest cost to produce. Since the cheapest quote gets picked off first on OpenRouter’s marketplace, loss-leader dynamics might naturally evolve if normalized for quality.To some extent, inference providers run a crack spread strategy on GPU-hours. In oil markets, a refiner’s “crack spread” is the margin between the crude it buys and the refined products (gasoline, diesel) it sells. The refiner is long crude, short products, and earns whatever the refinery in the middle can extract between the two prices. Similarly, inference providers are long GPU-hours forward, short tokens spot, with the serving stack acts as the refinery in between.We can write the inference provider’s margin per GPU-hour as:m=p⋅R⋅u-cwhere:p is the token priceR is the refining yield (tokens produced per GPU-hour)u is utilizationc is the GPU-hour costIt’s helpful to understand the above with an example. Let’s freeze our GPU/hr cost to $2.74/hr (Ornn H100 price on July 21) . A provider renting at the index and serving 1,000 tokens per second at $0.90 per million token produces 3.6M tokens per hour at full utilization and earns $3.24/hr against $2.74/hr of rent: a spread of +$0.50/hr. At 50% utilization, revenue halves to $1.62/hr and the spread turns negative to −$1.12/hr. Breakeven utilization on this “crack spread” sits at a utilization of 85%.

Two caveats. First, p and R pull against each other. Speed is sold by shrinking batch sizes, and smaller batches mean fewer tokens per GPU-hour. Serving users faster raises the price you can charge but lowers the yield you produce. That is why the same model on the same hardware sells for $0.56/M at 50 tok/s but $4/M at 125 tok/s. Providers often optimize their stack to serve a particular point on this curve.

*Anchor points from SemiAnalysis InferenceMAX[13] curve shape illustrative.
Secondly, the example’s 15% gross margin is much thinner than the reported 45–50% margin inference providers run today. They are able to:Charge higher prices (p ↑) by capturing flow from users further out on the throughput-cost curve.Compress costs (c ↓) by signing longer-term GPU commitmentsDrive utilization (u ↑) by dynamically managing or repurposing the GPU fleet (more on this below)Push yield (R ↑) with the serving-stack optimizations (more on this below)p is set by sell-side competition and c by the GPU market. R and u are the only two a provider have complete control over.As such, providers seek to maximize R and achieve differentiation on those axes against other providers. Common techniques to optimize costs and maximize R are as follows:Quantization (FP8 → FP4/INT4): Decoding a token is memory-bandwidth-bound: every output token requires streaming the model’s active weights from HBM. Quantization (using FP4 vs FP8) halves the bytes per weight and halves the bandwidth used. FP4 yields 1.8× over FP8 in production, and B200s running FP4 reach up to 3.65× the performance per dollar of H200s on FP8. However, quantization comes at the cost of model quality.Prefix/KV caching. Most tool call an agent makes resends mostly the same prompt with a little new text at the end. Rather than re-process that prompt from scratch each time, the provider stores the computation from the last call and only processes what’s new. Coding agents reuse 85–97% of their prompt this way in production, and going from no caching to 90% reuse takes roughly 10× off the GPU bill. For agent traffic, cache-hit is the most important metric in determining the compute bill.Speculative decoding: A small “draft” model guesses several tokens ahead, and the big model verifies the whole guess in a single pass. Checking is much cheaper than generating, so one read of the big model’s weights now yields several tokens instead of one.Prefill/decode disaggregation: Prefill (reading a prompt) is bound my compute decode and (generating a reply) is bound by memory bandwidth. Yet they share the same GPUs. Splitting them onto separate pools, each tuned for the respective bottleneck, allows for 10–30% improvements and up to 4.4× per GPU for large MoE models on rack-scale systems.Parallelzing MoE experts: Frontier MoE models activate only 3–5% of their parameters per token. Spreading the experts across 32–144 GPUs shrinks the weights each GPU holds, freeing HBM for larger batches, and expert load-balancing alone contributes a 1.5–2.5× throughput gain. DeepSeek runs its own fleet this way (prompts on 32-GPU units, generation on 144-GPU units ), SGLang reproduced the setup on 96 GPUs in the open-source engine, and NVIDIA’s rack-scale GB200 NVL72 systems are built around exactly this pattern.

These optimization levers compound multiplicatively. Despite models getting larger and GPU/hr prices increasing, inference costs have plummeted across generations. DeepSeek’s flagship output price fell ~8× since January 2025 (R1 at $2.19/M → V4 Flash at $0.28/M ), while the H100 index ended the same window 17% higher: $2.34 to $2.74.

Source: R1, Jan 2025 → V3.2-Exp’s −50% cut, Sep 2025 → V4 Flash, 2026 . GPU line: Ornn’s H100 SXM price index , daily, pulled Jul 21 2026.*
Inference providers differentiate by building proprietary depth in these optimization levers. Fireworks wrote FireAttention, a custom attention kernel that allows it to serve the same weights 4× faster than stock vLLM and excels at latency-sensitive flow. Together built ATLAS, a speculative-decoding system whose draft models learn from live traffic, designed to enable its speedups to compound with volume. Baseten trains custom EAGLE-3 draft heads per customer, and has excelled at dedicated deployments. SAIL tunes its whole stack for time insensitive work and has excelled at long-running background agents.However, these optimizations eventually diffuse into the open-source serving engines like vLLM and SGLang. As such, the “alpha” for an inference provider decays and the decay/diffusion rate has been accelerating. Prefill/decode disaggregation took 11–16 months, Multi-head latent attention (MLA) took 3–8 months, EAGLE-3 took 1–2 months and by DeepSeek V4 the release included the most performant serving stack out of the gate.

The edge decay is structural. Not every optimization is published but the largest ones keep arriving as papers because the labs that invent them want their models served widely and cheaply on day one. Red Hat pays vLLM’s core maintainers and NVIDIA contributes to both vLLM and SGLang.There is additional industry nuance here. Some open source labs work closely with inference clouds and let them access model weights pre-open launch in exchange for 15-30% of lifetime serverless revenue from that model. Inference providers basically give up a percentage of future revenue from that model to get a 10 day head start to optimize their gear and plan their capacity around the new model release. Providers can also unlock more storage to have higher cache hits to be able to attract more flow. Model life cycles are short and the initial surge in demand post model release is quite profitable – almost like market makers vying for flow during an IPO or a TGE.A serving-stack edge is therefore temporally short-lived and like any trading alpha must be continuously re-earned.As such, once the optimization stack (R) is exhausted, COGS management turns financial:Rebalancing capacity (u): Provider’s often split their fleets in two parts: dedicated capacity, (where a customer reserves specific GPUs for its own model) and a shared serverless pool everyone else draws from. Dedicated capacity is paid for around the clock but is rarely busy around the clock and its idle hours are predictable. The unlock is that most customer fine-tunes are LoRA adapters: small weight deltas layered on the same base model that is already loaded on the GPU. So when a dedicated customer goes quiet overnight, providers can swap that customer’s adapter out and route serverless traffic onto the reserved GPUs and swap them back on when the customer wakes up. In this manner, the same GPU-hour essentially gets sold twice — once as a reservation, once as serverless flow — pushing effective utilization from 50% to 120%. This is not dissimilar to airlines selling more seats than the plane holds, because the no-shows are predictable. Here the no-show is a dedicated customer’s idle hour.Managing compute cost (c): Compute is the largest cost item in the entire token delivery supply chain. Of every $100 of tokens created, roughly $50 is burnt in GPU-hours. As such, GPU-hours are the homogeneous input for producing any token and thus the most integral part of the entire token lifecycle. The all-in cost of an owned H100 in turn is as follows:

Today providers manage c with term contracts and short-term rental agreements while internalizing all depreciation, price and volatility risk. Financial derivatives like futures and forward curves for GPUs (and memory) can help inference providers transfer risk and manage their cost effectively.In other words, as an inference provider’s software and hardware optimizations asymptote, it’s business begins to look more and more like a trading book.
Compute Futures: The Two-Sided MarketA tradeable instrument requires standardization (one unit substitutes for another) and stability (a contract written today describes the same good at maturity).Tokens fail both today:Standardization: A token is a product tuple across model × quantization × context × latency tier. Fixing the model, one ends up with a Caretsian bundle for the model’s grades – 3 quantizations × 2 context configurations × 3 latency tiers is already 18 distinct, non-fungible products of the “same” model. Stability: The overton window for the newest model has been shrinking. New models now come out every 41 days, often rendering an entire class of older models redundant and plummeting demand for them.Could a token index repair this? Only halfway. Token prices are set at the labs’ discretion and are manipulable by construction. Even the SIT proposal , which fixes the inputs, grades the model rather than the served inference, where the quality games actually live (identical weights score 76–100% on tool calls depending on the host).As such, a token index can work as a reference rate but it cannot carry risk transfer. Risk transfer must happen one layer down in the homogenous input layer that is GPU-hours.GPU-hours already have emergent indices for standardized price discovery such as Ornn’s Compute Price Index and two-sided liquid trading venues like the Architect Innovation Exchange (both Galaxy Ventures portfolio companies)

Why an inference provider needs to manage GPU price risk? An inference provider’s entire cost side is one volatile spot input – their cost of compute. In m=p⋅R⋅u-c, the provider controls R and u and competition sets p but c floats on a spot market whose realized volatility averages 130% annualized with current realized vol sitting at 312%.

In practice a provider’s book is a blend of owned GPUs inventory, 1–3 year term commitments, and short-term rentals at prices near the spot index. Left unhedged, the blend loses in both directions.When rent spikes (May 2026: +101% off the trough), the spot leg’s cost doubles while token prices stay stagnant (token prices have been monotonically decreasing so far) and thus every marginal GPU-hour serves at a loss.

When rent collapses (the $1.63 trough), the longer-term commitments are over-paying above the spot market rate, and competitors renting at spot can quote token prices below the provider’s cost.

How would inference providers manage price risk in practice? Buy GPU-hour futures against the fleet’s forward rental needs. Locking the cost leg replaces the floating spot rent with the futures price plus the cost of running the hedge itself:m=p⋅R⋅u-(F_0+f)where F_0 is the futures price for the tenor being locked and f is the financing cost of the position (collateral tied up as initial margin plus daily variation margin). As with any future, you can have contango or backwardation. Let’s walk through with some examples of a dummy futures curve:Contango (F_0>c_spot): Futures curve slopes up, so the buyer bears carry costs — m=p⋅R⋅u-(c_spot+"carry"+f). Take the February glut: spot sat at $1.63, but our dummy futures quoted above it at $2.05 for May delivery, $2.20 for further out because the market expected rents to mean revert. A provider hedging then paid $0.40–0.60 over spot for locking in the futures price. When the squeeze took spot to $3.28 in May, the hedged provider was still paying $2 and saving the $1.28 delta in operating costs.

Backwardation (F_0>c_spot): Futures curve slopes down, so the buyer pockets a discount (positive roll) — 𝑚=𝑝⋅𝑅⋅𝑢−(𝑐𝑠𝑝𝑜𝑡−discount+𝑓). Take May’s squeeze: spot hit $3.28, but our dummy futures quoted below it at $2.90 two months out because the market expected the shortage to pass. Whoever needed a GPU that week paid the full $3.28 while a provider buying next quarter’s hours got them at a discount to the panic price.

Either way, an open price risk becomes a known, contracted cost which provides margin stability and the only risks left are the two the provider is actually able to internalize, R and u.There are still a few caveats to the above:Firstly, basis risk is not entirely removed: The contract settles on index-spec H100 hours, while a real fleet is a mix of vintages, regions, and interconnects that won’t track the index one-for-one. The hedge covers the market move, not the provider’s fleet’s spread to it.Second, locking c doesn’t lock demand: If a provider hedges more hours than they end up utilizing the position flips from a cost hedge into a directional long on compute. The hedge ratio therefore is somewhat a function of the provider’s confidence in their future projection of their u.Huge thanks to Brett and Ishanee from Architect, Kush, Wayne, and Jack from Ornn, and Vishwa from Anera in their help in reviewing and helping me with this piece. articles.title: Monetary policy in times of high public debt
articles.text: 02 NOVEMBER 2026 · RESEARCH BULLETIN NO. 148Monetary policy in times of high public debtBy Stéphane Dupraz and Anna Rogantini Picco[1] This article was written by Stéphane Dupraz (Monetary Policy Research Division, Banque de France) and Anna Rogantini Picco (Directorate General Research, European Central Bank). The authors gratefully acknowledge the comments of Alexander Popov, and Zoë Sprokel. The views expressed here are those of the authors and do not necessarily represent the views of the European Central Bank or the Eurosystem. High public debt around the globe has revived concerns that it could undo central banks’ ability to control inflation. Central banks can still control inflation when public debt is high, but must then take into account that higher public debt increases the level of interest rates consistent with price stability.Public debt has climbed sharply on both sides of the Atlantic since the global financial crisis (see Chart 1). Meanwhile, financing needs are expanding owing to the green transition and higher defence spending. This has revived an old concern: can high public debt fuel inflation? When the euro area was first pieced together, the Maastricht Treaty[2] The “Maastricht Treaty” refers to the Treaty on European Union, signed in Maastricht on 7 February 1992 and later amended by the Treaty of Lisbon. Since 1997, the EU’s framework for coordinating fiscal policies has commonly been referred to as the Stability and Growth Pact. imposed limits of 3% on fiscal deficits and 60% on debt-to-GDP ratios. This reflected concerns that looser national fiscal policies could strain the seams of the monetary union by weakening the central bank’s grip on inflation. And surveys suggest that households also associate high debt with higher inflation (see Andrade et al. 2025). By contrast, Milton Friedman’s dictum that “inflation is always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon” suggests that, as long as the central bank is independent and the government does not interfere, monetary policy can keep a firm grip on inflation.Chart 1General government debt-to-GDP ratios for the United States and the euro areaSources: “Federal debt held by the public” from Federal Reserve Economic Data (FRED) and Eurostat’s “General government gross debt (EA20)”. An issue that divides economistsSo, which is it: can we always expect the central bank to keep inflation hemmed in, or can fiscal policy weaken the central bank’s ability to deliver price stability? Among economists there is surprisingly little consensus on this.[3] For a review of the literature on the linkages between fiscal and monetary policy, with a focus on the potential risks to price stability in times of high public debt, see Checherita-Westphal et al. (2024). On the one hand, most monetary models follow the Friedman view according to which monetary policy always controls inflation. On the other hand, the fiscal theory of the price level argues that unless current public debt is backed by future fiscal surpluses then fiscal policy, rather than monetary policy, can determine inflation (Leeper, 1991; Sims, 1994; and Woodford,1995).[4] Woodford’s (2026) tribute to Chris Sims discusses how the role of fiscal policy in determining inflation was an increasingly recurrent theme in Sims’ later work. The range of views has only widened in recent years. Blanchard (2019) highlighted that when interest rates on government bonds are below the economy’s growth rate, debt does not need to be backed by future surpluses. In this situation, a government may be able to keep rolling its debt over without having to raise taxes later to repay it – though Blanchard cautioned that this would not necessarily be a good idea. Conversely, the fiscal response to the pandemic made another intuition hard to ignore: if you give households extra money and they spend some of it, but the supply of goods remains limited, then prices rise (see for example Angeletos, Lian and Wolf, 2024).Both arguments rely on the assumption that households are not fully “Ricardian”. Households are said to be Ricardian when they save all of any debt-financed transfer they receive in anticipation of higher future taxes and the level of public debt makes no difference to their spending. In contrast, non-Ricardian households spend some of the extra money transferred. This is because some people may realise they won’t live to see the future tax increases, while others may be unable to borrow and prefer spending more today even though they expect higher taxes tomorrow. The empirical evidence suggests actual household behaviour doesn’t fit the Ricardian pattern: Borusyak, Jaravel and Spiess (2024) found that US households spent 8-11% of their 2008 tax rebates on non-durable goods in the same quarter in which they received their rebates.How high can debt be without causing price stability to unravel?In Dupraz and Rogantini Picco (2025), we take a fresh look at how fiscal policy could put serious strain on price stability. While rising public debt is inflationary when households are not Ricardian, we note that this does not necessarily mean the central bank loses control over inflation. Public debt translates into wealth for households, and greater wealth tends to raise spending, putting inflationary pressure on the economy. But the central bank can normally lean against that extra demand by increasing interest rates – just as it can counter the inflationary effects of other kinds of shocks.Nevertheless, this only works up to a point. When households are not Ricardian, public debt can become so high that even very high interest rates cannot rein in households’ desire to spend. In fact, higher rates can even encourage spending, because higher rates on a household’s savings mean it needs less savings to maintain high consumption in the future. However, we find the implied limit on public debt to be quite high – our main estimate puts it at about 5.4 times annual GDP, far above current advanced-economy debt ratios.How can monetary policy prevent high debt raising inflation?A more immediate difficulty arises well before that limit is reached. A standard prescription for monetary policy is to hike policy rates as inflation rises. But when households are non-Ricardian, this can backfire. Higher rates curb spending today, but they also increase future debt, adding inflationary pressure tomorrow. Inflation becomes more persistent, so when the central bank tightens more strongly cumulative inflation may fall very little – or even rise.There is, however, a way for monetary policy to stay in close control of inflation. Rather than waiting for higher debt to generate inflation, the central bank can tighten interest rates directly in response to an increase in the level of public debt. This restores the ability of monetary policy to prevent fiscal shocks from increasing inflation.Public debt alters the natural rate of interestTo explain this, it helps to consider the natural rate of interest: the rate that keeps demand in line with what the economy can produce and therefore keeps inflation on target. The natural rate depends on all the factors that determine households’ desire to save rather than spend, such as demographics, productivity and risk preferences (see Marx, Mojon and Velde, 2021).But the natural rate depends not only on households’ demand for assets in which to invest their savings; it also depends on the supply of these assets. Government debt is an important source of asset supply, and therefore helps shape the natural rate (see for example Auclert et al., 2025). For the United States, estimates suggest that a 1 percentage point increase in debt relative to GDP raises long-term interest rates by about 3 basis points (see for example Plante, Richter and Zubairy, 2025).How the central bank can stay in control of inflationTo track the natural rate, central banks in our analysis therefore need to keep an eye on public debt. Given that the natural rate increases with the level of public debt, they need to raise interest rates when public debt increases – and not wait to respond to the inflation that higher debt can generate. That can be institutionally uncomfortable: central banks do not want to appear to react to fiscal decisions. But monitoring the level of public debt is not the same as conducting fiscal policy; it is part of understanding how to implement monetary policy in a way that suits the economy it needs to stabilise.ReferencesAndrade, P., Gautier, E., Mengus, E., Mönch, E., Schmidt, T. (2025), “Household Beliefs about Fiscal Dominance”, Working Paper Series, No 986, Banque de France.Angeletos, G-M., Lian, C. and Wolf, C.K. (2024), “Deficits and Inflation: HANK meets FTPL”, NBER Working Paper, No 33102, National Bureau of Economic Research.Auclert, A. Malmberg, H., Rognlie, M. and Straub, L. (2024), “Revisiting Event Study Designs: Robust and Efficient Estimation”, Review of Economic Studies, Vol. 91, No 6, pp. 3253-3285. Checherita-Westphal, C., Rogantini Picco, A., Schmidt, S., and Sigaux, J.-D. (2024), “Monetary and fiscal policy interactions: risks to price stability in times of high government debt”, ECB Discussion Paper Series, No 26.Dupraz, S. and Rogantini Picco, A. (1995): “Price-level determinacy without control of a monetary aggregate,” Carnegie-Rochester Conference Series on Public Policy, Vol. 43, No 1, pp. 1-46.Woodford, M. (2026), “Chris Sims and the role of money in economic fluctuations”, VoxEU.org, 9 May. The views expressed here are those of the authors and do not necessarily represent the views of the European Central Bank or the Eurosystem. Since 1997, the EU’s framework for coordinating fiscal policies has commonly been referred to as the Stability and Growth Pact. For a review of the literature on the linkages between fiscal and monetary policy, with a focus on the potential risks to price stability in times of high public debt, see Checherita-Westphal et al. From Permian-associated gas supply to hyperscaler power demand, the variables driving North American energy prices are shifting faster than traditional trading frameworks were built to handle. So, what do energy traders need to know to position for Q4 2026 and beyond?
At Wood Mackenzie’s Energy Trading Conference 2026, held in Houston on 15 October, our analysts were joined by industry-leading experts to discuss the structural shifts reshaping the US gas, oil and power complex. Fill out the form to download a complimentary insight summarising the key themes explored at the event, or read on for three quick takeaways.
1. Crude oil prices are writing the US natural gas supply curve
Our US Lower 48 oil production forecast has moved higher since the beginning of the year, driven by Iran conflict-related oil price gains and the resulting wave of rig additions — mainly by private companies. Higher oil production is resulting in increased supplies of associated gas, driving overall gas production forecasts higher at the expense of Henry Hub prices.
How much US Lower 48 gas production growth do we expect by the end of 2027? Find out by downloading the insight.
2. Behind-the-meter generation is redrawing gas-power connectivity
Data centre power strategy is changing the relationship between gas and power. The AI race means that behind-the-meter (BTM) generation is increasing popular — new project announcements keep coming and projects continue to progress through development.
Where are most BTM projects being sited and why? Download the insight to find out.
3. Cross-commodity oil-gas-power risk is increasingly important for gas trading
Geopolitical risk has caused huge swings in Henry Hub pricing in 2026 as algorithms and traders try to understand the implications of the Iran War for natural gas markets. This along with along with growing gas & power volatility are just two examples of how the increasing interconnectivity between oil, gas and power markets can affect gas trading.
Every trader, regardless of their commodity, needs to be increasingly aware of a range of other indirect factors that can impact their markets. You can learn more in the insight.

articles.title: How Democrats won big, and why 2028 remains an open question | Brookings
articles.text:
Commentary

How Democrats won big, and why 2028 remains an open question

Elaine Kamarck and

Elaine Kamarck

Founding Director
- Center for Effective Public Management (CEPM),

Senior Fellow
- Governance Studies

William A. Galston

William A. Galston

Senior Fellow
- Governance Studies, Center for Effective Public Management (CEPM),

Ezra K. Zilkha Chair in Governance Studies

November 6, 2026

Democrats’ sweep of the 2026 midterms was driven less by Republican voters switching sides than by discontented Republicans staying home while motivated Democrats turned out.
Voters turned against the GOP over Trump’s low job approval, high prices tied to tariffs and the Iran war, immigration enforcement that went too far, and growing concerns about corruption.
The midterms say little about who will win in 2028, since past midterm results have not reliably predicted the next presidential race and progressives and moderates both won in 2026, leaving open which kind of Democrat is most electable.

Supporters of Democratic U.S. Senate candidate James Talarico cheer after he won the Texas race during a midterm election night watch party at the Long Center for the Performing Arts in Austin, Texas, on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by RONALDO SCHEMIDT / AFP via Getty Images)

16 min read

Bluesky Streamline Icon: https://streamlinehq.comBluesky

Back to top

Introduction

With some ballots yet to be counted, it is already clear that the 2026 midterm election was a historic victory for the Democrats and a devastating referendum on President Donald Trump and his party. Democrats reached deep into longtime Republican bastions to seize control of both the House and Senate. With the outcome of Senate races in Alaska and Mississippi yet to be determined, Democrats flipped at least seven Senate seats. Voters sent Democrats to the Senate in Texas and South Carolina for the first time in decades, and in Kansas, for the first time since 1932. Democrats racked up gains throughout the agricultural Midwest, which had been hard hit by President Trump’s policies. Maine’s Troy Jackson sent Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) into retirement after 30 years in office. In the House, Democrats won the national popular vote by 13 points and will end up with a larger majority than anyone expected. In the Texas governor contest, Gina Hinojosa defeated three-term Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, putting a Democrat in the governor’s mansion for the first time since 1995. In Georgia, former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms became the first Black woman governor in the nation’s history, while Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayed became the first Muslim senator.

Back to top

Key factors behind the blue wave

Turnout
Turnout in midterm elections is always lower than in presidential contests, but the party that wins the midterms enjoys the smallest falloff from the previous presidential election. Throughout 2026, Democrats enjoyed a substantial lead in polls measuring the likelihood of voting, and the actual votes reflected this edge. As election season progressed, expectations increased that turnout would be high. As of the end of October, early voting totals had surpassed the totals seen in 2018 and 2022. The all-time highs for the 21st century midterms were 2018 (53.4%), when Democrats took over the House of Representatives, and 2022 (52.2%) when Republicans took over the House.
Although national turnout numbers are not yet available, the results from three large red states are suggestive. Compared to the 2024 presidential election, votes cast for Texas Republican Gov. Greg Abbott fell 30% from President Trump’s total while his challenger, Democrat Gina Hinojosa, exceeded Kamala Harris’ vote by 8%.1 Republican Byron Donalds fell short of Trump’s total by 32%, while Democrat David Jolly finished 14% behind Harris. And in Ohio, Democrat Amy Action received 5% fewer votes than Harris while Vivek Ramaswamy’s total fell short of Trump’s by 36%. Meanwhile, only 6% of Republicans crossed over to support Democrats in races for the House of Representatives. Discontented Republicans didn’t abandon their party in 2026; they stayed home, opening the door for highly motivated Democrats to score massive gains.
Demography and geography
In 2024, Donald Trump scored historic gains among Hispanics, Black voters (especially men), independents, and young adults, leading commentators to speculate about a pro-Republican realignment into a multiethnic working-class party. The midterm results will likely end this conversation. In 2024, President Trump received 48% of the Hispanic vote (up from 36% in 2020), 15% of the Black vote (up from 8%), 48% of Independents (up from 43%), and 39% of young adults (up from 35%). In this year’s national vote for the House, by contrast, Republican candidates received only 29% of the Hispanic vote, 8% of the Black vote, 38% of Independents, and 28% of young adults.
The substantial decrease in the Black vote for Republicans is attributable to two big changes that affected these voters. The first was the Supreme Court’s Callais decision which significantly weakened the Voting Rights Act, and the second, related to the first, was the Republican-led mid-decade redistricting which wiped out many formerly majority-minority districts represented by African Americans. Politico predicted this would lead to increased turnout and named it “blacklash.”
There were also signs of erosion in the heart of the Republican base—white voters without college degrees. In 2024, Trump received 64% of their vote. This year, Republicans garnered only 60%.
The shifts in Latino voting had a substantial impact on key House and Senate races. Talarico’s historic win in Texas was fueled by predominantly Hispanic counties in South Texas. Nationwide, in the House districts with the heaviest concentration of Hispanic voters, Democrats won 30 seats, for a net gain of 12, with the results still incomplete in two contests.2 Democrats also scored gains in rural areas. Of the 20 swing rural House districts, Democrats have netted a gain of at least seven seats, with one still too close to call. 3

Figure 1

Bluesky Streamline Icon: https://streamlinehq.comBluesky

Mid-decade redistricting
In the summer of 2025, Texas broke from tradition, drawing new congressional lines in the middle of the decade and setting off a series of redistricting efforts across the country. But the effects of this strategy fell dramatically short of Republicans’ hopes.
Republican-led redistricting in Florida and Texas rested on the assumption that this year’s Hispanic vote would echo Republican gains in 2024, which it did not, leading to disappointing results for the GOP. In Texas, Republicans picked up just one of the seats they targeted—the open seat in the 32nd Congressional District which was flipped to Republican by Jace Yarbrough—while the other four remained in Democratic control. In Florida, Republicans hoped to pick up four seats by drawing new lines, but Democrats held on to three of them. The fourth (Florida’s 9th Congressional District) is still to be called, with the incumbent Democrat Darren Soto in the lead as of this writing. Of the 19 seats identified by the New York Times as most affected by redistricting, Democrats actually netted three additional seats.
Pennsylvania
In recent cycles, Pennsylvania has emerged as the largest swing state and as a microcosm of the country. Although the state had no Senate race this year, it featured some noteworthy developments. Not only did Gov. Josh Shapiro win reelection in a 22-point landslide, garnering 60% of the popular vote, but also Democrats flipped all four swing House districts and won a majority in the state Senate while expanding its majority in the House.
Democratic socialist candidates
Beginning with the 2025 election of Mayor Zohran Mamdani in New York City, and continuing with the rise of Abdul El-Sayed as the 2026 Democratic nominee for Senate in Michigan, attention turned to the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA). Republicans rejoiced as they publicized the DSA platform and sought to portray the Democratic Party as out-of-touch communists. Some Democrats responded by reiterating that they were, in fact, capitalists.
Earlier this year, Kamarck and co-authors identified all the congressional candidates that were either endorsed or recommended by the DSA. These included those endorsed or recommended by the national organization or state and local chapters. All told, 16 DSA candidates won their Democratic primaries. Nine of these candidates were from California; the remainder were from other states. Four were incumbents.4
Only two of these candidates came from Republican districts—Tessa Lynn Hodge from California’s 23rd District, which has a PVI score of R+9, and Justin Pearson of Tennessee’s 9th District, which also has a PVI score of R+9. Hodge is behind in her district, but the race has yet to be called. Pearson ultimately lost but only by 1 point. The remaining DSA candidates were in solidly Democratic congressional districts with PVI scores averaging D+22. The outlier was Randy Villegas whose district (California’s 22nd District) had a PVI score of D+1. Villegas won. Of the DSA nominees, four were incumbents and will be returning to Congress. One other candidate is William Lawrence, the Democratic nominee for Michigan’s 7th District, who left the DSA in summer 2026 but until then was an active member. That district had a PVI of 0—meaning that it was evenly split. Lawrence won his district, flipping it from Republican to Democratic.
The bottom line: With all votes counted and races called, there could be as many as nine new DSA-backed candidates in the Democratic caucus. However, there likely will be more than twice as many “blue dog” or conservative Democrats joining the caucus as well. Potential new Speaker Hakeem Jeffries will have to balance these new voices against the influx of newly elected moderates, just as in the Senate Abdul El-Sayed’s voice will be balanced by the likes of North Carolina’s Roy Cooper and other newly elected senators.5

Back to top

The Republican weak spots voters punished

Trump’s job approval
It is axiomatic among political scientists that the president’s job approval does more than any other factor to shape midterm elections, and 2026 is no exception. As voters streamed to the polls, President Trump’s job approval averaged just 39%, compared to 59% disapproval. Of the 11 Senate races that remained competitive on Election Day, Trump’s job disapproval exceeded his approval in all of them, despite the fact that he had carried 10 of these states in 2024, most by double digits.
Post-election polls mostly confirmed what preelection polls had been saying for months: Voters were deeply dissatisfied with the president’s handling of the issue they cared most about—high prices. Making things worse, they saw a direct connection between high prices and two of the president’s signature policies during his second term—tariffs and the war in Iran. Large majorities of voters concluded that his tariffs had raised costs for U.S. consumers, and they saw for themselves what happened to gas prices after the president initiated hostilities in the Persian Gulf.6
Rural America
Rural America was particularly hard hit: As other nations retaliated against U.S. tariffs, agricultural exports were slammed, and the war jacked up the prices of key agricultural inputs, including diesel fuel and fertilizer. This is why Democrats were competitive in so many rural districts this year, and why they won statewide races in Iowa, Ohio, and Kansas that appeared out of reach a year ago.
Immigration
Immigration was one of President Trump’s strongest issues in the 2024 election, but his handling of the issue once he reentered the Oval Office ended up neutralizing its political impact. While voters gave him high marks for shutting down the southern border, a majority concluded that the conduct of ICE agents, especially in big city raids, had gone too far. During the election, Trump had focused on deporting hardened criminals (“the worse of the worst”), but immigration enforcement has swept up large numbers of law-abiding immigrants and even citizens who were making economic contributions to their communities in sectors such as agriculture, homebuilding, hospitality, and child care. Hispanic voters, many of whom supported stronger enforcement at the border, objected strongly to the administration’s policies in the interior of the country.
Corruption
Beginning in 2025, a series of reports raised questions about President Trump’s cryptocurrency business and its financial dealings with foreign representatives. In summer 2026, Trump’s financial disclosure forms showed that he had made roughly $2.2 billion during 2025, with more than half coming from cryptocurrency ventures. These revelations coincided with a sharp increase in public perceptions of corruption. According to Gallup, the share of Americans who believe government corruption is widespread jumped from 73% in 2024 to 89% in 2026—a striking increase after more than a decade of relatively little movement on this topic.
In one much-discussed poll, worries about corruption had, to the surprise of many, eclipsed worries about the cost of living and the price of gas. A CNBC poll found that 36% of voters put government corruption at the top of a list of the most important issues facing the country right now. Other polls found that Trump was using the presidency to enrich himself and that Trump’s businesses influenced his presidential decisions. By the end of the campaign, candidates on both sides (but especially Democrats) were regularly tying corruption to voters’ complaints about their own economic struggles. These concerns coincided with an outpouring of anger and suspicion toward AI and data centers.
The Trump factor
Despite the powerful Democratic tide, the Republicans could have held on to the Senate—if President Trump had not put his thumb on the scales during the Republican primaries. He intervened decisively in four Senate races—Texas, Georgia, North Carolina, and South Carolina—pushing candidates loyal to him over the finish line for the nomination. All four lost, including shocking defeats in South Carolina and Texas.

Back to top

Conclusion

Despite the dramatic results of the 2026 midterm election, Democrats would be well advised to curb their enthusiasm and Republicans to restrain their despair. The reason: History shows that the midterms do not predict the results of the ensuing presidential election. For example, Democrats lost more than 50 House seats in 1994, but Bill Clinton went on to win reelection easily in 1996. Democrats lost more than 60 seats in 2010, but Barack Obama’s standing rose in 2011-2012, and he won a comfortable reelection in 2012. On the other hand, after large Democratic gains in 2006 and 2018, Obama and Joe Biden both won the presidency by significant margins.
While the 2026 midterms have at best limited predictive value for 2028, they do point to the challenges both major parties face as the race for their presidential nominations begins and the country awaits its first presidential contest since 2016 with neither an incumbent president nor a former president on the ballot. After the crushing rebuke their party received in the midterms, Republicans must decide whether to keep their party on the course Donald Trump has charted over the past decade or to head in a different direction.
For their part, Democrats face an embarrassment of riches. Moderates won numerous statewide races, but so did progressives in Maine, Michigan, and Minnesota. The midterm results do not conclusively show which kind of Democrat would be more electable at the national level in 2028. The outcome of the party’s primaries will reflect the voters’ judgment not only on electability, but also about the agenda that is most likely to successfully address the country’s most important problems. One thing is clear: In both parties, the intraparty debate that was deferred in 2024 can be delayed no longer.

articles.title: Managing our Environmental Impact
articles.text:
Managing our Environmental Impact. Our Commitment. Our Targets. Our Progress.

Man Group is committed to reducing its absolute carbon footprint and to being consistent and transparent about the progress we are making. As a key part of our Corporate Sustainability strategy, you can read more about how we manage our environmental impact in our Corporate Sustainability Brochure.

We continue to implement changes to our operations to ensure we are on track to meet our emissions reduction target set for 2026 and are on the strategic pathway to net zero carbon in our global workplaces by 2030.

Environmental Policy

Our Environmental Sustainability Policy Statement focuses on: using natural resources responsibly; minimising the environmental impact of our activities through maximising energy efficiency; reducing greenhouse gas emissions and; recycling and / or minimising waste. We also commit to at least annual reporting of our environmental targets, data and any issues we encounter. In 2024, we achieved ISO 14001:2018 for our London office.

Board Oversight of Environmental Matters

Our Man Group Board has responsibility for Man Group's environmental impact and ensures that Man’s Environmental Sustainability Policy Statement is implemented and reviewed. The Board has a collective role in providing environmental leadership throughout Man's global operations and is committed to continual improvement in environmental performance.

Environmental Risk Management

Man Group considers operational climate risks 15+ years into the future. It does this through multi-disciplinary company-wide risk identification, assessment and management processes. The types of risks considered include current and emerging regulation, technological changes and upgrades, market risks, reputational risks, acute and chronic physical operational impacts as well as upstream and downstream risks.

Green Buildings

Minimising our environmental impact is at the centre of our real estate strategy. We occupy eight buildings certified by LEED (Leadership in Energy Efficiency and Design), one by Energy Star and one by NABERS (National Australian Built Environment Rating System), accounting for 92% of our global headcount. Man Group’s largest office, Riverbank House (RBH) in London, has a Building Research Establishment Environmental Assessment Method (BREEAM) ‘Excellent’ rating.

Riverbank House - London

Riverbank House is rated “Excellent” via the Building Research Establishment Environmental Assessment Method (BREEAM). The building has a green roof, rainwater harvesting and solar power generation.

Pfäffikon - Switzerland

Our Pfäffikon office is a short walk from Lake Zurich and is powered by renewable hydro-electric energy.

Environmental data compilation systems

We strive to deliver clear and transparent reporting that captures the measurable elements within our control. We monitor and track our global environmental impact using specialist specialist tracking software and an energy services consultancy which help us to mitigate risk, maximise opportunities and reduce our carbon footprint.

Responsible Procurement

Man Group’s offices procure goods and services that are in line with our environmental objectives. We utilise ISO standards and ratings systems (such as energy star for IT equipment and green star for paper supplies) to assist us in choosing sustainable products. We also ensure all our equipment complies with the Restriction of Hazardous Substances EU Directive.

Man Group’s Supplier Code of Conduct

As a condition of supplying services to Man Group, our suppliers are directed to adhere to our Supplier Code of Conduct. This code outlines the minimum standards Man Group expects of its suppliers, regarding economic activity, impact on the environment, as well as engagement with wider communities.

Man Group intends to lead by example, and we endeavour to work closely with our suppliers to rise to the opportunity of addressing the global, social and environmental challenges that we all currently face.

Environmental Improvements

Man Group’s largest office, Riverbank House, is continually assessed for energy and air-conditioning efficiency. The recommendations inform our investments.

During 2024, we achieved ISO14001:2018 for our Riverbank House office.

Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures (TCFD)

Man Group is a supporter and signatory of the TCFD, and is committed to taking action against climate change. The Board oversees the development of our climate-related financial disclosures which cover governance, strategy, risk management, and metrics and targets, as described in our Annual Report.

Institutional Investors Group on Climate Change (IIGCC)

Man Group is a signatory to the Institutional Investors Group on Climate Change, the European membership body for investor collaboration on climate change.

UN Global Compact

We are also proud, active signatories of the UN Global Compact, supporting the Ten Principles on human rights, labour, environment and anti-corruption.

Environmental Training and Awareness

Environmental awareness campaigns are run in offices focusing on areas such as increasing recycling, reducing energy use, cycling to work and removing single use plastics.

We have run a number of sustainable volunteering activities across our offices including litter pick-ups, local garden and park maintenance as well as educational awareness events.

articles.title: UK: Hawkish Monetary Policy Committee puts a December hike on the table
articles.text:
RESEARCH BRIEFING

05 Nov 2026

UK: Hawkish Monetary Policy Committee puts a December hike on the table

The Monetary Policy Committee raised Bank Rate by 25bps to 4% on Thursday. December’s meeting now looks like a coin flip, with the path of oil and natural gas prices set to be the decisive factor

The committee’s messaging was more hawkish than before. Higher energy futures prices and more evidence of domestic resilience both increase the risk of second-round effects emerging. The degree of inflationary pressure already in the system means another hike is likely, in December or February.

The majority gave the impression that once Bank Rate reaches 4.25%, subsequent decisions will be a closer call. We continue to think that second-round effects on pay and margins will prove limited, so we maintain our forecast that Bank Rate will peak at 4.25%, but the risks are skewed to the upside.
