articles.title: Daily: Chip rout tests AI investment case
articles.text:
Talk to a UBS Financial AdvisorFrom the studioVideo:The AI sell-off and US midterms: Live at the UBS Disruptive Tech Summit (6 mins)Video: Allocating Assets | Adding FX carry, hedging oil risks, managing volatility(6 mins)Video: CIO Monthly | Mark Haefele on AI earnings, energy prices, interest rates (4 mins)Thought of the dayWhat happened?
US technology stocks led broader markets lower on Thursday, as the post-election relief rally reversed and investors reassessed the implications of the Democratic gains, especially at the state level, for AI infrastructure and data centers. The Nasdaq 100 and S&P 500 fell by around 6.4% and 4.4%, respectively.Semiconductor and AI infrastructure companies were at the center of the decline, including Qualcomm, which fell sharply after its profit outlook disappointed investors. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell 12.3%, extending its drawdown since June to around 38.3%.Pressure extended into Friday, with North Asia's tech-heavy indices leading declines. Japan's Nikkei 225 and South Korea's Kospi closed 6% lower, and Taiwan's benchmark index shed 4.5%. Major European stock indices all stand roughly 1% lower at the time of writing.The sharp risk-off move followed an initial post-election rally, when the removal of political uncertainty and the prospect of policy gridlock were seen as supportive for stocks. Investors now appear to be focusing more closely on how greater congressional oversight and changes in state governments might affect electricity consumption, water use, permitting, and development costs for data centers.Oil and geopolitical developments remained a secondary source of volatility, with Brent crude rebounding to around USD 100 per barrel before coming down to around USD 98 at the time of writing. US Treasuries and perceived safe havens have gained since the market close on Tuesday. The yield on 10-year US Treasuries has fallen by 12 basis points to near 4.84%, while gold is holding near USD 4,070/oz.What do we think?
In our view, the decline reflects uncertainty about the cost and pace of the data center buildout rather than a sudden deterioration in the outlook. It also appears to represent a de-risking event rather than a material change in fundamentals.Further technology volatility would not be surprising. The sector has delivered strong gains in recent years, leaving valuations, expectations, and investor positioning elevated in parts of the market. Investors are hence moving from rewarding spending commitments to demanding clearer evidence of monetization, capacity utilization, potential returns, and the ability to raise capital. The sensitivity of AI-linked stocks to company guidance, regulatory developments, and changes in risk appetite has increased.Greater congressional oversight may indeed increase scrutiny of data center construction and AI regulation. However, except in the event of a widespread AI security issue, we believe broad federal restrictions would likely face legislative and presidential constraints.And while political opposition at a state and local level may delay, relocate, or raise the cost of data center projects, it is unlikely to change underlying demand. Proposed US capacity of around 400 gigawatts already far exceeds our buildout assumption of roughly 90 gigawatts by 2030. We therefore see regulation as potentially redistributing and extending the investment cycle rather than derailing it, with power access, permitting, financing, and execution increasingly separating leaders from laggards.Underlying AI-related demand also remains strong. Recent earnings have shown accelerating cloud revenue and growing advance orders for computing capacity. Recent reports point to significant chip backlogs among Chinese buyers. We forecast aggregate AI capital spending of USD 1.0tr in 2026, USD 1.4tr in 2027, and USD 1.5tr in 2028.For the sell-off to signal a lasting downturn in the AI investment cycle, we think we would need to see evidence that AI-related revenue growth is slowing, cloud utilization is weakening, or lower AI costs are failing to generate sufficient new usage to absorb expanding capacity. We would also reassess the outlook if advances in algorithmic efficiency sharply reduced compute requirements, larger investments failed to produce commensurate gains in AI capabilities, or tighter financial conditions constrained spending by the largest technology platforms and frontier labs.How do we invest?
We see potential for gains in broad equity indices over the next six to 12 months and believe the sell-off looks overdone, given our base case for only modest changes to the outlook for the pace, timing, and cost of data center deployment. We believe the AI investment cycle remains intact, corporate earnings growth is resilient, and a positive global cyclical backdrop should support equities.Nevertheless, we acknowledge that investors may need more certainty about the data center policy environment before volatility fully abates, and we could see a period of market indigestion following the election results. This reinforces the importance of diversification and disciplined portfolio construction.Investors should decide in advance how they would respond to further market swings rather than making allocation decisions during periods of stress. This could include identifying target weights for equities, technology, fixed income, and alternative assets, then addressing allocation gaps progressively as markets move. Structured strategies may enable investors to respond in a disciplined way.Manage concentration risks. Although broad indices were down sharply on Thursday, volatility was even more elevated at the individual stock level. To prepare for potentially greater differentiation within the technology sector in the weeks and months ahead, investors should review portfolios and progressively reduce excessive single-stock concentration relative to technology and broad market benchmarks.Within AI, we prefer diversification over concentrated exposure to individual companies experiencing bottlenecks. We favor financially strong platform and application companies that can monetize growing AI adoption, together with infrastructure businesses that have durable pricing power, strong competitive positions, and access to capital. We are more selective toward highly valued companies whose investment case depends heavily on a single component, capacity constraint, customer, or stage of the data center buildout. Diversified exposure across foundry, compute, networking, power, and other enabling technologies can provide participation in structural growth while reducing dependence on any one bottleneck.Rebalance across sectors and regions. We reduced our sector preferences for US IT and US communication services to Neutral in February. Investors whose US tech exposure has risen materially in recent years and now stands in excess of benchmark weights should consider using opportunities to rebalance toward other sectors. Within equities, our preferred sectors include industrials, health care, and financials. Regionally, we have a relative preference for the Eurozone, emerging markets, and Asia ex-Japan.Build a strong core portfolio. To prepare for possible further equity market volatility ahead, investors with significant bond underweights should prepare for opportunities to rebuild allocations: We see attractive diversification and income potential in fixed income, particularly in high-quality bonds with short- to medium-term maturities and in emerging market bonds. Allocations to alternatives and commodities can also provide investors with exposure to a broader, differentiated range of return drivers beyond traditional asset classes.

articles.title: Financial conditions: what’s priced in? − speech by Catherine L. Mann
articles.text:
Financial conditions: what’s priced in? − speech by Catherine L. Mann

Given at the Nomura London Macro Forum

Published on
01 October 2026

Catherine L. Mann discusses how UK financial markets have priced in greater risk premia since the Middle East conflict intensified. She uses several models to uncover their sources and considers how monetary policy and communication can help reduce premia to ensure inflation returns to target.

Speech
Introduction
The conflict in the Middle East has generated significant volatility and financial market repricing in the UK, relating to uncertainty around the evolution of the conflict, the outlook for UK inflation, and our monetary policy response. Financial conditions are an essential mechanism through which monetary policy transmits and therefore form an important input into my monetary policy decisions. In this speech, I will evaluate the information that financial conditions provide about the current monetary policy stance and transmission, and carefully examine what they reveal about the types of risks driving recent moves.
Financial conditions
Let me start with a headline indicator of financial conditions, which summarizes how a broad range of asset price movements contribute to changes in nominal and real financial conditions. The effect of policy tightening since 2022 on nominal financial conditions in the UK is clearly visible, as the pink line in Chart 1 shows. Despite a modest loosening over 2025, this measure of nominal financial conditions resumed a slight tightening since the escalation of the conflict in the Middle East on account of higher short and long-term nominal interest rates.

Chart 1: Changes in UK financial conditions since 2020
Index points

Footnotes

Source: Burr (2023) Opens in a new window using Bloomberg Finance L.P., Tradeweb and LSEG.
Notes: The real financial conditions index uses real interest rate variables, exchange rate and equity prices – that is, net of inflation compensation. Latest observation: August 2026.

Nominal financial conditions incorporate inflation expectations and inflation risk premia, which may distort the signal about real tightness, particularly following an inflationary shock. The real financial conditions index in Chart 1 (white line) strips out the effects of rising inflation compensation following the start of the conflict in the Middle East at the end of February. This index suggests that real financial conditions loosened around the beginning of the conflict (consistent with inflation compensation measures rising significantly in March), some of which have since retraced, albeit with a notable compression in spreads.
Given that inflation has been well-above target for five years already and the conflict in the Middle East has contributed to further upside risks to inflation, real and nominal financial conditions need to remain tight. There are two mechanisms through which I can tighten real financial conditions: reducing measures of inflation compensation, and/or, raising nominal yields (and expectations), both of which can be achieved through an increase in Bank Rate. In my view, our current monetary policy stance is not sufficiently tight, which is why I voted in the last two meetings for a 25 basis point increase in Bank Rate.
As financial conditions indices summarize a range of underlying market dynamics, I will unpack some of their key drivers and explore what they reveal about what is priced in. This assessment concludes that the MPC cannot simply rely on policy restrictiveness coming from an upward shift in the nominal yield curve. At some point, we need to follow-through with Bank Rate rises – to maintain credibility, and to avoid policy expectations repricing downwards and inflation expectations repricing further upwards.
What does the gap between markets and participants imply?
Overall nominal financial conditions have remained relatively tight, but what are financial market expectations for the future path of monetary policy? We can gauge market expectations of the policy rate path from a variety of sources. For the UK, these are the yield curve, such as the overnight index swap (OIS) curve, and the Bank of England Market Participants Survey (MaPS).footnote [1]
Chart 2 plots the OIS curve across the UK, US and euro area (EA), and survey-based policy rate expectations from the respective central banks’ latest surveys of market participants. The survey-based measures should offer a cleaner read on policy rate expectations than the OIS curve, because they do not include risk premia or other market-based technical factors. As the differences between the light and dark solid lines in Chart 2 show, there are gaps between the two measures for all three jurisdictions, but the difference is largest for the UK.
If the OIS curve only reflected expectations for policy rate changes, it would imply almost 75 basis points of tightening in Bank Rate over the next 12 months, in contrast to a prolonged hold (and subsequent cuts) implied by the MaPS. I have plotted the OIS curve at the respective dates of survey closure. Since then, the gap has widened further, implying over 100 basis points of tightening in Bank Rate over the coming 12 months. The swathes indicate the interquartile ranges of the survey-based distributions; however, taking that into account does only a little to explain the gap in the UK.

Chart 2: OIS curves and survey-implied expectations for policy rates
Percent

Footnotes

Sources: Bank of England, Federal Reserve Bank of New York, European Central Bank, Bloomberg Finance L.P. and Bank calculations.
Notes: UK survey data shows the median response (solid light aqua line) and the 25th-75th percentile of responses (shaded aqua area) to the September 2026 Market Participants Survey. US survey data shows the median response (solid light purple line) and the 25th-75th percentile of responses (shaded purple area) to the July 2026 Survey of Market Expectations Opens in a new window. Euro area survey data shows the median response (solid light orange line) and the 25th-75th percentile of responses to the September 2026 ECB Survey of Monetary Analysts Opens in a new window. OIS curves (dark solid lines) on the respective dates of survey closure (4th September, 20th July and 26th August). Survey measures typically ask for policy rate expectations (Bank Rate, Federal Funds Rate/Range and Deposit Rate Facility) for UK, US and EA respectively. These do not exactly match the interest rate underlying the OIS (SONIA, SOFR and €STR).

The UK seems to be an outlier internationally, but is the current gap also large by historical standards? Chart 3 shows how the average difference between the OIS curve and market participants’ median expectations for Bank Rate has evolved over a 3-year horizon (left panel). There has been a material increase in the gap since the beginning of the conflict in the Middle East, to levels last seen following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Because the survey-based measure only captures market participants’ expectations for Bank Rate, movements in the gap can be a crude measure of risk premia. The widening observed this year therefore suggests that investors are demanding greater compensation for UK risk.

Chart 3: Average gap between market-based and survey-implied expectations for policy rates over a 3-year horizon
Basis points

Footnotes

Sources: Bank of England, Federal Reserve Bank of New York, European Central Bank, Bloomberg Finance L.P. and Bank calculations.
Notes: The height of the bar reflects the average gap between the respective survey’s median ‘most likely’ (modal) profile for the policy rate and the average OIS curve observed across the survey window over a 3-year horizon.

What risks are investors demanding greater compensation for? There is no single model that allows us to decompose this risk premium into its various sources and drivers. In the remainder of this speech, I will go through various hypotheses, using a variety of different models and data, to pinpoint the types of risks relevant to driving this gap.
The role of the term premium
Movements in nominal government bond yields can be decomposed into contributions from changes in expected interest rates and a term premium. The term premium is the additional compensation required by investors (above and beyond their interest rate expectations) to hold interest rate risk. Before discussing what the charts show, it is worth noting that the term premium, and risk premia in general, are unobservable. We rely on a suite of models to estimate them.
Chart 4 shows a model-implied structural decomposition of a 3-year nominal yield into these two categories across the UK, US and Germany. The model decomposition is an average of three term structure models: Malik and Meldrum (2016) Opens in a new window, Vlieghe (2016) and Andreasen and Meldrum (2015). For the UK, this structural model-based decomposition complements the survey-based evidence from MaPS on policy expectations.footnote [2] In both the UK and Germany, 3-year government bond yields have risen by around 100 basis points over the past year, but the drivers appear to be different.
According to this term structure model, higher term premia account for around 24 basis points of the increase in the UK, compared with just 4 basis points in Germany. This contribution has been increasingly positive in the UK throughout the year. In the US, a positive contribution from the term premium is only visible more recently, accounting for around 25 basis points of the 140 basis points rise in yields.

Chart 4: Decomposition of UK, US and German 3-year nominal yields
Cumulative differences since January 2026

Footnotes

Source: Bloomberg Finance L.P., Tradeweb, Federal Reserve Bank of New York and Bank calculations.
Note: The expected rates and term premium contributions may not sum exactly to the observed nominal yield because they are averages of model-implied decompositions and contain residuals that reflect model fitting error. Latest observation: 25th September 2026.

To compare results across different models I show, in Chart 5, a decomposition from a different model (Lengyel and Walker, 2026) that adapts a standard affine term structure framework to identify near-term risk premia more cleanly. Relative to classic models, which are typically calibrated to fit the yield curve as a whole, this approach uses OIS instead of government bond yields, allows for a richer factor structure, and directly incorporates survey-based expectations for Bank Rate. While term premia make a larger contribution to yields overall across the UK, US and EA, the result that its contribution is largest for the UK is robust.

Chart 5: Decomposition of UK, US and German 3-year OIS yields
Cumulative differences since January 2026

Footnotes

Source: Bloomberg Finance L.P. and Bank calculations.
Note: The expected rates and term premium contributions may not sum exactly to the observed nominal yield because they are averages of model-implied decompositions and contain residuals that reflect model fitting error. Latest observation: 25th September 2026.

In a historical and international context, it is somewhat unusual that the term premium has contributed significantly to the rise in short-term yields. The term premium is often defined as the additional compensation investors demand to hold a longer-term bond relative to a series of shorter-term bonds (Kaminska, Meldrum and Young, 2015 Opens in a new window). It is therefore common for the term premium to show up at the longer end of the yield curve. That is, the further into the future you go, the more uncertain the future path of interest rates is. So why is the UK term premium such an outlier, and such a significant driver of short-term yields?
Chart 6 plots the model-implied 1-year and 3-year term premium between 2009 and today. Over this period, the 1-year and 3-year term premium have been negative throughout the 2010s and after the Russia-Ukraine shock. A negative term premium is not unusual. Joyce, Kaminska and Lildholdt (2008) discuss various drivers for the UK, including regulatory changes, excess liquidity, and “flight to quality” dynamics away from risky assets in times of uncertainty. This could also be explained by a negative inflation risk premium (Cieslak and Pflueger, 2023 Opens in a new window).

Chart 6: UK model-implied 1-year and 3-year term premium
Percent

Footnotes

Source: Lengyel and Walker (2026) using Bloomberg Finance L.P., Tradeweb and Bank calculations.
Note: Latest observation: 25th September 2026.

However, term premia rose at the start of the conflict in the Middle East and have recently turned positive. That is also true for the 3-year term premium, which stands out as particularly high in recent history, and was only exceeded during the post-GFC period and when Russia invaded Ukraine. The Middle East energy shock is notable, but not as large as the Russia-Ukraine energy shock.
Staff work finds that the UK term premium, especially at the short end, has become more volatile and responsive to news about economic and financial market developments. In part, this reflects higher sensitivity of (international) investors (Mann, 2026) and a different composition of demand for government debt, including a reduced role of preferred habitat investors such as insurance companies and pension funds, as Beltran and Li (2026) Opens in a new window also find for the US.
Lengyel and Walker (2026) argue that risk premia at the short end of the curve reflect the compensation investors require for uncertainty around the policy rate path. It is therefore important for monetary policymakers to understand whether changes in nominal yields reflect changing policy expectations or uncertainty around them – distinguishing between the two has important consequences on how to interpret the moves in financial conditions.footnote [3]
I explore the role of near-term policy uncertainty in the next section.
What is the role of uncertainty?
Chart 7 shows the option-implied distributions of SONIA (the risk-free overnight interest rate for sterling markets, and the rate underlying the overnight index swap) 12 months ahead, and its equivalents for the US (SOFR) and the euro area (€STR) based on the methodology of Clews et al. (2000).footnote [4] While the OIS rate shown in the earlier Chart 2 reflects a summary statistic of the underlying distribution, the full distribution in Chart 7 contains additional information. Prior to the conflict (orange), the distributions for all three jurisdictions are tight – implying little uncertainty, and high conviction, about the future path of policy rates. Since the conflict began, the distributions for all three have shifted to the right and widened. The UK distribution, however, has widened slightly more, implying that perceived risks and uncertainty about the future policy rate have increasingly been priced in by markets, and particularly more so for the UK.

Chart 7: Option-implied distribution of interest rates, 12 months ahead
For SONIA, SOFR and €STR

Footnotes

Source: ICE, CME and Bank calculations
Note: The underlying rate for the UK distribution is the 3-month SONIA rate 12 months ahead. Latest observation: 25th September 2026

Furthermore, the skewness of SONIA has turned sharply positive following the outbreak of the conflict in the Middle East, which implies that upside risks to interest rates are perceived to be materially larger than downside risks. This degree of positive skewness was last observed following the post-Covid supply chain disruptions in 2021 and Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
The increase in uncertainty and the positive skewness could simply reflect a repricing of the outlook for the economy – reflecting uncertainty about how the conflict in the Middle East could play out, how the resulting supply shock will affect the UK economy going forward, and how it is passed through to broader pricing dynamics. However, such trade-off inducing shocks (shocks that are inflationary but have contractionary effects on activity) also make it more challenging for monetary policymakers to set policy, and uncertainty about the policy rate path could also be higher.
Financial markets are trying to price in both: uncertainty about the economic outlook and uncertainty about the monetary policy response. There is no “textbook” monetary policy response to supply shocks, and therefore, the market’s understanding of how members of the MPC might respond (that is, our reaction function) could be incomplete or unclear. Given that inflation has remained above target for five years and is expected to increase further as the energy shock propagates, the market might be pricing in a reaction function that is not consistent with bringing inflation back to the 2% target sustainably in the medium-term.
Is there a monetary policy uncertainty premium?
Could uncertainty about the monetary policy response to the conflict in the Middle East have also contributed to the gap between the OIS curve and market participants’ expectations for Bank Rate? Research about the effects of monetary policy has generally focused on the effect of changes in the level of Bank Rate on the UK economy (see for instance Brandt et al., 2026 Opens in a new window; Braun et al., 2025 Opens in a new window; Di Pace et al., 2025 Opens in a new window). Uncertainty about future interest rates and its effects on financial markets and the real economy has received less attention.
Based on a methodology developed by Bauer et al. (2022) Opens in a new window, Raviraj (forthcoming) constructs a financial market-based measure of UK monetary policy uncertaintyfootnote [5] surprises that uses changes in the standard deviation of the option-implied distribution of SONIA around MPC announcement dates. Using the surprise series as an instrument for a monetary policy uncertainty shock in a structural VAR allows the author to causally identify the effects of monetary policy uncertainty on a set of outcome variables.
Let me start by showing what this monetary policy uncertainty variable looks like and how it relates to MPC announcements. On average across the sample period (1997 to 2026), a monetary policy announcement leads to a resolution of uncertainty about short-term interest rates, as the decrease in the aqua line following the day of an MPC announcement in the left panel of Chart 8 shows. Monetary policy and communications around MPC decisions have acted as a stabilizing force in the economy, resolving uncertainty around the future path of interest rates.

Chart 8: Changes in monetary policy uncertainty around MPC announcementdates
Percent (LHS) and factor score (RHS)

Footnotes

Source: Raviraj (forthcoming).
Note: The solid aqua line in the left chart shows the average change in short-rate uncertainty on trading days around MPC announcements from June 1997 until July 2026. The pink line shows the change in short-rate uncertainty around the March 2026 MPC announcement. The shaded area represents the 95% confidence interval. In the right chart, monetary policy uncertainty factors are constructed by applying Varimax rotation to principal components of changes in short-rate uncertainty and first moment interest rates around MPC announcements.

However, there is one notable meeting where our decision and communications do not seem to have played that role. In the left panel of Chart 8, I also plot (in pink) changes in uncertainty around the March 2026 decision – the first monetary policy meeting after the escalation of the conflict in the Middle East. One may argue that this simply reflects elevated levels of uncertainty following the outbreak of the conflict in the Middle East. However, the identification strategy for the monetary policy uncertainty shock isolates changes in uncertainty on MPC announcement days – these changes should therefore largely reflect news associated with the monetary policy decision and associated communications. It strips out any first moment, level effects of monetary policy and captures shocks associated with MPC announcements beyond what markets had already priced in. I plot the estimated monetary policy uncertainty factor in the right panel of Chart 8, which shows that monetary policy uncertainty increased significantly following the March decision, which cannot simply be attributed to uncertainty around the economic outlook resulting from the conflict.footnote [6]
What are the implications of an increase in monetary policy uncertainty? Using the monetary policy uncertainty shock series, we can evaluate the impact of such a shock on financial market variables. The left panel of Chart 9 shows the impulse response function of short rate uncertaintyfootnote [7] to a one standard deviation increase in monetary policy uncertainty. An increase in monetary policy uncertainty also leads to a rise in the 1-year OIS rate, driven by both a higher term premium and higher interest rate expectations. An increase in monetary policy uncertainty tightens financial conditions.

Chart 9: Impulse response functions of short rate uncertainty, term premium and expected interest rates to a monetary policy uncertainty shock
Percentage points

Footnotes

Source: Raviraj (forthcoming).
Note: Impulse response functions to a one standard deviation structural monetary policy uncertainty shock, proxied by the monetary policy uncertainty factor presented in the right panel of Chart 8. Shaded areas represent 68% and 90% confidence intervals.

Yet, why did such a clear signal, a unanimous decision to hold Bank Rate, result in higher uncertainty? It could be because our communication about the outlook for the economy, beyond what was already priced in by markets, was too focused on the uncertainty resulting from the conflict in the Middle East, rather than the underlying dynamics of the economy. Or our reaction function to the shock – the balance between looking through the shock and responding to signs of propagation – was not clearly articulated.
What does this mean for the role of monetary policy uncertainty in driving current risk premia? The committee’s vote splits in the past have revealed differences in views about both the economic outlook and the appropriate monetary policy response. The unanimous vote at the March meeting deviated from these previously communicated reaction functions in light of the conflict in the Middle East. Central bank communication – including our Monetary Policy Report, Monetary Policy Summary and minutes, press conferences, and speeches – is an important tool to explain past monetary policy decisions and to manage expectations about the economy and potential Bank Rate paths. Communication should provide clarity about our reaction function and reduce uncertainty around the future interest rate path (Blinder et al., 2008 Opens in a new window; Gebauer et al., 2024 Opens in a new window), even without having to provide explicit forward guidance.
Our communications in March highlighted larger uncertainties. Perhaps they were not clear on how the MPC’s reaction function would evolve with new information – it appeared we were in “wait mode”, which discounted our assurance to the markets that we would “act as necessary” to reach the inflation target. And, as discussed by my colleague Alan Taylor (Taylor, 2026), not publishing a baseline forecast in April most likely did not help either.
The March announcement and the uncertainty it reflected did trigger a strong upward shift in the OIS curve, contributing to the gap between OIS and MaPS. My concern is that this gap has continued to increase, and that one spike in monetary policy uncertainty may have had lasting effects, particularly in an environment with a higher sensitivity of term premia to shocks.
What about risk premia in other assets?
Risk premia and term premia are not synonymous. Term premia specifically refer to the additional compensation required for interest rate risk on risk-free bonds. Risk premia is a general term referring to the additional compensation required by investors for holding risky over risk-free assets.
One would expect uncertainty about the economic outlook arising from geopolitical and energy shocks to be reflected in risk premia for a range of assets. For example, the equity risk premium is the additional compensation for risk associated with holding stocks. Chart 10 plots model estimates of this risk premium (Kontoghiorghes et al., 2025). While there is a temporary spike following the conflict in the Middle East, equity risk premia do not appear elevated in historical context (other than in the US since 2020), likely driven by a robust demand for equities as an asset class in general, or reflecting lower perceived (relative) risk across asset classes.

Chart 10: Equity risk premium
Percent

Footnotes

Source: Kontoghiorghes et al. (2025).
Note: The measure used follows the lower-bound ERP estimate of Chabi-Yo and Loudis (2020) Opens in a new window over a one-year time horizon, and uses options on the FTSE 100, S&P 500, and EUROSTOXX 50 for the UK, US, and euro area, respectively. Latest observation: 16th September 2026.

But there is another source of risk premia that is of particular concern for an inflation-targeting central bank – the inflation risk premium. Chart 11 (left-hand panel) shows cumulative changes in the 3-year inflation swap since February, decomposed into contributions from changes in inflation expectations and inflation risk premia. It shows that the inflation risk premium has contributed significantly to the rise in the 3-year inflation swap this year. Rising CPI inflation expectations have also played a considerable role. This reduced slightly in June and July, when the Memorandum of Understanding between the US and Iran was in place, but subsequently rose again following re-escalation of the conflict.

Chart 11: Decomposition of UK 3-year inflation swap rate (LHS) and 3-yearnominal yield (RHS)
Cumulative differences

Footnotes

Source: Kaminska et al. (2018) Opens in a new window for LHS, and Bloomberg Finance L.P., Tradeweb and Bank calculations for RHS.
Note: The left panel is estimated using a model proposed in Kaminska et al. (2018) Opens in a new window. Latest observation: September 2026 (LHS) and 25th September 2026 (RHS).

The right-hand side panel shows that the contribution to the rise in 3-year nominal yields has been almost entirely accounted for by a rise in inflation compensation, which is a combination of inflation expectations and the inflation risk premium. This brings me back to my very first chart where I showed that while nominal financial conditions have tightened following the escalation of the conflict in the Middle East, real financial conditions remained looser.
Monetary policy strategy
What does all this mean for my monetary policy strategy?
The supply shock resulting from the conflict hit at a time when the disinflationary process from previous supply shocks was still incomplete, with nominal rigidities limiting the speed of normalization. Inflation has been above target for the last five years and the Bank’s updated short-term inflation forecast from September projects inflation to increase to over 4% in Q1 2027. This raises inflation above the attentiveness threshold of households and firms ahead of wage negotiations next spring.
Given rising upside risks to inflation, a risk management strategy to monetary policy is appropriate. When there is uncertainty about inflation dynamics and second-round effects, raising Bank Rate to commit to the inflation target can help ensure a sustainable return of inflation to the 2% target, with smaller losses to economic activity.
With the ‘sporadic continuance’ of the conflict in the Middle East, uncertainty around the outlook for the economy and inflation risks have remained elevated. Uncertainty about the MPC reaction function should not compound the problem. Ensuring that this communication is clear and that the reaction function is well understood is the purpose of collective communications. When a policy decision deviates from the collective, speeches such as this can provide additional clarity on the outlook, risks, and decisions.
Against this backdrop, as a monetary policymaker, I cannot take comfort from tighter nominal financial conditions when much of that tightening reflects a higher inflation risk premium and, possibly, a monetary policy uncertainty premium that our own decisions and communications may have contributed to. These premia raise nominal yields without necessarily tightening the real financial conditions that matter for demand and inflation. In my view, real financial conditions are insufficiently tight. The appropriate response therefore is not to rely on risk premia to do the work of policy, but to reduce inflation risk and policy uncertainty through a clearly communicated reaction function and a sufficiently restrictive path for Bank Rate.
The views expressed in this speech are not necessarily those of the Bank of England or the Monetary Policy Committee.

articles.title: Policy Options Are Available Now to Lower U.S. Mortgage Rates | PIMCO
articles.text:
Libby Cantrill, Daniel Hyman, Munish Gupta

10/29/2026

| 5 min read

Share via Email

Share via Linkedin

Share via Twitter

Download

Rising U.S. Treasury yields have added fresh strain to the U.S. housing market. The average 30-year mortgage rate, which generally tracks the 10-year U.S. Treasury yield plus a mortgage spread, rose to 7.5% in October 2026, according to Mortgage Bankers Association data, worsening an affordability crunch that remains a top concern among U.S. households.
Last week, President Donald Trump signed an executive order intended to reduce housing costs and expand access to homeownership. Among other measures, the order directs the Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA) to cancel mortgage insurance premiums under certain conditions and establishes a task force aimed at lowering homebuilding costs.
While reducing costs is positive for borrowers, we believe several of the order’s changes could ultimately increase mortgage rates if applied too broadly. As we describe below, any changes should be targeted toward new purchases only, in our view, not refinancings. Otherwise, the market could price in more compensation for the increased risk of refinancing (or callability), potentially pushing mortgage rates higher. We believe policymakers can avoid this unintended consequence by limiting these changes to new mortgages, not existing ones.
Beyond the executive order, we believe there are several available tools that policymakers could use to lower mortgage rates in the near term. Doing so could deliver meaningful relief, as a 1-percentage-point drop in the mortgage rate lowers a buyer’s monthly payment by roughly as much as a 10% house-price cut (for more, see our September 2026 commentary, “The U.S. Housing Market Becomes a More Local Story.”)
We outline three policy options, all achievable under existing authorities, that we estimate could collectively lower mortgage rates by about 65-90 basis points (bps), or 0.65-0.9 percentage point.
1) Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac could actively buy more mortgage bonds
Congress created government-sponsored enterprises (GSEs) Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac with a mandate to improve housing affordability and reduce risks to capital markets. The GSEs do this largely by buying mortgages from lenders and packaging them into agency mortgage-backed securities (MBS), a form of mortgage bonds, which they either sell to investors or purchase to hold on their own balance sheets.
Increasing mortgage bond purchases is within the GSEs’ existing authority and aligns with their Congressional mandate – and, importantly, it is what President Trump directed the GSEs to do in January 2026. The goal of increasing GSE purchases is to boost demand for mortgage bonds, which typically raises bond prices and lowers yields, thereby helping to reduce mortgage rates (for more, see our April 2026 commentary, “How Policymakers Can Lower Mortgage Costs and Increase Housing Affordability.”)
Fannie and Freddie have been slow to implement President Trump’s January instruction to buy an additional $200 billion of mortgage bonds, with Freddie Mac reporting that it had sold about $1 billion as of August and Fannie reporting that it had only purchased about $40 billion. If Fannie and Freddie were to simply follow through on this directive, we believe mortgage rates could be substantially lower.
Nor is a $200 billion increase necessarily the limit. Fannie and Freddie could potentially expand their purchases even further, though doing so may require their regulator, the FHFA, to increase the GSEs’ existing $450 billion investment cap. Raising the cap would involve amending the Preferred Share Purchase Agreement (PSPA) from 2008, a step the FHFA and the U.S. Treasury have taken several times, most recently in 2025.
To put it in perspective, the GSEs held about $310 billion of mortgages as of August 2026, according to Haver Analytics data, far below the roughly $1.6 trillion they held before 2008, despite the mortgage market doubling in size in that time. While there are good reasons not to return to pre-financial-crisis levels, Fannie and Freddie still have substantial firepower.
We estimate additional GSE mortgage-bond purchases could lower mortgage rates by 20–30 basis points, depending on the size of the program.
2) Regulators could cut fees for new home loans only, not refinancings
On 30 September, the FHFA released new mortgage pricing based on an alternative credit scoring approach, a change that could reduce mortgage rates for new homebuyers. We think this is a positive step, provided it applies only to new home loans and not to existing ones. Clarifying this distinction could be helpful for the market.
Measures that lower costs only for new-purchase loans may improve affordability without materially affecting mortgage investors. Extending those fee cuts to refinancings, however, would likely increase prepayment risk, prompting mortgage investors to demand more compensation and potentially pushing rates higher for all borrowers.
The clearest illustration of this dynamic is in the contrast between multifamily and single-family lending. Currently, JPMorgan data show that single-family mortgage borrowers pay a premium nearly 70 basis points, or 0.7 percentage point, higher than the premium paid by multifamily borrowers – mainly landlords – because multifamily loans are less refinanceable (or in mortgage-speak, less callable).
The broader lesson is that policies that reduce the callability of mortgages may lower mortgage rates for home purchases, in our view, while measures that make mortgages easier to refinance could potentially backfire and raise mortgage rates. We estimate that cutting fees for new borrowers only could lower mortgage rates by approximately 25-30 bps.
Similarly, some measures in President Trump’s latest executive order would apply the same changes to refinancing as to home purchases, which could widen mortgages spreads if fully implemented without adjustment. We continue to recommend a purchase only approach, which could lower mortgage rates for buyers without disrupting the mortgage market or putting upward pressure on rates and spreads.
3) The Federal Reserve could stop selling mortgage-backed securities
Another potential action is for the Fed to stop allowing its mortgage bond portfolio to “roll off” its balance sheet, which in practical terms is akin to selling mortgages and buying Treasury bonds. If the Fed simply stopped this (i.e., retained its mortgage portfolio at current levels), it could potentially bring down mortgage rates for homeowners – by about 20-30 bps, in our view. (For more, see our September 2025 PIMCO Perspectives, “A Fed Housing Fix That’s Hiding in Plain Sight.”) Ultimately, the Fed makes decisions about the size and composition of its balance sheet in accordance with its dual mandate of price stability and maximum employment.
Conclusion
For many households, the most immediate obstacle to homeownership is the cost of financing a home today. While policymakers have devoted considerable effort to expanding U.S. housing supply – a longer-term objective – policy choices that affect mortgage rates themselves could provide a more near-term path toward affordability.
The debate over mortgage affordability also sits at the center of renewed discussions about the future of the GSEs. In comments last week, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent indicated that the U.S. may not look to remove the GSEs from their longstanding government conservatorship until 2027 or 2028 and only if it could be done without pushing mortgage rates higher (for more, see our May 2025 commentary, “The Future of the GSEs: Do No Harm.”)
For investors, the flip side of mortgage rates being high is that mortgage bond yields are also high. PIMCO continues to see value in mortgage-backed securities at today’s historically wide spreads and high all in yields. If policymakers succeed at lowering mortgage rates, investors in agency mortgages could potentially benefit from spread compression and price appreciation. If policymakers take no action, investors may continue to compound returns at today's attractive yields.

articles.title: Localizing agency: Co-constructing meaning with girls and communities | Brookings
articles.text:
Commentary

Podcast
Localizing agency: Co-constructing meaning with girls and communities

Listen on

Apple Podcasts

Spotify

YouTube

Pod.link

More

Embedding Equality in Education

Embedding Equality in Education

Hosts:
Jennifer L. O’Donoghue and

Jennifer L. O’Donoghue

Deputy Director
- Center for Universal Education,

Senior Fellow
- Global Economy and Development

Edem Dorothy Ossai

Edem Dorothy Ossai

Africa Regional Coordinator
- NORRAG,

2021 Echidna Global Scholar
- Center for Universal Education, Brookings Institution,

Founder
- MAYEIN

November 4, 2026

Localization means centering girls, not just adapting for context. Girls name agency in their own languages, and the meanings differ from place to place. Kurongeka in Zimbabwe, for example, is relational and includes responsibility to family and community.
Barriers to girls’ agency look similar across contexts, but their roots differ. Feudal legacies in South Punjab and interpretations of religion shaping marriage in Nigeria produce different priorities in how girls define agency.
Inside-out change shifts ownership and legitimacy. When communities lead the conversation, it builds on trust that is already there and makes room for hard truths, as when girls and mothers in Karamoja raised abuse by police with the police commissioner in the room.
Every community has a starting point. From a chief opening a community center to a market leader making sure girls’ trainers treat them well, existing structures can be used more intentionally. Small shifts in belief and expectation add up over time.

Two girls drawing, in Zimbabwe. (Photo by Precious Farayi)

28 min read

Bluesky Streamline Icon: https://streamlinehq.comBluesky

In this episode of Embedding Equality in Education, hosts Jenn O’Donoghue and Edem Ossai continue their “Moving into Action” conversation with a look at co-construction: how girls, families, and communities build a shared understanding of what agency means and what stands in its way. They also take on the question of backlash and the claim that gender equality is imposed from outside, making the case for an inside-out approach built on trust and on the strengths communities already have.

Related Episodes

What agency means and looks like to girls – and why this matters

Education Access & Equity

What agency means and looks like to girls – and why this matters

Jennifer L. O’Donoghue, Edem Dorothy Ossai

October 21, 2026

Centering girls in practice: Ethics, methods, and shared power in research

Education Access & Equity

Centering girls in practice: Ethics, methods, and shared power in research

Jennifer L. O’Donoghue, Edem Dorothy Ossai

October 7, 2026

TRANSCRIPT

O’DONOGHUE: Please note, this episode contains mention of child sexual abuse.
[music; girls singing]
That’s the sound of a group of girls in the Karamoja region on the border of Kenya and Uganda warming up before a community dialogue. Our colleague Mary Otieno suggested we dance or play a game as a warmup, and this is what happened.
[singing continues]
Completely spontaneous, one girl stood to sing, and within seconds the others had joined her.
[singing continues]
And I still sing that song now almost a year and a half later. I’m not religious, but the words are, “When Jesus says yes, nobody can say no.” And every time I hear it, I think about how much those girls had brought into that room before any of us had asked them a single question.
[music]
Welcome to the Embedding Equality in Education podcast. I’m Jenn O’Donoghue.
OSSAI: And I’m Edem Ossai, an education leader in Nigeria and a member of the Learning in Action Alliance for Girls Agency.
[1:12]
O’DONOGHUE: Edem, one idea keeps coming back to me across this season. How we define something really shapes what we do about it. If we get the definition wrong, we get the action wrong.
[1:22]
OSSAI: Absolutely, Jenn. And in our last episode, we spent a lot of time on what agency actually is. We landed on the idea that agency is multidimensional and dynamic. It’s not one thing, and it doesn’t stand still. It shifts across a girl’s life, across relationships, across the spaces she moves through.
[1:43]
O’DONOGHUE: Right. And if agency looks different everywhere, if it’s shaped by who a girl is, where she lives, who she lives with, what’s possible around her, then we can’t understand it from the outside. We have to understand it within each context.
[1:56]
OSSAI: Which brings us to today. This is part two of our Moving into Action conversation, and we’re going deeper into what we call co-construction. How do girls, their families, and their communities build a shared understanding of what agency means, and what’s getting in the way of what they can do about it?
[2:16]
O’DONOGHUE: Yeah, and I’ll say upfront here, to everyone listening, there are no universals here. We won’t be saying, “Agency means this, and so this is what we do to strengthen it in every context.”
Instead, we’ll offer up and talk through processes that have emerged in our work with LAAGA to build understandings and identify challenges and solutions that support these multiple dimensions of girls’ agency within their local settings.
So, let’s start with that word “local.” Within global education, global development, “localization” is a frequently used term. But Edem, let’s unpack that a little bit. When when we talk about localization in LAAGA, what do we mean?
[2:53]
OSSAI: That’s a very important question, Jenn. So, for me, there are two ideas inside localization. The first is contextualizing, and that is, understanding agency within the specific sociocultural realities of a place.
And the second meaning for me is, which we can never forget, is centering girls’ own understanding in that process. So, localization without centering girls isn’t really localizing.
[3:20]
O’DONOGHUE: So, it’s not just like, “Let’s adapt this for the local context”?
[3:24]
OSSAI: No, not at all. It’s grounding agency in girls’ lived experiences and in their own languages. You know, that’s also very important, because if agency is contextual and relational, as we’ve said many times in previous episodes, if it’s shaped by the people and the systems around girls, then the meaning has to be developed by the people who are actually living it, girls themselves.
[3:49]
O’DONOGHUE: Exactly, and and language matters so much here. Right? So, sometimes there isn’t a direct translation for this word “agency” at all.
[3:57]
OSSAI: Precisely, which is exactly why girls have to name it themselves. Across all the contexts we’ve worked in, we’ve engaged girls to name this concept of agency using local languages, local words or phrases. So, let’s take a listen, in one of our communities where we did our work as one of the girls explains this from the Karamoja region.
[4:23]
KARAMOJA GIRL: In my own language, I can say agency is a girl being brave, being able to understand her problems, and also to come up with solution so that she can help herself and the problems around her.
MARY OTIENO: Is there, a mother tongue word that means the same as agency?
KARAMOJA GIRL: The one that I can recall it is akemkem.
[4:50]
O’DONOGHUE: Being brave, understanding problems, coming up with solutions, all of that in one word.
[4:56]
OSSAI: Yeah, and you know, the meaning girls give to agency shifts from place to place. Let’s also listen to Pami Mhongera, another member of the Learning and Action Alliance for Girls’ Agency, who led our research in Zimbabwe. She’s describing how girls in her context defined it.
[5:15]
MHONGERA: So, they defined the word “agency” as kurongeka. In that context, kurongeka would combine being organized. It means having your priorities right, thinking, self-assertiveness, being streetwise, knowing the community, and more more importantly, having good relationships and being responsible, someone who is able to plant back to the family and to the community.
[5:50]
OSSAI: Notice there that kurongeka goes beyond the individual. So, in that clip you just heard, it’s the term kurongeka, it’s relational. So, it covers your relationships, your responsibility to your family and community. That’s a very different emphasis from simply, you know, definitions of agency that only center the self.
[6:13]
O’DONOGHUE: And that connects to how carefully we’ve talked about marginalization in this work. Right?
[6:18]
OSSAI: Exactly. Exactly. People use a lot of words interchangeably. They use terms like “disadvantaged,” “vulnerable,” “hard to reach.” But for us in LAAGA, and as we’ve talked about this extensively in episode two, marginalization is about inequality tied to power imbalances. This is very important. It’s the outcome of structural inequities created by power dynamics in each context and resulting, you know, in exclusion and even the denial of basic rights.
In the next clip which you’ll listen to, our colleague Armene has some thoughts around this.
[6:59]
MODI: Well, the reason I feel it’s important to focus on girls in marginalized contexts is undoubtedly they face some of the biggest challenges to their agency, including gender discrimination, restrictive patriarchal social norms, limited access to education and health care, et cetera.
And while contexts differ in different countries, many of the barriers to girls’ agency are remarkably similar. What is more, these barriers often reinforce each other, and they can severely restrict the opportunities and choices that adolescent girls in marginalized contexts face.
[7:46]
OSSAI: Armene Modi, in that clip you just listened to, named something very important here. The barriers can look remarkably similar from place to place, but once you put localization and marginalization together, now what stands out in how girls define agency is going to be distinct community by community, because the structures behind those barriers are usually different.
So, for example, take South Punjab in Pakistan. Historically, structural imbalances there have been tied to feudal relations, which have shaped, you know, who has gotten in the past access to resources. Now, certain people have been excluded from resource allocation for generations, and that has resulted in deep poverty and forced underdevelopment.
Now, you want to compare that to a context like Nigeria, where structural imbalances may have more to do with particular interpretations of religion that shape systems of marriages, including dispositions towards child marriage. So, imagine girls in these contexts defining agency. Some of these girls might emphasize decisions about their bodies, their sexual and reproductive rights, or their right to keep learning.
Others might tie agency to moving beyond the barest minimum of survival to the pursuit of goals, you know, livelihoods, whether in terms of access to capital, businesses to start, starting a family, and it goes on from there. But the picture is very different given their realities in these two contexts.
[9:25]
O’DONOGHUE: So, similar systemic challenges. Right? But really shaped by very different histories and structures.
[9:30]
OSSAI: Exactly, Jenn. And here’s what I find immensely powerful. So, when you take a localized lens on agency, it becomes an entry point into a much broader understanding of how that society is structured. The girls may not know that they’re naming these structures. Right? But by defining agency in certain ways, and if you’re listening, immediately you begin to see the pillars that hold up their society.
[9:56]
O’DONOGHUE: Right, and that’s why also, you know, grounding this work locally is what makes the work we’re doing in in LAAGA and others who are doing this type of grounded work more relevant, more sustainable. It’s really owned by the people that are directly affected.
And maybe that is the perfect setup for the other side of this. So, not just what localization is, but why it matters so much right now. And this came up a lot when we presented our LAAGA research at a recent Around the World symposium that the Center for Universal Education did with some of our partners around the world, and people were really asking, you know, when we presented this LAAGA work and what we’d seen changing and with communities, and they would say, “But don’t communities push back or reject these ideas of girls’ agency?”
And it’s a very valid question. Right? We’re living in a moment where there is a real backlash against gender equality and gender equality work, and and there exists this sort of narrative globally that says, “Oh, you’re imposing gender equality on communities. Outsiders are coming in and forcing change.”
[10:59]
OSSAI: Yeah. Yeah, that’s true. And and that narrative has its own problems, you see, because, you know, it treats cultures as though they are monoliths, as if communities don’t have their own internal debates and their own, you know, shifting aspirations within themselves.
[11:13]
O’DONOGHUE: Exactly. Right? And and certainly this does happen when outside ideas are are placed upon communities.
But for me, a key lesson from our work in LAAGA has been, has been this, right, that localization shifts ownership and shifts legitimacy. The community is discussing this and deciding what it wants. It’s not an outside perspective coming in and saying, “Here’s what gender equality means. Here’s how girls’ agency relates to it, and here’s everything you are doing wrong,” right? “And here’s what you need to do.”
[11:41]
OSSAI: Precisely. So, it’s, you know, the outside in approach. Here are your problems.
[11:48]
O’DONOGHUE: Right. Right. And and what we’ve been doing with LAAGA is an inside out approach. Right? These are the realities we live. We all know this from our own lives. It’s very different to say, “These are the problems we have,” versus someone else coming in and telling us, “Let me tell you about your problems.”
[12:05]
OSSAI: Yeah. Nobody, nobody likes that second version.
[12:08]
O’DONOGHUE: Nobody. And this is exactly the question I put to our colleague, Sumbul Naveed, who leads LAAGA’s work in Pakistan, and her answer is one I told her I wish I could hand out at every global education meeting.
[12:20]
NAVEED: Whether it is about agency or any other social change that we want to have, it is always important to bring them on board right from the beginning. Because if we don’t bring them in as a part of the planning, then communities always have a feeling that there is some imposition. Somebody is imposing something as a foreign concept, and especially when when an organization from the West is engaged.
I mean, there is a common understanding here in Pakistan that if something is coming from the West, regardless of whether it was created here in Pakistan or not, it is something being imposed from outside.
We need to start with the mutual understanding of what they think agency is so far, how they have been supporting and promoting agency. Because while working with communities, we had seen that some of the parents were really supporting agency without even knowing that it is agency.
So, I think we need to really recognize them as the agents of change, as people who are the advocates of agency, and recognize them and say, like, this is something we need to promote. This is something we need to expand on.
And I think having local examples, engaging local people, local champions who are already working on agency really makes it more indigenous as compared to, you know, a concept coming from outside and teaching them. So, you know, as we say in education, asking is more important than telling. So, I think we should ask and not tell.
[13:49]
O’DONOGHUE: So, the first step is engaging girls to develop meaning grounded in their lived realities and in their own languages. Girls talk about their aspirations and their dreams, and then they bring those to their communities, to their families, teachers, local leaders.
Of course, their communities want to support their dreams. And girls understand this terrain. They are navigating gender norms and power dynamics every single day of their lives, so who better than girls to open up this space and this conversation?
[14:18]
OSSAI: And, you know, what’s equally fascinating is that when it comes from inside, people can be more honest.
[14:24]
O’DONOGHUE: Yes. Localization understood as building with communities, right, creates that space for honesty, creates space for vulnerability to talk about things that would be much harder to raise if it were an outsider asking.
Of course, it’s still difficult. It’s still painful. I think a lot about the community dialogue that was held in Karamoja, where the girls and their mothers raised sexual abuse by police in their community as one of their key challenges, and the police commissioner was sitting right in the room.
And so, the bravery, the strength that it took, you know, for these girls and and women to stand up and and talk about these things was a very difficult conversation. But it was possible because it was of the community. It was community-led. It was grounded in trust. They were the ones that were making it happen. We never asked them to go and share these stories.
[15:15]
OSSAI: Yeah, and Jenn, now that you raised that incident, the truth is, you know, it’s important to stress that trust isn’t something you can bring in from the outside. You see, it’s it’s already there. It’s it’s in the relationships that people have with each other, as we saw in the Karamoja region.
[15:31]
O’DONOGHUE: Which is exactly where we want to go next, so thank you for bringing up that great segue, Edem, because co-construction, this building with community, isn’t only about defining agency and naming challenges. It’s it’s really about solutions, too.
One thing that distinguishes this work from a lot of development programs and development initiatives is that in every community that we were working in with LAAGA, and again, a reminder, we were working intentionally in, in highly marginalized communities, there was always a starting point. There was always something the community could point to and say, “This is where we can start. These are the resources we have. This is what we’re doing now that we could do slightly differently. This is what we could shift. We don’t have to wait for something to come from outside.”
[16:14]
OSSAI: Yeah, very true. And, you know, that’s not to say that the community is saying they do it alone.
[16:19]
O’DONOGHUE: No, never. But it’s a recognition, right, of their own agency, of of the community’s agency. They have relationships, they have power dynamics, they have local resources to build on. And and so instead of adding new structures, what we did with LAAGA was build on the existing ones and really ask, what are we doing already? And how can this support girls’ agency? Or how can this better support girls’ agency?
And our colleague, Adefunke Akine, really saw this in Nigeria. She led LAAGA’s research with out-of-school girls in Iseyin in Oyo State. And as she told us, she was honestly surprised by who stepped forward when she asked these questions.
[16:58]
EKINE: And I remember one of the traditional ruler who actually opened the gate for us. We meet in his community center, which he opened for us. So, the community decided that they were going to form a support system for the girls. I was shocked that the man will be one of the supporters that we really have.
Then we have this other aspect of the market woman as the leader of the market because, you know, as I said, these girls are girls that are not going to school again. So, they are learning a trade, they are learning a skill. So, the market woman was really willing to support them and to encourage them to finish up with their skill acquisition and to make their, what we call here, their bosses or their trainer to support the girls instead of maltreating them.
So, the community was open to such. And so, for me, the man being the leader and being there, he came even for the community dialogue. He just says, “For you to be interested in our community, we will give you all the support that we can.”
[18:12]
O’DONOGHUE: So, a chief opening his community center, a market leader making sure the girls’ trainers treat them well. None of that was brought in from the outside. Those structures were already there, and the girls’ research helped people understand how to make them work more intentionally for girls and for girls’ agency.
[18:28]
OSSAI: And I think it’s important to really stress that, you know, the community dialogues are where that really comes together. So, now let’s hear from our colleagues Ellen Chigwanda and Nasrin Siddiqi, who organized LAAGA’s community dialogues in Zimbabwe and in Bangladesh.
[18:47]
CHINGWANDA: I’m Ellen Chingwanda. I’m from Zimbabwe. I’m an Echidna Global Scholar for 2016 and also a LAAGA member.
Co-constructing understandings of girls’ agency really involves providing an enabling environment for the girls themselves to kind of interrogate what agency means for them at different levels, individually and then collectively.
So, this includes, you know, whole families, their parents, their guardians, their caregivers. But we also go beyond the family to talk to other stakeholders, community leaders, traditional leaders, government stakeholders, so that everyone is coming in and contributing their perspectives.
And also, actually seeking to understand where girls are coming from, and understanding the challenges that they face, whether to exercise agency or to be able to collectively push through the agenda of girls’ empowerment.
[19:49]
SIDDIQI: I’m Nasrin Siddiqa from Bangladesh, and I’m the executive director of NGO ECS, Education and Cultural Society.
So, we started our community dialogue, and we sometimes say policy cafe, policy dialogue. So, with the community people, community leaders, journalists, policymakers, the teachers as we worked with the schools. So, teachers and students, student representative, and female role model.
So, we brought them in our room and to share their understanding and to learn from the girls that what they are thinking, what is their progress or where they are declining their progress and where they are facing challenges. So, ultimately it was a very good, shared dialogue.
[20:37]
O’DONOGHUE: I love that phrase Nasrin uses, “to learn from the girls.” The adults aren’t in that room to teach. They’re there to listen.”
[20:44]
OSSAI: Yes, very true. And and the work isn’t about convincing people. It’s really about inviting reflection and adaptation. I love how those, you know, reflections from our colleagues stress that because when change comes that way, it feels owned, it feels relevant, it feels achievable. Right?
So, next let’s take a listen to what our colleague Tran Tran in Vietnam also had to say around this very important theme.
[21:11]
TRAN: I think that in those community dialogue, what surprised me most is the confidence of the girls. And it, it’s very relevant to what they share with us during our research and during our follow-on case with them when they clearly described how how safe space matter to them. It is not just about the physical location, like the classroom, something familiar with them, but also about feeling emotionally safe where they are trusted and not judged by the people. And that is very important for the community space like that.
[21:51]
OSSAI: “Emotionally safe.” Wow, that’s a very important phrase here. So that’s the condition for everything else. Girls’ confidence doesn’t appear simply because we put them in a room or we put them on stage. And Tran emphasized that in her reflection.
And it gets at something that I really want to highlight because when we say dialogue, I think there’s a tendency for us to often picture a girl standing up and speaking to a room full of adults. Right?
[22:23]
O’DONOGHUE: With a microphone, yeah, with a microphone in hand.
[22:26]
OSSAI: Exactly, with a microphone, with fluorescent lights, you know, a huge crowd staring at her. And in in our well-meaning intention to bring girls into the room, we can also jeopardize girls, you see, because now many of these girls, they’re adolescents. Let’s think back to our own selves as adolescents. Right? They’re in transition. They’re experiencing self-discovery. Their confidence is growing. So, sometimes they’re not ready for those very public spaces. Does that mean they don’t have things to say? No, they do.
So, we have to really expand what we mean by dialogue. Dialogue has to be broadened to the many different ways that girls express their innermost desires. So, it could be a song, it could be a poem, it could be a letter she wrote to her friend or to, you know, a relative. It could be an entry that she makes in her private journal, right, which she might be willing to share, or even a drawing, and girls tend to scribble a lot, right, when they’re daydreaming, or a conversation she recorded that, you know, she allows us to play back.
Now, in the Nigeria research, which another colleague of ours conducted, for example, girls used the BRIDGE model, maps and illustrations, and those images, you know, were the voice of girls. They were expressing the dreams and desires that girls have.
So, imagine if we curate them and make them an exhibit and allow the community to walk through that exhibit. Just imagine that.
[23:57]
O’DONOGHUE: Exactly. Right? And and that is, you know, what you’re pointing to is so important and is how our methodology really starts, too. We we don’t start by asking direct questions, you know, “What does agency mean to you? Where do you express agency more or less?” But really was more like, “Oh, you drew this picture. Tell me about it.”
[24:16]
OSSAI: Precisely. You know? And so, while she’s explaining her picture, she’s sharing far more than the picture. The picture becomes, comes alive. Right? You can’t necessarily ask her abstract questions about agency. That simply doesn’t work. It has to be, you know, something that’s easy for her to understand in her own reality, in her own everyday lived experience.
It could be something about her that her grandmother told her. It might be a verse that she recites every day that keeps her going, right, through difficult times. She might even say it in her language. So, you have to give her multiple entry points, pretty much what we’re saying.
[24:56]
O’DONOGHUE: Exactly, exactly. And and when we’re true to these principles, right, of really building meaning with girls, building meaning with communities, it takes us to depths and to layers that we didn’t imagine at the start, or that we didn’t, we didn’t recognize at the start.
And when space is created to really listen to the research, listen to the girls’ voices through the research, and in these community dialogue spaces, when the community is having the conversation with and of itself, it’s completely different from an outsider going in.
So, Edem, let’s try to get concrete on this. What actually changes when girls share their experiences this way?
[25:34]
OSSAI: Hmm, interesting question. So, a few things happen at once. I think first it validates girls’ agency. Their perspective is taken seriously, in their own words or we said earlier, in their own drawings, right, or their own songs, or their own poems, whatever. Right? And that changes how people see them.
Suddenly, members of communities begin to understand girls’ realities in a way they may never have stopped previously to consider. Tran saw it in those dialogues in Vietnam. Right? And what surprised her most was the girls’ confidence.
[26:09]
O’DONOGHUE: Exactly. And I think on the flip side of that, we see that validation from adults and that validation also comes with girls beginning to see new possibilities for themselves. Right? When a girl watches the adults around her take her dreams seriously, when she sees that adults have taken, you know, an hour-and-a-half, three hours, in some cases five hours out of their regular day and responsibilities to listen to girls and to focus on girls’ agency.
So, when they see this happening, the seriousness, right, with which this is taken, what she believes is possible starts to shift. And, you know, I want to be careful here because it isn’t always a dramatic overnight transformation.
[26:49]
OSSAI: No, it isn’t. Sometimes, and actually often, it’s it’s really small shifts.
[26:55]
O’DONOGHUE: Exactly, right? And those small shifts add up. They they start to add up. Right? They become changes in beliefs and changes in expectations, both of girls for themselves, but also of the adults around girls. Expectations for what girls can do, how they can be involved in decision-making, how they can be engaged in in shaping things like their own education, their family decisions, community actions, and so on.
And, you know, I think I’ll return to our colleague, Sumbal, who we heard from earlier, because she shared one story of how this happened, what this really looked like from Multan in South Punjab.
[27:30]
NAVEED: One of the girls really wanted to, you know, support her family because they were all really poor. The girl really was committed, and I think mutually because of all of this conversation, the father also understood how important it is to support girls.
So, he started, you know, talking about restarting his work and also supporting his daughter in her goals and her dreams so that, you know, mutually they can do something.
So, I think that girl’s dream became a spark, a light for even the parents. So, this is just a small example of how a girl’s dream could even become a hope for the family.
[28:11]
OSSAI: Yeah. Change is gradual and it is cumulative. And because the community, you know, has defined it for itself, the community is able to carry it forward.
[28:21]
O’DONOGHUE: Exactly. And what we’re seeing is that’s what really makes it it last. It isn’t a program that ends when the funding ends. Again, it isn’t something that comes from outside and and pays attention to a community for a few months or even a few years but then leaves.
This is really something that belongs to the people who built it, in this case belongs to the girls and their communities.
So, I think as we begin to wrap up I, you know, want to say if there’s one thing we want listeners to take from today, it’s that agency efforts need to be locally defined, collectively owned.
[28:55]
OSSAI: True that. And that girls are the experts here. This is very key. They’re already exercising agency every day. Our job is to make space for it to be seen and heard in whatever form works for girls.
[29:09]
O’DONOGHUE: Right. And to remember that communities, including the most marginalized communities, already have entry points. They already have things they’re doing that we can build off of, that they can build off of. They already have the potential for change, and that’s where we need to start.
[29:23]
OSSAI: Yes. So, no standard definition, no standard solution, but a lot of shared wisdom about how to get to definitions and solutions together.
[29:33]
O’DONOGHUE: Which leads us to next time. Girls don’t live in isolation. They’re surrounded by families, schools, communities, and a whole bunch of systems and structures. So, in episode six, we’re gonna talk about why strengthening that whole ecosystem around girls matters so much, and about how LAAGA has been working to strengthen those ecosystems for girls’ agency.
OSSAI: I’m already looking forward to that next conversation. Thank you guys for listening once again. I’m Edem Ossai from Nigeria, and it’s always a delight to have these conversations with you.
O’DONOGHUE: Thank you, Edem. It’s always wonderful to be in conversation with you.
[music]
I am Jenn O’Donoghue and thank you all for listening.
O’DONOGHUE: Thank you for listening to Embedding Equality in Education, a podcast from the Gender Equality in and through Education team in the Center for Universal Education at Brookings. Our sincere thanks to all the LAAGA members and others who contributed to this episode.
OSSAI: The show is produced and published by the Brookings Podcast Network. Thanks to the production team, including Ike Blake, supervising producer; Fred Dews, senior producer; Arushi Sharma, co-producer; Daniel Morales and Teddy Wansink, video producers; and Chris Chang, audio and video producer. Plus, thanks to Benji Aliaga and Madeline Chandler for their contributions to the show.
O’DONOGHUE: Daniel Morales also designed the show’s artwork. And a very big special thank you to our former senior project assistant and co-producer, Anya Kasubhai, who did so much to get this show launched.
Brookings gratefully acknowledges the support provided by Echidna Giving, Stone Family Foundation, and The LEGO Foundation in support of this work.
I am Jenn O’Donoghue.
OSSAI: And I am Edem Ossai.
O’DONOGHUE: Thank you for listening.

What could RED IV mean for Europe’s renewable hydrogen market?
A leaked draft of the EU’s post-2030 renewable energy framework points towards a significant change in how renewable hydrogen demand could be supported. If adopted, the proposals could shift the market away from binding EU-level quotas and towards greater national flexibility, wider eligibility and an indicative long-term target

06 November 2026
5 minute read

Email
Share by email

Monica Trilho
Research Analyst – Hydrogen & Derivatives

Close

Monica Trilho
Research Analyst – Hydrogen & Derivatives
Mónica is a hydrogen-focused research analyst for the Power & Renewables department.
