Europe’s approach to supporting renewable hydrogen could change significantly after 2030.
The European Commission is developing the fourth Renewable Energy Directive (RED IV), which will shape the EU’s post-2030 renewable energy framework. A draft impact assessment leaked in September 2026 suggests policymakers are considering a different approach to hydrogen from that established under RED III.
The document is not adopted policy. The Commission is expected to publish its legislative proposal before the final framework is negotiated by the European Parliament and Council.
But the direction under consideration raises an important question for the hydrogen industry: if binding EU-level targets become less prominent, what will drive demand after 2030?
How could RED IV change renewable hydrogen requirements?
The leaked assessment points towards a more flexible framework for renewable and low-carbon hydrogen.
In transport, obligations on fuel suppliers could remain, but implementation would increasingly sit at member-state level rather than being driven by a standalone EU-wide quota. The proposals also contemplate broadening the types of hydrogen and electricity sources eligible for compliance.
For industry and refining, the change could be greater still. Instead of continuing the current model of binding national RFNBO requirements, the draft considers moving towards an indicative EU-level hydrogen target for 2040.
That distinction matters. A binding mandate creates a clearer compliance-driven source of demand. An indicative target may give governments and companies more flexibility, but it also puts greater emphasis on the policies, incentives and market mechanisms used to translate ambition into actual hydrogen consumption.
Why is the EU considering a different approach?
The proposals reflect a difficult reality for Europe’s emerging hydrogen market.
Renewable hydrogen has faced persistent challenges around production economics, infrastructure development and demand creation. These conditions have made the pace of market development slower and more uncertain than earlier European ambitions implied.
Broadening eligibility to include additional forms of low-carbon hydrogen could therefore give policymakers another way to support hydrogen deployment while maintaining decarbonisation objectives.
For developers and producers, however, the important issue is not simply the size or structure of a future target. It is whether the framework creates sufficiently predictable demand to support projects and investment decisions.
What would the changes mean for hydrogen producers and developers?
If the framework develops along the lines set out in the leaked assessment, hydrogen producers could face a more varied European market after 2030.
National implementation may become more important, while a broader range of hydrogen production pathways could compete to meet demand. That could create opportunities for some producers, including suppliers outside the EU, while changing the competitive environment for projects developed around the existing RFNBO framework.
The assessment also considers mechanisms intended to connect hydrogen use across different sectors. Depending on their eventual design, these could give producers greater flexibility in how they participate in European compliance markets.
Much will depend on the detail, however. The way targets are translated into national policy, the treatment of different hydrogen pathways and the interaction between industrial and transport demand could all materially affect project economics.
Could removing binding quotas weaken hydrogen demand?
This is arguably the central question raised by the draft.
Replacing binding requirements with a more flexible framework could help address some of the challenges policymakers have encountered in scaling renewable hydrogen. But greater flexibility can also mean less certainty over where demand will emerge and how quickly.
Parts of the hydrogen industry have already argued for continued binding RFNBO requirements beyond 2030, highlighting the tension facing policymakers: balancing achievable decarbonisation rules with enough long-term visibility to support investment.
From Wood Mackenzie’s perspective, the crucial issue will therefore be how policy ambition translates into bankable demand.
The headline targets matter, but so do the mechanisms beneath them: national implementation, incentives, compliance rules and the interaction between transport, industrial and refining demand.
Why does refinery hydrogen matter under RED IV?
One area requiring particular clarification is the treatment of refineries.
Under the existing framework, refinery hydrogen can interact with transport-fuel compliance requirements. The leaked proposals also bring refining into the scope of the future industrial framework.
How policymakers reconcile those two routes will have implications for member states that have developed hydrogen strategies around refinery demand, as well as for producers assessing where future European demand could emerge.
This illustrates a wider issue with the draft: the direction of travel may be becoming clearer, but many of the rules that will ultimately determine commercial outcomes are not.
What should the hydrogen industry watch next?
Three questions will be particularly important as RED IV develops:

How will Europe create durable hydrogen demand if binding EU-level mandates are reduced?

How will industrial, refining and transport demand interact under the new framework?

Will the eventual incentives and compliance mechanisms provide enough certainty to support project development?

The Commission’s eventual proposal will be only the next step. The European Parliament and Council will then shape the legislation before the framework is finalised.
For hydrogen producers, developers and buyers, the significance of RED IV will therefore extend beyond any single target. The bigger question is what type of European hydrogen market the post-2030 rules are designed to create, and whether that framework can provide the demand certainty needed for the sector to scale.
Wood Mackenzie will continue to assess how the evolving RED IV framework could affect hydrogen demand, project economics and market development across Europe and the wider global hydrogen value chain.

articles.title: Crypto Markets Recover as Rates and Lending Conditions Shift
articles.text:
Insights / Perspectives / Crypto Markets Recover as Rates and Lending Conditions Shift

Written by:

Max Bareiss
Head of Lending

Hannah Kip
Institutional Lending

Yoojeong Lee
Institutional Lending Associate

Kenzie Yang
Lending Analyst

Topics

DeFi

Lending

Markets & Macro

Tokenization

Products & Services

Onchain Financing

Lending

Trading

perspectives • September 17, 2026

Crypto Markets Recover as Rates and Lending Conditions Shift

In this report:Tokenized equities move onchain as collateralRobinhood Chain Brings Tokenized Equities and Lending OnchainMorpho Brings Fixed-Rate Lending OnchainCompound Targets Institutional Growth with $52M InitiativeArc Goes Live, and Credit Starts in Dollars
Lending Market UpdateJune through mid-September marked a clear transition from deep correction to recovery and, more recently, consolidation in crypto. June was the weakest stretch, with BTC testing multi-month lows around $58k in late June before stabilizing through July in a range roughly between $56k and $64k. In August, BTC rose 25% and briefly traded above $82k in early September before retracing to around $76k as of September 16 amid a more challenging macro backdrop. A notable catalyst was a reversal in ETF flows, where August saw $3.52B of net inflows, the strongest month of 2026, against just $172M in July and $4.5B of outflows in June. The rally was also coincided with the expansion of U.S. Treasury long-end bond buybacks, which initially pushed longer-dated yields lower and weakened the dollar, creating a more supportive backdrop for BTC and contributing to a sharp short squeeze. ETF flows have since become more mixed in September as momentum from August moderated. Optimism around the CLARITY Act also supported sentiment, though the bill failed to advance in the Senate on September 15, falling short of the 60 votes needed in a procedural vote and adding to regulatory uncertainty across the industry.

CME annualized basis broadly moved with the recovery. After troughing near 3.8% in late June, basis widened through July and August, peaking around 6.7% in late August. Basis has since moderated and become more volatile in September, generally trading in the 5 – 6% range and ending the period around 5.3%. Meanwhile, Treasury yields moved meaningfully higher, narrowing the pickup offered by CME basis over risk-free rates. With Treasury yields moving closer to basis levels, the trade appears relatively less attractive despite the recovery in crypto markets.

The lending market remained orderly, with deleveraging continuing across platforms. Galaxy Research’s The State of Crypto Leverage Q2 2026 report showed that the total crypto-collateralized lending market fell to $56.16B (down $11.33B QoQ, and down 40% from the Q3 2025 peak of $78.7B), with Q2 the first quarter since Q4 2022 in which all three legs declined together- CeFi, DeFi, and the crypto-collateralized portion of CDP stablecoin supply. On the DeFi side, borrows dropped 27.61% to $20.43B, roughly 3x the pace of CeFi's 9.62% decline to $22.98B. The net effect was CeFi gaining relative share even as the overall market contracted, the first quarter since Q3 2023 that CeFi loans outstanding exceeded those of DeFi lending apps, with Galaxy Research reporting that Galaxy, Coinbase, Ledn, Arch, Sygnum and Milo all growing their books. Notably, the contraction has been stepwise rather than cascading- three consecutive quarters of 10%, 5% and 17% declines, against a 55% single-quarter collapse in Q2 2022, which pointed to gradual risk reduction rather than forced liquidations.

Key trends
Tokenized equities move onchain as collateralCoinbase recently launched tokenized U.S. stocks natively on Base on August 24, beginning with NVDAc, METAc, AAPLc, and GOOGLc. Each token is a direct 1:1 claim on a real share, where institutional market makers buy the underlying stock, Alpaca Securities custodies it in segregated accounts, and Coinbase Onchain SPV Ltd holds it as bare trustee in a bankruptcy-remote structure. The tokens are composable across Base DeFi, with other protocols like Aave, Morpho and Euler live for lending and borrowing. The significance for credit markets is that this is the first time a major regulated issuer has put genuine equity claims into open lending rails, extending on-chain collateral beyond just digital assets. The implication is that on-chain credit could broaden from crypto’s own market cap toward the equity and fixed income complex, potentially making lending activity less dependent on the crypto cycle, which is a structural counterweight to the kind of collateral contraction seen this quarter where the decline from peak reflected asset prices. It also raises a topic that needs further clarification from lenders, as equity collateral carries different liquidity and settlement characteristics from BTC or ETH. Coinbase’s product is currently restricted to non-U.S. persons, and Chainlink’s feeds run 24/5 against tokens that trade continuously, meaning weekend collateral is marked to Friday’s close.
Robinhood Chain Brings Tokenized Equities and Lending OnchainRobinhood recently launched its own Arbitrum-based Ethereum L2 on its public mainnet on July 1, built for tokenized real-world assets and shipped with Uniswap, Morpho, Chainlink and BitGo integrated at launch. Stock Tokens went live for 24/7 trading (currently only available for non-U.S. persons), deployable into lending pools and usable as collateral across DeFi, alongside Robinhood Earn. Robinhood Earn is a Morpho-powered product offering roughly 7% on USDG. An important thing to note is a TradFi platform with nearly 28 million funded users choosing to operate its own settlement layer rather than route through existing chains, funded in part by a $2B convertible note priced in June. For lending markets, this matters in two ways. First, distribution: potentially routing ~28 million retail users into DeFi lending brings a scale of deposit supply that on-chain credit has not previously had access to. Secondly, the structure differs from a tokenized share, as Robinhood’s Stock Tokens are tokenized debt securities issued by a Jersey entity, conveying price exposure without ownership, voting rights or direct dividend entitlement, and Robinhood operates the sole sequencer and controls issuance. As equity collateral migrates on-chain, the underlying legal structure on whether a token represents a share or a claim on the issuer, becomes a central input to how these assets are evaluated.
Morpho Brings Fixed-Rate Lending OnchainIn a continued effort to bring traditional credit markets onchain, Morpho launched Morpho Midnight, giving lenders and borrowers access to fixed-rate, fixed-term lending. Much of onchain lending relies on variable rates and open tenors, which can make it difficult to plan around a known cost of capital or return. Midnight is designed to address this challenge, and its customizable KYC gating can further help to attract institutional participants.Existing attempts at fixed-rate markets are built on top of variable-rate markets rather than as a native primitive, where fixed rates are achieved by wrapping or tokenizing exposure to an underlying floating-rate pool. This can introduce basis risk against the underlying source, add a layer of risk on top of the base market, and can fragment liquidity. Morpho Midnight, by contrast, introduces fixed-rate lending at the protocol level rather than synthesized from a floating-rate position.Defined rates and maturities align more closely with institutional credit markets than the utilization curve model most DeFi lending uses. The initial launch features a single cbBTC/USDC market on Base, with a roadmap that includes expansion into financing backed by real-world assets (RWAs). In the meantime, Morpho sits alongside existing Morpho Blue markets: lenders can earn variable rates on Blue while quoting fixed-rate offers on Midnight, capital is only committed once matched so it doesn’t sit idle while it waits.
Compound Targets Institutional Growth with $52M InitiativeCompound is also making a concerted push to attract institutional capital, beginning with a new leadership team and a $52 million budget approved by the DAO. The initiative follows a decline in the protocols TVL which has fallen from $12B in 2021 to roughly $1.2B today. The program aims to draw institutions by introducing RWA products and building infrastructure for the likes of banks, asset managers, and fintech companies.Of the $52 million, $14 million is released at the onset, with the remainder held in reserve until the Foundation reaches specified development goals. The move positions Compound to compete with other protocols that have already established RWA lending markets.
Arc Goes Live, and Credit Starts in DollarsCircle brought Arc’s public mainnet live on September 16. The chain is EVM-compatible, gas is paid in USDC, and settlement is built for sub-second finality. A permissioned validator set is producing blocks, including BlackRock, DTCC, Visa, Mastercard, ICE, and Galaxy. Circle also minted 10 billion ARC tokens around launch, while saying that is not a commitment to sell the token to the public.Lending was on the network from the start. Aave, including a V4 market, Morpho, and Uniswap opened with the chain, and tokenized cash such as BUIDL and USYC is being lined up as collateral next to cirBTC. Galaxy curated two Morpho vaults on Arc – one USDC and one EURC – and Morpho on Arc took in more than $150 million of deposits on day one. That is the early read: dollar credit can now clear on Circle’s own rails, with fees in the same unit as the loan.Notable News:The State of Crypto Leverage Q2 2026: An Orderly, Measured DeclineFed approves interest rate hike, signals one more to come this yearCircle launches Arc mainnet with BlackRock and Visa among validatorsMorpho Launches Fixed-Rate Lending Protocol Midnight on BaseUniswap launches 'Earn' with Morpho to let users earn yield on idle cryptoEuro Stablecoins Hit All-Time High as Tokenized Equities Reach $4.45BVisa combines VisaNet data with onchain lending to power stablecoin card working capital

PERSPECTIVES Memo

US Midterm Elections 2026: Riding the blue wave

Ready to talk?

×

Deepak Puri, CFA®, Chief Investment Officer Americas; Wolf Kisker, Senior Investment Strategist; Shreenidhi Jayaram, Investment Strategist; Jon Byrne, Investment Strategist
November 04, 2026

Share

Share on Facebook

Share on LinkedIn

Share by Email

Key takeaways
Democrats emerged as the clear winner of the midterms, reclaiming both chambers of Congress with a 54-44 Senate majority (+7 seats, two races outstanding) and a 228-139 House advantage (+25 seats).
From ballots to budgets: data centers and deficits may define the next phase of the policy agenda.
Equities initially sold off overnight as a Democratic sweep became more likely before staging a relief rally this morning.

What happened?
The key question heading into Election Day was whether Democrats would make modest gains or deliver a more decisive victory. While some races remain subject to final certification, the results point to a clear Democratic win, with the party reclaiming control of both chambers of Congress. In the Senate, Democrats secured a 54-44 advantage, flipping seven Republican-held seats in Texas, Ohio, North Carolina, South Carolina, Kansas, Iowa, and Maine. Several of these gains came in traditionally Republican states, with moderate Democratic candidates helping expand the electoral map beyond the party's usual battlegrounds. Despite the strong showing, Democrats remain short of a veto-proof majority.

In the House of Representatives, Democrats reached 228 seats as of this morning, comfortably above the 218-seat threshold required for control and representing a gain of 25 seats. Republicans currently hold 139 seats, with several races still outstanding. At the state level, Democrats also recorded a number of notable gubernatorial victories, strengthening their position across both federal and state governments. Taken together, the results represent a broader-than-expected Democratic overperformance and a meaningful shift in the balance of political power heading into the final two years of the presidential term.

Attention now turns to the post-election agenda, with government funding, fiscal negotiations, and the debt ceiling remaining key areas of focus in the months ahead.

What does it mean for investors?
The initial equity selloff in the overnight trading session as a Democratic sweep became more likely has given way to a relief rally this morning. However, the rebound is marked by sector dispersion, with industrials underperforming and consumer discretionary outperforming. Weakness in industrials may reflect concerns that tighter regulation could slow the AI infrastructure buildout, weighing on industrial companies exposed to that investment.

From a cross-asset standpoint, Treasuries remain bid across the curve, standing in contrast to renewed risk appetite. This divergence suggests that investors are distinguishing between reduced election uncertainty and potential policy risks that loom ahead, particularly related to concerns about the implications for domestic growth associated with a potential slowdown in data center construction. In line with lower Treasury yields, the US dollar rolled over. Taken together, lower Treasury yields and a weaker US dollar supported gold as it rose above the psychological 4,000 level, which has served as support over the past six months.

Divided government shifts rather than removes policy risk. With fewer legislative options, the White House may lean on tariffs, sanctions, enforcement, regulation, and foreign policy. Key watchpoints for 2027 and beyond include Senate confirmations, spending negotiations, AI infrastructure power costs, and developments in Iran.

For investors, the election changes the policy landscape, but it has limited bearing on the underlying macroeconomic environment. Although short-term trading opportunities may emerge, investors should avoid knee-jerk positioning around the outcome and instead focus on evolving economic conditions and corporate earnings. Even so, state-level policy changes may prove more important for AI investment than the shift in congressional control, given the role state and local authorities play in permitting new data centers. A well-diversified, multi-asset portfolio remains a prudent way to navigate political uncertainty.

articles.title: AI Could Do My First Job. Not My Last.
articles.text:
Blog Name

RealTime Economics

AI Could Do My First Job. Not My Last.

Jason Furman (PIIE)

Date
November 1, 2026 9:46 AM

Photo Credit: IMAGO/Westlight via Reuters Connect

This blog post was originally published on PIIE senior fellow Jason Furman's Econvitals.org(link is external) website and republished here with permission. Furman wrote the blog post with assistance from AI (see his website(link is external) for details).

XLinkedInBlueskyEmailShare

Body
Warning: This is different from what my other Occasional Posts will be. It is longer, more personal and more opinionated, with almost no data and no charts. But it also addresses some important issues, so I hope you read it. Or if you're busy, paste it into an AI and have it produce a summary and critique at whatever length or depth works for you.
I want to talk about my comment to Neil Irwin(link is external) about the White House Council of Economic Advisers (CEA) when Econvitals(link is external) was released: "If I were running the CEA today and had a choice between 20 staff members who had a combination of current Ph.D.s and future Ph.D.s versus the AI systems that we have today, I would somewhat regretfully and sadly choose the AI systems." It would be fair to say the reaction to it(link is external) was generally negative, including from many friends and former colleagues. I confess that makes me a bit mad and a bit sad.
The mad is entirely at myself for choosing a provocative example in order to stimulate a conversation, when instead it backfired and closed off the conversation. And the sad is because we are facing some very difficult and challenging issues, at least in certain pockets of the labor market(link is external), and I worry that unrealistic denials of risks and tradeoffs—albeit not certainties—could get in the way of honestly confronting what we are facing. At a moment like this we need realism, honesty and a willingness to make difficult choices.
I am not saying my view is definitely right, just that it is not so obviously wrong. In this post I will try to do a better job explaining why and what it might mean. I am going to be granular about CEA because I think it is a useful thought experiment, in the ways it does and does not generalize to other organizations.
The Council of Economic Advisers: An Amazing Group of Thirty-Five Humans That Could Be Mostly Replicated by About Ten Humans Plus AI
So let me get to my specific claim: I believe that most of what CEA did when I ran it could now be done by about ten people. Which means AI could replace much of what a group of bright people, from recent college graduates to seasoned academics, could do. So my 20-person comment to Neil may have understated the case. (Later on I will get to the different and more important question: not reproducing what we did but figuring out what to do in the future, which shifts the issue from whether AI could replace people to whether it should.)
A bit of background. CEA is like an in-house think tank that provides economic advice to the President and the administration, as well as a set of public reports including the Economic Report of the President(link is external). It is a small, scrappy staff of about 35 people, most of them not permanent government employees—including about ten Senior Economists, many of whom are professors on leave from universities, and another roughly ten incredibly talented and hard-working junior staff who are often headed to or in the middle of Ph.D. programs.
When I ran the Council of Economic Advisers from mid-2013 to the beginning of 2017 we produced dozens of reports(link is external) that helped contribute to the conversation on everything from competition(link is external) to male employment(link is external) to how to extract the signal from macroeconomic data(link is external), not to mention contributing to myriad policy issues including Medicare payments, criminal justice reform and the Clean Power Plan. None of that would have been possible without the ideas, initiative and execution of the people who worked there.
AI on its own or AI with just me directing it could not replace all of that. As I told Neil, "You would need people at CEA to interact in meetings, to talk to the press, talk to Congress." But CEA would not need nearly as many humans for just these tasks.
AI is an outstanding research assistant and is doing increasingly sophisticated economic reasoning and analysis. But humans would still play a critical role. If I were running an AI-intensive CEA with only a skeleton staff, I would expect the remaining humans to be in frequent conversation with economists and policy wonks, both across the administration and outside it, to challenge our ideas, get new ones, share our results and try to persuade people. This is not complete automation. But it is AI doing most implementation.
The Messy Reality of Who AI Can and Cannot Replace
My expertise on these issues comes only partly from my time as Chair under President Obama. Perhaps even more relevant is what I learned and did as a CEA staffer under President Clinton. At that earlier time my job was mostly performing short analyses, tracking macroeconomic data and writing short memos on it, drafting reports, working on the administration's forecast, and working with Joe Stiglitz and then Janet Yellen on their speeches. It was amazing and challenging work. I would not be the person I am today if I had not gone through that intensive experience and the mentorship I got from them. But I look back on that time and truly believe that AI—guided and directed by Stiglitz, Yellen and other more senior people—could easily do 95 percent of what I did then. And the other 5 percent was staffing Stiglitz on trips, doing things like getting him a new tie when he spilled on the old one.
A few people responded to my argument with claims that the CEA Chair might even be more replaceable than many of the people who work for them. It might sound just, but it is also wrong. Jason as Chair could not be replaced by AI but Jason as junior staffer could be. That is not because Jason as Chair was smarter or better than Jason as junior staffer. It is because the task mix for the Chair is mostly about being in meetings, briefing the President, testifying to Congress, making speeches, reaching out to discuss issues with academics and the like—those just are not jobs that an AI can do. In contrast, the task mix for a junior staffer—and even for some senior economists with decades of experience—is mostly doing analysis and writing on a computer and emailing it to the people who use it. That could be done by AI.
The reality gets very messy in ways that measures of AI exposure are unlikely to capture. For example, the effect of AI on employment at the National Economic Council (NEC), where I did two stints, could be quite different from its impact on employment at CEA. The NEC and CEA are both White House economic advisers and employ similar types of people, especially in the junior ranks. But the NEC is a more strategic and political organization that manages the policy process and is heavily involved in the passage and implementation of policy. Most junior staffers at the NEC are probably safer from AI than even more senior staffers at CEA, not because NEC staffers are smarter and more talented than CEA staffers but because much of the job of NEC staffers is running meetings, building coalitions and working with a wide range of units to implement policies—none of which can be done by AI.
So the issue of who AI can replace is not one of who is more virtuous or smarter or better or even who is more senior or more junior. It is about what the nature of the job is. AI poses more of a threat to some of the smartest people in the academy, like mathematicians(link is external), than to people in many other disciplines, although I have heard a number of colleagues in different disciplines wonder if their days as active researchers are numbered.
Don't Underestimate How Capable AI Is: It Can Write Decent Economics Papers, Very Good Briefings and Excellent Blogs With Basically No Human Input
Part of the disconnect in the discourse is that people have different understandings of the current capabilities of AI. More and more people understand them, but I still sometimes hear people talking about AI hallucinations or how it repackages Wikipedia. These might have been true of badly used, weaker AI models a year or two ago, but they are barely relevant for understanding agentic AI today.
To understand it better, as an experiment I built an engine I call Paperwright(link is external). It takes a short prompt and spends two to ten hours turning it into an economics paper, drawing on a multi-step agent process that includes researchers, writers, fact checkers and referees. For example, I entered "data centers and electricity prices" and about six hours later I got this 65-page paper(link is external), which has a mathematical model, an analysis of county-level data drawn from Environmental Protection Agency permit records, the Energy Information Administration and other sources, references and appendices, plus a replication package(link is external). I don't think the paper is a great contribution to knowledge, and it should not be published in even a mid-level journal, but if it were a senior thesis it would probably get a grade in the Summa range at Harvard. And if you think that paper is wild, check out this one(link is external), produced with a one-word prompt: "Triffin."
I also created Blogwright(link is external) as an experiment to see if AI could write think tank-style blogs that explain things, organize and summarize data, or make a case. The results, in my judgment, would be among the better versions of the genre at the better think tanks, on topics including the case for reviving the Premium Tax Credit(link is external), how work from home has changed the labor market for women(link is external), why the budget problem is that taxes are too low(link is external) and why the budget problem is that spending is too high(link is external).
These blogs are better than what a chatbot could do today, given the ways I have architected the multi-step process for writing them and the links to over one hundred data sources. But I expect even a simple prompt into a chatbot will do better than this in a year or two. Moreover, what started as an experiment has turned into an input into my thinking—on many topics I would rather get up to speed with an AI-generated blog post than anything written by humans, which might be out of date, not match my interests or have inaccurate or misleading numbers (AI, used properly, can make fewer mistakes than people).
I also created Briefwright(link is external) to write briefings for me on various topics, ranging from literature reviews on audit studies(link is external) to analysis of the wealth effect in supporting current consumption(link is external) to an evaluation of the climate forecasting track record(link is external). None of them are fully reliable from beginning to end, but all of them are informative and generative as an input to my own thinking and writing.
Econvitals itself is built the same way. Almost every email you receive from it was written by AI. I don't approve, read or edit them before they go out. I iterated on the prompts, designed the pool of charts they draw on and architected the overall system. The exceptions are a paragraph I write in Morning Notes(link is external) about a chart I select and design, and these Occasional Posts(link is external). The emails have been timely, reasonably comprehensive and generally accurate.
But I also expect my own posts will be more interesting than anything the AI writes. I don't say that to brag about myself; most days the Morning Note links to two pieces it selects as interesting by different people and organizations, and those are also more interesting than anything written by AI. As are innumerable other human-written pieces it does not link to.
Some of the AI-generated papers, blogs and briefings are cutting-edge. Some need significant work and have big deficiencies that need to be remedied by humans. And some of the longer papers might even be garbage. But all of them were done by AI in 2026 (it will get better), by systems I architected (I'm decent at this but many people are much better), and with basically no human input or iteration beyond architecting the system and then entering a simple prompt.
I can think of people I know who overrely on AI and produce slop they don't understand. But I can think of many more people—including some economists and think tankers—whose error goes in the opposite direction: underusing the technology in ways that lead them to make too many mistakes and not think ambitiously enough about what they could accomplish. And if you're only making errors in one direction (underreliance or overreliance) you're using the technology wrong.
AI Can Also Enable Us to Do More and Better: But How Much More and Better Will People Want?
CEA was swamped with just 35 staff covering every single economic issue. If I were in charge I would not have ten humans plus AI replacing the CEA I knew; I would have something between ten and 35 humans plus AI doing something much better than CEA did when I was there.
One factor that influences whether technological change increases or decreases the demand for labor is how much demand there is for the output of that labor (more technically, how elastic that demand is(link is external)—so how much does it increase when the price falls). A far smaller share of American workers are farmers today than two hundred years ago because of the combination of technological progress in farming and the fact that people don't eat much more than they did two hundred years ago. In contrast, businesses use vastly more accounting services, so that even as accountants enjoyed huge productivity improvements we ended up hiring more and more of them(link is external) (although that has fallen off lately). The latter effect is known as the "Jevons paradox(link is external)"—when making something more efficient and cheaper leads to a huge increase in demand for it, so you end up using more.
In the case of CEA, I am not sure how elastic the demand for its output is—after all, it was already free. We would not have written more reports or memos; we could have covered a few more issues and done better analysis, but there is a limit to that as well. Plus many of our clients—in the NEC (which is less technical), the Hill, the media, etc.—could do a lot of this without CEA, so it is possible that demand for CEA's output could go down, not up.
That said, in most domains we have consistently underestimated the amount of demand for new and improved versions over time. We can usually picture a living standard slightly better than ours, maybe twice as good, but have a hard time picturing one ten or a hundred times as good. And yet that is what we end up wanting and producing—which is why so many people still work so hard even though they could easily have an amazing living standard by the standards of 1930(link is external) with many fewer hours of work per week. So it is possible I am underestimating just how much more sophisticated the analysis will get—and how it might even take more people to work with the AI on that analysis.
But I want to be honest and realistic here, even though it's hard. I have talked to dozens of colleagues at Harvard and other institutions. I have not met a single one who cites the Jevons paradox in their own hiring of research assistants. No one who says, "Now that research assistants have access to Claude Code they are so effective that I want to hire more of them." To be clear, there may be some I have never talked to who think this, but they are greatly outweighed by people who think they need the same number, fewer or perhaps even none. I personally no longer have a full-time research assistant but continue to work with a few outstanding part-time research assistants who contribute a lot of ideas as well as execution to what I do.
Going beyond anecdata, the evidence itself is mixed. One paper by two of our graduate students at Harvard, Seyed Mahdi Hosseini Maasoum and Guy Lichtinger, found that junior employment is down about 9 percent at firms adopting AI(link is external). But Martha Gimbel and the team at The Budget Lab(link is external) at Yale do not see the occupational mix changing in ways that clearly line up with AI. It's still early days.
I would not be surprised if the optimum was a CEA about half its current size, staffed with more senior people, selected to a greater degree than in the past on their ability to operate interpersonally (so in meetings with other administration staff) and their ability to manage AI agents. And as AI gets more capable and the government updates how it operates, the optimal number would be more likely to go down than up.
(I also think that people who like and believe in government being capable of doing good and important things have a responsibility to help make it as efficient as possible. That will not always mean cutting staff relative to what we have now. Statistical agencies, for example, are vastly underresourced and nothing on Econvitals would work without the thousands of people who work at them collecting and analyzing data. That said, where we can do more with less—and there will be many places that is the case—we should.)
The Difficult Question of How Much to Give Up to Cultivate the Next Generation of Talent
So far I've talked about the work that CEA does in producing analysis and public policy. But what about the work it does in helping to train people who have gone on to everything from winning the Nobel Prize(link is external) and the John Bates Clark Medal(link is external) to serving as Treasury Secretary(link is external) and Director of the Congressional Budget Office(link is external)? You can debate the causal impact of CEA in each of these cases—much of it is selection, not treatment. But the causal impact is not zero.
We need to take the pipeline seriously and be mentoring, training and investing in the future. The best paper I have read on this topic is "Pyramids, Diamonds, and Oscillations"(link is external) by Guido Friebel and coauthors, a model in which AI makes firms freeze junior hiring in the short run even if they eventually return to the familiar pyramid of many juniors and few seniors, while faster learning could shift them for good toward a diamond, with fewer juniors and a bulge of experienced people in the middle. I highly recommend it—or if you are not super technical about equations, I recommend you give it to your AI to rewrite in whatever format you most want to read it in (which could even be a music video).
But we also need to be honest about the tradeoffs. CEA was paid for by taxpayers. I could maybe justify hiring someone at $75,000 who produced $50,000 a year of output on the grounds that it would help train and mentor people to contribute more in the future. But I could not justify jobs where the person made only small contributions here and there and the bulk of what they did could be done by an AI, just because it would be good for them and the world more broadly if they got that training. Moreover, it is not clear what it means to get "training" if all you end up doing is botsitting.
Similarly, if a researcher gets a grant for economics research or cancer research, the grantors are usually looking for the maximum possible research output—more discoveries and cures. Although there are programs aimed at supporting the pipeline and requiring dedicated training and mentoring, most are not looking for Principal Investigators to run projects that either are more expensive or end up doing less in order to devote additional resources to mentoring and training so that ten or twenty or thirty years from now economics research or cancer research is better.
In universities our job is mentorship and training people for the future. I take that seriously, as do most of my colleagues. I also think organizations around the country will need to put some weight on that too. But there is a limit to how much weight.
How it works out in the workplace will be much less clear. Gary Becker(link is external) explained that while firms would not pay for training in skills when workers could take them elsewhere, the training will still happen because the workers themselves will pay in the form of lower wages. That works fine if an investment banking associate is producing $300,000 of value for the firm but is willing to work for a mere $200,000—while de facto giving up $100,000 in exchange for the valuable training they are getting. But if the investment banking associate is producing effectively zero for the firm but getting valuable training they will take to another firm in the future, then do we really think it is a viable equilibrium for them to pay the firm $100,000 a year for the privilege of being trained?
The government is not profit-maximizing and can care some about the social good it does. But it is hard for me to believe that a make-work program for junior economists who are not actually producing much of value (because the AI is producing it) would have large enough social returns over time to justify its upfront cost. Moreover, if the government has spare funds to hire extra people it does not especially need in the short run, then economists should do their objective best to figure out where those skills are needed (public health? AI safety? National security?), not just assume that their own profession should be the one to be protected using extra taxpayer dollars.
I don't know the full answer to the pipeline question. I worry about it. But I don't think anyone should think it is easy or obvious or that no one needs to worry. At a minimum, we will probably need to be intentional about paying for the pipeline explicitly, through fellowships and training grants, instead of hoping that organizations keep hiring people they no longer need. But we may simply need fewer of certain types of skills and activities in a future world where AI is becoming increasingly capable.
I Don't Know the Right Ratio of Joy and Terror, but You Should Be Feeling Both When It Comes to AI
I have generally been an AI accelerationist. When I was the Chair of CEA a common refrain in my remarks on the topic was this: "The biggest worry I have about AI is that we will not have enough of it."(link is external) My feelings now are much more complex, and if there were a button I could press to undo the last year or two of AI advances—and freeze the technology there for the next several decades—I would be seriously tempted to press it.
I personally feel alternately exhilarated at all the things AI can do for me and humbled and slightly depressed at everything I used to pride myself on that it is vastly better at. I feel excited for students using AI to make new advances in research and thinking but also depressed that they will not have to struggle, learn and grow in the ways I did, without which I could not imagine being who I am today.
I look at younger people setting out to do knowledge work and feel both sentiments, but with a higher weight on the scared and depressed, fearing that they won't need to struggle and learn and that career paths and possibly even entire careers will no longer exist. Manufacturing workers and communities have dealt with much worse for decades, but it would not be truthful to deny feeling it a bit more strongly when it comes to one's own family, friends and community.
I said I would be tempted to press the button, but I would not actually press it (although slowing a bit to get safety right would be a good idea). In part because there is no button. But mostly because the people I'm most worried about are at the upper end of the global population in terms of income or the meaning and purpose they get from their jobs. They have a lot of downside from this technology. But people who are much poorer, who suffer from terrible diseases or who will be adversely affected by climate change all have more upside than downside from more innovation, technology and productivity growth.
Regardless of our feelings about the button, the best advice for any person, organization, country or the world is to figure out how to use AI better while also thinking about what you can uniquely do that is not easily replaced by AI. Continuing to challenge yourself so your skills are not offloaded to AIs, while also building the full capabilities of AI into your life and work and improving your management and interpersonal skills and your unique, human value added, is the best shot you have for the future. It is not entirely clear how anyone can do all of this, and it may not be good enough, but I can't think of anything better.
As for the broader public policy response, well, this post is long enough already—I'll come back to that another time, likely in another venue.

articles.title: View from the markets: Financial market implications of the US midterm elections - BNP Paribas Asset Management - United States
articles.text:
By Daniel Morris, Chief Market Strategist

As it turns out, this time the polls were right. If anything, they understated how well the Democratic Party would do across a range of elections. How significant, though, are the implications for US economic growth and asset prices?

One ‘parlour game’ that strategists play is to compare market returns after midterms, or when different parties control the presidency and the Congress. While perhaps entertaining, such analysis has little practical value as it assumes ‘all else being equal’ –that the only variable that is changing is the make-up of the government.

Needless to say, everything else is actually far from equal, from interest rates to GDP growth and inflation, which are far more significant factors for the markets.

In general, what happens in Washington has only a marginal impact on the economy and markets. The exception is when one party controls both the presidency and all of Congress (House of Representatives and Senate).

When that is the case, it is more likely legislation can be passed (such as Obamacare or the One Big Beautiful Bill) that is significant enough to impact, if not the whole economy, than at least particular sectors. When government is divided, the inevitable compromises required to pass legislation means the impact is often less.

This configuration of full, single-party control has recently tended to occur only at the beginning of presidencies, with mid-term elections then giving partial or total control to the opposition party.

Not only is the legislation passed of less impact when control is divided, there is generally less of it, as compromises generally are difficult to reach.

So, the view that investors had prior to the recent state and local elections should generally still prevail. Our view remains constructive on the outlook for equities as recent macroeconomic data continues to be positive. The third quarter earnings season results were good (if slightly disappointing), and the outlook over the next few quarters is still encouraging. Non-tech heavy indices (like the Russell Value) have tended to move steadily upwards.

The recent tech market sell-off is a continuation of what began in late June. The mid-terms have added an extra bit of uncertainty as investors worry whether data centre buildouts, on which a large of share of expected earnings growth is predicated, will be slowed by Democratic control of governorships and state legislatures.

We expect economic growth to continue more or less as before, regardless of what happens in Washington, which would point to medium-term gains in equities, but with potentially above-average volatility.

Data sources: Bloomberg, FactSet, BNP Paribas Asset Management as of 5 November 2026 (unless otherwise stated). Past performance should not be seen as a guide to future returns.

articles.title: What Is a 401(k)? Key Facts About Saving for Retirement | BlackRock
articles.text:
What is a 401(k) plan?

A 401(k) is an employer-offered retirement account. Plans may require age 21 and 1 year of service, though some allow earlier entry. In 2026, the limit is $24,500, plus an $8,000 catch-up at 50+ if permitted, or $11,250 at ages 60–63. If prior-year wages exceeded $150,000, catch-ups must be Roth. Traditional 401(k)s use pre-tax dollars; Roth 401(k)s use after-tax dollars.

Key takeaways

01

Understand the rules around eligibility and contributions
Plans may require age 21 and 1 year of service, though some allow earlier entry. In 2026, the limit is $24,500, plus $8,000 at 50+ if permitted, or $11,250 at ages 60–63. If prior-year wages exceeded $150,000, catch-up contributions must be Roth (after-tax).

02

Know the differences between traditional and Roth 401(k)s
Traditional 401(k) plans use pre-tax dollars, while Roth 401(k) plans use after-tax dollars. Traditional plans require taxes to be paid upon withdrawal, whereas Roth plans offer tax-free withdrawals under certain conditions. Roth accounts are also not subject to required minimum distributions during your lifetime.

03

Look into your employer’s matching and vesting policies
Employers often contribute to employees' 401(k) accounts through matching contributions. The specifics of matching and vesting rules vary by employer, and employees should consider these provisions before changing jobs to avoid missing out on extra savings.

401(k) plans

What is a 401(k) plan and who is eligible?

A 401(k) plan is an investment account offered by your employer that allows you to save for retirement. If your company offers a 401(k) plan, it may have certain eligibility requirements. While these requirements vary by company, some employees may be excluded from participating if they are not at least 21 years of age or have not completed a year of service with the company.
If you’re considering a job offer, be sure to ask about the company’s retirement plan, including any waiting period.
How much can I contribute to a 401(k) plan?
401(k) plan accounts have higher contribution limits than individual retirement accounts (IRAs). For 2026, you can contribute up to $24,500 of your salary to a 401(k). This limit applies to your combined contributions across all 401(k), 403(b) and SIMPLE plans in which you participate, not to each account separately. Employer contributions don't count toward this limit.
To boost your contributions even further, you might consider catch-up contributions, if your plan offers them. If you are 50 or older, you can contribute an extra $8,000 (up to $32,500 total in 2026). Participants who turn 60 through 63 during 2026 have a higher $11,250 catch-up limit (up to $35,750 total). Beginning in 2026, if your prior-year wages from your employer exceeded $150,000, catch-up contributions must be made on a Roth (after-tax) basis. These increased limits can help boost your savings as you near the retirement finish line. But you don't actually have to be "behind" in your savings to take advantage of catch-up contributions.
What is the difference between a traditional and Roth 401(k) plan?
Many 401(k) plans let you make traditional contributions, Roth contributions, or both. These plans have some similarities: They are subject to the same annual contribution limit and may offer the same investment options. However, traditional and Roth 401(k) plans differ in terms of the tax benefits they offer.

Traditional

Roth

Contributions

Made on a pre-tax basis

Made on an after-tax basis

Withdrawals

Subject to income tax

Tax-free after age 59 ½*

*A withdrawal is qualified if at least five taxable years have passed since your first Roth contribution to the plan, and it is made after you reach age 59½, because of disability, or to a beneficiary after your death. Source: IRS.gov. Date as of Aug 2026.
A traditional 401(k) plan is sometimes referred to as a pre-tax 401(k) plan. You contribute to the plan with before-tax dollars. Because you don’t pay taxes on the money you put into the plan, you must pay taxes (both federal and most state income taxes) when you withdraw it. This structure could be an advantage if you’re in a high tax bracket today but expect to be in a lower one when retired.
With a Roth 401(k) plan, the opposite is true. You save after-tax dollars in the account. Because you’ve already paid taxes on what you’re saving, your withdrawals are considered “qualified” distributions and won’t be taxed as long as both of the following criteria are met:

It has been at least five years since your initial Roth contribution to the plan.
Distributions are made after age 59½, because of disability or to a beneficiary after your death.

How does 401(k) plan matching work?
One major benefit of 401(k) plans is that employers often contribute to your account and “match” what you save. Each employer has its own methods and rules for how it makes matching 401(k) plan contributions. Importantly, a match does not necessarily mean that an employer matches your contributions dollar for dollar. Instead, employers typically match up to a certain percentage of your salary or your contribution.
If your company offers a match, be sure to consider taking advantage of this benefit. It could be a simple and effective way to boost your retirement savings.
One important note: Employers often require you to wait for a certain amount of time before their contributions to your account “vest,” meaning they become yours to keep. Consider this provision before changing jobs so that you don’t inadvertently miss out on extra savings for your retirement.
When can I withdraw from my 401(k) plan?
59½, although your plan's rules determine when withdrawals are available, particularly while you're still working for the employer. Taking out your savings before that age could cost you an extra 10% federal tax on top of the regular federal and state income taxes you'd normally pay, unless an exception applies (for example, if you leave your job in or after the year you turn 55).
When it's time to start using your savings, be sure to consider the tax implications. In addition, you generally must begin taking required minimum distributions (RMDs) from pre-tax 401(k) savings at age 73 (age 75 if you were born in 1960 or later). If you're still working for the employer that sponsors the plan, you may be able to delay RMDs until you retire. Roth 401(k) accounts are not subject to RMDs during your lifetime.
401(k) plans can be very useful tools in saving for retirement, particularly if you take advantage of features that your plan may offer to help maximize your savings. And the sooner you start saving in your 401(k) plan, the longer any investment earnings have to produce earnings of their own.

Wrap up

Top questions about 401(k)s

First, you don’t have to actually be “behind” in your savings to take advantage of this benefit. If you are 50 or older and your plan permits catch-up contributions, you can contribute an extra $8,000 to your 401(k) account in 2026 (up to $32,500 total). Participants who turn 60 through 63 during 2026 have a higher $11,250 catch-up limit (up to $35,750 total). Beginning in 2026, if your prior-year wages from your employer exceeded $150,000, catch-up contributions must be made on a Roth (after-tax) basis. Catch-up contributions can help boost your savings as you near retirement.

Because you don’t pay taxes on the money you put into the plan, you must pay taxes (both federal and most state income taxes) when you withdraw it. Note that you generally must begin taking required minimum distributions (RMDs) at age 73 (age 75 if you were born in 1960 or later). If you're still working for the employer that sponsors the plan, you may be able to delay RMDs until you retire.

The money you contribute from your own paycheck is always yours. However, employers often require you to wait for a certain amount of time before their contributions to your account “vest,” meaning they become yours to keep. Consider this provision before changing jobs so that you don’t inadvertently miss out on extra savings for your retirement.

Because you’ve already paid taxes on what you contribute, your withdrawals are considered “qualified” distributions and won’t be taxed as long as you meet both of the following criteria:

It has been at least five years since your initial Roth contribution to the plan.
Distributions are made after age 59½ because of disability or to a beneficiary after your death.

Saving for retirement can be complicated – but it doesn’t have to be. Arm yourself with the information you need to make the best decisions for your financial future.
