articles.title: Growth and regulation - speech by Andrew Bailey
articles.text:
Growth and regulation - speech by Andrew Bailey

Given at The Financial and Professional Services Dinner, Mansion House

Published on
14 July 2026

In his speech, Andrew Bailey argues that well-designed regulation can support sustainable economic growth by providing stability, enabling innovation and protecting financial stability. He sets out why the UK needs stronger long-term growth, explains the role of bank capital in supporting a resilient banking system, highlights the potential of modern payments and tokenisation, and discusses the opportunities and risks posed by artificial intelligence. This includes the need for proactive public policy and international coordination on frontier AI and cyber resilience.

Speech
Back in early February I was foolish enough to remark to a colleague that on the economic front things were looking more settled, and of course that was a good thing. We seemed to be in more stable times. I was expecting inflation to return to its 2.0% target in around April or May, and then we would need to assess what level of interest rate would keep it there.
Well, that jinxed it. Shortly afterwards, the Middle East conflict broke out. Since then, energy prices have gone up and then returned to levels a bit above where they were before it started, although we are now seeing renewed volatility. Inflation hasn’t returned to target, though the evidence we have seen over recent months has tended to reinforce my view that it would otherwise have done so. Moreover, we are operating in a fairly soft economic setting activity-wise.
We will ensure inflation returns to target and the context is currently encouraging, although uncertainty remains a feature of the situation. But, it will take longer.
I want to step back this evening and consider the longer-term context for the UK economy. Two things stand out for me in terms of the economic context here in the UK. First, we have had lower growth in the economy for the last fifteen years or so. Second, the economy has been hit by a sequence of negative supply shocks which have contributed to the lower growth rate – we can think of Covid, the Ukraine war, the impact of Brexit, etc.
When we think about sustainable growth we have in mind an upper limit that can be achieved without over-heating the economy - something we call the growth of potential supply. This is a speed limit on sustainable growth, and it is influenced by the amount of labour in an economy and how productive it is. For around fifteen years before the financial crisis, the average annual rate of growth of potential supply in the UK economy was around 2.8%. Productivity contributed 2.4pp and labour supply 0.4pp. For the roughly fifteen years since the financial crisis, the potential growth rate has fallen to 1.3% pa, of which productivity contributed 0.4pp and labour supply 0.8pp.
This has had a direct effect on living standards in the UK. Between 1990 and the financial crisis, the average annual growth rate of national income per head was 2.0%, whereas post-crisis it has been 0.6%.
It must therefore be a priority to raise the potential and actual growth rates. Macroeconomic policy provides an important backdrop to doing that. And the best thing we can do on this front is to create and maintain stability – and here I am talking about monetary and fiscal policy. My strongly held view is that, notwithstanding the sequence of adverse shocks, including the latest one from the Middle East, we have the policy frameworks, and policies themselves, in place to provide that stability.
Longer-term growth – the sort we need more of – comes from the supply side. As well as being impacted by negative supply shocks, growth can also be spurred by positive developments that allow us to take leaps forwards.
In this context, what are the longer-run causes of growth in an economy? The list is quite long: physical capital accumulation; technological progress; human capital including education and skills; trade; financial development; markets and competition; infrastructure; and institutional development, both public and private, including public policy and regulation.
Tonight, I want to focus mainly on the role of the final item on that list, regulation.
There is a lot of commentary that regulation is having an excessive negative effect on growth. We shouldn’t ignore this. Well-designed regulation should support economic growth, not hinder it. It can correct market failures; reduce transaction costs; lower entry barriers; and support competition and innovation. In our world, regulation has lowered the probability and severity of financial crises, thereby supporting sustainable growth by safeguarding the supply of finance – in other words, allowing companies and households to plan with confidence for the long term.
Of course, if regulation isn’t well designed and executed, this will not be true. And, to be clear, this would be a real issue across the whole economy.
What do we mean by well-designed and executed? Regulation should always be defined in terms of a positive purpose. In other words, we want to achieve an objective and regulation should help to do that. We should then design the precise regulatory regime that achieves this positive objective as quickly and effectively as possible whilst minimising any undesirable side effects.
This framing should lead to a better debate on the principle and practice of regulation. Are we achieving our objective or not? This is a much better way of framing the issue than simply a too much / too little debate about regulation which is divorced from the objective. Yet too much of the debate on regulation is precisely of this too much / too little sort, in abstract from the outcomes we want to see.
Much of our regulation has the objective of maintaining financial stability. We strongly believe that financial stability is a prerequisite of economic growth. However, we should never say that therefore every one of our rules and regulations is perfectly formed. That will not be the case. But, likewise, to simply argue for less regulation is unhelpfully reductive.
With that in mind, let me move on to look at three highly relevant current policy issues that we face, which are important in their own right but which also bring out the role of the regulation in public policy and the sort of issues we can face. The three current issues are: the level of capital held by banks; payments; and artificial intelligence, particularly so-called Frontier AI.
I will start with bank capital and go right back to basics to make the point that simply arguing for “more” or “less” are not sensible positions in and of themselves.
The main reason for regulating banks is to protect deposits. This begs the question, what is special about deposits? They constitute for all of us the main stock of money that we hold. Regulation exists to ensure confidence in the nominal value of that money. We could achieve this by requiring all the assets of banks to be risk free. But this is neither practical nor helpful from the point of view of supporting activity in the economy, where a degree of risk-taking is of course essential to support growth.
We have, therefore, a banking system that combines deposits as money with lending in the form of credit creation, also known as fractional reserve banking.
This puts banks at the centre of the financial and economic system. It also means that as well as wanting an assured nominal value for deposits, as policymakers we want banks to be able to extend credit across a wide range of activities at all times, thereby supporting the economy right through the business cycle. Striking this balance is the basis of macroprudential regulation and the work of the PRA and the Bank’s Financial Policy Committee in deciding how much capital banks must hold.
Capital is there to absorb losses and thus preserve the nominal value of deposits. It provides assurance to a bank’s customers and counterparties that they can go about their business with confidence. This means that capital instruments are performing the essential function of backing up the assured value of money. They bear the risk, and the return they earn must exceed the amount of loss providers of capital might expect to bear. This gets to the heart of why calibrating capital sensibly – not simply seeking more or less of it – is critical.
This is an important point, because for much of the post-financial crisis period major UK banks earned returns below 10 per cent, a lower-end estimate of the return required by equity investors over the longer term. Aggregate returns rose above 10 per cent in 2023 and reached 15.4% earlier this year. These banks’ price to book ratios are also now around 1.7 times, indicating that equity investors expect future returns to exceed the cost of capital.
There should not, to be clear, be a cap on returns set by regulators. That is a matter of commercial strategy for firms and good regulation should help markets to flush out supranormal profits by reducing barriers to entry. But conditions of financial stability do require that the return earned by investors is above the cost of capital, else capital will simply not be supplied. Regulation must therefore strike the right balance.
That leaves the important question of how much capital should be required. That is a debate that we can have, and are having, but it must be set within the context of maintaining financial stability. We announced changes to the capital regime last week to remove some anomalies, set within the positive objective of financial stability. We are very much open to simplifying and adjusting regulations where needed. But, doing so must contribute to sustaining a healthy banking system which can support and foster stronger growth in the economy.
What does this mean in practice? Sometimes, I hear arguments made which bear some resemblance to the old lump of labour fallacy – except that here it would be a lump of capital. Just as the lump of labour argument assumed a finite amount of labour input could be used in an economy, there is also I fear assumed to be an invariant amount of bank capital, and therefore lightening regulatory rules is necessary to allow that sum of capital to support more lending.
But capital is not invariant. The health of the banking system, and thus the support it can provide to the economy, are in good part interlinked with the returns it earns relative to the opportunity cost of supplying that capital. Banks that earn healthy returns which exceed the cost of capital will be in a stronger position to justify retaining earnings – building capital - to support more lending.
Regulation can support this outcome. Effective regulation which is proportionate will support a lower cost of capital, while weak and ineffective regulation will tend to raise the cost of capital.
I would contend that the position of UK banks today is one of good health and resilience, and this is supported by returns that exceed the cost of capital. The lump of bank capital is therefore not fixed. The system is competitive. This is a positive state of affairs, to which regulation contributes.
Let me move on to the second case, payments, something I spoke about at the end of my remarks here at the Mansion House last year. I am going to talk about regulation in a very broad sense, including the operational role of the Bank of England.
The are two critical positive objectives in the regulation of payments. One is to achieve the so-called singleness of money – which is the assured nominal value of money across all its forms. The second is so-called finality of settlement – the knowledge that payments, once made can be relied on. Together, these anchor confidence in the role of money as a means of payment.
Let me give a simple illustration of why these anchors are important. If we make a payment to each other, we want to know – and not have to spend our time worrying about - two things. First, that the pound in my account and in your account are the same – the nominal value point. And, second, that the payment will be finalised both operationally and legally, so a payment gets made and stays made. Regulation and public policy can help these outcomes happen, while also supporting innovation and competition.
As I said last year, we want to modernise payment systems. We think doing so will enhance their efficiency and functionality and support confidence in the role of money in the economy, thus supporting growth in the economy. We must also continue to enhance the operational resilience of payments, notably to protect against fraud and cyber attacks.
These more modern systems bring the potential benefits of digital technology to payments, for instance so-called programmable payments – “money with instructions” if you like. We think there is scope for important progress in tackling fraud, reducing payment delays, and benefitting trade by increasing the speed of cross-border payments. Innovation can also reduce contracting costs and increase transaction scope in a more digital economy, for instance by allowing small firms to participate better in ecommerce and thereby support growth in the economy.
Last year, we implemented a key part of the infrastructure to achieve this through the renewal of the RTGS system. This will enable innovation – something the Bank is doing jointly with the private sector through our Synchronisation lab.
And in our Digital Securities Sandbox we are supporting the issuance of tokenised assets. The first DSS participant was approved for live activity yesterday. This development will help support the issuance of a UK digital gilt, known as DIGIT. We will work with HMT to enable DIGIT’s eligibility as collateral in the Bank’s market operations.
We are now working with the banks to design and implement the introduction of so-called tokenised money. This will create the ability to tokenise bank deposits and allow the exchange of money to happen on digital tokenised ledgers, in turn enabling programmable payments.
Tokenisation sounds gimmicky and nerdy I admit. Put simply, it is another enabling step, in this case enabling things like faster, more assured payments or the contingent performance of contracts through smart contracts and programmability – i.e. payments that will only be made conditional on the other party first delivering. What might that deliver in the real world? It could be formally making a payment linked to the delivery of goods. It could be formally making a payment dependent on the recipient delivering proof of identity. The first could reduce late payments, the second could reduce fraud. Critically, it changes the point of review or audit of the payment from ex-post to ex-ante. These benefits are worth having, but need a policy framework to enable them to be exploited in an orderly fashion.footnote [1]
We are also moving to enable competition in this field. Recently, we issued proposed rules for so-called systemic sterling stablecoins, to enable these to come into existence as a means of payment beyond the crypto world. These rules will put into effect the key principles of assured nominal value and settlement finality.
This is all about making innovation happen, something that as a public authority and regulator we also do by working closely with industry. In the field of payments innovation using commercial bank money we now have the Bank chaired Retail Payments Infrastructure Board up and running to drive forward work on the design of the next generation retail payments infrastructure. It issued a consultation document on 25 June covering what types of retail payments are likely to be demanded by end-users in the future, and the resulting design issues and principles. The next stage will be to produce a Blueprint and Requirements which will be handed over to an industry owned Delivery Company to build. We are looking for feedback on this consultation by 11 September.
In turn, this kind of regulation supports outcomes that can spur growth in the economy, a positive outcome that we can do best by defining the public good outcomes that we want – these include setting the conditions for assured nominal value of money and settlement finality – and then getting on with them.
This brings me to the third case that we are dealing with, the impact of artificial intelligence. Obviously, it’s a big subject on which much can be said, so in no sense do I pretend to be comprehensive here. On a modest scale, I will make some more general comments relevant to the issues around economic growth and some big public policy and regulatory issues, and then I will add some thoughts on so-called Frontier AI.
I think that General Purpose Technology (GPT) innovation has been, and will continue to be, a major source of longer-run growth in the economy. A GPT is a technology with broad, economy-wide applications that advances over time and enables complementary innovations across many sectors of the economy. Looking back, I would say the following qualify as GPTs: the steam engine; the internal combustion engine; electricity; and information processing and the internet. GPTs come in long cycles, but there can be gaps between them which demonstrate lower growth.
Is this a reasonable description of the last fifteen years or so? Yes. The internet is everywhere but, as it has become so, its contribution to growth will have diminished. You can only get so much of it – honestly. One clue for this as a characterisation of the last fifteen years or so is declining productivity growth.
The obvious question is what will be the next GPT? It’s most likely to be AI, though I would add that AI – like most GPTs – will act to support advances elsewhere: in diagnostics, in research, or with robotics. This underscores that GPTs are enabling technologies – they make other things happen which support growth. The first invention often triggers a sequence of secondary innovations which spread its reach.
But timing is everything, and I think we are between two major cycles of technological innovation showing up in the productivity and growth statistics – between the internet and AI if you like. And innovation can take time to show up in productivity and growth at the economy-wide level. In 1987, the economist Robert Solow commented that “you can see the computer age everywhere but in the productivity statistics”.
A similar thing could be said about James Watt and the steam engine and Thomas Edison and electricity. This is not so surprising. Change can be gradual, and it often requires complementary innovations – as well as trial and error -to get the economic benefit of the GPT, and those take time. And, for now, we are really experimenting with the new technology before we get the economic benefits, which is certainly true of me and AI.
This does not detract from the view that AI is likely to be the next GPT and is likely to raise growth levels in the economy.
But, in doing so, it will raise very big public policy and regulatory issues which we will need to solve, and I would argue we should do so positively and promptly. In other words, we should be regulating for the positive outcome of safe, productive use of AI.
I could set out quite a few big questions of this sort which AI prompts. I am going to stick to two, to provide illustration. These are not questions for the Bank of England to answer, but certainly ones in which we all have a great interest.
First, there are questions on resource allocation. It is said to me by people in the AI industry that there is not enough foreseeable clean power supply (here I mean “clean” in the technical sense of high quality, uninterrupted supply) needed by datacentres to meet all the likely demand from AI. This ultimately, creates the need to make trade-offs. So, should we prioritise medical research (which has great potential), drone technology, finance, entertainment, etc? Markets can always answer that question, but they may well not do so in ways that capture the public interest. This is a big issue, at least potentially.
Second, the rise of AI creates problems of law. Consider so-called agentic AI where we can create AI agents to act on our behalf – say, to buy or trade things. But a feature of AI, including AI created agents, is learning from its own experience, and this learning capacity is growing rapidly. And they can develop bad habits of their own – like lying, or covering up gaps in knowledge in an attempt to please us. These are not new issues.
But, typically, in law a principal becomes responsible for an agent while the agent operates within the remit given to it by the principal. If the agent goes beyond that remit, or acts improperly, it becomes responsible. Traditionally that had depended on the agent having a legal persona, i.e. being a human or a company etc.
But when the agent has no legal persona does that leave the principal responsible at all times? If so, principals may need to constrain agents in ways that cut against the direction of innovation in AI models.
Put another way, is agentic AI in this context more a tool of the principal rather than strictly an agent, with the principal fully liable for all that is done and not done? Does this apply when real money is spent in ways that are final and binding, as and when agentic AI is allowed to hold the purse strings? This removes questions around the boundary of authority but should leave principals wondering how their governance frameworks can effectively operate with this technology. We must think about these things now: and I use this case study to illustrate why we must take a positive and pro-active approach to solving problems which are critical to ensuring effective innovation.
These are very big questions, on which there will need to be public policy input, and probably a mixture of law and regulation. My general argument is that we should tackle them pro-actively and positively, and not get stuck in a negative debate on regulation.
Let me turn to another aspect of AI, namely frontier AI and the risk it poses to the security of IT systems and the potential for cyber attacks. Suffice to say, it appears to have moved on very rapidly, and represents a major threat to the security of systems and thus in our world to financial stability.
To cut the story short, the ability of cutting-edge models to find, and potentially to exploit, vulnerabilities in systems poses some very important public policy and regulatory challenges, as well as challenges for all of us in relation to the systems we use ourselves. Here there are two big challenges relevant to the world of financial stability.
First, we need much stronger co-ordination of testing of frontier models before they go into wide circulation. This needs to be co-ordinated internationally because no country can seal itself off from the cross-border nature of systems that are prevalent today. Such co-ordinated testing needs to start at the level of public authorities. Here, the UK is in a strong position because the AI Security Institute is world leading. And, new models need to go on to testing across the Critical National Infrastructure. Again, the UK is well placed because of the strengths of the National Cyber Security Centre. We at the Bank are working very closely with firms we regulate, including establishing forums to share and improve the efficiency of work on patching systems where needed.
Second, we need to move to much more robust approaches to allow us to recover when things do go wrong. This is often described as Bare Metal recovery – think of it as restoring systems from scratch to a fully operational state. A bigger and more immediate threat means we simply must have the right capabilities. Again, these are big issues, and ones where the best sort of regulation involves working together to facilitate an agreed positive outcome.
To conclude. Economic growth is hugely important and regulation – done right - can play a hugely important role. Growth will come from innovation on the supply side of the economy. I believe technology is a source of growth, and AI is the most likely next big contributor. Inevitably, very big issues come with such change, ones that must be solved with a strong input from public policy and regulation.
But, as in other aspects of regulation, we must do this in a positive way – define what we want to achieve, by when, and then work out how to achieve it in the most effective way. We have to roll our sleeves up and get on with it. Yes, we must question existing regulation, but we must do so in a positive spirit of what we want to achieve.
I would like to thank David Bailey, Sarah Breeden, Victoria Cleland, George Johnston, Karen Jude, Tom Mutton, Nicola O’Keefe, Rhys Phillips, Rob Price and Francine Robb their assistance in preparing these remarks

There are other benefits of Tokenisation. Atomic Settlement – whereby all legs of a financial transaction either complete together or not at all, thus simultaneous settlement - can enable greater efficiency and less risk in wholesale markets.

Footnote [1]
There are other benefits of Tokenisation. Atomic Settlement – whereby all legs of a financial transaction either complete together or not at all, thus simultaneous settlement - can enable greater efficiency and less risk in wholesale markets.

Andrew Bailey
Governor, Bank of England

articles.title: The top Latin American cities in 2026
articles.text:
Blog

30 Oct 2026

The top Latin American cities in 2026

Liam Sides
Associate Director, Cities & Regions

Discussion of the world’s major cities often overlooks the role and dynamics of Latin America. Yet, to ignore the region would be to ignore around a quarter of the world’s land mass and almost a 10th of its population.

In the 2026 edition of the Global Cities Index, Latin American cities are at the forefront of our analysis. Not only has the region seen some the largest increases in their ranking relative to last year, but we have also introduced a new ‘Cities to Watch’ section for the region allowing our analysts to highlight the top five city-economies they are most excited about and think investors should take notice of. The five we covered—Brasília, Lima, Medellín, Monterrey, and Santiago—are a group of cities with diverse drivers, united by their productivity-led expansion as they progress up the value chain.

In terms of the overall rankings for the region, Buenos Aires, the capital of Argentina, takes top spot in the region and 138th overall (Chart 1). The city has the region’s second largest economy and has a deep skills base centred around strong universities and the many corporate headquarters. Second up is Chile’s Santiago, boasting similar credentials but higher housing costs and weaker Environmental scores cost it the top spot. Rounding off the top three is rapidly developing Lima as a combination of rural-urban migration, infrastructure investment, and rising trade volumes positions Peru’s capital as a key regional leader.

Major capital cities lead the index in Latin America

The megacities of São Paulo and Mexico City also rank highly, supported by their large GDP size and elevated scores in the Human Capital category. In fact, the Human Capital category is an area of relative outperformance across the region, with cities benefitting from good universities and high levels of educational attainment. The strength of Human Capital in driving Latin American cities’ performance in the index is perhaps best illustrated by the fact that nine of the 10 cities topping the overall rank for the region also top the Human Capital score, with only Medellín breaking into the top, as Costa Rica’s San José falls out.

The region’s poorest-performing category is Quality of Life, which may sound odd when one thinks of the golden beaches of Rio de Janeiro or the cosmopolitan streets of Santiago and Buenos Aires. However, the region has high levels of inequality, severe poverty, and some of the highest crime rates in the world (Chart 3). Cities as far afield as Port-au-Prince in Haiti, Guatemala City, and Fortaleza in Brazil are emblematic of this reality.

While it would be easy to say that reducing crime will shoot Latin American cities up the rankings, it is much more nuanced than that. This is because of the strong link crime has with other socioeconomic factors, like poverty and inequality, explaining the poor performance of Latin American cities across each of these metrics. Instead, the region needs broad-based interventions to stem to the drivers of crime, which in turn means stronger economic performance as much as it does stronger law enforcement.

Peru’s major cities will continue their strong momentum

Looking ahead, the region is set to see several of its cities climb the rankings and become more prominent in the index. Chief among them is Lima. GDP growth in the city will significantly outpace all other major Latin American cities and, over the next decade, will average 3.2% per annum, more than double the rate of São Paulo and rivalling the growth expected in some of Europe’s and the Middle East’s most dynamic cities. Moreover, this will open up substantial consumer market opportunities—having already surpassed Rio de Janeiro in 2021, Lima is projected to have higher average disposable income than both São Paulo and Bogotá by 2050—despite having a level just 82% and 93%, respectively, of the two today.

Slightly further south, Arequipa, Peru’s second-largest city and one of the world’s leading copper producers, is also set to rise in the rankings. Industry accounts for close to two-fifths of the city’s output, and this specialisation has supported one of the fastest rates of economic expansion among Latin American cities over the past two decades, averaging 5.1% per year. Supported by a strong investment pipeline and sustained demand for copper as electrification advances, we expect Arequipa’s largest gains to come in its Economic score, lifting it into the top 10 Latin American cities in our index over the next decade.

Panama City and Georgetown (Guyana) are also set to climb the rankings, reflecting their roles as both capital city economies and centres of national economic activity. Panama City will remain among Latin America’s top-performing cities, supported by deep human capital, high income per person, and its strategic location at the Pacific mouth of the Panama Canal. Georgetown, by contrast, stands out more for its vast natural resources. It is already Latin America’s fastest-growing city economy, with average annual growth of 12.6% over the past two decades. Offshore oil discoveries and rising infrastructure spending are at the centre of this, driving strong employment growth and higher incomes. These dynamics should support further progress over the coming decade, even if income disparities remain among the highest in our Global Cities Index.

Weaker momentum across some of the region’s more established urban centres will see them lose ground in our index over the coming decade. Rio de Janeiro is one such example, with growth set to remain subpar and substantially weaker than in other vital cultural epicentres, such as Buenos Aires and Santiago. A mature urban economy, softer demographic trends, and limited productivity gains are likely to constrain its performance. A similarly weak outlook applies to Cancún, where the same tourism reliance that drives its global appeal also leaves the city with a less stable economic footing than its more diversified city peers.

articles.title: Physical shocks and economic resilience: a central bank perspective − speech by James Talbot
articles.text:
Physical shocks and economic resilience: a central bank perspective − speech by James Talbot

Given at the 2nd Annual Conference on Sustainable Finance at the Banco de México on 21 October 2026

Published on
23 October 2026

James Talbot, Executive Director for International at the Bank of England and the Bank’s Executive Sponsor for climate, explains how physical climate shocks can affect inflation and output, and how central banks can assess and respond to them. He considers two connected horizons: their near-term effects on monetary policy, and the longer-term role of economic resilience, adaptation and insurance in helping economies absorb future shocks and support price and financial stability.

Speech
Physical shocks increasingly matter for central banks
Governor, distinguished guests, I am sorry that I cannot be there with you in person at such a prestigious event. It is very much an honour and a pleasure, and my thanks to Dr. Fabrizio López-Gallo Dey for inviting me to speak today.
The physical impacts of climate change are becoming larger and more proximate, and their short-term economic impacts are also increasing. Annual global damages from weather-related events have more than doubled since the early 2000s, reaching over $200bn in 2025footnote [1].
In light of that, the economic effects of climate change are increasingly on the radar of central bankers. When extreme weather events affect production, output and inflation, that matters for our primary goal of maintaining price stability.
Let me take two examples that are close to home:
Increasingly high summer temperatures reduce water levels on key transport arteries for industrial trade, like the River Rhine in Germany. When water levels fall, ships reduce the amount of cargo they carry, disrupting the movement of goods and increasing transport costs.
Such exceptionally low water levels have become a recurring feature in recent years. The economic effects have also been material: recent research estimates that 30 days of low water on the Rhine reduces German industrial production by around 1%footnote [2].
In October 2024, extreme rainfall caused devastating flash floods in Valencia. Aside from the tragic loss of human life, economic losses amounted to over 20% of regional GDP. Spanish Q4 GDP growth was reduced by between 0.1 and 0.2 percentage pointsfootnote [3].
The economic impact would have been larger were it not for the high level of insurance protection for affected households and businesses. Around 250,000 insurance claims were filed following the floods and Spain's Insurance Compensation Consortium had paid more than €4bn in compensation by late 2025, making this the largest event the scheme has ever managedfootnote [4].
Even countries like the UK, which may be less susceptible to large physical shocks, can be affected by the impact of events abroad.
Over the past four years, as chair of the NGFS Workstream on Monetary Policy, I have worked together with more than sixty central banks to set out a framework to assess the impact of climate change on the economy, to measure its effects and to determine what monetary policymakers should do about it.
I’ll talk today about how the physical impacts of climate change can affect the economy in the near term; how we diagnose their magnitude, persistence and propagation; whether their effects belong in the central forecast or in the risks around it; and how that diagnosis informs monetary policy judgements. We set out each of these steps in an NGFS guide for monetary policymakers that we published earlier this yearfootnote [5].
I also want to look beyond the near-term policy horizon. In particular, how repeated losses, adaptation, fiscal space and insurance protection gaps shape the capacity of economies and financial systems to absorb future shocks.
I will argue that these two horizons are connected: The resilience an economy has built determines the scale and persistence of the macroeconomic impact of a shock over the monetary-policy horizon. And, in turn, repeated shocks can erode that resilience over the longer term, eventually exacerbating the effects of climate shocks when they occur.
How physical shocks transmit through the economy
Let me start with how physical shocks can affect the economy.
Physical hazards can operate through several channels at once: They can damage capital. They can reduce labour supply and lower productivity. They can disrupt transport and supply chains. They can weaken demand and confidence among economic agents, tighten credit conditions and raise uncertainty.
Importantly for monetary policymakers, those channels can interact and may also move output and inflation in different directions, making the policy response more challenging.
But different physical hazards can transmit through the economy in different ways. To give some examplesfootnote [6]:

Heatwaves transmit as a shock to productive capacity and labour supply. They push down on GDP while increasing inflation volatility, making them relevant for monetary policy even though direct physical damage is not as visible as for a flood or storm.
Droughts reduce productive capacity in agriculture pushing down on production and up on prices. They can raise inflation both through the effect on domestic production and through more expensive imports.
Floods and cyclones damage the capital stock, reducing demand and investment, which can in turn push down on output and inflation. But floods can also be inflationary where they hit food supply, logistics or essential infrastructure.

So while there is no one-size-fits-all pattern for the effects of a physical shock, there are some common themes:

Shocks are often transmitted through a disruption to production;
That usually means that output and inflation often move in opposite directions; and
Even when shocks occur overseas, these can be transmitted through changes to exports and commodity prices, particularly for open economies. Indeed, a 2022 study for the euro area showed that for every 1% unanticipated increase in globally traded food prices, overall inflation rose by 0.1%footnote [7].

This latter channel is also particularly important for the UK since we import around 40% of our food. In recent work at the Bank of England, we have looked at the impacts of extreme weather events on commodity prices and UK inflationfootnote [8]. The estimates from the model suggest that global weather-related disruption has played a non-trivial role in UK food and headline inflation over the past two decades
This makes climate-related shocks relevant to our regular inflation forecasting. Indeed, many central banks are now assessing the impact of food, energy, supply-chain, and weather-related shocks. That is because these shocks are affecting inflation and output forecasts, or the risks around them, in an increasingly meaningful way.
The NGFS note on the economic and financial impacts of extreme weather events, produced for the 2026 French G7 Presidency, uses 31 case studies to show that these effects repeatedly appear in output, employment and prices across a geographically diverse range of countriesfootnote [9]. Supply-chain and trade linkages can also propagate these shocks beyond the country or region directly affected.
With that in mind, let me turn next to consider how central banks should diagnose the shock, assess its impact on their forecasts and the risks around them and therefore their monetary policy judgements.
A framework for assessing the impacts of climate shocks
Here I will draw on the recent NGFS guide on monetary policy strategy that I mentioned earlierfootnote [10]. The report provides a five-step approach to assess these impacts: identify, assess the propagation, assess whether a trade-off arises, set policy, communicate and monitor.
Step one is to identify the nature of the shock itself: How large is it? How long is it likely to last? Which regions and sectors are affected? Is it localised or widespread? And is it a one-off event or one in a sequence of shocks?
Those distinctions matter.
A short-lived disruption affecting a relatively narrow part of the economy during the low season of economic activity poses a very different challenge from a shock affecting food, energy, or critical infrastructure, or services such as tourism during peak season. And a sequence of individually temporary shocks may have quite different macroeconomic consequences from an isolated event.
Having identified the shock, step two is to assess how it propagates through the economy.
Here, the familiar distinction between direct, indirect and second-round effects is particularly useful.
Direct – or first round – effects are the immediate relative-price effects from the shock: for example, a drought raising food prices, a heatwave reducing labour productivity, or a flood disrupting production and logistics.
Monetary policy cannot repair infrastructure, restore a harvest, or offset the initial physical damage. If the shock is short-lived and expectations remain anchored, the standard monetary policy response is usually to look through the first-round effects, because policy operates with a lag and tightening in response to a temporary supply shock can impose unnecessary output costs.
But the initial shock can spread more widely, having indirect effects, as firms pass higher input costs across supply chains. And there can be second-round effects through wages and inflation expectations. Workers may seek compensation for higher living costs; businesses may adjust their price-setting behaviour; and households and firms may revise their inflation expectations.
Food and energy prices can be particularly important here. Households observe them frequently and a well-established literature shows that they have an outsized effect on expectations about future inflation. Research conducted at the Bank of England reinforces that result for the UK, finding that more than 60% of households report that food prices heavily influence inflation perceptions. Food prices also matter significantly more for household inflation-expectations dynamics than other components, with effects at short, medium and long horizons.
Frequency of shocks matters too. An isolated rise in prices will feel different to a series of repeated upward moves. Indeed, a sequence of individually temporary shocks which arrive before the effects of previous disturbances have dissipated can look and feel like more persistent inflationary pressure. Repeated disruption can also erode fiscal buffers and weaken private-sector resilience.
Central banks should therefore focus closely on frequency, persistence and pass-through to overall inflation and inflation expectations.
From diagnosis to the monetary-policy response
Step three is next: does the identified shock create a trade-off between inflation and output?
As I noted earlier, hot and dry events provide relatively clear examples. By reducing agricultural production, a drought can weaken output while putting upward pressure on food prices. A heatwave pushing down on productivity can increase inflation volatility at the same time as hitting output. But if shocks primarily damage capital and reduce output, such as floods and storms in some circumstances, they can push down on inflation where demand effects dominate.
If you permit me a brief digression at this point, the situation becomes no easier when considering the economic impact of the policies enacted by governments to ensure that the necessary climate transition happens. These policies can also drive large and persistent relative price movements, shifts in investment and reallocation of production across sectors of the economy. Modelling the impact of these shocks is therefore no less important. Here, the NGFS and IMF published joint work earlier this year on how countries’ Nationally Determined Contributions to reducing emissions under the Paris Agreement will affect inflation and output across a range of economiesfootnote [11].
Step four is to set policy and communicate the decision.
Here, the assessment depends importantly on the wider economic environment at the point the shock arrives. If inflation is already elevated and expectations are less firmly anchored, the risk that an initial price increase develops into broader inflationary pressure may be greater, and the case for responding becomes stronger. If the economy has spare capacity and demand is weak, the case for looking through is stronger.
This is also where a central bank faces an important judgement: if the effects of a physical shock are material and sufficiently well understood, they may belong in the central forecast.
But where there is substantial uncertainty around the scale of a shock or the way it will propagate, scenarios can allow policymakers to explore and communicate risks. Scenarios can complement the central forecast by helping us explore precisely the kinds of uncertainty I have described today: whether a shock proves temporary or persistent; whether supply or demand effects dominate; and whether initial price increases generate material second-round effects.
The fifth and final step is to monitor and assess whether the economy is evolving in line with expectations and adjust policy in response to new data developments. Since there is also evidence that climate shocks can affect credit supply, collateral values or financial intermediation, central banks should also monitor the operation of the monetary transmission mechanism.
You will notice, of course, that the process I describe here is not that different to how central banks assess and respond to other economic shocks. That is because the impact of climate change is now one of the set of economic shocks that monetary policymakers consider.
From immediate shocks to the resilience threshold
Since climate shocks are likely to increase in both magnitude and frequency, another important question is whether economies and financial systems can continue to absorb rising losses from these shocks over the longer term.
The capacity of households, businesses, governments and financial systems to absorb losses is a key determinant of the recovery profile from a climate shock. Fiscal space, insurance penetration, climate adaptation, infrastructure quality, financial-market depth and institutional capacity all help to determine a country’s resilience threshold. Where those buffers are stronger, shocks are more likely to be absorbed. Where they are weaker, the effects can become more persistent and can spill into credit, financial stability and public-finance channels.
Less developed economies typically have lower resilience thresholds, meaning similar physical hazards can generate larger and more persistent macroeconomic damage. A previous study by Raddatz (2009) estimated that a climate-related disaster resulted in a cumulative per capita output loss of 0.25%, 0.5% and 1% for high, middle and low-income countries respectivelyfootnote [12].
But resilience is also not fixed. Repeated shocks can gradually erode the very buffers that help economies absorb losses in the first place, including fiscal space, private-sector balance sheets and insurance capacity. Without effective mitigation and adaptation, economies may therefore become less resilient over time, with the same physical hazard generating increasingly persistent effects on output, inflation, credit and public finances.
There is also evidence that these interactions can be non-linear. The NGFS’s 2023 work on compound risks examines precisely what can happen when shocks combine, either across time or across locations. It shows that the overall macroeconomic impact of compounding shocks can be materially greater than the sum of the partsfootnote [13].
This in turn feeds back to the short-term policy response. Resilience directly affects the scale and persistence of the macroeconomic consequences of a shock, and therefore how difficult it is for monetary policy to look through it. But if losses are absorbed quickly through insurance mechanisms or other buffers, the inflation-output trade-off may be shorter-lived.
There is therefore an important interaction between resilience and monetary policy. The more resilient an economy is, the easier it is to absorb physical shocks. As resilience erodes, the same shock can become progressively harder to look through.
Insurance protection gaps and why they matter for central banks
The provision of insurance helps economies to cushion the effect of physical shocks by pooling and transferring losses. High insurance penetration and rapid payouts can reduce household distress, firm insolvency and credit losses as well as supporting a faster recovery in output.
But as physical risks increase, rising and repeated losses could place pressure on the availability and affordability of insurance in areas exposed to these shocks. If insurance coverage falls, losses will instead fall on households, businesses, banks and governments.
Two recent events provide a sobering comparison. In Spain, public-private insurance arrangements helped absorb a significant share of losses from the 2024 floods whereas in Pakistan, following the 2022 floods, only around 1% of total damages were insured, leaving households and small firms far more exposed to income and wealth losses, generating larger macroeconomic impacts.
From a microprudential perspective, withdrawal of insurance provision may enhance the safety and soundness of insurance firms, because rising insured damages can significantly dent profitability and potentially threaten firm resilience.
As the insurance supervisor, our role is not to direct underwriting decisions by individual firms. But as a macroprudential authority, we will need to take a broader view of the implications for the financial system as a whole. Indeed, the Bank of England’s Financial Policy Committee highlighted this issue at its September 2026 meetingfootnote [14].
Where insurance coverage falls, uninsured risks will need to be redistributed:

For households, this means higher repair costs when physical risks strike, lower property values and potential difficulties obtaining a mortgage.
For businesses, it can mean bearing losses from the destruction of physical goods, capital and infrastructure.
For banks, it can mean weaker collateral values and higher credit losses.
For governments, it can mean more frequent pressure to act as insurer of last resort.

For the UK, Bank of England staff have modelled how a widening flood-insurance protection gap could spill over to the UK mortgage marketfootnote [15].
This analysis suggests that the share of UK mortgagors without insurance could rise from around 5% today to around 7-10% in 2050, or up to 16% following a severe flood event. The aggregate effects on house prices and mortgage impairments in that modelling are relatively small compared with the severe macroeconomic stresses against which the UK banking system is tested. But that does not mean the issue is trivial: the consequences for affected households, exposed lenders and local economies could still be significant.
There is an important lesson here: the answer cannot simply be more of the same insurance. Insurance capacity cannot sustainably compensate for underlying physical risks that continue to rise. Insurers will likely increasingly need to include risk prevention in product design, underwriting, and pricing practices.
Indeed, while a successful transition to net zero can limit the future increase in physical hazards, we will also need to consider the role of adaptation in a world where climate shocks are more frequent.
Investment in ensuring resilience to climate shocks can support insurability. This may require collaboration between businesses, households and governments. Updates to planning rules and building regulations could further mitigate the impact of increased physical hazards.
Actions to improve climate-related risk identification, measurement and modelling capabilities across the insurance sector, as envisaged under the recent update to the Bank of England’s supervisory expectations, should strengthen firms' ability to assess and price climate-related risksfootnote [16].
But the financial sector also has a long tradition of coming up with innovative solutions to difficult problems. In this regard, there may be scope for greater collaboration between insurers, reinsurers and banks to share data, develop products and risk-transfer mechanisms that support resilience and help narrow protection gaps.
International cooperation
Let me finish with a word on international cooperation. Climate change is an issue which transcends borders and cannot be fixed by one country acting alone. In recent years, great strides have been made in multilateral fora like the NGFS to assess and model the impacts of climate change on the financial system. The NGFS’ flagship climate scenarios are an important tool in underpinning climate risk assessment in the financial sector. The work of the International Sustainability Standards Board to ensure consistent and better climate disclosures is helping financial firms to better manage climate-related risks and to make better decisions on where to allocate capital.
The 2025 South African G20 Presidency focused on the issue of natural catastrophe protection gaps, drawing on joint work from the World Bank and the International Association of Insurance Supervisorsfootnote [17]. That work helped to raise our collective understanding of these issues as well as suggesting a range of approaches to tackle them, tailored to country circumstances.
In 2026, the French G7 Presidency took this work forward by strengthening the evidence on the macro-financial consequences of extreme weather, while examining how to tackle protection gapsfootnote [18]. This issue is also on our radar as the UK develops priorities for its own G20 Presidency in 2027. In my view, there is value in better understanding how insurance protection gaps affect the economic impact of extreme-weather events and in exploring what can help sustain insurability and resilience as physical risks increase.
That could include looking at what constrains insurability, which approaches appear capable of operating at scale, and the conditions needed for them to work sustainably.
Insurance cannot close protection gaps on its own. But better data, investment in adaptation and more resilient infrastructure can help sustain affordable cover. Timely mitigation also remains essential to limit the future increase in physical risk.
That brings me back to the two connected horizons. In the near term, central banks will need to understand how physical and transition-related shocks affect inflation, output and expectations in order to deliver on their price stability mandate.
Further ahead, the availability of insurance will determine both the economic impact of climate shocks and the capacity of economies to absorb the resulting losses. It will also shape the prevailing environment in which central banks will pursue their price and financial stability goals.
As macroprudential policymakers, we understand that the availability of insurance matters to the resilience of the financial system as a whole. So as protection gaps widen, addressing them will require concerted action across governments, regulators, international institutions and the private sector. Multilateral fora can play an important role in supporting that dialogue and sharing lessons on what works.
As climate change increasingly affects our economies and financial systems, central banks will need to understand these effects, just like any other shock. This will enable us to make sure that the financial system remains stable and that price stability is maintained. And in turn that can provide a sustainable platform for governments to deliver the climate transition.
I would like to thank Danae Kyriakopoulou for assistance in writing this speech. I would also like to thank Lukasz Krebel and Fergus Booker for their input and helpful comments, as well as India Rimmer, Hannah Copeland, Boromeus Wanengkirtyo, Dario Bonciani, Riccardo Masolo, Silvia Sarpietro, Nikoleta Anesti, Vania Esady, Matthew Naylor, Will Banks, Kemal Erçevik, Alex Curtis and Jemima Hall for their underlying research.

There is only one Goldman Sachs.Discover CareersWORKING AT GSStudentsLife at GSBenefitsFeatured OfficesOpen RolesGoldman Sachs Chief Economist Jan Hatzius Joins CNBC to Discuss the US Jobs Report and the Economic OutlookNov 6, 2026ShareThe recent stronger-than-expected employment report indicates a stable labor market, according to Goldman Sachs Chief Economist Jan Hatzius. He joined CNBC to discuss his views on the data and his outlook for the year ahead.
Transcript:
Host: Welcome back. The October jobs number came in hotter than expected: nonfarm payrolls rose by 165,000, above nearly every forecast. Joining us is Jan Hatzius, Goldman Sachs Chief Economist, to discuss the report, the midterms, markets, data centers, and more. Jan, it is great to have you.
Jan Hatzius: It is great to be here.
Host: There is nothing wrong with this number, I assume you agree. Do you think it marks the beginning of something new?
Jan Hatzius: Definitely nothing wrong with it. It is a very solid report, certainly as far as payrolls are concerned. There is some month-to-month volatility, but we think the underlying trend in job growth is probably back above 100,000. That is more solid than it was earlier in the year.
What we are not seeing is sustained downward pressure on the unemployment rate. It edged down a little, but it has remained in the 4.1% to 4.2% range. To me, this still looks like a labor market that is stable at about full employment. We think it will probably stay roughly in that range over time, which remains consistent with relatively subdued wage growth and low inflation.
Host: How low can claims get? Are we scraping the bottom of that historic range?
Jan Hatzius: It is the lowest we have seen in a series that goes back more than five decades. Layoffs are at extremely low levels, which is consistent with what we see in other indicators.
Hiring continues to be relatively subdued as well, so we have not really seen a major pickup in hiring. It is still a more stagnant environment, but at a very solid level.
Host: The markets this week have been rethinking the possibility of a more elongated buildout cycle. Does that lead you to lower your nominal GDP estimates for next year?
Jan Hatzius: We are growing at a very rapid pace right now. GDP numbers fluctuate, but we are talking about growth with a three-handle in the second and third quarters, and likely in the fourth quarter as well.
I do think growth will be softer next year. We have thought that before, but we have not made a change to our underlying growth estimate. We think it is probably in the 2% to 2.5% range, which should keep the unemployment rate roughly stable.
There are some downside risks to that growth outlook. We have seen tightening in financial conditions of about 50 basis points according to our index. There are also questions around energy prices, the war with Iran and its implications for real income growth, as well as the AI buildout and its effects on both GDP and the labor market.
But our baseline remains relatively stable growth.
Host: Goldman also closely monitors increases in enterprise efficiency from AI use, or at least expected productivity gains. Where are we now, and what are your expectations for 2027?
Jan Hatzius: We have seen some effects on the labor market, mainly in the technology sector. That has been worth roughly 10,000 to 15,000 fewer jobs per month in employment growth.
There are some indications that this is broadening into the service sector. For example, we have begun to see a correlation across service-sector industries between employment growth and unemployment rates on one hand, and AI adoption on the other.
But the relationship is still not particularly strong, and you would not expect it to be if you looked at overall labor-market outcomes. Over the next year or two, I think that relationship will probably strengthen. By 2028, it is likely to become somewhat more of a headwind for employment growth.
I have a fair amount of conviction that AI will be more of a macroeconomic story by 2027, though the timing remains one of the open questions.
Host: That could also affect profit margins.
Jan Hatzius: Yes, although at the moment it is clearly still a tailwind.
Once we get into 2028, you would expect the volume of investment to flatten out, and eventually investment spending will come down. That is what tends to happen in historical investment booms: infrastructure is built out, the necessary capital stock is achieved, and investment then begins to decline.
That is probably still some way off, but there is, of course, substantial uncertainty around the path.
Host: We are glad we will have you around for 2027 and 2028. I hope we will speak many times.

articles.title: Financial Conduct Authority Primary Market Bulletin No 66 | Norges Bank Investment Management
articles.text:
We refer to the Financial Conduct Authority’s consultation GC26/6 (Primary Market Bulletin No. 66), published on 30 September 2026, on draft Technical Note 803.1 (TN 803.1), the proposed amendments to TN 801.4 and the proposed deletion of TN 802.3. We welcome the opportunity to contribute an investor perspective on how the “comply or explain” approach in Policy Statement PS26/19 should operate in practice.
Norges Bank Investment Management (NBIM) is the investment management division of the Norwegian Central Bank (Norges Bank) and is responsible for investing the Norwegian Government Pension Fund Global. NBIM is a globally diversified investor with approximately NOK 22,700 billion under management, or 1,724 billion GBP. Of these, about GBP 90 billion was invested in the United Kingdom at end June 2026.
As a long-term, global investor, we consider our returns over time to depend on sustainable development in economic, environmental and social terms, as well as on well-functioning, legitimate and efficient markets. We need consistent, comparable, reliable and decision-useful information from companies on sustainability-related risks and opportunities that are financially material to their business. We support the IFRS Sustainability Disclosure Standards (ISSB Standards) as the global baseline for such information, and we strongly support the UK’s adoption of UK SRS.
In our response to Consultation Paper 26/5, we recommended that the FCA keep climate-related disclosures under UK SRS S2 mandatory, make Scope 3 and UK SRS S1 reporting mandatory on a defined timeline, and avoid an open-ended “comply or explain” regime[1]. PS26/19 instead places all UK SRS disclosures on a “comply or explain” basis. We recognise that this policy decision has been taken and that this consultation concerns the accompanying guidance. We therefore focus our response on how the Technical Note can limit the risk that “comply or explain” results in incomplete and non-comparable disclosure.
The draft note sets out how to comply and what an explanation should contain, but it does not yet say when it is acceptable to explain. A “comply or explain” regime is not equivalent to a mandatory one. It can allow issuers to withhold material information, reduces comparability across companies and over time, and can produce explanations of variable quality. The effectiveness of the regime will depend on issuers choosing to comply, and on the FCA’s approach to its supervision. Our key messages are as follows:
State the regulatory intent. Technical Note 803.1 should say that the FCA expects issuers ordinarily to disclose in accordance with UK SRS, and that the option to explain is exceptional flexibility beyond the proportionality provisions and transition reliefs already in the standards.
Apply materiality and proportionality first. UK SRS already allows issuers to omit immaterial information, to use estimates, simpler data and qualitative disclosure, and to rely on “reasonable and supportable information available without undue cost or effort”. The Technical Note should clarify that existing provisions of UK SRS already address the scope of information to be disclosed and provide reliefs.
Limit explaining to exceptional and transitional circumstances. The note should state that explaining is available only where an issuer is unable, despite reasonable and proportionate efforts, to disclose in accordance with UK SRS, and that it is not available because an issuer prefers not to disclose, finds disclosure inconvenient, or has not put the necessary systems and processes in place. Explanations should give specific reasons, the steps being taken and indicate the timeline to compliance.
Refine the illustrative examples. Examples 2, 3 and 4 risk signalling that disclosure of financially material information is optional. We propose specific changes in the Annex.
Supervise and review. We encourage the FCA to monitor how issuers use the option to explain and to commit to a review, with a view to moving towards mandatory disclosure as market capacity increases. This would bring the UK market in line with several other capital markets which have already moved towards mandatory disclosure.
Our detailed responses to the consultation questions are set out in the Annex. We would welcome the opportunity to discuss our views with you.
Yours sincerely
Carine Smith IhenachoChief Governance and Compliance Officer
Elisa Cencig Head of Policy Engagement

[1] FCA Consultation Paper CP26/5: Aligning listed issuers' sustainability disclosures with international standards | Norges Bank Investment Management
