articles.title: Europe's Resilience Re-Rate | Franklin Templeton
articles.text:
A Different Kind of European Shock

As we touched on in our recent paper “European Exceptionalism on Sale”, Europe has spent much of the past decade being priced as something of a fragile region. The critique is familiar: low trend growth, an economy hostage to imported energy and little exposure to the technology themes that have driven global returns. Fragmented policymaking and heavier regulation complete the charge sheet. Much of it has been grounded in real experience, from the sovereign debt crisis to the inflation shock that followed Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

The latest shock has again tested Europe's energy sensitivity and geopolitical exposure, this time through the US-Iran war and renewed volatility in oil and gas markets. Yet eurozone equities have performed broadly in line with US and global markets year-to-date, with the region having recovered much of the relative ground lost in the immediate aftermath of the conflict. UK equities have also delivered strong gains and have marginally outpaced continental peers in local-currency terms—the FTSE All-Share Index is up 13.4% against 12.2% for the MSCI EMU Index year-to-date.1

The market recovery partly reflects intermittent optimism about a negotiated settlement between the United States and Iran, although the conflict has proved more protracted than markets hoped in the early summer and energy prices remain above pre-conflict levels. Europe also appears better prepared to deal with the energy-related challenges than in previous shocks. It has already lived through one major energy crisis, and the behavioural response is visible in company meetings as much as in policy design. Russian pipeline gas supplied roughly 40% of European Union (EU) imports in 2021; it now supplies 6%, and storage entered the conflict at 63% of capacity against 30% at the same point in 2022.2

The European Central Bank's (ECB) September decision captured this balance. The Governing Council raised its three key rates by 25 basis points, taking the deposit rate to 2.50%, its second increase since the conflict began. It noted that the war continues to generate inflation pressures and that inflation is set to remain above target for an extended period, with staff projections now showing headline inflation averaging 3.0% in 2026 and 2.5% in 2027. The response was measured: a quarter-point move with no pre-commitment to a rate path.

Earnings Have Absorbed the Pressure

According to our numbers, FY 2026 earnings per share (EPS) expectations for the MSCI Europe Index have been upgraded by around 5% year-to-date, despite the disproportionate impact that the Iran war and energy costs might have been expected to have on the region.3 Those upgrades now imply expected growth of around 12.5% year on year versus 2025, with limited upgrade contribution from the second half so far.

Exhibit 1: European Earnings Expectations Held Up Through Market Volatility

Source: Bloomberg. Period shown: June 2025 to October 2026. EPS figures are analyst estimates and are subject to revision.

If Europe were still behaving like the fragile earnings region of the old stereotype, a renewed energy shock would have translated quickly into downgrades. Instead, the earnings base has held. Energy, financials, and defence have led the upgrades, with consumer discretionary (specifically autos and luxury goods) the only major group to see estimates cut.

None of this makes Europe the highest-growth equity region in the world. Aggregate EPS growth still lags global markets, at 12.5% against 14.2% for MSCI ACWI, largely because Europe does not have the same concentration in artificial intelligence (AI) and mega-cap technology.

What the Discount Pays For

By our current measures, the MSCI Europe Index trades on 17.6x trailing earnings, compared with 22.3x for MSCI ACWI Index and 25.4x for the S&P 500.

Better performance from here requires only that European earnings prove more durable than investors assume, and that the discount be recognised as too wide relative to the region's improved resilience. US-style growth is not part of the requirement. In that context, the valuation gap is the compensation investors receive while waiting for a more durable earnings story to be recognised.

Listings First, Then Deals

The value in European stocks has been discussed for years, but the duration and depth of the discount now appear to be producing action. The first phase was listing arbitrage. CRH and Ferguson moved their primary listings to New York in search of deeper capital markets and broader investor pools, with CRH completing its transition in 2023; Linde consolidated on the NYSE by delisting from Frankfurt the same year.

The second phase is mergers and acquisitions (M&A). As Exhibit 2 shows, the value of announced M&A involving publicly listed European companies in 2026 had already surpassed every full-year total since 2007 by 30 October. Intesa Sanpaolo’s US$35.3 billion bid for Monte dei Paschi, the largest European deal since 2018, is one prominent example.4

Exhibit 2: Announced M&A for Publicly Listed European Companies

Notes: Deal value in US$ billion. 2006 to 2025 show full-year totals; 2026 is year to date. Source: Bloomberg. Data as of 30 October 2026.

The deal list is also broadening. Recent activity around easyJet, Rotork, JDE Peet's, InPost, Allfunds and AkzoNobel suggests that strategic and financial buyers are increasingly prepared to underwrite European assets before public markets fully re-rate them. The largest example is Prologis' agreed £14bn acquisition of SEGRO, which the SEGRO board recommended in August at a 39% premium to the undisturbed share price. It takes the United Kingdom's biggest real estate investment trust out of the London market, and Prologis intends to take a secondary London listing as part of the deal.

Fiscal Push, Monetary Drag

Policy change in Europe is usually slow and dispersed, but its direction is becoming more supportive. Defence and infrastructure spending are rising. At the EU level, the Savings and Investments Union is intended to channel more European savings into productive investment, and the simplification agenda targets a material reduction in administrative burdens. The Commission has framed the Savings and Investments Union around Europe's need to finance strategic investment, citing the 2024 Draghi Report's estimate that the region requires an additional €750bn to €800 billion of annual investment by 2030.5

The most immediate fiscal impulse is likely to come from Germany. The €500bn Special Fund for Infrastructure and Climate Neutrality is designed to fund additional investment over a 12-year period, from transport to hospitals to grid and climate-related infrastructure. Delivery has disappointed so far: €24bn had been committed by the end of 2025, against the roughly €40bn a year the fund's size implies.

The interest-rate backdrop has turned into a modest headwind. The Bank of England held the Bank Rate steady at 3.75% in September for the sixth consecutive meeting, although three of the nine Monetary Policy Committee members voted for an increase, UK inflation rose to 3.1% in August, and the Bank expects it to peak slightly above 4% in the first quarter of 2027. Alongside the ECB's two quarter-point increases, that is a tightening bias across the region.

For equities, the level of rates matters as well as their direction. Even after those hikes, the ECB's 2.50% deposit rate remains below the UK’s 3.75% and the US federal funds target range of 3.75% to 4.00%.6 It also remains below its 4.00% peak in 2023, while UK inflation is 3.1%, against 11.1% at its 2022 peak. Markets have priced in a quarter-point rise at the Bank of England’s 5 November meeting as more likely than not.

Investment Conclusion

Europe may still lack a single moment-in-time catalyst. The structural change taking place does not depend on one. Earnings expectations are improving through an external shock and a tightening cycle, valuations remain at a discount to global markets and announced deal value has risen. German fiscal money is starting to move, and EU-level reform is increasingly focused on competitiveness and scale.

Europe is proving more resilient than investors assume, while still being priced as though fragility is the default. That is the basis for a resilience re-rate—a gradual recognition that European earnings and corporate value are stronger than the old narrative allows.FOOTNOTES

Source: Bloomberg As of 30 October 2026. Past performance is not an indicator or a guarantee of future results.
Source: European Council, based on European Commission calculations; gas storage data from Gas Infrastructure Europe (GIE) via Bruegel. Data as of 2025-2026.
Source: LSEG I/B/E/S, consensus FY2026 EPS estimates for the MSCI Europe Index, year-to-date change as of 30 October 2026. There is no assurance that any estimate, forecast or projection will be realized.
Source: Bloomberg. Data as of 30 October 2026.
Source: European Commission, The Future of European Competitiveness (Mario Draghi Report, September 2024).
Source: European Central Bank, Monetary policy decisions, 29 October 2026; Bank of England, Monetary Policy Summary and Minutes, 17 September 2026; Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, FOMC statement, 28 October 2026. Policy rates as at 30 October 2026.

How best to measure the breakneck pace of US AI and data centre roll-out? Well, there’s hyperscaler capital expenditure, which has increased four-fold since 2023 and is set to exceed US$750 billion this year, more than either the global spend in renewable power or upstream oil and gas.
Hyperscaler electricity consumption is another metric, skipping along at 23% a year so far this decade – way ahead of total US power demand, which did not grow from 2006 to 2024. Perhaps best is the 201 GW of new data centre capacity that US utilities have committed to connect to their grids, which would increase electricity demand by 30% if it’s all built.
Speed to power is the buzz phrase. All hyperscalers want their data centres plugged into reliable power supply as soon as it is ready to run their large language models and satisfy consumers’ growing reliance on them. The problem is that the US electricity industry, regulators and the entire supply chain alike are not yet capable of moving at the pace, or scale, required.
Chris Seiple, Vice Chair Power and Renewables, and I spent last week in New York talking with power sector investors and financiers about the challenges and opportunities ahead.
What are the biggest challenges for the power sector?
Among multiple challenges there are three big ones. First, the timetable for getting a data centre connected to the grid keeps getting longer. It varies by state but in Virginia, a hot spot for data centre location, the wait is 54 months at best. In Ohio, it’s 84 months – that is, no power supply until 2033 for a project going ahead today.
Second, public opposition to data centre development is growing. Lawmakers have called 400 moratoriums on data centre proposals. One-fifth of projects under development have been delayed by a moratorium, some by more than one.
Third, there’s an acute lack of essential components in the supply chain. Gas-fired power plants will dominate data centre power supply and the waitlist for the heavy frame gas turbines has stretched out to 278 weeks – roughly early 2032. Not much use if you want your data centre up and running before 2030 and weren’t early in the queue to order. Wire infrastructure is not much better with waitlists for transformers coming in at 162 weeks and circuit breakers at 137 weeks. Skilled labourers are also emerging as a bottleneck – not an easy problem to solve quickly.
Is it easier to build generation in regulated or unregulated markets?
Unregulated markets are easier in some ways in that the data centres are free to choose their power supplier and often have more flexibility in developing behind-the-meter generation (BTM) solutions. The main challenge is the disconnect between the planning for large loads and the planning for generation interconnections, and connecting the two.
In short, there are numerous independent decisions being made in unregulated markets that can get in the way of building out the grid in the most cost-effective way and that makes sure supply growth keeps up with demand growth. Regulated markets can mitigate some of the planning uncertainty and grid inefficiency.
What’s the timetable to deliver the power?
Realistically, there are no solutions that deliver new supply at any scale in 2027 or 2028 beyond what has already been committed. The task for regulators, the electricity industry and hyperscalers is to ensure that supply is connected by the time that demand ramps up beyond 2028. And the focus should be on delivering the 201 GW capacity already committed – adding more capacity to the pipeline before the current logjam gets moving will only hinder progress.
What solutions are there for power supply challenges?
First, BTM projects – which account for 15% of the pipeline by project count and 40% of planned capacity – skip the need for grid connection and the regulatory hurdles that go with it. Most BTM plans will be gas-fired capacity, backed increasingly by new high-discharge batteries. These projects will be expensive, complicated from an engineering perspective, and few data centres view the BTM solutions as a long-term plan, preferring to connect to the grid at some point.
The ‘ERCOT solution’ could be a pragmatic way forward for unregulated markets. The Texas system operator analyses the planned locations and scale of large load demand in the market, then makes assumptions where developers are likely to build generation. It can then make an ‘80/20’ decision on investment in transmission and connection and hope it all works out.
Interruptibility of demand is emerging as another solution. Data centre developers are trying to figure out how dedicated BTM resources, such as generators or batteries, might offer more flexibility to the grid. At the same ime, regulated utilities are working to communicate to data centre developers what type of flexibility will best optimise getting new load connected faster. Lastly, deregulated market rules are evolving to accommodate flexible interconnect.
Is AI-driven demand changing utilities?
Yes. For one thing, hyperscalers are currently price-insensitive. That’s a new experience for regulated utilities, which can leverage that price insensitivity to deal with affordability concerns and to find innovative ways to get load connected faster or to pursue new generation technologies, such as advanced geothermal or long-duration energy storage.
After operating in a low-growth bubble for decades, utilities are coming up with solutions for a new breed of customers with large loads in grids that are already constrained.

articles.title: In UK Budget, No News Is Good News
articles.text:
In UK Budget, No News Is Good News

Anatole Kaletsky

Gavekal Research | 30 Oct 2026

Sometimes a non-event is a great event. This can obviously be true in geopolitics, when a war or terrorist attack is avoided. But it can also apply to economic policy. A good example is Britain’s annual budget charade, which inflicts on the country a curse of fiscal fundamentalism unknown in any other mature democracy by twinning the crazy tradition of “budget secrecy,” which turns any discussion of fiscal plans into a crime worse than treason, with the even crazier convention of “parliamentary confidence,” which demands immediate resignation of any government that loses a budget vote.Between them, these two absurdities of Britain’s “unwritten constitution” exempt tax legislation from the rational debate and technocratic scrutiny taken for granted before any new legislation on infinitely less consequential issues like the regulation of bus routes or the protection of newts.

articles.title: View from the markets: The earnings season has been good, but is it good enough?
articles.text:
FRONT OF MIND | ARTICLE – 2 min read
View from the markets: The earnings season has been good, but is it good enough?

By
DANIEL MORRIS 30.10.2026

LinkedIn
Twitter
Facebook
Email

In this article
Sector drivers

LinkedIn
Twitter
Facebook
Email

By Daniel Morris, Chief Market Strategist

At first blush, there is little to complain about regarding the third-quarter earnings results so far (about half of the companies in the S&P 500 and MSCI Europe have reported). Compared to the third quarter in 2025, profits have risen by 26% for the S&P 500 and by 40%(!) for Europe, with double-digit figures for other major indices, based on data from FactSet (see Exhibit 1). This is well above historical norms.

The worry is that those values are not far off what was expected by analysts, and in one case it was below. Earnings have come in only 2% better than expected for the S&P 500. Typically, earnings surprises (how much better or worse results are versus consensus) run in the 3-4% range. Over the previous few quarters, they were even higher. This quarter few indices have matched that.

The chart shows clearly what the source of the disappointment has been: technology. The surprise for the Nasdaq 100 index is -3% and for emerging market (EM) tech stocks it is -8%. The disappointments in emerging markets were almost entirely driven by tech stocks; results for the other sectors were 1% better.

There are two questions: Are these disappointments surprising and how much do they matter?

Given not only how high expectations have been for technology stocks, and how rapidly the artificial intelligence theme is developing, it is not surprising that companies have reported results that are further off the mark than is typically the case.

Though there has been some disappointment in the short term (which will drive the short-term performance of the stock), the more important consideration for investors is the medium-term outlook (which will determine the stock’s medium-term path).

It is worth recalling that consensus estimates for Nasdaq 100 earnings growth in 2027 is 35% and for emerging market technology stocks it is 39%. Even if actual results are a few percentage points lower, and if valuations do not change significantly, indices would typically appreciate in line with earnings.

Sector drivers

It is not only the tech sector that has boosted EPS (earnings-per-share) growth rates. Higher energy prices have contributed to strong results for indices like MSCI Europe and Russell Value. Excluding the energy sector, earnings growth for MSCI Europe is a (still good) 17%. But even setting aside the gains from tech and higher oil prices, results across other sectors are robust. The automobile industry continues to be a drag on the consumer discretionary sector, but most of the others are seeing high single or double-digit earnings growth (see Exhibit 2).

Whether this broadening in earnings continues, or even accelerates, will partly depend on the rate of adoption of AI technologies. There is already significant anecdotal evidence of companies finding meaningful productivity improvements through AI. One example is insurance companies reducing their claims review times and credit losses by using micro-expression recognition technology.

Stories of CFOs becoming alarmed by high AI bills also suggests adoption is accelerating. This will be critical not only for the future rate of non-tech company earnings growth, but also for the hyperscalers, as they look for the return on their massive capital expenditure.

Norges Bank Investment Management (NBIM) is the investment management division of the Norwegian Central Bank (Norges Bank). We are responsible for investing the Norwegian Government Pension Fund Global. As of year-end 2025, we managed EUR 1.79 trillion in assets, invested in the shares of 7,201 companies across 67 countries. As a long-term, global investor, we believe our returns depend on sustainable development in economic, environmental and social terms.
We appreciate the opportunity to respond to the consultation by the European Financial Reporting Advisory Group (EFRAG) on the ESRS-40a Exposure Draft. This response builds on our engagement throughout the simplification of the European Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRS).[1] ESRS-40a will apply from financial year 2028 to non-EU groups with significant activity in the EU, setting out the sustainability information they must report under the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD). Unlike the ESRS that apply to EU companies, it covers only companies’ impacts on people and the environment, not how sustainability matters affect the companies themselves (sustainability-related risks and opportunities). The CSRD does not require non-EU groups to report on the latter.[2]
Many of our largest holdings are non-EU groups likely to fall within the scope of ESRS-40a. A growing number of them report, or will soon report, on sustainability-related risks and opportunities under the standards issued by the International Sustainability Standards Board (ISSB), known as the ISSB Standards, either directly or through local standards based on them. We have long supported the ISSB Standards as the global baseline for sustainability reporting, given their focus on information that is material to investors.
For groups that already report under the ISSB Standards, ESRS-40a will add a further set of requirements. Although the two frameworks have different objectives, they overlap considerably, particularly on climate, where both require information on matters such as greenhouse gas emissions, targets and transition plans. As an investor, we therefore have two main interests in how they fit together. First, companies that report under the ISSB Standards should be able to meet ESRS-40a as efficiently as possible. Reporting the same information twice or in different ways would add to their burden and make companies harder to compare across markets. Second, the resulting report should remain understandable for investors such as ourselves, who rely on the financially material information it contains. Our response focuses on interoperability between ESRS-40a and the ISSB Standards with these two aims in mind.
Overall, we welcome EFRAG’s proposals in this area, which already support both aims. They allow companies to build on their ISSB reporting and add the disclosures ESRS-40a requires (the “ISSB+” approach). Companies could do so either through a single report that meets both sets of standards, or by referring to information already published in other reports (incorporation by reference). This is in line with the ISSB’s building-block approach, under which the ISSB Standards provide a global baseline that jurisdictions can add to. Because companies can reuse the reporting they already prepare, the proposals also encourage wider adoption of the ISSB Standards. As currently drafted, however, the approach would be available to fewer groups than intended. To help this approach work in practice, we would encourage EFRAG to:

Widen the reports companies can build on. We would welcome confirmation that companies can base their reporting on the ISSB Standards as issued by the ISSB, including where they apply them voluntarily or instead of a local version. At present, companies can only incorporate by reference reports that are required by law. This excludes, for example, groups that report under the ISSB Standards, or local standards based on them, voluntarily or before their local requirements come into force, as well as groups that choose the ISSB Standards as issued over a local version. We therefore suggest allowing incorporation by reference even where the report is not legally required, whether it is prepared under the ISSB Standards as issued or under local standards based on them. The content table that companies must provide when a large part of the report is incorporated by reference could usefully apply to these reports as well.
Make the level of assurance visible. As more types of reports become eligible, investors will need to be able to judge how reliable the referenced information is. Some of these reports may not be subject to the same level of assurance as the rest of the ESRS-40a report. Rather than excluding them, we would suggest that companies state clearly what level of assurance applies to each referenced source.
Allow ISSB disclosures to be used as they are. ESRS-40a sometimes treats matters that the ISSB Standards also cover differently, such as time horizons.[3] Companies may then need to adjust their ISSB disclosures or report the same information twice. It would be helpful to confirm that companies applying the ISSB Standards as issued by the ISSB can use those disclosures unchanged wherever ESRS-40a requires information on the same matter. They would then add any other impact information that is material under ESRS-40a.
Simplify how the ESRS-40a information is identified. As drafted, ESRS-40a appears to require companies preparing a single report to label each disclosure according to whether it meets both sets of standards, ESRS-40a only, or the ISSB Standards only. Neither framework requires this level of detail elsewhere and, in our view, it would add work for companies without making the report more useful to investors or other readers. Information for investors does need to be identifiable, but it should be sufficient for the ESRS-40a information to be clearly identifiable, as the Exposure Draft already requires in line with ESRS. We would therefore suggest that companies should not be required to label ISSB-only information separately. An appendix to ESRS-40a listing the additional disclosures that companies starting from the ISSB Standards may need to provide would also help them apply the standard consistently and, where they use incorporation by reference, prepare the content table.

We believe that allowing companies to build efficiently on their ISSB reporting, while keeping the resulting report understandable for investors, would best serve both investors and companies. We value EFRAG’s work on ESRS-40a and its ongoing cooperation with the IFRS Foundation, and we hope our perspective is helpful as EFRAG finalises its advice. Our answers to the relevant questionnaire questions are set out in the Appendix.
Thank you for considering our perspective. We remain available for further discussion.
Yours sincerely
Carine Smith IhenachoChief Governance and Compliance Officer
Dr Shilpi NandaSenior Policy Advisor

[1] See our responses to EFRAG's calls for input on the revision of the ESRS (May and September 2025) and to the European Commission's consultation on the draft revised ESRS (June 2026).
[2] These requirements are set out in Article 40a of the Accounting Directive (Directive 2013/34/EU), which was added by the CSRD.
[3] ESRS-40a sets fixed time horizons for reporting purposes: the short term is the period covered by the financial statements, the medium term runs up to five years beyond that, and the long term is more than five years. The ISSB Standards instead require companies to explain how they define these time horizons themselves.

articles.title: Euro Tax Flash from KPMG's EU Tax Centre: 05 November 2026
articles.text:
Go back to the Euro Tax Flash homepage.

European Commission publishes its 2027 work program

At a glance: the Commission is streamlining its EU direct tax agenda, prioritizing the Tax Omnibus and clearing out several long-standing Directive proposals that have failed to secure sufficient Member State support – including BEFIT, HOT and the Corporate taxation of a significant digital presence.Taxpayer impact: the work program provides a useful indication of where the Commission’s focus will lie in the year ahead, with tax simplification as the key priority for EU direct tax policy.

European Commission – Tax Omnibus proposal – 28th legal regime – EU Inc. – BEFIT – Head office tax system – Significant digital presence – EU digital services tax – Gold-plating – Simplification

Background

Following the 2024 European Parliament elections, the new European Commission took office on December 1, 2024 for a five-year term. In January 2025, the Commission presented its Competitiveness Compass, setting out its policy priorities for the new legislative cycle. Building on the report on the future of European competitiveness by Mario Draghi (the Draghi Report), the Compass placed a strong emphasis on strengthening EU competitiveness and simplifying the regulatory environment, including a target to reduce reporting burdens by 25 percent for companies generally and by 35 percent for SMEs.This focus on simplification was subsequently reflected in the Commission’s 2026 work program. In the field of direct taxation, the program announced the Tax Omnibus initiative, which resulted in the Tax Omnibus and DAC recast proposals published on June 24, 2026 – for more details, please refer to Euro Tax Flash Issue 582 and Issue 583.At the same time, the Commission announced the withdrawal of several pending direct tax initiatives that it considered no longer aligned with its priorities or unlikely to progress. These notably included the following initiatives.Rules to prevent the misuse of shell entities for tax purposes (Unshell) - 2021: The initial proposal set out a list of indicators to filter entities at risk of being misused for tax purposes. High-risk entities were supposed to be required to report on a series of substance indicators through their annual tax return. Companies failing to meet the substance indicators would have been deemed to be ‘shell’ entities, potentially triggering tax consequences.Enhanced cooperation in the area of financial transaction tax (FTT) - 2013: Proposed introduction of a tax on qualifying financial transactions.Debt-equity bias reduction allowance (DEBRA) - 2022: The proposal provided for an allowance in respect of equity increases in a given tax year. In addition, the DEBRA initiative proposed the introduction of a new limitation on interest deductibility, which would apply alongside the interest limitation rules under the Anti-Tax Avoidance Directive (ATAD).Transfer Pricing Directive – 2023: The proposal aimed to incorporate common transfer pricing principles into EU law – specifically the OECD arm’s length principle and a reference to the OECD Transfer Pricing Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises and Tax Administration.The withdrawal of these initiatives was published in the Official Journal of the European Union on October 29, 2026, formally closing the respective legislative procedures.For more details on the Commission’s 2026 work program, please refer to E-News Issue 220.

Commission 2027 work plan

On November 4, 2026, the Commission published its work program for 2027opens in a new tab. The program includes a list of new initiatives that would be tabled by the EC in 2027, a list of pending priority proposals, as well as list of proposals that will be withdrawn or repealed.New and pending initiativesThe 2027 work program does not announce any new initiatives specifically in the field of taxation. However, one pending tax-related proposal has been identified as a priority, namely the Tax Omnibus. The proposal was published on June 24, 2026 and is aimed at simplifying EU tax rules, reducing compliance burdens for businesses, and strengthening the competitiveness of the Internal Market by proposing updates to the EU legislative framework for corporate taxation (including the Parent-Subsidiary Directive, Interest and Royalties Directive, Anti-Tax Avoidance Directive, Dispute Resolution Directive and Merger Directive). The proposal is currently being discussed by Member States in the Council, with a political commitment to reach agreement by the end of 2027. As amendments to EU direct tax legislation require unanimous agreement, the final scope and timing of the package will depend on the outcome of those negotiations.On a related note, the “28th regime corporate legal framework – EU Inc.” was also included in the in the list of priority proposals. The regulation provides for a voluntary, EU‑wide corporate form called ‘EU Inc.’ as part of its broader ‘28th Regime’ initiative. The proposal aims to establish a single, optional and harmonized set of corporate rules covering the entire lifecycle of a company. This new regime would not replace existing national company law frameworks. Instead, it would operate as a parallel system alongside the national regimes of the 27 Member States. The proposal does not introduce an EU‑level corporate tax system, i.e., the tax rules of the Member State of incorporation would generally apply. Nevertheless, the proposal includes a tax-relevant feature, i.e., the taxation of qualifying EU Employee Stock Option Plans (EU-ESO). On October 23, 2026, EU Member State ambassadors in the Committee of Permanent Representatives (COREPER) agreed on the Council’s negotiating mandate on the proposed 28th regime corporate legal framework, paving the way for negotiations with the European Parliament. Directive proposals to be withdrawnThe work program also identifies a number of pending proposals that will be formally withdrawn within six months. From a direct tax perspective, key initiatives to be withdrawn include:Business in Europe - Framework for Income Taxation (BEFIT) - 2023:
The proposal provided for common rules for determining the corporate tax base for EU-based entities that are part of a group with global consolidated revenues above a certain threshold. BEFIT also included provisions for the allocation of profits to relevant Member States. Once allocated, profits would have been subject to the corporate income tax rate of the respective Member States.The Commission indicates that the file has been pending in the Council for almost three years without progress and is unlikely to obtain the necessary support within a reasonable timeframe, particularly as EU taxation matters require unanimity in the Council. The EC has been actively promoting the idea of a common consolidated corporate tax base (CCCTB) since 2011, but none of the past initiatives achieved consensus. Head Office Tax system for micro, small and medium sized enterprises (HOT) - 2023:
The Directive proposal allowed certain EU-based standalone SMEs that operate in other EU Member States only through permanent establishments (PEs) to make a five-year election to determine the taxable results of the PEs according to the rules of the Member State of their head office.Similar to the BEFIT proposal, the Commission indicates that the proposed withdrawal is due to the lack of progress in the Council over the past three years, with agreement considered unlikely to be reached within a reasonable timeframe. Corporate taxation of a significant digital presence - 2018:
The Directive proposed the introduction of a taxable nexus for digital businesses operating within the EU. Significant digital presence would have covered any digital platform where annual revenue from providing digital services in a given Member State, the annual number of users of such services, or the annual number of online contracts concluded with users in a given Member State exceeds certain thresholds. The proposal would have also introduced principles to attribute profits to businesses having such significant digital presence.The 2027 work program notes that the file is intended to be withdrawn as it has been pending with the Council for more than eight years and it is unlikely to secure support.

Next steps

The withdrawal of Commission proposal needs to be formally published in the EU Official Journal in order for the legislative process to end.

ETC Comment:

The work program does not provide a comprehensive list of pending proposals that have not been designated as priorities.One noteworthy tax file is the EU Digital Services Tax (DST) proposal, tabled in 2018, with the aim of establishing a coordinated EU approach to taxing revenues from certain digital services and avoiding fragmentation resulting from unilateral national measures. Notably, the proposal has not been identified for withdrawal, despite the Commission’s continued preference for a multilateral solution to the taxation of the digitalized economy.The 2025 Polish Presidency progress report noted that several Member States remained open to a common EU DST in the context of a potential new own resource, although they questioned whether it could be introduced in time for the 2028–2034 Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF), while others cautioned against potential retaliatory measures by international partners. More recently, the OECD/G20 Inclusive Framework plenary outcome agreed to renew its examination of the challenges posed by digital business models under the existing international tax framework before considering the merits and practicalities of coordinated solutions, and asked the OECD Secretariat to develop a work plan by end of 2026. Against this background, it remains to be seen whether the developments at OECD level could influence the future of the EU DST proposal.Another noteworthy tax file that has not been identified for withdrawal, but is also not included on the priority list, is the proposed revision of the Energy Taxation Directive. The initiative seeks to better align the taxation of energy products with EU energy and climate objectives and promote the use of renewable energy sources. Negotiations have been ongoing since 2021, but Member States were not able to reach agreement on a compromise text.The withdrawal of several long-standing tax proposals reflects the challenges of reaching agreement at Council level, where unanimity is required on tax matters. One possible avenue where EU-wide agreement cannot be reached is enhanced cooperation, a procedure that allows a minimum of nine Member States to pursue closer cooperation within the EU framework without the participation of all Member States. The procedure has been successfully used in non-tax related areas. In the tax area, enhanced cooperation was pursued for the Financial Transaction Tax (FTT) after agreement among all Member States could not be reached. However, the participating Member States were ultimately unable to agree on the substance and design of the FTT, rather than being prevented from proceeding by the enhanced cooperation procedure itself. Against this background, a June 2026 report from the European Central Bankopens in a new tab suggested that harmonizing tax rules among smaller groups of Member States could, in some cases, be more effective than seeking unanimity among all 27 EU countries.Notably, the Commission’s work program also reiterates its commitment to simplifying EU regulation and reducing administrative burdens, including by addressing the “gold-plating” at Member State level. The Commission plans to work towards a Pact against gold-plating, aimed at increasing transparency around additional national requirements introduced when EU legislation is transposed and their impact on businesses and the Single Market. The initiative would also include a ‘review and remove’ mechanism under the European Semester to tackle unnecessary burdens resulting from gold-plating. It remains to be seen how this approach would be applied in the tax area. The issue has already proved politically sensitive in the context of public Country-by-Country Reporting, where efforts to discourage Member States from going beyond the EU framework attracted pushback from the European Parliament.Similar tensions have emerged in the negotiations on the Tax Omnibus, where several Member States have raised concerns about provisions that would restrict their ability to derogate from harmonized EU rules.

*This Euro Tax Flash edition was updated on November 6, 2026 to clarify that the Unshell, FTT, DEBRA and Transfer Pricing Directive proposals were officially withdrawn on 29 October, 2029.

Should you have any queries, please do not hesitate to contact KPMG’s EU Tax Centre or, as appropriate, your local KPMG tax advisor.

articles.title: Daily: Gridlock and diplomatic hopes lift US stocks
articles.text:
Talk to a UBS Financial AdvisorFrom the studioVideo: CIO Monthly | Mark Haefele on AI earnings, energy prices, interest rates (4 mins)Video: Why China's equity markets have lagged (6 mins)Thought of the dayWhat happened?
The S&P 500 closed 1.6% higher on Wednesday, reversing the initial negative reaction in futures markets to the Democrats taking control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate in the US.The Nasdaq Composite gained 1.4%, while the 10-year US Treasury yield fell 8bps from its level before the election result. The US dollar weakened against most other major currencies, with the DXY dollar index down 0.5%.Hopes for progress toward ending the US-Iran conflict also supported market sentiment. Qatar has stepped up mediation efforts following signs that Washington and Tehran are seeking to resume talks. Iranian officials, however, sounded less optimistic about a deal, reiterating that an agreement would only be possible if the US accepts Iran’s seven points. Brent crude oil fell 8.2% overnight, and has since stabilized around 95/bbl, as investors assess whether diplomacy could reduce the risk of further disruption to energy supplies.Still, overall risk sentiment remains fragile in early Thursday trading, with AI-heavy indices in South Korea and Taiwan down 5.3% and 3.2%, respectively, and Nasdaq futures pricing a 0.5% decline at the time of writing.What do we think?
The election result has removed a source of uncertainty. With Democrats controlling both chambers of Congress and President Donald Trump retaining the presidency and veto power, abrupt changes to tax and spending policy should be more difficult to enact.While this is not a forecast of future performance, the S&P 500 gained an average of 15.5% in the six months following the previous 14 midterm elections since 1970. This pattern may partly reflect the removal of election uncertainty and investors’ tendency to refocus on the economic and earnings outlook.Political risks remain, however. The next Congress will need to address government funding and the debt ceiling, potentially increasing bond market volatility. Democratic gains in key data center states could also delay projects, raise development costs, or influence capacity location. Trump retains broad executive authority over tariffs, foreign policy, and regulation.Individual stock performance is already beginning to reflect these differences in exposure. On Wednesday, large technology platforms performed strongly, while some companies linked to data center construction declined. Investors were concerned that Democratic gains in states including Texas and Georgia could lead to greater scrutiny of electricity consumption, water use, and permitting.Investors appear to favor financially strong platforms that can fund investment flexibly from existing cash flow. They are becoming more cautious about businesses exposed to financing, construction, permitting, or execution risks. This suggests that broad equity gains may be accompanied by greater dispersion in technology sector performance.Overall, the election does not change our view that economic growth, corporate earnings, inflation, and interest rates should remain the primary market drivers. Earnings remain supportive, with recent corporate results providing further evidence of robust demand
across parts of the technology sector and the broader economy.Prospects for US-Iran diplomatic progress offer another potential source of stability. Both sides have incentives to avoid a prolonged conflict that keeps energy prices elevated and increases economic pressure. However, global inventories have fallen sharply, and pledged releases from strategic oil reserves are largely complete. Continued undersupply could further deplete commercial stocks and support oil prices. Record freight costs, constrained tanker capacity, and recovering Chinese imports are also likely to keep prices elevated.Comments from Trump that no military strike is imminent have helped weigh on prices, but the risk of renewed military action leaves markets vulnerable to further energy price volatility, while open questions remain on how long the US will support energy flows with military escorts.How do we invest?
We remain constructive on global equities, but the uneven rally and uncertainty surrounding US-Iran negotiations reinforce the importance of diversification.Stay invested in diversified equities. Strong earnings, resilient economic growth, and robust demand for AI infrastructure continue to support our constructive view. Our preferred sectors include industrials, health care, and financials. Regionally, we prefer the Eurozone, emerging markets, and Asia ex-Japan.Rebalance concentrated technology exposure. Greater scrutiny of data centers, alongside existing questions about AI monetization, could increase single-stock volatility. Investors with oversized positions in individual securities should use periods of strength to reduce concentration and diversify across the AI value chain. We favor financially strong platforms and high-quality infrastructure providers over businesses that rely more heavily on external funding or the rapid completion of individual projects.Maintain protection against geopolitical disruption. Diplomatic progress could push down oil prices further, but renewed attacks or a breakdown in negotiations could trigger another rise. Broad commodity exposure can help diversify portfolios when geopolitical disruption weighs on both stocks and bonds. Investors should consider exposure across energy, precious metals, industrial metals, and agriculture, rather than rely on a single commodity or geopolitical outcome.

articles.title: New Bank Start-Up Unit
articles.text:
New Bank Start-up Unit

The New Bank Start-up Unit provides information and support for those thinking of setting up a new bank in the UK.

On this pageIntroductionThinking of becoming a bank in the UK?Engaging with the NBSUNew Bank Pre-application engagementSubmitting the applicationThe application feeThe authorisation (including decision making) processRegulatory expectations as part of the assessment approachThe assessment – authorisation with restrictions (mobilisation)Life as an authorised bank (with restrictions - mobilisation)Life as an authorised bank (without restrictions)Resource links, new banks authorised since 2013 and contact details

Introduction
Firms that want to operate as banks in the UK (see ‘thinking of becoming a bank’ section) must be authorised by the Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA), with the consent of the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA).
International banks seeking to establish a banking subsidiary and/or branch in the UK should, in parallel with referring to the NBSU website, consult SS5/21 (International banks: The PRA’s approach to branch and subsidiary supervision), as well as the FCA’s Approach to international firms publication Opens in a new window.
The New Bank Start-up Unit (NBSU) is a joint initiative set up by the UK financial regulators, the PRA and the FCA, to provide information and support for firms interested in, or currently applying for, authorisation as a bank in the UK.
To advance the PRA and FCA’s primary and secondary objectives (information on the PRA’s objectives, goals and latest business plan. Information on the FCA objectives Opens in a new window, both regulators will assess whether a firm meets the Threshold Conditions, which are the minimum standards that all firms must meet at their point of authorisation, and on an ongoing basis while operating as a bank.
The Threshold Conditions for the PRA and FCA (below) are set out in Schedule 6 to the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 Opens in a new window.

Legal status: Deposit-takers must be corporates or partnerships;
Location of offices: A UK incorporated corporate body must maintain their head offices and, if one exists, their registered office in the UK;
Prudent conduct of business: The firm must conduct their business in a prudent manner, which includes having appropriate financial and non-financial resources;
Suitability: The firm must satisfy the PRA that they are a ‘fit and proper’ person with regard to all circumstances to conduct a regulated activity; and
Effective supervision: The firm must be capable of being effectively supervised by the PRA.

Effective supervision: The firm must be capable of being effectively supervised by the FCA;
Appropriate non-financial resources: The firm’s non-financial resources must be appropriate in relation to the regulated activities they seek to carry on, having regard to the FCA’s operational objectives;
Suitability: The firm must be a fit and proper person. The firm’s management must have adequate skills and experience and act with integrity (fitness and propriety). The firm must have appropriate policies and procedures in place, and it must appropriately manage conflicts of interest; and
Business model: The firm’s strategy for doing business must be suitable for a person carrying on the regulated activities it undertakes or seeks to carry on and must not pose a risk to the FCA’s objectives.

Thinking of becoming a bank in the UK?A ‘bank’ is an entity that carries out deposit-taking business. The PRA and the FCA glossaries define a ‘bank’ as a firm with a Part 4A permission, which includes accepting deposits and is a credit institution, but is not a credit union, friendly society, or building society.The Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (Regulated Activities) Order 2001 Opens in a new window defines the regulated activity of accepting deposits (see Chapter II Accepting Deposits) and stipulates that, to accept deposits, one of the following statements must be true:a) Money received by way of deposit is lent to others or;
b) A firm uses deposits to materially fund a business line.Firms must consider if their proposed business satisfies the definition of accepting deposits and be able to justify this assessment to regulators. You should also consider the following:

Firms should consider their options for accessing payment systems as early as possible and adequately reflect this in their plans. Payment systems are critical to allow the transfer of funds between people, businesses and financial institutions – new banks are unlikely to be able to operate without access to a payment system. The NBSU encourages firms to consider the guidance on payment systems access.
New banks can access a payment system in the following ways:
Full direct access – where the new bank will have a direct technical and settlement relationship with the payment system provider (PSP);
Direct technical access – where the new bank will have a direct technical relationship with the PSP but use a sponsor for settlement; or,
Indirect access – where an Indirect Access Provider (IAP) acts as the new bank’s sponsor for both technical and settlement sponsorship.
There are a variety of software vendors with products and services that may reduce the cost and complexity of the direct access option, as well as several IAPs providing indirect access offerings. Further information about direct and indirect access can be found on the Payments Systems Regulator Opens in a new window and Payment System Operators’ websites, and in the Code of Conduct for Indirect Access Providers Opens in a new window.

If the firm is already FCA solo-authorised (for example an investment firm seeking to broaden their funding base to take on retail deposits), they will need to apply to vary their permissions to add deposit-taking. Whilst this is a different regulatory transaction, the firm should follow the same authorisation process as fully unauthorised firms. In this instance, the NBSU recommends that, like unauthorised firms, the solo-regulated firm should follow the pre-application stages before applying to become authorised. In addition, the NBSU encourages FCA solo-authorised firms seeking dual authorisation to consider their capital and ownership structures and ensure that those are as simple as possible.

The use of certain sensitive words such as ‘bank’ and ‘banking’ in registered company names is controlled by legislation to prevent the public from being misled. Firms cannot call themselves a ‘bank’ until they have been authorised by the PRA. Prospective firms must take care when liaising with press, prospective investors, and posting on social media, prior to obtaining authorisation.
Firms may begin the application process as ‘Example Ltd’ but only once they are authorised as a bank can they call themselves ‘Example Bank Ltd’.
Firms must seek the FCA’s consent before using domain names that include sensitive words including ‘bank’ and ‘banking’. Further information can be found on the FCA’s sensitive business name Opens in a new window page.

Please refer to ‘Should I become a bank Opens in a new window’ guide to help firms understand whether being a bank is the appropriate model for them.
Are there alternatives to being a bank?
Yes, please refer to the ‘alternatives to being a bank Opens in a new window’ guide for further information on some of the alternatives.

The NBSU is open to listening to proposals and answering any questions you may have - before any significant work has been undertaken towards becoming a bank in the UK. If you have a proposal that you would like to raise or discuss, please email NewBankstartupunit@bankofengland.co.uk with your proposal/enquiry – someone from the team will get back to you within five working days.

Engaging with the NBSUTo navigate the authorisation process as efficiently as possible and achieve their objective of setting up a bank, firms should be ready, willing and organised. We have provided below some examples of how firms can demonstrate this. Please note that this is not an exhaustive list:
Ready and thinking ahead – Firms should ensure that they have a well thought through proposition which has undergone robust challenge and consideration of the inherent risks (this should also be appropriately reflected into their key documents). Firms should ensure that they will have in place appropriately skilled staff and operational infrastructure to commence trading at the point of being authorised. This includes a robust IT framework, a robust governance framework, risk management framework, premises, and finances;
Willing – Firms should demonstrate that they have done their research, understanding not only the activities that they will be undertaking but the rules and regulations which their business will be governed by; and
Organised – Firms should ensure that they are operationally ready to carry out the regulated activities at the time of their authorisation (if successful).
We aim to have positive regulatory relationships with firms along their journey, from pre-authorisation to becoming authorised and later becoming established banks. We do this by keeping an open and constructive dialogue:

Be open and honest;
Have considered the guidance provided on this website
Provide all the necessary information to undertake our assessments
Notify us of any changes, challenges or concerns as soon as possible
Develop plans, complete the necessary work, and prepare and send materials in good time for meetings with us;
Fully consider and address the feedback we provide on key documents such as the Regulatory Business Plan (RBP)/the Internal Capital Adequacy Assessment Process (ICAAP)/the Internal Liquidity Adequacy Assessment Process (ILAAP) documents
Understand, consider and demonstrate how they will meet the required standards at authorisation and on an ongoing basis.

To clearly set out the process and requirements for setting up a bank;
To host pre-application meetings to discuss the firm’s proposals and highlight any concerns;
To provide firms with clear feedback on their proposals including formal written feedback;
We will end our pre-application engagement with firms if our feedback is not adequately addressed in the development of their proposition and key documents
To help firms understand the standards required of being an authorised bank.

New Bank Pre-application engagement
(Optional but recommended)
The NBSU offers firms a ‘complimentary service’, which includes enhanced engagement and support as firms build out their proposals before applying for a banking licence.
Although pre-application engagement is optional and not part of the statutory authorisation process, it is something that the NBSU encourages firms to take advantage of at an early stage (feedback from previous applicant banks has shown how valuable they have found it).
Early engagement allows the NBSU to provide input into the development of regulatory business plans, by guiding potential applicants towards what the PRA and FCA are most interested in, as well as helping them understand regulatory requirements. It also allows the NBSU to identify any significant issues or showstoppers at an early stage.
Pre-application engagement with the NBSU is usually focussed around three stages (although this is flexible and all three stages might not be necessary):
i. business proposition;
ii. draft regulatory business plan; and
iii. technical sessions.
If you would like to take advantage of this complimentary pre-application engagement service, then please contact NewBankstartupunit@bankofengland.co.uk.

Although still early in a firm’s preparations, you will have reached the stage where you can present (usually as a PowerPoint presentation) high level information on your business model, financial forecasts, governance, source of funding, ownership, controllers and risks. You should also provide an indication of the timeframes that you are working towards and indicate whether you will be applying for full authorisation or authorisation with restrictions (also known as mobilisation), as this will impact your planning, as well as the information requirements for your application.
Upon receipt of your business proposition, the NBSU will review and schedule a meeting, typically within three weeks from date of receipt (this meeting may be over MS Teams so progress can be made as efficiently as possible). You will also receive written feedback within three weeks of the meeting.

The RBP forms a critical component of the assessment of a potential application, and therefore the NBSU expects your RBP to already be at a detailed stage prior to submission and should include the following:

Business model and financials covering business strategy, route to profitability, financial projections;
Market analysis and research that underpins the business model assumptions;
Corporate governance setting out board and committee structure as well as proposed approach for recruiting senior managers;
Risk register and stress testing;
Risk management and control framework;
Funding plans, which includes details around the owners and controllers. Where funding is still being sought, you should provide details of your plan to bring in investors;
Conduct risk of harm and consumer duty (if applicable);
Financial Crime Risk Management Framework;
Operational resilience covering outsourcing, IT infrastructure timescales to implement/test and business continuity;
Details of the regulated activities you wish to undertake (please refer to the application form for further information on the regulated activities that can be applied for);
Mobilisation plan (if applicable);

Please refer to the Regulatory Business Plan guide for further information on why an RBP is important, what should be included and the common challenges.
Once you have submitted your RBP (it is useful to be notified of the planned RBP submission date two weeks in advance), the NBSU will review and schedule a face-to-face or hybrid MS Teams meeting, typically within three weeks from date of receipt. You will also receive written feedback within the three weeks following the meeting.

At this stage, the expectation is that you have addressed all the feedback provided and can submit a fully developed RBP. For UK start-ups and subsidiaries of international banks, you will also have drafted and submitted your ICAAP and ILAAP documents by this stage.
The firm’s management team should own ICAAP and ILAAP and be able to discuss these in detail at the technical session. The ICAAP and ILAAP should have gone through a full review and challenge by someone other than the author (the Board or the key guiding minds of the firm), before they are submitted to the NBSU.
At this stage, the PRA will assess the ICAAP and ILAAP, which includes engagement with the relevant technical specialists. The assessment will focus on whether the ICAAP and ILAAP meet the relevant regulatory expectations and consider whether the documents would be sufficient to set capital and liquidity requirements during an application.
The NBSU will also consider the latest RBP to assess if there is any further feedback prior to the firm submitting the application. Further, depending on the nature of the proposed business model and operational design, the FCA may also look to hold focused technical sessions on the financial crime control framework.
Following the submission of the near final RBP, ICAAP and ILAAP, the NBSU will schedule a face to face or hybrid MS Teams meeting. Typically, this will be within six weeks from date of receipt. As this review involves technical specialists, it is important to give both the PRA and FCA as much notice as possible prior to submitting, and to provide at least two weeks' notice, so that both regulators can line up the necessary resource and avoid delays. You will also receive written feedback within three weeks of the meeting.

Submitting the application
The application process commences with the submission of the New Firm Authorisation application (and supporting documentation), and the payment of the PRA and FCA’s non-refundable application fee. It is entirely up to the firm to decide when it should submit its application, but this should be at a point where the firm can demonstrate that their business is ready, willing and organised to be authorised as a bank.
There are two routes available for applying to be a bank in the UK:

Full authorisation; or
Authorisation with restrictions (mobilisation) – this route is primarily targeted at UK start-ups. Although the Threshold Conditions still need to be met, the NBSU’s approach to the information requirements will be proportionate to the restrictions that will be put in place, and therefore will likely result in a quicker authorisation (the information instead will be required during the mobilisation period and will be assessed as part of the application to remove the restrictions). Please refer to the further information on mobilisation.

The application forms
Please note, firms will need to send an email with an electronic copy of their application (and supporting documentation) to the PRA at the following mailbox: NewBankstartupunit@bankofengland.co.uk.
If the file size exceeds 25 MB, please use multiple emails to accommodate your submission.

The application fee
The PRA and the FCA Regulatory Transaction fees for applications for new authorisations are payable in accordance with PRA Rulebook Opens in a new window and FCA Handbook Opens in a new window.
The total fee payable (covers both PRA and FCA fees) to seek permission to accept deposits (other than a credit union) is £56,300.
The preferred method for payment is via BACS to the FCA, who will provide a single invoice covering both the PRA and FCA fees.
Please make the payment to the FCA using the details below:

When you make the payment, please reference it with the following: Title: ‘New authorisation application’ and the ‘firm name’ (name of the firm applying for authorisation).
Please then email your remittance advice and payment details to: fcafees@fca.org.uk and NewBankstartupunit@bankofengland.co.uk.
Information on how to pay the fee is also contained within the application form.
Please note that in the case of a firm withdrawing its application, and later re-submitting another application, they would likely need to pay the full fee again.

The authorisation (including decision making) process
The NBSU will acknowledge receipt of your application within two working days.
Usually, the NBSU will communicate whether your application is complete or incomplete within three weeks of receiving it (if incomplete, the regulators will inform you of any missing information).

For complete applications (i.e., the NBSU has received the application fee and all the necessary applications and supporting documents, which should be of sufficient quality and detail for completion of the assessment) – the PRA targets four months to determine the application (with a statutory timeframe of within six months).
For incomplete applications – the PRA targets 10 months to determine the application (with a statutory timeframe of within twelve months).

During the assessment period the NBSU welcomes regular dialogue and encourages you to reach out as and when you need. The NBSU will keep you informed on the progress of any reviews and proactively highlight any significant risks or issues identified. In addition, the NBSU will typically meet monthly with the firm’s senior management.
The PRA aim to issue a decision as quickly as possible, but this depends on how complete your application is and how promptly you respond to our requests for information. We may have questions or need more details from you during our assessment. Responding quickly and thoroughly will help speed up the process.
The decision-making process:

Both the PRA and FCA will independently decide whether to authorise your bank.
Without FCA consent, the PRA cannot authorise your bank

If authorised, you'll receive:

An authorisation letter
A Scope of Permission Notice detailing your permissions and any requirements
A welcome pack

Your bank’s details will be added to the Financial Services Register on the date shown in the authorisation letter.

Initial notification
If during our assessment of the application we think there are grounds for refusing your application, we'll inform you both verbally and in writing where you'll have time to address our concerns.

Minded to refuse letter
If you can't address the concerns, we'll send you a letter explaining why and which rules or threshold conditions haven't been met.

At this point you can either withdraw your application (and reapply later when issues have been addressed) or, if you want to proceed, the PRA and FCA will follow its decision-making process
Issuing statutory notices (Warning Notices and Decision Notices)
Please refer to SoP1/24 - The Prudential Regulation Authority’s allocation of decision making and approach to supervisory decisions, which sets out

the PRA’s allocation of decision-making regarding statutory notices (Warning Notices, Decision Notices, and Supervisory Notices);
the PRA’s approach to decision-making on statutory notices in relation to supervisory decisions under the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000; and
the PRA’s approach to publication of decisions in supervisory cases.

Regulatory expectations as part of the assessment approachThe assessment – full authorisationThe areas that the NBSU assess as part of a new bank application are set out below but should not be considered an exhaustive list. Firms are responsible for considering in detail all relevant laws, rules and regulatory policies, and ensuring that they understand and can fully comply with them.

Read information on ‘regulatory expectations’ (including where expectations are different for branches)
The assessment – authorisation with restrictions (mobilisation)
It is up to firms to propose to the NBSU which activities they complete in mobilisation (please refer to the application form for details of the activities that can be applies for). Therefore, the key for the NBSU’s assessment is that all the design work is complete with a clear plan to deliver everything with a plausible timeframe.
Further information is contained within the mobilisation page.

Life as an authorised bank (with restrictions - mobilisation)
Once a new bank is authorised with restrictions, it enters a mobilisation period, which typically lasts no longer than 12 months. During this time, the bank's deposit-taking permission is restricted to a total of £50,000, while it completes the remaining build-out of its operations. This period allows new banks to secure further investment, recruit staff, invest in IT systems, and commit to third-party suppliers, as they are now an authorised bank.
Further information is contained within the mobilisation page.

The PRA and FCA anticipate that new banks will want to progress quickly through the mobilisation phase. This could take as little as a few months but cannot continue indefinitely and should take no longer than 12 months. For a new bank to exit mobilisation, they should submit a Variation of Permission (VoP) application via Connect.
Further information is contained within the mobilisation page.

Further information is contained within the mobilisation page.

Life as an authorised bank (without restrictions)
At this stage, the firm should be fully operational and in a position to fulfil its business proposition as agreed with the PRA and FCA.

Authorisation is only the start of the journey towards becoming an established bank.
New banks must always meet their capital and liquidity regulatory requirements and the Threshold Conditions.
New banks must ensure that they submit their regulatory returns on time and keep up to date with the latest regulatory information.
New banks must ensure that risk management frameworks and controls evolve commensurately with the scale of business growth.
The PRA and FCA will assess how new banks are managing the key prudential and conduct risks, respectively, to their businesses through supervisory engagement.
Read: Life as an authorised bank (without restrictions).

Resource links, new banks authorised since 2013 and contact details

SS3/21 Non-systemic UK banks: The Prudential Regulation Authority’s approach to new and growing banks – This outlines the PRA’s expectations of firms and new banks and how those evolve throughout the authorisation journey.
Climbing mountains safely – a speech by Sarah Breeden – This speech, published alongside the CP on the PRA’s approach to new and growing banks, sets out key aspects from the consultation (i.e. what firms need to consider becoming an established bank).
PRA’s approach to banking supervision – This sets out the PRA’s approach to supervising regulated firms.
SS5/21 International banks: The PRA’s approach to branch and subsidiary supervision – This sets out the PRA’s proposals regarding its approach to supervising the UK activities of PRA-authorised banks and designated investment firms that are headquartered outside of the UK or are part of a group based outside of the UK.
Financial Services Register Opens in a new window – Where a new bank’s details will appear and includes the mobilisation restriction applied.
Read: New banks authorised since 2013.
If you have any queries about becoming a new bank, please contact NewBankStartupUnit@bankofengland.co.uk.

21 July 2026 - Application forms updated to reflect that the complaints contact does not need to be an approved SMF holder.
16 July 2026 - Application fee amended from £55,740 to £56,300 (new fee amount applicable from 2 July 2026).

16 March 2026 - Refreshed more concise NBSU website, updated application forms and regulatory expectations (including new section on group and consolidated supervision). Guides on Regulatory Business Plans and Mobilisation have been created (linked within this page).
