articles.title: Tokenised stocks Q3 2026 report | CoinShares
articles.text: Tokenised stocks were worth $3.91B on 30 Sep 2026, up +842% year on year1. No other tokenised asset class came close. Over the same year, tokenised commodities grew +267%, tokenised funds +97% and stablecoins +4%1.A tokenised stock is a digital token, recorded on a blockchain, that tracks the price of a listed share or ETF. The Hybrid Finance Q3 2026 Update, produced by CoinShares with Token Terminal, finds that these tokens serve demand that already exists. Of the market's total value, 87.2% tracks US-registered shares and ETFs, and 85.4% is issued under terms that exclude US persons1. The typical buyer is an investor outside the US who wants exposure to US equities. Foreign investors already hold $24.3T of US equities2, and tokenised stocks equal just 0.016% of that amount.The market is also spreading out: Since September 2025, the number of issuers holding more than $1M of tokenised stocks has risen from 10 to 25.Over the same period, the number of underlying shares and ETFs above $1M has gone from 83 to 1721.Onchain holder positions reached 4.88M, 8.5x the level at the end of June1. Custody is the exception.One US broker-dealer, Alpaca Securities LLC, holds the shares behind 81.3% of the market, down from 94.6%1. The report names this as the market's largest single point of failure.The report's main argument is about policy. The US has the most influence, but no single country's decision is likely to stop the market growing. If US regulators support tokenisation, issuance can move into the US. The SEC's March 2026 approval of tokenised trading on Nasdaq points that way. If they do not, issuers in Jersey, the British Virgin Islands and the UAE already serve investors outside the US. If the US blocked tokens backed by US shares, demand would probably move to derivatives. Perpetual futures on US stocks traded on Trade.xyz already have $1.51B of open interest, the value of outstanding contracts1. Most tokens are backed by shares bought in the US, so Washington has an economic reason to prefer them over derivatives. For comparison, a BIS working paper finds that inflows into stablecoins lower 3-month US Treasury bill yields by 2.5 to 3.5 basis points3.Download the full report in PDF for the complete data, the breakdown by issuer and the risk indicators. If you would rather explore the charts yourself, the interactive version is at coinshares.research.tokenterminal.com.Download the report

articles.title: Data and analytics transformation at the Bank of England to enable, equip and empower − speech by Ben Martin
articles.text:
Data and analytics transformation at the Bank of England to enable, equip and empower − speech by Ben Martin

Speech to be given at DAMA Data and AI Conference Europe 2026

Published on
04 November 2026

In this speech Ben Martin explores how the Bank is transforming its use of data, analytics and AI. From building stronger data foundations to safely adopting new AI capabilities, he explains how the Bank is enabling, equipping and empowering colleagues to make the most of these tools.

Speech
Good morning. It is a great pleasure to be here today at the DAMA Data & AI Conference. This event is about sharing practical experience of building trusted, responsible and effective data and AI capabilities, so I thought it would be a good opportunity to share some of the work we are doing on this at the Bank of England.
In recent years, my colleagues at the Bank have spoken publicly about the implications of AI on the wider economyfootnote [1] footnote [2]. Today, I want to talk about this from a slightly different perspective: what data and analytics transformation means for the Bank of England itself, as an organisation.
But first, let me introduce myself: my name is Ben Martin and I am the Bank’s Chief Data Officer. I took up this role just under a year ago, following a career across the Bank’s economics, markets and supervision areas. This experience gave me a deep understanding of the Bank’s data needs. Taking on the CDO role has allowed me to bring those perspectives together at an enterprise level. It has been encouraging to see how much progress we have made – and continue to make – in improving our data, analytics and AI capabilities. Even though we are making good progress, this is by no means job done. The pace of change in this field is rapid, and our ambitions need to keep pace with it. So today, I want to reflect on the journey we have been on, where we are now, and some of the opportunities and challenges that lie ahead.
Our mission at the Bank of England is to promote the good of the people of the United Kingdom, by maintaining monetary and financial stability. Across our offices in London and Leeds, our people are working to deliver that mission. Central to this is our ability to make the best possible decisions using the most effective data and analytics to achieve our public policy objectives. Data and analytics are integral to our work. They support our understanding of the economy, our supervision of the financial firms within it, and the operations through which we fulfil our responsibilities.
A couple of years ago, we published our Data & Analytics Strategyfootnote [3]. Our overarching aim is to make the best use of data and analytics to fulfil the Bank’s mission. Our ambitions are summarised by three missions.

First, making it easy for people in the Bank to work with and analyse data.
Second, bridging data gaps to increase the value of what we collect and share.
Third, enabling safe and effective innovation, including artificial intelligence.

Those missions rest on two foundations: a modern enterprise data platform on the cloud; and investment in business change, skills and culture to embed this.
That combination is important. We are not simply replacing systems. We are seeking to change how people find and use data, how they collaborate on it with each other, and how they develop new analytical tools and techniques to gain the best insights to make good decisions.
Today I want to focus on how we are enabling, equipping and empowering our organisation to deliver this strategy. Let me give a quick overview before we dive into each in more detail later on.
First, what do I mean by enablement? This covers the work we are doing to build solid foundations by providing transformed systems and high-quality data for our colleagues.
Second, we are equipping our colleagues with new capabilities including AI, with effective guardrails and associated training, so they can safely achieve new insights.
Last, but by no means least, I will cover empowerment – our approach to supporting colleagues to make the most of the investment we have made and to have the confidence to explore these new tools.
I am a big fan of the television programme Grand Designs, watching people use exciting, modern solutions in an innovative way to build something truly special – not just special on paper or to look at, but special for the people who live there. I sometimes think about our strategy in the same way. We are using modern techniques and the latest thinking on how to use data, but not as an end in itself or to wow anyone. Instead, the point is to deliver the Bank’s mission effectively and to make sure our colleagues can flourish. We are enabling colleagues by putting the foundations in place, equipping them with new capabilities to continue building on those foundations and empowering them to make the most of those new capabilities. Thankfully, the one thing we don’t have is Kevin McCloud turning up every few months to see how we’re getting on!
I will say a bit more about the work we are doing on these three Es – enable, equip and empower – at the Bank of England.
Enable – by building solid foundations
As I have said, we are building solid foundations, so we can enable our colleagues by providing effective systems and high-quality data as the bedrock of good analysis. At the Bank, we are part way through a multi-year investment programme to build solid data foundations. This includes investing in new systems and technology, but also continuing to invest in the ‘bread and butter’ of good data management: quality, governance and trust. AI may be grabbing the headlines, but AI runs on data. This audience knows well enough that without high-quality, well-governed and trusted data, even the most sophisticated AI will struggle to deliver. So I will share some reflections on how we are bringing together the new systems and the good old basics to ensure solid foundations.
New systems
At the foundation of our Data & Analytics Strategy is a new Enterprise Data Platform, or EDP. This is our central, cloud-based data and analytics ecosystem. It will bring together a wide range of data needed across the Bank’s responsibilities, including macroeconomic and financial market data we bring in from partners, and the regulatory and statistical returns we collect directly from the financial sector. But the EDP is about much more than storing data. It provides a structured and governed way of bringing data into the Bank, and transforming it into trusted, reusable data that can be readily used for analysis. Alongside this, the EDP provides modern analytical tools and capabilities, including access to approved AI models, helping colleagues to work with data more effectively and strengthening analysis and decision-making across the Bank.
Earlier this year, we deployed the core of the platform. We are now migrating data services and data systems onto that foundation in stages. Those new data systems are being completely transformed from the legacy systems we are retiring. Alongside this technology, we are building the operating model needed to support it. Together, the platform and its operating model are intended to help us move beyond data silos, establish a shared foundation for future data initiatives, and make greater use of cloud-native capabilities to develop new products and services.
The word ‘enterprise’ really matters here. The Bank of England brings together a number of different responsibilities within one institution, in part because of the connections and synergies between them. Our approach to data should reflect that same principle. Data collected or created for one purpose can often have value elsewhere, and insights can be richer when we are able to connect information from across the organisation. So rather than recreating a collection of separate systems, we are building shared data and analytical capabilities that can be used right across the organisation to support delivery of the Bank’s mission.
Good basics
Now, there is no point in building new systems but immediately filling them with poorly managed data. I know that data management is familiar territory for this audience. DAMA gives us a useful way of thinking about it: not as a standalone control, but as the coordinating mechanism that connects ownership, quality, metadata, architecture and use. For us, the real test is whether those disciplines show up in the everyday experience of colleagues working with data. That is why, since launching our Data & Analytics Strategy, we have focused on putting those practical data management foundations in place.
We have an organisation-wide data management policy and an ownership and stewardship framework, alongside data management learning within our wider data fluency programme.
We have numerous Data Owners and Stewards across all areas of the Bank who support over 2,000 registered data assets. These arrangements combine accountability for data with the day-to-day work needed to manage it.
These are important foundations helping us improve consistency, transparency and trust across an increasingly complex data estate. But the existence of a policy, a register, or an assigned owner, is far from being the end of the task. Our objective is that data can be found, accessed, trusted, understood and used, where data management acts as an enabler, not a barrier.
That is the practical test of data management. Does it help someone coming with fresh eyes establish what a dataset contains? Or understand whether it is appropriate for their purpose? Do they know who can answer their questions about it? And can they use it with confidence?
Like other long-established institutions, we face particular challenges in modernising our data estate. The Bank has a long history and with that comes years of accumulated data, systems and processes. Recent independent reviews by the Independent Evaluation Officefootnote [4] and Dr Ben Bernankefootnote [5] have reinforced the importance of tackling these challenges. It is clear we cannot simply build something new and expect all that complexity to disappear. Our Enterprise Data Platform is a good example – as we move datasets across, we are ensuring we look carefully at what we are bringing with us, to improve our data quality and embed those enduring data management basics from the outset. To stick with the theme of houses, this is a bit like moving house. If you live somewhere for a long time, you inevitably accumulate things along the way, which get shoved in drawers or the loft. Moving gives you the opportunity to decide what you really need, tidy things up and organise them better, rather than simply packing everything into boxes and recreating the same clutter in your new home.
Equip – by providing new capabilities
Next, we want to equip our colleagues to safely achieve new insights by using new capabilities including AI, with effective guardrails, and by providing the right training.
New capabilities
Much of the focus on data tooling over the past couple of years has been around the opportunities from new AI capabilities. We have been open about our approach to using AI at the Bank of England, which we outlined in our AI strategy that was published last yearfootnote [6]. To support a consistent and coherent approach to AI across the Bank, our AI strategy rests on a set of principles that set the tone for how we approach AI. Although frontier AI models and their capabilities have advanced rapidly over the past year, these principles are enduring. The principles are embodied in the ‘TRUSTED’ framework, which is for our AI solutions to be:

Targeted on tightly defined use cases that have a clear business purpose.
Reliable with high performance standards and grounded in high-quality data.
Understood in the context of their intended purpose.
Secure so we protect ourselves from risks such as unauthorised access.
Tested thoroughly for their technology standards and impact on behaviour.
Ethical including being beneficial and scientifically rigorous, fair and inclusive, transparent and secure, and compliant and accountable.
Durable so they remain effective despite changing conditions and usage patterns.

To bring this to life, I thought I would share some examples of how we have implemented this framework in practice. Our approach combines broad access to general purpose tools across the Bank with a more tailored applications for specific business needs.
A significant milestone has been the organisation-wide rollout of Microsoft 365 Copilot. Nearly all colleagues at the Bank use it each week. Some colleagues also use GitHub Copilot to support code development. As colleagues have become more confident, this has extended to the creation of many custom Copilot agents over the past year, typically to improve personal productivity in day-to-day tasks or to help navigate internal services. Many began as experiments, but some are now being used more widely across the organisation. For example, our ‘AskHR’ agent provides answers to questions on leave, pay and our people policies. Another agent, called ‘AskTech’, helps with technology-related questions and can direct colleagues to further support where needed. As you can see, our approach to naming them has been slightly less experimental!
Alongside these general-purpose tools, we are also developing bespoke AI applications for important business processes.
One example is our Agency Retrieval and Insights App, known as ARIA. The Bank’s regional Agents, based in 12 agencies across the nations and regions in the UK, maintain close relationships with businesses of all sizes, providing the Monetary Policy Committee with real-time insight into economic conditions and perspectives from across the country. Those relationships and the judgements of our Agents remain at the heart of that work, but ARIA complements this by helping them make sense of this wealth of intelligence they gather, using capabilities such as theme detection and quantitative analysis to identify patterns and draw out insights. It is a good example of technology augmenting human expertise and strengthening one part of the evidence base that supports the MPC in making its policy decisions.
Another example is called GRACE, which provides retrieval-augmented AI to enable colleagues to draw deep insights from large and trusted internal knowledge repositories. But what I particularly like is that it does this through an email interface, a tool colleagues already know how to use every day. They can send off a query, get on with something else and come back to the response when it arrives. The interaction is also captured naturally in the email chain. It is a simple example of designing AI around people and the way they work, rather than the other way round. These applications address different needs. What connects them is the effort to make technology useful within the work people already do.
Effective training
The pace of technology change can be dizzying, and with new capabilities emerging all the time, it can be difficult to know where to start. That is why we need to equip colleagues not just with the access to these tools, but to also equip them with the confidence and skills to use them safely and effectively. We want to help them feel confident navigating that change and so we have maintained a focus on training which is one of the two foundations of our Data & Analytics Strategy. It focuses on business change, skills and culture, recognising that successful adoption requires practical support, as colleagues move to new services and learning that goes beyond narrow technical training.
To put this in practice, we have a dedicated data and analytics learning function. To date, I am proud to say it has delivered more than 250 courses to many colleagues across our data science and analytical toolset.
Our aim is not simply to provide more training. It is to make learning more relevant to the work people need to do. On Copilot, we began with introductory learning to establish a common baseline for everyone. Many colleagues then attended application-based deep dives. We have subsequently introduced clinics offering more personalised support for local and role-specific use cases.
That progression from training course to back at the desk matters. General awareness can help people get started. Practical support helps them move from experimenting with a tool, to using it effectively and achieving results.
But formal learning is only part of the picture. We have a thriving Data Community, with almost 2,000 members. It actively supports collaboration, sharing and peer-to-peer learning. During our ‘Data & Analytics Fortnight’ in June, over 1,000 colleagues turned out to one of our events, which included a wide range of internal and external presenters sharing their expertise. Beyond this, the community also organises regular hackathons which have turned out some brilliant solutions.
Bringing people together is incredibly important but the value of a community is not only in the events it organises. It is in the opportunities it creates as a place for people to ask questions, share experience, and learn from colleagues who have faced and overcome similar challenges.
Beyond catalysing an organic approach to building capacity, we are also developing more structured pathways for embedding data skills professionally.
We launched the Data Profession last November, bringing together colleagues from across the Bank whose work involves data into a single professional community. It covers disciplines including data science, data analytics and data governance, helping us take a more joined-up approach to the data skills we need, how we recruit and develop people, and the career pathways and support available to them.
Building our capabilities also means broadening access to opportunities. I am pleased to say that our recently established partnership with Women in Data helps this through a range of initiatives supporting our commitment to greater representation and inclusivity in the workplace.
Like our data tools and technology, our learning approach must also keep evolving. We are working to understand shifting skills requirements across different time horizons, using a role-based approach to assessing skills profiles to help us to map the work different colleagues need to do, against the skills required to do it effectively, and the most appropriate ways to support them in addressing any gaps.
So, we are equipping colleagues to safely achieve new insights by using new capabilities including AI, with effective guardrails, and by providing the right training.
Empower – by supporting colleagues to innovate
Investing in equipping and enabling our people is important, but to unlock its full potential, we need to empower colleagues to try innovative new approaches in their roles. This is not just about doing what we already do more efficiently. It is also about opening up new possibilities, helping colleagues work differently and undertake types of analysis that simply were not possible before. Ultimately, it is about giving people the tools and confidence to evolve with the world around us.
Support
Like many organisations, we want to reduce the costs to trying new innovative approaches and to avoid the risks of this happening in siloes. To do so, we are bringing together a dedicated team of experts from both our data and technology functions to act as an innovation hub for the Bank as a whole. The aim is to support colleagues to understand the range of tools available to facilitate innovative work and to support them to bring insights from across different teams. The idea is not that we try to do the innovative analytical work centrally, but instead to be a centre of excellence and smooth the way for the innovative work that the various business functions of the Bank want to achieve. This includes a forum where local business and central support functions’ representatives can meet, share developments, and to prioritise work to achieve the biggest benefits.
Culture
Finally, we need a culture that gives colleagues the confidence to try something new. Sometimes trying something new feels daunting. We want colleagues to feel that innovation is part of their role – that they are empowered to question how something is done today, explore whether there might be a better way, and have a safe environment in which to test new approaches, which can be supported by the innovation hub. It gives colleagues somewhere to experiment with the right support and safeguards around them, reducing some of the barriers to trying something new. Of course, the design of this needs to be appropriate for the evolving culture of the Bank, just like a well-designed house needs to work in the place where it’s built and for the people who live there.
Senior leaders have an important role here too. We need to visibly take the lead in encouraging people across the organisation to innovate, make space for them to do it, and celebrate the examples that demonstrate what is possible. Over time, that is how we make innovation feel more like a natural part of how we work, and why we are launching in the coming months a new leadership programme focused on leading in an increasingly digital, data and AI enabled world.

Conclusion
Let me conclude by returning to the main theme of my remarks today. Data and analytics transformation is not primarily about technology for its own sake. It is about making sure the Bank of England can continue to fulfil its mission effectively in a world where the volume of data, the sophistication of analytical tools, and the pace of technological change are all increasing rapidly.
For us, that means doing three things together. First, we need to enable colleagues by putting the right foundations in place: modern platforms, well-managed data, clear ownership and the enduring disciplines of data management. Those foundations matter because high-quality analysis, effective decision-making and responsible AI all depend on trusted and accessible data.
Second, we need to equip people with new capabilities and the confidence to use them safely. That includes making general-purpose tools such as Copilot available at scale, developing more tailored applications where there are specific business needs, and applying clear guardrails through our AI framework. But it also means investing in training, communities and professional pathways, so that people can use these tools well and understand their limits.
Third, we need to empower colleagues to innovate. The opportunities from data, analytics and AI will not be realised by a central team alone. They will come from colleagues across the organisation identifying better ways to do their work, experimenting responsibly, sharing experience, and building on each other’s successes. Our role centrally is to reduce the friction, provide expertise and make it easier for good ideas to move from the drawing board to practical use.
We cannot stand still and our job is not done. At the Bank, our ambition is to build on the progress we have made and keep moving forward: enabling colleagues with trusted foundations, equipping them with safe and effective capabilities, and empowering them to innovate in support of the public good.
The technology around us will continue to evolve and expectations of what is possible will continue to rise in the era of AI. But keeping pace is not just about technology. It is also about continuing to learn from one another. The work of communities such as DAMA has a vital role to play in bringing people together, sharing practical experience as we are today, and ensuring that even as technology moves quickly, the standards underpinning our data remain strong. Thank you.
And if Kevin McCloud is in the audience, ignore what I said earlier – you're welcome to come to the Bank any time you want!
Acknowledgements
I would like to thank Aimee Newmarch and Miranda Hewkin Smith for their assistance in drafting these remarks. I would also like to thank, Nay Assassa, Karen Bassett, David Bradnum, Jane Cathrall, Benjamin Crampton, Elizabeth Hall, Rachel Heppinstall, Alan Hicks, Rebecca Jackson, Sarah John, Neil Kisserli, Georgios Kyriakopoulos, Leslie Lambert, Clare Lombardelli, Phillippa Loveridge, Pat O'Connor, Arshadur Rahman and Paul Robinson for their input and helpful comments.

articles.title: Main findings from the ECB’s recent contacts with non-financial companies
articles.text: Main findings from the ECB’s recent contacts with non-financial companiesPrepared by Davide Fantino, Alex Melemenidis, Richard Morris, Zsuzsanna Riedel and Moreno RomaThis box summarises the main findings from recent contacts between ECB staff and representatives of 64 leading non-financial companies operating in the euro area.[1] For further information on the nature and purpose of these contacts, see Elding, Morris and Slavík (2021). The exchanges mainly took place between 28 September and 7 October 2026.Reports from contacts pointed to ongoing moderate growth in activity in the third quarter and towards unchanged momentum in the fourth quarter (Chart A and Chart B). Activity in the manufacturing sector was uneven with a very strong rise in demand for high value-added electronics, electrical equipment and related machinery. Meanwhile, many other industries continued to struggle with low, flat or declining volumes amid intensifying import competition. Construction and real estate activity were also losing momentum. The hot and dry summer weighed on agricultural output and food production, but it increased the demand for air conditioning and thereby raised energy output. Retail trade and related transport services remained relatively subdued, but most other business and consumer services experienced good growth.Chart ASummary of views on activity, employment, prices and costs(averages of ECB staff scores)Source: ECB.Notes: The scores reflect the average of scores given by ECB staff in their assessment of what contacts said about quarter-on-quarter developments in activity (sales, production and orders), input costs (material, energy, transport, etc.) and selling prices, and about year-on-year wage developments. Scores range from -2 (significant decrease) to +2 (significant increase). A score of 0 denotes no change. For the current round, previous quarter and next quarter refer to the third and fourth quarters of 2026 respectively, while for the previous round these refer to the second and third quarters of 2026. Discussions with contacts in January and in March/April regarding wage developments normally focus on the outlook for the current year compared with the previous year, while discussions in June/July and September/October focus on the outlook for the next year compared with the current year. The historical average is an average of scores compiled using summaries of past contacts extending back to 2008.Chart BViews on developments in and the outlook for activity(averages of ECB staff scores)Source: ECB.Notes: The scores reflect the average of scores given by ECB staff in their assessment of what contacts said about quarter-on-quarter developments in activity (sales, production and orders). Scores range from -2 (significant decrease) to +2 (significant increase). A score of 0 denotes no change. The dot refers to expectations for the next quarter.Contacts painted a mixed but still mostly subdued picture of consumer spending. Retailers continued to perceive consumers’ price sensitivity and resulting downtrading as a major determinant of consumption dynamics, especially in Germany and France where consumer sentiment was particularly low. Contacts in – or supplying – the consumer durable goods sector reported weak or falling demand for furniture and household appliances, attributed in part to subdued housing investment. However, they noted rising demand for consumer electronics (in anticipation of rising prices) and passenger cars. In the case of passenger cars, this was reflected in surging demand for battery electric vehicles owing to high fuel prices and rapidly growing purchases of hybrid vehicles imported from China. Growth in spending on consumer services was said to be relatively robust, especially for digital services (mobile data etc.). Despite being negatively affected by the conflict in the Middle East, tourism-related spending was proving resilient as destinations in the euro area benefited from the diversion of tourism away from destinations closer to conflict areas.Growth in business investment and spending was increasingly driven by AI, electrification, defence and aerospace, although activity and investment in many sectors remained subdued. Contacts in the software and IT consulting industries reported ongoing, exceptional growth as customers accelerated their digital transformation, modernised legacy infrastructure, adopted cloud solutions and increasingly integrated AI into their processes. Such demand was particularly strong in the public, defence, health, life sciences, technology and utility sectors. Geopolitical independence was an important consideration with firms increasingly seeking to keep data within sovereign frameworks. Euro area engineering exports were already benefiting from the global data centre construction boom and data centre construction was also gathering pace in the euro area. Geopolitical concerns underpinned surging demand for defence and aerospace equipment, while high oil and gas prices, as well as data centre construction, were generating increasing demand for renewable energy infrastructure. Activity and investment in the steel industry was starting to benefit from recent policy changes – most notably, the application of stricter import quotas and tariffs since 1 July 2026. However, other process industries, such as food, chemicals, textiles, pulp and paper, continued to face weak demand amid high energy, labour and regulatory costs and intense international competition, causing them to scale back investment. Concerns about rising government bond yields and upcoming elections in some countries also weighed on the business outlook.Employment dynamics remained subdued. On balance, contacts reported declining headcounts in both the manufacturing sector and, albeit to a lesser extent, the services sector. Reductions in employment remained strong in manufacturing industries undergoing structural cost-cutting to regain international competitiveness. However, this was partly offset by growth in sectors such as IT, aerospace, defence and energy, as well as in firms supplying those sectors. In services, many contacts reported a stable employment outlook as a rise in demand could be met through productivity gains, with AI increasingly cited as a facilitator. Meanwhile, recruitment agencies pointed to moderating declines or modest increases in staffing, although this was mainly driven by temporary placements rather than permanent hiring.Contacts reported stronger increases in selling prices in the third quarter, amid higher than anticipated cost pressures, with some moderation expected in the fourth quarter (Chart C). This pass-through was particularly difficult – and more limited – in consumer-facing sectors. Around 90% of contacts from consumer-facing firms said that the pass-through to selling prices was only partial or limited, compared with less than half of those from business-facing firms (Chart D). The main reasons were cited as weak demand and competitiveness pressures. Consistent with this, selling price growth was expected to moderate somewhat in the coming months. However, contacts expected that cost pressure would continue to be felt by many into 2027 as hedges would continue to expire, agricultural commodity prices would rise and supplier price increases would continue to feed through.Chart CViews on developments in and the outlook for prices(averages of ECB staff scores)Source: ECB.Notes: The scores reflect the average of scores given by ECB staff in their assessment of what contacts said about quarter-on-quarter developments in selling prices. Scores range from -2 (significant decrease) to +2 (significant increase). A score of 0 denotes no change. The dot refers to expectations for the next quarter.Chart DAssessment of the pass-through of higher costs resulting from the Middle East conflict to selling prices(percentage of responses)Source: ECB.Expectations for decelerating wage growth have moderated somewhat (Chart E). On average, the quantitative indications provided by contacts imply that wage growth is expected to slow from 3.2% in 2025 to 3.0% in 2026 and 2.9% in 2027. This is a milder deceleration than in previous survey rounds. Consistent with this, around 40% of contacts thought that the uptick in inflation caused by the conflict in the Middle East would result – or risked resulting in – higher wage demands (up from 20% during the previous survey round). Most, however, still did not anticipate any notable impact on wage growth, citing the subdued economic conditions and employment outlook.Chart EQuantitative assessment of wage growth(percentages)Source: ECB.Notes: Averages of perceptions of wage growth of contacts in their sector in 2025 and their expectations for 2026 and 2027. The averages for 2025, 2026 and 2027 are based on indications provided by 50, 55 and 51 respondents respectively.Contacts had been negatively surprised by the duration of the conflict in the Middle East but positively surprised by how firms had adapted to it. This round, we asked our contacts how they assessed the impact of the conflict in the Middle East on business conditions in their sector and how this compared with their expectations at the onset of the conflict. Around 40% said that activity in their sector had decreased as a consequence, while 20% said it had increased. Most, however, emphasised the impact on costs with almost 80% saying that costs had risen. Views were rather equally split between those saying that the impact on their business had been “worse than” or “better than” expected. Those that thought the impact had been worse than expected tended to point to the duration of the conflict, which contrasted with prior expectations for a more rapid resolution. Those that thought the impact had been better than expected instead pointed to the surprising resilience and adaptability of businesses and their supply chains. Some attributed this to what firms had learned and how they had adapted, as well as the information systems they had put in place, following a series of shocks (tariffs, pandemic and war) over the past decade.ReferencesElding, C., Morris, R. and Slavík, M. (2021), “The ECB’s dialogue with non-financial companies”, Economic Bulletin, Issue 1, ECB. For further information on the nature and purpose of these contacts, see Elding, Morris and Slavík (2021).

articles.title: Corporate bonds: Finding alpha in an efficient market - BNP Paribas Asset Management - Corporate English
articles.text:
Corporate bond markets may be well researched, but that doesn’t mean opportunities for investors are hard to find. The key is knowing where to look. As Charles Cresteil, Investment Specialist, and Anthony Desrousseaux, Portfolio Manager, explain to Chief Market Strategist, Daniel Morris, active managers can uncover opportunities by identifying mispriced bonds, comparing securities from the same issuer and exploiting temporary market dislocations.

Differences in liquidity, investor behaviour and bond characteristics can create opportunities to generate additional returns without making big bets on the direction of interest rates or credit markets. A systematic, multi-factor approach can help investors avoid securities that appear cheap but may carry hidden risks.

Portfolio managers can pursue additional returns while keeping risk close to that of a benchmark through disciplined security selection, diversification and careful control of interest-rate sensitivity, credit exposure and issuer concentration. “A research-driven approach to corporate bond investing can seek modest but repeatable improvements in returns while keeping unintended risks in check.”

Listen to the full Talking Heads podcast for insights into effective approaches when investing in corporate bonds.

You can also listen and subscribe to Talking Heads on YouTube, Spotify, or wherever you normally get your podcasts.

XXX

Read the transcript

Daniel Morris: Hello, and welcome to the BNP Paribas Asset Management Talking Heads podcast. Every week, Talking Heads will bring you in-depth insights and analysis on the topics that really matter to investors. In this episode, we’ll be discussing enhancing returns in corporate bond markets. I’m Daniel Morris, Chief Market Strategist, and I’m joined today by Charles Cresteil, Investment Specialist and Anthony Desrousseaux, Portfolio Manager. Welcome, gentlemen, and thanks for joining me.

Charles Cresteil:

Happy to be here.

Anthony Desrousseaux:

Hello, Daniel.

DM: When we think about investing in corporate bonds, initially we think about what’s going on with central bank policy rates, with spreads, economic outlook and so on. But once you’ve taken that decision to invest in corporate bonds, what you’re really going to be looking for is how to generate the most alpha out of that investment. Where are the relative opportunities? What parts of the market do you want to invest in? And that is what you guys focus on.

If I could start with you, Charles, we think of corporate bond markets as fairly efficient. That makes the challenge of finding alpha all the more difficult. Where, for you, does the alpha come from?

CC: At first sight, corporate bond markets look highly efficient. They are widely researched, institutional investors dominate trading, and a great deal of information about issuers is available publicly. But that doesn’t mean that every bond is always perfectly priced. In fact, the structure of the market creates many small recurring opportunities. There are four main reasons for that.

The first is breadth. A large company may have five, 10 or even more bonds outstanding. Those securities were all issued by the same company but can differ in terms of maturity, seniority, currency liquidity, or even some ESG (environmental, social & governance) characteristics like green or social use of proceeds.

As a result, two bonds from the same issuer can offer different compensation for broadly the same fundamental risk. That gives us a much broader opportunity set than a market in which each company only has one listed security.

The second reason is fragmentation. Corporate bonds do not trade on a single central exchange as large-cap equities do. Liquidity varies significantly from one issue to another, and different investor groups may value the same bond differently. Insurance companies, pension funds, banks, ETFs (exchange-traded funds) and total return managers all operate with their own constraints, and their buying and selling can create temporary dislocations that are not necessarily linked to a change in the issuer[s[ long-term risk.

A third source of opportunity comes from the benchmark itself. A traditional corporate bond index is usually weighted by the amount of debt outstanding. In other words, the companies that borrow the most receive the largest index weights. That makes sense when the objective is to be representative of the overall market, but it doesn’t mean the index is optimal from an investor point of view in terms of expected risk-adjusted returns.

An active process can therefore be more selective about which issuers and which individual bonds provide good reward for their risks. And finally, prices do not always adjust at the same speed. A company’s fundamentals may improve before all its bonds fully reflect the change. A new issue may come with an attractive concession on the primary market. Or a bond may become temporarily cheap because a large investor needs to sell. These opportunities can occur repeatedly over a large investment universe.

Our objective is not to make calls on the direction of interest rates or credit markets as a whole; it is to identify a large number of small, relative value opportunities, referring one bond to another with comparable characteristics, avoiding securities where the reward looks poor compared to the credit risk and diversifying those decisions across the portfolio.

Each individual position should contribute only modestly, but together they can create a consistent source of excess return. That is the central idea: alpha in corporate bonds doesn’t have to come from big bets. It can come from a disciplined security selection approach applied across a broad market that remains fragmented and imperfectly efficient.

DM: Anthony, even though theoretically markets are supposed to be efficient, we know the reality is somewhat different. It’s nice to know there are these discrepancies in the market, but finding them is the real challenge. What are the signals you use to identify those opportunities?

AD: We use a multi-factor framework because there is no single indicator that can reliably identify attractive bonds in every market environment. A bond may look cheap, but it may be because the issuer is deteriorating. Another bond may have strong fundamentals but offer too little spread to compensate investors. The purpose of combining signals is to obtain a more balanced view of each security.

The first family of signals is valuation. How much compensation are we receiving for the risk we are taking? We compare bonds spread with those of relevant peers while adjusting for characteristics such as sector, rating, maturity and duration.

We may also compare different bonds from the same issuer. The objective is not simply to buy the bond with the wider spread, but to identify securities that appear attractively priced relative to their underlying risk.

The second family is quality. We examine the financial strength and resilience of the issuer using measures linked to profitability, leverage, cash flow, generation, balance sheet stability and the ability to service debt.

Quality is particularly important in credit because the return distribution is asymmetric. The upside on a bond is limited while the downside from a downgrade or default can be significant. A quality signal helps us avoid being paid a little more spread in exchange for a disproportionate deterioration risk.

The third family is momentum. Credit markets often adjust gradually as information is absorbed by different investors. Improving spread trends, supportive price behaviour or positive changes in market perception can indicate that a bond is moving in the right direction.

Conversely, a bond that looks statistically cheap but continues to underperform may be signalling that the market sees a problem not yet fully visible in accounting data. We also use technical and low risk indicators. Technical signals can capture elements such as issuance, liquidity, investors flows and supply demand imbalances.

Low-risk indicators help distinguish securities whose apparent return potential depends on taking excessive credit or market risk. These signals matter because a theoretically attractive valuation may not be investable. Once trading cost, liquidity and portfolio constraints are considered, we then combine the different signals into an overall assessment for each bond.

Importantly, the comparison is made within appropriate peer groups. We are generally not trying to forecast whether the entire credit market will rally or sell off. We are asking whether one bond is more attractive than another with broadly comparable characteristics.

The advantage of a systematic process is consistency and scale. The same questions can be asked across thousands of securities every time the data is updated. That does not eliminate judgement. The model, data, constraints and portfolio construction all require careful design and oversight. But it prevents the process from depending on a small number of subjective convictions.

In practice, the strongest opportunities are usually those where several independent signals agree [a] bond is reasonably valued, issued by a sound company, supported by market momentum and sufficiently liquid to trade. That combination is more robust than relying on any single factor alone.

DM: Anthony, you’ve talked about the different ways you can evaluate the markets to look for opportunities. But when it comes to portfolio management, there’s risk and return. How do you manage keeping tracking error low when you’re taking many active positions?

AD: The key is to separate active security selection from broad market exposure. We want the portfolio to remain close to its benchmark in the dimensions that investors expect, while using a limited risk budget to favour the bonds that our process finds more attractive.

Let us start with duration. If the portfolio has much more or much less interest-rate sensitivity than the benchmark, performance can be dominated by a view on government bond yields that may produce a positive result, but it’s not the type of alpha we are trying to deliver. We therefore keep duration tightly aligned with the benchmark, both at the portfolio level and, where relevant, across maturity segments.

We apply the same discipline to credit exposure. A portfolio could outperform simply by holding systematically lower-rated bonds or by taking more exposure to volatile sectors. Again, that would be a broad beta decision rather than evidence of successful security selection. We therefore control rating spread, duration, sector allocation and other measures of credit sensitivity. The objective is that the portfolio does not need a strong market rally to succeed.

Issuer concentration is another important control. Even when the model identifies a very attractive bond, we do not want the result to depend excessively on one company.

Corporate credit has an asymmetric risk profile. A single adverse event can have a meaningful impact, while the upside from any individual bond is naturally capped. Position limits help ensure that no single issuer or security dominates the portfolio.

Active risk portfolio construction then brings all these elements together. The process looks for the best combination of expected attractiveness and controlled risk. For example, if we overweight one bond in one sector, we may underweight a less attractive bond with similar duration and credit characteristics. The broad exposures largely offset one another, leaving the relative value preference as the main active decision. This is how we try to isolate alpha from beta.

Diversification is crucial. Instead of making a few large calls, we spread the risk budget across many modest positions. Each preference may have only a small impact on tracking error but the portfolio can contain a large number of such decisions. If those signals contain useful information and are sufficiently independent, their combined contribution can become meaningful while the effect of any individual error remains limited.

We also account for liquidity and turnover. A portfolio that looks attractive before cost may be much less compelling after bid/offer spreads and market impact. Trading therefore needs to be selective. We do not want to react to every small change. The expected benefit of a trade should exceed its likely cost. Low tracking error is not achieved by avoiding active positions. It is achieved by being precise about which risk we want to take and which we want to neutralise.

We accept diversified research-based security selection risk. We tightly constrain unintended duration. Market beta sector and concentration risk. The result is a portfolio designed to preserve the benchmark characteristics that matter to investors while seeking a modest but repeatable improvement in return.

DM: Well, Charles, Anthony, thank you very much for joining me.

CC: Thanks for having us.

AD: Thank you, Daniel.

DM: That’s it for this week’s episode of Talking Heads. If you would like more information about our capabilities in investing in corporate bonds, please reach out to your asset management contact or check out Viewpoint, our website, for investment insights at viewpoint.bnpparibas-am.com. The Talking Heads podcast is available on Spotify and on YouTube. For YouTube, visit YouTube.com bnppam playlist and tap or click on Talking Heads.

You’ve been listening to the BNP Paribas Asset Management Talking Heads podcast with me, Daniel Morris, Charles Cresteil, Investment Specialist, and Anthony Desrousseaux, Portfolio Manager.

Please do join me next week. Until then, take care.

There is only one Goldman Sachs.Discover CareersWORKING AT GSStudentsLife at GSBenefitsFeatured OfficesOpen RolesMarketsEmerging Market Credit Shows Resilience amid Energy ShockNov 5, 2026Share Weathering recent global shocks with newfound stability, emerging market credit has matured into a resilient and diverse asset class, according to Goldman Sachs Asset Management. As their capital markets and economies have developed over the past decade, emerging market bonds are less constrained by the US dollar. Robust improvements in the quality and depth of financial data are helping drive the growth of emerging market corporate bonds. Investors must be selective in a diversifying market with a rising number of issuers of government and corporate debt.When the Iran war triggered a surge in oil prices this year, many investors may have expected credit markets in the developing world to slide into a selloff.
Instead, emerging market sovereign and corporate bonds weathered the shock with a newfound stability and solid performance for investors.
The development is a key sign that emerging market credit is maturing into a resilient asset class, according to Anupam Damani, co-head and senior portfolio manager of emerging market debt at Goldman Sachs Asset Management. At the same time, investors are rethinking their approach to the market, which has trillions of dollars in outstanding debt.
“Emerging market credit is now unrecognizable, and I mean that in a good way,” Damani says. “These bonds used to come with a crisis label, but this market is no longer monolithic. In my view, it has become a more diverse and resilient asset class, though risks remain.”
To be sure, emerging market bonds run the gamut in terms of risk, and investors must be selective about what they trade in a marketplace with myriad issuers, she adds.
We spoke with Damani about the changing dynamics in the asset class, including the growth of emerging market corporate bonds and a less binding US dollar.
Emerging market credit used to be a byword for volatility. What has changed and what opportunities does the asset class now offer investors?

For a long time, emerging market credit (EM credit) was considered a risk-on or a risk-off trade. Now, there are what we like to call more dispersed opportunity sets, or more names to choose from. We believe this reflects fundamental improvements that may have reduced binary tail risk—the all-or-nothing quality that used to define EM credit. In our view, this has become an asset class where credit selection really matters. The market has matured.
In the sovereign space, for example, you’ll see deep local-currency markets with stronger reserve buffers. This means more liquidity. There are also more credible inflation-policy frameworks and deeper domestic investor bases.
This policy shift seems significant.

It is, and this trend is unfolding across regions, from Asia to Latin America, Eastern Europe, and Africa. I believe these changes have anchored the market very differently than in the past. There used to be only a few countries in the EM sovereign space. Now, there are more than 80 countries offering a far wider range of potential opportunities.
How are investors responding to these changes?

Well, it’s been an evolution. There are countries that are developing strong institutions, and there are always going to be a few countries that are moving backward. This isn’t a linear progression across the asset class. But on an aggregate level, I think there has been a greater focus on fiscal orthodoxy and monetary orthodoxy.
And to see the results, look at how many major emerging markets are running close to their inflation targets, with significant GDP growth, even in the face of the energy supply shock this year. When you look at developed markets, investors are struggling to see the same kind of discipline. Indeed, investors are increasingly demanding a higher risk premium to own some developed market assets.
In my view, what’s interesting is that in emerging markets, there has always been a demand for higher risk premiums because of perceived notions around governance and weakness in policy frameworks. I think this has moved quite a bit.
And corporate bonds? Has that market changed as well?

EM credit used to be largely a sovereign-only market. Today, we have a rapidly evolving market for corporates. And issuers are companies with footprints that extend beyond their borders—they are globally competitive, industry leaders that deal in hard currency. They are supported by local markets, with domestic consumer investor bases that have become larger and deeper in recent years.
In fixed income, we believe emerging market corporates have historically offered attractive Sharpe ratios, or risk-adjusted performance, relative to many other sectors. In our view, this reflects the bonds' strong resilience, credit quality, and lower duration.

Has the role of the US dollar changed in emerging market debt?

Yes. The US dollar constraint is less binding than it used to be in previous cycles. In the 1990s, for instance, issuance was overwhelmingly dollar-driven, so when the dollar appreciated massively, your payment capacity was reduced as the local currency cost of servicing the debt rose. Now that effect is decreasing with the growth of local-currency sovereign debt markets. Emerging market countries are also issuing more debt in euros and renminbi.
Fixed income investors need reliable data to size up credit risk. Are issuers improving the quality of information?

We believe this is an underappreciated development in the EM credit story. There used to be a transparency discount for investors because data on issuers was considered too opaque. If you look at the investable universe in EM corporates today, disclosure looks much closer to what we see in developed markets.
There is standardized reporting of data under International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS) or IFRS-aligned frameworks. This improves comparability across regions and sectors, which we didn’t have in the past. Balance sheet transparency is also far stronger.
Issuers have also improved communications with investors—quarterly reporting, presentations, earnings calls, roadshows—just as we see in developed markets. When there are negative developments in a country or broader industry, those communications tend to pick up. You didn’t see this type of healthy dialogue between issuers and investors in the past.
Global markets have recently sustained two shocks: US tariffs and the Middle East energy supply crunch. What is the fallout for emerging market credit?

It’s a pertinent question for the asset class. In our view, what’s important is the convergence around institutional frameworks, orthodox policies on inflation, and stronger fiscal reserve positions. These developments may have increased the ability of emerging markets to better absorb these types of shocks. In this cycle, for example, we have not seen uniform stress across the market but rather a dispersion across credits.
This is an important point. If you look at what’s happening in the Middle East, we have oil prices shooting up. In emerging market credit, we have energy exporters and importers, right? This creates greater differentiation across issuers in the marketplace rather than the broad-based selloffs seen in some prior EM crises.
And it shows that over the years, many developing economies have learned from their mistakes and tried to make changes that make them more resilient. So returns are increasingly driven by fundamentals and valuations, and that is a very different proposition from simply owning what we used to call the EM beta trade.

articles.title: From commitment to delivery: How institutions turn development and climate priorities into results
articles.text:
Published on
Voices

From commitment to delivery: How institutions turn development and climate priorities into results

Arturo Herrera Gutierrez

Jamie Fergusson

November 05, 2026

This page in:

English

Français

Español

English

Français

Español

Copyright: tomperry.com.au/ World Bank Group.

Countries have their own climate and development goals and priorities, often ambitious ones. The key challenge is turning these goals and priorities into action. Finance matters, but so do the institutions that translate ambitions into investment decisions, carry priorities through budgets, and implement projects effectively. Drawing on evidence from 103 economies, this year’s Country Climate and Development Report (CCDR) summary, Governance for Climate and Development, examines how governments can bridge the gap from commitment to results.
Opportunities for smart development are clearer than ever
Five years of CCDRs show that climate and development are inseparable. Without action, climate impacts could reduce GDP by roughly 1 to 20 percent by 2050, depending on the country. The right policies can change that trajectory. In Nigeria, for example, climate change could push an additional 5.1 million people into poverty by 2035, while adaptation measures assessed in the country’s CCDR could protect about 3 million of them.
The potential benefits go beyond avoiding losses. Across low- and middle-income countries, adaptation interventions could raise labor income, creating and protecting the equivalent of 150 million jobs by 2050.
The harder task is prioritization and allocation
In some low- and lower-middle-income economies, investment needs for climate and development exceed 5 percent of GDP a year. Governments must balance priorities and determine how much to spend and how to spend it well. About 57 percent of CCDR recommendations propose spending better, compared with 42 percent that call for more investment.
Three functions that turn commitment into action
The report identifies three institutional functions for delivering climate commitments: designing and enacting laws that establish responsibility, planning to turn goals into programs, and ensuring that public financial management links those programs to budgets and implementation. Each function builds on the previous one.

Laws create the authority to act. Climate framework laws turn policy goals into legal obligations, assign responsibilities, and help commitments outlast changes in government. More than 50 of the 103 economies benefiting from CCDRs have enacted such laws or have them in draft or preparation. The most effective frameworks extend responsibility across the public sector. For instance, Argentina requires every jurisdiction to prepare a climate response plan, while Fiji’s law applies to state entities, including state-owned enterprises. These examples show how laws can distribute responsibility, but delivery also depends on regulations, mandates, staff, and resources.
Planning translates long-term goals into sequenced priorities. Climate and development challenges cannot be solved overnight. Governments must decide which problems to address, when, and in what order. Country cases show how development and climate priorities can align: one-third of Uganda’s Fourth National Development Plan overlaps with its updated national climate commitment; and Türkiye’s climate objectives are included in its latest National Development Plan. Yet alignment alone is not enough. When budgets are formally linked to plans, planning becomes a powerful driver of delivery; when that link is weaker, success depends on whether priorities carry through into budget decisions.
Public financial management turns plans into results. Priorities need funding, and funds need to be spent well. More than 40 economies have adopted or are developing climate budget tagging to track how spending supports climate goals. Georgia now applies it across programs representing more than 80 percent of expenditure. However, execution matters as much as allocation. In Colombia, the CCDR finds that climate-informed municipal spending would increase if local governments had greater capacity to design and implement projects.

Governments have extensive experience in regulating citizens and the private sector when it comes to climate change. But only recently has it been acknowledged that as governments function, they also contribute to climate change. For example, state-owned enterprises account for 30 percent of global greenhouse gas emissions and include many of the largest energy, transport, and industrial firms. To capture the public sector's impact, IPSASB SRS 1, the first public-sector climate disclosure standard, was launched this year, with reporting to start in January 2028.
Additionally, as major buyers, governments can create demand for cleaner goods. Public fleets, from postal vans to ambulances, illustrate this influence. The Azerbaijan CCDR proposes procurement to electrify the public fleet and expand charging infrastructure. Buying cleaner vehicles at scale sends a signal to manufacturers to invest in sustainable transport technologies.
The road ahead
CCDRs provide evidence for client-driven, climate-smart development, helping countries identify priorities and integrate them into broader development strategies. Around 85 percent of recent World Bank Group Country Partnership Frameworks reflect CCDR findings. With more than 100 economies covered by CCDRs, we will build on the first generation of reports, with a greater emphasis on jobs, nature, and private capital mobilization.
No single reform path fits every country. Governments can start where change matters most: putting mandates into practice, linking plans to budgets, or improving execution. Institutional capacity and finance reinforce each other; countries investing in both are better positioned to turn climate ambition into development gains.
As countries prepare for COP31, the challenge is to ensure that governments can deliver. Finance and institutional capacity need to advance together.

articles.title: Margins matter in US midterm elections | RBCCM
articles.text:
The U.S. military escalation against Iran appears increasingly likely despite growing pre-election pressure, with both Washington and Tehran maintaining entrenched negotiating positions. The conflict has proven impervious to pre-election off-ramps, expanding in scope with Houthi entry into the war. Regional talks in Tehran and Vice President Vance's reported outreach to Iran's hardline Supreme National Security Council secretary suggest the administration is calibrating rather than reversing course.
The critical strategic question is whether U.S. military action will constitute a final strike before withdrawal, or will be a more extensive operation designed to finish the job and orchestrate regime change. Some regional actors warn that a brief escalation followed by hasty exit would essentially amount to an Iranian victory despite reconstruction costs. Others caution that a sweeping military campaign dramatically increases the risk of Iranian retaliatory strikes on critical civilian infrastructure, including desalination facilities, alongside expanded proxy attacks on U.S. allies throughout the region.
While Congress cannot force an end to the war, Democratic control of either or both chambers will likely intensify efforts to control the purse strings. Even if the administration maintains veto authority over broad policy reversals, Democratic gains could embolden Republicans to challenge the administration's authority on Iran war funding through year-end defense legislation. With the size of Tuesday's Democratic victory determining the degree of Republican defections likely, the midterm results will substantially influence congressional leverage over military spending and escalation decisions heading into 2027.
A Democratic House victory would trigger a wave of hearings and investigations on energy deals involving administration insiders and military actions affecting major global producers. Venezuela will face intense scrutiny, with lawmakers seeking to determine whether oil companies had advance knowledge of the January military operation against Nicolás Maduro. Inquiries could expand to examine whether companies received privileged information or benefited from the operation, and challenge the Pentagon's authority to take a 35 percent stake in North American Blue Energy Partners.

"Even if the [Democratic] party only captures the House of Representatives, we anticipate a wave of hearings and investigations on energy deals involving administration insiders, as well as military actions/foreign policy decisions involving key global producers."
Helima Croft, Head of Global Commodity Strategy and MENA Research, RBC Capital Markets

Russia sanctions waivers and the recent diesel deal will draw bipartisan criticism, particularly from GOP Russia critics including Senators Susan Collins, Mitch McConnell, and Lisa Murkowski. Democratic-led committees will review the administration's suspension of sanctions measures mandated by the Graham Act, which authorizes 100 percent secondary tariffs on imports from Russia oil purchasers and imposes further restrictions on Russian banks and energy investment.
The scale of a Democratic victory could influence whether Republicans defect to challenge the administration's waiver authority through defense legislation. Beyond Venezuela and Russia, congressional reviews will likely examine government equity stakes in critical mineral firms and CFTC investigations into large energy trades around Iran war developments.
Growing concerns over electricity affordability could reshape the administration's data center acceleration initiative, despite likely bipartisan backing for AI and data center infrastructure expansion. The House's bipartisan passage of the Ratepayer Protection Act signals growing support for requiring data centers to shoulder their own costs. Democratic control would pursue stricter oversight, with House Judiciary ranking member Jamie Raskin already investigating major hyperscalers over nondisclosure agreements with local governments regarding data center projects.

View detailed data

Figure 2, titled "Iran War Tops Midterm Voter Priorities*," is a horizontal bar chart ranking nine political, economic, and geopolitical issues by their mean importance rating from voters on a 1-to-5 scale, with the x-axis displaying a truncated range from 3.0 to 4.0. From highest to lowest, the issues and their approximate mean scores are: Iran War at approximately 3.87 (highlighted in yellow), Jobs at approximately 3.80, Tariff Policy at approximately 3.72, Immigration at approximately 3.69, Gas Prices at approximately 3.69 (highlighted in yellow), AI Regulation at approximately 3.66, Interest Rates at approximately 3.55, Israel-Gaza at approximately 3.32, and Data Centers at approximately 3.21 (highlighted in yellow). The remaining bars are dark navy blue. The footer notes the sources as Emerson College and RBC Capital Markets, based on a National Poll conducted September 21–22, 2026, where respondents rated each issue from 1 (least important) to 5 (most important), with scores representing mean ratings and a sample size of n=1000.

Democratic congressional control could complicate broader efforts to expand conventional energy production and roll back environmental regulations. New majorities could investigate federal leasing decisions, environmental deregulation, and DOE funding allocations. Clean energy developers could benefit from heightened oversight of restrictions on offshore wind and solar approvals, though presidential veto authority and existing executive powers would limit Democrats' ability to reverse policies or reinstate repealed incentives.
Bipartisan permitting reform offers the clearest avenue for legislative cooperation, yet skepticism remains that this historical nonstarter could succeed post-election. The recently introduced American Affordability and Jobs Act seeks to accelerate energy infrastructure development across conventional and renewable technologies, though Democrats increasingly demand assurances against discriminatory treatment of clean energy projects. A sizable Democratic victory could strengthen their leverage, potentially complicating passage in the lame-duck session.
Ultimately, Democratic gains could constrain the administration's energy agenda through congressional oversight and legislative leverage, even as the administration pursues priorities through executive and regulatory authority.

Helima Croft authored "Washington Strategy: Margins Matter," published on October 28, 2026. For more information on the full report, please contact your RBC representative.

PERSPECTIVES Weekly Podcast

November 2 – US midterm elections, AI, and the Fed

Ready to talk?

×

The US midterm election takes centre stage this week, and the outcome will have a big impact on markets for a long time, says Markus Müller, the Private Bank's head of the CIO office and Chief Investment Officer for Sustainability.

“The interesting question isn't simply who wins,” Markus says. “It's what the result ultimately means for fiscal policy, US debt, and then finally the bond market.”

In addition to counting ballots, markets also remain preoccupied with the AI buildout – the spending behind it, and signs that it is bearing fruit. “Financial markets are increasingly focused on one fundamental question, which is, will the enormous amount of investments going into AI ultimately be justified by the returns?”, Markus says.

On the data front this week, “the US labour market remains absolutely central”, Markus says, pointing to the monthly US jobs report, but also data on job openings, labor turnover, and a private reading of employment numbers. “Taken together, they can give us a better understanding of what's actually happening in the US labour market.”

articles.title: A Silver Lining Or A Shovel?
articles.text:
A Silver Lining Or A Shovel?

Louis-Vincent Gave

Gavekal Research | 3 Nov 2026

In recent meetings with North American clients, the first question clients asked is whether bond yields in the US have risen enough to buy US treasuries (answer: most likely “yes”, at least in the short term, see Reasons To Start Buying Bonds and Why Bonds Respond To The Fed, Not To Inflation). And almost invariably, the second question has been: who are the mugs that will end up holding the bag on the now rapidly evolving French debt crisis? (answer: the European Central Bank and European insurance companies). These divergent perceptions underline an uncomfortable fact: as things stand, and for many investors, France has now become “uninvestible”; or at the very least too much of a career risk for most portfolio managers. After all, if France was to end up defaulting on its debt, or collapsing into some kind of civil disorder, portfolio managers would be blamed for failing to foresee an event even pre-announced on the cover of The Economist… not once but on an almost annual basis over the past decade.
