articles.title: Transitioning to mid-cycle – Market Outlook
articles.text:
30 October 2026
Global Market Outlook

Download Report

Transitioningto mid-cycle
We now favour a more balanced stance between stocks and bonds. Near-term event risks and high earnings expectations prompt us to trim equities to a Core holding. The US and Asia ex-Japan (AxJ) remain our preferred regions. We upgrade India to Overweight.

Higher bond yields are improving the outlook for future returns and offering increasingly attractive income opportunities. We are Overweight Emerging Market (EM) USD bonds and favour corporate over sovereign debt, but limit duration to 3-7 years.

We remain Overweight gold. Prices are likely to grind higher as near-term headwinds from higher bond yields are offset by EM central bank demand.

Where are the tactical opportunities?

Are central banks likely to continue hiking rates?

Are quantitative models still bullish on equities?

Strategy
Investment strategy and key themes

Steve Brice

Global Chief Investment Officer

Manpreet Gill

Chief Investment Officer, AMEE

Raymond Cheng, CFA, CPA

Chief Investment Officer, North Asia

12m Foundation Overweights:

Gold
US, Asia ex-Japan equities
Emerging Market USD bonds

Opportunistic ideas – Equities

Global: High dividend
US: Healthcare^
Euro area (EA): Banks, MSCI Switzerland^
Asia: Japan banks

Top Global Sectors:

US: Technology, healthcare^, financials, materials
EA: Financials
Asia: Japan financials

Opportunistic ideas – Bonds

US: Treasury Inflation-protected Securities (TIPS), AAA-rated collateralised loan obligations (CLOs), US High-yield (HY)
Others: AUD corporates

^New

Transitioning to mid-cycle

We now favour a more balanced stance between stocks and bonds. Near-term event risks and high earnings expectations prompt us to trim equities to a Core holding. The US and Asia ex-Japan (AxJ) remain our preferred regions. Within AxJ, we upgrade India to Overweight.
Higher bond yields are improving the outlook for future returns and offering increasingly attractive income opportunities. We are Overweight Emerging Market (EM) USD bonds and favour corporate over government bonds, but limit duration to 3-7 years.
We remain Overweight gold. Prices are likely to grind higher as near-term headwinds from higher bond yields are offset by EM central bank demand.

Great expectations
Individual risk events, high earnings expectations and a higher cost of capital point to a more moderate return environment ahead. In the very near term, financial markets must navigate key event risks, such as (i) the US mid-term elections, which have historically been associated with elevated market volatility and (ii) renewed geopolitical tensions, with several reports suggesting the US is considering renewed strikes on Iran. These concerns have pushed the Brent oil price well above USD 110/bbl despite significant ongoing crude oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz.
Higher bond yields combined with high earnings expectations raise the risk of an expectations reset. The US Q3 earnings season is attracting significant attention given high earnings expectations, particularly for the AI sector. However, higher US bond yields may start to bite as debt-financed capex takes on a greater share of total capex over the coming year. This, combined with already-high expectations, raises the risk of disappointment and a near-term repricing of expected earnings growth pace.
Despite the current challenges, healthy growth continues to underpin the economic backdrop. The US economic outlook remains well supported, and the absolute level of year-ahead earnings expectations is high. We do not expect Fed rate hikes to result in overly restrictive policy. Our caution, thus, stems from the risk of an expectations repricing rather than an outright economic slowdown.

Fig. 1 Our quant model score has fallen to levels associated with flat-to-modestly-negative equity returns
Our quantitative stock-bond model

Source: Bloomberg, Standard Chartered

A more balanced stock-bond mix
We trim global equities to a Core holding, leaving us Neutral on both equities and bonds and Overweight gold. The concerns laid out earlier point to near-term volatility risks and a somewhat lower long-term growth trajectory for equities. Our quant model also reflects this cautious outlook, having downgraded equities to a level usually associated with flat-to-modestly-negative returns.
From a relative perspective, though, the higher yields on offer from bonds also raise the bar by presenting an increasingly compelling return outlook after several years of very low yields. We believe this argues for portfolios that are increasingly balanced between equities and bonds.
Ways to diversify equity exposure
We continue to favour global equity market diversification, with a preference for US and AxJ equities. We remain Overweight US and AxJ equities, expecting them to outperform other major regions. Earnings growth remains the main driver of this view – while growth rates could decelerate somewhat, we still expect them to remain higher than those of other major regions.
Japan and Euro area equities remain attractive as regional diversifiers. Our positive view on both markets’ financial sectors supports our Core holding view on them.
Within Asia, we are Overweight Taiwan and India. Indian equities have lagged the region this year, in part due to limited listed AI-related exposure. However, we believe this is increasingly likely to become an advantage as investors seek greater diversification away from excessive concentration in the AI theme. This comes at a time when the economic and earnings growth outlook for Indian equities is starting to improve. We retain a more Neutral view on Chinese equities amid a still-challenging growth outlook.
We also favour greater sector diversification. In the US, we favour diversifying across our Overweight sectors of technology, financials, materials and healthcare. We also favour financials in Japan and the Euro area.

Fig. 2 Negative gold-USD correlation has held back gold amid USD strength. This is unlikely to persist
Gold and USD correlations over the last 15 years

Source: Bloomberg, Standard Chartered

Changes to our equity opportunistic ideas also reflect a more defensive stance. In recent weeks, we have closed our global semiconductors, MSCI Taiwan, US communication services and global power & electrification ideas and have opened new ideas on US healthcare and MSCI Switzerland.
Riding the yield train
We believe bond markets offer an attractive opportunity to lock in yields. The 10-year US government bond yield is now in a range last witnessed in 2007. While the process of rising yields results in lower bond prices – as painfully experienced in recent months – the yield level itself starts to significantly improve the outlook for future returns.
Favour corporate over government bonds, but check your duration. Still-high credit quality means that we continue to favour taking on credit risk to earn a higher yield (EM USD bonds are preferred, but we also see investment-grade (IG) and high-yield (HY) bonds as Core holdings). However, limiting duration to 3-7 years remains key to avoiding excessive exposure to any inflation surprises.
Changes to our bond opportunistic ideas also reflect a more balanced stance. We close our EU bank contingent convertible bonds (CoCos2 – please refer page 27) and US utilities corporate hybrids ideas. We also close our opportunistic idea on US 10-year government bonds following the recent pullback in yields, locking in gains.
Alternatives and gold to remain relevant
Alternatives are an effective tool for portfolio risk management. Hedge funds and private markets provide a differentiated return stream, while rotating into alternatives helps reduce equity beta exposure. We examine downside capture and how beta is reduced via hedge fund sub-strategies and private markets in our asset allocation section.
Gold remains a key Overweight. We trim our three- and 12-month forecasts modestly, but see gold forming a strong base above USD 4,000/oz. Rising bond yields and the USD were recent headwinds, but we expect a softer USD and continued EM central bank demand to result in 12-month gains.

Foundation asset allocation models
The Foundation and Foundation+ models are allocations that you can use as the starting point for building a diversified investment portfolio. The Foundation model showcases a set of allocations focusing on traditional asset classes that are accessible to most investors, while the Foundation+ model includes allocations to private assets that may be accessible to investors in some jurisdictions, but not others.
Fig. 3 Foundation asset allocation for a balanced risk profile

Fig. 4 Foundation+ asset allocation for a balanced risk profile

Fig. 5 Multi-asset income allocation for a moderate risk profile

Source: Standard CharteredNotes: (i) Developed Market (DM) IG Bonds is an aggregate of DM IG Government and DM IG Corporate Bonds; (ii) EM Bonds is an aggregate of EM USD and EM Local Ccy Government Bonds
Foundation: Our tactical asset allocation views

Fig. 6 Performance of our Foundation Allocations*

Source: Bloomberg, Standard Chartered; *12-month performance data from 28 October 2025 to 28 October 2026, Six-month performance from 28 April 2026 to 28 October 2026, Three-month performance from 28 July 2026 to 28 October 2026
Fig. 7 Opportunistic ideas performance

Macro overview – at a glance

Rajat Bhattacharya

Senior Investment Strategist

Key themes
Core scenario (soft landing, 45% probability): An economic soft landing remains our core scenario, with the global economy overcoming this year’s oil price shock thanks to a surge in AI investment in the US and Asia. Record wealth generation driven by the stock market rally is supporting US consumption. Fiscal easing in the US, Germany and Japan is supporting growth. Meanwhile, inflation has reaccelerated due to a rebound in fuel prices as the Middle East conflict drags on. Against this backdrop, the Fed, ECB and BoJ all hiked rates in the same month (in September) for the first time. Although all three subsequently paused in October, we expect the Fed to hike twice more, the ECB once more and the BoJ thrice more by June 2027. Nevertheless, we expect the energy and tariff effects on inflation to fade by H2 2027, enabling the Fed and the ECB to cut rates by Q3 2027. Meanwhile, China is likely to target credit easing and accelerate fiscal spending in H1 2027 to revive domestic growth.

Upside risk (no landing, 30% probability): We maintain the probability at 30% as AI-driven investment growth continues. There is a reasonable chance that lower oil prices next year, the AI-fuelled wealth boom and fiscal easing in Germany and Japan will boost ‘animal spirits’. A potential global defence spending boom, led by the US and Europe, could also lift global growth.
Downside risk (25% probability): We raised the risk of a recession to 15%, especially if central banks are forced to accelerate the pace of rate hikes to douse rising inflation. A stock market downturn negating the wealth effect or a bond sell-off due to fiscal concerns are other tail risks. We cut stagflation probability to 10% as we see low risk of oil prices sustaining above USD 120/bbl.
Key chart

The US-led AI-focused investment boom has lifted business confidence. The resulting equity market rally has boosted US household wealth, supporting consumption

Fig. 8 Robust business confidence amid AI boom; equity rally lifts US household net worth

Purchasing managers indices; US household net worth as percentage of personal disposable income

Policy rates watch
We expect the Fed to hike twice more by Q2 2027, then ease in H2 2027, as AI-led expansion continues. The US economy remains firmly in expansion. In Q3, annualised GDP growth accelerated to 3.4%, led by AI investments and consumption. In October, the composite Purchasing Managers’ Index (PMI) remained strong at 57.6. Since our last monthly report, the consensus estimate for 2026 GDP growth has been nudged up to 2.3% from 2.1%, and the 2027 estimate has risen to 2.2%. That matches the Fed’s upgraded growth projection of 2.3% for 2026, but remains below the Fed’s 2.4% estimate for 2027. AI investment, fiscal support and household wealth are the main growth drivers, although consumer activity lags business spending. Higher bond yields and elevated oil prices are headwinds, but recession risks look contained. Our core scenario remains a ‘soft landing’, at 45%, with a meaningful 30% chance of a ‘no-landing’ upside.

Rising gasoline and diesel prices pushed US core personal consumption expenditures (PCE) inflation to 0.3% m/m and 3.1% y/y, matching estimates. Consensus sees core PCE inflation slowing from 3.2% in Q4 2026 to 2.4% by Q4 2027 as energy and tariff effects fade. Underlying price momentum is softening, and recent PCE methodology revisions have lowered core inflation. However, fuel costs passed on to wider consumers and AI-driven chip shortages remain upside risks.
In October, the Fed held rates at 4.0%, after hiking in September for the first time since 2023. We expect the Fed to hike rates by 25bps in December and 25bps more in H1 2027 due to elevated near-term energy inflation. It is likely to follow with a 25bps cut to 4.25% in Q3 2027 as disinflation returns. This aligns with the Fed’s projected policy path, although it implies a more dovish trajectory than money markets, which are pricing another 56bps of hikes over the next 12 months. Political uncertainty after the mid-term election is a key risk.

ECB to hike once more in December, then pause. The Euro area recovery is firming. GDP grew 1.2% y/y in Q2 2026, up from 0.6% in Q1, and the manufacturing PMI stayed robust at 52.4 in October. Consensus 2026 growth has been raised to 1.0% from 0.9%, and 2027 is unchanged at 1.3%. The main supports are resilient exports and German infrastructure and defence spending. However, cautious consumers and soft private investment limit the recovery, and energy costs are squeezing household incomes and business margins. Recession is not the central expectation. French fiscal stress and sustained high energy costs remain the key risks.
Higher energy prices pushed Euro area headline inflation up to 3.8% y/y in September from 3.2% y/y in August, while core inflation rose to 2.5% y/y. Consensus expects headline and core inflation to ease to 2% y/y and 2.4% y/y by Q4 2027, respectively. Encouragingly, energy has had limited impact on core prices, and longer-term inflation expectations remain stable at around 2.1%. Together, these should allow inflation to moderate in 2027. The main risk is that energy, and especially gas, prices stay high for longer than expected.
The ECB held its deposit rate at 2.5% in October after raising it by 50bps this year. Inflation data continue to favour an additional hike in December. We expect an ECB rate hold in H1 2027, followed by a cut by Q3 2027 as disinflation returns. This policy path is more dovish than money markets, which are pricing more than 60bps of hikes over the next 12 months.
China to provide targeted support to defend growth floor. China’s growth momentum recovered in September. Both the manufacturing PMI (50.1) and the non-manufacturing PMI (50.2) moved back into expansion. The construction PMI rose above 50 for the first time this year as infrastructure spending started to take effect. Exports grew 36.3% y/y, pushing the trade surplus to a record USD 133.5bn. We expect growth in 2026 to meet the lower end of the 4.5-5.0% target. Growth is increasingly bifurcated, though, with technology firms and exporters doing well, while household demand stays weak.
Prices are rising again, but only narrowly. Consumer inflation edged up to 0.9% y/y in September, and producer inflation surged to 5% y/y, its highest since 2022, driven by energy and metals prices and concentrated in upstream sectors. With domestic demand weak and a high comparison base next year, the boost from energy prices is likely to fade in 2027.

domestic demand weak and a high comparison base next year, the boost from energy prices is likely to fade in 2027.
Policy is in ‘targeted easing’ mode. We expect a modest fiscal package to defend the growth floor rather than a large stimulus. The PBoC cut a key rate by 25bps to 1.5% to fund ‘Six Networks’ infrastructure projects and raised its relending quotas. A new interest subsidy on first-home mortgages provides limited support to demand. We expect no policy rate cut this year. There is still room to speed up fiscal spending, including by using CNY 500bn of unused local-government debt quota. If the PBoC switches to an overnight reverse repo rate as its policy rate, that would imply a de facto rate cut as the overnight rate is lower than the 7-day official policy rate.
BoJ to hike at a quarterly pace until Q2 2027. Japan’s economy remains solid. Wages are growing above 4%, and the labour market is tight. The main headwind is high energy prices, which is slowing growth. Fiscal spending gives some support: the FY27 draft budget includes ambitious spending plans, alongside a proposed two-year cut to the consumption tax on food and a new five-year defence programme. However, this extra spending raises questions about fiscal sustainability. The BoJ unveiled plans to triple the pace of ETF sales from January 2027, potentially funding the tax cut.
Price pressures now look firmly established. Headline and core inflation rose above 2% for the first time this year, and core-core inflation (ex-fresh food and energy) jumped to 2.4% and is expected to rise towards 3% in Q1 2027. Breakeven inflation rates have stayed above 2% most of this year. Real interest rates remain negative, hurting savers and pensioners.
The BoJ held its policy rate at 1.25% in October, after raising it in September, only three months after its previous hike. This points to an accelerated quarterly hiking pace. We expect the quarterly pace of hikes to continue, taking the rate to 2% by June 2027. Money markets have caught up with our hawkish view in recent months. The BoJ noted for the first time that underlying inflation has reached its 2% target, marking a shift from creating inflation to containing it. Politics could slow the hiking cycle in H2 2027. Two government-appointed board members voted against the September hike, and the two most hawkish members are due to leave in July 2027.

Fig. 9 Inflation is likely to ease globally by H2 2027
Consensus inflation estimates across major economies

Source: Bloomberg, Standard Chartered

Fig. 10 We expect limited central bank hikes over 12m
Our estimates of key central bank policy rates over 12 months

Asset classes
Fixed Income – at a glance

Jonathan Liang, CFA

CIO, Fixed Income & FX

Cedric Lam

Senior Investment Strategist

Ray Heung

Senior Investment Strategist

Anthony Naab, CFA

Investment Strategist

Our view
Foundation: Bond yields remain near multi-year highs, offering an attractive entry point. We view fixed income as a Core holding (ie, a Neutral allocation) in our multi-asset portfolios. Within the asset class, we maintain an Overweight stance on EM USD government bonds, given their attractive risk-reward. We hold an Underweight view on Developed Market (DM) government bonds due to the tail risks associated with term premia.
The Fed’s decision to hold rates at 3.75-4.00% in October amid still-elevated energy prices suggests that every Fed meeting from here is ‘live’, with a rate change possible on incoming data. With US inflation still running hot and the labour market tight, we expect two more 25bps hikes (one by year-end and one in H1 2027), bringing the Fed’s target range for the federal funds rate to 4.25-4.5%. We continue to favour the 3-7-year part of the US government bond yield curve as the best hedge against any risk-off move driven by AI-related growth fears. As inflation pressures ease in H2 2027, we see room for the Fed to consider a rate cut, which should pull nominal yields lower. Solid corporate fundamentals and supportive technicals should keep spreads tight, but there is limited room for them to tighten further. We still favour EM USD over local-currency (LCY) government bonds.

DM rates – Underweight
We remain Underweight DM government bonds. In the US, government bond yields have retraced meaningfully after a sharp bear steepening through September and early October. We expect real yields to stay elevated over the next six months as AI capex and productivity growth continue to drive above-trend economic growth. We expect two more 25bps rate hikes by June 2027.
Over the next few months, we expect US government bond yields to remain rangebound. The near-term path hinges on five factors: 1) the 3 November US mid-term election, where a ‘Democratic sweep’ would likely be bond-supportive by constraining US President Trump’s fiscal spending agenda, while a ‘Republican sweep’ would likely weigh on bonds as markets price in further fiscal expansion and a higher term premium; 2) Fed communication at upcoming policy meetings;

3) the US Treasury’s quarterly refunding announcement on 4 November, where any signal of reduced long-end issuance would likely compress long-end yields; 4) softening auction demand and repatriation by foreign investors, which add uncertainty around demand for US government bonds; and 5) the fluid geopolitical situation in the Middle East, which is keeping oil prices elevated, with a risk of further upside.
Going into H2 2027, we expect moderating oil prices and the fading inflationary impact of tariffs to give the Fed room to consider rate cuts. The US 30-year yield, however, is likely to stay elevated as fiscal deficit remains substantial next year.
We expect a final ECB hike to 2.75% by December 2026, then a pause in H1 2027, followed by a 25bps cut in Q3 2027. In Japan, we expect quarterly pace of BoJ hikes, with one hike that takes the policy rate to 1.50% by December 2026 and two more in H1 2027, reaching 2.00% before pausing at mid-year.

DM corporates – Core holding
We maintain a Neutral allocation to both DM IG and DM HY corporate bonds, with a tactical bias to add exposure on episodic weakness, as carry continues to dominate total returns across DM credit. Credit spreads have widened from their lows but remain close to historical tights, while yields are still attractive, reinforcing a carry-led stance. This tight-spread regime is anchored by robust issuer fundamentals, strong profitability and resilient balance sheets, despite a visible moderation in rating upgrades over the past quarter.
Technical supply dynamics are reshaping sector dispersion, especially in the IG space, where heavy AI-related issuance is weighing on the long end of the curve. AI-driven supply is surpassing USD 250bn in 2026 and making up a growing share of US IG gross issuance, but there are growing signs that hyperscalers are turning to private markets for funding, which should help ease public bond market supply pressures.
We remain selective at the long end of the yield curve and favour a duration of 3-7 years, where risk-adjusted carry remains most durable. Issuance-driven concessions in sectors with strong capex cycles (notably technology, capital goods and basic industries) present opportunities for investors who can stomach near-term volatility.

DM HY spreads have widened to roughly a six-month high. Persistent doubts about whether hyperscalers can generate adequate returns on massive AI capex investments triggered a broad risk asset sell-off. The CCC tier has become the focal point of genuine credit concern, with yields hovering near the high-15% range and spreads near a four-year high. Market focus has shifted to the funding pressures facing AI-related neocloud companies. We view this as idiosyncratic for now and see a limited impact on the broader HY universe. The underlying credit picture is mixed. Leverage is elevated and interest coverage is thin, but the broad market has not yet shown signs of systemic stress. The US HY default rate remains below trend in 2026.

HY offers an attractive income proposition, with all-in yields of over 8%. Its shorter-duration profile, combined with its lower sensitivity to changes in the term premium and rate volatility, make it an attractive sleeve in the current phase of the cycle. We remain attentive to evolving credit rating migration trends and sector-specific supply pressures, particularly as upgrades slow and new issuance clusters around key themes. However, healthy issuer fundamentals and stable credit metrics continue to support it as a Core holding allocation.

EM government bonds – Overweight USD/Core holding for LCY
We are Overweight EM USD government bonds and retain EM LCY government bonds as a Core holding, reflecting a balanced perspective across both regional performance and currency dynamics. In EM USD sovereign debt, the recent spread widening offered an attractive entry point to gain exposure to areas benefiting from resilient global growth and stable external conditions. Technicals remain favourable, with supply being front-loaded and investor positioning remaining relatively light compared with historical levels.
Many EM central banks having tightened earlier and more aggressively post-pandemic, preserving credibility and maintaining positive real rates. External balances have improved, reserve buffers have increased and greater reliance on domestic funding reduces external vulnerability. Lula’s surprise win in Brazil’s presidential election raises political risk. The country’s fiscal trajectory under the incoming administration is a key risk to monitor. Fiscal slippage could trigger a broader repricing of LATAM risk. In Asia, higher-rated issuers continue to offer a valuable buffer during bouts of global rate volatility, while select frontier exposures in EMEA remain more sensitive to liquidity shifts and changes in risk appetite. Index composition also shapes resilience: the EM USD benchmark is less exposed to oil price shocks, as countries that are not oil importers account for a larger share of the benchmark than in the LCY benchmark. We expect returns to be primarily driven by carry rather than further spread compression.

EM LCY debt faces additional headwinds, especially as elevated US real yields and an appreciating USD dampen demand from foreign investors and reduce the comparative attractiveness of broad-based duration strategies. However, real yields remain comparatively supportive in several markets, and current valuations signal selective opportunities, especially given the restrictive monetary policy stances prevalent across many EM economies. Accordingly, EM LCY bonds retain their Core holding status, with portfolio emphasis

placed on country selection and measured duration exposure, reflecting the differentiated currency dynamics at play.
Key risks to both the USD and LCY segments include a potential escalation of the Middle East conflict, higher oil prices, renewed hawkishness from the Fed that could support further USD strength and weather-related disruptions, such as the effects of El Niño. Climate risks could prolong inflation pressures and hinder disinflation in vulnerable EM regions.
Asia USD bonds – Core holding
We retain a Neutral allocation to Asia USD bonds, an asset class that continues to reward investors with attractive nominal yields, favourable supply-demand technicals and robust credit fundamentals. Healthy corporate cash flows, low leverage and a high share of sovereign-linked issuers lend the segment a defensive quality relative to broader credit.
The resilience has been evident year to date (YTD). Asia USD bonds have outperformed both DM government and DM IG corporate bonds on a total-return basis. We expect this relative strength to persist. The combination of carry and credit quality (over 60% of issues are sovereign or sovereign-related) anchors our conviction in the asset class, even as we maintain a Neutral stance.

Shifting to a mid-cycle bull market

The last few years have seen strong annual returns of 15-20% for global equities, consistent with the early cycle of a bull market, driven in large part by a rapid AI buildout. As the AI infrastructure buildout is increasingly debt funded – we estimate 40% of AI capex in 2027 would be debt-financed – the market is increasingly concerned about the quality of this growth and execution risks. We remain positive on the structural AI theme, but we expect investor focus to shift from rapid buildout to monetisation. During this transition, we expect market leadership to broaden beyond technology. We believe this shift will also be accompanied by higher near-term volatility and a moderation in global equity returns, consistent with a transition to a mid-cycle bull market.

US equities – Overweight
US equity valuations have declined this year, with the 12-month forward P/E falling to 19x from 22x at the start of the year. This reflects higher rates, a valuation headwind, and worries about the quality of growth, which is increasingly debt-funded. As market leadership broadens and the US mid-term election nears, we expect higher near-term volatility in the US market. Nonetheless, US equities have broad-based strength, with the ongoing Q3 earnings season pointing to a robust economy. In a world of rising geopolitical risks, the US is also relatively insulated by its domestically driven growth.

AxJ has the strongest earnings growth among major markets, as its technology sector remains a key beneficiary of the AI capex cycle. AxJ’s P/E valuations have also dropped to attractive trough levels, the lowest among major regions. Within AxJ, we are Overweight Taiwan, which benefits from clear visibility on AI-driven growth and dominance in manufacturing advanced AI chips. We also upgrade India to

Overweight due to its resilient domestically driven earnings, providing diversification beyond AI-related growth. India offers the highest exposure to defensive sectors (healthcare, consumer staples and utilities) within AxJ. Both Taiwan and India offer attractive returns on equity.
South Korea equities remain a Core holding. We are positive on long-term agreements that improve earnings visibility for memory chipmakers. Valuations are attractive (the lowest in AxJ), with supportive corporate governance reforms. Still, extreme volatility remains the key overhang. China remains a Core holding, given inexpensive valuations, but re-rating potential appears delayed amid AI monetisation struggles, lingering regulatory risks and weak domestic demand. We remain Underweight ASEAN, as Indonesia’s downgrade warning, oil shocks and a well-supported USD could weigh on the region, although Singapore offers defensive growth.

USD view
USD consolidation with limited upside: Our three-month US Dollar Index (DXY) forecast stands at 101, revised upwards from 100.20 last month, reflecting a higher expected Fed rate path. With the October Fed rate pause and a potential December rate hike largely priced in, further tightening would offer limited additional USD support. Persistent inflation, elevated US government bond yields and resilient business activity continue to underpin the USD’s interest-rate advantage. However, in September, payroll growth slowed sharply to 29,000 (from 133,000 in August), the unemployment rate rose to 4.2% from 4.1%, annual wage growth eased to 3.0% from 3.1% and housing starts fell 5.2% m/m. These signs of cooling demand temper expectations of more aggressive Fed tightening. We expect DXY to remain rangebound between 101 and 103, with our three-month forecast at 101.00.

Peaking Fed rates and narrowing rate differentials favour gradual USD weakness: We maintain our 12-month DXY forecast at 98.50. We expect a Fed rate hike in December 2026 and another in H1 2027, taking the federal funds target range to a peak of 4.25-4.50%, before easing in H2 2027. Further BoJ normalisation and the ECB’s relatively restrictive policy stance should progressively narrow the USD’s rate advantage. Persistent fiscal and current account deficits increase reliance on foreign capital inflows, adding to medium-term pressure on the USD. Resilient US growth, AI-related capital inflows and elevated US government bond yields remain important offsets, supporting DXY’s gradual decline towards 98.50.

Summary
Our stock-bond model (3-6 months) is at -2 (minimum: -5) in October, signalling a modest Underweight (UW) in global equities. Historically, a decline in the model score to -2 has been associated with flat to slightly negative returns. The shift was driven by stretched valuations in both global and Asian equities, weaker fundamentals and deteriorating market technicals. On fundamentals, market risk aversion has risen sharply, while PMI new orders have declined over the past three months, pointing to a slowdown in the pace of industrial expansion. On technicals, the share of equity markets trading above their 200-day moving averages, a key gauge of long-term support, has fallen below 60% for the first time since January 2025. The model rebalances in the middle of each month and has generated 11bps of alpha from the equity Underweight initiated on 15 October 2026, lifting YTD alpha vs. the 60/40 equity-bond benchmark to 4.0%.
Our 1-3-month equity market regime model indicates contained bear market risks across US and global equities. Estimated bear market probabilities are 4.2% for the S&P500 and 7.7% for the MSCI AC World, compared with 0.9% and 6.4% respectively in the September outlook. Across both models, volatility measures are the main factors keeping probabilities low, supported by momentum signals. Together, these outweigh modest upward contributions from macro and cross-market factors, leaving little evidence of a bear market regime over the next 1-3 months.
Our market diversity indicator flags reversal risk in MSCI Europe Real Estate and MSCI China Industrials, which are down over 12% and 19% respectively from their August peaks. US equity and USD positioning remain broadly neutral.

articles.title: Quick Thoughts: Bluer Than Blue—Investment Implications | Franklin Templeton
articles.text:
The 2026 midterm elections have delivered a significant political shift, with Democrats projected to control both the House of Representatives and the Senate, along with important gubernatorial victories in Texas, Georgia, Ohio and Iowa. Although not all results are in and the final congressional margins remain uncertain, the implications for President Trump's remaining two years in office are substantial. For investors, the key questions concern legislative gridlock, fiscal policy, interest rates and the prospects for industries ranging from artificial intelligence (AI) to cryptocurrencies.

Affordability is a key issue. The cost of living was a dominant factor in this election, with voters expressing concerns about housing, health care, energy and everyday expenses. The conflict with Iran, higher energy prices and tariffs have contributed to these pressures. The results suggest that affordability will remain a central political issue through 2028. Both parties have incentives to address these concerns, potentially creating opportunities for bipartisan initiatives involving housing, infrastructure and energy costs. For investors, affordability will influence consumer spending, corporate margins, inflation expectations and Federal Reserve policy. Companies perceived as contributing to higher prices may also face increased regulatory and political scrutiny.
Gridlock: Markets are usually up the year after midterms. History suggests investors should not necessarily fear divided government. Franklin Templeton Institute research covering the nine midterm elections from 1990 through 2022 found that the S&P 500 Index gained an average of 14.5% during the following 12 months, with positive returns in all nine periods. Markets have historically benefited as election uncertainty recedes and attention returns to fundamentals. However, gridlock should not be confused with fiscal discipline. A Democratic Congress will constrain major new tax and spending legislation, but substantial federal deficits and Treasury issuance are unlikely to disappear. The immediate market reaction has included declines in equity futures and Treasury yields, reflecting uncertainty about regulation and future fiscal policy. Longer-term interest rates will remain particularly important for equity valuations, housing, real estate and the financing of infrastructure investment. Historical returns are not a guarantee of future performance.
AI and data centers: An increasingly political investment theme. The expansion of AI infrastructure became an important election issue, particularly in states where data centers have contributed to concerns about electricity prices, water consumption and infrastructure costs. Democratic gubernatorial victories in Texas and Georgia are especially noteworthy, as both states are important locations for data-center development. The incoming Texas governor has advocated restricting new projects until developers bear more of the associated infrastructure costs. However, concerns about data-center economics and electricity affordability extend across party lines. The election is unlikely to reverse the structural demand for AI infrastructure, but it could change where facilities are built, how quickly projects proceed and who pays for the necessary infrastructure. Power generation, transmission, electrical equipment and grid infrastructure should remain important investment opportunities, although developers and utilities could face increased regulatory costs and construction delays.
Investment impact—Industries most affected. Elections tend to have a greater influence on the relative performance of industries than on the overall direction of financial markets. Health care companies could face increased scrutiny over drug pricing, insurance costs and reimbursement policies. Financial institutions may encounter tougher congressional oversight, while defense contractors could face changes in spending priorities. Energy companies, including renewable-energy developers, may be sensitive to permitting decisions, regulation and federal incentives.
Cryptocurrencies deserve particular attention. Republican control of Washington had supported expectations for a more favorable regulatory environment for digital assets. Democratic control of Congress could complicate further market-structure legislation and lead to increased scrutiny of cryptocurrency exchanges, decentralized finance and investor protections. The CLARITY Act failed to advance in the Senate in September, and the new congressional composition may make agreement on comprehensive legislation more difficult. However, the GENIUS Act, which established a federal framework for payment stablecoins, remains law. Bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies declined as the election results emerged, reflecting investor concerns about the regulatory outlook. Near-term volatility may increase, but greater regulatory clarity over time could support institutional adoption, tokenization and the development of digital financial infrastructure. For investors, the distinction between speculative crypto assets and the longer-term investment opportunities associated with blockchain technology remains important.
Governors' races may have a greater investment impact than expected. Democratic victories in Texas, Georgia, Ohio and Iowa represent important changes in state leadership. Governors and state regulators exercise significant influence over electricity pricing, utility investment, infrastructure permitting, economic development and taxation. Their decisions may have more immediate consequences for AI infrastructure and energy investment than changes in congressional control. State policy will also influence manufacturing investment, industrial development and the availability of incentives for new facilities. Municipal bond investors should pay particular attention to state fiscal policies, infrastructure spending and credit quality. Differences in tax policies, demographic trends and economic growth could create attractive opportunities for active management across state and local bond markets. These elections reinforce the importance of evaluating investment conditions at the state level rather than treating US policy as a single national issue.
A tougher Trump? With Democrats controlling both chambers of Congress, President Trump will face greater legislative constraints, congressional oversight and potentially more investigations. Democratic control of the Senate will also complicate judicial and other presidential appointments requiring confirmation. However, the president retains considerable executive authority over tariffs, trade, immigration, sanctions and foreign policy, subject to legal constraints. This could encourage greater reliance on executive actions rather than legislation. Congressional budget negotiations and debt-ceiling discussions may also become more contentious. For investors, divided government may reduce the likelihood of sweeping legislative changes without necessarily reducing policy uncertainty. Indeed, greater confrontation between Congress and the White House could increase volatility, particularly for companies exposed to international trade, government spending and regulatory decisions.
What is different this time? Several factors distinguish the 2026 midterms from previous elections. First, the AI investment boom has become a major contributor to economic growth, corporate earnings and equity-market performance, while simultaneously creating new political tensions around electricity demand and affordability. Second, geopolitical uncertainty, particularly the conflict with Iran, has added pressure to energy markets and inflation. Third, substantial federal deficits, elevated Treasury yields and a Federal Reserve that has resumed raising interest rates present a more challenging environment for both equities and fixed income. As discussed in a recent Franklin Templeton Institute Quick Thoughts commentary on bond markets, the increase in Treasury yields has been driven predominantly by higher real interest rates rather than inflation expectations. Higher real yields increase the cost of capital and could weigh on economic growth and corporate earnings in 2027. Meanwhile, equities have already benefited from strong earnings growth and substantial AI-related investment. The election is likely to create greater dispersion among industries and individual companies rather than fundamentally alter the long-term drivers of financial markets. Earnings growth, real interest rates and the sustainability of the AI investment cycle should remain more important than the political composition of Washington.

And now on to 2028... Attention will quickly turn to the next presidential election. With President Trump constitutionally limited to two terms, both parties will begin positioning their prospective candidates, and the Democratic victories in Congress and several key governorships will influence the political landscape. Affordability, economic growth, trade, energy policy and America's leadership in AI are likely to remain central issues. The next two years could bring increased political confrontation and shifting policy expectations, but investors should remember that markets are ultimately driven more by earnings, economic fundamentals and interest rates than by election outcomes. The challenge will be to distinguish political noise from policy changes that materially affect investment returns—and to recognize the opportunities that political uncertainty can create.

articles.title: Municipal Bonds: Are They Having A Moment?
articles.text:
Municipal Bonds: Are They Having A Moment?

Despite its size and quality, the $4.4 trillion municipal bond market is often
overlooked in core fixed income portfolios.

October 2026

KEY TAKEAWAYS

Municipal (muni) bonds may
present attractive after-tax income opportunities, particularly for investors in the
highest tax bracket.1
In our view, the scale and complexity of munis can create opportunities for active managers to generate value
beyond income.
Munis are generally considered
to be high quality, with
historically low default rates
compared to corporate bonds.

Despite its size and quality, the $4.4 trillion municipal bond market is often overlooked in core fixed income portfolios. However, at certain maturities, the highest-quality AAA municipal bonds can sometimes offer higher after-tax yields than high yield corporates. In our view, the market’s size and complexity can create opportunities for active managers to add value.
Municipal bonds currently offer their highest yields since 2008, climbing close to 7.9% on a calculated tax-equivalent yield basis for investors in the highest tax bracket.2
Longer-dated AAA municipal yields are even higher and may surpass equivalent BB high yield corporate yields on a tax-equivalent basis for the highest taxpayers, potentially reflecting material relative value and inefficient pricing.3

These yields indicate that municipal bonds may be able to deliver compelling income potential through their coupon payments.
Additionally, municipal bonds may benefit from price appreciation over time. Because the municipal yield curve is steeper than those of Treasury and corporate bonds, investors may benefit from the “roll-down” effect, where a bond’s yield falls over time (and thus its price rises) if the yield curve remains steep and credit conditions are stable.
Further, we believe that if wider macroeconomic and global interest rate volatility subsides, high grade municipal bonds could be favorably positioned to rebound from their current levels.
Municipals’ High Credit Quality May Offer Stability
72% of the tax-efficient municipal bond market is rated AA or above, versus only 10% of the U.S. investment grade corporate bond market. In addition, 10-year historical municipal bond default rates have been 0.15%, compared to 10.82% for global corporates.4

We believe munis could provide diversification benefits to a core fixed income allocation. They also present a direct opportunity to invest in local communities, financing infrastructure such as hospitals, schools, transportation, and utilities.
Potential Opportunities for Active Managers
The scope of municipal bonds is vast, with over 65,000 investment grade taxexempt municipal bonds available – far surpassing the total available in related bond markets.5
California and New York account for about a third of the tax-exempt municipal bond market. As a result, national municipal strategies may hold bonds issued outside an investor’s home state, and depending on the applicable tax rules, income from such bonds may be subject to state or local taxes.

Many municipal bonds are small issues spread across local governments throughout the U.S. As a result, comprehensively covering the full market can be difficult, particularly for investors without significant resources.
We believe credit spread pricing is inefficient and there are mispricing opportunities across the universe. In many cases, our internal credit assessments differ from those of the rating agencies.
In our view, active managers can seek significant value through independent credit research and opportunistic trading.

Outcomes Matter
Learn more about Insight Investment’s capabilities, philosophies & solutions:
Getting to Know Insight Investment

ABOUT INSIGHT INVESTMENT
BNY Investments’ fixed income platform can deliver a wide range of solutions, and leverages Insight Investment’s deep active fixed income expertise across traditional, specialized, municipal bond, and absolute return strategies.

Endnotes
Municipal bonds currently offer attractive tax-equivalent yields for investors in the highest federal tax bracket; at certain maturities, AAA municipal taxequivalent yields may exceed yields on certain below-investment-grade corporate bonds.Bloomberg (Bloomberg Municipal Bond Index), September 28, 2026. The municipal tax-equivalent yield (TEY) is calculated using an assumed 40.8% tax bracket, which includes a 37.0% top federal marginal income tax rate and a 3.8% Net Investment Income Tax (NIIT).At certain longer maturities, AAA municipal tax-equivalent yields may exceed yields on comparable BB-rated corporate bonds for investors subject to the assumed 40.8% federal tax rate.Moody’s, 1970-2024, July 2025.Source: Insight Investment, Bloomberg Municipal Bond Index, October 2026.

Risks
All investments involve risk including loss of principal. Certain investments involve greater or unique risks that should be considered along with the objectives, fees, and expenses before investing.
Bonds are subject to interest rate, credit, liquidity, call and market risks, to varying degrees. Generally, all other factors being equal, bond prices are inversely related to interest-rate changes and rate increases can cause price declines. The amount of public information available about municipal securities is generally less than that for corporate equities or bonds. Legislative changes, state and local economic and business developments, may adversely affect the yield and/ or value of municipal securities. Other factors include the general conditions of the municipal securities market, the size of the particular offering, maturity of the obligation, and the rating of the issue. Income for national municipal funds may be subject to state and local taxes. Income may be subject to state and local taxes for out-of-state residents. Some income may be subject to the federal alternative minimum tax for certain investors. Capital gains, if any, are taxable.
Appendix
Asset-Backed Securities (ABS) are financial securities such as a bond or note collateralized by a pool of assets such as loans, leases, credit card debt, royalties, or receivables. Mortgage-Backed Securities (MBS) are investments made up of a bundle of home loans bought from the banks that issued them. Investors in MBS receive periodic payments similar to bond coupon payments. Commercial Mortgage-Backed Securities (CMBS) are fixed-income investment products that are backed by mortgages on commercial properties rather than residential real estate. Bond ratings are an evaluation of a bond’s credit quality and the issuer’s ability to meet scheduled interest and principal payments, assigned by NRSROs on a scale from AAA (highest) to D (default). Ratings of BBB- and above are investment grade; BB+ and below are non-investment grade (speculative/high-yield), with BB, B, and CCC representing progressively higher credit risk. Tax-equivalent yield (TEY) calculates the pre-tax yield a taxable bond needs to offer to match the after-tax return of a tax-free investment. Roll-down return is the potential price appreciation a bond may experience as it approaches maturity. Net Investment Income Tax (NIIT) is an additional federal tax that applies to investment income above certain income thresholds.
Bloomberg Municipal Bond Index tracks the performance of the USD-denominated long-term tax-exempt bond market in the United States. articles.title: Cybersecurity & Fraud: Protecting Your Information | KKR
articles.text:
Security and Fraud Awareness
KKR prioritizes the security of our clients’ information and assets and is committed to ensuring that clients and employees are made aware of fraudulent schemes and activities when communicating with KKR. Fraud is an issue that companies may face regardless of size, industry, or country.
While we maintain robust cybersecurity measures, cyber criminals may seek to impersonate or claim affiliation with KKR and create fraudulent websites, email domains, applications, and social media accounts. Fraudsters may pose as legitimate organizations and send emails or make phone calls to extract personal data that can be manipulated for the use of financial crimes. These scams are complex as the perpetrators may use real employee names and replicate proprietary documentation.
KKR encourages clients to be aware of the different types of fraud and to exercise caution when disclosing personal information. To help improve awareness and knowledge, we offer the following information about cyber threats and guidance to help protect from falling victim to a cyber-attack or scam.
When communicating with KKR please note:
KKR does not engage in cold calling or in sending unsolicited messages or emails to clients. KKR only contacts people from official kkr.com e-mail addresses. Confirm you are visiting a KKR authorized website.Do not share your password and login ID with anyone, including anyone from KKR.Do not communicate or deal with personnel who are not affiliated with an authorized KKR office. All authorized office locations are listed on our locations page.KKR does not conduct business over chat platforms. Imposters can use the KKR name in furtherance of a variety of criminal activities. In particular, beware of scams purportedly affiliated with KKR that promise extraordinary returns on your investment at little to no risk.
KKR provides links to the resources below for informational purposes only and is not responsible for their content.
United States
U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission - Information on high-yield investment programs and how to avoid themFBI Cyber Threats - General guidance on cyber crimesFBI Scams & Safety - Safety resources on internet scamsU.S. Securities and Exchange Commission - Webpage on how to avoid fraudIf victim of internet crime, you may file complaint with the following government entities: Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3)Federal Trade CommissionU.S. Postal Service (for crimes involving U.S. Mail)

Europe
OLAF – European Anti-Fraud OfficeTake Five to Stop Fraud – Impartial advice to help everyone in the UK protect themselves against financial fraudAction Fraud – The National Fraud & Cyber Crime Reporting CentreFCA Scam Smart – Check an investment opportunity and avoid scamsMoney Advice Service – How to spot an investment scam
Asia
Hong Kong Police Force – Fight Scams TogetherHong Kong Monetary Authority – Beware of FraudstersIndia Cybercrime Reporting PortalIndia SEBI Platform for Securities Markets InquiriesSingapore Police Force – Scam AdvisorySingapore Scam Alert – Spot the signs, stop the crime
Contact Us
If you come across any websites, mobile applications, e-commerce accounts or social media accounts in the name of or affiliated with KKR; or receive emails, text messages or phone calls from KKR that you are uncertain about or which you believe to be fraudulent, please either contact your KKR Representative, email us at Client.Services@kkr.com or call us at +1 (212) 230-9700.

articles.title: AI winners and losers: A global sector view
articles.text:
Webinar

AI winners and losers: A global sector view

Register Now

12 November 20262 sessions:12 November 2026 – 1.00pm HKT (Hong Kong/ 4pm Sydney)12 November 2026 – 2.00pm GMT (London / 10am New York)

online

AI is already changing the shape of the global economy, but the gains are far from evenly spread. Indeed, AI investment is concentrated on a narrow set of products, mainly chips, servers, software, and data centres, and much of the hardware is made in a handful of tech-focused economies.

Consequently, a continuation of the boom or a sharp bust would impact some industries and economies much more significantly than others. Over the longer term, our research shows differences in AI exposure and levels of adoption could open large gaps in productivity and output across sectors. In this webinar, Makoto Tsuchiya and Charlie Muir will present the global sector level results of our AI scenarios, covering:

Short-term boom and bust: changes in data centre demand affects tech-exporting economies the most, with impacts concentrated in electronic components and semiconductors. In a tech downturn, a stock market correction would also drag on consumer spending, spreading to household-facing and other non-AI sectors.

Long-term productivity: how exposed each industry is to AI in production, and how widely AI is adopted, drives differences in productivity gains, with implications for economic activity across sectors and economies.

This webinar is being held on our new platform, ON24. If you do not receive your confirmation email, please check your junk and spam folders.

Speakers

Charlie Muir

Charlie is a Senior Economist in the industry team, based in London. He works on the global industry service, where his main focus is improving the service through model development and research alongside the regular forecast updates. He also runs the industry climate service and works on AI strategy for the team. Previously, he coordinated the forecast updates for the global industry service and was responsible for forecasting the consumer goods sectors.He achieved a first-class degree in Economics at the University of Bath and joined Oxford Economics in July 2021.

Senior Economist, Industry

Makoto Tsuchiya

Makoto Tsuchiya is an Economist at Oxford Economics. He oversees the forecast and analysis of the electronics sector, including semiconductors. He also works on a wide range of client projects, by way of producing bespoke forecasts as well as written reports. Makoto has a Bachelor’s degree from Temple University Japan where he majored in Economics with a minor in Business Studies. He also has sophisticated knowledge in the corporate accounting field.

articles.title: Daily: Build resilience as tech volatility rises
articles.text:
Talk to a UBS Financial AdvisorFrom the studioVideo: CIO Monthly | Mark Haefele on AI earnings, energy prices, interest rates (4 mins)Video: Why China's equity markets have lagged (6 mins)Thought of the dayMarket sentiment came under pressure on Friday as tech earnings raised fresh concerns about capital expenditure. Stocks in Japan, South Korea, and Taiwan fell after a tech-led selloff on Wall Street, while Nasdaq futures were pointing 2% lower ahead of the US market open on Friday. Signs that the US may resume military strikes against Iran also pushed oil prices higher, with Brent crude trading at around USD 117/bbl at the time of writing.But further volatility does not make retreating from markets an effective way to protect portfolios from potential drawdowns, in our view. We continue to see scope for equity gains overall and believe investors should focus on building a resilient portfolio that includes exposure beyond tech.AI demand remains robust, but we see a rising risk of mid-cycle capex indigestion. Weaker-than-expected growth in megacap tech companies’ core businesses was at the center of investors’ concerns, as markets questioned how the next phase of AI capex would be funded amid continued signals of higher spending from hyperscalers. We are seeing a shift in the funding mix for AI investment after four years of relying on hyperscalers’ cash flows, with incremental capex increasingly drawing on debt, equity, leases, and supplier-backed financing. In our view, the health of underlying demand remains a key metric to watch. Latest results showing accelerating cloud revenue growth and expanding advanced orders for cloud computing capacity point to still-robust demand for AI infrastructure, but we acknowledge the rising risk of mid-cycle capex indigestion, as financing and execution risks are emerging in the more capital-intensive areas of the AI buildout.Resilient growth underpins opportunities beyond US tech. The US economy expanded at an annualized rate of 3.4% in the third quarter, ahead of the 3.1% estimate and up from 2.2% in the second quarter. This growth has helped keep inflation elevated, but the economy’s resilience also supports the outlook for sectors beyond tech. In fact, the equal-weighted S&P 500 has outperformed its market capitalization-weighted counterpart year to date, suggesting that an improving cyclical backdrop, healthy consumer spending, and structural trends—such as the growing longevity industry—are also supporting market performance. Outside the US, robust earnings growth across the Eurozone and Asia gives investors a broader range of opportunities to participate in potential further equity gains.Quality bonds can help stabilize portfolios. As equities have come under pressure, bonds have rallied, with the 10-year US Treasury yield falling by 37 basis points in October. This shows that quality fixed income is once again serving as a portfolio stabilizer, and we believe still-elevated yields provide sufficient income to compensate for the risk of potential yield volatility. Bonds could also benefit if inflation moderates or economic growth weakens, adding valuable diversification to portfolios.So, with cash unlikely to overcome the combined portfolio challenges of inflation, taxes, longer lifespans, and withdrawals, staying invested remains critical for the long term. Within tech, we continue to like leading megacaps, defensive names in payment networks and consumer electronics, as well as quality semis and hardware companies. But those with an outsized allocation to US tech should diversify across sectors and regions. We also believe investors should maintain a well-diversified portfolio that includes exposure to quality fixed income. Those willing and able to tolerate relevant risks can consider broad commodities and hedge funds to access additional return drivers.
