04 November 2026 – The International Energy Agency (IEA), the International Energy Forum (IEF), and the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) today convened key stakeholders and leading industry experts to discuss maritime energy flows, shipping and insurance in a ‘Joint IEA-IEF-OPEC Technical Workshop on the Security of Energy Flows: Maritime Routes and Market Stability’.The technical workshop comes at the request of the consultation meeting of ministers of the Declaration of Cooperation (DoC) which was held in Riyadh on 12 October 2026, following the IEF17. At that meeting, ministers underlined the critical importance of ensuring uninterrupted flows of energy, expressed concern about elevated shipping and insurance costs, and noted their wish to continue engaging with the IEF, the IEA and other international partners on these issues.The technical workshop builds on the IEA-IEF-OPEC trilateral programme of work and their shared concerns such as reflected in the IEF 17 Ministerial Concluding Statement, including the protection of energy infrastructure and trade routes.Today’s online meeting was convened under the leadership of OPEC Secretary General, HE Haitham Al Ghais, IEA Executive Director, HE Dr. Fatih Birol and IEF Secretary General, HE Eng. Jassim Alshirawi.In highlighting the importance of the meeting, HE Al Ghais said: “Participants in the DoC remain fully committed to supporting the stability of global energy markets. In this regard, our discussions will be vital to help identify possible solutions to the challenges facing both producers and consumers in relation to current maritime trade.“HE Al Ghais also stressed that maritime energy flows remain a core pillar of global energy security and noted that shipping and insurance costs in 2026 have increased significantly to a level of more than one-third of the underlying value of crude oil. Furthermore, the elevated transportation and risk expenses have been passed along the entire oil and energy value chains, straining both producing and consuming economies, and placing additional inflationary pressures on the global economy.HE Birol said: “Energy markets are facing a crisis of unprecedented proportions, affecting the production and transportation of the oil and gas on which the global economy relies. While producers have worked hard to maintain supply, under extremely difficult circumstances, we must all work to safeguard freedom of maritime navigation, a central pillar of global energy security. That is why we are here today, together with our colleagues from OPEC and the IEF, to help find durable solutions to these challenges.”HE Alshirawi said: “Safe maritime passage is essential to energy security and market stability for producers, consumers and transit countries alike. Disruption can raise energy, food and transport costs far beyond the region affected, with the greatest hardship falling on vulnerable communities. Building on IEF17, our cooperation with the IEA and OPEC can strengthen the dialogue and data transparency needed to restore confidence, support investment and build more resilient global energy markets.”Today’s workshop underscores the flexibility of the joint programme of work agreed upon by the IEA, the IEF and OPEC and endorsed by energy ministers at the 12th International Energy Forum, held in Cancún, Mexico in March 2010, as part of the ‘Cancún Declaration’.

articles.title: Global responsible tax: How complicated is simplification?
articles.text:
KPMG International hosted a virtual roundtable discussion in July 2026, as part of the Global Responsible Tax Program, to explore what it would really take to simplify tax systems and what might be lost, gained or exposed in the process.Everyone wants tax to be simpler. It is a perennial challenge, with questions of certainty, compliance burden and basic comprehensibility consistently raised. A simpler system, many argue, would support growth, improve investment confidence and make it easier for taxpayers, businesses and revenue authorities to ‘do the right thing’. But the harder question is, what trade-offs are organizations prepared to make to get there?Tax systems are asked to do many things at once: raise revenue, support growth, redistribute fairly, encourage certain behaviors, deter others, provide certainty, prevent avoidance and remain administratively workable for taxpayers, advisers and revenue authorities alike. Complexity is often the result not simply of bad design, but of competing political, economic and social objectives being layered into the system over time.But how complicated can simplification be? Removing a relief may broaden the base and reduce distortion, but it may also remove targeted support. Fewer rules may make a system easier to understand, but they also may create more discretion, uncertainty or perceived unfairness. Harmonization across borders may help businesses and tax authorities operate more consistently, but it may also reduce national flexibility. Strong anti-avoidance rules may protect revenue and public trust, but it can also add complexity for those simply trying to comply.Technology and AI add a further dimension. Digital administration, data analytics, real-time reporting and automation may offer ways to make tax easier to navigate and administer. But if tax rules become more automated, who is responsible for interpretation and how can taxpayers understand and challenge decisions? If systems become easier to comply with but harder to see, has tax really become simpler? Held under the Chatham House Rule, the discussion brought together academics, policymakers, business representatives and civil society voices. The write-up below summarizes the personal views expressed and does not necessarily represent the position of any organization, including KPMG International Limited or any KPMG member firm.

Executive summary

Complexity is increasingly experienced as uncertainty
Discussion moved beyond the volume of legislation toward legal, administrative and policy uncertainty. Predictability, including confidence that rules, incentives and interpretations will endure, may matter as much as formal simplicity.

Process and design require different responses
Technology, pre-filled returns and better data can streamline administration, but they cannot resolve unclear policy choices or subjective rule design. Digitalizing a complex system may make compliance easier without making the underlying tax system simpler.

Shorter legislation is not necessarily simple
Detailed rules may provide certainty, while concise and principles-based laws may transfer complexity to guidance, tax officials and disputes. Legislative length is therefore an unreliable measure of practical simplicity.

Incremental reform may be more credible than wholesale redesign
Comprehensive reform could create disruption, implementation risk and an ‘economic freeze’ while businesses await clarity. Periodic pruning, improved data use, clearer thresholds and targeted procedural changes may offer a more practical route.

Rules should produce clearer outcomes
Regardless of legislative length, rules should generate yes or no answers wherever possible. This would improve certainty and remove cognitive burden for taxpayers and revenue authorities while making greater automation possible.

Small businesses bear disproportionate costs
Compliance costs, uncertainty and administrative friction are often regressive. Rules designed around large organizations, followed by exemptions or accommodations for smaller firms, may fail to reflect the limited financial and internal capacity of small and medium enterprises.

The economic case for simplicity remains central but can be complex to quantify
Some participants suggested that complexity can discourage hiring, investment and use of incentives, particularly among smaller businesses. However, further evidence quantifying these effects may be needed before simplification gains sustained political traction.

Tax may be carrying too many objectives
Some participants questioned whether redistribution and other equity goals should be pursued primarily through tax design or more directly through public expenditure and services. This raised a wider question about whether layering multiple social objectives into taxation contributes to unnecessary complexity.

Beyond the length of the law

Is complexity about how much legislation exists, or how effectively people use it?

It was agreed by many in the discussion that legislative length (or indeed number of taxes) is a poor proxy for the practical difficulty of a tax system. The length of the UK’s tax code is often cited in exasperation, but a lengthy provision may be relevant only to a narrow group and provide those taxpayers with valuable clarity. Conversely, a short or principles-based rule may create considerable uncertainty if it leaves important questions to interpretation.It is therefore important to distinguish between the volume of law and its effectiveness.The relevant test may not be how many people ultimately claim a relief or fall within a provision, but how many must spend time determining whether it applies to them. A narrowly used rule need not create widespread complexity if its intended users can identify and apply it easily.Clear drafting was seen as particularly important. Terms such as ‘reasonable,’ ‘normal’ or ‘just’ may permit flexibility, but they can also create blurred lines. Several participants favored rules that allow taxpayers to reach a clear yes or no answer in as many circumstances as possible.Periodic pruning of obsolete or duplicative provisions was supported, but not as a substitute for improving the usability of the law.

From complexity to uncertainty

Is the deeper economic problem unpredictability rather than complication?

As the discussion developed, many participants increasingly framed the challenge as one of uncertainty. Complexity and uncertainty are related, but they are not identical. A technically detailed system can still be relatively predictable, while a shorter and more discretionary system may produce divergent outcomes across regions, officials or taxpayers.Different forms of uncertainty were identified. Legal uncertainty concerns whether legislation provides an intelligible answer. Administrative uncertainty arises when the interpretation or behavior of a revenue authority is difficult to anticipate. Policy uncertainty reflects the frequency of rule changes and the possibility that taxes, reliefs or thresholds may be altered with limited notice.Long-term predictability was considered particularly important for investment. A business may be able to comply with a complicated incentive, but it may still decide not to invest if it cannot be confident that the relief will apply, that its claim will be accepted or that the policy will remain in place.One participant also raised the cognitive burden created by uncertainty. Businesses must devote management attention to interpreting rules and anticipating challenges, while governments and tax authorities must understand the interaction of numerous provisions before making further changes.Greater access to binding clearances was also suggested as a means of reducing the cost and risk associated with uncertainty over difficult legal interpretation and boundary questions.

Separating rule design from administrative process

Technology can streamline compliance, but can it simplify the underlying policy?

A central distinction emerged between the design of a tax and the process used to administer it. Either can be simple or complex independently of the other.Process simplification may offer the most immediate opportunities. Third-party reporting, pre-populated returns, integrated data systems and faster digital filing can reduce the information taxpayers must gather and submit themselves. Better use of third-party data may also narrow the tax gap by reducing non-reporting. However, some participants cautioned that the burden does not disappear; it may be transferred to banks, platforms, employers or other institutions required to provide the information. Where businesses are required to provide more third-party data, this should be considered holistically alongside opportunities to streamline or remove other tax or wider regulatory reporting requirements.It was also suggested that administrative complexity can also arise from limitations in revenue authority systems, particularly where these are fragmented or have not been upgraded for a significant period, requiring businesses to devote substantial time and resources to resolving issues that are not caused by the underlying tax rules.Several participants argued that machine-readable rules will increasingly require more structured conditions and clearer decision points. AI may assist by summarizing legislation, navigating guidance and identifying relevant provisions. However, one participant was wary that AI was the right way forward for tax legislation as its simplistic style can leave things out and hallucinate.

Designing for the smallest taxpayer

What would change if tax rules were built around small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) rather than adapted for them afterward?

The burden of tax complexity was described by one contributor as highly regressive. Large organizations can draw upon in-house tax teams, established relationships with revenue authorities and external advisers. Small and microbusinesses often lack comparable resources, making the same rule considerably more expensive for them to understand and administer. One contributor argued that tax jargon makes life harder and that language should be recognizable and understandable to taxpayers.Some participants argued that governments frequently ‘think large first’: rules are designed around the structures and capabilities of major organizations, with exemptions or simplified treatments added later for SMEs. This can produce a patchwork of thresholds, elections and special regimes that itself becomes difficult to navigate.The discussion of research and development incentives illustrated the problem. Some smaller businesses were said to be withdrawing from claims because the process, uncertainty or risk of challenge outweighed the expected benefit.Ideas included allowing microbusinesses to base tax more closely on their financial accounts, with reduced access to bespoke reliefs in exchange for lower compliance costs. Such approaches would involve trade-offs. Taxpayers might gain simplicity but lose opportunities to optimize their position.

International models

What can jurisdictions learn from one another without assuming that systems are inherently transferable?

International examples demonstrated that simplicity takes different forms.Singapore was cited as an example of a highly streamlined filing process supported by employer reporting and a relatively narrow range of taxable personal income. An individual with straightforward circumstances may be able to complete a return in minutes.At the same time, it was noted that this administrative simplicity is connected to wider choices about the tax base, redistribution and the role of government. A process cannot be separated entirely from the policy system it administers.India was mentioned as an example of technology and third-party data being used to pre-populate income information, facilitate electronic filing and accelerate processing. This illustrated how administrative reform can generate significant practical benefits even within a large and complex economy.The European Union (EU)’s emerging tax simplification agenda was discussed as an example of reform focused less on wholesale redesign than on cleaning up an increasingly layered body of rules. Participants pointed to the proposed tax simplification omnibus and the recast of the Directive on Administrative Cooperation as attempts to consolidate successive amendments, remove obsolete provisions and reduce overlaps between reporting regimes.Some proposals were seen as relatively straightforward administrative improvements, while others were more ambitious, including reducing withholding tax frictions on certain cross-border payments and reconsidering whether some anti-avoidance rules remain necessary where newer regimes, such as Pillar Two, already address similar risks.The central constraint is that EU tax measures generally require unanimous agreement among member states. This makes simplification both legally and politically demanding. The likely outcome is that the most pragmatic measures may progress, while more ambitious proposals are diluted, delayed or removed. The EU case therefore illustrates a broader lesson from the discussion: simplification is often easiest where it involves consolidation and duplication, but much harder where it requires governments to surrender discretion or accept a different balance between competitiveness, enforcement and national autonomy.

Incrementalism over wholesale reform

Can tax systems be improved without destabilizing economic activity?

Some participants were skeptical that wholesale reform could be implemented safely or sustainably. Rewriting numerous elements simultaneously would place significant demands on legislative drafters, revenue authorities, software providers, advisers and businesses. It could also create an ‘economic freeze’ as taxpayers delay decisions while waiting to understand the new system.The discussion therefore pointed toward incremental reform. Better use of third-party data, removal of duplicative reporting, clearer language, periodic review of thresholds and targeted improvements to areas of disproportionate burden may be more achievable than a single comprehensive redesign.Incrementalism is not without risks. Repeated small changes can themselves add complexity if they are not guided by a coherent direction. Participants’ comments therefore suggested a need for an enduring framework: reforms should be assessed against accessibility, certainty, administrative cost and economic impact, even when introduced separately.

Conclusions

Some participants were skeptical that wholesale reform could be implemented safely or sustainably. Rewriting numerous elements simultaneously would place significant demands on legislative drafters, revenue authorities, software providers, advisers and businesses. It could also create an ‘economic freeze’ as taxpayers delay decisions while waiting to understand the new system.The discussion therefore pointed toward incremental reform. Better use of third-party data, removal of duplicative reporting, clearer language, periodic review of thresholds and targeted improvements to areas of disproportionate burden may be more achievable than a single comprehensive redesign.Incrementalism is not without risks. Repeated small changes can themselves add complexity if they are not guided by a coherent direction. Participants’ comments therefore suggested a need for an enduring framework: reforms should be assessed against accessibility, certainty, administrative cost and economic impact, even when introduced separately.

Saturday Nov 7, 2026 1:50 P.M. EST Update:Reactor, KYT (UI and API) and Address Screening are now back online. We’ve restored these products with enhanced security measures, and we’re asking customers to reconnect in a specific way to keep accounts and data protected. We’re sending our customers an email with instructions. We know this week has been difficult, and we appreciate your patience. We’re here to help 24/7. If you’re having trouble, please contact support.Friday Nov 6, 2026 3:30 A.M. EST Update: We have begun restoring access to KYT and Address Screening through a phased approach, with additional customers expected to regain access over the next several hours. We are proceeding carefully, monitoring each phase and validating our enhanced security controls to ensure services are brought back online safely.As we confirm that each phase is operating as expected, we will expand access to all remaining customers.To help us facilitate the restoration of your access, please take the following steps:
Submit your trusted IP addresses: If you have not already done so, please send your trusted IP addresses for our allowlist to support@chainalysis.com or to your Chainalysis account team.
Prepare to reset credentials: Once access is granted, all users will be required to reset their passwords and rotate API keys, as applicable, before registering transactions.
In parallel, we are continuing to work around the clock with our external security experts to harden our systems and safely restore access to Reactor and Data Solutions. We will provide further updates as our restoration efforts progress.We recognize the disruption this incident has caused and appreciate your continued patience and partnership as we work to restore our services safely.Wednesday Nov 4, 2026 11:00 P.M. EST Update: On Monday, we discovered certain customer information including names, usernames, password hashes and live tokens for all Chainalysis users were exposed to a malicious actor. While we investigated, we removed access to Reactor and Data Solutions. At this time we continue to have no evidence that any investigations data has been accessed or Chainalysis attribution data has been manipulated.Recognizing the importance of our compliance transaction monitoring products to our customers’ businesses, we implemented additional proactive monitoring systems for unusual activity. Today, we discovered abnormal activity and took KYT (the user interface and API) offline alongside other address screening products and the login page. We are directly notifying customers whose KYT accounts appear to have been accessed without authorization.Next StepsWe intend to begin restoring access to KYT and Address Screening tomorrow. Contact support@chainalysis.com or your Chainalysis account team with trusted IP addresses for our allowlist. We will then grant access for users to reset their passwords and rotate API keys to register transactions.We are working around the clock to harden our systems and bring Reactor and Data Solutions back online. We will require additional protections to access accounts, including that every user will have to reset passwords and rotate API keys as appropriate. We will communicate these changes as necessary.We know how business critical these services are to our customers, and we are working expeditiously alongside our outside experts to restore them securely.Wednesday Nov 4, 2026 10:30 A.M. EST Update: We have been actively monitoring our transaction screening products for suspicious activity. Due to abnormal activity, we have taken KYT (the user interface and API) offline alongside other address screening products and the login page. Reactor, Data Solutions, and Chain (Beta) are still offline while our team completes critical work. We are working to bring all of our products online as soon as possible.For customers who just received an email from us instructing you to reset your Chainalysis password, resetting this password won’t be possible right now. We still encourage you, where necessary, to reset your password on other systems where you may be reusing credentials.Wednesday Nov 4, 2026 9:50 A.M. EST Update: Our teams are working to respond to ongoing cyber threats, ensure the safety of our systems, and bring offline products back online. We are sending the email below to certain customers whose Chainalysis passwords were exposed in an “on-path attack.”Our investigation is ongoing, and we will update this blog as new information becomes available.Dear customer,Chainalysis teams are working around the clock to investigate an ongoing multifront cyberattack, review the security of our systems, and bring our products back online. Today, we confirmed that as a part of this incident, an “on-path attack” exposed a subset of customer passwords, including yours. This attack vector has been contained and remediated. Given this sensitive and urgent information, we are requiring you to reset your password. We are locking your Chainalysis account as a precaution. Please reset your password through the usual Chainalysis login page before signing in again:For your security, go directly to the Chainalysis login page noted above rather than clicking links in any password-reset emails you may have received. If you need help regaining access, please contact support@chainalysis.com.As of this time, we have no evidence that your account has been improperly accessed. If you used this same password for any other non-Chainalysis service, we recommend resetting it there as well and choosing a unique password.Our investigation is ongoing, and we will share relevant updates as we have them.Sincerely,Your Chainalysis TeamMonday Nov 2, 2026 Update: Chainalysis continues to respond to ongoing cyber threats associated with the security incident described below.Out of an abundance of caution, we have proactively taken certain products offline, including Reactor and Data Solutions, and are working alongside our third-party cybersecurity experts to complete additional security assessments before restoring service.Recognizing the importance of our compliance transaction monitoring products to our customers’ businesses, particularly their role in detecting money laundering across the ecosystem, we have made the decision based on information available to date to continue operating those products while we conduct our investigation. We are closely monitoring these systems for unusual activity and will keep you apprised of new information so you can make informed decisions for your business and operations.As our investigation continues, we recommend that our customers continue to follow their organization’s established security protocols, remain vigilant for suspicious communications or activity, and promptly report any concerns to your IT or security team. We will share relevant updates and any recommended additional actions as more information becomes available.Friday Oct 30, 2026 Update: Chainalysis was recently the target of a cybersecurity incident, similar to many other tech platforms in recent weeks. Based on the investigation to date, we have found no evidence of unauthorized access to investigation content, authentication credentials, or session tokens.Our team is working with leading cybersecurity experts to investigate this activity and harden our systems. We’ve proactively notified all of our customers and will keep them updated as our work progresses. This security incident is not related to the recent crypto theft at Binance.Below, you can find the full text of the email that was sent to impacted customers.Chainalysis is committed to the security of our platform and the protection of our customers’ data. We are seeing an industry-wide rise in AI-driven cyberattacks, and we are taking a whole-of-company approach to make sure our security posture meets the evolving environment and our customers’ expectations. In keeping with our commitment to transparency, we are writing to inform you of a security incident affecting your organization. Some of you have been previously notified and we want to provide an update on our work. Please note that this security incident is unrelated to the recent crypto theft involving Binance. What happenedThis month, Chainalysis detected an external actor using offensive agentic techniques to gain unauthorized access to Chainalysis systems and internal tools. Our teams have been working around the clock to investigate unauthorized activity, patch vulnerabilities, and harden our systems. Customer data impactBased on the evidence available to date, we have found no indication that these incidents resulted in the unauthorized access of investigation content (such as graphs, notes, or cases), transaction or query results, passwords in clear text, MFA secrets, or user session tokens.Some non-sensitive customer data, such as user IDs, full names, email addresses, and organization role labels for users provisioned on our platform were accessed, including such information relating to your organization and users. We are in the process of determining the records for your organization that were accessed and will provide a detailed breakdown as soon as that analysis is complete.What we have doneWe have engaged world-class third-party cybersecurity experts and are using sophisticated large language models to support a broader review of our platform’s security and strengthen our defenses. This work extends beyond the exploited vulnerabilities to enhance our security posture across the platform. What you can doChainalysis users should continue to be hyper-vigilant of unexpected password reset requests or authentication prompts. If your organization has not yet enabled two-factor authentication, we strongly recommend doing so. Your Chainalysis account manager can help you complete that process.What happens nextWe will provide you with updates relevant to your organization as our investigation progresses. We take the security of your data seriously and regret that this incident occurred.Respectfully,Your Chainalysis Team

articles.title: Zcash NU7: Faster Private Payments With 25-Second Blocks
articles.text: Zcash implemented its NU7 upgrade at block 3,543,405 at 02:34 UTC on the 6th of November. The main change within this upgrade is block time: cutting the expected wait time for a first confirmation from 75 to 25 seconds once difficulty settles at the target. An exchange that keeps a usual 3-confirmation requirement would see its expected on-chain wait fall from about 3:45 minutes to approximately 75 seconds.This is an important step as Zcash addresses one of its main bottlenecks, which is not privacy, but friction. Shielded transactions hide sender, receiver and amount, as we have explored in detail, but they were slow to confirm and expensive for wallets to find. NU7 addresses both of these issues directly. NU7 also limits shielded activity in each block, cutting the maximum amount of data light wallets need to download each day from 271 MB to 169 MB. But with blocks arriving 3 times as often, estimated capacity for standard private payments still more than doubles, from 2.9 to 6.6 transactions per second.In the first 2 and a half hours after activation, blocks arrived every 39 seconds on average as mining difficulty adjusted to the faster pace. Separately, the Zakura team tested full 2 MB blocks across 80 nodes in 11 regions. Faster blocks meant more competition between miners producing blocks at similar times, with the share of blocks discarded by the network rising from 1.57% to 3.43%. This seems like a pretty reasonable tradeoff for faster payments.Source: ZIP 259Retiring Sprout and funding future securityNU7 retires Sprout, Zcash’s original shielded pool, freezing roughly 12,224 ZEC, less than 0.1% of supply. Coinholders backed the change to remove it, as it had become a security risk. Sean Bowe has outlined a possible way to recover the funds in a future upgrade, but nothing has been approved.The fee change redirects 60% of transaction fees into a reserve for future mining rewards. These funds leave circulation now and begin returning through block rewards around February 2031. The 21M supply cap and scheduled halvings remain exactly the same as before. Fee contributions are small today, but Bowe’s separate proposal to redirect the 8% of issuance allocated to Zcash Community Grants would add roughly 144 ZEC a day, providing substantially more funding for future network security. There is no timeline on implementation of this.It will be important to see whether faster confirmations translate into greater use of Zcash for private payments. Sources: ZIP 218, ZIP 259, ZecStats

Opinion

El Niño's long shadow over fuel demand

View Edgar Manzano's full profile

A very strong El Niño, peaking in northern winter 2026-27, could reduce global demand for gasoline, diesel and jet fuel. At the aggregate level, the figure looks like it is contained. At the regional and sectoral level, it does not.
Wood Mackenzie modelled the demand impact by averaging GDP per capita losses from the three strongest El Niño events on record: 1982-83, 1997-98 and 2015-16. Income elasticities, adjusted for product type and region, convert each country's projected income loss into reduced fuel consumption.
Fill in the form to download the full report, or read on for a preview of some of the key themes explored.
1. How income loss, not weather, drives the demand shock
El Niño does not simply warm the planet. It redistributes rainfall and heat, bringing drought to some regions and floods to others. For energy markets, that redistribution is the critical variable, not the temperature shift itself.
Agriculture, hydropower, freight, and electricity demand all absorb the disruption. Those channels cut GDP and household income, and lower income translates directly into lower fuel consumption. The weather event ends. The income shortfall does not.
How does this translate into fuel demand across the most exposed markets? Find out more in the full report.
2. Road transport carries the heaviest burden
Road transport carries the heaviest burden, with gasoline and diesel accounting for much of the overall loss. Aviation accounts for most of the remainder, with jet fuel the most income-sensitive product per barrel.
The trajectory of the loss matters as much as its size. Each year after the event, affected economies fall further behind the growth path they would otherwise have followed. Lost growth compounds. This is a multi-year income drag, not a seasonal disruption.
Explore the impact across road transport, gasoline, diesel and aviation in the full report.
3. US income response shapes the global outcome
North America records the largest volume loss, with the United States accounting for the majority of the regional total. Its prominence reflects the scale of the market, not the depth of its climate exposure.
Latin America and Africa carry the steepest proportional losses. These markets include economies that rely heavily on rain-fed agriculture and hydropower, shortening the distance between weather shock and income loss.
Asia Pacific also faces country-level dynamics moving in different directions, with hydropower, back-up generation, aviation and other factors shaping the impact on liquid fuel markets.
Find out how the impact differs across North America, Latin America, Africa and Asia Pacific in the full report.
4. A demand loss that builds, not fades
The final intensity of the 2026-27 event will determine the scale of the income shock in the most exposed economies. US economic performance through 2028 matters most for volume. The pace of recovery in Andean markets shapes the Latin American share and the overall depth of the loss curve.
The two dimensions of the impact point to the same underlying dynamic. El Niño's effect on fuel markets extends well past the weather event that triggers it, and the income channel is the mechanism that sustains it.
For energy companies, commodity traders and infrastructure investors with exposure to affected regions, that distinction carries direct implications for capital allocation.
Download the full report to explore the implications for fuel demand, infrastructure investment and supply assumptions.

articles.title: Measuring Consumption with Credit Card Data: Benchmarking and Beyond
articles.text:
Finance and Economics Discussion Series (FEDS)

Twitter

Share

RSS

October 2026

Measuring Consumption with Credit Card Data: Benchmarking and Beyond
Aditya Aladangady, Ricardo Duque Gabriel, and Carlo Wix

Abstract: We introduce a novel monthly county-level consumption dataset constructed from spending data on over 350 million credit cards in the Federal Reserve’s Y-14M reports, covering over 3,000 U.S. counties since 2014. We first show that the data closely track traditional consumption measures, explaining 92 percent of the variation in monthly adjusted personal consumption expenditures (PCE) growth at the national level, capturing meaningful cross-sectional variation in annual adjusted PCE growth at the state level, and reproducing the impulse response of official consumption measures to identified monetary policy shocks. We then use the county-month panel to estimate heterogeneous consumption responses to monetary policy shocks across the county-level income distribution, an analysis infeasible with traditional consumption data. We find suggestive evidence that low-income counties exhibit larger spending declines than high-income counties, consistent with heterogeneous-agent New Keynesian models. Finally, we provide practical guidance for researchers working with similar data, discussing coverage, sample composition, and the approximation of credit card spending from credit bureau data.
Keywords: Measurement and Data, Consumption, Credit Card Spending

articles.title: Here We Go Again: Binance Loses $6.3b in Largest Robbery in History
articles.text:
Insights / Research / Binance Loses $6.3b in Largest Robbery in History 

Written by:

Alex Thorn
Head of Firmwide Research

Thaddeus Pinakiewicz
Vice President, Research

Topics

Bitcoin

Cryptocurrency

Ethereum

research • October 30, 2026

Binance Loses $6.3b in Largest Robbery in History 

This article originally appeared in Galaxy Research's weekly newsletter. Subscribe to get timely insights delivered to your inbox every Friday morning. Find our past reports and newsletters at galaxy.com/research. Send feedback to research@galaxy.com. Binance, the world’s largest crypto exchange, was drained of roughly $6.3b across 10 blockchains on Thursday night. TRM Labs and Chainalysis attribute the attack to TraderTraitor, North Korea’s Lazarus-linked unit. As of writing, the exchange has not yet re-enabled withdrawals. Start with scale. The benchmark for the largest robbery ever has long been the roughly $1b Saddam Hussein’s regime took from the Central Bank of Iraq on the eve of the 2003 invasion, about $1.8b in today’s dollars. Bybit beat that in nominal terms but not after inflation. Binance beats it on any measure. Even after roughly $2.5–3bn in freezes, this is the biggest heist of all time. Binance’s BTC outflows yesterday were 11 standard deviations higher than their 30-day average.

Then the method. On Ethereum, the attacker used EIP-7702 to turn a Binance hot wallet into a sweeper contract that took orders only from the attacker. It was backed by 50 pre-signed authorizations, one for each upcoming transaction number (nonce), so whichever one came up next would work. The code was rehearsed on three test wallets hours beforehand. Within minutes of each other, nine more chains were emptied, each with different key types and signing schemes. That is someone with intimate knowledge of how Binance’s withdrawal systems work. This is Binance’s preliminary finding: a compromised DevOps engineer’s laptop gave access to a service container, with “no evidence of any wallet private key leak.”

Our take We believe our previous thesis from Bitget is consistent here. Nobody attacks the private-key math. They attack whoever, or whatever, tells the math what to do. The biggest mitigating factor of this exploit was stablecoin issuers. Tether froze about $1.77b in USDT, Circle about $825m in USDC, Ripple about $40m in RLUSD, and World Liberty about $28m in USD1. That’s a big part of why this appears to be a painful week rather than an existential one, and we believe Tether deserves credit for moving fast and at scale. We also believe Circle deserves credit for the freeze. Circle has long said it freezes only when directed by law enforcement or a court, not in real time during an active hack. After April's $285m Drift exploit, CEO Jeremy Allaire went further, saying a private company deciding "what is the right path or not" would be a "moral quandary." During the Drift exploit, about $232m in stolen USDC moved through Circle's own cross-chain transfer protocol over roughly six hours without being frozen. But, on Thursday, Circle froze $823m about 40 minutes after the Ethereum sweep, "in coordination with law enforcement." Does Binance have enough to cover the hole? The SAFU fund, about $1b in BTC, does not come close to covering it, so Binance says it will cover all losses from its own corporate funds. Last year’s 10/10 liquidation event cost Binance about $283m in depeg compensation plus its $400m “Together Initiative” ($300m in user vouchers and $100m in low-interest loans to institutions). That’s under $700m; this hack is roughly nine times that. A better yardstick is the BNB burn. 2026’s three quarterly burns so far have retired about $3.2bn of BNB. Net of freezes, the hole is roughly one year of burns, or about 4% of the ~$144bn in assets Binance held before the attack. It is a staggering amount of money, but Binance does appear to have it, or at least the ability to earn its way out of a hole based on our own calculations of their revenue-funded BNB burns. While we can’t independently verify Binance’s whole financial condition, and we don’t know exactly what Binance plans to do, Binance Co-CEO Richard Teng said plainly: “Binance will cover all losses from the SAFU fund and company funds.” What’s left: when will withdrawals reopen, where will the roughly $2.4b in ETH and BTC still in the attacker’s hands go next (THORChain, Tornado Cash, etc.), and how did an outsider come to know Binance’s systems this well? These are among the key specific questions we will be following in the coming days and weeks. But how the market reacts to the event broadly is also top of mind. Bitcoin and other crypto assets are trading lower on the news. Alex Thorn’s piece from Monday (Why Now Is the Time to Add and Hold BTC) relies heavily on the 50-week moving average as a key level to maintain a bullish trend, with a break below that is not retaken within 1 month cited as invalidating the paper’s thesis. That 50w MA currently sits at $76,103, and at the time of writing BTCUSD is trading at $77,000. So far, the 50w MA has held, with BTC trading as low as $76,301 overnight on Coinbase. Whether the 50w can hold this weekend is a key test that could be consequential for the next several months of Bitcoin’s technical market structure.

CareersThere are many chapters in a career. There is only one Goldman Sachs.Discover CareersWORKING AT GSStudentsLife at GSBenefitsFeatured OfficesOpen RolesMARKETSGlobal Music Revenues Are Forecast to Rise as Subscriber Growth Beats ExpectationsNov 5, 2026ShareMusic industry forecastThe outlook for recorded musicGrowth markets for streamingOpportunities to grow subscriptionsWhat's boosting live music?How will AI impact music?In Summary Goldman Sachs Research expects global music revenues to grow at an annualized rate of 5.8% to almost $200 billion in 2035 from $112 billion in 2025. Paid subscriptions for music streaming have ample room to grow relative to gaming and on-demand video services. Our analysts see an opportunity for increased conversion from free to paid subscription tiers among older age groups. The market for live music is forecast to grow 6% in 2026 despite economic uncertainty, driven by a strong global arena and stadium business. AI represents an opportunity for the industry as streaming providers and tech companies use the technology to personalize algorithms, curate content, and transform passive listeners into active creators.Global music industry revenues are expected to reach approximately $200 billion annually by 2035 amid an improving outlook for subscription streaming. New subscription models, AI, and direct-to-consumer offerings are creating opportunities for the industry to reach audiences in new ways, according to Goldman Sachs Research.
The music market undershot growth expectations over the last several years. The new forecast represents the first time in three years that Goldman Sachs Research has raised its long-term outlook for the industry, Stephen Laszczyk and Eric Sheridan write in the team’s 2026 edition of the annual “Music in the Air” report. Goldman Sachs Research expects global music revenues to increase at 6.7% year-on-year in 2026 and at a compound rate of 5.8% per year between 2025 and 2035.
“While growth is likely to moderate from the pace observed during the industry's streaming adoption phase, we continue to see a long runway for industry expansion supported by favorable consumer behavior and an increasingly diversified monetization model,” Laszczyk and Sheridan write.
Music streaming subscriptions are growing faster than expected
Paid streaming subscriptions are helping to shore up the outlook for recorded music. After three consecutive downgrades to its forecast for 2030 recorded music revenues, Goldman Sachs Research’s outlook for the segment this year reflects improvements in streaming revenue, physical revenue, and download and other digital revenue.
Subscription streaming revenue is growing faster, mainly because subscriber numbers are increasing more quickly than expected and revenue per user is rising in developed markets. Our analysts are factoring in more consistent price increases from streaming platforms as music labels increasingly incorporate higher royalties into their contracts and streaming platforms introduce new premium service tiers.
At the same time, increasing fan demand for vinyl and CDs is helping lift the outlook for physical music revenues in markets like Japan, South Korea, and the US. “We expect these trends to continue as fans increasingly view physical formats as collectibles rather than as a way to listen, and as artists incorporate physical formats into their album rollouts and tour experiences,” Laszczyk and Sheridan write.
Which markets will drive the growth of music?
Paid subscription streaming revenue beat our analysts’ expectations in 2025, and Goldman Sachs Research expects further growth ahead, driven by emerging markets. Laszczyk and Sheridan forecast the percentage of internet users with paid streaming subscriptions in emerging markets to rise from 10% in 2025 to 15% in 2035, with subscriber numbers boosted by growing populations and increasing internet penetration.
Paid subscriptions in developed markets also have room to grow, according to Laszczyk and Sheridan, who expect the number of paid subscribers in the US, Canada, Europe, and Australasia to rise to 568 million in 2035 from 398 million in 2025.
Only around 53% of Americans subscribed to paid music streaming in 2025, compared with around 60% for gaming and 90% for on-demand video. Goldman Sachs Research expects most developed markets to approach peak penetration for paid music streaming at 60% by 2035.
“Subscribers have been growing at a healthy clip. Going forward, we expect subscribers to grow in the mid-single-digit range over the next 10 years, driven by emerging market penetration and continued growth in developed markets.”Stephen LaszczykGoldman Sachs ResearchOlder age groups and new products could help drive paid music users
Older listeners could be an untapped audience. Data from the UK shows that older listeners are less likely to use paid streaming and less likely to convert from free to paid users.
“We see opportunity for increased conversion from free to paid among older age groups, especially as younger age cohorts who are heavy users of paid streaming services grow older, and as streaming providers adapt their marketing strategies to target older demographics,” Laszczyk and Sheridan write.
Introducing an ad-light tier could also help streaming providers drive subscriber acquisition. Goldman Sachs Research estimates that a small incremental fee of around $1-2 per month for a reduced advertising load could result in subscriber growth. “This follows a similar playbook to what has already been implemented in video streaming,” Laszczyk and Sheridan observe.
If 10% of free streaming users in developed markets shifted to a $1 ad-light tier, global ad-supported revenues would rise by around 8%, Goldman Sachs Research estimates.
Another emerging opportunity in streaming is direct-to-consumer offerings, where artists build a direct relationship with their fans without an intermediary platform controlling access to that audience.
This innovation is still in its early stages, Laszczyk and Sheridan write. But “if this ecosystem continues to develop the way it has been, the direct-to-consumer opportunity could grow from representing tens of millions of dollars of revenue today to hundreds of millions over the next decade.”
Increased touring and new venues are buoying live music
Despite pressure on consumer wallets from tariffs, gasoline prices, and higher interest rates, our analysts expect the market for live music to grow 6% in 2026, driven by a strong global arena and stadium business.
This supports Goldman Sachs Research’s thesis that demand for live events has increased globally since the Covid-19 pandemic, and that the sector is less exposed to economic downturns than other forms of discretionary spending.
Looking ahead, our analysts expect live music to grow at a similar 6% compound rate through 2035, underpinned by an increasing supply of diverse and popular artists touring over the next decade.
Stronger financial incentives to tour and efforts by record labels to promote new talent are set to drive the live music sector, Laszczyk and Sheridan project. And they expect venue capacity to grow, with operators poised to open several dozen new music venues around the world in the next five to seven years.
“Live music is a durable form of spending. If your favorite artist is making their way through town once every so many years, you are likely to prioritize that concert over other forms of discretionary spending.”Stephen LaszczykGoldman Sachs ResearchHow will AI impact the music industry?
AI’s impact on the music industry has been “the biggest debate among music investors over the last year,” Laszczyk and Sheridan say. One concern is that AI-generated music will displace human artists, but Laszczyk and Sheridan believe that fear is overblown for higher-profile artists in the near term. While the team does see some potential for cannibalization by AI over the long term, they expect that it will mostly be limited to lower-value music (including background and study music as well as mid-tier artists).
Only a mid-single-digit percentage of consumers used an AI music generation tool at least monthly as of the fourth quarter of 2025. As of the third quarter of 2025, around 55% of music creators had used an AI tool in the past year, but mostly for production workflow or mastering rather than to generate entirely new songs.
At the same time, AI represents an opportunity for music labels and rights holders: Streaming providers and tech companies can use the technology to personalize recommendations, curate content, and turn passive listeners into active creators.
“We believe that monetization will ultimately make its way back to the rights holders in a way that we think will disproportionately benefit some of these higher-end artists where AI music is likely created off of their image and likeness, their melodies, or their lyrics, given how popular they are,” Laszczyk says.

articles.title: New horizons: the legal and commercial frontier of digital assets − speech by Sasha Mills
articles.text:
New horizons: the legal and commercial frontier of digital assets − speech by Sasha Mills

Given at Hogan Lovells and Global Digital Finance Digital Assets Summit

Published on
01 October 2026

In this speech, Sasha Mills sets out five ways the Bank will continue to support responsible innovation. It will focus on outcomes, support testing and growth, clarify its processes, bring firms together and work with overseas authorities. Together, these steps will foster innovation while protecting financial stability.

Speech
Good afternoon. It is a pleasure to be with you today. Thank you to Hogan Lovells and Global Digital Finance for bringing together financial institutions, policymakers, regulators and technology innovators at a moment when the digital-assets debate is changing in an important way.
For several years, much of this debate has been about technical possibility. Can a security be issued on a distributed ledger? Can a smart contract automate an event in its lifecycle and embed AML/KYC checks? Can cash and assets move together across different systems? Increasingly, the answer is yes.
The harder question is whether those possibilities can become trusted, widely-used and commercially sustainable. We must ask not only whether the technology works, but who owns the asset; which record is authoritative; when settlement becomes final; what happens on insolvency; who is accountable; where the regulatory perimeter falls; and whether the service solves a problem that customers are willing to pay to solve.
Those are not peripheral questions. They mark the difference between an interesting experiment and working part of the financial system's infrastructure. Technology can create a token in an instant. Creating a trusted market around it is the more consequential task.
There is a useful parallel in the history of medicine. When Alexander Fleming observed the antibacterial effect of penicillin in 1928, the scientific insight was extraordinary. But the observation in a petri dish was not yet a medicine that could improve outcomes at scale. Other researchers had to turn that insight into a stable treatment. Manufacturers had to find ways to produce it reliably and in large quantities. Clinicians needed evidence and confidence to use it. A breakthrough became transformative only when a wider system developed around it.
I do not want to stretch the analogy too far. Financial markets are not medicine. But the lesson is helpful. Discovery matters. So do trial and error, evidence, standards, production, distribution and trust. Innovation succeeds when invention becomes everyday practice.
That is the journey I want to discuss today: how useful innovations in digital finance, led by industry with convening and coordination from the authorities where appropriate, can move from possibility to practical use, and from practical use to permanence.
Innovation founded on stability
For the Bank, financial stability is the foundation. But stability and innovation are not opposing objectives. Confidence in the system enables firms to invest, users to adopt and new approaches to achieve scale. Our secondary innovation objective recognises that innovation, pursued safely, can improve efficiency, strengthen resilience and support broader economic growth. We therefore support innovation in ways that preserve, and may ultimately reinforce, financial stability.
Our ambition is to create conditions in which new entrants and incumbents can explore responsible change, and in which successful initiatives can progress from experimentation towards scale. The secondary innovation objective has applied to the Bank’s regulation of central counterparties and central securities depositories. The Government has proposed extending that statutory focus to the Bank’s regulation of payment systems, including those using digital settlement assets, and related service providers. We welcome this proposal from Government, in particular that it will bring the objective to a further core part of our financial-market-infrastructure remit, reinforcing the approach we are already taking: working with government, other authorities and industry to maintain trust while enabling innovation.
We will not know in advance which technologies, products or business models will deliver the greatest benefits. Commercial users, not the authorities, should drive that selection. The Bank's role is to preserve strong foundations, remove unnecessary barriers, provide proportionate pathways for firms to learn and grow, and convene where a system-wide outcome cannot be achieved by firms acting alone. As authorities our role is to ensure that there is a platform for open competition and that what succeeds commercially can do so safely and responsibly. But we should not pick winners; that’s for the market. It is industry’s job to identify solutions, test them, and implement them.
From commercial value to trusted markets
Let me start with commercial value, because innovation will not be useful if it is not commercially viable. Tokenisation may enable faster processing, reduce reconciliation and operational costs, automate lifecycle events, mobilise collateral more efficiently, and make information available in more usable forms. But a technically successful pilot that cannot attract users, connect to liquidity or generate sustainable activity will not transform finance.
The prize is not merely that an individual firm makes one process quicker. It is that successful innovation becomes normal market practice. That requires continuity of confidence across the system. Cross-market adoption is hard and may cut across individual firms’ incentives. The benefits depend on other firms investing too, on compatible operational arrangements, on common legal understanding and on standards that allow systems to interoperate.
Structural change, such as tokenisation, also requires different parts of the financial system to move together. Issuers, investors, trading venues, infrastructures, banks, custodians and technology providers may all need to adapt. These sectors have different systems, incentives, and regulatory frameworks. And because financial markets operate across borders, new arrangements must be capable of connecting across platforms and jurisdictions. Otherwise, innovation intended to reduce friction could create new technological, legal or regulatory fragmentation.
Let’s go back to penicillin. Penicillin became transformative not because every institution pursued an isolated solution, but because research, testing, production and clinical practice developed together. In financial markets too, a good idea may work within one firm yet fail across firms if the connections are missing. The investable frontier within an institution can remain uninvestable across the market.
Strong foundations therefore matter. A tokenised security needs a legally authoritative record. Ownership must be evidenced and transferred. Competing claims must be resolvable. Settlement must be final and irrevocable. Insolvency protections must work. Responsibility for maintaining the record must be clear. Faster technology does not automatically produce clearer legal effect.
The same is true operationally. An asset cannot realise its full value unless the cash leg can settle with comparable certainty. Nor will a new platform scale if it cannot connect to existing infrastructure, liquidity and custody arrangements. Interoperability is therefore about more than a technical bridge: it requires compatible rulebooks, data, operating hours, legal arrangements and risk controls.
This is why the Bank - working closely with the Financial Conduct Authority, HM Treasury and industry - has focused on providing the foundations for tokenised markets to thrive in the UK. In May, we, with the FCA, published a Call for Input on Tokenisation which set out our commitment to enabling the benefits of tokenisation in the UK's wholesale financial markets. We pointed to work already underway and made commitments in several key areas where we can use our regulatory, operational, and policymaking levers to drive change. Later this year, we will publish a full Roadmap which will provide a clear forward path, to help ensure all parts of the financial system move together to grasp the gains of tokenisation. Industry must engage actively with that Roadmap, align investment and delivery plans around it, and work collectively to turn those foundations into scalable market activity.
The role of industry and the authorities: an end-to-end system
Industry collaboration and coordinated action is essential to identifying what stands in the way of responsible innovation, and which combination of solutions can remove those barriers. Some obstacles may require targeted legal, regulatory or operational changes. Others will demand market-wide coordination, common standards and shared approaches. Because tokenisation cuts across products, institutions and infrastructures, no single intervention will be enough. Progress will depend on complementary changes that reinforce one another.
That is also why the work of the Wholesale Digital Markets Champion matters. By bringing firms together around practical use cases, such as the repo market, the Champion can expose dependencies, align incentives and build momentum where coordinated investment is needed. This can help industry and the authorities distinguish between problems that require a coordinated action plan and those that market forces will solve by themselves. Public authorities should focus on genuine public-policy obstacles, rather than assume that every barrier to adoption has a regulatory answer.
The Digital Securities Sandbox: evidence before permanence
But coordination alone is not enough. Firms also need a way to test their ideas, capabilities and market appetite for their products and services. And they need to do this under real-world conditions and with real users.
That is one reason why the authorities created the Digital Securities Sandbox. I should explain, sandbox does not mean playing with a child's version of reality, it means allowing real trades with real customers in a way that won't break the financial system if something goes wrong. Along with the FCA we have changed the rules to allow new market structures and products to be created and tested. The DSS allows firms to issue, trade and settle digital securities, on new technologies and combine trading and settlement in the same legal entity. This was not previously permitted and enables firms to set up efficient new market structures that exploit new technologies. They can use distributed ledger (DLT) and other new technologies to record and transfer assets and offer completely new financial instruments that may unlock new sources of liquidity, offer new investors access to markets previous unavailable to them, and make post trade processes significantly more efficient.
While the DSS does use limits, these have been set at levels that allow for meaningful activity - for example, £8-13.1 billion for gilts, and £17-28 billion for sterling corporate bonds – while ensuring appropriate financial stability safeguards are in place.
The Bank has already adjusted the DSS in response to feedback and as the market has developed, including broadening the settlement assets that firms may use to include stablecoins, subject to minimum requirements and case-by-case assessment.
A deep understanding of the legal operational and practical barriers that need to be removed or overcome help us be more proportionate and, taken as a whole, these activities have the potential to drive significant innovation and growth. We are working with the Wholesale Digital Markets Champion and the industry to build this future for UK markets.
A well designed permanent regulatory regime that supports innovation and allows a whole new generation of firms, products, and market structures to flourish is an important prize. By serving as a starting point for a permanent regulatory regime, and enabling firms and authorities to see the real-world benefits and risks of these technologies before it’s put in place, the DSS provides a real benefit to the system as a whole – beyond simply the institutions participating in it. In this way, the DSS promotes greater certainty, competition and innovation compared to alternative ‘sandbox’ approaches.
I am encouraged by the number of firms in the DSS, the steady flow of firms passing the ‘Go Live Gate’ and breadth of business models being explored. The prospect that the Digital Gilt Instrument, or DIGIT, could further our collective learning. DIGIT, as a digitally native government bond issued in the DSS, provides a real instrument around which firms can develop and test the connections needed across issuance, ownership records, trading, settlement, custody and collateral use. It does not determine the design of every future security, but it could provide a practical catalyst for the ecosystem around digital securities and demonstrates the UK’s commitment to digitising its markets.
Integrated market structures, efficiency from on chain assets born out of experimentation and business growth through and after the DSS is the aim. Not all ideas or firms will be successful, but we are allowing them to try so market forces, not regulatory constraints, determine the future.
Progress is not linear in innovation. The value of all the work by firms and the authorities below the waterline will only become truly apparent when this new generation of businesses have scaled up in the DSS and the successful ones are operating seamlessly with the wider market as it transforms to greater digitisation.
The longer-term legal architecture
This is why the future of CSD regulation and settlement finality belongs firmly in the innovation agenda. On the infrastructure side, we need to consider whether the definition of a CSD remains fit for new business models, whether the scope of securities required to settle on a CSD is set appropriately, and how requirements should apply proportionately to firms that may look different from today's FMIs. On the legal side, settlement finality must continue to provide certainty for CSDs and the wider system, while the framework for financial collateral arrangements responds to the emergence of different asset types. Efficient technology is insufficient if ownership, transfer and finality remain uncertain.
The evidence generated in the DSS will be important as the authorities consider the future framework and possible steady-state paths for successful activity. The objective should be a framework capable of supporting established and new structures while retaining the confidence on which both depend.
Pathways: same risk, same regulatory outcome
Our guiding principle in forming regulation going forward continues to be ‘same risk, same regulatory outcome’. That does not mean rules and supervisory approaches must always apply in exactly the way they have before. They may need to be amended, interpreted or calibrated so that a different technology, product or entity achieves the same underlying outcome. Innovation does not receive a lower standard. The standard remains the same, even where the route to meeting it changes.
This approach recognises that not all experimentation will scale. A model may prove operationally sound but commercially unattractive. Another may be commercially attractive but unable to manage the risks it creates. Either conclusion is useful evidence. Penicillin is widely known because the discovery ultimately worked at scale. Responsible experimentation must also make room for ideas that do not. The point is to learn, not to predetermine success. That learning will support further innovation.
And learning must run both ways. Industry must be candid about business cases, dependencies and risks. Regulators must listen, test whether rules remain justified and adapt where evidence demonstrates that change is needed. A flexible framework is not one without standards. It is one that can calibrate its requirements to the risk, the evidence and the stage of development.
The relevant questions are therefore functional. What service is being provided? What risks does it create? Where do those risks travel? Could they become systemic? Which authority has the tools to address them? As activities and risks change, the perimeter must remain capable of recognising the substance of what is being done.
Trusted functions and a safe transition
Consider tokenised collateral. Tokenisation may make collateral faster or easier to identify, transfer and mobilise. That could reduce operational friction. But collateral exists to absorb risk, especially in stressed conditions. Its legal enforceability, settlement finality, liquidity, valuation, custody, operational resilience and accessibility in stress matter even more.
The same is true of central clearing. Tokenisation may change how services are delivered, but it does not remove the value of multilateral netting, disciplined default management and trusted risk management. Innovation should improve those functions, not ignore or impair them.
A safe transition therefore matters as much as the destination. New and established arrangements may coexist for a considerable period. Links between them must not create hidden dependencies, ambiguous ownership or new channels of contagion. Incumbents and new entrants both have an essential part to play.
Practical foundations
Digital assets also need to be paid for. The cash leg is not a secondary implementation detail. Asset and payment transfers must be coordinated so that neither party bears unnecessary principal risk. Central bank money remains the ultimate risk-free settlement asset and an anchor for the singleness of money, even in a future in which private forms of digital money also play important roles.
Synchronisation is not simply an experiment: the Bank intends to deliver a live synchronisation capability in 2028, enabling innovative platforms to settle transactions in central bank money. We are testing that capability now through the Synchronisation Lab, where prospective operators can develop use cases, test design choices and refine business models in a non-live environment ahead of launch. Building on Project Meridian, this work is helping us ensure that the live service provides a trusted settlement capability on which the market can build, without prescribing every platform or use case that connects to it.
This puts the UK in a good position to scale digital asset adoption, because it will be built on the foundation of programmable risk-free money.
The Bank's commitments
Let me draw these points together into five commitments from the Bank, with some corresponding challenges to industry. Progress will not come from regulatory action alone: it will require firms to invest, collaborate and turn technological possibility into services that customers use.
First, we will not make regulatory judgements in isolation from the technology, activity and risks before us. We will remain agnostic about which technologies industry chooses, while applying the principle of same risk, same regulatory outcome. Different technologies may require different regulatory approaches, but each must deliver an equivalent outcome that protects confidence in the financial system. Industry, in turn, must demonstrate how its chosen technology delivers that outcome.
Second, we will support experimentation, scaling and, where appropriate, transition towards systemic scale by incumbents and new entrants. We will use proportionate requirements, conditions and activity limits, and we will learn from live activity. Industry must match that pathway with ambition: move beyond proofs of concept, commit capital and senior attention, bring real users and transactions into testing, and build credible plans for commercial scale.
Third, we will improve our processes. We will be clear about what we require, realistic about response times and prepared to adapt where evidence shows that unnecessary friction can be removed without weakening standards. Industry must engage early and candidly, submit robust evidence, identify dependencies and risks, and tell us where requirements create genuine barriers, with practical proposals for resolving them.
Fourth, we will support the Digital Markets Champion and the Government's Wholesale Financial Markets Digital Strategy. In particular, we will support the Champion’s work to convene industry where coordinated action is necessary to deliver a system-wide outcome, while leaving commercial choices to the market. But convening is not delivery. Firms must be prepared to invest together, agree workable standards, resolve collective-action problems and build the connections that allow successful propositions to operate across the market.
And fifth, we will work with domestic and international authorities to reduce fragmentation and support responsible paths to cross-border growth. Interoperability across systems must be matched by coherence across standards, legal frameworks and regulatory approaches. Industry must design for that reality from the outset: participate in standard-setting, build interoperable services and avoid closed solutions that reproduce fragmentation in digital form.
Assets, market participants, infrastructures and financial flows operate internationally. And so the benefits of innovation will be greatest where firms can operate across borders with confidence, rather than navigate fragmented legal, regulatory and technical frameworks.
That does not require every jurisdiction to adopt the same technology or market structure. But it does require cooperation on outcomes. Authorities, market infrastructures and industry will need to work together internationally to promote interoperability, support common standards where appropriate, and ensure that differences in legal frameworks, regulatory expectations, supervisory approaches, settlement arrangements and risk-management practices do not create unnecessary barriers to cross-border activity.
The Bank attaches considerable importance to international engagement. Through our work with overseas authorities, standard-setting bodies and market participants, we want to help shape an environment in which innovation can scale across borders while preserving financial stability and confidence. Modernisation will succeed more quickly, and deliver greater benefits, if markets evolve in ways that are capable of working together internationally.
These commitments are not a promise that every experiment will succeed. They are a commitment that good ideas can be tested fairly, regulatory expectations will focus on outcomes, and successful innovation will have a credible route towards permanence. But the route will only matter if industry uses it. The challenge to firms is to bring forward propositions with real commercial value, invest for scale, collaborate where markets need collective solutions, and demonstrate that innovation can meet the same outcomes of trust, resilience and stability. That is the partnership required to move from possibility to permanence.
Conclusion: from possibility to permanence
The UK begins from strong foundations: a trusted legal system, established market infrastructure, deep capital markets, active government and regulatory programmes, and firms willing to experiment. The challenge now is to use those assets to their fullest potential.
Technology, law, money, infrastructure, standards and commercial demand must develop as one ecosystem. Industry must identify propositions that solve genuine problems and make the investments needed to realise them. Authorities must preserve confidence, remove unnecessary obstacles and provide proportionate pathways. Government must provide the strategic and legislative architecture. And all of us must keep learning from evidence.
The penicillin story began with a striking possibility. Its enduring impact came from the difficult work that followed: testing, refinement, production and adoption across a whole system. Digital finance is at a different frontier, but it faces a related test. We have demonstrated much of what the technology can do. We now need to build the conditions in which the best applications can be trusted, connected and used at scale.
The Bank will not pick the winning token, ledger or business model. Commercial value should drive adoption. But commercial success will be sustainable only where it is safe and responsible, where legal and operational foundations are strong, and where confidence can continue as activity grows through strategic coordination between actors to adopt, adapt and scale.
The new horizon is not a financial system in which everything is tokenised. It is one in which innovations that offer real value can move from possibility to practical use, and from practical use to lasting scale, on foundations strong enough to retain the confidence of the market.
Thank you.
I would like to thank Shane Scott, Andrew Bailey, Sarah Breeden, Michael Yoganayagam Richard Spooner, Priya Mistry, Kushal Balluck, Mark Strasshine, Steven Dyer, Nina Turnbull and Edward Denbee for their help in preparing these remarks

Sasha Mills
Executive Director, Financial Market Infrastructure
