articles.title: View from the markets: The earnings season has been good, but is it good enough? - BNP Paribas Asset Management - Corporate English
articles.text:
By Daniel Morris, Chief Market Strategist

At first blush, there is little to complain about regarding the third-quarter earnings results so far (about half of the companies in the S&P 500 and MSCI Europe have reported). Compared to the third quarter in 2025, profits have risen by 26% for the S&P 500 and by 40%(!) for Europe, with double-digit figures for other major indices, based on data from FactSet (see Exhibit 1). This is well above historical norms.

The worry is that those values are not far off what was expected by analysts, and in one case it was below. Earnings have come in only 2% better than expected for the S&P 500. Typically, earnings surprises (how much better or worse results are versus consensus) run in the 3-4% range. Over the previous few quarters, they were even higher. This quarter few indices have matched that.

The chart shows clearly what the source of the disappointment has been: technology. The surprise for the Nasdaq 100 index is -3% and for emerging market (EM) tech stocks it is -8%. The disappointments in emerging markets were almost entirely driven by tech stocks; results for the other sectors were 1% better.

There are two questions: Are these disappointments surprising and how much do they matter?

Given not only how high expectations have been for technology stocks, and how rapidly the artificial intelligence theme is developing, it is not surprising that companies have reported results that are further off the mark than is typically the case.

Though there has been some disappointment in the short term (which will drive the short-term performance of the stock), the more important consideration for investors is the medium-term outlook (which will determine the stock’s medium-term path).

It is worth recalling that consensus estimates for Nasdaq 100 earnings growth in 2027 is 35% and for emerging market technology stocks it is 39%. Even if actual results are a few percentage points lower, and if valuations do not change significantly, indices would typically appreciate in line with earnings.

Sector drivers

It is not only the tech sector that has boosted EPS (earnings-per-share) growth rates. Higher energy prices have contributed to strong results for indices like MSCI Europe and Russell Value. Excluding the energy sector, earnings growth for MSCI Europe is a (still good) 17%. But even setting aside the gains from tech and higher oil prices, results across other sectors are robust. The automobile industry continues to be a drag on the consumer discretionary sector, but most of the others are seeing high single or double-digit earnings growth (see Exhibit 2).

Whether this broadening in earnings continues, or even accelerates, will partly depend on the rate of adoption of AI technologies. There is already significant anecdotal evidence of companies finding meaningful productivity improvements through AI. One example is insurance companies reducing their claims review times and credit losses by using micro-expression recognition technology.

Stories of CFOs becoming alarmed by high AI bills also suggests adoption is accelerating. This will be critical not only for the future rate of non-tech company earnings growth, but also for the hyperscalers, as they look for the return on their massive capital expenditure.

articles.title: Testing times require time for testing − speech by Ruth Smith
articles.text:
Testing times require time for testing − speech by Ruth Smith

Given at UK Finance

Published on
13 July 2026

Ruth Smith reflects on the Bank’s resolvability assessments of banks and building societies, and discusses how the Bank engages with firms at different stages on the journey to resolvability. She emphasises the importance of realistic testing and ongoing maintenance of resolvability capabilities, so they are ready for use if needed.

Speech
Good afternoon. It’s a pleasure to have the opportunity to speak to you today. Thank you to UK Finance for hosting us. Resolvability is a journey that the Bank and firms are on together, and engagement with industry has been essential to the progress we’ve made so far. Resolution matters because, as we have been reminded in recent years, when a financial institution fails, resolution enables the ongoing provision of critical financial services, protects customer deposits and prevents disruption to the wider economy. Maintaining a credible, effective and responsive resolution regime is at the heart of financial stability in testing times – supporting a resilient financial sector, which in turn enables households and firms to thrive. In January, my colleague Dave Ramsden spoke about this need for responsiveness and evolution in the Bank’s approach to resolution, so the regime’s outcomes are met in an ever-changing landscape.footnote [1]
Today, I want to focus on the idea of outcomes, and the goal we as the Resolution Authority have in mind for all firms – ongoing resolvability.
I will discuss our outcomes-based approach to the assessment of different firms, how we apply the Resolvability Assessment Framework, or RAF, to different groups of firms, and how we use testing and assurance to maintain progress.
I also want to look ahead to the principles we expect to guide us in evolving our approach to assessing resolvability. While our end destination remains the same, how we get there must respond to the growing maturity of firms’ capabilities, and the changing terrain and system that they are a part of.
The Resolvability Assessment Framework
The RAF applies to our major and mid-tier banks and building societies.footnote [2] The starting point is that it is proportionate by design and inherently risk-based. Firms are different, and they pose different challenges in resolution. While our objective is for all firms to be resolvable, the path to getting there will not be the same for everyone.
That is why the RAF is focused on outcomes. As firms grow in size and complexity, we expect more from them because their failure could have a greater impact on financial stability. To maintain that proportionality, we recently updated the calibration of the framework, raising both the MREL and Resolution Assessment thresholds.
The proportionality steps are broadly:

one, the RAF applies to firms where we will use our resolution powers if they fail – typically those with more than £25 billion in assets.
two, firms with bail-in resolution strategies need more capabilities than transfer firms:footnote [3] including financial resources to enable recapitalisation and capabilities to plan for post-resolution restructuring.
and three, major UK firms – those with £100 billion or more in retail deposits – must meet the RAF reporting and disclosure requirements, providing a layer of additional, public transparency and scrutiny for both firms and the Bank.

In all cases, we expect firms to own their resolvability, regardless of where they are on their journey. This means that firms’ senior management and boards are responsible for ensuring that their firm has the capabilities necessary for resolution and that these are tailored to the individual attributes of the firm.

Chart 1: RAF overview of requirements

The RAF also sets out three outcomes we want to see for the Bank to consider a firm resolvable: firms having adequate financial resources for resolution, being able to continue to do business through resolution and restructuring, and co-ordinating and communicating effectively.footnote [4]
This is not a box-ticking exercise: each firm needs to take the necessary steps to be ready for orderly resolution. What is needed for an established G-SIB differs to a neobank. And once capabilities are in place, they should be maintained to ensure they remain ready, including as the firm and the market evolve. Ongoing testing is crucial, to ensure capabilities operate effectively and are ready for use when required.
For international firms, the Bank works intensively in BAU so we are ready to support home authorities to implement a co-ordinated resolution if needed. While we expect international firms in the UK to achieve broadly the same outcomes as our home firms, how they do this may differ as they focus on having the capabilities required to deliver their group resolution strategy.
Assessing resolvability in these cases is not a one-size-fits-all exercise. We consider the approach of the home jurisdiction, alongside each firm's own preparations and UK business model. And we maintain active, practical engagement with international authorities to ensure we are all ready to use our respective powers if required.
Maintaining these close relationships enables us to respond with speed and agility in a crisis. We did this during the failures of Silicon Valley Bank and Credit Suisse. Such strong co-operation and co-ordination between authorities is a lesson from the financial crisis we cannot forget. Effective co-operation and co-ordination is the core purpose of the work of the Financial Stability Board’s (FSB) Cross-Border Crisis Management group for banks, which I chair. Structures like the FSB, Trilateral Principal Level Exercises (with the UK, US and Banking Union authorities), firm-specific Crisis Management Groups and regular bilateral engagement are essential for authorities to build resilience and readiness which can be relied upon in a crisis.
Our approach to assessing resolvability to date
I’ve led the RAF journey since 2018. At this point I think it is important to reflect on what we, as an authority, have done to foster progress towards firms being fully resolvable, as well as the progress that firms have made over their own resolvability.
We’ve now completed two assessments of the major UK firms and two assessments of mid-tier firms under the RAF. These assessments provide confidence that we can manage UK bank failure in an orderly way. The findings also support the Financial Policy Committee’s judgements on the optimal level of capital needed in the banking system.footnote [5]
Our first RAF assessment for major UK firms was largely desk-based. Our focus was on the capabilities firms had built and how they assured themselves that their preparations were adequate.
Our accompanying RAF public statement in 2022 provided transparency on our resolution strategies for individual firms and the areas each of them needed to focus on. We shared thematic findings and examples of good practice.
Our second RAF assessment gave us an improved view on each firm. Our assessment approach developed from being mainly desk-based to being underpinned by targeted tests of the Adequate Financial Resources outcome, providing us with a better idea of how policy would work in practice for each firm. We found continued progress by firms along with areas for further work.
Moving to our mid-tier assessments, we have mirrored our approach to the major UK firms while keeping proportionality and specificity at the forefront of our thinking. We have used the assessments to identify areas where we need to guide firms more explicitly on what we are looking for, without undermining the principle of firms’ responsibility for their own resolvability and keeping to an outcomes-based approach.
Our second assessment of the mid-tier firms last year included targeted testing of firms’ continuity capabilities, where the ultimate aim is to ensure the continued provision of services that are critical to the economy.footnote [6] Events such as the failure of Silicon Valley Bank have underlined that continuity is essential for keeping the lights on while we execute resolution. This matters for all firms and especially for mid-tiers, which are more likely to have a preferred resolution strategy of transfer. It is also an area where we saw weakness in our first mid-tier assessment.

Chart 2: RAF timeline

All this work with firms has enabled us to fine-tune what we need from firms, for example we have been able to reduce loss-absorbency requirements for transfer firms, increase thresholds, extend the time between RAF assessments, delete reporting templates, clarify requirements and share best practice. This makes the regime more efficient and targeted and demonstrates its responsiveness.
We are also streamlining our own internal processes for reviewing resolution plans, again being responsive while maintaining readiness. For example, we are leveraging the information gained through the RAF for our statutory resolvability assessments and, where firms’ capabilities have reached a steady state, we plan to use the flexibility the Bank has in legislation to review resolution plans less frequently.footnote [7]
We are reviewing our lessons from the delivery of the RAF to make further amendments to reporting requirements. This includes reviewing Supervisory Statement 19/13 on resolution planning, where we hope to tailor the requirements for the different firms in the system, while ensuring that the Bank can deploy its resolution powers across the population of firms it is responsible for. In particular, these changes aim to enhance the resolvability of smaller firms that are not in scope of the RAF.
The value of testing
Testing – whether as part of firms’ assurance or led by the Bank – is a valuable way to enhance our collective readiness. At this point we all have a mutual understanding of what it means to be resolvable, but resolution will always be a high-pressured transaction that requires both the Bank and firm. That is why we focus on outcomes and flexible capabilities.
For the Bank, testing is crucial to assess if firms’ capabilities can deliver what we need to execute a resolution in the public interest. Our testing complements our review of firms’ assessments of their capabilities and our review of their own assurance exercises. For firms, Bank-led testing is an opportunity to understand how the Bank will engage with them in resolution and how their capabilities may be utilised.
So testing cannot be seen as a narrow regulatory compliance exercise: firms should use it to think realistically about what they would have to do and how easily they could use their capabilities at pace and under pressure in resolution.
In short, realistic testing must be a priority. By realistic I mean testing that is time-bound, end-to-end, dynamic and involving relevant decision-makers or third parties. Realistic testing ultimately forces decision-makers to exercise the muscle of making decisions in uncertainty. We have seen that firms performing more strongly in assessments are likely to have undertaken dynamic, resolution-focused, integrated fire drill exercises that test across barriers and seniority levels using different scenarios.
Questions firms should be asking themselves as part of their assurance include:

Are data and data processes operable and effective at speed under the unique stresses of resolution? Bluntly, poor data and overly manual processes hinder rapid decision-making by senior management and the authorities, introducing unnecessary risk.
Have firms engaged realistically with the uncomfortable options that may be necessary? Resolution is more than just deep recovery. Firms need to ensure they embed this reality in their capability design and assurance. We all need to be clear that resolution may result in significant business model and senior leadership changes to respond to the causes of failure.
And have previous issues been remediated? Resolvability isn’t static so we will inevitably find more issues requiring remediation. Senior management need to own remediation and track progress when issues are identified.

For major firms, we have evolved our assessments to provide firms with space to perform their own assurance and to undertake specific work at the Bank’s request. That was why we chose to delay the third RAF assessment by a year.
In our third assessment we will review the clarity of firms’ assurance plans and the outputs from the valuations and restructuring planning exercises we have asked firms to undertake. Questions we will be asking include: is the assurance provided by the firm appropriate to the scale and complexity of the firm? Does it consider interdependencies between capabilities? Is it realistic? How are findings being remediated and tracked?
For mid-tier firms, we also provided an indicative scope for undertaking a valuations exercise to help firms understand our assurance expectations. This replaced a Bank-led test we had planned for this year.
We have also shared more information on how we expect to use the Bank’s powers to help firms prepare. We recently had a helpful roundtable with UK Finance to discuss the updated operational guide to bail-in and the new operational guide to transfer resolution. We issued these guides not to establish new capabilities we are asking firms to build. But to help firms and wider stakeholders understand more about how the Bank could execute a resolution transaction and what it would involve in practice. We also engage firms in a targeted way on topics where we see a need to do so, such as the recent roundtable on resolvability for building societies which was hosted by the BSA.
Third RAF assessment: assessing resolvability with agility and precision
Looking forward, we are already well underway with our third assessment of the major UK firms focused on the Continuity and Restructuring outcome. The assessment will conclude with the publication of the findings on 10 June 2027.
As I set out in my letter to CFOs Opens in a new window in February this year, our testing and assurance work for the third assessment has evolved and is:

More agile: recognising firms are doing their own testing, we have reduced overlaps in scope and sequenced or streamlined firm-specific engagement, without compromising our thematic, cohort-based approach.
More precise: we have worked with firms, supervisors and our Resolution Procurement Framework suppliers,footnote [8] building in their feedback to ensure we test effectively and realistically core capabilities for continuity and restructuring, including how they need to work together to deliver timely and robust outputs across the different phases of resolution contingency planning and execution.
And more holistic: our testing across barriers is for the first time guided by a resolution scenario, to provide a single thread running through the different tests and enhance realism. But ultimately the scenario is a means to an end of testing the capabilities.

The path ahead – for established firms on the resolvability journey
We are now at a level of maturity with bank resolution planning where we consider the policy landscape is well-established. That doesn’t mean we won’t continue to be responsive to learnings, nor will we stop considering the efficiency and proportionality of the regime. But the outcomes we need for resolution are timeless and cater for the different firms in scope of the UK resolution regime. Where the context surrounding firms is changing, we may need to look at how that alters our view of firms’ resolvability, in line with the RAF being a point-in-time assessment.
Within the major and mid-tier cohorts there are two broad groups of firms: those established on their resolvability journey and those newly coming into scope.
For the more established firms, ongoing maintenance is a key focus. This recognises these firms are resolvable. That doesn’t mean they don’t all have areas to work on or new issues won’t be identified by testing. For these firms, we will focus on remediation of past lessons, targeted testing, and reviewing assurance. But our approach will continue evolving, based also on feedback from the industry and our internal preparedness work.
We expect these firms to increasingly take even more of a lead on testing capabilities as part of their own assurance work, with a focus on holistic and realistic testing across barriers. The Bank will support firms, but we won’t be prescriptive – and rightly so, given where firms’ capabilities are. This approach will enable firms to structure their assurance in a way that works best for them, helping management achieve business objectives.
At the end of our third assessment in summer 2027, we will ask the major firms to present testing plans to us, informed by our RAF feedback. We will then engage bilaterally in a risk-based, proportionate way as firms undertake their testing plans. Where relevant, we will also engage with host authorities bilaterally and via Crisis Management Groups. I want to be clear though that we recognise that the cost for firms of maintaining resolvability is likely lower, all else equal, than the design and build phase, and this will be reflected in firms’ assurance plans.
We are planning that the fourth RAF assessment of major UK firms will not be before 2029-30. This will allow firms to focus on their testing plans and for the Bank to engage with firms and stakeholders to plan the assessment.
We will say more next summer, but as with the third assessment, we want to keep advancing and focusing on outcomes and how the Bank expects to use capabilities in a resolution.
The content and approach will reflect the findings from the third assessment, work done by firms in the interim and the circumstances at the time. But we will have a focus on the Co-ordination and Communication outcome.
Management, communication and governance capabilities lend themselves to assessing how resolvability barriers come together as a whole through the lens of simulations and senior management and board walkthroughs. So, it is likely this will be a feature. We will also maximise efficiencies between the Bank’s plans and firms’ multi-year testing plans.
Beyond that is very much in the medium term! But my expectation is that we will continue to embed resolvability assessment within firms.
Our approach to mid-tier firms with established capabilities will draw from our assessments of the major firms. But we will continue to take a proportionate approach. We will engage firms next summer on the scope and approach to the 2028 mid-tier assessment. Firms should expect a structured information request and Bank-led tests focusing on how capabilities would be used in practice. Following the third mid-tier assessment, we will consider our future approach based on firms’ progress.
The mid-tier cohort is a broad one, especially following the PRA’s doubling of the threshold for firms to be in scope of the major firm RAF.footnote [9] So, we will increasingly take a tailored approach to assessing the resolvability of mid-tier firms, based on size, complexity and resolution strategy. More complex mid-tier firms will rightly need to do more than simpler, smaller ones.
As a final thought on established firms, it is important that firms consider not just their own resolvability but their broader role in the financial system. For example, some firms act as FMI intermediaries by providing access to clearing, settlement or payment services to other banks and building societies. In these cases, providers of the intermediary service should continue to provide services, and plan accordingly, when clients are in resolution, so long as they continue to perform their obligations. They should also make information available to support clients’ resolution planning.footnote [10]
The path ahead – for those just joining us on the resolvability journey or those with more ground to cover
I will turn now to another group of firms – those just joining us on their resolvability journey or those with relatively more ground still to cover. We recognise that these firms are at a different stage on their resolvability journey and that requires a different approach from us.
This group comprises firms in a variety of situations. First, it includes firms that are growing into our thresholds and have work to do to build up their capabilities. Building capacity for resolution is essential and there is no time to waste. We will engage in a targeted and technical way with these firms, supporting them to get up the curve as quickly as possible. These firms must own their resolvability and build quickly and effectively, making the most of our established policy landscape.
More established firms may also find themselves in this group where there is substantially more work to do on their resolvability. This could happen for various reasons such as because firms are making material changes to their business, such as mergers or acquisitions, which affect their ability to achieve the resolvability outcomes. We expect firms to consider their resolvability as they go through these changes, to update us on material changes and to remediate issues that would impede resolution. We will engage with firms closely throughout this process until they reach a steady state again. It may take time for firms to make the necessary changes. But we expect firms to demonstrate they have a plan and that they have considered the impact of any integration actions on resolvability.
Established RAF firms may also have more work to do where the issues we have identified have persisted and are not being adequately remediated. In such cases, you should expect us to co-ordinate our engagement closely with the PRA. You may also see us deploying our powers to appoint skilled persons. We will do this in a targeted way and as part of a wider engagement plan with each firm.
Testing has an important role to play for all of these firms as they build or enhance their capabilities. A common feature of our approach to all these groups is the involvement of technical, dedicated specialists to support our firm-facing teams where needed. Third-party advisers on our Resolution Procurement Framework have a crucial role to play here. You should expect us to work more regularly with them as providers of market and operational expertise to support the design of the Bank’s assessments and in undertaking skilled persons reviews if required.
Beyond banks
Banks are not the only firms with resolution regimes, as Dave Ramsden noted in January. We are building out our regime for UK central counterparties (CCPs). While the capabilities will be different than for banks, the underlying expectation of resolvability is the same. In May, we published a Discussion Paper that sets out three draft outcomes for a CCP to be considered resolvable.footnote [11] This is a first step to invite feedback from industry on our thinking. Subject to the responses to the Discussion Paper, we expect to consult later this year on more detailed resolvability expectations, which are proportionate and reflective of the risks that a CCP failure would pose.
Conclusion
So, we have collectively come a long way towards the outcome of ongoing resolvability. This matters because a credible, effective and responsive resolution regime which is proportionate underpins financial stability and supports growth. But resolvability is a journey that can never be ‘done’. Firms, whatever waypoint they have reached on their resolvability journey, need to make sure they build and maintain their capabilities, so they are prepared for resolution on an ongoing basis. Testing must increasingly be at the heart of this. And we need to remain agile and responsive, and focused on outcomes, so we are ready and able to execute a resolution if needed in testing times.
I would like to thank Adam Cull, Kat Hind, Pauline Maburutse, Jane Maxwell and Matt Wooderson for their help in preparing these remarks. I would also like to thank Andrew Bailey, Dave Ramsden, Jackie Tibbetts and Robert Zammit for their helpful comments.

Capitulation... You On Stocks Or Trump On Iran

Marko Papic, Chief Investment Strategist & Head of GeoMacro

Iran

US Election

Geopolitics

Published on
03 Nov 2026

October has been a bad month for equities — particularly AI/tech ones — and a great month for oil. We do not think that the AI supercycle is ending, it has more room to go. Token price decline is a sign of a price war between LLMs, not a decline in demand. In fact, that price war is what is driving datacenter profitability, which is what the bull market is actually based on.As such, what matters on a tactical time horizon is whether Trump capitulates on Iran. If he does not, the market will have to correct. We take the bullish side and expect oil prices to decline imminently, forcing a short squeeze and powering equities higher.

PERSPECTIVES Quarterly update

PERSPECTIVES: Economic and asset class update – March 2026

Ready to talk?

×

Robust economic growth is expected due to solid consumption and sizeable investment, although geopolitical tensions could act as a drag. We see stable sequential quarterly growth in the US in 2026, while in the Eurozone extensive German fiscal stimulus should keep growth near potential. In Japan, the government’s pro-growth policy will help sustain robust economic activity. Policy support for strategic industries and households will continue in China.

On investment, we argue that discipline will continue to beat drama. Equities started the year on a strong footing and, despite recent reverses, are still on track for future gains. A strong earnings outlook is supportive and sectoral strength is broadening. On fixed income, deficits are keeping the US long end elevated but investment grade is steady despite AI disruption risks. Recent events in the Middle East and investors’ reactions have underlined the case for gold; oil remains fundamentally well-supplied but more short-term price spikes are possible. In FX, previous USD weakness has not been sustained but future possible headwinds from asset diversification are still relevant.

As of May 2026, Arctos is part of KKR Solutions, a new global investing business at KKR spanning investments in premier sports franchises through Arctos Sports and private equity and real assets through Arctos Keystone. Together, these businesses provide bespoke capital solutions, differentiated insights and purpose-built operating capabilities to industry leaders across both markets.
Within Arctos Sports, we focus primarily on investing in professional sports franchises across the four major North American leagues (NFL, NBA, MLB and NHL), supported by deep sector expertise and proprietary research into the factors driving long-term franchise valuations. A key component of our investment thesis is the enduring value of premium live sports media rights, which we believe are becoming increasingly important as streaming reshapes the media landscape and artificial intelligence accelerates content proliferation.
In the analysis below, we examine the evolving sports media rights landscape, the key developments shaping the market in 2026, and why we believe the scarcity and resilience of premium live sports will continue to support long-term growth in franchise valuations.

Sign up to subscribe to the latest insights from KKR

Email Address

Please enter your business email.

Please enter a valid email address.
Please enter a professional email address.

SUBSCRIBE TO INSIGHTS

Key Takeaways
The media rights business is transforming in ways that benefit the Big Four (NFL, NBA, MLB, NHL) and other premium sports leagues.Competition in the video business has changed forever due to streaming, which now represents over 50% of industry economics. Because the industry is so fragmented, retaining must-have content has never been more important.Streaming created an explosion of undifferentiated content, and AI is set to worsen this problem.We believe premium live sports is a safe haven that is both AI-resistant and reliably monetizes audiences at scale – an increasingly scarce asset in the content landscape.

Introduction: The Great Content Glut
Media rights represent an important revenue source for global premium sports leagues, including the “Big Four” in North America (NFL, NBA, MLB, NHL). Media rights deals are typically contracted over multiple years, with annual escalators, and represent a durable driver for franchise valuations. As a firm dedicated to investing in the Big Four and other premium sports, we have spent considerable time and resources on the data and models necessary to understand and forecast media rights values.
We believe three key shifts in the U.S. media marketplace are driving growth in premium sports media rights:
First, the market is digesting the reality of content proliferation, competition and commoditization. Put simply, there is too much video content chasing the same number of eyeballs across the same 24-hour day. Second, a new cohort of streaming-first, diversified tech platforms have emerged as real competitors for sports rights. These businesses are more than just media companies and can amortize rights costs across a broader set of commercial goals. Third, AI is an accelerant: it will make it even easier to create undifferentiated, copiable content at scale, which will worsen the “content glut” and raise the value of anything truly differentiated, authentic and uncopiable.
As a result, traditional media companies face a dilemma. How do media companies protect our subscriber base and advertising business in the face of increasing commoditization and formidable new competitors?
How We Got Here
Media companies, both legacy media companies and Big Tech, generate direct revenues from content via subscriptions and advertising – Subscriber Value (SV) and Advertiser Value (AV). Sports media rights packages represent some amount of future SV and AV that leagues and teams sell to media companies in exchange for fixed, contracted revenue – providing certainty and visibility to franchises in exchange for reliable, often exclusive access to must-have content for networks and streamers. That basic set up is in large part not changing, but the number and kind of partners interested in buying rights packages is.
Just over a decade ago, the media business was highly concentrated and consolidated. There was, in fact, only one television product that most households bought: the cable / linear TV bundle. There were only five, scaled, active bidders on sports rights, and even worse for leagues, losing a rights package was less consequential: no one unsubscribed from the bundle because ESPN/ABC lost NASCAR rights in 2014; they just changed the channel. Margins at media networks were ~40%+ - extremely high by any industry standard.
EXHIBIT 1: Video Landscape In the U.S. Is Highly Fragmented

Estimated Household Penetration by Service Offering (Millions)

Source: SNL Kagan, Company Financials, and Arctos Estimates. As of July 2026.

EXHIBIT 2: Sports Rights Competitors – Then and Now

Source: SNL Kagan, Company Financials, and Arctos Estimates. As of July 2026.

Now, there are at least 11, scaled and capitalized bidders on national and local Big Four sports rights. Most of these players are either streaming-only (Amazon, Netflix, YouTube, Apple) or have both linear and streaming products. Streaming is now >50% of overall industry revenue and ~50% of total media industry EBITDA. The streaming genie is not going back in the bottle: consumer choice is far higher today, and the value proposition is much better. Today, customers can self-curate their own bundle, across many different linear and digital options, and churn at any time. This makes it better than ever to be a media consumer, but harder than ever to be a media company.
As a result, losing must-have sports content today is far more consequential than it was in the bundle world. That would mean risking one of your highest-value subscriber segments to a competitor for as long as the next media deal lasts (often a decade or longer).
Three Updates for 2026
There were several important highlights in 2026 worth addressing.

First, viewership and engagement fundamentals in 2026 are stronger than ever. To unpack this, some context-setting is useful. Over the last 10 years, the media business has “unbundled” – this has meant ever increasing fragmentation and narrowing of audiences. Netflix and YouTube have learned your preferences to such precision that they can use machine learning to curate an engagement-maximizing portfolio of content just for you. There is less “mass media” today – in 1980, 52M homes simultaneously watched the evening news on ABC, CBS, or NBC; today that number is 19M, and falling ~2% per year. Movie theater unit ticket sales are half of what they were in 2002. If the market average ratings point for everything in mass culture is facing this headwind, then (as we like to say) “flat is the new up”. And indeed, viewership has been strong in the Big Four and is growing in part due to new measurement standards. Pro sports is one of the last remaining content niches that durably delivers mass, diversified and heterogeneous audiences at scale.

EXHIBIT 3: Viewership Fundamentals Continue to Deliver for the Big 4
Regular Season Viewership Indexed to 2014

Source: JP Morgan and NBA. As of July 2026. Note: Weighted average of regular season.

Second, some legacy media companies have raised the prospect that they cannot support additional step-ups for must-have sports. Our work suggests that there is more than enough room in aggregate to afford rights just among those incumbents, and that in fact, given the amount of SV and AV that sports rights drive, it could be worse to let must-have rights fall to a competitor than to simply retain them at a step-up. We estimate that legacy media companies spend over $55B on non-sports, non-live content, most of which is less protected from threats like commoditization and competition; they spend $28B on live sports, and only $16B on the Big Four.

EXHIBIT 4: Big Tech Still Has Enormous Dry Powder

Source: SNL Kagan, JP Morgan, Morgan Stanley, Goldman Sachs, and Arctos Estimates. As of July 2026.

Now, this doesn’t mean that leagues and teams will default to the status quo: increasingly, media companies offer different value propositions to leagues in terms of the amount and diversity of audience they can offer. The 11 active media companies that compete for rights are not all created equal, do not all have equal capabilities or have equal balance sheet strength. At the same time, leagues want and need a diverse set of partners. Threading that needle isn’t easy, but it also isn’t new: that is what leagues have done for decades. We think leagues will continue to grow the SV and AV potential of their programming, and over the long-term, the partners with the capabilities to maximize SV and AV will win.
Finally, there’s the topic of “rebundling”. We are seeing signs of rebundling, led by Charter, who has been able to reintegrate the ad-supported streaming platforms of the major network groups (think: Peacock, Paramount+, Disney+, etc.) into their Spectrum basic cable package. However, this is far from a reintroduction of the “one big bundle” market structure that prevailed in pre-internet era. We think this is a rational market evolution that gives these platforms reliable subscriber access for a fair price; but nonetheless, ceding market share to competitors by allowing sports rights to lapse will remain painful, especially if those losses occur to Big Tech, whose platforms live entirely outside of the linear business.
Scarcity Economics
In short, premium sports rights are seeing their already high scarcity value accelerate, driven by persistent market forces that show no signs of letting up. Programming that is evergreen, can retain mass audiences, reliably delivers both SV and AV, and is AI-resistant is in short supply. There are few if any content bets available that can check all four of these boxes – premium sports does.
The specialness of the fan relationship undergirds this – a relationship that takes decades of authentic engagement and powerful memories to build. Authentic fan connection is not something AI can threaten easily. The gap between haves and have-nots is widening in the content world, and premium, global sports is benefiting.

articles.title: Equities update - Week 44 - October 30 2026
articles.text: Week 44 brought further equity-market volatility as disappointing mega-cap technology updates and the Fed’s hawkish hold weighed on risk appetite. The Fed maintained rates at 3.75–4.00%, while firmer PCE inflation kept the December FOMC meeting a live at 76% odds of a hike down from 85% at the beginning of the week. Higher oil prices, supported by renewed threats to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, added to inflation concerns. Gold also weakened as expectations of higher interest rates increased the opportunity cost of holding non-yielding assets, illustrating how inflation risks can complicate its defensive role. Concerns over the cash-flow impact of substantial AI spending added pressure to technology shares and broader equities, increasing scrutiny of the financing assumptions supporting the infrastructure buildout. On the corporate front, ICE’s agreement to bring Hyperliquid-based markets into a regulated US framework, alongside further stablecoin initiatives from Ripple and SBI, demonstrated the continuing integration of blockchain infrastructure with traditional finance. Listed-platform earnings also showed revenues diversifying beyond crypto trading, while the Binance and Polymarket breaches reinforced the importance of custody, governance and the investment vehicle used to access the sector.Week 44 Key Developments in Blockchain Equities:Index Performance: The Index declined -2.6%, compared with a -4.5% fall in Bitcoin, as persistent inflation and renewed pressure on technology shares weighed on risk appetite. The FOMC held interest rates at 3.75–4.00%, although two officials favoured a 25bp increase, keeping the prospect of further tightening in focus. September PCE inflation accelerated to 3.6% year-on-year, with core inflation at 3.1%, reinforcing concerns that price pressures remain above the Fed’s target. Resilient economic growth and higher oil prices amid renewed Middle East tensions further complicated the inflation outlook. Meanwhile, disappointing updates from Alphabet and Amazon added pressure to the technology trade, as investors scrutinised the impact of substantial AI capital expenditure on cash generation and the timing of investment returns. Weakness in these heavily weighted companies also weighed on broader equity indices.Block Index Key Movers: 7-day top performers: Hyperliquid Strategies (+41.6%), Galaxy Digital (+18.6%), AMD (+11.5%) 7-day worst performers: Nu Holdings (-18.2%), GMO Internet (-13.2%), MercadoLibre (-9.0%) ICE announces agreement to bring Hyperliquid-based perpetual futures to the US – ICE, the parent of the New York Stock Exchange, announced an agreement with Trade[XYZ] to establish US-regulated perpetual futures markets built on Hyperliquid. ICE would provide the regulated market and clearing framework, Trade[XYZ] would contribute product design and deployment expertise, and Hyperliquid would supply the underlying blockchain infrastructure, with customer access expected through brokers and futures commission merchants. The agreement marks a significant step in the convergence of traditional finance and crypto infrastructure, with an established exchange operator adopting crypto rails to expand how financial assets are traded. The proposed market would offer around-the-clock exposure across equities, commodities, currencies and crypto, combining onchain trading capabilities with established distribution and regulatory oversight. Subject to approvals, this could open a new retail growth channel operating separately from ICE’s existing institutional franchise.Stanley Druckenmiller’s public backing reinforces the significance of the announcement. He confirmed an investment in Trade[XYZ] and said he looked forward to using its product to enhance his investment process. Separately, Duquesne Family Office reported a holding in index constituent Hyperliquid Strategies (PURR) valued at approximately US$23m as of 30 June 2026. For PURR, the potential benefit comes through its HYPE token treasury and staking operations. Broader adoption of Hyperliquid could increase trading activity and fee generation, potentially supporting HYPE’s economics and the value of PURR’s holdings. The agreement therefore strengthens the commercial adoption thesis behind PURR, although the eventual equity benefit will depend on the scale of adoption and how economic value accrues to HYPE.Binance’s US$6.3bn hack and Polymarket breach reinforce the case for listed blockchain equities - The security incidents at Binance and Polymarket on 29 October reinforce the importance of how investors access the digital-asset ecosystem. Binance estimated the impact at approximately US$6.3bn and pledged to cover losses through its SAFU fund and company resources. Polymarket temporarily halted its international platform following a third-party security breach and also promised reimbursement. Both incidents highlight the operational and counterparty risks that can accompany holding funds directly on trading platforms.Blockchain equities provide a route to participate in the industry’s growth through an established securities framework. Investors can hold shares through regulated brokers and custodians, with applicable client-asset protections, while assessing businesses through published audited financial statements, corporate governance and ongoing disclosure requirements. US domestic issuers, for example, generally must disclose material cybersecurity incidents within four business days of determining materiality. These arrangements provide a framework for scrutiny and accountability without requiring investors to manage private keys or maintain balances on crypto trading platforms.The week’s results also demonstrated how listed businesses are monetising demand across the ecosystem. Coinbase reported prediction-market revenue exceeding US$173m of quarterly event-contract revenue. Visa’s annualised stablecoin settlement volume exceeding US$25bn provided further evidence of adoption within established financial infrastructure. For equity investors, the opportunity is to participate in the revenues and earnings generated by these activities.Earnings Recap – Key Holdings:Coinbase, Standard Chartered, Mastercard, Galaxy Digital – PositiveSamsung Electronics, Strategy Inc, Robinhood – MixedFlow Traders, PayPal - NegativeOther news - Index constituents:SBI Holdings announced several initiatives connecting stablecoins with asset management, banking and cross-border payments. Alongside BlackRock and Startale, it signed an MOU to explore linking tokenised money-market funds with JPYSC, its yen-denominated trust-type stablecoin. SBI also agreed a strategic alliance and preliminary framework for a Japanese joint venture with Cross River Bank’s parent, CRB Group, covering tokenised loans, cross-border payments and agentic commerce, alongside a proposed strategic investment and potential integration of JPYSC. Separately, SBI announced a capital and business alliance with Sumitomo Mitsui Financial Group to develop services using stablecoins and tokenised assets, and participated in PhotonPay’s US$65bn of annualised platform-wide transaction volume. Together, these developments broaden SBI’s potential role across asset management, distribution and payment infrastructure, although several initiatives remain exploratory or subject to final agreements and regulatory approvals.Circle and ACI announced a collaboration to demonstrate USDC settlement within existing banking and payments infrastructure, initially in Colombia. The work combines Circle’s infrastructure with ACI Connetic and builds around ACI’s role in Bre-B, Colombia’s interoperable instant-payments ecosystem. The opportunity is to embed stablecoins within established financial-institution workflows.Bullish advanced its tokenised securities strategy with the addition of Qube Research & Technologies, Vertalo and zerohash to the Issuer Sponsored Token Coalition strengthens Bullish’s efforts to build an ecosystem spanning tokenised securities issuance, shareholder registration and trading. Co-founded with Equiniti, the coalition is developing standards that connect tokenised shares with official shareholder records, preserving investors’ dividend and voting rights. This supports the strategic rationale behind Bullish’s proposed acquisition of Equiniti: combining issuer relationships and registry capabilities with Bullish’s exchange infrastructure.Galaxy applied to the OCC to establish Galaxy National Bank. If approved, it would bring digital-asset custody, trading, staking and fiduciary investment advisory services under a federal trust framework. A national structure could support broader institutional relationships and simplify the regulatory architecture around these services.IREN and Wingspire Equipment Finance closed US$363m of financing against revenue-generating GPU servers and networking equipment. The six-lender group included commitments from Eldridge Capital Management and Silver Point Capital. The transaction releases capital already invested in deployed infrastructure backed by multi-year customer contracts. Ripple expanded RLUSD distribution across Coinbase Prime, Exchange and the retail app, with support across XRPL, Base and Ethereum. Global Exchange access and collateral functionality are to follow. RLUSD is also live on Robinhood Chain and Bitstamp, with Robinhood app access expected later this year. Robinhood plans to integrate Ripple Treasury, while the partnership also extends institutional financing and market access through Ripple Prime.HIVE’s BUZZ subsidiary agreed approximately US$129m of equipment financing at a fixed 9% rate over three years, with principal and interest amortising during the term. The equipment supports the previously announced three-year Cohere contract. Asset security, limited recourse support and an equity pledge underpin the facility.Soneium backed by Sony Group, outlined plans for an ecosystem token and introduced ipUSD and IP Vault, with access scheduled to open on 28 October. The vault offers eligible users exposure to a US$549m Partners Group royalties fund tokenised by Asseto; this is the underlying fund’s size. The initiative connects financial infrastructure with entertainment and intellectual property, although customer adoption and the contribution to Sony’s earnings remain early considerations.Nu Holdings and MercadoLibre – Brazil election repricing: Lula’s surprise runoff victory triggered a sharp reversal in Brazilian markets, with the Bovespa closing down 13.9% on Monday and the real falling 8.1% against the dollar. For Nu and MercadoLibre, the immediate implications include country risk, FX translation, credit conditions and consumer demand, which can affect group earnings independently of digital-asset initiatives.Other news – Non - Index constituents:Visa reported revenue of US$12.1bn, and adjusted EPS of US$3.48. Management described more than US$25bn of annualised stablecoin settlement volume, over 225 stablecoin-linked card programmes and commercial production for Visa Direct’s stablecoin prefunding. These disclosures demonstrate adoption within an existing distribution network.Aviva Investors launched a tokenised share class of its GBP22bn Sterling Liquidity Fund on XRPL with an initial GBP50m investment. The development extends institutional cash-management applications, with the commercial opportunity resting on distribution, servicing and assets retained in the new share class.BNY and Ripple expanded their collaboration across institutional custody and potential tokenised trade finance. The work aims to connect assets with payments and collateral workflows. For BNY, the commercial question is whether these capabilities deepen custody, servicing and financing relationships sufficiently to generate recurring fees.

articles.title: Santa's sleigh will be weighed down by tariffs
articles.text:
Blog Name

RealTime Economics

Santa's sleigh will be weighed down by tariffs

Cullen S. Hendrix (PIIE)

Date
November 2, 2026 9:18 AM

Photo Credit: SipaUSA via Reuters/Anthony Behar

XLinkedInBlueskyEmailShare

Body
Believe it or not, the holiday shopping season is just around the corner, with holiday lights and artificial Christmas trees already crowding store aisles. Many parents are eager to give presents that encourage young people to put down their screens and pick up something else: a bat and ball, a sketchbook and colored pencils, or a musical instrument. Others want their gamers to have the latest consoles. But if you have an athlete, artist, musician, or gamer on your shopping list, be ready: your gift-giving dollar won't stretch as far as it did in the 2024 holiday shopping season, or even last holiday season, when tariffs on these goods hit a recent peak.[1]
Each of these hobbies runs largely on imported gear, especially the entry-level items most parents buy. Musical instruments, sports equipment, paints, pencils, and crayons are overwhelmingly made abroad. The trade and price data tell a consistent story: tariffs on these goods have eased a bit since last year but remain high, and imports have fallen. Retail prices are higher, and they aren't coming back down despite some tariff relief. Even video games, the hobby many parents are trying to pull kids away from, weren't spared.
Tariffs peaked last holiday season and remain high
Before 2025, imports of these goods—athletic equipment, art supplies, and musical instruments—were lightly taxed at the port. In the 2024 holiday season (September through December), the effective tariff rate, meaning calculated duties as a share of the value of imports for consumption, was 5.6 percent on sports equipment, 5.0 percent on pencils and crayons, and 5.7 percent on instruments. Something else, of course, happened during that window, too: Donald Trump was elected to serve a second term as US president, having campaigned on a pro-tariff platform that he claimed would lead to a manufacturing renaissance.
When Trump returned to office in early 2025, he quickly ratcheted up the trade war against China, where most of these goods are made. By the 2025 holiday season, effective tariff rates had jumped to 27.7 percent on sports equipment, 26.6 percent on pencils and crayons, and 21.2 percent on instruments. The rates have declined a bit since the Supreme Court struck down some of Trump's tariffs, but not by much. Through August,[2] effective rates were 17.2 percent on sports equipment, 16.1 percent on pencils and crayons, and 14.1 percent on instruments.
Higher tariffs mean fewer goods
At least so far, Trump's tariffs have not resulted in a US manufacturing boom, either in terms of employment(link is external) or construction(link is external). They have, however, reduced imports of these goods, a pattern clearly evident in the 2025 data. Holiday-season imports from all countries in 2025 fell 24 percent for musical instruments and 17 percent each for sports equipment and for pencils and crayons, compared with 2024.[3] Football may be life on Ted Lasso, music may nourish the soul, and coloring outside the lines may foster creativity—but for most households these goods are wants, rather than needs, and among the first things households cut when prices climb. In the main, price increases for these imported goods didn't drive consumers to domestically produced alternatives because these products largely don't exist at entry-level prices. Instead, the tariff-driven higher prices destroyed US demand, which here meant fewer kids finding a hockey stick, trumpet, or colored pencils under the tree.
Tariffs are down—but prices are not
Tariff relief has been welcome, especially for the importers of record who are now receiving refunds, little of which is likely to be passed on to the consumers who ultimately paid(link is external). But slightly lower tariffs are not translating into lower prices: prices for all three classes of goods rose in 2026 relative to 2025, and they have risen faster than core goods prices (excluding food and energy) since 2024 (see figure). There are three reasons. First, many importers anticipated the Trump tariffs and spent much of 2025 selling stock imported before the tariffs took effect. Prices in 2026 thus reflect the higher tariffs that prevailed until the Supreme Court decision in February 2026. Second, retail prices tend to rise quickly when costs go up and fall slowly, if at all, when they come down, so tariff relief rarely shows up at the register. Third, underlying inflation remains elevated: core consumer prices are up 5.7 percent over the past two years, stoked by spillovers from the war with Iran and large fiscal deficits. This further erodes general purchasing power, forcing harder choices about needs versus wants.

But general inflation can't explain these increases on its own. Core goods prices rose just 2.3 percent over the same period, a small fraction of the 9.1 percent increase for musical instruments. Of the three, musical instruments have been hit hardest, with the steepest price increases and the largest drop in imports.Video game consoles and machines faced the same tariff surge. Their effective rate went from zero in the 2024 holiday season to 19.7 percent in 2025, and calculated duties rose from nothing to $508 million. Imports spiked in early 2025 as importers front-ran the tariffs and Nintendo launched the Switch 2, then fell 33 percent over the 2025 holiday season; through August 2026 imports were 10 percent below 2024 levels. List prices rose, too, and kept rising.[4]
Why it matters
These economic losses are significant, and not only for US-based sellers of imported instruments, sports equipment, and art supplies. Cheap imported beginner gear doesn't so much compete with American manufacturing as feed it: the kid who learns on an imported starter guitar or drum kit is tomorrow's buyer of a US-made Gibson or Ludwig. Similar dynamics are evident in sporting goods like mountain bikes—Trek(link is external) makes its entry- and mid-tier models in Asia while producing its top-tier bikes in Wisconsin—and in footballs, where Wilson's Ohio factory makes the NFL's game balls. Firms like these already split production this way, making entry-level lines abroad and high-end ones at home. That is the pattern Bernard, Fort, Smeets, and Warzynski(link is external) find more broadly: firms that offshore keep making the same goods at home, upgrade to higher-quality varieties, and shift their workforce toward technology jobs. Tariffs on beginner gear thin out the next generation of customers for the very domestic producers they are meant to protect. And the losses are not confined to importers, retailers, or manufacturers.
First, alternatives to screen time are getting harder to come by, even as the US grapples with childhood screen addiction(link is external) and rising obesity rates(link is external). Tariffs raised the price of video games too, but they have also made the alternatives scarcer and, in the case of instruments, considerably more expensive. Second, parents aren't the only buyers. School music, art, and athletic programs buy instruments, sports equipment, paints, and pencils on fixed budgets, so every tariff dollar means less gear for the kids who use it(link is external). For many low-income families, those programs are the only point of access: the school-owned trumpet or the team's equipment locker is the only way in. When schools buy less, low-income families feel it first.
Third, much of what is lost simply cannot be priced. The look on a child's face as they unwrap their first guitar, baseball glove, or set of colored pencils lasts a few moments. But the gift itself can lead to a lifetime of playing, competing, and making art—and, for those who eventually stop, a lifelong appreciation of these pursuits. School music, sports, and art programs are how poor and working-class kids like Quincy Jones(link is external), Wilma Rudolph(link is external), and Andy Warhol(link is external) started their journeys to becoming global icons. Those losses never show up at any port, but they are real.
Tariffs aren't just taxing imported goods. They're taxing the tactile, offline activities that enrich young lives and feed American culture. Tariffs were supposed to shield American industry, but they haven't: there's no domestic manufacturing revival to show for them. What they may be doing instead is snuffing out the next generation's sparks of passion before they're ever lit. And while the administration has handed out firm-specific tariff relief(link is external) to producers of many other products, the goods that build skills, human capital, and joy in kids have gotten no such break.
Bah, humbug.
Notes
1. To paraphrase Homer Simpson, "You mean peaked so far."
2. Data cover January through August 2026; August is the most recent month for which USA Trade Online has published data.
3. Imports are measured as imports for consumption, the basis on which Census calculates duties. Values are deflated with the relevant Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) import price indexes.
4. Sony (link is external)raised the price of the PS5 from $499.99 to $549.99 in August 2025 and to $649.99 in April 2026. Microsoft (link is external)took the Xbox Series X from $499.99 to $799.99 in three steps between May 2025 and August 2026. Nintendo(link is external) raised the price of the original Switch by $40 in August 2025 and the Switch 2 by $50 this September.

Data Disclosure

The data underlying this analysis can be downloaded here [zip].

The big question for onshore wind: what to do with ageing turbines?

View Charles Coppins's full profile

Wind and solar are infinite sources of renewable energy. But the equipment that generates power from these resources – the turbines and panels – physically degrades over time and must eventually either be removed or replaced. After a quarter of a century of deployment, renewable project developers are now facing the choice of decommissioning, extending asset life or repowering sites with the latest technology.
What is the scale of decommissioning? Does repowering make economic sense? Who stands to gain most? Soren Lassen and Charles Coppins from our Power and Renewables team explain how the next generation of renewables could deliver more power at lower cost.
How big is the decommissioning challenge?
Large, and growing fast. Of the more than 3.5 TW of wind and solar capacity operational worldwide by the of 2025, Wood Mackenzie forecasts that over 70% will face a decommission, extend or repower decision in the 2040s.
Ageing wind projects are the most pressing. Our latest Horizons report shows that almost 50 GW of wind is now over 20 years old, broadly the design life of these earlier turbines. The number quickly rises to over 230 GW by 2040. And while the rapid deployment of solar PV may have started later, global solar capacity more than 20 years old will overtake wind before 2040.
Does repowering make economic sense?
There’s a compelling case. With capital and operating costs on a par with greenfield projects, the economic advantage of repowering comes mainly from higher output as technology advances. Given the site will always outlast the equipment, repowered projects can also skip grid-connection queues and often clear permitting faster. Location matters. In Germany, for example, decommissioned sites have average wind speeds 4% higher than new greenfield projects, delivering higher capacity factors and a lower levelised cost of energy.
And it isn’t only about economics. Without repowering, growth in global annual wind and solar installations risks stalling. If greenfield renewables additions can’t keep pace as policy support softens, more coal and gas will be required to fill the gap. 
Is technology changing the equation?
Substantially. The average wind turbine rating has increased fourfold over the past two decades and continues to rise. Meanwhile, the efficiency of solar modules has risen by almost 70% over the same period and average solar sites now require around a third less land for the same capacity.
Hardware is also getting more robust. Wind turbine design life has climbed from 20 years to more than 30, while warranties for solar panels have increased by five years as degradation levels continue to improve.
What does this mean for power markets?
Simply decommissioning ageing wind and solar projects does nothing for meeting capacity targets. Take the European Commission's 500 GW wind goal for 2030. Reaching this requires about 37 GW of additions a year through to 2030. If all end-of-design-life projects are decommissioned, around 2 GW more would need to be added annually to achieve published goals.
Repowering can side-step this. Sticking with Germany, we estimate repowering existing projects would raise the country’s onshore wind output by 16% in 2050, which would represent almost a third of the country's current annual wind generation. This matters not only for installation targets but also for consumers as repowered supply could significantly lower power prices.
Who gains most from repowering?
Aside from customers enjoying lower electricity bills, equipment suppliers stand to benefit most. Repowering existing sites means global equipment sales could be more than 60% higher in 2050 than at present even as the pace of annual net additions declines.
The distribution of repowering opportunities is uneven, however. While decommissioning will drive 44% of wind and almost a quarter of solar buildout worldwide in the 2040s, the figures are notably higher in established markets across Europe, Asia and the Americas.
Repowering could usher in an era of renewal and lead to more wind and solar installations than ever before. The impact of this will take years to fully materialise but is already relevant to strategic decision making today. As governments and consumers grapple with volatile fossil fuel prices, planning for future energy renewal opportunities should already be on the agenda.

articles.text:
Day One With Your Financial Advisor

Preparing for your first meeting

Your first meeting with your Financial Advisor marks the beginning of an important professional relationship. Just as you rely on your doctor with your health and your mechanic with your car, you’ll be entrusting your Financial Advisor with something of great value too — your financial goals.

call out

Your Financial Advisor will want to know you as a person — not just as a client.

end call out

Our Financial Advisors work with many types of investors and value their diversity. Your Financial Advisor will want to know you as a person — not just as a client — so he or she can understand the best way to help you with your investment needs and life goals.

The right fit

Meeting with a Financial Advisor for the first time, you should expect a friendly, casual conversation — you’re just getting to know each other. There’s no obligation, no pressure, no judgment — and no cost for your first meeting. You should be candid about your level of investing experience, overall financial situation, and financial goals. You should also feel comfortable asking as many questions as you’d like.
It’s important you choose a Financial Advisor who listens to your concerns, understands your financial needs, and values your input. The relationship between you and your Financial Advisor is a critical one — through the years, you should have many sensitive, private conversations. The relationship may even expand to include friends and future generations of your family.

Getting ready

Before the meeting, your Financial Advisor should send you a checklist of items to bring. Your privacy is a top priority, and your Financial Advisor is committed to maintaining strict confidentiality.
A good Financial Advisor will want the right fit for you as much you seek the right fit in him or her. Before your first consultation, you’ll want to reflect on and be prepared to discuss:

Your values about money and your vision for your future
What life events are happening or could potentially happen
Short- and long-term life and financial goals
Investment questions
Your current financial situation
Preferred account management style

Remember, the more you share about your financial picture, investment goals, and risk tolerance, the better your Financial Advisor will be able to recommend strategies and create an investment plan. You’ll find the initial meeting with your Financial Advisor will set the stage for many conversations to come.

Next steps

Think about how you prefer to work with your advisor and what types of investments you’re interested in.
Gather the necessary documentation for your initial meeting and prepare answers to questions your advisor may ask.

articles.title: What's behind young workers’ job struggles?
articles.text:
Expert insight

What’s behind young workers’ job struggles?

November 05, 2026

Adam Schickling, CFA

Vanguard Senior Economist

Get Vanguard's insights delivered straight to your inbox. Subscribe now

Get Vanguard's insights delivered straight to your inbox. Subscribe now

Entry-level workers often support more experienced colleagues by gathering information, conducting initial research, and handling routine client communications—work that firms can increasingly accomplish with AI. With recent college graduates struggling to find jobs, it’s easy to view AI as the culprit.

The logic is intuitive, but labor market data tell a different story. Our research finds little evidence that AI is the main reason why recent college graduates are struggling to find jobs. In particular:

Employment among recent college graduates in occupations highly exposed to AI remains relatively close to its prepandemic level.

Firms positioned to benefit from AI adoption have hired younger workers at a greater pace than firms less exposed to AI.

In other words, the evidence points elsewhere for the source of young job seekers’ struggles.

Stagnant job environment constrains young workers

To be sure, the current “low-fire, low-hire” labor market, where both new employment and job termination are down, is particularly challenging for young workers. While established workers are benefitting from historically low layoffs, those just entering the workforce depend on hiring to get their start. When companies pull back on hiring, young workers are the first to feel it.
But our research suggests that AI isn’t to blame. Employment of 22- to 26-year-old college graduates in occupations with high AI exposure is only modestly below its benchmark trend, as the chart that follows shows.

Occupations highly exposed to AI persevere

Notes: AI exposure is measured using a task-level framework, mapping AI capabilities identified in the Stanford AI Index to the task composition of roughly 800 occupations and grouping occupations into exposure terciles. Current Population Survey employment estimates cover 22- to 26-year-old college graduates. Employment is X-13 seasonally adjusted with COVID intervention controls and shown as annual averages. Benchmarks extrapolate 2015–2019 employment trends, adjusted after 2019 for slower college-graduate population growth.
Sources: Vanguard calculations, based on data as of September 30, 2026, from O*NET, the Stanford University 2026 AI Index Report, and the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics

We mapped AI capabilities to roughly 800 occupations and grouped them into high, medium, and low AI-exposure categories, then specifically examined activity among 22- to 26-year-old college graduates in each group. The patterns we found don’t line up with an AI-displacement story.
Recent college graduates frequently enter professional and cognitive occupations in which generative AI has relatively high task exposure. If AI were an important driver of recent labor market weakness, that weakness would be expected to be particularly pronounced in occupations highly exposed to AI.
Employment among recent graduates in occupations with high AI exposure is only modestly below its prepandemic trend. The bigger shortfall shows up in occupations with medium AI exposure, and that weakness started before the 2022 introduction of ChatGPT marked the public arrival of AI.
Meanwhile, low-AI-exposure employment has bounced back more strongly, helped along by teenagers leaving the labor force after a pandemic-era surge, freeing up leisure and hospitality positions for older recent graduates.

Employer behavior tells a similar story

Notes: The chart shows the change in the difference between AI-beneficiary and AI-agnostic firms in the measures of gross hires, work separations, and net hires pre-AI (February 2016 through February 2020) and in the AI era (November 2022 through June 2026). AI-beneficiary employers are firms where analyst review identifies clear, material, near-term upside from AI. Benefits may come from AI-related demand, such as compute and infrastructure buildout, or from firms’ own adoption through lower costs, automation, and improved products. Classifications cover large Vanguard plan sponsors across nine industries. Workforce outcomes come from Vanguard 401(k) recordkeeping data.
Sources: Vanguard data, as of September 12, 2026.

A separate Vanguard analysis classifies firms based on how AI is expected to affect their businesses, including firms positioned to benefit from AI-related investment and expected productivity gains.
If the AI displacement narrative were right, AI-beneficiary firms would likely be pulling back hardest on young workers. Instead, since the release of ChatGPT, AI-beneficiary employers have outhired AI-agnostic employers overall. And the net hiring advantage is largest among workers ages 22 to 26. The firms best positioned to leverage AI are hiring more young people, not fewer.

The first step of the talent management ladder

Companies hire young workers for many reasons. For one, given aging demographics, companies expect elevated retirements; those that don’t hire entry-level workers may find their workforce shrinking.
Companies also benefit from representation across the career spectrum. Today’s entry-level workers are the more experienced midcareer workers of tomorrow.
And younger workers are more likely forward-thinking on technology, such as the AI that we foresee automating some tasks, augmenting others, and creating an array of products, services, industries, and occupations that the technology will make possible.
