There is only one Goldman Sachs.Discover CareersWORKING AT GSStudentsLife at GSBenefitsFeatured OfficesOpen RolesTalks at GSHow Aaru Uses Advanced AI Simulations to Predict Human BehaviorNov 5, 2026ShareSubscribe:SpotifyAppleYouTubeDownload TranscriptAaru, a two-and-a-half-year-old startup valued at $1 billion, is redefining market research and consumer intelligence by deploying multi-agent AI simulations to predict how humans will make decisions. Cam Fink, co-founder and CEO, and Ned Koh, co-founder and president, discuss Aaru's founding story and how advanced behavioral simulation overcomes the limitations of traditional consumer polling. In this conversation with Goldman Sachs Chief Information Officer Marco Argenti, they also explore the real-world enterprise applications of such predictive simulations across retail, financial services, and utilities, which are driving Aaru's rapid rise.
Transcript:
Cam Fink: We help you understand the composition of any population on the globe, and what decisions they make. What marketing campaigns they're going to click on, what subway lines they're going to ride.
Ned Koh: Our model is able to process how humans are able to think.
[MUSIC INTRO]
Marco Argenti: Welcome to Talks at GS. And also welcome to Ned and Cam from Aaru. Nowadays with AI almost like anything is possible, including being 19 and then, you know, having a $1 billion valuation startup, which is pretty incredible. So, since then, Aaru has become one of the most closely watched companies in the research and intelligence space. Thank you for being here.
Cam Fink: Thank you, Marco, for hosting us. We're really glad to have the opportunity today to talk a bit more about what we do.
Marco Argenti: The first question I'm going to ask you is, when was the first time you kind of realized that AI was something big?
Cam Fink: So, it's interesting you ask this because the ChatGPT moment was right in our senior year of high school. So, I remember, you know, having worked in the NLP space, in the computer vision space, where Ned and I were researchers before ChatGPT was released. You could tell that like AI was gaining a lot of capabilities very quickly.
But it wasn't until it became actually productized into something consumers could use that all of a sudden it felt like not only was AI going to gain capabilities, but actually that it would create serious change in how people work on, you know, ideas, on products. But even still, like I remember the most enterprising students were already using AI to evaluate their answers to papers or come up with new ideas or test new things.
And if you were even more enterprising before that, you would have been using the GPT-3 API to try and finish papers. So, you know, I think that was truly the moment that it became clear AI was going to be inevitable.
Marco Argenti: Was there another ah-ha moment recently? Because, you know, right now it feels like things are changing so fast. What's another inflection point that you've seen?
Ned Koh: The tools are incredibly powerful for being used for incredibly rudimentary application: note taking, you know, or summarization as like the key use cases or demonstrations of like how this can help you. And I still think in many businesses it is. It's easy to get behind. There's not really any friction to adopting those technologies. And so, I think that the larger change is this wave of product-first AI businesses. You saw that in health care. You saw that in, you know, financial services and beyond. But I think it was when it went beyond just those into more complex applications, for sure.
Marco Argenti: So, rolling back, like, kind of two basics. If you're in front of a CEO that doesn't know what Aaru is and you have a few seconds to explain, what would you say to them? What's your pitch? Like you're 30 second pitch.
Cam Fink: We predict human behavior. So, we help you understand the composition of any population on the globe and what decisions they make. We can help you understand how U.S. household purchase decision makers are going to purchase products, what marketing campaigns they're going to click on, what music they're going to stream, what subway lines they're going to ride. That's really the core of what we do: predicting behavior to make better business decisions.
Marco Argenti: And I think we met maybe two years ago for the first time. So, really early on. So, what have you learned in terms of sort of what kinds of decisions is AI really good at predicting and what others are not that good?
Ned Koh: Yeah, I think the first place that you look when you define what good means is understanding like the relative for how people make those decisions today. Right? So, let's take something that's like very simple - product launches. So, you have someone who's going in front of a survey, you're asking people questions. It's easy to benchmark. And that's a very interesting market. Product innovation is massive for us.
But when you think about like use cases and how that's kind of diverged across the board, the most relevant ones for us and where we offer the most amount of value, of course, are places where you may not traditionally have data. Right? And so, that may exist in a population who doesn't respond to surveys. The example I like to give is like everybody in this room is wearing a shirt. Did anyone tell someone how much they were willing to pay for it? Probably not. Right?
But then you get into like other categories. Right. You know this answer better than I do. But you know, there are four industries that make up about like 15% of the GDP of the U.S. Airlines, telecom, utilities, insurance. What are the times that matter to those companies about their behavior? When do you remember who your cell provider is? When your cell service goes out. When do you remember that you pay bills to Con Ed? When your power goes out. When do you remember that you fly a specific airline versus another? When your flight gets delayed. Right? And so, on and so forth. When do you remember who your insurance is? When you crash a car.
And so, those businesses, despite being massive, the most important place and time for them to understand the behavior of their customers is somewhere where it's fundamentally impossible to get inside their head inside that moment. Right? And so, the most interesting use cases to us have always been those areas that have the most challenging to reach groups. The time frames of traditional research, it can take weeks and weeks or months to get people in a room and ask them questions or show them a product. You don't have the ability to do that. Right?
So, things that are compressed in timeline are the use cases that are most relevant for simulation because human insight just doesn't reach that same level.
Marco Argenti: But why can't you just ask ChatGPT?
Cam Fink: Language models themselves alone can't understand human behavior with the depth and the capability that is required to actually allow a business to trust their decisions. There are a lot of startups out there now doing what you might call synthetic personas. That's sort of like the last generation of the technology we build. They can be useful. Those startups can help you get like a really quick read on marketing copy. But if you want a decision that you can trust, you need something that's grounded in real world outcomes. And that's where someone like Aaru would come in.
Everything we do is AI. Right? So, what underpins our capabilities to predict human behavior are models. Models that we train. Models that leverage LLMs but aren't LLMs alone. But through fusing kind of LLMs with statistical models and traditional mathematical models, we're able to be far more accurate and take advantage of all of LLMs’ advantages without falling into those kind of gaps with LLMs and predicting behavior.
Marco Argenti: And how do you verify the accuracy and the results? I mean, what is what's ground truth for you guys?
Ned Koh: At the end of the day, if you're trying to predict and make a decision better, what you should be aiming for is a better business outcome. That was very first principle to us, right? You want to benchmark it to the sales result, to the product selling better or selling worse or the limited time offer not flying off the shelves like you wanted it to.
The way that we've been able to grow our business so quickly is by making sure that people walk out of a pilot with us and don't just say, "Yes, we came to a decision faster," but rather we came to a decision better than we otherwise would have.
Marco Argenti: So, let's actually kind of bring it to life a little bit with some examples. What does the client actually get? Give us some examples of that.
Cam Fink: So, we do a lot of work with CPG companies. We do a lot of work with retail, beauty, apparel, kind of like anything that touches a consumer brand. And every kind of business ultimately sells a product. But for consumer brands, it's typically really linear. You can hold the product in your hand, right? A canned beverage, a carton of milk, whatever it might be.
So, we do a lot of product innovation work where we'll go work with, you know, a canned sparkling water company, for example. And that sparkling water company will come to us and say, "Hey, we've built this great business around this one core product. What is our next new product line, right? Is it still hydration? Is it a shelf-stable dairy product? Is it an energy drink? Is it--," you know, all of these things.
And we can use Aaru to do everything from the very core conceptual stage of what is the next frontier, right, all the way into figuring out who exactly is the purchasing audience. Then into the product concept itself specifically. So, say we pick out that it's an energy drink. We figure out who the energy drink purchaser is going to be from this brand. And then we figure out, okay, what flavors of energy drink do we want to put out in the world? And then we can do everything from getting as niche as optimizing the caffeine content to helping figure out the right pack size and carry that entire product innovation cycle from start to finish in just a few weeks.
And one of our clients we worked with, their product innovation cycle traditionally was nine months long, right? That's actually pretty quick for the CPG industry. A lot of the big global companies might be taking 12 months, 18 months, to go from product idea or, you know, new market entrant to ready for manufacturing. We managed to squeeze it down into eight weeks. That was a really, really, really powerful case study. And now the product ended up hitting the shelves earlier this year. And they saw more success than they had with any of their previous product launches before.
Marco Argenti: And if I remember, that you guys can decide the size of the core. Tell us a little bit about that spectrum.
Cam Fink: Yeah, we don't go down to individual-by-individual level, right? We're never processing PII or any kind of individual data. So, we can't recreate Tom Smith from Iowa or Cameron Fink from New York City, right? We can get down to audiences that in the real world might only be a couple hundred people.
I remember at one point doing hospitals that have to purchase this third-party risk management software. You're probably talking only a few hundred to low thousands of people nationwide. And yet we were still able to recreate that audience. And for the company that we did do that study for, they saw a massive impact from the work we could do together.
So, we're getting really niche. We can talk about very small groups of buyers or social media influencers or Gen Z in one particular city metro. And then we can go as wide as US household purchase decision-makers or British residents or, you know, even residents of the EU if you want it.
Marco Argenti: And where do you get your data?
Cam Fink: I mean, it's a massive wealth of data sources, right? So, when we talk about how we leverage that data, we have audience data and we have behavioral outcomes data. On the audience data component, that's what helps us understand who actually exists inside of a population. So, when you come to me and you say, "Hey, I want to talk to ultra high net worth individuals in, you know, the United States and Canada," we can actually tell you what the distribution of that population looks like.
And then we have behavioral outcome data. That helps us figure out what decisions are they going to make. So, that would, you know, be for each of these given value propositions, how will UHMW individuals react to them?
Now, when it comes to where that data actually comes from, you can think about three different buckets for each of the data sources that we leverage. The first would be publicly accessible data. We're leveraging tons of things like the census, academic research where there's license to train on top of it, you know, anything else available publicly that our model is able to use.
Then there's a lot of data we purchase. So, we buy data from everyone from credit card, you know, purchase history data providers to receipts, there are music streams, social media data. And then I would say really the final component is proprietary partnerships that we leverage. So, we do a lot of work with organizations that wouldn't fit the shape of traditional customers of ours but still want access to the impact of our software. We have done data sharing through those sorts of engagements before that's been incredibly powerful for what we do too.
Marco Argenti: How do you make your clients comfortable that they can share their most valuable data?
Cam Fink: Every client is sandboxed entirely. We're SOC 2 compliant. I didn't expect that I'd be saying that up on stage. But just in case anyone was worried, we have any InfoSec people in the room, we are SOC 2 compliant. We have all the compliance certifications we can. Most importantly, we do not train on customer data. And all of our clients are sandboxed.
So, we actually end up being trusted as one of the most secure places to store, you know, that data because you would never be able to leverage a traditional research provider for anything sensitive. Right? You wouldn't want to go survey people and then someone takes a screenshot and says, "Hey, you know, my favorite brand was polling me about this on the internet." Instead, when you're leveraging our software, it's kept entirely secure to, you know, the model that we train.
Marco Argenti: You just said the models that we train. So, has your attitude and approach shifted over the years with regards to kind of using your own models versus using frontier models versus using quasi frontier open-source models?
Cam Fink: Yeah, our approach has definitely changed. I mean, when we started the business, we were definitely more in this realm of like, hey, can you take an LLM and train it on top of survey results? We found some of our own issues with that, right? Historically, we found it wasn't extensible. And that's what really led us to the next generation of our technology.
So, those are all the models that we built ourselves. And that was really the big leap forward in terms of how our technology was able to reach the accuracy level that it is today.
And so, we've been on, you know, all of our own models ever since that point in time. LLMs help us write analysis. They help us do tons of tasks as part of the simulation pipeline. But LLMs aren't driving the fundamental underlying prediction and behavior themselves.
Now, when it comes to the LLMs we integrate, we use tons of different providers. We default to whatever is the best provider for each task that we have to do.
Marco Argenti: Which could be, you know, somehow maybe filtering all the data or explaining or prompt interpretation. But then the actual prediction machine or the simulation machine is your own. And that's your secret sauce.
Ned Koh: That is the secret sauce. Every single economist in the history of like behavioral science and everything else that you can go into has dreamed to be able to build a model off of something that's based on outcomes. You want to be able to remove as much bias as possible. Right? And so, not always is the magic and the data exclusively. It's much more in how our model is able to process things that are in many ways useless by their own right into something that can become a holistic view of how humans are able to think.
Marco Argenti: If every customer is protected and everything, how do you evolve the model?
Cam Fink: We're integrating new data sources all the time, right? So, the data that we have alone is enough that we are able to go out and make tons of valuable predictions. We can generate a lot of insight without having to integrate client data. Integrating client data for us is the key to unlock, you know, much deeper capabilities and integrations, both in terms of, you know, the simulation component and also in terms of how simulation results end up getting used.
Marco Argenti: I get that. But within, let's say, client engagement though, let's say we use it in private wealth in GS and then we want to kind of continue to learn, so do you allow your clients to continuously learn on the model that you provide and that stays theirs?
Cam Fink: It's actually interesting. A huge part of what we're talking about now is this idea of compounding intelligence. One of the biggest issues that our clients feel, one of their biggest pains, is this idea that traditional insight is very static, right? You run one survey, you run another survey, maybe you run a quarterly brand tracker, but it's not like those survey results are propelling forth the next survey that you run.
And when you think about simulation, what's really incredible about the difference with our platform is that it's not just the power to like access more accurate, faster results. Our simulations can also contain the insights from all the simulations before it. And what that means is that it actually builds and compounds in value over time.
You can imagine someone using our platform at the end of running nine projects about studying the Gen Z audience together, could come to us and say, "What are the insights, you know, we didn't even know we had about the Gen Z audience?" And that can go into helping build the next product that people might be interested in. So, a big focus for us is that compounding intelligence piece.
Marco Argenti: Are you guys mostly focused on the US, or do you have a lot of international customers?
Cam Fink: Yeah, we're a totally global business in terms of what we support. So, when you think about the range of Aaru today, it's over 130 countries across the globe. All of the EU, all of North America, much of South Asia, Southeast Asia, you know, and beyond. In the future, we are actually planning international expansion starting soon. But today, the bulk of our customers are based in North America.
Marco Argenti: And so, on that note, so do you think you need to tune sort of your models by culture and by countries?
Ned Koh: I think one of the best markets that is super relevant for a lot of the biggest enterprises that we work with today is expansion into Germany is really interesting, right? I've seen this across customers of ours in consumer electronics. I've seen this across customers of ours in financial services, right? Like it really goes across so many areas.
The amount of safety regulations that people care about in like South Florida versus in, you know, Central Germany are vastly different. I can tell you that, right? Like the reality is, you know, you talk about why do we train models within this time when you're actually in runtime? Why do we keep them updated? These sorts of elements. The news, the way they digest social media, the things that changed their environment is what we like to call it within a given sim. Absolutely do. The context of how you and I make decisions on today versus tomorrow, absolutely do change.
Does my race change? No, that's not the most important part to measure. So, we absolutely have to do that and have to do it on a hyper localized basis.
Marco Argenti: What's your biggest bottleneck at this point?
Cam Fink: 100% hiring. Like it's the best people in the world is the number one thing you need for any fast-growing business. And so, when we think about what is going to-- has defined the last six months, going to define the next six months, next six years of Aaru, it's all going to be about working with the best people in the world.
Marco Argenti: And what kind of people are you looking for?
Cam Fink: The first thing that we evaluate for is raw capability. We do look for people who are the best in the world at something. Right? People who are truly excellent at the craft or at their craft, so to speak, and represent the pinnacle of understanding knowledge capability in a given area. That's something that every person wants. Right? I'm sure Goldman wants people who are the best in their craft as well.
We also look for people who are really high slope. So, even if you're not the absolute best in the world at something today, do you have the potential to be that in the future? Can you learn quickly? Can you adapt is something that's really important to us as well.
And then finally, we look for people who are real collaborators. Every time someone joins our team, it's not just about whether or not they themselves are a really, really brilliant individual. Tons of people who are super smart and, you know, would be lucky to work at any incredible business on the globe. We spend a lot of time focusing on who is exactly right for Aaru and the people who have much to teach our team, much to teach myself, but we also have much to teach them and they can be, you know, leverage, exponential or multiplicative leverage to the people around them.
Ned Koh: Most of our research team, right, you'll have people who are pure math backgrounds. You'll have people who have done Alzheimer's and dementia research, right, who are able to tie in these really interesting areas. On the other side, we've recently brought on the head of research and data science from Qualtrics, who was there for over 13 years. Right? It's like you need some of those incredibly experienced perspectives to understand how to solve these problems. But you also need very fresh ones to think outside of the box to be able to do it as well. It's all about a combination and a balance.
Cam Fink: I think what we believed was true when we started this business is still true for the most part. Right? Like, we've always believed in being open communicators. We've always believed internally in, you know, the power of learning from each other, the power of collaboration. I think those are all important things. We've always believed in wanting people who are excellent at their craft.
When we started to think about it, it's that as a growing business, it's actually time to write that down for the first time and distill it into the things that matter most for us. And that is what led us to kind of starting to think more about culture and principles in the last few weeks than we had previously.
Ned Koh: To that point, a really interesting thing that we've been discussing, especially with some of the larger implications of being able to model behavior, is this idea of like trustworthiness of a model. There's a very big difference between being worthy of trust and being a trustworthy company. And we certainly try to stay on the prior, right? We define that as being worthy of trust to the people who work next to you, right? That you're going to do an incredible job. It's being worthy of trust of your investors. It's being worthy of trust of your customers. It's being worthy of trust of the world that you're using the technology for the biggest impacts you can.
Marco Argenti: Ned, Cam, thank you so much.
Ned Koh: Thank you so much for having us, Marco.
Marco Argenti: Was great. And good luck. Thank you so much.
Cam Fink: Thank you. Thank you.

articles.title: How markets react when hidden debt comes to light
articles.text:
Published on
Let's Talk Development

How markets react when hidden debt comes to light

Reina Eskimez

Jiwon Lee

Franz Ulrich Ruch

November 04, 2026

This page in:

English

English

Markets react differently to hidden debt revelations, but a few lessons for governments are clear. | © Shutterstock.com

Governments sometimes borrow more than they publicly admit. Loans taken out by state-owned companies, debts guaranteed behind closed doors, payments owed to contractors but never recorded — these liabilities can accumulate for years without appearing in any official figure. To outside observers — investors, credit rating agencies, international lenders — the public balance sheet can therefore look stronger than it really is. Then, suddenly, that picture changes.
Recent research has shown that such “hidden debt” can be large. It tends to come to light in one of three ways: an incoming government inherits the books and discloses what it finds; an international audit or IMF review uncovers discrepancies; or a financial crisis forces a full accounting of what the state actually owes. When that moment arrives, the numbers can be startling — in some countries, reported public debt burden has been revised upward by billions of dollars. But the revelation itself is only the beginning. What happens next — to borrowing costs, to investor confidence, and to a country's ability to access financing — is less well understood. Do markets react immediately or gradually? Do reactions differ depending on how the government responds? And how persistent are the effects?
To answer these questions, we examined seven well-documented episodes of hidden debt coming to light between 2005 and 2025 in the Dominican Republic, Ecuador, Mozambique, Pakistan, Senegal, Türkiye, and Zambia tracking daily borrowing costs and stripping out global market swings to isolate each country's specific experience. The results highlight important differences in how markets respond to hidden-debt revelations — and offer clear lessons for governments navigating the aftermath.
Three lessons emerge.

1. Borrowing costs rise steadily, and the reaction builds for weeks
Markets do not anticipate revelations — borrowing costs are broadly unchanged in the 10 days leading up to these events. Once the information becomes public, however, the cost of borrowing rises sharply and persistently. On average, spreads widen by about 80 basis points within 10 days and by about 150 basis points by day 20, peaking at nearly 250 basis points around day 50 (Figure 1). Strikingly, the adjustment is gradual. By day 10, less than half of the eventual two-month repricing has occurred, and spreads stay elevated well into the second month. Investors appear to spend weeks reassessing not only the larger debt burden but also how promptly the country's fiscal reporting is revised.

Figure 1. Sovereign risk spreads climb steadily after hidden debt is revealed

-1000100200300400500-100102030405060Days relative to revelation (t=0)Basis points

Sources: Authors’ calculations based on J.P.Morgan EMBI Global spreads. Note: The line shows the pooled mean of country-specific spreads across the seven episodes, normalized to the pre-event baseline (day 0 = revelation). Shaded band shows the 90 percent confidence interval.

2. The size of the hidden debt is not the whole story
It is tempting to assume that the larger the concealed liability, the larger the market reaction. But in our sample, the link between the size of the revealed debt and the spread response is weak. The two extremes make the point: Senegal had the largest revision in our sample, yet its market reaction was far from the worst. Mozambique’s “tuna bond” revelation involved a more modest revision but triggered the sharpest repricing of any episode, with spreads jumping by roughly 700 basis points within three months (Figure 2). Mozambique's case stands out because the borrowing appeared deliberate and covert — when the loans came to light, the IMF suspended its program and donor support collapsed, compounding the market shock well beyond what the debt figures alone would have warranted.

Made with Flourish • Create a scatter plot

3. Credibility matters too
How governments handle hidden debt after it is revealed matters as much as the revelation itself. We split the episodes into two groups: those where authorities promptly reconciled the newly revealed liabilities, with independent validation within a year (Dominican Republic, Türkiye, Ecuador, and Pakistan), and those where the true debt picture remained contested or the audit process dragged on (Zambia, Mozambique, and Senegal).
The difference is stark. Where reconciliation was prompt, spreads rose about 123 basis points after 60 days, and much of the initial increase later reversed. Where it was delayed or contested, spreads climbed about 324 basis points and remained elevated for longer (Figure 3). Markets price not only the debt they see but also the uncertainty about what else might still be hidden. Prompt, verifiable disclosure helps close that uncertainty; delay keeps it alive and costly.

With only seven episodes, the evidence on the role of reconciliation should be viewed as suggestive. But the pattern points to an important policy implication. Hidden debt is costly the moment it surfaces, but those costs are not sealed at the point of revelation — what governments do in the days and weeks that follow also matters. Markets are not simply pricing a larger debt stock; their response may also depend on how much they trust the numbers still on the page. A government that moves quickly and invites independent verification can help limit the increase in borrowing costs, while one that delays faces more persistent market repricing. The lesson is not only that transparency can reduce the risks associated with hidden debt — it may also help contain the costs once hidden liabilities come to light.
For further details, please see Sovereign Risk Repricing after Hidden-Debt Revelations.

Reina Eskimez

Economist, Prospects Group, World Bank Group

A Fractured World: How geopolitical tensions could reshape global trade

online

We take a deeper dive into the scenario assumptions, exploring a possible future in which geopolitical tensions continue to rise, populists gain political power, and the world fragments into trading blocs.

In this webinar, we revisit our Fractured World scenario. We discuss the economic impacts of a deglobalised world, using our TradePrism service to disaggregate the impact on trade flows at the bilateral and commodity level. Join us to start planning for a fractured, deglobalised world.

This webinar is being held on our new platform, ON24. If you do not receive your confirmation email, please check your junk and spam folders.

Speakers

Paul Moroz

Paul Moroz holds an undergraduate degree in Philosophy, Politics, and Economics (PPE) from the University of Oxford and an MSc in Economics from Birkbeck, University of London. Paul contributes to the Global Climate Service, the Global Scenarios Service, and bespoke client scenarios.

Senior Economist - Scenarios and Macro Modelling

Harry Murphy Cruise

Harry Murphy Cruise is the Head of Economic Research and Global Trade at Oxford Economics Australia. He leads the Australian Macroeconomic Service and global trade initiatives, including TradePrism. Harry frequently provides insights to major media outlets, including CNBC, BBC, Reuters, and the Wall Street Journal. His research primarily focuses on global trade and investment flows, with particular interest in the challenges and opportunities of economic decoupling.

Harry holds a master’s degree in international and development economics from the Australian National University and a bachelor’s degree in arts and commerce from Monash University. He is a PhD candidate at ANU, exploring the role of China’s diverse households and firms in the country’s economic transition.

Prior to joining Oxford Economics, Harry was the Head of China and Australia Economics at Moody’s Analytics. He was previously responsible for Australian state and territory analysis at Deloitte Access Economics.

Investment Insights

The Mega Themes Driving Asia’s (Still) Untapped Private Capital Opportunity

November 2026

4 minute read

Key Takeaways

Asia’s private capital opportunity has been decades in the making. Converging structural forces are creating a larger, more diverse investment opportunity set.Corporate transformation is fueling private equity opportunities in Japan. Governance reform, succession needs and shifting priorities are unlocking deal flow and avenues for value creation.Asia’s AI ambitions are driving significant private capital demand. Trillions are needed to close an infrastructure funding gap larger than those in the U.S. and Europe.Private credit is gaining ground in Asia. Even dominant banks increasingly recognize the need for flexible private financing.Capturing Asia’s opportunity requires more than exposure to growth. Selectivity, active ownership and underwriting discipline remain critical to generating returns.

Sign up to subscribe to the latest insights from KKR

Email Address

Please enter your business email.

Please enter a valid email address.
Please enter a professional email address.

SUBSCRIBE TO INSIGHTS

Henry Kravis and Joe Bae thought they had stumbled upon a take-private Shangri-La.
When KKR’s co-founder and its soon-to-be head of Asia-Pacific operations visited Japan on their 2005 Asia Exploration tour, they asked the chairman of one Japanese conglomerate how many subsidiaries it had.
“Two thousand,” he responded.
They thought they misheard. Did he mean core subsidiaries or just tax designations?
Two thousand core.
That’s when it hit them: the scale of what lay buried inside corporate Japan was unlike anything they had ever seen.
Hiro Hirano, CEO of KKR Japan, shared the story at KKR’s 2026 Asia Investment Forum in Singapore. His point was twofold: It has taken nearly 20 years and several waves of corporate governance reform for the potential Kravis and Bae identified to fully materialize. Second, the scale of the private capital opportunity emerging across Asia may be even more staggering today.
Joining Hirano were Diane Raposio, Head of Asia Credit & Markets, and Waldemar Szlezak, Global Head of Digital Infrastructure. Moderated by Bhavit Patel, Head of Institutional Sales and Family Capital for Asia Pacific, the discussion explored three mega themes reshaping private capital across the region.

1. The dam finally breaking in Japan
It took six years from the exploration tour before KKR completed its first (small) corporate carve-out in Japan, and another three years for its first major one, Panasonic’s health care division. Deal activity gained momentum over the next decade, but only really reached escape velocity following two landmark reforms in 2023: Tokyo Stock Exchange rules pressuring companies to address their cost of capital and low valuations, and government takeover guidelines making it harder for boards to dismiss bona fide acquisition offers.
Japanese buyout and exit value nearly tripled between 2022 and 2025 to a record US$92.5B.1 That was also the first year when more Japanese companies were taken private than went public.
“The Japanese corporates are not looking for cheap money,” said Hirano. “They’re looking for the right solutions — how the provider can help make the right acquisition outside the country or help with post-merger integration.”
Governance reform is only one driver. Some 90% of Japan’s small and medium-sized companies are family-owned. In a rapidly aging society, this has created a “succession cliff,” with succession-driven deals now accounting for two-thirds of Japanese buyouts.2
Demographics are also accelerating Japan’s embrace of automation. Where other countries worry about AI displacing workers, Japan sees it as a solution to a chronic labor shortage. But the automated society policymakers envision will require far more compute and power. The government estimates electricity output must rise 35%-50% by 2050, reversing two decades of stagnant demand.3
2. The sheer scale of Asia’s AI infrastructure needs
Japan is only one manifestation of a vastly larger Asian infrastructure problem. Szlezak put the scale of the mismatch — and the resulting investment opportunity — in stark perspective.
The U.S. attracts approximately two thirds of global data center investment, leaving the remaining third roughly split between Asia ex-China and Europe.4 Excluding China, all of Asia attracts investment comparable to Northern Virginia’s data center belt.5
At the same time, Asia accounts for 60% of the world’s internet traffic6, has more than four times the combined population of the U.S. and Europe7, and a GDP growing two to three times faster.8
Current compute capacity tells the story: 160 watts per capita in the U.S., 50 in Europe, and just six in Asia.9
Closing that gap requires more than data centers. AI needs power, transmission, cooling, and related infrastructure. And as AI becomes increasingly intertwined with national security, Szlezak expects countries to prioritize domestic capacity — perhaps eventually treating it as a strategic reserve much like oil.
Greater efficiency is unlikely to dent the need for investment. The cost of producing an AI token has fallen 99% over the past four years10, yet cheaper compute has so far fueled dramatically higher consumption.
Estimates vary widely, but PwC projects that Asia-Pacific alone could require US$8.2 trillion in AI infrastructure investment through 2050 — roughly a quarter of the global total.11 Where will all that capital come from?
3. Asia starts to bank on private credit
Asia has historically relied primarily on banks for credit. They still provide 88% of the region’s credit capital, compared with 50% in Europe and just 31% in the U.S. But the forces reshaping Japan and driving AI infrastructure investment are testing that model.12
Asia already has roughly US$3.8 trillion in private equity — nearly twice Europe’s total — but less than US$90 billion in private credit. Applying Europe’s debt-to-equity mix would imply roughly US$900 billion of additional private-credit opportunity from sponsor-backed companies alone.13
This isn’t about replacing banks. Unlike in the U.S. and Europe, regulators aren’t forcing Asian banks to retrench. Instead, private credit is emerging as a complementary source of flexible capital alongside institutions deeply embedded in corporate financing.
Broadly speaking, Raposio explained, Asian banks offered “very, very cheap capital, but usually in a very rigid and inflexible way.” Corporates, particularly those seeking to retain more equity, are turning to private credit to plug the gap.
And on AI, she added, “We’re even being told by the banks in Japan, ‘We can’t finance all of this. We need other forms of capital’” to support data center and energy investment.

Very, Very Essential
Capturing an opportunity of this scale will require discipline and the right capabilities. Szlezak emphasized the importance of drawing on experience from previous technology cycles, assessing the staying power of customers and leveraging strategic partnerships. In credit, Raposio pointed to selective underwriting, thoughtful portfolio construction and structures designed to protect capital, while Hirano highlighted the importance of aligning management and employees to “think like an owner, act like an owner.”
Together, these approaches reflect the increasingly important role private capital can play in Asia's transformation. As Patel summed up the discussion, private capital in Asia has gone from “complementary to very, very essential.”

The Case For More Mega-Cap Outperformance

Tan Kai Xian

Gavekal Research | 2 Nov 2026

October was a tough month for the mega-cap tech stocks that have driven US market outperformance over the last 10 years. Since early October, Nvidia has fallen -14.5%, Meta -17.1% and Alphabet -20.4% as investors have grown nervous about how the AI capex boom is being financed and jittery about the returns big tech companies will earn on the trillions they have poured in so far. As a result, since the end of September, the S&P 500 market-cap-weighted index, which is dominated by mega-cap tech stocks, has underperformed the S&P 500 equal-weighted index by -6pp.So, is the era of mega-cap outperformance coming to its end? There are solid reasons to think not.

(Photo by Mandel Ngan/AFP via Getty Images)CommentaryEmissaryAfter the Midterm Rout, Can Trump Change Course Without Giving Up Tariffs?Even if the administration maintains its broader trade policy, it should use tariffs more strategically and work with U.S. partners, not against them.Link CopiedBy Barbara WeiselPublished on Nov 6, 2026Among the factors driving the midterm election results, affordability and price increases were often cited as voters’ top issue. The results should motivate the administration of President Donald Trump to adjust its approach to its economic policies, but it may choose to stand firm on trade. Trump proudly embraces the “tariff king” label and views tariffs as an all-purpose tool for securing agreement on trade, investment, and economic security demands.But there are places where the administration can fine-tune its policies without a wholesale shift. Even if it otherwise stays the course, the administration should deploy tariffs more strategically, use them more judiciously in support of a broader U.S. economic agenda, and use carrots—not just sticks—to encourage cooperation from foreign partners. And while it may be tempted to continue to rely on executive action, it should work with the new Congress, which likely will begin to reassert its trade authority and seek more influence in shaping U.S. policy when it takes office in January. More Targeted TariffsOver the past year, the Trump administration has used across-the-board tariffs to pressure U.S. trading partners into bilateral trade agreements. Although tariffs increased government revenues, this blunt instrument also raised business costs and consumer prices, disrupted supply chains, delayed business investment by creating uncertainty, and strained U.S. ties with many partners and allies.In February, the Supreme Court struck down the administration’s broad-based tariffs, ruling that the president does not have the authority to impose tariffs under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA), the statute on which it relied. Then, the administration launched two investigations under Section 301, which allows the government to investigate and take action against unfair trade practices. The result is expected to produce combined tariffs equal to the invalidated IEEPA rates.The first Section 301 investigation, focused on forced labor, resulted in across-the-board tariffs on sixty economies beginning in July. The administration demanded action on specific labor concerns but offered no clear path to tariff removal even if its demands are met.The second Section 301 investigation covers structural excess manufacturing capacity—for example, a factory with unused capacity that’s kept open by government subsidies—across sixteen economies, including major U.S. trading partners in the Indo-Pacific and Europe, as well as Mexico. The findings, due shortly, will likely include broad-based tariffs but—as with the forced labor investigation—are not expected to outline a path to removing them.Meanwhile, the U.S. government has been negotiating trade agreements with about twenty economies, with commitments that overwhelmingly fall on the partners. Facing U.S. threats of tariffs above IEEPA rates if they fail to agree to U.S. demands, these partners are committing to lowering tariffs on U.S. goods, addressing specific trade barriers, and curbing unfair competition from subsidies or state-owned enterprises, among other requirements.These agreements render the Section 301 tariffs unnecessary. If those tariffs were intended as pressure to get U.S. trading partners to lower their tariffs on U.S. goods and make other changes, they have achieved their goal. U.S. partners will be bound by the obligations in these deals, including those related to excess manufacturing capacity and labor. Additional tariffs merely impose further taxes on U.S. businesses and consumers. They also will not advance the administration’s goal of slashing the U.S. goods trade deficit, which reached a record $135 billion in September—up 2 percent from August and 63 percent year over year.At a minimum, the administration should set out a clear roadmap to phase out all Section 301 tariffs as trading partners address U.S. concerns. The U.S. government should begin by removing tariffs on consumer goods and raw materials or other manufacturing components not already exempted, providing some financial relief to U.S. businesses and consumers in what amounts to a regressive tax on consumers. Speed is essential: The longer the tariffs remain, the harder it will be to give up the revenue and persuade companies to forgo protection they do not need.More Coherent Trade Policy AgendaThe second Trump administration has failed to set clear trade priorities and has pursued policies that lack coherence. Rather than targeting priority countries, Washington imposed sweeping Section 301 tariffs on sixty economies, as though they were all of similar economic significance. It has relied heavily on tariffs as a means to bring manufacturing back to the United States, although they have created business uncertainty and higher production costs. In addition, different government agencies seem to operate in silos. For example, tariffs on steel, aluminum, auto parts, lumber, advanced semiconductors, and other inputs that were imposed under Section 232, which aims to protect national security, have further raised the cost of the domestic industrial production that the Section 301 tariffs were supposed to promote.Trade policy should advance a more holistic approach toward U.S. innovation, competitiveness, resilience, job creation, and growth. Washington should sequence actions to address issues in priority order rather than overload the system and better coordinate both affirmative and defensive actions across agencies. It should use tariffs sparingly and judiciously, employing other tools to achieve its economic goals, protect genuinely strategic sectors, or address specific problems. Going forward, the Trump administration should weigh the downstream effects of tariffs and the costs to consumers more carefully and favor affirmative policies that create new business and market opportunities, rather than reach for tariffs in the first instance.Greater Cooperation with PartnersU.S. trading partners have grown increasingly frustrated with the administration’s unilateral trade actions and have sought to expand their trade with other partners. Over the summer, Trump escalated his trade war with Canada by imposing 50 percent tariffs on a range of Canadian products. The move drew intense opposition on both sides of the border, with many citing the close and longstanding relationship between the neighbors, and it led Canada to intensify its trade diversification efforts. But the United States is deeply integrated in the global economy, which does not operate by zero-sum rules, and its actions will have strategic implications. Moving ahead, the administration should seek to better use its partnerships to advance its economic goals and avoid unnecessarily damaging relations with foreign partners, whose support is essential to addressing international economic challenges and advancing broader U.S. interests. Washington has attacked its partners, often more harshly than its rivals, while demanding their cooperation on multilateral initiatives. Some have participated, but distrust of the United States limits what they can achieve together. Canada would be a good start for this effort. In addition, some countries, such as those in the Indo-Pacific, worry that Washington is missing opportunities to cooperate on shared concerns, including China’s exports of excess industrial capacity and its growing manufacturing trade surplus. They have sought to curb soaring Chinese imports, which have weakened local firms and caused factory closures and job losses, through a variety of measures. But they do not trust that the U.S. government will work with them to manage the issues, despite Washington viewing Beijing as its primary economic, technological, and strategic rival. Instead, these Indo-Pacific countries are attempting to avoid triggering both Chinese retaliation and U.S. accusations that their countries have become bases for China to circumvent U.S. trade restrictions. In other cases, Washington is working with countries that share U.S. concerns about the global impact of China’s industrial overcapacity and recognize the need for collective action. In late September, fourteen G20 trade ministers (including the United States) issued a joint statement on this issue. Without naming countries, the group warned that inaction would cripple industries, cost jobs, and damage economies and agreed to cooperate, initially focusing on autos and electric vehicles, batteries, chemicals, foundational semiconductors, and solar panels. But at the same time, Washington is poised to impose unilateral tariffs on some of these key trading partners.Cooperation on this initiative will already be slow and painstaking, not least in defining excess capacity and agreeing on concrete initiatives to tackle the problem. The Trump administration seemingly believes its unilateral Section 301 tariffs can proceed alongside international coordination efforts, but it minimizes how its action will weaken partners’ commitment to cooperation. It also incorrectly assumes their reliance on the U.S. security umbrella gives them no other choice. Instead of imposing tariffs, the administration should use incentives that reward countries for implementing agreed principles on excess capacity and support them as they take steps to curb China’s massive exports. The ASEAN Summit, which Trump will attend later this month, would be an ideal opportunity to signal a shift in U.S. approach.Congress Should Reassert Its AuthorityCongress has played virtually no role in trade policy during the second Trump administration, but the midterm results may embolden lawmakers. The new Congress may struggle to curb the White House’s use of executive authority, and Trump could veto legislation requiring congressional approval. Still, the scale of the Democratic wave and public anger may prompt the administration to rethink its approach, and it can do so without completely abandoning Trump’s beloved tariffs. Congress may also be able to begin reasserting constitutional authority over trade—a welcome development that will provide healthy checks and balances on the administration’s trade policy.Get more news and analysis fromCarnegie This WeekUnderstand the world with the latest from our scholars around the world.About the AuthorBarbara WeiselNonresident Scholar, Asia ProgramBarbara Weisel is a nonresident scholar in the Asia Program at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace and the former U.S. chief negotiator of the Trans-Pacific Partnership.Recent WorkCommentaryThe Fallout of the U.S.–Canada Trade War Won’t Be Limited to North AmericaBarbara WeiselCommentaryPost U.S.-China Summit: Managed InstabilityBarbara WeiselTradeForeign PolicyEconomyChinaUnited StatesCarnegie does not take institutional positions on public policy issues; the views represented herein are those of the author(s) and do not necessarily reflect the views of Carnegie, its staff, or its trustees.More Work from EmissaryCommentaryEmissaryCentral Asia Wants U.S. Investments. Frequently asked questions

BulletShares are a suite of defined maturity exchange-traded funds (ETFs) designed to help investors build targeted fixed income portfolios. Each fund holds a diversified basket of bonds that all mature in the same calendar year, helping investors target specific maturity timelines, risk preferences, and investment objectives. By combining the precision of individual bonds with the structural benefits of ETFs, BulletShares offer diversification, transparency, and liquidity. The funds typically distribute income monthly.

A bond ladder is built with individual bonds of varying maturities. As the bonds mature, the anticipated proceeds can be used for income needs or reinvested in new bonds that mature in subsequent years. Investors may use bond ladders to help create some predictability and stability regardless of market volatility and interest rate environments. Since they have specific maturity dates, investors can use BulletShares to build bond ladders without the time and expense of using individual bonds.

BulletShares can provide investors with an efficient way to establish potential protection from rising rates because the duration of the fund slowly rolls down to zero over the life of the ETF. Most traditional fixed income mutual funds and ETFs typically have a perpetual duration target, making them more sensitive to rising interest rates. Investors using BulletShares in bond ladders can also take advantage of rising interest rates by reinvesting the proceeds at maturity into BulletShares that mature in subsequent years and invest in bonds with higher interest rates.

BulletShares provide targeted exposure to investment-grade corporate bonds, high-yield corporate bonds, corporate bonds, municipal bonds and treasury bonds.

BulletShares have defined maturities to simulate the investor experience of buying and holding individual bonds to maturity for use in bond ladders and other strategies. BulletShares have designated years of maturities that are included in the fund’s name. Each BulletShares is designed to terminate in December of the designated year and make a final distribution at maturity. At each fund’s expected termination, the net asset value (NAV) of its assets is distributed to investors without any action on their part.

As BulletShares approach maturity, their durations decrease. In the last six months of the ETF’s maturity year, it is anticipated that the bonds in the portfolio will either mature or be called. Proceeds for these events will then be held either in cash or in cash equivalents such as US Treasury bills or commercial paper.

Title: Why build a bond ladder with BulletShares ETFs
Description: Our BulletShares ETFs offer a flexible and cost-effective solution to help you achieve your income goals now and — and in the future. Our Head of Fixed Income and Alternatives ETF Product Strategy Jason Bloom explains why.
Hello, I’m Jason Bloom head of the Fixed Income ETF Product Strategy team.
Having a flexible and resilient income strategy is crucial because markets are everchanging. Bond ladders are a solution and our BulletShares ETFs offer a convenient and cost-effective solution to implement a ladder to help you achieve your income objectives now — and in the future.
Here’s how.
Think of a bond ladder as a series of bonds on rungs on a ladder with each bond maturing at a different time. As each bond matures, you can use the proceeds to either meet specific financial needs — such as college tuition or an upcoming tax bill — or reinvest the proceeds into new bonds with longer maturities and maintain the ladder.
There are two key reasons why bond ladders can be advantageous:
First, they can provide a predictable and steady income.
Second, you have the flexibility to tailor your portfolio’s maturity and duration profiles and adjust for interest rate changes. If interest rates increase, you can reinvest any proceeds from maturing bonds at higher future interest rates. If interest rates decrease, only a segment of your laddered portfolio has to be reinvested during the low-rate period.
BulletShares ETFs can help make building bond ladders easier and more efficient. They have designated maturity years and cover a range of bond types, including investment-grade corporate, high-yield corporate, and municipal bonds. This allows you to build a bond ladder that matches with your financial goals.
They also combine the best of both worlds ­— the benefits of individual bonds and the advantages of exchange-traded funds.
Like individual bonds, BulletShares offer the potential for monthly income and a final distribution at maturity. You choose your portfolio’s maturity, yield, and credit quality.
As ETFs, BulletShares provide enhanced diversification, liquidity, transparency, convenience, and cost-effectiveness.
Whether you’re looking to generate steady income, customize your portfolio, or insulate against interest rate fluctuations, BulletShares ETFs provide a robust and versatile tool for building bond ladders.

articles.title: Access to finance is not enough: What the International Debt Report 2026 tells us
articles.text:
Published on
Data Blog

Access to finance is not enough: What the International Debt Report 2026 tells us

Haishan Fu

Evis Rucaj

November 05, 2026

This page in:

English

English

Between 2022 and 2025, low- and middle-income countries paid $436 billion more in principal and interest than they received in new financing. / Image: World Bank Group

Developing economies need financing to build roads, power grids and schools, to create jobs, and to raise living standards. That is why access to capital has been a central goal of development finance for decades. But does access alone deliver these results?
The newly launched International Debt Report (IDR) 2026, the World Bank Group's annual publication on external debt, puts this question front and center. Here is the paradox it reveals: access to international finance has improved, but the price of that finance has not. Low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) are borrowing more, paying more, and, in many cases, leaving less for long-term development.
External debt in LMICs rose to a record $9.4 trillion, marking the strongest increase in five years. Growth was even faster in IDA-eligible and low-income countries. For several years, private lending to LMICs was either declining or barely growing. In 2025, that trend reversed. Private lenders returned, and bond markets reopened after years of tight financial conditions and investor caution. On the surface, these developments point to a recovery. But beneath the headline numbers, the picture is more complicated.

Total debt service for LMICs rose for a fifth consecutive year in 2025, to $1.4 trillion, while payments to bondholders reached $363.1 billion. Between 2022 and 2025, LMICs paid about $436.1 billion more in principal and interest than they received in new financing. That means more public resources are being absorbed by debt servicing just when countries need to invest more in infrastructure, jobs, education, health, and the other foundations of long-term growth.

The poorest countries are paying the most
The return to international capital markets, while welcome, has been highly uneven. The poorest and most vulnerable countries now face borrowing costs not seen since the late 1980s. New private lending to IDA-eligible countries carry an average of 8.2 percent in 2025. The gap between what they pay private creditors and official creditors has widened from 3.4 percentage points a decade ago to 5.5 percentage points today, making private borrowing expensive.

Bond market borrowing has continued into 2026 even as yields have risen. That raises a fair question: are the terms sustainable on all this new financing, and is the money reaching the people and places that need it most?

A world full of shocks
These questions matter even more in an economy prone to shocks. Over the past decade, countries have faced a pandemic, disrupted trade and supply chains, sharp jumps in food and energy prices, geopolitical fragmentation, and repeated bouts of financial market volatility. Any economy would struggle to absorb that, and it is harder still when governments already have large financing needs and little room to respond.
Debt is not just a financial concern, either. When debt service squeezes productive and social spending, households feel it through weaker investment and fewer opportunities. The report finds that during external shocks, countries with heavier debt burdens tend to see larger adverse changes in the share of people who cannot afford a healthy diet. Sovereign borrowing costs and household welfare are closely connected.

Why debt transparency matters
Given all this, knowing how much countries owe, to whom, and on what terms has never been more important. For more than five decades, the World Bank has worked with borrowing countries to build the most comprehensive source of comparable external debt data for developing economies.
But transparency can't rest on what borrowers report alone. Since the creditor data-sharing exercise began in 2022, successive rounds have helped reconcile loan-level records, identify discrepancies, validate information, and close critical data gaps, strengthening the quality and consistency of external debt statistics. Round after round, this has helped reconcile records, flag discrepancies, validate information, and close critical data gaps.

That is debt transparency in practice. It is not just about publishing more data. It is about borrowers and creditors sitting down with their records, resolving differences, and steadily improving the shared information behind debt decisions.
This work matters even more as sovereign financing gets more complex. New creditors, instruments, guarantees, restructurings, and financing arrangements make it harder to see a country's full obligations. Without reliable, reconciled data, governments can't manage debt well, creditors can't assess risk accurately, and restructurings get harder.
Transparency is a shared responsibility. Borrowers need to keep comprehensive, timely debt records. Creditors, both official and private, need to disclose what is required to understand those obligations. And international institutions need to strengthen standards, close data gaps, and support better debt management systems.

The bottom line
Better information must lead to better financing. Countries with some of the greatest development needs still face some of the steepest borrowing costs, and borrowing that merely rolls over costly debt is no substitute for financing that expands productive capacity and raises future incomes.
The goal shouldn't be more debt. It should be finance that is affordable, transparent, sustainable, and able to support investment and growth.
That is the message of this year's report: access to finance is not enough. We have to know the debt, understand its terms, and make sure the financing developing countries receive helps them grow, withstand shocks, and improve people's lives.

articles.title: How Vanguard builds accountability into AI
articles.text:
Technology

How Vanguard builds accountability into AI

November 03, 2026

In financial services, AI offers the opportunity to provide personalized advice at scale, enable faster decision-making, and streamline workflows. Yet as firms race to deploy these capabilities, a crucial question emerges: How do companies harness the potential of AI while keeping the focus on investors?

At Vanguard, the answer lies in designing governance directly into the technology rather than layering it on afterward. Our approach balances innovation with oversight, embedding accountability mechanisms designed to keep pace with the AI systems they evaluate. The goal is not to slow AI adoption but to ensure it scales responsibly.
For investors, responsible innovation means applying AI in ways that support reliable experiences, appropriate oversight, and confidence in how the technology is used.

Governance that keeps pace with innovation

As AI development accelerates, governance must evolve alongside it. Vanguard addresses this challenge in part through AI-enabled oversight tools that can help review outputs, identify potential concerns, and surface relevant regulatory or policy considerations for human evaluation. This approach is sometimes described as “supervisory AI.”
This layered architecture pairs generative capabilities with built-in oversight. Content-generation tools work alongside compliance validators, helping teams develop client-ready materials while maintaining required standards. The technology supports, rather than replaces, human judgment by surfacing potential risks and compliance considerations before output reaches clients.
“We’re building AI systems that can operate at scale while maintaining the same standards of accountability that have defined Vanguard for decades,” said Mani Iyer, Vanguard’s chief AI and technology officer. “The key is embedding governance into the technology itself, not treating it as a separate review step.”

Evaluation that stress-tests before deployment

Before any AI solution reaches investors, it undergoes rigorous evaluation of its technical performance, ethical integrity, and resilience against misuse. Vanguard’s evaluation capability uses large-scale simulations to validate accuracy, identify potential failure modes, and ensure alignment with firm standards.
The process examines how systems respond to a range of conditions, including adversarial scenarios designed to expose potential vulnerabilities. This stress-testing approach can help uncover use cases that might not arise in standard development cycles, allowing teams to proactively address issues.

Real-world application across client experiences

These principles extend to how AI is used in client experiences. AI-enabled tools support advisors in delivering personalized guidance more efficiently, while embedded compliance layers help ensure that recommendations align with regulatory requirements and firm policies. For example, Vanguard advisors can use AI-generated summaries of market content tailored by tone and audience level, with integrated oversight supporting appropriate disclosures and review prior to use.
The architecture recognizes that productive AI workflows require end-to-end integration. Generation and governance must operate as connected capabilities rather than separate functions, reducing friction in advisor experiences while preserving the oversight necessary for trust.

Moving from pilots to governed scale

As Vanguard transitions AI initiatives from proof of concept to production, the focus shifts from novelty to durability. That requires clear policies, continuous monitoring, and transparent communication about how AI is used and governed. Technology partnerships, including legal and compliance AI platforms, can further extend these capabilities.
“In order to realize the productivity gains of AI, we need to build for a world where AI does work end to end where appropriate, while humans serve as supervisors for use cases,” said Iyer. “This is not about replacing human judgment; it is about augmenting it with technology that operates within clear guardrails.”
As AI capabilities evolve, Vanguard’s operating models must evolve with them, ensuring that human oversight remains central even as automation increases. This partnership approach positions AI as an enhancement to human judgment rather than a replacement for it.
Responsible AI is the foundation for sustained innovation, not a constraint on it. Embedding governance into technology workflows from the start helps Vanguard use AI to help deliver better outcomes for investors with the accountability they expect and deserve.

articles.title: Le Déluge: On the Brink of a French Fiscal Crisis?
articles.text:
Le Déluge: On the Brink of a French Fiscal Crisis?

Is France moving closer to a crisis? French government bond spreads are at their widest in almost 15 years driven by high inflation, rising global yields, and ongoing fiscal challenges, among other factors.

October 2026

KEY TAKEAWAYS

Is France moving closer to a crisis? French government bond spreads are at their widest in almost 15 years driven by high inflation, rising global yields, and ongoing fiscal challenges, among other factors.
Polls indicate a dramatic political shift: Surveys suggest Marine Le Pen is the most likely to win the presidential election in April 2027. Addressing the fiscal situation has not historically been a high priority for Le Pen.
French assets will likely stay under pressure though default risk remains very low in our view: Long-term investors may find current spread levels attractive. However, historical comparisons suggest spreads could widen further, offering potential opportunities within dynamically managed active portfolios.

Markets signal rising concerns over France
Persistent deficits and rising debt mean the French fiscal situation has become increasingly unsustainable, and risks associated with the 2027 presidential election are becoming more acute.
The spread between French and German 10-year government bond yields recently widened to 140 basis points (bp), the highest level since the 2012 eurozone sovereign crisis (see Figure 1).

Figure 1: French government bond spreads relative to German bunds have widened dramatically

Source: Bloomberg, as at 9 October 2026. For illustrative purposes only. Past performance is no guarantee of future performance.

There are several interrelated reasons why French spreads have widened.
Prices are rising: The latest French inflation reading (HCPI) shows prices over the year to September rose 3.4%, up from the equivalent August reading at 2.6%. Inflation is above central bank targets globally and so interest rate hikes have led to rising bond yields, and widening yield spreads within the eurozone.Changing dynamics for Japanese investors: Rising Japanese government bond yields offer an increasingly attractive alternative for Japanese investors, who have historically been supportive holders of French government bonds.Ongoing fiscal challenges for France: The French budget plans are in progress, but the deficit is likely to stay high – the government now expects a deficit of 5.4% this year and is unlikely to get parliamentary support for meaningful consolidation ahead of the presidential elections next April.
Against this backdrop, a key focus for investors are French political dynamics. Attempts to shore up the French fiscal situation have so far failed.

A dramatic political shift looks likely
The outlook for the 2027 presidential elections signals a dramatic shift, with polls showing Marine Le Pen of the right-wing Rassemblement National (RN) party far in the lead. Significantly, Édouard Philippe of the Horizons party, the leading centrist/centre-right candidate, has now fallen behind Jean-Luc Mélenchon of the left-wing La France Insoumise party (see Figure 2). It is important to note that the final candidates who will stand for election in the first round are as yet unclear.
It appears that Philippe and other centrist candidates have failed to generate political enthusiasm or momentum. The polls suggest that voter preferences are being driven by the same issues that are driving voters in other countries, such as the cost-of-living crisis and its impact on median real wages. Diesel and petrol prices are playing a significant role (see Figure 3). These have been an issue in French politics before, driving the ‘gilets jaunes’ (‘yellow jacket’) protests which began in 2018.

Figure 2: Polls show Marine Le Pen has a commanding lead ahead of the next election

Source: Politico, as at 1 October 2026. For illustrative purposes only.

Figure 3: Rising diesel prices in France are a key political issue

Source: Macrobond, as at 1 October 2026. Index shown is France, Consumer Price Index, Transport, Operation of Personal Transport Equipment, Parts & Accessories for Personal Transport Equipment, Fuels & Lubricants for Personal Transport Equipment, Diesel, Index.

Polls consistently show Le Pen winning the first round in the presidential election. In the last two weeks, Mélenchon has overtaken Philippe: it appears to be a roughly even chance of a second round vote between Le Pen and Mélenchon, rather than Le Pen and Philippe which previously seemed likely.
If this were to occur, Le Pen is expected to comfortably beat Mélenchon, with polls suggesting a vote split of about 68%-32%. By comparison, a contest between Le Pen and Philippe would be closer – though in such a contest polls show Le Pen’s support has been rising from 51% (July) to 57% (September) of the vote.
Overall, these numbers suggest an increasing probability of Le Pen taking the presidency in April 2027. Focusing purely on the implications for French government bonds, we believe unsustainable debt dynamics are likely to remain under a Le Pen presidency. Le Pen has outlined planned cuts to spending, reportedly increasing proposals for net savings of €123bn to €140bn by 2032 relative to 20261.
French bond spreads tightened slightly on the day Le Pen announced these plans, but questions remain over the feasibility of the proposals.
History suggests French spreads could widen much further
Given the level of French debt, markets are likely to punish fiscal mis-steps, and in our view spreads are likely to widen further as the election approaches, even though default risk remains very low in our view.
The question is how far spreads might widen. Would the highs in 2011 be attractive? Any comparison between French debt today, and back in 2011, must bear in mind that the French rating then was Aaa/AAA, and the nation’s debt/GDP ratio was 86%. Today, its rating has fallen to Aa3/A+, and its debt/GDP ratio is 118% and rising.
It may be more instructive to look at the spreads on Italian and Spanish debt in 2010 (see Table 1).
In May 2010 Italian and Spanish spreads were at similar levels to French spreads today, approaching the highs from the global financial crisis a few years before. Spreads went on to widen much further.

A positive outcome for French bond markets is still possible
There are three potential scenarios that might improve the outlook for French government bonds.
A centrist resurgence: Philippe or another centrist candidate might recover. Catalysts for this could include a new candidate; a sharp decline in diesel prices, though this currently seems unlikely; or if there is a geopolitical shock of sufficient magnitude that makes voters reconsider their priorities. If the probability of a more centrist candidate winning the presidential election meaningfully rises, this may provide a rationale to cover underweight positions.Positive fiscal action under Le Pen: Assumptions around Le Pen’s proposals and attitude toward the fiscal situation in France may prove mistaken. If new president Le Pen gives the right fiscal signals, and if RN achieves a legislative majority, this could be a signal to cover underweight positions and consider building overweight positions in French government bonds.Action by the EU: If a crisis does develop and a bailout is required from the EU, French government bond spreads will likely have widened materially – this would potentially be an attractive opportunity to buy French debt, as it was previously for Italy and Spain (but not Greece).
For long-term investors, current spread levels may offer an opportunity to buy French government bonds at attractive levels. Scenarios like the three above might lead markets to recover from here, although currently we expect the crisis to deepen and opportunities to arise for long-term investors to add further to positions. For more active portfolios, there is a rationale to remain cautious on French assets until one of the scenarios above emerges and only seek to move overweight if the political backdrop changes. Active investors looking for other ways to position for a deepening crisis could look to underweight positions in Belgium, the EU, or the eurozone periphery.

Endnotes
1. Source: Le Pen eyes bond markets with promise of bigger spending cuts if far right wins presidency, 6 October 2026, Reuters.

Appendix
Basis points (bp) is a unit of measurement equal to one one-hundredth of one percent (0.01%), commonly used to describe changes in interest rates and bond yields. One basis point equals 0.01%, so 100 basis points equal 1.00%.
Bond spread is the difference in yield between two bonds, typically between a riskier bond and a safer benchmark bond such as a German bund, used as an indicator of perceived credit risk. A widening spread generally signals growing concern about the riskier borrower.
Consumer Price Index (CPI) is a measure of the overall change in consumer prices based on a representative basket of goods and services over time.
Credit rating is an assessment of the creditworthiness of a borrower, such as a government or corporation, typically assigned by rating agencies such as Moody’s, S&P, or Fitch on a scale from AAA (highest quality) to D (default). A lower rating indicates higher perceived risk of non-payment.
‘Gilets jaunes’ (‘yellow jacket’) is a protest movement that began in France in 2018, initially in opposition to higher fuel taxes and rising living costs. It was named after the high-visibility yellow vests worn by protesters.
Government bond is a debt security issued by a national government to borrow money from investors, with the government promising to pay periodic interest and repay the principal at maturity.
Gross domestic product (GDP) is a measure of the overall change in consumer prices based on a representative basket of goods and services over time.
Debt/GDP ratio is a measure of a country’s government debt compared to its gross domestic product, used to assess the sustainability of its borrowing relative to the size of its economy. A higher ratio indicates a heavier debt burden.
Default risk is the risk that a borrower, such as a government or company, will be unable to make required payments on its debt obligations, potentially leading to default.
Fiscal relates to government revenue, spending, and debt management, particularly through taxation and budgetary policy.
Fiscal consolidation is the process of reducing a government’s deficit and debt levels, typically through spending cuts, tax increases, or a combination of both.
HCPI (Harmonised Consumer Price Index) is a standardised measure of inflation used across European Union countries, calculated using a common methodology
to allow consistent comparison of price changes between member states.
