articles.title: Mixed signals, research findings, and policy judgements − speech by Catherine L. Mann
articles.text:
Mixed signals, research findings, and policy judgements − speech by Catherine L. Mann

Given at the Natixis CIB Private Debt Forum

Published on
02 July 2026

Catherine L. Mann highlights how disaggregated data can improve our understanding of trends in headline economic variables. She also examines how volatility in inflation and financial markets has influenced financial conditions. Catherine then explains how research about de-anchoring of inflation expectations and the speed of monetary policy transmission has underpinned her activist policy strategy.

Speech
Introduction
As I think about my recent policy decisions, my assessment has evolved with incoming data and ongoing research. At the start of this year, moderation in price and wage growth, alongside slowing activity, had brought me closer to considering a reduction in Bank Rate. However, since the onset of the conflict in the Middle East, the reemergence of the trade‑off between inflation and activity has led me to place more weight on inflation persistence, shifting my view towards a longer hold, and potentially a need to lean against that risk.
This remains my view, as notwithstanding a sporadic reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, infrastructure rebuilding, future-proofing, and restocking supplies imply that higher energy prices will likely persist. Associated firm pricing reactions are also likely to keep inflation from moderating to the two percent target within the monetary policy horizon. That said, the discussion for today addresses the timing of a hike versus hold decision. The first topic is how an assessment of disaggregated data provides important nuances to the economic picture relative to the headline numbers. The second topic is how key research findings for both inflation persistence and monetary policy transmission inform my policy strategy.
The disaggregated assessment of the data shows mixed signals across key indicators. Realized inflation and expectations differ across households, firms, and financial markets, and have been influenced in the aggregate by fiscal measures. Wage developments differ across the public and private sectors, with further variation across industries. Public sector activity growth continues to outpace that of the market sector, alongside continued government budget overruns, including on account of interest costs. Volatility in both inflation and financial conditions has increased, affecting the degree of restrictiveness as well as the signal-to-noise assessment.
Interpreting mixed and noisy signals is nothing new for central bankers, but it is more challenging in the current environment where more frequent shocks are building on already persistent inflation with embedded second-round effects, amid higher volatility with elevated uncertainty (see Mann 2024b). In this speech, I will evaluate some of these mixed signals, explain how I interpret them and how – in light of research – they have shaped my recent decisions, especially the last one in June, and what they could mean for my monetary policy strategy going forward.
Uncertain underlying trend inflation
Prior to the conflict in the Middle East, inflation – as indicated in the February 2026 Monetary Policy Report – was expected to come down to our two percent target by the second half of 2026. However, that sanguine projection masked the underlying economic patterns, as increases in administered prices and national insurance contributions (NICs), which contributed 0.7 percentage points to the inflation hump in 2025, were assumed to dissipate in Q2 2026. The projected fall in inflation also reflected the energy bills package introduced in the Autumn Budget. The latter accounted for a reduction of nearly 0.25 percentage points to CPI inflation, as Chart 1 shows. Finally, slack in the economy was projected to weigh on inflation through the projected tightening of the fiscal position. The latter two factors underscore the importance of fiscal measures in getting us back to the inflation target.

Chart 1: Contribution of budget measures to deviation from inflation target
Percentage point deviation from the 2% inflation target

Footnotes

Source: ONS and Bank calculations.

Notes: ‘Administered prices, NICs, and electric vehicle (EV) mileage charge’ includes the estimated direct effects of changes to Vehicle Excise Duty, bus fares, VAT on school fees, and water charges. The NICs component represents Bank staff’s allowance for the effects of the recent increase in employers NICs on CPI inflation. The EV mileage charge component relates to the mileage-based charge on electric vehicles announced in Budget 2025.The ‘Energy budget measures’ bars represent the estimated direct effects of the energy bills package. The ‘Import prices’ bars includes an MPC judgement on the price of tradables (see May 2024 Monetary Policy Report) which has little effect on the profile beyond 2026. The ‘Other’ bars represent other deviations of inflation not attributable to the listed influences including the estimated effects of changes to tobacco and vaping products duties.

Of course, that projection was prior to the US-Israel-Iran war. The economy and our projections have evolved since then. For starters, the conflict resulted in a higher forecast for CPI inflation across all three scenarios presented in the April 2026 Monetary Policy Report. While outturns for price growth – so far lower than expected – continue to reflect lagged pass-through from pre-war moderation in commodity and domestic cost pressures, household inflation expectations have picked up materially since the conflict.
Because inflation shocks are amplified and attention to inflation rises when inflation is elevated – both with thresholds of around 3 to 3.5 percent CPI inflation – inflation expectations could pick up even more (Weber et al., 2025 Opens in a new window; Gaffney and Potjagailo, 2026).footnote [1] Staff research also shows that the latest rise in households’ short-term inflation expectations move back into the non-linear region, even if not quite as far as in 2022 (Buckmann et al., 2025). While the most recent observation of the Citi/YouGov measure of household inflation expectations has decreased from its April peak, it remains within the region of these non-linear dynamics, and both short- and long-term expectations remain elevated relative to historical averages and their pre-Iran war levels.
On the firm side, research surveys reveal that the recent inflationary episode spurred an increase in the share of firms setting prices in response to changes in economic conditions – so-called state-dependent pricing – instead of adjusting their prices at fixed intervals (Bunn et al., 2026a). State-dependent firms increased their prices more quickly when inflation rose but also raised their prices by less relative to time-dependent firms as inflation decreased (Chart 2) as the time-dependent firms’ adjustment caught-up. A higher frequency of price adjustments yields an upside inflation bias as well as more volatile inflation, as prices respond more quickly, more often, and more strongly to positive inflation shocks.

Chart 2: Firm output price growth by price-setting behavior
Own-price growth and expected year-ahead own-price growth, percent

Footnotes

Source: Bunn et al. (2026a).

Notes: Chart depicts trends in own-price growth (solid lines) and expected year-ahead own-price growth (diamonds), split by firms’ price-setting behavior. Firms are split into state-dependent and time-dependent pricing based on each firm’s most recent response to this question (as of April 2026). The series are three-month moving averages, with the latest data up to May 2026. Percentages in brackets denote share of firms using state- and time-dependent pricing.

To get a better understanding about the current conjuncture and prospects for nominal conditions, I look at firms’ responses to the Decision Maker Panel (DMP) survey, particularly the distributions of responses to questions about expected CPI inflation and expected one-year-ahead price- and wage-setting. Following the outbreak of the Iran war, the survey data show that firms’ CPI inflation expectations quickly responded, (left panel in Chart 3). Although the distribution has shifted to the right in the latest quarter (purple) relative to the three months preceding the Iran war (orange), it remains below 2022 (aqua) and is also much less dispersed. This implies that the pattern of firms’ responses does not yet exhibit the same degree of uncertainty about future inflation as it did during the
Russia-initiated inflation surge.
The distribution of firms’ expectations for their own-price growth in the year ahead has shifted modestly to the right, too. This is most apparent for consumer-facing firms and goods producers, while services firms and business-facing companies have adjusted their expectations by less. These changes in firms’ expectations and price-setting behavior are a key ingredient for the evolution of CPI inflation itself.
The DMP survey data also show that some firms have modestly altered their realized prices in recent months, with the distribution for goods-producing firms exhibiting a bit more mass in the right-hand side of the distribution, suggesting that there could be more inflation in the pipeline. Input and output PMIs have also been elevated.

Chart 3: Distributions of firms’ inflation and wage growth expectations
Expected one-year-ahead CPI inflation (left panel) and expected year-ahead wage growth (right panel)

Footnotes

Source: Decision Maker Panel.

Notes: Charts show kernel density plots for expected one-year-ahead CPI inflation (left panel) and year-ahead wage growth expectations for 2022, December 2025 to February 2026 (three months prior to the Iran war), and March 2026 to May 2026. Distributions are weighted by industry and employment shares.

Widening the aperture on potential wage dynamics from the firm-level survey data, current official wage statistics show mixed signals. Despite a continued easing in private sector regular pay growth (left panel in Chart 4), which is now within the Bank staff’s estimates of target-consistent wage growth, whole-economy total pay has not decelerated to the same degree. We therefore continue to see a wedge between the two pay measures, as illustrated by the right panel in Chart 4.
Over the past year, that wedge has largely been driven by stronger public sector wage growth and the impact of bonuses. In recent months, the contribution from the public sector has eased somewhat. Drawing on the evidence from February 2026 Monetary Policy Report on heterogeneity in wage setting, this pattern is consistent with stronger pay growth in sectors characterized by more structured or collective bargaining where inflation and inflation expectations play key roles. This includes the public sector and similar “union-type” segments within the private sector, as well as cost-minimizing firms, which together account for around 80% of private-sector workforce.
Pay settlements have largely been finalized for the year, and there is limited evidence (as shown in Chart 3 above) from firms in the DMP of a pick‑up in what they expect to offer their employees next year. Looking ahead, the risk is that wage pressures are deferred rather than dissipated, particularly if future pay settlements – including in these more collectively bargained segments – are set against the backdrop of higher realized inflation and elevated expectations in the second half of this year.
Furthermore, even if energy prices moderate, the temptation will be to maintain the own- price and wage strategies to partially rebuild margins, which, according to the survey data, have been absorbing the current shock (Bunn et al, 2026b Opens in a new window). All told, distributions are important indicators to evaluate whether inflationary pressures, the wage setting process, and resulting price setting feed into overall inflation.

Chart 4: Regular pay growth and contributions to the wedge between whole-economy and private sector pay growth
Three-months-on-year growth (left panel) (a) and percentage point contributions to the difference (right panel)(b)

Footnotes

Source: ONS and Bank calculations.

Notes: Left panel (a) depicts three-months-on-year public and private sector regular pay growth in percent and the range of target-consistent estimates for regular pay growth. Right panel (b) depicts percentage point contributions by bonuses and public sector regular pay growth to the wedge between three-months-on-year whole economy total and private sector wage growth. Latest data: April 2026.

The trade-off re-emerges
Alongside the higher projected paths for inflation in the April Monetary Policy Report is a slower projected pace of GDP growth across all scenarios relative to February (Chart 5). The trade-off between inflation and activity has re-emerged, as I have noted in previous speeches (see Mann 2025a, 2025b).

Chart 5: Real GDP in the February and April 2026 Monetary Policy Reports
Index (2025 = 100)

Footnotes

Source: ONS and Bank calculations.

Notes: Aqua line shows the forecast for real GDP from the February 2026 Monetary Policy Report. Orange, purple, and gold lines show the respective forecasts for scenarios A, B, and C from the April 2026 Monetary Policy Report.

While headline GDP growth remains subdued, looking beneath the aggregate number reveals a divergence between the role of public and private sector activity. While GDP growth has recently been primarily driven by market sector output (MSO, right panel in Chart 6), public sector output has grown by around 4.5 percent since Q4 2023, outpacing the cumulative growth of market sector output by around one percentage point (left panel in Chart 6).

Chart 6: Growth in market sector and public sector GDP and their contributions to GDP growth
Cumulative change since 2023 Q4 (left panel) and contributions to change since 2023 Q4 (right panel)

Footnotes

Source: ONS and Bank calculations.

Notes: Notes: The government sector comprises public administration, education, and health, while the market sector comprises all other industries, including agriculture, wholesale and retail trade, accommodation and food services, and other market-based activities. Latest data: April 2026.

Why do I highlight the different growth rates of government and market sector GDP? The MPC’s forecast is conditioned on announced fiscal policy, as reflected in the Office for Budget Responsibility’s (OBR’s) projections. In simple terms, fiscal policy is funded by a mix of public sector borrowing and taxes. As noted in the Bank’s recent Forecast Evaluation Report, “looser-than-expected fiscal policy has […] contributed to there being less spare capacity” (Bank of England, 2026b). As shown in Chart 7, this reflects higher outturns for public sector borrowing than embodied in the OBR’s forecasts, consistent with the OBR’s own forecast evaluation Opens in a new window (Office for Budget Responsibility, 2026 Opens in a new window). Using a structural VAR model, Brignone and Piffer (2026) demonstrate that upward revisions in inflation forecasts following the post-pandemic inflation surge can be attributed to a combination of expansionary shocks on the demand side, revisions to past shocks, and contractionary supply-side shocks. Going forward, the question is whether there will be upside surprises in fiscal policy,footnote [2] which could provide additional support to public sector activity and can have broader implications for productivity, aggregate demand, inflation, and financial conditions.

Chart 7: Successive forecasts and outturns of public sector net borrowing
Public sector net borrowing as a percent of GDP

Footnotes

Source: Office for Budget Responsibility.

Notes: Data shows successive forecasts (grey) and outturns (orange) of public sector net borrowing as a percent of GDP. Latest forecast: March 2026.

Labor market data also show a mixed picture, with implications for the strength of demand. Beneath the rise in headline unemployment in recent years and its projected increase, the dispersion in unemployment rates across industries has also increased. Chart 8 illustrates how unemployment rates across different industries have changed since 2022. The shaded area (aqua) shows that the dispersion of unemployment rates across different sectors has increased since mid-2025, suggesting that unemployment is more unevenly distributed across industries. For instance, the unemployment rate remains higher in accommodation and food services and has risen faster in that industry compared to overall unemployment since mid-2025. By contrast, the professional and technical sectors are closer to the lower end of the distribution of unemployment rates across sectors.
Some of these differences may reflect varying exposure to recent changes in fiscal policy, such as changes to national insurance contributions and the national living wage, as well as sector-specific demand conditions, including exposure to the energy shock. The result is a labor market that is far from uniform, indicating that some industries are more resilient than others, and that headline unemployment may overstate weakness in the labor market. Therefore, demand may be more resilient than projected by the aggregate numbers.

Chart 8: Dispersion in unemployment rates across industries
Unemployment rates by previous industry (percent)

Footnotes

Source: April 2026 Monetary Policy Report.

Notes: Data show ONS estimates of unemployment by previous industry. This measure will not fully capture new entrants to the labor market who do not find a job as they have no previous industry, nor will it reflect the capacity for workers to transition across industries. The shaded area shows the range of industry-level unemployment rates by previous industry over time. Given data limitations and relatively small sample sizes, it can be difficult to draw firm conclusions from changes in these data. These data are not seasonally adjusted. The latest data shown are for the three months to April 2026.

Financial conditions are volatile
I also considered financial conditions in forming my June decision, as has always been the case. Global spillovers, as discussed in one of my speeches last year, have importantly contributed to the volatility of financial market variables, particularly in a small open economy like the UK. That remains the case today (Chart 9).
Looking at the time-varying volatility of asset price factors extracted from a daily structural VAR based on Brandt et al. (2021) Opens in a new window, we see that the Iran conflict has been associated with a material increase in the volatility of international monetary policy factors but also in the volatility in the UK-specific risk factor. In fact, the UK-specific risk factor is now furthest away from its historical normal. By contrast, volatility in the model's macro factors and global risk (which is a flight-to-safety factor) is little changed. This divergence suggests that markets are interpreting the conflict less as a shock to the growth outlook and more as a source of uncertainty about inflation and the associated monetary policy response, as well as perhaps the consequence of the behavior of an evolving investor base in the gilt market, a topic I discussed in my speech on the UK's external exposures (Mann, 2026).

Chart 9: Volatility of asset price factors
Rolling standard deviation of shocks

Footnotes

Source: Mann (2025c), Bloomberg Finance L.P. and Bank calculations.

Notes: The calculations are based on a structural VAR identified using sign and magnitude restrictions following Brandt et al. (2021) Opens in a new window. The model is extended to analyze monetary policy spillovers between the UK and its two most important trading partners and dominant currency blocks, the US and the euro area (as described in Mann (2024a)).

We can also directly observe the increase in financial market volatility in how UK overnight index swap (OIS) curves have evolved since the onset of the Middle East conflict. Following the outbreak of the Iran war, OIS curves have become increasingly volatile, as the widened range in their movements post-conflict (aqua) relative to pre-conflict (purple) in Chart 10 (left panel) shows. During this period, these large increases in OIS rates have been passed-through rapidly into mortgage rates faced by households: interest rates on two- and five-year fixed rate mortgages with a 75% loan-to-value ratio have risen by 87 and 73 basis points, respectively (right panel in Chart 10). The asymmetry in price and wage developments I highlighted earlier – more robust adjustments to upside shocks and relatively slow adjustment to downside shocks – can also be observed in financial markets, as increases in OIS rates pass through to mortgage rates more quickly than do decreases.
As I noted in my 200-word paragraph in the latest MPC minutes, higher financial market volatility acts as a headwind to both consumption and investment. For firms, increased uncertainty around financing conditions raises the hurdle for investment. For households, more volatile inflation can result in uncertainty about future inflation, which tends to encourage precautionary behavior and the maintenance of higher savings buffers (Fischer et al., 2025). At the same time, my preferred measure of financial conditions (see Burr, 2023 Opens in a new window), has not tightened that much. Taken together, just like other parts of the economy, financial conditions are sending mixed signals, too.

Chart 10: Volatility in OIS curves and pass-through to mortgage rates
UK instantaneous forward OIS curves (left panel) and daily quoted mortgage rates and OIS rates (right panel)

Footnotes

Source: Bloomberg Finance L.P., Bank of England and Bank calculations.

Notes: Swathes of UK instantaneous forward OIS curves in the left panel cover an equivalent period of time. Range of moves in OIS curves pre-Iran war (purple swathe) observed from 28 October 2025 until 27 February 2026. Range of moves in OIS curves since the Iran war (aqua swathe) observed from 27 February to 26 June 2026. Right panel shows 2-year and 5-year OIS rates and 2-year and 5-year fixed rate mortgages with 75% loan to value ratios. Latest observation for daily quoted mortgage and OIS rates: 26 June 2026.

Research informs my monetary policy strategy
Against the backdrop of the data and prospects discussed above, two research strands inform my strategy. The first strand emphasizes the importance of leaning against upside risks to inflation to reduce risks of de-anchoring and to ensure that monetary policy remains credible. I’ve discussed research on persistent upside risks to inflation and the consequences in numerous previous speeches.footnote [3] The second research strand emphasizes the speed with which firms adjust their expected pricing strategies and the capacity for Bank Rate decisions to feed through relatively quickly into expectations, firms’ price-setting behavior, and overall inflation, a topic that I addressed last in 2023 (see Mann, 2023a).
Let’s look at what’s new in the first research strand. This research on de-anchoring examines how responsive medium- to long-term inflation expectations are to changes in short-term inflation expectations by regressing the former on the latter alongside a set of control variables.footnote [4] A regression coefficient close to zero indicates firmly anchored expectations – in that case, expectations about inflation in the medium- and long-term are insensitive to short-term fluctuations. By contrast, a coefficient close to one suggests that expectations are de-anchored. Chart 11 shows the analysis for households, firms, and financial markets.
Data from household and firm surveys show an increased responsiveness of their inflation expectations to near-term inflation developments since the Covid pandemic and the energy shock following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, suggesting that these two groups are not firmly anchored (left and center panel in Chart 11). Financial market participants’ expectations are more anchored relative to households and firms, despite the responsiveness of their long-term expectations to short-run expectations being more volatile (right panel in Chart 11). Taken together, these findings point to some erosion in credibility and potential risks of de-anchoring among households and firms.

Chart 11: Responsiveness of medium/long-term inflation expectations to short-term inflation expectations
Regression coefficients (percentage points)

Footnotes

Source: Bank of England/Ipsos Inflation Attitudes Survey, Decision Maker Panel, Market Participants Survey and Bank calculations.

Notes: Household measure shows the slope of 5-year-ahead inflation expectations on 1-year-ahead inflation expectations from the Bank of England/Ipsos Inflation Attitudes Survey. Firm measure shows the slope of CPI 3-year-ahead expectations on CPI 1-year-ahead expectations from the Decision Maker Panel. Financial Markets measure shows the slope of 5-year-ahead inflation expectations on 1-year-ahead inflation expectations from the Market Participants Survey. Shaded areas denote 95% confidence bands.

Staff research has also used the Boosted Inflation Model – a machine learning model based on boosted decision trees that is designed to capture non-linear relationships between a range of indicators and CPI inflation (Buckmann et al., 2025). It can decompose inflation into its underlying drivers, reflecting the price Phillips curve as well as potential drift of that curve. Chart 12 shows the model’s decomposition of predicted inflation relative to the two percent target. The contribution of the trend inflation component (aqua), which comes from elevated household inflation expectations has started to increase since the Iran war, but remains below the levels last seen in 2023 and 2024. Since household expectations can feed into both wage and price developments, this can be a harbinger of second-round effects.
These developments increase upside risks to the inflation process and raise the risk of
de-anchoring, particularly given the extended period of above-target inflation and the increase in inflation volatility. As discussed in Mann (2022), once expectations drift from the two percent target, monetary policy needs to tighten more, to both control expectations and to moderate inflation itself. So, considering this research strand alone would typically point towards a tighter policy stance.

Chart 12: Decomposition of CPI inflation from Boosted Inflation Model
Annualized and smoothed (left) and annualized month-on-month (right)

Footnotes

Source: Buckmann et al. (2025).

Notes: Colored bars show the block-wise predictive contributions to 1-month-ahead annualized month-on-month CPI inflation (white line), around 2% target. Blockwise boosted inflation model estimated via cross-validation over 1989m1-2026m5 sample. Dashed line: CPI inflation, annualized.

What’s new in the second strand of research – the speed of transmission of monetary policy. Evidence points to a relatively more rapid transmission of monetary policy to borrowing costs, but also directly to inflation expectations as compared to what is embodied in most traditional slack-driven models of inflation process. Although even the more familiar approach finds that monetary transmission to GDP has been quicker.footnote [5]
With regard to the first stage of transmission of monetary policy,footnote [6] the relatively quick increase in mortgage rates in response to the rise in inflation and market expectations of tighter monetary policy that I showed in Chart 10 illustrates a key channel through which the financial environment will affect households considering a new mortgage or seeking to remortgage by making their monthly repayments more expensive. Note as well that the moderation from the peak has been slower than the advance, pointing to asymmetry in the institutional response to the policy environment.
Besides the fast pass-through to financial variables, Brandt et al. (2026) Opens in a new window use
high-frequency credit and debit card spending data to show that monetary policy shocks can affect real economic activity very quickly, too. They show that consumer spending declines within a few days in response to a contractionary monetary policy shock, while web searches for terms related to unemployment rise. This result suggests that a fast adjustment in households’ expectations about their economic prospects can drive a change in consumption behavior.
Firm-level research by Yotzov et al. (2026) Opens in a new window also shows that firms update both their CPI inflation perceptions and expectations as well as their own-price growth expectations upon CPI releases. Specifically, the authors find that between 2022 and 2024, a one percentage point increase in headline CPI inflation raises firms’ expected year-ahead own-price growth by 0.3 percentage points. On CPI perceptions, they respond quickly within a few hours of data releases. Firms’ expected own-price growth also increases a few hours after a positive change in CPI inflation, although to a smaller extent.
Research by Di Pace et al. (2025) Opens in a new window analyses how firms update their price expectations in response to monetary policy announcements by the Bank of England. They find that within days following the Bank Rate decision, firms revise down their year-ahead price growth expectations if the increase in Bank Rate is sufficiently large. As Chart 13 shows, Bank Rate increases of 50 basis points or more result in a statistically significant and economically sizeable downward revision in firms’ expected price growth for the year ahead. While this pattern is evident across the distribution of firms’ expected own-price changes, it is more pronounced in the left tail. This means that firms revise the lower-price outcomes in their pricing plans more than the higher-price outcomes, suggesting an asymmetric updating of expectations. Chart 13 also shows that firms do not seem to significantly alter their price growth expectations in response to announcements of Bank Rate changes smaller than 50 basis points.

Chart 13: Responsiveness of firm price expectations to Bank Rate changes
Regression coefficients

Footnotes

Source: Di Pace et al. (2025) Opens in a new window.

Notes: The chart plots regression results for different moments of the distribution of firms’ price expectations on monetary policy shocks within a 5-day window around policy announcements. Monetary policy shocks are measured using actual Bank Rate changes. The series is normalized so that coefficients correspond to the response to a 25 basis point shock. BR change < 50 bps indicates a Bank Rate change below 50 basis points in absolute value. BR change >= 50 bps indicates a Bank Rate change equal or above 50 basis points in absolute value. Analysis uses data from November 2016 until December 2023. Error bars denote 95% confidence intervals.

Implications for monetary policy strategy
How do I use the underlying data and these two strands of research to inform my policy strategy? Consider the following three dimensions generally, but with specific reference to my June decision.
First, the importance of a disaggregated assessment. Disaggregated data is always key to how I evaluate the economic conjuncture. In June, these data exhibited mixed signals, which provided a more nuanced view of the inflation-activity trade-off than the macro data. Wage growth has differed between private and public sectors. Pricing behavior of firms has varied in speed of responsiveness. The administered one-off changes in prices masked underlying trend inflation. Disaggregated labor signals in some sectors were less weak than the overall unemployment rate. Tracking fiscal outturns has been important, especially given the gap between GDP and market-sector output, and the evidence from the Forecast Evaluation Report.
Second, on the topic of volatility and noise versus signals. Whereas both higher inflation and financial market volatility do make it harder to distinguish signals from transitory movements, because inflation volatility goes hand-in-hand with inflation rates, and financial volatility is reflected in risk premia, the noise contributes to the signal. It puts upside pressure on inflation and tightens financial conditions, at least in nominal terms. The source of inflation pressures – from costs versus from demand matters. The source of financial risk premia – from domestic drivers versus foreign spillovers – matters. In June, the cost-oriented inflation pressures were being offset by domestic-oriented financial restrictiveness. Bearing these factors in mind has been key to many of my policy decisions.
Third, on the topic of timing. Energy price developments, profit margin behavior, and the underpinnings of the 2027 wage negotiations will be critical in determining whether current cost pressures become more embedded. All these conditions are still unfolding. Given the seasonality of wage negotiations and their dependence on previous inflation and inflation expectations, data outturns (including the expectations for one-year-ahead) in the second half of this year are particularly important for my future decisions.
Considering my June decision, by the disaggregated data assessment, there was more upside risks to inflation compared to downside risks for activity. On that basis and considering the research about risks of de-anchoring alone, tightening Bank Rate could have made sense. But, at the time of the June meeting, financial markets had tightened considerably at least in nominal terms.
Research on the responsiveness of pricing and consumer behaviors to CPI announcements and to monetary policy shocks is clear evidence that monetary policy can have quick effects on the key variables of inflation expectations and CPI inflation, which is the Bank of England’s remit. In June, observing these forward-looking and high-frequency data in the context of both strands of the research meant that an activist hold was the appropriate decision.
Going forward, as I evaluate the disaggregated data, the sources of signal-to-noise in financial conditions, and the inputs to firms’ pricing strategies, I am confident that if outturns – especially in expectations – are unfavorable to the underlying inflation process, an activist move can bring inflation expectations and outcomes toward the two percent target.

articles.title: Managing Payment Fraud Risk
articles.text:
Managing Payment Fraud Risk

Payment fraud is rising sharply worldwide1, costing businesses tens of billions of dollars2 each year.Organizations handling large volumes of financial flows are particularly targeted.In a large majority of cases, despite strengthened technical security measures, human factor remains a key source of vulnerability3. Raising awareness and training your teams are key levers in protecting against these types of fraud.Stay ahead of key fraud risks and support your organization's resilience.Main fraud scenarios observed:Phishing or smishing (email or SMS phishing)An email or text message impersonating a trusted individual or a recognized organization (bank, internet service provider, etc.) in order to collect your personal information.Fake bank advisor fraud / Impersonation scamA call or message from someone claiming to be a representative of your bank, citing technical checks or a supposed fraud attempt on your account, to pressure you into urgently approving a fraudulent transaction or handing over your bank card via a fake courier.IBAN fraud / invoice redirection fraudThe fraudulent alteration of the bank details of one of your counterparties, such as suppliers or service providersCEO fraud / Business Email CompromiseAn urgent and confidential request allegedly coming from a senior executive within your company, aimed at getting you to approve a banking transaction.Malicious QR codesQR codes that redirect users to fraudulent websites designed to collect personal information or prompt the installation of malicious software.Email account compromiseHacking of email accounts, allowing fraudsters to monitor interactions between the client and their bank and/or insert fraudulent messages. 1- Corporate treasurers report significant rise in fraud | The Association of Corporate Treasurers 2- According to World Metrics, Businesses lost $32bn to payment fraud in 2022: Payment Fraud Statistics (2026): Latest Research 3- Discover how human error and manipulation pose risks to B2B payment security and learn strategies to mitigate these vulnerabilities effectively

articles.title: Settlement reached in Silicon Valley Bank investor class action case | Norges Bank Investment Management
articles.text:
Norges Bank Investment Management and the Swedish pension fund Sjunde AP-fonden (AP7), as Co-Lead Plaintiffs, have reached a settlement in principle of $224.5 million with KPMG LLP, the former external auditor of Silicon Valley Bank (SVB), on behalf of the class of investors in the U.S. securities class action arising from the bank’s collapse in March 2023.
The fund and other SVB investors suffered significant losses on their investments in SVB securities.
“The settlement is an important first step toward recovering investor losses from one of the largest bank failures in U.S. history. It was reached after more than three years of litigation that has helped strengthen legal protections for investors. Investor confidence depends on well-functioning markets and on investors’ ability to enforce their rights”, says Nicolai Tangen, CEO of Norges Bank Investment Management.
The settlement is subject to court approval. The case continues against the other defendants.

articles.title: ETF Innovators: Goldman Sachs Asset Management on client-first ETFs  | RBCCM
articles.text:
With $90 billion in assets under management, Goldman Sachs Asset Management is moving beyond traditional index replication to tackle what investors actually need: solutions to specific financial challenges.
In this edition of ETF Innovators, Brendan McCarthy, Global Head of ETF Distribution and Capital Markets at GSAM, points out that the lines between investment vehicles are blurring, and GSAM is positioning itself as “wrapper-agnostic.” A client might access the same strategy through an ETF, mutual fund, separately managed account, or private vehicle, depending on what suits their needs. The product offers the liquidity and transparency of an ETF alongside the characteristics of illiquid private equity – without forcing investors into a false choice between the two.
Income-oriented strategies are another growth area. Demand for yield is evergreen, but the nature of that demand is shifting. Clients now want enhanced income, diversified sources of yield, and upside participation simultaneously. Rather than settling for traditional dividend or fixed income products, sophisticated investors are turning to strategies that use derivatives to improve returns while managing downside risk. GSAM is expanding its offering here, with several new products in the pipeline.
Looking ahead, the firm is no longer thinking about managing individual products, but about being a portfolio construction partner. This evolution is supported by its European expansion and the strategic Innovator acquisition, which strengthens GSAM's defined outcomes capabilities.

“That is a big part of our value add — to truly provide solutions where we truly are wrapper agnostic.”
Brendan McCarthy, Global Head of ETF Distribution and Capital Markets, Goldman Sachs Asset Management

Looking ahead, the firm is no longer thinking about managing individual products, but about being a portfolio construction partner. That represents a meaningful shift in how asset managers compete and how investors should evaluate them.

About ETF Innovators
ETF Innovators is a short-form video series hosted by Valerie Grimba, Director, Global ETF Strategy, that spotlights how RBC clients are driving innovation in ETFs. The series tracks the evolution of the global ETF landscape and spotlights the leaders, ideas, and strategies powering the next wave of performance.

The fund seeks to maximize current income exempt from federal income tax to the extent consistent with the preservation of capital. For additional yield, the fund may invest up to 30% of its net assets in municipal bonds rated, at the time of purchase, below investment grade ("high yield" or "junk" bonds) or the unrated equivalent as determined by the fund's sub-adviser.

The complexity and urgency of the world’s challenges require meaningful collaboration among members of the development community and other stakeholders if the goal of ending poverty on a livable planet is to be realized. With overlapping crises threatening global development and a growing global demand for a bold and coordinated response to these crises, the World Bank is working to strengthen partnerships and utilize every resource available to maximize development impact.The Bank works with a growing array of development partners, both traditional and non-traditional, formal, and informal, to help meet our shared goals. From the ongoing partnership with our sovereign donors, through engagement with foundations and civil society, to an increased focus on leveraging private capital, the Bank recognizes how transformative partnerships can be when new ideas, perspectives, and experiences are combined with the necessary financial resources.Development partners work with the Bank through trust funds, financial intermediary funds, and co-financing arrangements:to align and pool funding support with other development partners within agreed strategic frameworks.to benefit from the Bank’s convening power, at both the international and country level, to maximize coordinated action and achieve impact at scale.to benefit from the Bank's extensive technical expertise, country experience and supervision capacity, its financial control framework, and its ability to monitor and report on results.to provide grant funding in fragile, conflict-affected, and other complex situations enabling the Bank to engage and provide critical assistance in circumstances where traditional instruments are not well-suited.to support innovative or emerging policy areas, which the Bank and Partners view as a priority.Trust FundsThe World Bank uses trust funds, a financing arrangement set up with contributions from one or more development partners, to complement core funding from the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (IBRD), and the International Development Association (IDA) to help attain its institutional goals. Trust funds support the achievement of these goals by providing financial resources, contributing to the knowledge agenda, and leveraging the Bank’s convening power and global and local presence to contribute to country, regional, and global development. Trust funds allow the Bank to mobilize and direct concessional resources to strategic development priorities and to mobilize the resources and capabilities of other development actors through partnership programs.Financial Intermediary FundsFinancial Intermediary Funds (FIFs) are financial arrangements that leverage a variety of public and private resources in support of international initiatives, enabling the international community to provide a direct and coordinated response to global priorities. FIFs are a key financing arrangement for the World Bank, where the Bank acts as a trustee of large multilateral financial mechanism to support global development initiatives and partnerships. As a FIF trustee, the World Bank provides financial services, including receiving, holding, and investing contributed funds, and transferring them when instructed by the FIF governing body.Co-FinancingCo-financing is an important financing mechanism of the World Bank. The World Bank works with Multilateral Development Banks (MDBs), bilateral agencies, and other development partners to allow funds to flow directly from co-financers to the recipient client country and finance activities within the scope of a World Bank operation. Under these arrangements, World Bank resources and third-party resources are deployed in a coordinated manner to World Bank operations that are led by the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (IBRD) or the International Development Association (IDA).

Our FirmWe aspire to be the world’s most exceptional financial institution.Our Purpose and ValuesABOUT USOur People and Leadership157 Years of ExcellenceCommunity TransformationOur Focus on SustainabilityOur Vendor ProgramPartnershipsLocationsFEATUREDCommunity TransformationWe invest the power of Goldman Sachs' financial and intellectual capital to advance enduring economic growth and opportunity.
CareersThere are many chapters in a career. There is only one Goldman Sachs.Discover CareersWORKING AT GSStudentsLife at GSBenefitsFeatured OfficesOpen RolesExchangesBrookfield’s Connor Teskey on the Real Bottleneck in the AI BuildoutOct 30, 2026ShareSubscribe:SpotifyAppleYouTubeDownload TranscriptThe bottleneck in the artificial intelligence (AI) buildout is neither capital nor demand, but rather the operational capability to develop land, secure a grid connection, and build the power supply, says Brookfield Asset Management CEO Connor Teskey on Goldman Sachs Exchanges: Great Investors. Indeed, one market misconception is that demand for data centers is somehow “fragile,” he says in this conversation with Alison Mass, chairman of Investment Banking in Goldman Sachs Global Banking & Markets. Teskey also shares his perspective on long-term investing, Brookfield's approach to building businesses and the evolution of its private credit platform.
Transcript:
Connor Teskey: Demand has become the critical input to growth for every major company in every major country around the world, and there is a scarcity of it.
The growth we're seeing across critical infrastructure assets and the overwhelming need for energy around the world goes so far beyond simply artificial intelligence.
Demand is up here and supply is down here. Even if demand growth was to slow, even if it was to plateau, even if it was to decline, there would still be a huge supply-demand imbalance to the providers.
It is perhaps the greatest capital need in the history of mankind. It's pretty exciting.
Alison Mass: Welcome to Goldman Sachs Exchanges: Great Investors. I'm Alison Mass. Today, I'm sitting down with Connor Teskey, CEO of Brookfield Asset Management. Connor joined Brookfield in 2012 at age 24. 14 years later, he runs the entire asset management business, managing approximately $1.3 trillion dollars across infrastructure, renewable power, real estate, private equity, and credit, while continuing to lead its energy group.
In this episode, we discuss Connor's transition to the CEO seat, Brookfield's AI infrastructure buildout across the US and Europe, and the firm's strategic expansion in credit.
Connor, welcome to Great Investors. It's so fantastic to have you here.
Connor Teskey: Thank you for having us.
Alison Mass: So, across all those asset classes that you play in, is there one that you're most excited about right now?
Connor Teskey: I'm probably a little bit biased. I have spent the last 10 years as part of the energy team, a business that's grown very, very rapidly. I still lead that business today. I think if there was one theme across Brookfield that is quite dominant right now, it's energy and infrastructure.
And a lot of the growth in that space, a portion of it is undoubtedly being driven by AI, and AI infrastructure is a huge theme at Brookfield. But the growth we're seeing across critical infrastructure assets and the overwhelming need for energy around the world goes so far beyond simply artificial intelligence.
And that is one that the capital needs are bigger than at any point in history. It is perhaps the greatest capital need in the history of mankind. And the returns are very attractive, and we see this theme not enduring for quarters or years, but through the end of this decade and beyond. It's pretty exciting.
Alison Mass: Yeah. Must be really fun for the energy team investors to have you sitting at the table.
Connor Teskey: Yes and energy's just a fun place to play right now. You know, in only four or five years, electricity is something that everyone took for granted, and now all of a sudden it is the single biggest bottleneck to growth for the greatest companies around the world and the largest countries around the world.
And being a provider of that is an exciting place to be.
Alison Mass: So let's continue on the theme of AI which you brought up. What's your read on the buildout?
Connor Teskey: If there was one headline or narrative that we hear a lot in the market that is detached from what we're seeing in the fundamentals on the ground, it's that the demand for AI infrastructure and the demand for the energy that supports it is in some way fragile. You know, we've seen the market react quite heavily to certain announcements.
Or a potentially more efficient model comes out, or a large hyperscaler walks away from one of its multiple thousands of data center leases, and the whole market reacts. That seems a little divorced from what we're seeing on the ground. Right now, demand is exceptionally high, and supply is only a small fraction of that demand.
Demand is up here, and supply is down here. And therefore, even if demand growth was to slow, even if it was to plateau, even if it was to decline, there would still be a huge supply-demand imbalance to the providers of those assets and those inputs into that ecosystem. So, obviously a huge amount of discipline is required.
These are huge projects. It's a large sum of capital that's going to go into the ground for multiple decades going forward, but the demand is absolutely overwhelming and that imbalance is not going to be disturbed by small changes. The other thing that we're seeing on the AI side is so much talk goes to the big numbers, cause the numbers are quite frankly --
Alison Mass: Staggering.
Connor Teskey: Staggering. Thank you. That is not the bottleneck. There is no shortage of capital, and there is no shortage of demand. The bottleneck is who can actually pull these projects out of the ground. Who has the capabilities to complete the land development, secure the grid connection, build the power supply, build and operate a large-scale gigafactory, provide the redundancy.
That is the scarce input. It is not capital. It is not demand. And we are increasingly seeing the market flow to not just simply those that can show up with big dollars, but those that can show up with both big dollars and big operating capabilities as well.
Alison Mass: All right, so you've already built significant AI infrastructure in the US, and now you're taking that push into Europe. So what is driving that expansion, and what do you think travels across the Atlantic well and what doesn't?
Connor Teskey: So both are going to see very significant buildouts, but the origins of those buildouts and the demand factors are going to be a little bit different.
We can have a thoughtful debate, but of the 15 greatest technology companies in the world, the vast majority of them are based here in the United States. And those corporates are driving a ton of corporate demand in an organic buildout of the AI infrastructure in this country. And that's really being driven by the large technology companies, the hyperscalers, and all of society in the United States is going to benefit from that.
What's interesting is Europe doesn't have that same concentration of homegrown, large-scale technology companies that can provide that corporate demand. That doesn't mean we're not seeing significant growth, but it's coming from two different places.
One, the large global technology companies. Yes, most of them are American, but they are global, so they are, of course, expanding into Europe as well. But the other demand driver that we think is underappreciated is we're actually seeing sovereigns step in, in places where that corporate demand is not going to be the catalyst for the AI buildout.
We're seeing the nation-states... What is AI? At its core, it's a productivity tool. It's designed to drive efficiency and enable more growth. We're seeing nation-states step in and say, "We don't want our population, our country, to be left behind in having access to those tools and those productivity gains in the future," so they will actually backstop the buildout of AI infrastructure.
And we've signed agreements in France, in Sweden, in Qatar, where the initial off-taker to support the buildout of AI infrastructure is not a hyperscaler, but actually a sovereign, and we call that sovereign AI. And we see that demand much more in places outside of the United States and or APAC where, where you do have those domestic global technology leaders.
Alison Mass: That's an interesting perspective. Sovereign AI.
Connor Teskey: Sovereign AI.
Alison Mass: So the power side of this isn't new territory for you, as you've talked about. It's where you started. You built most of the renewables business that's been long core to Brookfield. But the argument has changed. It used to be a climate case, and now it sounds like more of a commercial one, speed to market, availability, energy security. So has the thesis changed in your view, or has the customer changed? What has changed?
Connor Teskey: A lot has changed in the last five to 10 years. But the one thing I would say about our approach that's been quite helpful, and this existed long before my time, is our approach has always been driven by commercial. We don't take technology bets. We don't ever accept one basis point of return discount because of the decarbonization or energy transition impact of an investment.
We think you can make very attractive risk-adjusted returns that also provide those benefits to society. What has changed is demand has become the critical input to growth for every major company in every major country around the world, and there is a scarcity of it. There is a supply-demand imbalance that started at the end of the last decade, the late twenty-teens.
Interestingly, at that point, it wasn't driven by AI. It was driven by these global trends of reindustrialization and electrification. That created a supply-demand imbalance that in and of itself was going to exist for decades and provide multiple decades of electricity demand growth. And then AI took off and took that supply-demand imbalance and exaggerated it even further.
What we would say that we're seeing in our business is two things. Electrons are a commodity, but there is a lot more sophistication around electrons now. Counterparties don't just phone up and say they want power. They want power that's a certain shape in a certain location from a certain source for a certain duration.
And being able to evolve and meet those ever-evolving customer needs is very, very critical to us, and that's leading to the development of new technologies. I'll tell you, the fastest-growing segment of our energy business right now is energy storage. How do you get the joys of low-cost renewables but offset the issues of intermittency?
You offset it with energy storage and batteries, which is undoubtedly the fastest. That wasn't true five years ago. The other thing that we are seeing is because electricity has become such a critical bottleneck, the largest buyers and users of electricity around the world don't always just go to who can provide it at the lowest cost.
It is a very negative for a hyperscaler if they want to turn on a data center but the power supply isn't available yet. So rather than having 10,000 small suppliers who may or may not get a project delivered on time or on budget, we're increasingly seeing the largest users of electricity increasingly focus on a smaller number of scale providers who have the credibility to work through problems, deliver on time, deliver on budget, and really can be a partner to them in providing what is one of the most critical inputs.
And our business over the last five or 10 years, 10 years ago, we essentially sold power to utilities and governments. Today, we sell the most, majority of our power directly to corporates. And we work very much with those corporates to meet their evolving needs. And our relationships with them go beyond individual contracts to global scale framework agreements that just continue to grow and grow over time.
Alison Mass: That makes sense, certainty and ability to deliver.
Connor Teskey: It's far more value than picking up a penny here or a penny there on power price.
Alison Mass: So everything that you've described gets built with borrowed money, which brings me to credit. And in your story, there's a mix of organic and inorganic.
You've built a lot in-house, but you've also bought a majority stake in Oaktree, Howard Marks' firm back in 2019, and now full ownership, plus stakes in several other managers. So how do you decide what you're going to build versus what you're going to buy?
Connor Teskey: The build versus buy decision is one that we make every time we look to grow at Brookfield. It is always a build versus buy decision. And in general, we prefer to build it ourselves if we think we have the capabilities to do so because it's often less expensive.
And two, you can build it exactly how you want it. Sam Pollock, who's built our infrastructure business over the last 20 years, he's built an incredible market-leading franchise. It does not have a peer. If he wants to launch a new strategy, he's not going to go buy someone else to do it.
He's very likely going to use some internal resources to build the strategy from the ground up. However, from time to time, we see capabilities that we think it would be very difficult to replicate, or it would take us too long to replicate in order to capture what we think is a very large and attractive market opportunity.
And that, that was exactly Oaktree for us in 2019. We had a very large and market-leading equity franchise on the private investment side, but we did feel that credit was becoming a core pillar of private markets going forward. And could we have built a market-leading credit franchise over 10 or 15 years? Absolutely.
But we thought it was worth it to accelerate that process, and in hindsight, we think it was a great decision, and we couldn't be more thrilled with the partnership with Oaktree.
Alison Mass: So, staying on Oaktree for a second, how did that deal start, and how did you end up at the center of it?
Connor Teskey: Like a lot of things, some good fortune. I actually started in the private equity group at Brookfield when I joined the firm in Toronto almost 15 years ago.
One of the first things I was asked to review was actually an investment in another asset manager that was in need for capital, and I didn't really know where to start. I'd never looked at an asset management business before.
And after spinning my wheels for probably a few days, I had this idea, which was, well, if I can understand Brookfield's business model, I can probably use that as a base case to try and understand this other asset manager's model. And from that initial review we began, as part of that process, we simply began to track some of the other publicly traded alternative asset managers, largely to see how Brookfield could be doing better and how are we doing versus our peer set.
And at the beginning of 2018, we felt that Oaktree was not trading appropriately in the market, it was one of the names we tracked, relative to the incredible quality of that franchise and what we thought the long-term's earning potential would be.
And it's funny, I went to Bruce and I said, "Well, maybe we can just buy some shares and make a little bit of money." And Bruce said, "Fine, but, you know, maybe think could we do something a little bit more strategic with them?" And we took that away into our little lab and came up with this idea of privatizing the company but partnering with the founders and the existing management. And that was the transaction we did about 12 months later.
Alison Mass: Yeah, and the rest is history.
Connor Teskey: Yeah, it's been great.
Alison Mass: How would you characterize your approach to making investment decisions in general?
Connor Teskey: We have incredible resources around the world, expertise by asset class, by geography.
I think it is very important to try not to be an expert at everything. On any individual decision, there is probably someone at Brookfield who is more of an expert and more informed than I am, and I think being a great investor is knowing where that information is and pulling all that appropriate information in to make the most informed decision.
That would be point one. The second thing is there are no certainties. There absolutely are no certainties. When you get to a level of confidence where things are extremely likely and largely in your control, that's when you pull the trigger and you invest with conviction.
If you try and remove absolutely every risk and turn every variable into an absolute certainty, you will have a perfect track record, but you will make no investments. And I think it is very important to pass judgment of we are in control of enough of the variables here, and we have certainty over enough of the outcomes that we have a return profile that is downside protected and asymmetric to the upside.
And that's really our investing style. And then the last thing I would say is it's very important to be able to simplify things. We invest in extremely large assets on a scale that few around the world do. These are large businesses. It's always important to understand the very small number of key value drivers and understanding which ones do you have a strong view on, which ones are you in control of.
I think being able to simplify large but amazing businesses is very important to making good investment decisions.
Alison Mass: So, most of our listeners have heard of Brookfield, but fewer appreciate the range or the scale. So, give us the rundown, and one thing to flag for any of our listeners who still file you away as a Canadian company, you're headquartered in New York now. So, tell us a little bit about that journey.
Connor Teskey: Sure. So today, Brookfield is the leading global alternative asset manager focused on real assets. The firm and its predecessors were founded in 1899, and yes, our original origins were Canadian, but as we've become a scaled global financial firm, we operate in 50 countries around the world, and we're increasingly concentrated in the global financial centers with our headquarters here in New York.
Alison Mass: So we’ve seen a lot of transition in the leadership of the alternative asset management space over the last five years. You recently stepped into the CEO seat at the asset management business, taking over from Bruce Flatt, who built it, and who's still running Brookfield Corporation.
So, did you feel ready, and how did that transition happen?
Connor Teskey: So a lot of credit goes to not only Bruce, but the other senior leadership of Brookfield. This has been an incredibly methodical, incremental, continuous transition. Yes, we announced a change in titles earlier this year, but this transition has been happening for three years, and it probably has a number of years still to run.
And I remember, and I think we announced it on a Wednesday. Monday and Friday of that week didn't feel a whole lot different. And I think it really comes down to two things. One, Brookfield has created a culture where there's incredible senior mentorship, and they really coach young talent up from an early age and put people in a position to take on more responsibility early and be in a position to win.
And I was fortunate to have incredible mentors and be some of the beneficiary of that. To your question of whether or not you can feel ready, I always feel that there's a certain healthy level of insecurity is good. It keeps you sharp, it keeps you focused. But the fact that it was such a seamless and incremental transition, made it feel very easy.
Alison Mass: You’re a new leader at a relatively young age, and probably a decade younger than some of your peers who've been put into similar positions. Has that been an advantage?
Connor Teskey: One of the things that Bruce and other members of the senior leadership do feel is very important at Brookfield is mixing excellent experience and tenure and knowledge with young energy.
And that's something we do across all of our businesses. I'm fortunate coming into the role to have the most amazing set of senior partners and mentors who have decades of experience that we can draw on. But we love to continuously inject young energy and young perspective into our leadership, into our decision-making.
We think it's, one, important for having fresh perspectives, but two, it's also important to being relatable to an extremely large workforce of Brookfield employees that many of whom are on the younger side as well.
Alison Mass: So, what was the most useful thing that Bruce told you before you took the job that helped you in your first six months in the job?
Connor Teskey: Undoubtedly the thing, having been fortunate to work with Bruce and the other senior leaders for a number of years now that I find most helpful is just how calm and balanced they are when markets inevitably change. We like to forecast, we like to do due diligence, remove risk, things like that, but markets are always moving.
And one of the things that at the very beginning you almost feel a bit unnerved by it, but then you become accustomed to it. It's just the thoughtful, balanced, moderate approach to adjusting to the evolving environment that we all work and live in every day. When Bruce did tell me for the first time about the succession, the succession plan, your mind goes to a lot of places very, very quickly, and I'm sure he said a lot of things that day.
The one that always sticks out to me, which really grounded me very quickly, is he said, "Don't worry whether or not you're the right person. That was our choice, not yours. We just want to make sure this is what you want, and you're committed to doing it for decades to come." And I remember mind going a lot of different directions, and the second he said that, immediately things slowed down and it all became a bit more digestible.
Alison Mass: Yeah. That's very thoughtful because to your point earlier about we're all a little insecure, it takes your insecurity away because you didn't make the decision, they did.
Connor Teskey: Yeah. I'll be honest, I use Bruce's line now.
Alison Mass: Yeah, no, I think it's a good one. I may have to incorporate it myself. So how are involved are you now in the day-to-day investment decisions?
Connor Teskey: So, I sit on all the investment committees, so, oversee any time around the world that Brookfield deploys capital, but I think it's important to recognize with the scale of our operation, how we deploy capital. And the way Brookfield operates is we source, execute, and operate in an incredibly decentralized manner.
For every region around the world that we want to own or invest in assets, and for every asset class around the world, we have a dedicated local team, and those teams are empowered to know everything about that market, go find... know all the themes, know the value levers that are coming, position the business to capture that value, see the risks that are coming, position the business to mitigate that risk in a very decentralized manner. We actually allocate capital in a quite centralized group. And it's in that way that we can grow fast and be local in so many markets around the world, but we can also consolidate all that knowledge to use that global perspective to allocate capital to where we see the best risk-adjusted returns.
So myself and a number of the members of the senior team sit on that centralized investment committee. I always feel it would be the wrong approach for me to try to be the expert in a specific asset class or region where we've got a dedicated team that does it 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, 365 days a year.
I'm rarely questioning underwriting assumptions. We have experts for that. What we do on that investment committee is think more high level, more strategic in terms of our comments and our feedback.
One of the things your question triggers a little bit is, it seems to us a little bit silly to bet on a competitive advantage of simply being smarter than everyone into perpetuity.
You want to create structural and enduring competitive advantages that allow you to deploy capital very attractive risk-adjusted returns at an incredible scale and consistency that few can match. That is our brand.
So, we spend a lot of time focusing on enhancing those strategic, competitive and enduring competitive advantages such that it's not just making the next good investment, it's putting the firm in a position to make several good investments in the years and decades to come.
And that's things like focusing on changes in global themes, where is capital flowing, do we have the right people and the right expertise in the organization? That's where we spend a lot of time.
Alison Mass: So let's widen it out a little bit to the industry. What kind of growth do you expect in alternatives from here?
Connor Teskey: The growth in the alternatives industry is going to be very significant. I actually think it's very tough to see a scenario where the allocations in either the individual market or the institutional market slow. And very simply, the alternatives industry has grown over the last 20 plus years essentially on institutions beginning to and then increasing their allocation to alternatives.
And that's grown the industry for the last 20 years, and that, in and of itself, growing institutional demand could drive the growth of the industry for the next decade and beyond. But now there is this second additional growth lever, which we call the individual market. That's your, your high net worth or private wealth investor, that's your life insurance policy or annuity holder.
That is your 401k or your retiree market. In that segment of the market, the penetration is very low. If institutional investors are allocated somewhere in the, call it mid-teens range to alternatives and probably going up to 20% or 30% over time, that individual market is 2% or less today.
So, in terms of directional trend line, we don't see it slowing down. And it's not a trend or a fad, it's because of what alternatives can provide to those investors' portfolios that traditional portfolios don't have. Private market investments over the long term do come with a return premium because they are private and there is a slight liquidity premium.
But more importantly, they provide a huge amount of stability in portfolios, especially relative to public markets that are becoming increasingly volatile. Secondly, with many of the leading companies around the world staying private longer and with certain industries much more concentrated in the private markets, it can provide diversity to what they can get in a public portfolio.
And then, the last thing I would say is private capital very simply works better for certain types of investments. Think large infrastructure projects that are going to take two, three, four, five years to build and are going to be non-income producing for that period of time, then they turn on and they produce cash for the next four or five decades.
It's really different after they're producing cash, and that works really well in a quarterly-over-quarter reporting cycle. Those early years of putting dollars, non-income producing dollars in the ground doesn't work great in the public markets. So, whether it's returns, whether it's stability, whether it's diversification or access to some of the biggest growth trends and growth themes around the world, we view it as directionally a pretty strong certainty that the growth will continue to be there going forward.
Will it ebb and flow over that very strong growth trend line? Absolutely. And that will be driven by markets, that will be driven by performance of certain vehicles and things like that, but I think the trend line is pretty definitive.
Alison Mass: And as you say, as long as the asset classes continue to outperform the public market indices over any periods of time you look at, one, three, five, 10 years, the investments will flow in.
Connor Teskey: Absolutely. And they've proven to do that over decades.
Alison Mass: So last one before we go to our lightning round. You were a rower in college, I understand. So what did that teach you about leading?
Connor Teskey: Feels a long time ago. I wasted all my time growing up watching, following, playing sports.
Alison Mass: That's not a waste of time.
Connor Teskey: I still spend a lot of time on ESPN. Rowing is a kind of a funny sport. There's very little that's actually enjoyable about rowing itself. It's very - You get up early in the morning, you go somewhere that's often cold or wet in the dark, and you twist your back and pull as hard as you can 3,000 times in a row.
But it is one of the greatest team environments I think you can get in sports because it really is an environment where a crew is only as good as the weakest link. And it doesn't matter if you're the strongest person in the boat or the weakest person in the boat, if you do a little bit better, the whole boat goes faster.
And I think what it teaches you about discipline, what it teaches you about working really hard, and what it teaches you about teamwork, I'd say that those are some of the things we use every day in a much more different environment that we work in now.
Alison Mass: Okay, we like to end these conversations with sort of a quick answer round. So, what is your greatest strength as an investor?
Connor Teskey: Ability to simplify things.
Alison Mass: And what is the best advice you've ever gotten from outside the business?
Connor Teskey: To always remember that this is a people business. People will always do more deals and do more business that people they enjoy working with. This will always be a people business.
Alison Mass: Yeah, I agree. People want to do business with people they like and people they trust.
How do you spend your time out of the office? And I'm assuming it's not on a boat in crew.
Connor Teskey: No, with my family. I have a very young family, so 100% of my time out of the office is with my wife and kids.
Alison Mass: That sounds fun. Which investor do you admire most?
Connor Teskey: Sam Pollock, built our infrastructure business
Alison Mass: Okay. And what are you most excited about in the world right now?
Connor Teskey: I wear two hats at Brookfield, the asset management business and the energy business. It's very fun waking up in industries and markets where the question is not, "Can you grow?" It's, "How much can you grow, and can you do the right growth?" That is exciting. That makes it easy to get out of bed in the morning.
Alison Mass: Well, Connor, thank you so much for joining. It was a fun discussion, and I hope you enjoyed it as well.
Connor Teskey: Thank you for having us.
Alison Mass: We're good to go. Great thank you all for listening to this episode of Goldman Sachs Exchanges: Great Investors, which was recorded on Wednesday, September 16th, 2026. I'm Alison Mass. Earlier this year, Jason,

Andrew and I argued that the AI economy is based on a flywheel.

AI based productivity leads to more demand,

which leads to more CapEx, which begets more AI productivity.

And to examine that thesis.

Our team at UBS has answered

some of the most pertinent questions

about the AI economy and answers it with data.

Here are three of the questions

we answer in our quarterly AI economy update.

So the first question is why have token prices fallen

while demand keeps rising?

Since June, the cost of running AI models has roughly halved

thanks to efficiency

gains in software and hardware and some LLM subsidization

of tokens to compete

with more open source models with cheaper prices.

Volume of tokens processed has risen about five fold.

That's the so-called Jevons paradox.

Cheaper chips, more efficient models and open source competition

keep pushing prices down and lower prices open up new uses.

That strong demand

is why we expect Hyperscaler CapEx to top $1 trillion next year.

So where is AI actually showing up in the labor market

in aggregate, barely at all.

The effect on the unemployment

rate is around 2/10 of a point or less.

But beneath that employment for 22 to 25 year

olds in the most

AI exposed jobs is down around 4% from a year ago.

And at the same time,

construction jobs tied to data centers are up nearly 3%.

So AI isn't shrinking.

The labor market is reshuffling it.

How did the AI trade perform in Q3?

The key word is rotation.

The leaders and the laggards switch places semiconductors,

which has been the most crowded trade on Wall Street. Cool.

Despite strong earnings, software,

which has been punished as an AI casualty

at the start of the year,

rallied about 40% since the end of June.

Hyperscalers benefited from strong Q2 earnings,

but greater scrutiny on these CapEx plans

have led to wider spreads of Hyperscaler debt.

So this is just a little taste of what's in the AI report.

To read more,

please go to ubs.com/CIO and search up the AI economy.
