articles.title: Macro Signposts | Campaign Spending: The Hidden Boost Behind U.S. Consumer Resilience | PIMCO
articles.text:
Tiffany Wilding, Graeme Westwood

11/4/2026

| 7 min read

Share via Email

Share via Linkedin

Share via Twitter

Key takeaways

Record midterm election spending gave consumption growth a significant boost. U.S. economic data count a significant portion of political spending as personal consumption expenditures (PCE). That added roughly 50 basis points to real consumption growth through the first three quarters of 2026 – enough to offset some of the drag from higher energy prices.
Retroactive tax provisions also put cash in household pockets. New or enhanced deductions from the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) reached many households as larger refunds or smaller tax bills during the 2026 filing season. We estimate these provisions added roughly $160 billion to what households had available to spend this year.
Consumer resilience in 2027 is far less certain. With election outlays and larger tax refunds both fading after the midterms, the outlook for U.S. consumers depends more heavily on energy prices.

Following the U.S. midterm elections, investors will naturally focus on what the results mean for fiscal policy, geopolitics, and the regulatory outlook. But there’s another more immediate way the midterms have already mattered for the economy: The campaigns themselves have provided a meaningful boost to U.S. growth.
Unprecedented election spending, plus retroactive household tax cuts, help explain why U.S. consumption has been resilient in 2026 in the face of 40% higher household energy prices – something that would normally be a substantial headwind on real spending.
Looking ahead to 2027, however, election-related spending will fall sharply, and the one-time boost from larger tax refunds will not repeat. The outlook for continued consumer resilience, therefore, may increasingly depend on whether higher energy prices reverse.

Untangling the puzzle of resilient U.S. consumption

One of the biggest puzzles of 2026 has been the resilience of the U.S. consumer in the face of what has been a substantial increase in energy prices. Higher spending from wealthy households, who have enjoyed several years of strong equity gains, is one plausible explanation for some of the resilience. However, a detailed look at the National Income and Product Accounts (NIPA) data from the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) reveals a much simpler accounting: Unprecedented political campaign spending was an offset to the impact of energy costs.
Higher energy prices are a headwind for households. In a typical economy, households cannot easily substitute away from the gasoline and other energy products needed to power their cars and heat their homes. Although the rise of work-from-home arrangements, electric vehicles, solar power, and other energy-saving products have reduced the dependence on energy over time, higher energy prices still act much like a tax on consumption for most households.
The shale revolution in the mid-2010s and the rise of U.S. energy production, which turned the U.S. into a net energy producer and exporter, hasn’t fully mitigated the impact. Higher energy prices effectively shift real income from households toward the owners of energy-producing companies. Most households are not participating enough in energy sector gains (via investments, for example) to offset the direct hit to their purchasing power.
Simple accounting gives us a sense of the magnitude of the increasing energy “tax.” Gasoline and other energy goods prices have risen roughly 40% this year, according to the U.S. Consumer Price Index. Energy goods account for around 3% of consumer spending, according to the BEA. Assuming households don’t reduce consumption of energy goods in reaction to higher prices, a 40% increase in prices therefore must result mathematically in a 1.2-percentage-point (ppt) decline in household spending elsewhere. Even if consumers absorb half of the shock by saving less of their income or dipping into accumulated savings, the implied drag on real consumption growth is still 0.6 ppt – an estimate that is consistent with the findings of empirical studies.
There is surprisingly little evidence of that kind of drag in the aggregate data, however. Through the first three quarters of 2026, U.S. real consumption grew at roughly a 2.75% annualized pace – a similar pace as in 2025, when energy prices were far lower.
What has supported the consumer amid this year’s energy shock? The reported saving rate has indeed declined, suggesting that strong U.S. equity returns may also have reduced households’ perceived need to save at the same rate.
But a detailed look at the BEA data unveils another major factor. In particular, the election-driven increase in professional advocacy spending reportedly boosted real consumption growth by roughly 0.5 ppts on average over the first three quarters of the year (see Figure 1) – effectively offsetting the energy drag.

Figure 1: Election-related spending added roughly 0.5 percentage points to U.S. consumption growth this year

Source: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis National Income and Product Accounts (BEA NIPA) and PIMCO calculations as of September 2026

Yes, political ads count as consumption

Political spending has grown substantially over the past decade and a half, following legal changes (most notably the Supreme Court’s 2010 Citizens United decision) that expanded the scope for corporations, unions, and other organizations to make independent political expenditures.
Political campaign activity is recorded in the NIPAs as personal consumption expenditures (PCE), and since the pandemic in particular, it has become a substantial impulse to overall growth in election years. The logic for including this activity in the consumption data is that these organizations ultimately provide services to households rather than producing goods or services for sale in the traditional sense.
In the NIPA framework, the “persons” in PCE encompass both households and nonprofit institutions serving households. This accounting recognizes that a nonprofit can provide a final service to households even when households do not purchase the service directly at a market price. Think, for example, of a food bank or free health clinic. The BEA measures the consumption of these nonprofits largely as the cost of providing their services, including compensation and purchases of goods and services, net of receipts from sales to households.
That accounting treatment matters for elections because political organizations are also categorized within that nonprofit sector serving households. Their spending on political advocacy is recorded as the production and consumption of a final service on behalf of households.
In other words, whether a household prefers to watch political campaign ads or not, NIPA records the resulting advocacy service as “consumed.”
Election-related spending has steadily grown since 2010. However, an unusually competitive political landscape helped turn 2026 into the most expensive midterm election on record. Campaign finance watchdogs estimate that candidates, political parties, political action committees, and outside groups spent nearly $12 billion on federal elections alone, up from $8.9 billion during the 2022 midterms. And that figure does not include state and local election activity. State ballot-measure campaigns alone attracted roughly $1.25 billion in contributions by early November, while tight gubernatorial races – with campaigns focused on anti-AI policies and slowing data center investment – also saw significant spending.
Using the NIPA data, our calculations suggest that nominal spending on professional advocacy services in the first three quarters of 2026 outpaced the annualized 2025 rate by roughly $22 billion. Not all of it represents campaign spending, of course. The category is broader, and some of the increase would have occurred regardless of the election. But the timing and magnitude are striking.
The source of the money is important as well. Political campaigns are disproportionately financed by wealthy and ultrawealthy households. In the 2024 election, estimates suggest that billionaires and their families alone accounted for nearly one-fifth of reported federal political contributions. Academic research has similarly documented the increasing concentration of campaign contributions among a very small group of extremely wealthy donors.
Campaign contributions also likely explain at least part of the substantial decline in the measured household saving rate this year. To the extent that these contributions are financed from income or wealth that otherwise would have been saved, campaign activity effectively transfers resources from high-saving households to political organizations that rapidly spend those funds on advertising, consultants, staff, travel, and events.
The composition of advertising spending also matters for measured growth. When a private company buys advertising, GDP doesn’t count it as a separate purchase: The ad is treated as a cost of doing business, like electricity or raw materials, and its price is built into whatever the company sells. Counting both the ad and the final product would count the same spending twice. Political organizations are different. When a nonprofit political organization purchases advertising and other inputs to provide advocacy services to households, the resulting final nonprofit service is recorded as consumption.
A temporary shift in advertising demand from businesses toward political organizations can therefore raise measured final consumption and GDP.

Tax changes also provided indirect support to consumption

Campaign spending wasn’t the only thing that temporarily boosted consumption this year. The one-time household tax windfall from the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) also likely supported U.S. consumption indirectly in 2026. The legislation enacted several new or enhanced household tax provisions with retroactive effects, including the higher state and local tax deduction cap, deductions for tips and overtime, and the enhanced deduction for seniors. Because some of the provisions applied to 2025 income but were enacted after withholding schedules had already been established, part of the tax relief reached households through larger refunds and lower final tax payments during the 2026 filing season.
We estimate that these provisions boosted U.S. household cash flow by roughly $160 billion in calendar year 2026. (Our calculations focus on the new or enhanced household provisions, not simply the extension of the existing tax regime.) That significant, albeit temporary, boost also helped consumers maintain spending in the face of higher energy prices.
Figure 2 provides our estimates of the growth impact of the Trump administration’s tax, spending, and tariff policies, using Congressional Budget Office (CBO) estimates of the impacts of various government activities. Individual tax cuts were likely a significant contributor to GDP in early 2026.

Figure 2: Individual tax cuts were a significant boost to consumption and GDP in 2026

Source: BEA, Congressional Budget Office (CBO), Joint Committee on Taxation (JCT), Piper Sandler, and PIMCO calculations as of September 2026. Figure includes forward-looking estimates (based on current policy) through the end of 2027.

Energy headwinds delayed?

Higher energy prices should have imposed a substantial headwind on household consumption. But that shock coincided with two unusually large offsets: an election-related surge in nonprofit consumption and a tax-law-induced boost to household cash flow. So perhaps it is not so surprising that consumption growth has remained resilient at around 2.5% year-over-year.
The more important question is what happens next. Election spending will fall sharply, and the one-time tax-refund boost will fade. That leaves energy prices as an increasingly important swing factor for the consumer in 2027. If energy prices retrace toward pre-conflict levels, the resulting improvement in household real incomes should offset some of the disappearing policy support. If they don’t, the drag from higher energy costs may finally become visible in aggregate consumption growth.
In other words, one-time factors likely delayed the visible impact of higher energy prices on consumption. We expect that higher energy prices will eventually start to bite.

articles.title: Learning about earnings: Can we rely on labour market slack to mitigate the latest supply shock? − speech by Megan Greene
articles.text:
Learning about earnings: Can we rely on labour market slack to mitigate the latest supply shock? − speech by Megan Greene

Given at London School of Economics

Published on
20 October 2026

The extent to which the latest energy price shock feeds into more persistent inflation through second-round effects remains a key consideration for policymakers. The presence of slack in the labour market could suggest that wage pressures will remain contained, limiting the scope for second-round effects. But is this likely to be the case?
In this speech, Megan challenges this argument, drawing on a wide range of wage indicators to assess recent developments in pay growth and the likely path ahead for wages and domestically-generated inflation. She then turns to broader measures of labour market slack to examine whether current conditions are likely to restrain second-round effects via the wage-setting channel.

Speech
Introduction
Thank you for inviting me to the LSE to speak. It’s nice to be back here—I often studied in your library when I was an undergraduate in the US working in London for the summer. Come to think of it, I may have snuck in so please don’t alert the authorities.
Over the past few months, a lot has happened in the world of geopolitics…and yet very little has fundamentally changed. Passage through the Strait of Hormuz remains beset by attacks and potential new chokepoints in shipping have emerged such as the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. Although Middle Eastern oil flows have at times returned to near pre-war levels, expensive and inefficient workarounds have kept energy prices high (Figure 1). Wholesale gas prices are close to triple their level at the start of the year, with oil spot prices just under double their early-January level.footnote [1] And the prices for refined products have remained elevated despite volatile spot prices. Even if the conflict in Iran ends tomorrow, we have already been hit by a protracted energy shock.

Figure 1: Evolution of energy prices since start of 2026
Index, 100 = price at 1 Jan 2026

Footnotes

Source: ONS, Bloomberg Finance L.P. and Bank calculations.

(a) Dashed vertical lines denote selected key events. Dates may not be exact due to frequency of data. Latest datapoints are for 19 October 2026.

I have previously laid out the various avenues via which such a negative supply shock can propagate through the UK economy, highlighting the important role of second-round effects in embedding inflation in the economy. As I set out in my last speech Opens in a new window in June, they can take hold through the price- or wage-setting channel, or both. For today’s purposes, I will focus specifically on the wage-setting channel.
Wages represent a material cost for firms, particularly in the services sector where labour accounts for a large share of total costs. Wages are also a significant determinant of incomes, thus underpinning consumption. As a result, measures of wage growth offer useful insight into domestically-generated inflation. Of course, not all wage growth is inflationary. If wages rise because productivity improves, the implications for inflation may well be limited. But wages can also act as the mechanism through which temporary negative supply shocks become embedded in domestic inflation, particularly when workers seek to protect real incomes and firms then raise prices to protect their margins.
The MPC has judged that there is slack in the labour market, as evidenced by the ratio of vacancies to unemployment relative to equilibrium (Figure 2). Some of my colleagues and I have argued that the wage-setting channel poses a smaller risk of generating second-round effects than the price-setting channel. If firms are facing higher costs and have experienced years of margin compression, they are likely to pass on some of their higher costs by raising prices. This is consistent with intelligence that we’re hearing from our Agents. But if there is slack in the labour market, worker power is relatively weak. Even if workers demand higher pay as their costs go up, employers may deny that request given the large pool of talent from which to choose.

Figure 2: Vacancy-unemployment (V-U) ratio and V-U equilibrium
Ratio(a)

Footnotes

Source: Advertising association/ World Advertising Research Centre Expenditure Report, ONS and Bank calculations. Latest data point is for 2026Q2.

(a) The equilibrium V/U ratio is estimated using an error-correction model over the period 1982–2024. The real cost of vacancy posting and hourly labour productivity are included as long-run determinants for the level of vacancies. The model also includes controls for short-term movements in these variables (Stelmach, Kensett , & Schnattinger, 2025 Opens in a new window)

Given our monetary policy strategy has relied partly on slack mitigating the impact of second-round effects, it’s worth exploring how much labour market slack there really is. The wider economy has proved surprisingly resilient, implying there is less slack than some labour market indicators suggest. If so, there is a greater risk of second-round effects emerging through the wage-setting channel than we initially thought.
We may not have a clear steer on whether the shock from the Iran conflict gives rise to material second-round effects through wage- or price-setting until early next year when our Agents’ pay survey is out in February and the brunt of 2027 pay settlements are agreed in January and April. But if we wait for this evidence to lean against second-round effects with a tighter monetary policy stance, we will already be too late given the lags with which monetary policy affects the economy and inflation.
As outlined in our Forecast Evaluation Report and the Macro-technical paper Opens in a new window alongside it, predicting wage growth has been a challenge for the Bank, particularly since the Global Financial Crisis. As shown in Figure 3, Bank forecasts tended to systematically predict higher wage growth than what we experienced until the Covid period, after which our forecasts systematically underestimated the strength of wage growth.footnote [2]

Figure 3: MPR forecasts and outturns of wage growth(a)
Annual growth (%)(a)

Footnotes

Source: ONS and Bank calculations.

(a) The grey lines show forecasts from different vintages. The aqua line shows the outturns k=12 quarters after the first data release.

Our suite of wage models, like many macro forecasting models, are largely driven by historical relationships. The recent persistent undershooting of wage growth forecasts may suggest something structurally shifted in the labour market during the pandemic. As I argued in my 2024 speech (Greene, 2024), this could reflect reduced matching efficiency, lower search intensity, labour hoarding, persistent recruitment difficulties and weaker participation. It could also reflect stronger real wage resistance following the 2022 energy shock than historical relationships have implied (Pill, 2025). Wage growth has generally decelerated since 2023, suggesting these upward pressures have been unwinding, but they may not have unwound entirely.
Models inevitably simplify reality, and their performance depends critically on the quality of the signals they are trying to capture. One important development over the past decade has been an expansion in the range of wage indicators we look at, reflecting efforts to measure underlying wage pressures from multiple perspectives.
But this richer information set has brought its own challenges. At the moment, wage data are like a Rorschach Test; they can be used to confirm anyone’s preconceived view of slack in the labour market because they are giving mixed signals (Figure 4). Different indicators often tell different stories, reflecting differences in coverage, frequency, composition and methodology (Villar, Moyon, & Ahn, 2025 Opens in a new window). The task for policymakers is therefore not simply to monitor wages, but to understand the dynamics underpinning different metrics.

This brings me to my main focus today. Given the importance of understanding wage-setting behaviour and what it might mean for slack and second-round effects, I want to dig into some of our key wage indicators to parse signal from noise. I will start by examining how these indicators differ and where in the wage-setting process they are likely to be most informative. I will then consider what they can tell us about the recent developments and what signal we might glean about wage dynamics going forward. Finally, I will examine how confident we can be that a material degree of slack will restrain second-round effects and inflation via the wage-setting channel.
Getting into the weeds isn't always glamorous, but in policymaking as in gardening, sometimes you just have to get your hands dirty.
Measures of wage growth
When confronted with a range of indicators, it is often useful to take a step back and consider exactly what information each one conveys. After all, wage indicators measure different things and are collected in different ways. This is a feature, not a bug - the differences between measures allow us to build a richer picture of wage developments within the domestic economy to assess the degree of current and emerging wage pressures.
In light of this, Table 1 brings together some of the key metrics used by the Bank of England to monitor UK wage growth. While not exhaustive, the selection illustrates the breadth of information available to policymakers and the different insights a variety of measures can provide, as demonstrated by the range of questions presented in the second column: each of these metrics has something different to offer when it comes to understanding wage pressures.

Naturally, some measures receive more attention than others. Chief among these is the average weekly earnings (AWE) series, which helps us answer the question “what is the growth of the average wage?”. AWE is an accredited official statistic published with a two-month lag by the Office for National Statistics (ONS), derived from the Monthly Wages and Salaries Survey (MWSS).footnote [3] The MWSS is issued to around 9,000 businesses and covers approximately 15 million employees across Great Britain. While adjustments are made to account for smaller firms, the survey includes only businesses with 20 or more employees. Nevertheless, AWE provides a broad measure of the change in pay levels across the economy and is thus useful for gauging domestic inflationary pressures stemming from changes in wages.
At the Bank, we tend to focus on private sector regular AWE growth as opposed to the whole economy (including the public sector) for a few reasons. Private sector pay feeds more directly into the CPI measure of inflation, particularly when it comes to services, where labour costs make up a large chunk of total costs. In addition, UK public sector pay is often determined by government policy decisions. As such, wage-setting in the private sector is generally more closely tied to labour market conditions, whereas institutional pay setting arrangements and fiscal constraints can often influence public sector pay outcomes. Monetary policy therefore has more influence over private sector pay. Furthermore, private sector regular pay excludes volatile bonuses while they’re included in total pay. For these reasons, I’m going to focus on private sector regular AWE pay growth for the rest of this speech.
Pay As You Earn (PAYE) Real Time Information (RTI) data provides an alternative read on wage growth. This is published by the ONS on a monthly basis, in conjunction with HMRC, and can be used to help answer the same question as the AWE: “what is the growth of the average wage?”. Median estimates of the data are available with less of a lag than the official AWE measure, though they are often heavily revised. In addition, its production does not rely on survey responses. Instead, the information comes directly from HMRC’s PAYE RTI system, which covers the whole population of employees payrolled by employers, allowing for more detailed breakdowns of the data. The data is presented as gross pay, which includes bonus pay and other one-off payments (but not pension contributions) unlike private sector regular AWE. Arguably, this can make it harder to gain a clear view on wage growth and makes it more difficult to compare RTI and AWE.
We can also draw on wage growth measures derived from responses to the Decision Maker Panel (DMP) survey to answer the question “what assessment do firms make of their own wage growth?”. The DMP is a large, monthly panel survey of Chief Financial Officers from small-, medium- and large-sized UK businesses. Since 2022, the survey has included a number of questions focused on firms’ wages. This means that the back data available for wage analysis is limited. In 2026, the survey included wage growth data from approximately 700 firms, covering around 300,000 employees each month. Responses are used to construct measures of both realised and expected wage growth. The former tells us what has actually happened to firms’ own wage growth over the last year, while the latter gives us an idea of what firms anticipate will happen to their wage growth over the next year. Forward-looking indicators are hard to come by – an unfortunate truth for those of us in the forecasting business – but they are particularly useful given that both shocks and monetary policy take their time to work their way through the economy. As such, I am monitoring this measure closely as the current shock unfolds.
Pay settlements data can also provide us with a glimpse into the future path for wage growth. Such data allows us to shed some light on the pay decisions firms are making with regard to their current employees, helping us answer the question “what pay increases are firms agreeing for their existing employees?”. However, settlements data captures changes in basic pay and does not capture all sources of earnings growth, such as progression, merit and performance-related pay, or bonuses. We can access pay settlements data through the Bank of England’s settlements database. This database brings together information collected from businesses across the UK economy by the Bank’s Agents and external data providers, collected at various frequencies. Given that these figures can be updated retrospectively as more settlements are finalised, they are subject to some revision. We also get a sense of how pay settlements are likely to evolve over the next year in the Agents’ pay survey, released in February but with intelligence coming in from our Agents in the lead up to that.
Settlements data can only tell us so much. By its nature, its focus is on those workers already employed. But what are firms willing to pay new hires? The Indeed Wage Tracker provides insight into this, measuring the median annual change in advertised wages and salaries found on the Indeed platform across job title, region and salary-types. The sample size of each is reliant on a number of different factors, including the amount of total job vacancies, the proportion that is posted online and the share of these postings that contains wage or salary information (Adrjan & Lydon, 2023 Opens in a new window). This data is collected in the UK and a range of developed countries, allowing for cross-country comparison.
This is a whistle-stop tour of wage growth metrics. Each tells us something slightly different about wage growth pressures in the economy. I’ll now put them to use to explore present and future developments in wage growth.
Recent and current wage growth: two measures, different stories
Having gone through the various wage metrics, let’s use them to try to work out how much slack there is the labour market now and whether the wage-setting process has changed. For this, I’ll look at private sector regular AWE and its median RTI equivalent (proxied for the private sector), which both answer the question “what is the growth of the average wage?”. The good news is that both metrics show wage growth broadly continuing to moderate since recent peaks in 2023 (Figure 5). But these two indicators tell very different stories about the extent of that progress.

After almost 3 years of gradual easing, recent AWE data broadly suggest a further and more rapid leg down in wage growth, coming in at 3.0% in August (the aqua line in Figure 5). In contrast, our primary RTI metric of private sector wage pressure – growth in median pay – remains at a considerably higher rate of 4.4% in September (the orange line in Figure 5). Historically, these measures have tracked each other reasonably closely, albeit over a relatively short sample given RTI data are only available from 2014. Since early 2026, the divergence between them has become unusually large by historical standards.
RTI and AWE measures are answering the same question and both are constructed using sectoral wage growth and weighted according to the level of employment.footnote [4] So what's behind their divergence now? To decompose the wedge between these different measures, I’ll use a measure of mean pay growth derived from the RTI data (showing annual wage growth of 5% in August), which is more comparable to mean private sector regular pay growth from AWE (showing annual wage growth of 3% in August).
The wedge between these measures is explained primarily by three factors:

Differences in wage growth within industries: for a given industry wage growth in AWE is different to that in RTI. This is possible due to the different data underlying the two (a survey in the case of AWE, administrative data for RTI).
Between-industry compositional effects: This arises because the industry shares underlying the two differ and can change over time as employment shifts between industries.
Differences in flexible pay such as bonuses: AWE regular pay doesn’t include bonuses and arrears, whereas RTI does.

Differences in wage growth between industries and within industries can both help us understand underlying wage dynamics. Wage growth driven by changes in industry shares has implications for aggregate wage pressure and can give us a sense of overall slack. Wage growth within sectors reflects firms’ pay-setting decisions and can reveal whether they have changed in the face of a shock.
Figure 6 isolates the contributions to the wedge from the three sources. In August the wedge was 2 percentage points and has grown since late 2025 due to steadily rising compositional differences (pink area), fluctuating contributions from within industry differences in pay growth (purple area) and bonuses (blue area).

Of the three main components explaining the wedge between AWE and RTI, let’s first address the easiest to interpret: flexible pay. AWE private regular pay data exclude bonuses and arrears, while private sector RTI data include them. We want to compare apples-to-apples when we are gleaning signals from the two series. To do this, we assume that the bonuses (and arrears) captured in the AWE measure of total pay are also present in the RTI data and subtract their contribution from the RTI measure. This is necessarily a simplifying approximation and so the results should be interpreted with some caution. Bonuses and cost of living payments played a significant role in explaining the wedge between the two series in 2022-23 and earlier this year before waning more recently. During 2022-23 bonuses and one-off payments were common across sectors, whereas more recently these have been concentrated primarily in finance and professional services.
Now let’s turn to the role of compositional effects in creating a wedge between AWE and RTI. We can do this by comparing the changes in sectoral employment weights in private sector AWE and private sector RTI over the past year (Figure 7). This chart shows the year-on-year changes in the latest data, but it reflects trends that have persisted throughout 2026. AWE shows employment shifting towards lower-paid sectors, with rising weights for industries such as accommodation and food services and falling weights for higher-paying sectors such as financial and professional services. RTI, however, paints the opposite picture, with employment shifting slightly away from lower-paying sectors towards higher-paying ones.

What signal can we draw from this? There is really no silver bullet here, and this is exactly why we look at multiple indicators to get a complete picture of the labour market. But on balance, I’d put slightly more weight on the compositional story from the RTI. The RTI series is drawn from administrative data rather than a survey. RTI doesn’t require imputing employees who work in small firms (under 20 employees) as the AWE series does. Finally, the narrative from the RTI data chimes with the Labour Force Survey (LFS), which also indicates that employment has shifted to higher paid industries over the past year. There are reasons to treat the LFS with caution; it suffers from low response rates and the industry classifications are self-reported and may not always be accurate. On balance, I place slightly more weight on the RTI’s narrative that workers are shifting towards higher paying industries. This means that the AWE may be giving us an artificially low reading of wage growth because of the specific compositional effects it incorporates.
Let’s now take a look at differences in pay growth within industries in the AWE and RTI series. Figure 8 shows wage growth within various sectors in the latest AWE and RTI releases. This chart shows year-on-year changes in the latest data, but this is consistent with the trends we have seen over the past year. The AWE data suggests that, on balance, wage growth in lower paying sectors was running hotter than for higher paid sectors. The RTI data, however, suggest wage growth was faster in higher paying sectors.footnote [5] For the reasons I’ve just explained, I have a bit more faith in the RTI data. But again, these discrepancies point to the importance of making use of a range of metrics.

Where does this leave us? Our adjusted measures of wage growth remain above levels consistent with our inflation target of 2%. The most frequently cited indicator that we use, private sector regular AWE, seems to have been consistently undercooking actual private sector wage growth since late-2025.
Looking ahead: what can guide us?
Over the past year, different metrics of wage growth have told different stories. However, there is strong evidence to suggest that underlying wage growth is higher than that reported by private sector regular AWE. What we ultimately want to know, however, is how wage setting will evolve going forward, particularly in light of yet another negative supply shock. For this, I’ll look at some forward-looking indicators—specifically the DMP, pay settlements and the Indeed Wage Tracker.
The DMP has been an invaluable source of information on wages since wage questions were introduced in 2022. The survey directly asks firms about wage changes for their employees, and so arguably provides the clearest window into firms’ wage-setting processes. Realised wage growth has broadly tracked the trends in AWE and RTI, though there have been some periods of divergence. The DMP recorded a lower peak in 2023 and indicated more gradual moderation in wage growth thereafter. We can see this in Figure 10, which plots DMP realised wage growth and one-year ahead expected wage growth, at the time of the survey, alongside the RTI and AWE measures.

The noticeable gap between private regular AWE and pay settlements over the past five years can be explained by the state of the labour market. Faced with recruitment difficulties and elevated staff turnover, firms had stronger incentives to raise pay to attract and retain workers. As a result, there was ‘pay drift’; actual wage growth often exceeded that implied by pay settlements, reflecting pay for new workers, retention-related pay increases and other adjustments outside formal settlement rounds. This is consistent with academic literature that finds that workers achieve faster pay growth when outside job opportunities improve, and that the threat of higher turnover can prompt firms to raise pay more broadly across their workforce (Jäger, Roth, Roussille, & Schoefer, 2024 Opens in a new window) (Sokolova & Sorensen, 2021 Opens in a new window).

As I outlined in a recent speech (Greene, 2026), the labour market is considerably weaker now than it was in 2022. As aggregate demand has softened, demand for labour has also eased, reducing recruitment difficulties and, in turn, the pressure on firms to grant large pay increases. Expected pay settlements may therefore provide a more reliable guide to future wage growth than they did during the post-pandemic period.
At present, our Agents report that expected settlements for 2027 will be similar or only slightly lower than in 2026, suggesting the wage disinflation process may be stalling. For the past two years, actual settlements have come in above what was projected in the Agents’ pay survey (4% in 2025 vs 3.7% in the pay survey; current estimate of 3.6% in 2026 vs 3.4% in the pay survey), so I expect the risk to the latest guidance is to the upside. Moreover, the vast majority of pay settlements will be agreed between January and April (Figure 15), when we expect inflation to be above 4%. This is well above the threshold in which households are more sensitive to inflation outturns in forming their expectations.

Finally, the Indeed Wage Tracker offers a highly forward-looking and high frequency insight into wage pressures. The Indeed Wage Tracker captures the pay firms are willing to offer new recruits and therefore captures those workers that the pay settlements data omits. Their main limitation is that they – typically – represent a small proportion of the work force who have in recent years made a relatively small contribution to overall wage growth. However, as retention pressures have eased and firms are less reliant on large pay increases to retain staff, wages offered to new recruits may play a somewhat larger role in explaining overall wage developments as they did in the years before the pandemic.
Since late 2023, the Indeed Wage Tracker has tended to imply slightly higher wage growth than private sector regular AWE (on average about 0.8pp) (Figure 4). In August, the UK Indeed UK Wage Tracker stood at 4% (Figure 15) and while UK wage growth remains high relative to many of its peers, it has become less of an outlier in recent months. However disinflationary wage momentum here also seems to be levelling off, with the wage tracker remaining stuck at around 4% since the turn of the year.

Taken together, I place considerable weight on the DMP and pay settlements, while monitoring the Indeed Wage Tracker as a higher frequency indicator of broader labour demand conditions. Collectively, these measures suggest that the wage disinflation process is stalling out with pay growth likely to stabilise over the coming year closer to 3.5% than 3%. I believe this remains above levels consistent with our inflation target and suggests there is less labour market slack than we thought.
What will I be monitoring for the emergence of second-round effects?
There is a plethora of wage growth indicators that can help inform our view of slack in the labour market. Our investigation of these different measures leads me to believe that underlying wage growth is running above rates consistent with our 2% inflation target and this looks set to continue. This suggests there is not as much slack as we had expected, and so there is a greater risk of second-round effects emerging from the wage-setting channel.
But we need not only focus explicitly on wage measures in making our assessment of slack. Other labour market and activity measures can provide insights on the degree of slack in the economy, and as I have demonstrated previously Opens in a new window, wider economic conditions play a role in determining the extent to which second-round effects are likely to take hold. Taking stock of these conditions suggests that it may be unwise to assume that labour market slack and weak demand will mitigate the risks. Other labour market indicators also suggest there is less labour market slack than we thought and that it may have peaked. As with wages, there is no one perfect metric of employment growth – particularly in recent years given issues with the Labour Force Survey. Bank staff produce an estimate of underlying employment growth drawing on a range of surveys and hard data. Figure 17 shows that employment growth was essentially flat in 2025 and below the rate of population growth—consistent with a degree of slack opening up. However, underlying employment growth has been steadily rising this year. This has recently been corroborated by the KPMG/REC jobs report, according to which measures of employment and labour demand have risen above pre-conflict levels.

Meanwhile, there are other signs that labour market slack may have peaked: the unemployment rate has fallen from 5.2% in the three months to January 2026 to 4.7% in August; redundancies have come down from their peak of 150,000 in the three months to October 2025 and are currently running at just above 100,000, in line with the average observed since 2012; and vacancies show signs of stabilising.
A stable or slightly improving labour market is consistent with more resilience in activity than we and other forecasters had been expecting. In April, HM Treasury’s summary of independent forecasts for the UK economy showed a median GDP forecast of 0.7% in 2026, roughly in line with our middle projection (Scenario B) in April of 0.8% growth this year. By September, HM Treasury’s summary of forecasts showed median growth of 1.3% this year and our central projection in July predicted 1.1% growth in 2026 . There has been a trend towards revising UK GDP forecasts for this year up, particularly as stronger-than-expected data has come in.
Surveys of firms and consumers tell a similar story. September's flash PMI ticked down modestly but remained in positive territory, reflecting an expansion of output. Purchasing managers are reasonably positive about the future as well, with the future output index at 67.4, just a little below the long-run average of 68.2.
The economy has proven surprisingly resilient even in the face of tighter financial conditions. Since the outbreak of the Iran conflict, financial conditions have tightened largely as short-term interest rates and mortgage rates have increased. But while the price of credit has risen, the impact on credit volumes has been muted. Although mortgages for home purchases have fallen since the conflict began, overall gross mortgage lending was £23.6bn in August—slightly below pre-conflict levels (an average of £24bn in the second half of 2025), but above the average level since 2024 (£21.9bn). Monthly consumer credit (credit cards, car finance and other non-mortgage credit) hit a high of £2.5bn in August, and over the past 6 months monthly net finance raised by corporates has remained above the average level since 2024. It is not obvious to me from this data that our monetary policy stance is meaningfully restrictive.
Meanwhile, household and firm inflation expectations remain elevated. As I have previously argued Opens in a new window, attentiveness to inflation has risen after over five years of inflation remaining above target. Inflation is also currently already within the threshold at which outturns impact expectations. Greater inflation attentiveness is reflected in an increase in the frequency of UK Google searches for a variety of inflation-related terms in recent years (Figure 18).

Conclusion
Our monetary policy strategy since the outbreak of the Iran conflict has relied to some degree on labour market slack mitigating the risks of second-round effects taking hold. But not all of our wage metrics support this argument. A closer look at the two main metrics we use to understand the recent evolution of wage growth—private sector regular AWE and private sector RTI—suggests wage disinflation has stalled at levels above those consistent with inflation at 2%.
If getting a better handle on the evolution of wage growth to date is tricky, devising a clear view of the future is trickier. The forward-looking indicators we consider—the DMP, pay settlements and the Indeed Wage Tracker–all point to wage growth that is likely to plateau closer to 3.5% than 3% over the coming year. The risks to this are skewed to the upside, in my view. Not only have we tended to underpredict wage growth since the pandemic, but realised pay settlements have been above those predicted in the Agents’ pay survey the past two years. Furthermore, the majority of 2027 pay settlements will be agreed at a time when inflation is above 4%.
Our broad range of wage indicators suggests there is less slack in the labour market than we thought and it may have peaked. This is reflected in broader indicators for the labour market and activity. All together, this suggests the risk of second-round effects taking hold is higher. This is even more so the case as energy prices have remained high and volatile for longer. In my view, this makes a risk management approach to our monetary policy strategy even more appropriate.
When it comes to managing risks around second-round effects, we face two main scenarios. In the first one, we proactively lean against second-round effects by hiking interest rates and later discover this was unnecessary and adjust our policy stance. In the second one, we are too sanguine about second-round effects and set policy accordingly before course correcting. I believe the evidence laid out in this speech shows the risk of second-round effects is greater than we thought. Furthermore, staff simulations suggest setting policy as if you were in a stronger second-round effects scenario and then adjusting policy upon learning you are in a minimal second-round effects scenario leads to better outcomes than doing the opposite. I therefore continue to believe we should proactively lean against the risk of second-round effects.

As in the FER and macro-technical paper, here I focus on aggregate whole-economy average earnings due to the availability of older forecast vintages. In practice, and as discussed later in this speech, the MPC often focuses on private regular pay but results are broadly invariant to that distinction.

The AWE measure is also used to calculate earnings growth under the current Triple Lock framework.

The RTI data provides mean and median figures, AWE provides only the mean.

Another reason weekly (as measured by AWE) or monthly pay (as measured by RTI) could be changing is due to changes in hours worked. If pay is rising because people are working more hours that has different implications for wage pressure than if their hourly pay is rising. The LFS is the only timely source of data on hours worked but comes with an additional health warning. The ONS recently explained Opens in a new window that declining response rates on the LFS, coupled with the non-response imputation method and reliance on respondent recall, had led the LFS to overstate hours worked on average. Nevertheless, across the whole economy, the LFS suggests average hours worked for employees increased from 31.8 to 32 per week in the year to the second quarter of 2026. In some sectors where pay growth has been weak according to the AWE data – such as accommodation and food services – average hours worked have fallen. Similarly, in some sectors where the RTI data suggests monthly pay growth has been strong – such as finance and insurance – there has been a rise in average hours worked. Overall, we can tentatively conclude that shifts in hours may account for a marginal part of changes in wage dynamics over the past year.

The ONS provides its own decomposition of private sector regular average weekly earnings. In August it estimated that the wages contribution was 3.4%.

The wage growth consistent with an inflation target of 2% depends on labour productivity growth, the share of imports in consumption and import price inflation, and margins. As set out in the February 2026 Monetary Policy Report, labour productivity growth of 1%, imports’ share of consumption of 25% and import price inflation of 1%, with growth in margins of 0% gives target-consistent wage growth of 3.25%. I think that labour productivity growth is likely to be lower and import price growth higher than 1% and so my estimate of target-consistent wage growth is closer to 3%.

articles.title: A unique vantage point − speech by Nathanaël Benjamin
articles.text:
A unique vantage point − speech by Nathanaël Benjamin

Given at the ISDA Derivatives Trading and Treasury Forum

Published on
01 October 2026

Nat Benjamin sets out how the Bank of England has a unique vantage point from which to understand the UK’s ever more complex and interconnected financial system, and how such surveillance can be used to strengthen its stability. He then illustrates this with gilt repo market resilience as one policy area that has benefited from that mindset.

Speech
Why surveillance matters more than ever
Good afternoon, and my thanks to ISDA for inviting me to speak at this year’s London Derivatives Trading and Treasury Forum. It is a pleasure to be here.
ISDA has played a key role in shaping the modern derivatives market through its work on legal standards, market infrastructure, data, and risk management. At a time when markets are becoming more interconnected and increasingly vital for the provision of financial services to the real economy, that contribution matters more than ever.
The nature of risks to financial stability has changed a lot over the last two decades.
Before the global financial crisis, the attention of authorities was often focused primarily on individual banks. The resilience of individual institutions is still fundamental today, of course. But many of the vulnerabilities that matter today emerge not within a single bank, but from interactions across non-bank financial institutions (NBFIs), markets, and funding structures.
Recent episodes have demonstrated that stress can originate in one part of the financial system and propagate rapidly through funding markets, collateral demands, margin calls, and leveraged positions. And the actions taken by individual market players can, even when rational from their own perspective, combine to amplify stress across the system. We have talked about these risks on numerous occasions – including in this forum.
As the risks have changed, so has our financial stability perspective, adopting a resolutely system-wide lens that can observe their complex interconnections and interactions.
That scrutinising lens, how surveillance is evolving, and what it can help us achieve, is the first thing I’m going to talk about today. And then I will turn to one policy area which has benefited from that mindset: the resilience of gilt repo markets.
A unique vantage point
Over the past decade, the post-crisis reform agenda has transformed the information available to authorities.
One of the shortcomings identified following the global financial crisis was the lack of visibility into activity in important financial markets, and into the interconnections between market participants. Transaction-level reporting was introduced in response, allowing authorities to better understand how markets function and how market participants interact.
Today we can draw on transaction-level reporting across derivatives, securities financing, and trading activity, together with fund-level reporting and supervisory data. We've been using these insights for years to better understand how markets function, how risks propagate, and where vulnerabilities may be building across the financial system. They have informed our analysis during episodes such as the “dash for cash” that followed the outbreak of the Covid-19 pandemic, the stresses in energy markets following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, or the 2022 gilt market disruption. Yet as the nature of vulnerabilities changes, the way we use this data has changed too. Having access to millions of transaction records is not the same as being able identify how shocks might propagate through a complex web of funding relationships, collateral chains, and leveraged investors.
No single reporting regime was designed to provide a complete view of the financial system. Each dataset offers a different lens. As the UK’s central bank with macro- and micro-prudential authority, we have a unique vantage point that allows us to bring multiple sources of data together, building out a picture of chain reactions that would otherwise be unforeseeable.
Our institutional set-up makes us particularly well placed to do so for UK markets. As a participant in these core markets ourselves, and through the gathering of market intelligence from that position, we obtain invaluable insight that brings colour and context to reporting data. And through close collaboration with our colleagues at the Financial Conduct Authority, we can bring together information from derivatives markets, securities-financing markets, trading activity, fund reporting, and prudential supervision within a shared analytical framework.
This allows us to answer questions that would have been much harder to address in the past. We are increasingly able to identify where leverage resides, how it is financed, who is providing that financing, and how funding and liquidity shocks might propagate through the financial system. These capabilities are helping us to understand the behaviour of leveraged market participants and to evaluate how changes in market structure, such as greater central clearing, broader clearing access, or minimum haircut frameworks, could affect the resilience of core funding markets.
To show what a system-wide perspective can do, let's turn to a sector where these insights have been invaluable: hedge funds.
Data, and the case of hedge fund leverage
Increasingly, hedge funds contribute to liquidity, price discovery, and risk-bearing capacity across important financial markets. The financial stability question for us is not the fact that they use leverage to support their activities – that is a commercial matter entirely up to them, and indeed well-managed leverage is a positive thing for the economy. The question is rather about where that leverage resides, how concentrated it is, how it is financed, and how it interacts with the rest of the financial system.
Those questions cannot be answered using any single dataset, or by looking at hedge funds in isolation. They require combining transaction-level data, fund-level reporting, supervisory intelligence, market engagement, and deep market expertise.
Doing so has already generated insights that would have been difficult to obtain in the past. For example, in our July 2026 Financial Stability Report (FSR) we showed that, over the past four years, hedge funds have shifted from being net cash lenders to net cash borrowers in repo markets across a range of currencies, reflecting the important role of the banks as by far the major providers of leverage.footnote [1] We were also able to show that growth in hedge funds' gilt repo borrowing has coincided with increasing futures open interest, consistent with an expansion in basis trading activity. We were able to spot and track the growth of the cash-futures basis trade in the UK over the last 18 months – which was corroborated by our market intelligence.footnote [2] These insights help us understand where leverage is being created, how it is financed, and which transmission channels may matter during periods of stress.
That said, transaction data can only tell us part of the story. They help us understand positions and interconnections. They do not necessarily tell us how firms will behave if conditions deteriorate. To understand that, we complement our datasets with analysis of behaviours and reaction functions.
That is why we have started to run system-wide scenario exercises in collaboration with the industry. Our first one, two years ago, focussed on core sterling markets. During that exercise, many hedge funds originally assumed that additional repo financing would be available if needed. But it was clear from dealer banks that this would not necessarily be forthcoming. So we shared that feedback with hedge funds and asked how they would respond if banks reduced the amount of gilt repo financing available. Many reported that they would need to unwind positions financed through repo, illustrating how pressures on dealer balance sheets could be transmitted to leveraged investors and potentially amplify market moves.footnote [3]
Hedge funds play an important role in supporting market functioning, including in government bond markets, by warehousing risk and providing liquidity. But they are also generally more responsive to changes in market conditions and financing costs. As a result, the unwinding of leveraged and often crowded positions can have a disproportionate impact on market liquidity and may amplify stress during periods of market turbulence.
This is precisely why a system-wide perspective matters. A hedge fund can observe its own financing relationships. A dealer can observe its own clients. However, only the authorities can bring these perspectives together, helping identify vulnerabilities and interconnections that may not be visible to any single firm. Publishing analysis through our Financial Stability Reports, Staff Working Papers, and other publications allows market participants to benchmark their own exposures against broader market developments, improve risk management playbooks, understand which avenues would or wouldn’t be open to them in a stress, and identify vulnerabilities earlier.
As a concrete example of this, in our Financial Stability Report we have started to publish regularly aggregated data and charts that can help market participants understand wider developments and aid their own risk management. Examples of this in our latest FSR include how the preferred maturities of the gilt investor base have changed over the past decade, investor positioning in gilt repo, and breakdowns of the term and collateral maturity of those transactions.footnote [4] As part of our ongoing market engagement we look to understand which other areas might benefit from increased transparency, such as deep dives into specific market segments like retail investors in gilt markets and transparency on basis trade dynamics.
So please do take a look at our FSRs! I am not sure all the market participants who might find this information helpful actually clocked that we had very deliberately started to publish it. So far the feedback from hedge funds about its usefulness has been positive, and our message is: please put your thinking caps on and let us know what other aggregate data you would find helpful to see for your risk management. If we have it and can share it, we will.
At its best, surveillance is not just about helping authorities understand the system, it is also about helping the system understand itself better. Equipped with better information, market participants can be a more effective first line of defence, and the market as a whole is better able to self-stabilise when shocks hit – reducing the need for us to intervene.
And because we’re better placed than anyone else to see the overall picture, assembling it and sharing it back is an increasingly important policy tool in our toolbox.
But in addition to allowing market transparency to play out more effectively and do its work, surveillance also helps us identify in a discerning way the select few areas where the structure of markets does need to evolve to enhance resilience. Which brings me to a market where we have been asking such questions: the government bond repo market.
Leverage and funding in core markets
Like much of the financial system's infrastructure, the repo market is probably most visible only if it stops working properly. But its day-to-day role is essential – it keeps cash and collateral flowing through the financial system, supports liquidity in government bond markets, and facilitates the transmission of monetary policy.
Our first system-wide exploratory scenario (SWES) several years ago illustrated the crucial role that this market plays. Its resilience has improved, as was demonstrated by the fact that it has withstood successfully all the recent shocks in a heightened global risk environment. But that improved resilience isn’t yet locked permanently into its fundamental structure – it can still not be taken for granted.
Specifically, a key issue on our radar is how leveraged positions that are extremely large, concentrated, or correlated with respect to the size of the market have the potential to amplify shocks if they are unwound abruptly. Market corrections as a result of economic fundamentals are natural and healthy. What we want to avoid is such corrections getting amplified by structural features, as happened in the 2022 LDI crisis. That does not mean eliminating risk, though. Quite the opposite. The repo market performs crucial economic functions precisely because participants take and manage risk, often in the form of leverage. In principle leverage supports market liquidity and efficient risk transfer. Margin protects counterparties. Intermediation connects investors with different funding and investment needs.
Our intention is not to reduce leverage financed through the repo market. It is to ensure that the way it is provided and accessed supports market liquidity, efficient risk transfer, and the allocation of capital in all environments – not just when the sun shines. That might require limiting the particular forms of risk-taking that make the system more fragile.
So well-managed and well-understood leverage is welcome. Out-of-control leverage is unwelcome.
The challenge for policymakers is therefore to identify the combination of measures that best strengthen the resilience and efficiency of the system as a whole, in both normal and stress times. These properties depend on the ability of the financial system to supply liquidity when it is most needed. And they depend on limiting the build-up of vulnerabilities that can generate sudden and disruptive demand for liquidity during periods of stress.
On the supply side, greater central clearing has the potential not only to reduce counterparty credit risk, but also to strengthen the resilience of the market structure itself. The benefits for risk management are well understood, including more transparent and risk-sensitive margining practices. Less often appreciated are the market-wide benefits arising from greater netting efficiencies, lower balance sheet usage and a greater capacity for intermediaries to absorb positions, warehouse risk, and supply liquidity during periods of stress. Bank of England researchers have estimated that greater central clearing could have reduced gilt repo exposures on UK bank dealers' balance sheets during the “dash for cash” by between 40% and 60%.footnote [5] So this could free up a lot of capacity.
Experiences in other jurisdictions suggest that greater use of central clearing can encourage innovation in market structure and access models. In the United States Treasury repo market, for examplefootnote [6], market structures are evolving alongside clearing reforms, with new intermediation models and broader clearing access arrangements developing over time.
This is why access models matter. Different access arrangements can broaden participation in central clearing while preserving the diversity of participants that supports market liquidity. In the indirect model, clients access the central counterparty (CCP) via a clearing member. Sponsored access allows eligible firms to become direct participants of the CCP with support from a sponsoring clearing member, typically a dealer bank. Such support might include managing the connectivity to the CCP; managing collateral and settlement processes; and funding default fund requirements. In some ‘guaranteed’ sponsored models, direct access can be extended to an even wider range of participants, supported by greater obligations of the sponsor, for example to step in and make margin payments on behalf of the sponsored member. Arrangements can therefore sit at different points along a spectrum. By allocating responsibilities differently between clients, clearing members, and the CCP, they create different trade-offs between market access, balance sheet efficiency, incentives to provide intermediation, and overall market resilience.
Improvements in access to client clearing may themselves encourage greater use of clearing and catalyse the evolution of markets over time.
The measures I have discussed so far operate primarily through the liquidity supply channel. But recent episodes have demonstrated that liquidity stress is often driven not simply by a shortage of liquidity supply, but by sudden increases in liquidity demand.
This is where margining and haircut practices become important, reducing the build-up of extreme and unmanageable leverage, strengthening counterparty risk management, and lowering the likelihood of abrupt position liquidations.
In some circumstances, zero or near-zero haircuts can be justified by risk-reducing features such as netting and portfolio margining arrangements, which lower the overall exposure of the lender of leverage to its counterparty by recognising offsetting positions across different portfolios. However, while these arrangements can explain an important share of observed near-zero haircuts, we found that competitive considerations also play a role in the setting of very low haircuts – whereby the haircut is not set on risk grounds, but to avoid losing the client to competitors.footnote [7] This matters because near-zero or negative haircuts that are not directly linked to underlying risk can facilitate the build-up of unmanageable levels of leverage at little cost, and increase vulnerabilities in periods of market stress. More broadly, these findings support ongoing efforts by policymakers to strengthen the resilience of core funding markets and reduce vulnerabilities associated with extreme leverage in non-bank financial institutions.
Considering policy across these areas inevitably involves trade-offs. Poorly calibrated measures could reduce market-making capacity, shift activity elsewhere, or create unintended incentives. Margin and collateral arrangements that limit netting opportunities or prevent the recognition of genuine risk offsets can increase funding pressures precisely when market participants are already under stress.
From a financial stability perspective, the objective is not simply to demand more collateral from market participants. It is to ensure that collateral and margin requirements reflect underlying risks while avoiding unnecessary demands on liquidity during periods of stress.
This raises an important question: can the same level of risk protection be achieved while reducing unnecessary liquidity demands? This is one reason why appropriately designed cross-margining arrangements are attracting increasing interest, as they can improve collateral efficiency and reduce unnecessary liquidity demands where genuine risk offsets exist. However, cross-margining is not a free good. The scope for recognising offsets has to be determined by genuine offsets in the risks, noting asset correlations that appear stable in normal times may become less reliable during periods of stress. Realising the benefits of cross-margining also requires effective legal and operational arrangements and close cooperation across infrastructures and jurisdictions.
No single measure is likely to be a silver bullet for the resilience of gilt repo markets.
Measures that promote the appropriate pricing and management of leverage, support clearing adoption, broaden access to central clearing, and improve collateral efficiency should be viewed as complementary rather than substitutes. Considered together, they may offset some of the costs or limitations that would arise if any individual measure were implemented in isolation.
As it happens, and thankfully, that is what system-wide surveillance is helping us understand. It will certainly inform which policy package we put forward.footnote [8] As we said in the past, doing nothing is not an option.footnote [9] We intend to publish a comprehensive update on this, including potential policy proposals, in early 2027.
Many of these issues are inherently cross-border, and we continue to work closely with international partners through the Financial Stability Board and other fora to strengthen the resilience of market-based finance globally, where surveillance is high on the agenda. We are strong supporters of initiatives such as the FSB’s Nonbank Data Taskforce to break down barriers to transparency in these inherently global markets. The changes we see to the UK’s financial system are also being seen by our fellow regulators around the world, so we are far from alone in investigating these issues.
Conclusion
Of course the challenge of interpreting vast quantities of data to make sense of complex, interconnected systems is not unique to financial regulation. Let me conclude with a famous example of system-wide thinking from history. Often, the deployment of newly invented radar technology is credited with winning the Battle of Britain. But it was not one innovation that won out: not superior radar, better guns, or faster pilots. RAF fighter command understood that it was getting the right data where it needed to go that would win the battle. It was in setting up the famous Dowding System in the 1930s – a central command that could filter thousands of data points from radar systems, civilian spotters, and reconnaissance planes, turn those observations into system-wide insight, and relay them back out to gunners and fighter squadrons, giving them the information they needed to make front line decisions – that made British air defence so effective.
They had a system-wide mindset. And that mindset is bound to be powerful as we adapt to a new era of complexity and interconnectedness in the financial system. As central banks and regulators we have a unique vantage point over the whole system. Post-crisis reforms gave us more data than ever before. But our objective is not more and more data for its own sake. It is to draw from it genuinely system-wide insight. And then to share that aggregate data and insight back with the financial system to support its enduring ability to self-stabilise autonomously.
The more reliably it does that, the more selective we can be with policy interventions.
Thank you.
I would like to thank Gerardo Ferrara, Emily Evans, Nicholas Butt, Shefalika, Waris Panjwani, Michael Wood, Bradley Hudd, Julia Giese, David Bailey, and Sasha Mills for their comments and help in the preparation of these remarks.

China as an AI disruptor

Equity markets: The tech and non-tech divide

Equity markets have diverged into two different worlds: tech and non-tech, with correspondingly different interactions with global bond yields. Over the summer, the oil price was the key driver of bond yields. Rising oil prices and bond yields led – as expected – to declines in non-tech equities. Tech equities, however, were largely impervious as the positive earnings outlook mattered more.

The recent sell-off in tech stocks, however, has led investors to seek safety in government bonds, driving yields lower even as oil prices rise. Defensive (non-tech) equities have also benefited from the lower yields and inflows from investors looking for perceived safe havens.

What happens next will depend on whether tech market volatility subsides. Investors have been disappointed by the earnings of some tech stocks. Given the high expectations implicit in the strong gains for tech indices year to date, there may be little room for further disappointment.

Government bonds: Many moving parts

Government bond yields have increased significantly this year, worsening financial conditions and sparking worries about debt sustainability. While no second-round effects are yet visible, the unanticipated inflation acceleration is certainly a key variable behind bond yields.

Another important variable is major central banks’ monetary policy U-turns. For example, market-based expectations initially indicated the Fed would cut interest rates in 2026. Instead, the Fed hiked rates and current market expectations suggest another two hikes over the next 12 months.

However, this is just one side of the story. There are structural factors as well; in particular, the oversupply of long-term bonds resulting not only from governments’ need to fund their spending, but also from changing demand. The government bond market has transitioned from being driven by price-insensitive investors with seemingly infinitely elastic balance sheets, to highly price-sensitive investors with constrained balance sheets. Therefore, the expected interest rate peak, government bond risk premiums and the shape of the yield curve have become once more an integral part of fixed income allocation decisions.

An industrial renaissance in progress

The artificial intelligence buildout is generating a capital investment cycle of an historic scale, reshaping industrial supply chains, power infrastructure, manufacturing geography, and sovereign economic strategies across both developed and emerging markets. Surging financing and extensive order backlogs confirm the structural nature of this wave, anchored primarily by the US and China.

However, this industrial renaissance is highly uneven and bottlenecks are shifting. US-led AI capital expenditure is driving the growth disparities; non-AI driven-economies are facing slower expansion. Moreover, China’s investment and production-biased policies are adding pressure to traditional manufacturing sectors.

Simultaneously, as a byproduct of its own tech competition drive, China could emerge as a disruptor within the AI trade. Operationally, power availability and grid interconnection timelines are increasingly outweighing core tech infrastructure, land, and labour as the primary deployment constraints.

Consequently, development is shifting toward behind-the-meter and off-grid facilities –connected directly to solar, batteries, or power plants – to accelerate energisation and reduce grid dependence. These trends will likely lead to divergent investment outcomes in 2027 and beyond.

Implementation ideas

Flexibility within euro credit

The euro credit market remains resilient, supported by strong fundamentals, despite geopolitical tensions and elevated energy prices. While investment grade spreads remain relatively tight, high yield spreads have widened in recent weeks. This has restored some value in the higher-yielding segments of the market, but it also calls for greater selectivity.

With the third-quarter reporting season now under way, company results will be key to confirm the strength of corporate balance sheets. Overall, conditions remain supportive with elevated all-in yields and an attractive income. Tactical duration positioning could potentially be beneficial, particularly given the market has already priced in expectations of future European Central Bank interest rate hikes. An agile, flexible approach could help investors capitalise on opportunities across the euro credit spectrum, including high yield and subordinated debt, while mitigating idiosyncratic risks.

Inflation and rates fluctuation protection

Geopolitical tensions are sustaining high levels of inflation uncertainty, particularly due to volatile energy prices, while financial conditions remain restrictive. The distinctly hawkish turn by various central banks means short-dated inflation-linked bonds look attractive, given their near-term growth potential and inflationary risks. Given that multiple interest rate hikes are already embedded in market pricing, both inflation indexation – bonds where the principal is linked to inflation – and the potential returns investors can earn from holding the bond offer potential attractive opportunities through year-end. Short-duration strategies can potentially help protect against the risk of higher inflation as they are less sensitive to interest rates compared with all-maturities strategies.

Environmental solutions enabling AI development

The artificial intelligence revolution is not just about investing in semiconductors and technology. Behind the rapid growth of AI is a significant build-out of critical enabling infrastructure, particularly power and water. Rising data centre demand requires more electricity generation, stronger and smarter grids, transformers, battery storage, energy efficient cooling, and reliable water infrastructure. Meeting this growing demand while supporting the transition towards a lower-carbon power system will require significant investment in environmental solutions. We believe this creates a broad, multi-year potential investment opportunity in the providers that enable the continued expansion of AI.

The North American power landscape is evolving
Utilities, hyperscalers, and other offtakers are seeking a broader mix of resources to balance affordability, reliability, and emissions goals – from collocated solar and storage to SMRs and gas. Solar and energy storage are gaining share, bolstered by their cost profile and development timeline. These advantages help meet the surge in demand from data centers and reshored manufacturing. At the same time, geopolitical volatility and supply-chain pressures are reshaping market conditions.
In this environment, utilities, developers, IPPs, and investors need a broad view of the power market to make sound decisions. To reflect this shift, Wood Mackenzie’s longstanding Solar & Energy Storage Summit is expanding to become the North American Power & Renewables Forum.
On the agenda for 2027, we discuss the forces reshaping the power market in North America:
• Can the U.S. achieve energy leadership over the long-term without greater policy consistency?• Tariffs, international conflicts and rising interest rates are adding cost pressures. What level of increase will stifle demand growth?• Has FERC interconnection reform successfully removed blockers to transmission development?
