Why attend the North American Power & Renewables Forum 2027?

The solar & energy storage journey
For 20 years, the Solar & Energy Storage Summit has grown alongside the solar and storage sectors to become a key industry gathering for developers, IPPs, and investors. The new North American Power & Renewables Forum will continue to cover solar and storage markets in depth, while placing them in the broader context of North America and global power markets. As the audience expands, the solar and energy storage community will gain greater access to their utility and C&I customers, along with crucial interconnected intelligence across technologies and markets.
What’s new at the North American Power & Renewables Forum?
The expanded Forum will bring together leaders from across the power sector, including renewables, conventional generation, utilities, data centers, other commercial and industrial offtakers, and government, to examine the forces reshaping North America’s power market.
What will remain the same at the North American Power & Renewables Forum?
The Forum will continue to showcase the deeply researched data and insight from Wood Mackenzie’s interconnected intelligence. It will dive deep into technology and market issues that drive North America’s power mix to allow attendees to understand the root of the problem and different viewpoints on solutions.

articles.text:

News Release
One in five refineries at closure risk as global oil demand peaks in 2032

05 November 2026
6 minute read

Email
Share by email

An estimated one in five of the world's oil refineries faces increasing risk of closure as global oil demand peaks and enters structural decline within the next decade, according to new research published today by Wood Mackenzie. For the refining industry, the firm says, hope is not a strategy.
Global refined product demand stands at 105 million barrels per day. Wood Mackenzie forecasts a rise to 108 mb/d by 2032, after which decline sets in. Roughly 20% of existing global capacity sits on what the report terms a "downward escalator," facing falling or negative operating net cash margins and increasing risk of closure. Demand peaks in 2032, but with 2040 only three to four refinery turnaround cycles away, the window for major investment decisions is closing. Despite this, some refinery investments will continue in locations such as India, driven by domestic demand growth and energy self-reliance policy, though it remains capacity added locally into a global market in structural decline.
"The sector has navigated structural change before, from the oil shocks of the 1970s to the investment capacity wave across the Middle East and Asia in the 2000s,” said Alan Gelder, SVP Refining, Chemicals and Oil Markets, Wood Mackenzie. “The current pressure is different in kind, not just degree. For the first time, the industry faces sustained decline in end-market demand rather than a temporary supply disruption. Scale, complexity and location determine which assets have genuine options. For those without structural advantages, the absence of a credible adaptation plan is not a deferral. It is a decision."
The demand decline is not uniform
Gasoline faces the sharpest pressure from electric vehicle adoption. Diesel, gasoil and jet fuel are more resilient, as heavy road transport and aviation have no clear decarbonisation pathway. LPG and naphtha benefit from petrochemical feedstock demand, while specialty products including lubricants, bitumen and waxes are largely insulated, as bio-based alternatives do not yet exist at scale.
The current elevated refining margins, driven by the Middle East conflict and damage to Russian refineries, will return to more modest levels when the conflict ends. Refining margins are determined by crack spreads, not the oil price, and long-run average benchmark margins are slim. The sector generates lower returns on capital than upstream operations, making the investment required for adaptation harder to access when the need is greatest.
Five archetypes, sharply uneven exposure
Large-scale, high-complexity refineries, including major assets on the US Gulf Coast, modern export-oriented facilities in the Middle East and the Dangote refinery in Nigeria, are the most competitive. Complex chemical-integrated sites, increasingly common in China and parts of Europe and Asia, can redirect output from declining transport fuels into petrochemicals. These two archetypes have the broadest adaptation options and are best placed to become the integrated energy parks that define the sector's future.
Coastal cracking refineries, the most common OECD configuration, face direct international competition and narrower options. European assets face the most acute regional pressure. Small-scale specialty assets, focused on lubricants, bitumen and waxes, carry limited exposure to transport fuel decline. Small-scale, low-complexity refineries, many of them NOC-owned in developing countries, survive only through subsidies.
Many pathways exist, but not all are equally available
Wood Mackenzie identifies several adaptation strategies, though high capital costs and market uncertainty make many difficult to execute. Petrochemical integration is the primary route for large, complex sites, redirecting LPG and naphtha into olefins, aromatics and polymers; Asian and Middle Eastern operators, backed by state capital, lead here. Bio and circular conversion, producing renewable diesel and sustainable aviation fuel from used cooking oil and recycled plastics, suits EU coastal refineries. Conventional upgrading is most viable for Middle Eastern and Asian refiners with capital, land and export access. Carbon capture and storage is relevant primarily to European and OECD operators. For mid-tier assets, the options are capacity consolidation, a pivot to specialty products, full value-chain integration or diversification into tangential sectors such as power, LNG and ammonia.
"The capital required for the most of these adaptation strategies is substantial, and the sector's return profile makes raising it harder than it appears from the outside,” said Chris Barry, Vice President, Downstream Consulting, Wood Mackenzie. “The risk is a mismatch between ambition and balance sheet capacity. Petrochemical and renewable fuels integration may be an attractive growth or diversification opportunity for large, complex, well-positioned assets. For structurally weaker sites, consolidating around local market strength or moving into specialty products is the more defensible route to long-term viability."
A bifurcated future
Oil products remain central to the global economy for several more decades, and well-positioned refineries have a viable future. The sector's long-term shape is bifurcated: world-class integrated energy and molecule parks producing fuels, petrochemicals and speciality products at one end; terminal conversion, repurposing or closure at the other. Sector specialists will survive by monetising local advantages in feedstock access, regulatory environment or state support. For investors and asset owners, the question is not whether a refinery will face pressure, but whether its archetype, location and ownership structure give it the tools to adapt.
Key details:

Refined product demand: 105 mb/d in 2025, peaking at 108 mb/d in 2032, then declining
Estimated 20% of existing global refining capacity at increasing risk of closure
More than 700 refineries worldwide
India: 40% of global refining capacity additions to 2030
Sustainable aviation fuels: up to 80% emissions reduction versus conventional jet fuel
Refinery complexity scored on a scale of 1 to 25; higher scores generally correlate with higher net cash margin
2040 is three to four refinery turnaround cycles away

Background
Wood Mackenzie's Horizons series draws on proprietary data from the firm's Refinery Evaluation Model and Product Markets Service. Net cash margin is defined as cash from refining operations after payment of feedstock, fixed and variable operating costs on a per-barrel-of-throughput basis. All demand forecasts and capacity risk estimates reflect Wood Mackenzie's analytical view as of the date of publication.

articles.title: Running with purpose: Supporting families when they need it most | RBCCM
articles.text:
What began as a single race in New York in 2009, RBC Race for the Kids has grown into a series of 17 events around the world. Together, they have attracted more than 525,000 participants and raised over CAD$118 million for youth-focused charities.
In Sydney the event brings together RBC employees, their families, friends and clients to take part in one of the city’s most iconic races, the Voltaren City2Surf. Funds raised help charity partner Ronald McDonald House Sydney provide a “home away from home” for families caring for sick or injured children.
Ronald McDonald House Sydney supports people whose children are being treated at the Sydney Children’s Hospital in Randwick – particularly those traveling from regional and remote communities. It provides them with a comfortable place to stay, practical support and the reassurance of being close to their child throughout treatment.
“Fundraising for Ronald McDonald House Sydney through RBC Race for the Kids is a natural fit with our broader commitments to making a positive and measurable impact in the communities where we operate,” says Blair Wark, Chief Financial Officer, APAC; Chief Operating Officer APAC CM, Country Head, Australia.
“We are helping to make a real impact – delivering positive outcomes for people in need. We’re helping these families access lifesaving healthcare, which is at the heart of our Purpose Framework.”
Maximizing impact through a partnership
While the purpose of RBC Race for the Kids in Sydney has remained unchanged since its 2014 launch, the way it brings that purpose to life has evolved.
What was initially launched as a small-scale standalone event 12 years ago has transformed into a partnership with the world’s largest fun run, the Voltaren City2Surf. On August 9, 2026, RBC participants joined more than 90,000 people on a scenic but challenging 14km course from Sydney’s CBD to Bondi Beach.
RBC participants took part under the RBC Race for the Kids banner, while the greater scale and visibility of the Voltaren City2Surf creates more opportunity to raise awareness and funds. “Our new approach allows RBC Race for the Kids to retain its identity while connecting with a much larger event and community and, most importantly, generating greater support for Ronald McDonald House Sydney,” Wark adds.

“Our new approach allows RBC Race for the Kids to retain its identity while connecting with a much larger event and community.”
Blair Wark, Chief Financial Officer, APAC; Chief Operating Officer APAC CM, Country Head, Australia.

Going beyond fundraising
Around 300 RBC staff, their families, friends and clients took part in this year’s Voltaren City2Surf – the event’s 56th year – raising more than A$72,000 for Ronald McDonald House Sydney. The funds will contribute to the House’s Meal Coordinator role, led by a qualified chef who prepares home-cooked meals for families. The role also oversees the Home for Dinner volunteering program, in which RBC employees regularly participate.
The Home for Dinner program gives corporate volunteers the opportunity to prepare, cook and serve an evening meal for families staying in the House. The program has recently evolved, with the Meal Coordinator taking responsibility for menu planning and sourcing ingredients, which volunteers previously managed. The new model provides families with greater variety and more nutritious meals while helping reduce food waste.
“After a long and often exhausting day at the hospital, the last thing we want families to worry about is what they are going to cook for dinner,” explains Simone Daher, Chief Executive Officer, Ronald McDonald House Sydney.
“Patrick, our Meal Coordinator and qualified chef, is helping us deliver on a simple but important commitment – to have a nourishing, home-cooked meal available for our families every day.“
“It’s about much more than food. Sitting down to a home-cooked meal can bring a little bit of routine and normality back into a family’s day at a time when almost everything else feels uncertain. RBC’s support is helping us make that possible.”
The partnership between RBC and Ronald McDonald House Sydney will mark 10 years in 2027. Over this time, RBC has donated over A$1 million to the charity, supporting not only the Meal Coordinator but also practical improvements at the House. These have included the refurbishment of an isolation unit, learning services for children and siblings staying for extended periods, and renovations to the outdoor play area and kitchen.
“When a child is seriously ill or injured, families often have to leave their homes, their jobs and their support networks behind to access specialist treatment in Sydney. Our role is to take away some of the everyday pressures so families can focus on what matters most – being together and being there for their child,” Daher adds. “That means providing much more than a place to sleep. It’s meals, education, practical and emotional support, spaces for siblings and, importantly, a community around families during what can be one of the most difficult times in their lives.”
That support has contributed to countless individual stories that demonstrate the role the House can play during some of the most difficult periods in a family’s life. One family spent more than 900 nights at the House, demonstrating the long-term role it can play during an extended course of treatment. In another remarkable example, a young girl staying at the House was found to be a bone marrow match for a fellow resident in need of a transplant and later went on to become their donor.
Wark says stories like these reinforce why the program is such a strong fit with RBC’s commitment to communities. “It is a powerful reminder that these partnerships are about people, not just numbers. It’s about bringing people together and encouraging them to understand the importance of giving back,” he says.

“These partnerships are about people, not just numbers. It’s about bringing people together and encouraging them to understand the importance of giving back”
Blair Wark, Chief Financial Officer, APAC; Chief Operating Officer APAC CM, Country Head, Australia.

articles.title: Operational resilience of the financial sector
articles.text:
Operational resilience of the financial sector

We make sure banks and financial services firms in the UK can overcome disruption

Related links

Co-ordinating the response to disruption of financial services

On this pageOverviewStrategic outcomesFirm-level outputsSystem-level outputs

Overview
Operational resilience is the ability of firms and the entire financial sector to prevent, adapt, respond to, recover from and learn from disruptions.
Financial firms and financial market infrastructures (FMIs) must have robust plans to deliver important services, no matter the disruption. This includes man-made threats such as physical and cyberattacks, IT system outages and third-party supplier failure. It also includes natural hazards such as fire, flood, severe weather and pandemic. These can affect firms’ safety and soundness, undermine policyholder protection and, in some cases, affect financial stability.
The Bank of England and our Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA) carry out this work with the UK's two other financial authorities: the Treasury and the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA).
Our approach assumes that sometimes disruptions that prevent firms from operating as usual will occur and mean they cannot provide their services for a period.

External links

Operational Resilience - Financial Conduct Authority Opens in a new window
The National Cyber Security Centre Opens in a new window

Prudential and Resolution Policy Index related links

Banking - Operational resilience
Insurance - Operational resilience

Strategic outcomes

Build firms' resilience: when severe but plausible disruption occurs, it should not affect financial stability, safety and soundness or policyholder protection. Firms must ensure high standards of IT and cyber resilience, third-party dependency risks.
Build systemic operational resilience: firms and the Bank work to ensure that when systemic operational risks crystallise, they do not impact the UK's financial stability. Third parties must be sufficiently resilient to support this outcome. It is important that firms can contribute to sector-wide incident response and can learn and evolve from failures.
Manage risks: limit the likelihood and impact of losses. Firms must set aside capital so that the crystallisation of risks is unlikely to affect firm safety and soundness.

The following outputs are designed with these outcomes in mind:

Monetary Policy Committee voting history

Firm-level outputs

Operational resilience policy
Our Financial Policy Committee (FPC) looks at the entire system. Our Prudential Regulation Committee (PRC) and Financial Market Infrastructure Committee (FMIC) focus on the firms and FMIs we regulate.
In summary, we ask firms to:

identify important business services: boards and senior management must prioritise services that, if disrupted, would affect our objectives and the public interest;
set impact tolerances: firms must say to what extent they could continue important business services after severe but plausible disruptions; and
make sure they can stay within impact tolerances: firms must map their important business services and test their capacity to continue to the agreed extent – they should address any vulnerabilities they have identified.

The operational resilience policy SS1/21 requires firms to prepare a written operational resilience self-assessment of compliance. The aim is to document a firms’ resilience journey, identifying risks that could prevent them from delivering important business services within tolerances in severe but plausible scenarios. It helps the firms’ boards and senior management make informed investment decisions to address resilience gaps.
We assess the status of a firm’s implementation of our policy. This includes reviewing:

their important business services, impact tolerances and additional metrics
scenario testing details, results and assurance that the firm can remain within impact tolerances in severe but plausible scenarios
firms’ identification of risks, threats, and vulnerabilities through mapping, testing and live incidents
response and recovery actions, remediation plans and timelines

Self-assessments allow us to identify good practices at an individual firm level while also facilitating thematic comparisons, helping us build a clearer picture of the wider systemic operational resilience picture across the industry.
Incident management and reporting
The PRA has published a policy that details requirements for reporting certain operational incidents, and notification and reporting of material third-party arrangements. It sets out expectations for regulatory reporting, which aim to enhance the PRA’s understanding of firm and sector threats and vulnerabilities.

CP17/24 – Operational resilience: Operational incident and outsourcing and third-party reporting

Third-party management
The PRA’s current policy is set out primarily in Supervisory Statement (SS) 2/21: Outsourcing and third party risk management, which was published in March 2021. The Bank has a near-identical set of policies for FMIs, such as clearing houses and payment systems.
Operational risk framework
Our role is to assess whether a firm's operational risk management framework allows them to effectively identify, assess, monitor, report and manage material operational risks to which it is or might be exposed, in line with board-approved strategy and risk appetite.
We are also responsible for assessing whether firms hold sufficient capital to mitigate the impact when operational risks crystallise.
This supports the Internal Capital Adequacy Assessment Rules, which require us to assess whether firms’ own funds and internal capital is adequate to cover the level of the risks to which it is or might be exposed and is reflective of the firm’s operational risk profile.
Cyber resilience
Firms and FMIs should assess their cyber risk and build adequate resilience capabilities to prepare for, and respond to, potentially disruptive cyber incidents. To maintain the financial sector's cyber resilience and to support our supervisory oversight, we have developed cyber assessment tools. They include CBEST, STAR-FS and CQUEST.
CBEST
This provides a framework for regulators to work with firms using a simulated cyberattack. This allows firms to explore how to counteract an attack on the people, processes and technology of cyber security controls. We base the simulated attacks on present threats.
The aim is to test:

a firm's defences
its threat intelligence capability
its ability to detect and respond to external and internal attackers

Firms use the assessment to plan how they can strengthen their resilience.
An accredited service provider carries out the simulation, acting within legal, ethical and moral constraints. It aims to get through a firm's defences using the cyber kill chain. They also assess if the confidentiality, integrity or availability of systems and processes that deliver a firm's important business services can be compromised.

CBEST Threat Intelligence-Led Assessments

CBEST thematic review
The annual CBEST thematic is intended to inform the sector on the findings and lessons learned from our CBEST programme, which assesses the cyber resilience of key financial institutions through security testing performed in ‘live’ corporate environments.

2023 CBEST thematic findings
2024 CBEST thematic findings
2025 CBEST thematic findings

STAR-FS
STAR-FS (simulated targeted attack and response assessments for financial services) is part of the PRA and FCA supervisory toolkit, to assess the cyber resilience of firms' important business services. This allows regulators and firms to better understand vulnerabilities and take remedial actions, thereby improving their resilience and, by extension, the wider financial system.
It promotes a threat-led penetration testing approach that mimics the actions of actors' intent on compromising an organisation's important business services as well as the technology assets and people supporting them.
An implementation guide and supporting templates are available. If your firm is interested in conducting a STAR-FS please contact your supervisor. It aims to provide:

an outcome-based assessment of financial institutions' protection, detection and response technical capabilities against cyber-attacks;
an approach, conducted through a firm-led delivery model, that can identify cyber resilience vulnerabilities within systems, people and processes;
reduced regulatory and firm effort relative to other supervisory technical assessments such as CBEST;
levels of independent technical assurance beyond those ordinarily included in firms' own penetration testing programmes; and
a testing approach accessible by a larger number of financial institutions to experience and learn from.

STAR-FS Implementation guide – Threat Intelligence Led Penetration Testing for Financial Services (PDF 2.1MB) Opens in a new window
STAR-FS Scope Specification (PDF 0.7MB) Opens in a new window
STAR-FS Targeting Report Specification (PDF 0.6MB) Opens in a new window
STAR-FS Threat Intelligence Report Specification (PDF 0.7MB) Opens in a new window
STAR-FS Penetration Test Report Specification (PDF 1.4MB) Opens in a new window
STAR-FS Remediation Plan Template (PDF 0.8MB) Opens in a new window
STAR-FS Regulator Summary (PDF 0.6MB) Opens in a new window
STAR-FS Threat Intelligence Maturity Assessment Guide (PDF 1.3MB) Opens in a new window
STAR-FS Detection & Response Assessment Guide (PDF 0.7MB) Opens in a new window

CQUEST
We use the CQUEST (Cyber resilience questionnaire) to gauge the cyber risk and resilience capabilities of the sector. Firms can also use it as a self-assessment tool to consider their own cyber risk and resilience maturity. It comprises 50 questions with multiple-choice answers across six domains:

governance and leadership
identify
protect
detect
respond
recover

To achieve a reliable outcome, an organisation should identify and direct a competent party with appropriate knowledge of the business to complete the CQUEST. When it is used to inform regulatory activities, supervisors might provide additional guidance and/or they could request evidence or clarifying information in response to the answers.
The latest version of CQUEST builds upon the previous one, and encompasses lessons learned from good practice frameworks and feedback from supervisors and firms.

Download the CQUEST

System-level outputs

Collective action and incident response
The Cross Market Operational Resilience Group (CMORG) leads sector-wide collective action on operational resilience. It comprises about 25 members: firms across retail, wholesale, FMIs, insurance, the financial authorities and the National Cyber Security Centre. Its co-chairs are senior executives of the PRA and UK Finance.
CMORG has three core objectives:

identify risks to the resilience of the financial sector.
develop solutions to improve the operational resilience of the sector.
share knowledge

Industry has developed CMORG-endorsed capabilities (including good practice guidance, response frameworks and contingency tools) to support the operational resilience of the UK's financial sector. The financial authorities support the development of these capabilities and efforts to improve resilience. However, their use is optional and they do not constitute regulatory rules or supervisory expectations. As such, they may not necessarily represent formal endorsement by the authorities.
Specialist subgroups support CMORG. They design, manage and deliver operational resilience improvements for the sector. Their work is voluntary. Their chairs meet regularly to discuss CMORG's activities and identify areas for more collaboration. A project management office (PMO) also supports CMORG. It is jointly resourced by us and UK Finance.

Find out more about CMORG Opens in a new window

The Financial Services Cyber Collaboration Centre (FSCCC) is a CMORG-led partnership. It aims to help identify, investigate and co-ordinate the response to incidents that may have consequences for the financial sector. It analyses and distributes information to produce timely outputs for the sector's benefit.

The Financial Services Cyber Collaboration Centre (FSCCC)

What happens if there is a disruption?
Firms should get in touch with their usual business or supervisory contacts at the Bank or the FCA. The sector's response is facilitated by the Sector Response Framework (SRF). It sets out how organisations across the sector and government are connected. It also explains how they may respond to incidents when the impact becomes broader than a single firm or FMI and requires co-ordination, information-sharing or collective action.
Its purpose is to:

allow firms, FMIs and the sector to make collective, timely and informed decisions in response to incidents
provide a reference to good practice, contingency tools and plans, which may be invoked as part of a sector response
include decision makers and subject matter experts
be organised on a modular basis, so that components of the SRF can respond
be recognised by the financial authorities as the principal structure by which the sector will respond to incidents
support collaborative engagement between the sector and the UK's financial authorities (see below)
be able to engage with frameworks in other jurisdictions, if required

The UK's three financial authorities are the Bank (including the PRA), the FCA and the Treasury. If disruptions could affect the whole sector, these authorities act together.

Find out about how we co-ordinate our response to the disruption of financial services

Sector exercising
The Bank works with the sector to co-ordinate and deliver exercises to strengthen the operational resilience of the UK's financial system.
The most prominent is SIMEX – a biennial, market-wide simulation conducted through a public-private partnership between industry participants and financial authorities. SIMEX performs a unique role in bringing the sector together to address the most challenging and complex risks that individual firms cannot manage alone.
These sector-wide exercises are based on our collective approach to resilience, working together with industry to identify emerging risks and build capabilities to enhance the system’s overall resilience.

SIMEX 24 – A major market-wide simulation exercise to test the UK's financial sector’s resilience to a major operational disruption
SIMEX 22 – A two-day market-wide simulation exercise to test the UK's financial sector’s resilience to a major operational disruption

Critical third-party oversight
The Bank, the PRA and the FCA (the regulators) are responsible for overseeing critical third parties (CTPs) to the UK's financial sector, following their designation by HMT.
Regulated firms and FMIs are increasingly dependent on a small number of third parties for the delivery of functions and services that are essential to the stability of, or confidence in, the UK's financial system. In some cases, third parties can become so critical that no single firm can adequately monitor or manage the systemic risks they pose.
The aim of oversight is to reduce systemic risks arising from the failure of, or disruption to the systemic services they provide to firms. The regulators will assess CTPs against outcomes-focused rules and expectations with the aim of ensuring the systemic services CTPs provide to the financial sector are resilient and therefore any failure of, or disruption to, those services does not threaten the stability of the UK's financial system.
The CTP regime complements, and does not replace, the existing requirements and expectations for firms on SS1/21 operational resilience and SS2/21 outsourcing and third-party risk management policy.

SS6/24 – Critical third parties to the UK financial sector
PS16/24 – Operational resilience: Critical third parties to the UK financial sector
Approach to the oversight of critical third parties

Find out more about the CTP regime:

Critical Third Parties

Cyber and operational resilience stress test (CORST)
The cyber and operational resilience stress test (formerly the Cyber Stress Test or 'CST') is a key part of the Bank’s toolkit on macroprudential operational resilience. The outcomes of cyber and operational resilience stress testing inform the FPC's monitoring of sector operational resilience and its articulation of its tolerance for disruption to vital services. The objectives of testing are to:

provide insight into sector vulnerabilities and the financial stability impacts and residual risk of severe but plausible operational disruption to vital services
explore firm and sector capabilities to respond to, and recover from operational disruption, and to mitigate its impact on financial stability
share lessons to support firms in maturing their approach to operational resilience and financial stability, including firms' roles as systemic risk managers

We invite firms to participate in CORST on a voluntary basis and they identify their own lessons and remediation actions. Actions that require cross-firm co-operation are often progressed through established collective action forums or voluntary groups.
The test aims, over time to explore all systemically important firms and provide insight into not just the impacts of disruption to the services they provide, but also the impacts to their customer firms and from their third parties. Participation may be direct, indirect through co-operation with a direct participant, or through engagement at cross-firm workshops.
The CST24 thematic letter, which provides thematic findings from the 2024 test, also provides resources to support firms’ role in mitigating potential financial stability impacts of disruption to their services.

Thematic findings from the 2024 cyber stress test
Thematic findings from the 2022 cyber stress test

FPC impact tolerance for financial stability
The FPC updated its impact tolerance for payments and settlements after CST22. This was published in the March 2023 FPC Record:

it expected the financial system to be able to complete critical payments by the end of the value date in severe but plausible scenarios; timely recovery of service delivery was the first best way firms could prevent adverse material economic impacts;
in such instances where restoring services would be harmful for financial stability, or impossible, alternative mitigating actions might be appropriate; firms should, therefore plan, prepare and test for such situations and invest so that their response could effectively mitigate any impact on financial stability until service delivery was restored; and
an example of mitigation may be providing an overdraft to a retail Banking customer, so that they can still make purchases, despite a disruption to the payment systems which may have prevented the normal 'payment' being completed

Financial Policy Summary and Record – March 2023 (see paragraphs 101-108)

In Financial Stability in Focus (FSIF), the FPC noted it would regularly review the operational resilience policy toolkit and will explore ways to continue to build system-wide resilience to operational disruption.
In addition to the tools mentioned above, the FPC does this, for example, through:

assessing potential system-wide gaps in, or risks to, operational resilience which are not adequately covered by firm-level or microprudential policies
considering whether to set impact tolerances for additional vital services beyond payments.

The committee has published its macroprudential approach to operational resilience in FSIF and sets out its priorities twice a year in its Financial Stability Report.

What do you need to know?

The Federal Reserve decided to keep interest rates on hold at 3.75%-4% by a vote of 10-2, with two of the 12-member committee favouring a 25-basis-point rise. The Fed stated that while inflation remains high, “the accumulation of more information” is first needed to guide its return to the 2% goal – though expectations of a further rate hike by year end remain strong. Meanwhile, an advance estimate for US GDP growth in the third quarter showed expansion at an annualised 3.4%, up from Q2’s 2.2% and above expectations of 3.2%.

Around the world

The European Central Bank voted to keep interest rates steady last week, despite annual inflation accelerating to 3.8% in September, a three-year high. The ECB noted that rising energy prices are likely to drive up inflation and lower growth within the region. The eurozone economy grew 0.4% on a quarterly basis in Q3, a slowdown from Q2’s 0.6%, according to official data released after the ECB meeting. Elsewhere, the Bank of Japan kept rates unchanged at 1.25% and said underlying inflation had reached its 2% target, the first time since the goal was set in 2013.

Figure in focus: 37%

Foreign direct investment increased by 37% globally in the first half of 2026, compared to the average half-year level in 2025, according to the United Nations’ Trade and Development arm. The rise was largely driven by developed economies which saw investment flows rise by more than 70% in the first half of 2026. However, overall activity weakened, with the number of new projects falling by 15% and international project finance deals declining by 11%. The slowdown in activity reflects global uncertainty over geopolitical tensions, energy prices and supply chain disruptions, the UN said.

Chart of the week

About a third of US and Europe-listed companies had released their third quarter earnings as of last week. Things are going well. In the US, earnings have risen by 37%, though a big contributor to that growth is the technology sector. Excluding technology stocks, the earnings growth rate is a still good 17%. In Europe, earnings are up 25%. Investors also look at how much better or worse the results are compared to what was expected. So far, earnings have surpassed expectations by 3%-4%, in line with historical averages.

Words of wisdom: Big Bang

The deregulation of the London Stock Exchange, referred to as the Big Bang, marked its 40th anniversary last week.On 27 October 1986,the open outcry trading floor was replaced by electronic order books, and fixed broker commissions were abolished, leading to a sudden surge in trading volumes and lower costs for investors. This transformed London into a leading global financial centre. As investment from the US and Asia flowed into London, the Big Bang caused a ripple effect across Europe with the region accelerating the pace of modernising its own trading models.

What’s coming up?

On Tuesday, the Reserve Bank of Australia convenes to set interest rates. Wednesday sees the eurozone release a flash estimate for October’s inflation rate. Several final Purchasing Managers’ Indices for October are issued on Wednesday covering the eurozone, China, UK, and the US. The Bank of England meets to set interest rates on Thursday. On Friday, the US releases its latest jobs data.

articles.title: Reimagining U.S. development at home and overseas
articles.text:
Commentary

Reimagining how the United States advances development in the 21st century: At home and overseas

Sarah E. Mendelson

Sarah E. Mendelson

Nonresident Senior Fellow
- Global Economy and Development, Center for Sustainable Development

November 6, 2026

Development happens everywhere, no matter the income level of a country. The United States’ ability to be a credible champion of global development needs to involve getting its own house in order.

When the 120th Congress takes office in January 2027, members ought to consider creating a Development Officer Corps, where experts would embed in communities in the United States as well as serve tours overseas.

This commentary argues for ending the earmarks that previously shaped “foreign assistance” in favor of locally led, demand-driven development.

“Global engagement ought to deliver positive impacts at home.” (Image: Rachel Rose Boucher/Shutterstock)

7 min read

Bluesky Streamline Icon: https://streamlinehq.comBluesky

For some time, the American approach to development has been misaligned with how most of the world conceives of development. Since 2016, the framework of sustainable development has reflected the fact that “development” happens everywhere, no matter the income level of a country. Societal issues such as poverty, health, and well-being are deeply interconnected rather than existing in policy silos.
To talk about “foreign assistance” or international development as disconnected from what happens inside countries, including this one, is to leave the United States (and millions of Americans) behind, out of step with best practices. Indeed, the implicit impetus driving the “America First” approach to the world is the not unreasonable recognition that global engagement ought to deliver positive impacts at home. While this administration’s approach has been largely transactional, eroding trust, causing damage diplomatically, and undermining U.S. national interests, there is a way in which the pursuit of development both here and abroad can lead to more sustainable and equitable partnerships that benefit Americans as well as citizens in other countries.
The United States should re-engage as a leader in development overseas, while also applying the discipline of sustainable development at home. Simply put, our ability to be credible champions of global development needs to involve getting our own house in order. As detailed daily in press accounts and academic research, our democracy is not delivering for large swaths of Americans on numerous issues, including significant gaps in life expectancy, increasing numbers of families who are food insecure, and growing wealth inequality. These are urgent harms to the health of our democracy. As Columbia University historian Kim Phillips-Fein recently noted, “Societies in which there is an extreme division between the wealthiest and the rest tend to be politically unstable ones as well.” Making progress on domestic priorities, such as expanding economic opportunity and mobility, addressing persistent poverty, and strengthening democratic practices, will offer stronger ground and credibility to pursue a modern global development agenda.
A new Development Officer Corps
What does this look like practically? When the 120th Congress takes office in January 2027, members ought to consider creating a Development Officer Corps, where experts would embed in communities in the United States as well as serve on tours overseas. This idea is not entirely new; there was a long-standing program placing a limited number of USAID and State Department officials inside the United States. Brookings Senior Fellow Anthony F. Pipa wrote about this concept as it relates to diplomacy in 2021, and more recently, Matt Perit, a former Foreign Service officer, similarly wrote about the idea in Just Security. Yet development and diplomacy are distinct disciplines. Therefore, yes, American diplomats ought to have expanded tours in the United States, and so should American development experts.
Development officers can play an important role in the United States, listening to local communities, sharing trends in urgent needs with local, regional, and federal government agencies, and recommending policy changes that impact communities in positive ways. These officers would also serve as local ambassadors explaining to Americans why global development is important to U.S. national security and prosperity, ideally generating awareness and public support for this work, growing the resilience that failed to emerge during the rapid dismantling of USAID.
Development officers serving internationally can also help American communities by bringing advances from elsewhere—“reverse innovation”—to the United States as well as highlighting innovations emerging in towns and cities across the country. Particularly in an era of rapid technological change, Americans can benefit from lessons and adaptations occurring in many places on a range of issues, such as reducing maternal mortality or advancing innovations in agriculture.
In the 21st century, the gold standard advanced by the United States should be data-driven. Such efforts will likely involve bespoke, open-source AI models and could also involve cultivating a younger workforce composed of digital natives to surface, in real time, social and economic issues that need to be addressed rather than waiting months or even years for data. These digital natives could then look forward to productive careers working both domestically and internationally. Congress should create a program to grow this Development Officer Corps with a dedicated digital cone, or career track.

Related Content

The US is leaving millions behind: American exceptionalism needs to change by 2030

Economic Security & Mobility

The US is leaving millions behind: American exceptionalism needs to change by 2030

Sarah E. Mendelson

April 10, 2023

Doing development differently
For years, experts have recognized that development should ideally be locally led and demand-driven, involving communities in the design of programs. Instead, it was commonplace at USAID to talk about ramping up locally led efforts, only to be stymied by Congress. What will strike some as controversial may emerge as common sense to others: A commitment to locally led, demand-driven development would entail reining in the power that a handful of Senate Appropriations staffers have had over who gets to do what, and where. Congress should end the earmarks that previously shaped “foreign assistance.” This system has been a good business model for the U.S.-based NGOs and contractors receiving the funds. It has not been a good model for local organizations and may even have helped fuel the global trend of “closing space” for civil society, in which governments label NGOs receiving U.S. funds as “foreign agents.”
Perhaps nowhere is the evidence stronger that the supply-side (earmarked) approach was problematic than in democracy assistance, amid a 20-year worldwide decline in democracy. A 2021 CSIS study found that 95% of “Democracy, Human Rights, and Governance” (DRG) funds were earmarked. While it is unlikely that the relatively small amount of DRG funding (between $2 billion and $3 billion a year) could alone have stemmed the tide of global decline, the heavily earmarked sector of DRG work could not meet the needs of local communities while simultaneously being subjected to the demands of appropriators.
Moreover, the Cold War hangover across multiple administrations of refusing to acknowledge socioeconomic rights—such as access to food and health—as rights, and instead focusing exclusively on political and civil rights, has contributed to the disconnect between foreign funding and local needs. It has left the United States trailing peer countries on numerous socioeconomic indices—particularly health outcomes. It has helped marginalize the United States in multilateral settings, opening the door for others, such as China, to lead. The United States should finally acknowledge the importance of the full scope of rights in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights because, when realized, they can be instrumental in helping democracies deliver for their populations, including this one.
Finally, one of the most important efforts to emerge in the last two years has been archiving the knowledge and lessons from USAID’s decades of work, known as “the Development Knowledge Commons.” Congress should consider supporting a consortium of universities to mine this work and study the discipline of sustainable development that has emerged in the last 10 years. Since 2016, the world (except Haiti, Myanmar, and the United States) has communicated about sustainable development through hundreds of voluntary reports on national and local-level progress. These reports and the Knowledge Commons are repositories of under-told stories of impact. As many experts reimagine development, how the United States supports this work at home and overseas is an opportunity to drive a paradigm shift for the 21st century that none can afford to waste.

Author

Sarah E. Mendelson

Nonresident Senior Fellow
- Global Economy and Development, Center for Sustainable Development

articles.title: US Affordability challenges cut across every state and local election
articles.text:
RESEARCH BRIEFING

30 Oct 2026

US Affordability challenges cut across every state and local election

The rising cost of living has emerged as the primary issue in the upcoming midterms.

The central driver of this has been higher oil prices, which have rippled across consumer categories such as groceries, electricity, and housing vis-a-vis elevated interest rates. Higher living costs have been exacerbated by cuts to ACA insurance subsidies, which have forced many to drop health insurance; the surge in data centers, which has heightened electricity prices; and tariffs, which have hurt Midwestern economies.

The US-Israel war with Iran has pushed up the cost of gasoline, utilities, and food, three non-discretionary categories. Low-income consumers are especially affected by rising costs as they spend a larger share of their disposable income on non-discretionary categories. Southern states and metros have been the most exposed, as they have the highest share of low-income households burdened by the high cost of necessities.

The rising interest rates that have accompanied these cost pressures have eroded housing affordability more than it had declined in prior years. Although coastal metros are most cost-burdened, no metro has escaped the material deterioration in affordability. The average household needed to earn $115,600 in income to afford median housing costs in Q3 2026, up from $111,500 in Q3 2025, and 75% more than the $66,200 needed five years ago.

Ballooning healthcare costs, data center-driven electricity price increases, and tariffs all add further cost pressures to consumers and businesses across the US. Southern states have weathered the steepest drops in ACA enrollment due to insurance subsidies cuts. Northeastern states are bearing the brunt of higher electricity costs, while manufacturing-heavy Midwestern metros are most exposed to tariffs.

articles.title: Europe gets the thumbs up from global investors – Deutsche Bank
articles.text:
Macro and Markets

Europe gets the thumbs up from global investors

04 November 2026
Will Monroe

Despite its competitiveness challenge, Europe remains an attractive destination for international companies, according to a new Deutsche Bank survey. But why do many business leaders outside of Europe see a more positive picture than the headlines might suggest?

9 min read
Reading time could not be calculated{{@root.language.[rwd.flow.readingTime.error]}}

Much has been made of sluggish European growth in recent years, with the September 2024 Draghi report laying bare Europe’s productivity and competitiveness challenges.1
But a new survey published by Deutsche Bank, Global Sentiment Survey on Europe 2026, paints a much rosier picture. As the survey highlights, international companies are far more optimistic about Europe than recent reports would suggest.
This article summarises the core findings of the survey – which featured inputs from 1,200 senior leaders and decision-makers from companies in 13 non-European markets – to explain why international companies see plenty of promise in Europe as an investment destination.

Europe: an attractive proposition for global investors

More than one-third of survey respondents cited Europe as the world’s most attractive region for their business, putting it ahead of Asia (excluding China), North America, the Middle East and Africa, China, and Latin America. Among companies already invested in Europe, 45% rank it as their first choice. That falls to 15% among those not yet invested, pointing to a significant opportunity to convert broader confidence in Europe into future investment.
Europe’s appeal as an investment destination is also gaining momentum. Some 81% of business leaders say the region has become more important to their investment decisions over the past three years (see Figure 1 below), while just 3% report that its importance has declined.
As confidence in Europe remains robust, future capital allocation looks set to be strong, with a large majority of firms intending to deepen their presence in Europe – or establish one – over the coming years. Asia-Pacific (APAC) is notable for its future potential; the region has the largest share of companies planning to enter Europe (see ‘The Asia story’ section below).

Figure 1: Importance of Europe vs. 3 years ago, by regionSource: Global Sentiment Survey on Europe 2026, B2B online survey. Base: n = 1,200 (APAC 600, Americas 400, Middle East 200)

Why is Europe an appealing investment destination?

Investors/companies value certainty and predictability; two factors that have been in short supply in 2026 in a global landscape characterised by geopolitical tensions and economic uncertainty. These factors are increasingly influencing investment decisions. In this environment, Europe stands out for its perceived resilience: 71% of C-suite respondents consider the region highly or rather resilient as a place to do business, while only around 10% view it as not resilient.
If Europe ticks the boxes for companies who value resilience, it also scores highly in areas such as ‘opportunities’ and ‘innovation potential’, with these two factors helping to underpin the region’s attractiveness.
Europe’s consumer market is another major draw. Almost all respondents (99%) consider the region important to their growth over the next three to five years, reflecting the attraction of its “large, wealthy and stable base of consumers”. And the appeal extends beyond access to customers: 92% also rate Europe as an important location for production, research and development, and supply chains.

Figure 2: Current and planned investment in EuropeSource: Global Sentiment Survey on Europe 2026, B2B online survey. Base: n = 1,200

Germany: Europe’s ‘investment magnet’

At a country level, Germany leads the field as Europe’s most attractive investment destination. Some 56% of respondents rank it among their top three European markets, while 29% place it first, ahead of the United Kingdom and France.
This strong showing reflects a wide range of perceived strengths, from innovation, technology and industrial capabilities to skilled talent, infrastructure, logistics and access to capital. These are themes that have previously been explored by flow – see ‘Germany update: breaking from the brake’ and ‘View from the top: raising the bar’.
European banks are of course playing a key role in facilitating international investment across the region. As investors translate confidence in Europe into concrete decisions, the choice of financial partner becomes increasingly important. For international companies navigating multiple markets and regulatory regimes, financial strength, robust risk and compliance capabilities, and local expertise are all important considerations. Against this backdrop, 60% of respondents say they would prefer to work with a European bank.
Yuliya Trupp, Head of US Regional Corporate Coverage EMEA at Deutsche Bank, notes that the bank’s international network and strength in Germany is “particularly valuable for companies seeking to expand across multiple markets”. She adds: “Our role is to bridge global strategy and local execution. We support clients with everything from establishing banking and liquidity structures to payments, FX, funding, trade finance and working-capital solutions.”

At a glance: investor appetite in Germany

Germany is Europe’s no.1 investment destination
56% include Germany in their top 3 markets
29% rank Germany as their first choice
59% see infrastructure and logistics as a strength
Germany leads on innovation and technology (58%)
Germany leads on industrial capability and skilled workforce (56% each)

Source: Global Sentiment Survey on Europe 2026, B2B online survey. Base: all respondents, n = 1,200

The Asia story

APAC investor appetite for Europe is notable for its room for growth. While 55% of surveyed firms are already invested in Europe (see Figure 3 below), APAC (excluding China) has the largest share of companies planning to enter Europe (44%).
One example of APAC capital allocation in Europe is seen in the growing presence of Taiwanese technology companies in Germany. As the global AI build-out drives a multi-year investment cycle, Taiwanese firms are expanding production, building overseas facilities and strengthening supply chains, increasing demand for financing along the Taiwan-Germany corridor.
Figure 3: Companies currently invested in EuropeSource: Global Sentiment Survey on Europe 2026, B2B online survey. Base: n = 1,200 (APAC 600; Americas 400; Middle East 200)
Fintech payment companies are another growing APAC segment seeking to expand in Europe. In June 2025, Deutsche Bank and Ant International announced a strategic partnership that will see the latter deepen its commitment to Europe via a series of global treasury management and cross-border payment innovations.2
“Continued geopolitical risks are accelerating the pace at which APAC corporates are investing and expanding into Europe”Chintan Shah, Head of Corporate Bank and Corporate Coverage, Asia Pacific and Middle East, Deutsche Bank
In August 2026, Deutsche Bank was appointed by the People’s Bank of China as a Renminbi (RMB) clearing bank for Europe in Frankfurt. As the first foreign bank to receive the designation in Europe, Deutsche Bank can provide direct end-to-end processing, clearing and settlement for cross-border RMB transactions, providing European financial institutions and businesses with a local bridge to China’s payment systems.
Chintan Shah, Head of Corporate Bank and Corporate Coverage, Asia Pacific and Middle East, Deutsche Bank notes of the overall picture: “Continued geopolitical risks are accelerating the pace at which APAC corporates are investing and expanding into Europe. From semiconductor fabs in Germany to EV battery manufacturing across Central and Eastern Europe, our position as a European bank with a strong APAC presence uniquely positions us to support clients through this next phase of cross-border growth.”

The US story

Across the Atlantic, 82% of US multinationals already have a presence in Europe, but its importance as an investment destination continues to grow. Some 85% of decision-makers say Europe has become more important to their investment decisions over the past three years, while 39% believe it has become much more important, compared with 24% in APAC and 20% in the Middle East.
According to the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis, total US direct investment abroad rose by US$438bn in 2025, with Europe accounting for most of the increase: investment in the region grew by US$350bn year on year.3

Figure 4: US direct investment abroad by region, 2024–2025Source: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis
A recent example is Uber’s takeover bid for German takeaway company Delivery Hero in a deal worth US$14.8bn. The transaction will increase the number of markets in which the company operates from 79 to 99. Alongside strategic M&A advice, Deutsche Bank is also participating in bridge financing for the transaction.4
Trupp highlights that „Europe remains a key investment destination for US multinationals“, driven by its scale, skilled workforce, infrastructure, and attractive consumer markets. „Recent investment trends include healthcare manufacturing expansions in Germany and Spain, investment in the European data centre ecosystem, and fintech firms establishing a presence in the UK. US multinationals also continue to choose Europe as their Regional Treasury hub, reinforcing its role as a gateway for international business and treasury management.“
“Europe remains a highly compelling investment destination for US multinationals”Yuliya Trupp, Head of US Regional Corporate Coverage EMEA, Deutsche Bank

The Middle East story

Europe is also attracting growing interest from the Middle East. Some 89% of investors say its importance to their investment decisions has increased over the past three years (20% much more important, 69% somewhat more important), while a further 33% are planning to invest despite not yet having done so. Resilience appears to be part of the attraction, with a region-wide high of 82% viewing Europe as resilient (25% highly resilient, 57% rather resilient).
One example of Middle East-to-Europe investment collaboration came in November 2025, when Qatar’s Al Mirqab Capital partnered with Deutsche Bank and DWS on a mandate initially targeting €1bn of investment in Germany and the wider European economy, spanning sectors from energy and transportation to telecommunications and technology.

What does Europe need to do next?

While the survey highlights that Europe remains highly attractive to global investors, respondents also note there is room for improvement when it comes to competitiveness, market integration and innovation. These three factors are identified as essential to improve and sustain if Europe is to remain an attractive location for international investment.
Europe’s biggest obstacle is arguably Europe itself; Trupp points out that it is not a single homogeneous market, so “companies need to navigate different jurisdictions, regulations, currencies, and tax regimes, which can create considerable complexity as they scale”.
It remains to be seen if these hurdles will be overcome and Europe can tap into its full growth potential, but, for now, investors appear to be ‘voting with their capital’ when it comes to confidence in Europe as an investment destination.

The Global Sentiment Survey on Europe 2026 was conducted as a business-to-business online survey in July and August 2026 among 1,200 senior decision-makers at companies with 100 or more employees. All participating companies are headquartered outside Europe, across 13 markets in three regions.

articles.title: The PRA’s second decade − speech by Katharine Braddick
articles.text:
The PRA’s second decade − speech by Katharine Braddick

Given at Mansion House

Published on
22 October 2026

In her first Mansion House speech as Chief Executive Officer of the Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA), Katharine Braddick sets out her vision for the PRA's second decade. She outlines plans for a new five-year strategy centred on four priorities: resilience, growth, innovation and transparency, alongside a series of reforms to strengthen operational resilience, streamline regulation and improve regulatory processes for firms.

Speech
Lady Mayor, thank you for inviting me to speak this evening. It is an honour to address you and your guests and a pleasure to be speaking alongside Nikhil, who I have known for many years and who I look forward to working with in this new role.
When I joined the PRA in July I joined an organisation that in a little over a decade had succeeded decisively in its initial core mission, a mission that is vital to the success of the United Kingdom and its economy: to restore the resilience of the financial sector, so that it can properly support businesses and households across the nation.
Thanks to the work of the PRA, and significant effort by industry, that resilience has not only been restored but significantly strengthened. This hard-won stability is a source of advantage for our financial sector and this country, and it underpins our position as a leading and trusted financial centre. It is also the principal legacy of my predecessor Sam Woods: we might all wish to say we had achieved such a thing in our careers.
In that decade or so the world has also, of course, changed. Security threats increase, exacerbated by a more fractured geopolitical landscape. Interconnected financial vulnerabilities are arising from stretched sectoral valuations, rising sovereign debt levels and increased market leverage. Technology presents extraordinary opportunities and material and novel risks. And society demands accountability and transparency from its public institutions to maintain their legitimacy.
A new long-term PRA strategy
In this context, then, our task is to determine what the PRA must deliver in its second decade and how to create the regulator the UK will need for the future. Next year I will publish for the first time a five-year strategy for the PRA. The strategy will set out how we intend to deliver four priorities I believe are central for the PRA’s future success:
Resilience
The first priority is resilience. Maintaining the resilience of the UK’s banking and insurance sectors is the foundation of our mission; the PRA identified early on that the need to address operational resilience as well as financial resilience is a prudential matter. Addressing non-financial resilience is an ever wider and more complex task, not least as the frequency and materiality of cyber incidents grows. Firms need to continue to invest in their capabilities, not only to prevent incidents, but to ensure they can respond to and recover from severe disruption.
The PRA similarly needs to evolve. We will significantly increase our focus on firms’ operational and cyber resilience. The cyber challenge, in particular, is an area where we can and do partner effectively with industry and our international counterparts to progress our understanding of both risks and mitigants. We will create a new PRA directorate, reporting directly to me, to act as a centre of excellence for operational and cyber resilience. We will also consult jointly with the FCA on a new supervisory statement by the end of the year, clarifying our expectations of firms as we develop our experience and understanding.
Growth
Our second theme is growth. Achieving sustained and sustainable growth is the key economic policy question of this moment and regulation has its part to play, even if it is rarely the determinative factor.
In the coming period we will further develop our framework for the secondary competitiveness and growth objective. It will address not only the costs and benefits of regulation, but how our work influences the investment environment, the availability of capital for the firms we regulate and the pricing of the services they provide. We will set out how that framework is embedded in our day-to-day decision-making, and how we will track the effect our work is having on the growth and international competitiveness of the UK.
This framework will help ensure our regime remains relevant, effective, and proportionate. We will engage industry and Parliament as we shape, use and learn from it. It will enable us to be clear and confident about our role, and articulate a well-founded understanding of our contribution to the economy. This is not just a means to deliver against the secondary objective but is ultimately a foundation for good regulation.
Of course, the PRA has already taken steps to keep our regime up to date, most recently working with our FCA colleagues to devise a new captive insurance regime to enable innovation and growth in the insurance market. And to remove barriers to growth and provide predictability, we consulted earlier this month on a framework to automatically index our regulatory thresholds with nominal growth, a first among major financial regulators.
As a next step, we have today set out with the FCA a second set of significant reforms to streamline the Senior Managers and Certification Regime. These proposals reduce the number of senior management functions requiring pre-approval and remove requirements relating to the certification regime, halving its regulatory burden on firms whilst retaining clear accountability of their senior leaders.
Innovation
Our third priority is innovation. The PRA is a world-class regulator. To continue to be so, we must become a world leading technologically enabled regulator. Working with industry, we will go further in refining the data we collect and how we collect it to ensure we can react to emerging issues and risks in a timely manner, while shrinking the need for ad hoc collections and removing collections whose benefits are not justified. We will take feedback from you on this as we go, refining our approach and prioritising the changes that add the most value.
We will accelerate our deployment of data analytics and new technologies, enabling supervisors to rapidly identify emerging themes and trends in risks. Working with industry, we will make it easier and more efficient to work with us by taking innovative approaches to data collection and enhancing the clarity and accessibility of our rulebook and supervisory guidance, streamlining communications so that firms can quickly and easily understand what we expect.
Transparency
And our fourth priority is transparency. A sound understanding of the intentions and priorities of the regulator is crucial for firms to be able to effectively plan and manage their risks. And a stable and predictable business environment is essential to enable investors to deploy capital in the UK economy. So we will provide a clear and transparent line of sight to firms, Parliament and society about our plans and priorities, not least through the publication of and reporting on the new strategy. That will provide the means for us to be held accountable for meeting our commitments and demonstrate that we are a listening and learning organisation.
As an early example of this approach, we will take decisive steps to improve the experience of banks and building societies in relation to internal models for residential mortgages. This has been a source of particular difficulty for many firms, and we need to learn the lessons of this experience.
The PRA has already improved the approval process for firms, and we will go further by providing additional transparency about our operational performance. We will consult in Spring next year on material policy changes to improve firms’ access to a modelled approach. These proposals will be subject to challenge by an independent panel of industry and regulatory experts to ensure their feasibility, learning the lessons of the past to ensure our future policy is grounded in operational realities. Working with our colleagues in the wider Bank, we will also examine the interactions between hybrid mortgage models and stressed buffer requirements.
And we will conduct an independent review of the UK’s implementation of hybrid mortgage model requirements to identify tangible ways to assist firms as they maintain and develop their models. The work of that review will be sequenced to ensure it does not jeopardise the delivery of ongoing model approval and policy work.
Delivering the strategy
The delivery of our strategy will rely on the considerable strengths that characterise the PRA: our deeply expert and purpose-driven people; our comprehensive knowledge of the firms we regulate; and our established approach to supervision – judgement-led, forward-looking and focussed on key risks to safety and soundness. That work has underpinned the success of the PRA’s first twelve years and must never be taken for granted.
As we take the PRA into its second decade, we will build on our strengths and track record by evolving our approach to meet the challenges of today and of tomorrow. We will ensure the financial sector remains resilient to the increasingly volatile environment we now face. We will set out clearly and confidently how we contribute to growth. We will exploit technology to retain our position as a world-leading regulator and supervisor. And we will operate transparently to underpin confidence in our work and thereby in our financial sector and economy.
The PRA in 2032 will be a forward-looking regulator that is respected and trusted. A regulator that is recognised for its work supporting a resilient, competitive and innovative financial system that in turn supports a thriving UK economy. I look forward to working with my PRA colleagues, and importantly also with you all, to deliver that vision.
Now, would you please join me in raising a toast to the Lady Mayor and the Mayoral Consort.

Katharine Braddick
Deputy Governor for Prudential Regulation and Chief Executive Officer of the Prudential Regulation Authority
