articles.title: More than a change of address: Reflections from previous part VIII transfers − speech by Manuel Sales
articles.text:
More than a change of address: Reflections from previous part VIII transfers − speech by Manuel Sales

Given at Association of Financial Mutuals Annual Conference 2026

Published on
05 October 2026

Speech
Opening remarks
Thank you for inviting me to speak today.
Having been in my role for a few months, I have been reflecting on the insights it has given me into how firms operate. One thing that has stood out about mutuals is not just that they are owned by their members, but how that ownership shapes the decisions they make. We can see this in the important role they play in serving parts of the market that may otherwise be underserved.
Against this background, you can understand why the Mutuals Landscape Report sets out our ambition to support the sector’s sustainable long-term growth. What that means will differ from one mutual to another. Many mutuals will continue to operate sustainably. Some will grow organically, while others may pursue acquisitions.
For some mutuals, the strategic challenge is different. They have told us that their current business models may not be sustainable over the longer term. The reasons for this include high levels of competition, keeping pace with technological change, and responding to rapidly-changing economic pressures. Some of these firms are responding by adapting their strategies and exploring new opportunities. Others are considering whether a solvent exit, including through transferring some or all of their business to another firm, may provide the best outcome for their members.
Where the firm being acquired is a friendly society, the transaction will take place through the Part VIII transfer process under the Friendly Societies Act 1992, with the PRA being ultimately responsible for deciding whether a transfer should proceed. While that process is grounded in legislation, we heard feedback that firms would benefit from having a clearer understanding of both the process itself and the factors that inform our decisions. In the Mutuals Landscape Report, we committed to providing more clarity, and CP12/26 (the CP) fulfils that promise. It sets out proposals intended to make our approach clearer and gives firms a more structured sequence of steps to follow. And alongside that, we are also improving the way we manage these transactions internally.
With these initiatives, we aim to promote a dynamic market and support sustainable growth of the mutuals sector.
But the PRA is not the only one working to make this process more efficient. We have also observedfootnote [1] practical approaches developed by firms to improve how these transactions are managed. Today, I want to provide an overview of the Part VIII process. As I do so, I will weave practical insights on how we have seen firms successfully navigate that process, so that others can benefit from the experience of previous transactions.
Reflections from a recent mover
Before turning to those insights, let me take a step back and explain why the process matters.
A Part VIII transfer can offer significant strategic benefits, such as realising economies of scale, improving service standards, and becoming more resilient. All of these improve outcomes for members. But it also requires firms to commit considerable time and resources, with the costs ultimately borne by members. At the PRA, we are very conscious that if a transfer cannot be confirmed, those costs may still have been incurred without the expected benefits being realised. That’s why we work with firms to try to help them build the evidence needed to demonstrate that the legislative requirements have been met.
Meeting those requirements is not just about ticking a legal box. Members rely on the safeguards built into the Part VIII process, including scrutiny by the PRA and FCA, to protect their interests.
So, how should firms approach the Part VIII process?
While no analogy can fully capture the significance of a Part VIII transfer, particularly for mutuals with long histories and strong member communities, it may be helpful in illustrating the process itself, especially for those who are less familiar with Part VIII transfers. The decisions surrounding a transfer are often complex and significant. But when it comes to the process, it has some parallels with moving house. Driving the moving van into your new driveway may feel like the culmination of the journey, but a successful move depends on everything that happened beforehand. You need to understand why you are moving, weigh up the options, complete the necessary checks, and prepare carefully for what follows.
The same is true of a Part VIII transfer.
As the slide shows, we have split that journey into five parts. Let me take each in turn.

Chart 1: Part VIII Transfer Process

Part A: Planning and preparation
Let me start with planning and preparation.
Every house move begins with a reason for moving. When my wife and I bought our home, we spent as much time discussing why we wanted to move as we spent choosing the house. Did we need more space? Or a shorter commute? Once we were clear about our objectives, many of the decisions that followed became easier.
A1: Intention to transfer, A4: Details of transfer plans
When similar questions are considered in the context of a Part VIII transfer, firms may have many avenues to explore. To help firms navigate these factors, the CP highlights the matters the PRA is likely to focus on early in the process, including members' interests.
Of course, firms will generally pursue a transfer because they believe it will deliver better outcomes for members. However, those benefits may not be shared equally between all members, and they may emerge at different times. It is possible that in some circumstances, particular groups of members could be worse off. The key question then is whether the transfer is in the interests of the members of each friendly society participating in the transfer.
Part of answering that question comes from how the benefits are expected to arise. Where a proposal relies on cost savings, operational changes, or integration programmes, those assumptions help explain how the combined business is expected to operate after the transfer. They can provide an important indication of whether there is a credible strategy and a realistic plan to deliver the expected benefits to members.
We have also found it helpful to consider the proposal from another perspective: in what circumstances might some members be worse off? Firms often undertake careful analysis of that question to understand whether potentially adverse impacts have been appropriately considered.
We can work with you as you develop your thinking in this area, which will help with later stages of the transfer. For example, some benefits may depend on integrating the two firms and could take several years to emerge. Whilst there are different ways to ensure that members will be protected in the meantime, the PRA can work with firms to establish what evidence could help show that the legal test has been met. These discussions could inform the transfer documentation, actuarial analysis, and communications with members.
A2: Preparations, updating rules, and applying for permission
Moving on to the preparations step, we have seen firms take a careful and considered approach to the practical aspects of the process. That includes considering whether the acquirer has the necessary regulatory permissions. This matters because permissions do not transfer with the business.
As an extra check, some firms have used the FCA’s register to compare the transferring society’s permission with the acquirer’s permission. This has allowed the acquirer to confirm whether it has identified and addressed any gaps in its permission.
This has also helped firms explain why a permission will no longer be required to cover specific regulated activities and, in doing so, show that the relevant statutory test has been met. These checks may appear relatively small. But when carried out early, they help the wider process run more efficiently.
A3: Considerations of overseas members and regulators
Turning to overseas members, this relates to one of the statutory tests, where the PRA must assess whether there is a substantial risk that the acquirer will be unable legally to carry on the business being transferred. This is usually relatively straightforward for members in the UK, but firms have found it more challenging for members based overseas.
Much of that work begins with a simple question: where are your members based? Maintaining up-to-date member records has helped firms with this work. There are other useful ways of checking those records. Some firms may find it helpful to consider payments to and from non-UK bank accounts to identify any other overseas members.
With that information in hand, firms can consider their overseas members in the context of the legal test and develop a reasoned explanation of why the legal test is met. There is a range of different forms of evidence to consider, from local legal advice to the relevant EIOPA recommendationfootnote [2]. The CP highlights engagement with overseas regulators, which firms may find to be a practical and cost-effective way of exploring the position.
While these steps should help, we recognise that firms continue to face challenges in this area. Indeed, we engaged with the Law Commission on the issue ahead of its recently published proposals. At our recent roundtablefootnote [3], firms also suggested ways in which the PRA could help firms with the overseas member part of the process. We are considering if we can further clarify what information we might need from firms in order for the PRA to assess the legal test under the existing legislation. We will, of course, consider this feedback alongside any responses we receive to the CP.
A5: PRA’s approach to special resolution: consent for Part VIII transfers
Let me turn to the final part of planning and preparation: what many firms call the dispensation process. This is where the acquiring society can seek the PRA's consent for the transfer to be approved by its board, rather than through a special resolution voted on by its members.
Giving the acquirer’s members the opportunity to vote is an important safeguard, so it is not a requirement the PRA will dispense with lightly. But we also recognise that holding a vote comes at a cost, which is ultimately borne by members.
In the past, firms have told us that this is one of the less predictable parts of the process, so we have added more clarity on our approach in the CP. It provides some reference points for how the PRA is likely to consider whether to consent to a dispensation. One of these is that firms will also need to show that the transfer is in the interests of the acquirer’s members and that there are no factors likely to lead a material number of them to vote against it. Firms are likely to benefit from discussing this with their transfer partner and considering this point together.
For example, that collaboration may bring to light a history of tension between the societies that could influence how members would vote if they were given the opportunity. Factors like this don’t necessarily mean that consent couldn’t be granted. But open discussions on such matters can help the PRA understand the position more quickly and reduce the need for further questions.
Part B: Recording and analysing the transfer
Let me move on to recording and analysing the transfer.
Once my family had decided which house to buy, our attention turned to the practicalities. The paperwork began, surveys were commissioned and the important decisions had to be documented.
The same is true of a Part VIII transfer. Once firms have developed their proposal, the focus shifts to documenting the terms of the transfer and analysing its effects.
B1: Instrument of Transfer
Once firms are clear about the purpose and structure of the transaction, that understanding must be captured in the Instrument of Transfer. Producing the Instrument is a statutory requirement, but it can also provide important protections for the members of both firms.
The Instrument can cover a wide range of matters, from service standards to membership rights. We have seen firms benefit from bringing together legal, risk, and actuarial specialists to develop it. It has also helped firms consider not only what is needed to give effect to the transfer, but what additional protections could be provided to members, both now and over the long-term.
Those protections will depend on the circumstances of each transfer. We have seen firms consider important safeguards for the management of transferred funds, appropriate governance arrangements, and commitments about the future treatment of policyholders.
Where with-profits policies are involved, firms have found it helpful to specify the fund to which those policies will be allocated and how expenses will be apportioned. They have also considered what support may be available from other funds, particularly where this could affect the receiving fund’s investment strategy. Setting out these details in the draft Instrument can then provide a clear basis for the actuarial analysis supporting the transfer.
B2: Internal actuarial reports, B3: Independent actuary report and supplementary report(s)
The actuarial analysis is an important part of the process. Internal actuarial reports help boards and regulators understand how a proposed transfer is expected to affect members. Clear and balanced reports can also provide a strong foundation for communications with members, particularly where outcomes are uncertain or depend on judgement. The more useful reports explain the assumptions, evidence, and reasoning behind the conclusions they reach.
In our experience, the more complete internal actuarial reports consider how members are expected to be affected before the transfer, immediately after the transfer, as well as after any integration of the two businesses. This helps all of us – including members – understand both the destination and the journey to get there.
The firms’ own analysis is important. However, in some cases, the process also requires an independent perspective. Much as an independent surveyor provides an objective assessment when someone is purchasing a property, the Independent Actuary provides independent scrutiny of the firms’ analysis. The CP provides greater clarity on when we are likely to require a report from an Independent Actuary. We hope this will help firms better understand the likely costs of a transfer.
Where an Independent Actuary provides a report, the legislation requires it to address the likely effects of the transfer on members who are long-term policyholders. We have found that reports are most useful when they explain both the positive and adverse effects, how those effects may differ between groups of policyholders, and the basis for any conclusions about materiality. Of course, this balanced analysis helps members understand the proposal. But it also supports the PRA’s assessment of whether the transfer is in members’ interests, alongside the FCA’s consideration of fairness.
As an aside, we have found that it is often a good idea for firms to also consider any FCA requirements that apply to the transaction (for example, if the FCA's reattribution rules for with-profits business apply).
There is also an important relationship between the internal actuarial reports and the Independent Actuary’s report. If an internal report contains material information that is not reflected in the summary of the Independent Actuary’s report included in communications sent to members, firms will need to consider whether members have received all the information they need to understand the proposal and make an informed decision. This is one of the statutory tests the PRA must assess. In previous transfers, we have worked with firms to understand how they have met it.
Even where an Independent Actuary is not appointed, another form of independent review may still be valuable. We have seen firms benefit from independent peer review of their internal actuarial analysis and key judgements. This can strengthen the overall assessment and give members greater confidence in the analysis, particularly where they are considering whether to make representations about the proposed transfer.
Part C: Member engagement and member vote(s)
Having considered the key documents supporting a transfer, the next stage is to translate them into communications that members can understand and engage with.
When my family moved house, it wasn’t enough for me to know the plan. Everyone needed to understand what was happening, why it was happening and what it means for them (or, in our case, who was getting the biggest bedroom). Member engagement is similar. The technical analysis may be robust, but it only serves its purpose if members can understand what the transfer means for them.
C1: Member engagement: general approach, C2: Member engagement: Schedule 15 statement, C3: Resolutions
Member communications play an important role in informing how members vote. So, as you would expect, the FCA considers them through the lens of the Consumer Duty, with a focus on ensuring that they are clear and easy to understand. What makes the Part VIII transfer process slightly different is that the PRA also has a statutory role in reviewing one of the key communications sent to members: the Schedule 15 statement.
The CP provides more details on what the PRA considers as part of that review. I want to reflect on some practical approaches that we have seen work well in previous transfers.
The more developed Schedule 15 statements are those that clearly explain what the transfer means for members. They present the key considerations fairly and help members reach their own view. One approach that could work well is testing communications before they are finalised. We have read documents that include all the relevant technical details, but it is not always clear whether these messages are framed in the best way for members to fully understand them. To ensure that the proposed messages can be understood, it may be helpful to run the proposed communications past a colleague who has not been involved in the transfer or seek feedback from a small group of members.
We have also seen the value of careful and balanced drafting. The stronger summaries of the Independent Actuary’s conclusions tend to be those that faithfully reflect the full report while focusing on the matters most relevant to members’ decisions.
Of course, even the clearest communication is only effective if it reaches the people for whom it is intended. The legislation requires the Schedule 15 statement to be sent to all eligible voting members. Where firms have faced challenges contacting members, we have seen a range of practical approaches, including tracing exercises, updating records, using alternative contact methods, and contacting members directly to confirm their details. Firms have also used press notices and other engagement channels to raise awareness of the transfer and the voting process. In some cases, firms have supplemented this with dedicated webpages containing information about the transfer.
Although I have focused on the Schedule 15 statement, we have seen firms engage with their members in different ways. This includes with letters, frequently asked questions, presentations, webinars, and online material. The aim is to help members understand the proposed transfer and give them a genuine opportunity to engage with the proposal before casting their vote. Where members are effectively engaged, it helps firms address issues and reduce the likelihood of unexpected representations arising later in the transfer process.
Part D: Formal application, public notices, and representations
When buying a house, arguably the most important stage is the period leading up to the exchange of contracts. During that stage, surveyors, solicitors, mortgage brokers, and banks can all raise questions, identify risks or challenge assumptions underlying the proposed purchase.
D1: Formal notice of the application
The formal notice of the application plays an important role in the period leading up to the transaction, bringing it to the attention of interested parties and ensuring that those affected have an opportunity to engage with the process.
Firms will submit the formal notice after the member vote. So, whilst the progression of these tasks remains subject to member approval, there is preparatory work we can do ahead of that. In previous transfers, firms have provided draft notices for our review.
The PRA will also direct firms to publish the notice in the London, Edinburgh, or Belfast Gazettes as well as other newspapers where appropriate. However, firms can suggest which Gazette(s) and newspapers they feel would be the most appropriate.
D2: Approach to representations, D3: Representations Hearing
Once the formal notice has been published, the representations period begins. It gives members and other stakeholders an opportunity to raise concerns about the transfer.
But the representations process is about more than formal representations submitted directly to the PRA. Firms also consider whether concerns, complaints, or queries received through their own channels raise issues that are similar in nature to a formal representation. These interactions can provide valuable insight into the matters that are most important to members.
Part E: Confirmation Assessment Meeting(s) and related processes
The final stage of buying a house is exchanging contracts and moving into the property. By that point, much of the hard work has already been done. The legal issues have been addressed and the financing agreed. What remains is to finalise the purchase arrangements. The same principle applies to the final stage of a Part VIII transfer.
E1: Preparations for the Confirmation Assessment Meeting(s), E2: Confirmation Assessment Meeting(s)
The Preclusion Grounds Analysis sits at the heart of this stage. It explains why none of the statutory grounds that would prevent the PRA from confirming the transfer have been met. The stronger submissions tend to be balanced and leverage the evidence already generated throughout the transfer process and present it in a thorough and structured way.
Let me give you an example. When looking at the solvency ground, some firms carefully consider whether the acquiring society will maintain an adequate margin of solvency after the transfer. They bring together the evidence supporting that conclusion, such as post-transfer financial projections, actuarial analysis, audited financial information, and any material changes since the latest valuation date.
We have seen a similar approach taken when considering whether the members’ vote was representative. Firms’ analysis usually explains why the requirements of the legislation and the relevant society rules have been met. The more developed analyses also consider factors such as how voting turnout compares with previous member votes and whether the outcome would have changed under different assumptions. For example, where some members could not be traced despite reasonable efforts being made to contact them, firms could consider whether the outcome of the member vote would have been different if those members had voted against the transfer.
Perhaps the area where we have seen the greatest variation is the assessment of whether the proposed transfer is in the interests of the members of both societies. The more developed analyses bring together actuarial, risk, and legal evidence to consider factors such as benefit security, benefit expectations, service standards, and membership rights. They also identify situations in which some members may be disadvantaged and explain how those risks have been assessed and mitigated.
In considering firms’ post-transfer target operating models, we have taken a proportionate approach, with discussions often centred on three related questions.

How will the enlarged business operate immediately after the transfer?
What is the target operating model?
How does the firm intend to move from one to the other?

E3: The PRA’s decision, E4: Processes after the Confirmation Assessment Meeting(s)
After the PRA has reached its decision, it is not the end of the journey. There are a few procedural steps left including issuing the decision notice and registering the Instrument of Transfer.
Firms will also continue implementing aspects of their target operating model after the transfer has completed. Boards should continue to satisfy themselves that members are seeing the expected benefits from the transfer.
Closing remarks
I appreciate that this statutory process may feel a long and complex journey. But members rely on the safeguards built into the Part VIII process, including scrutiny by the PRA and FCA, so it’s right that we approach the statutory requirements with care.
At the same time, we recognise that members ultimately benefit from an efficient process. CP12/26 sets out our proposals to make our approach clearer, more transparent, and easier to navigate. Your engagement has already informed those proposals, and I would encourage you to respond to the consultation so that we can continue refining our approach together.
I don’t want to close without recognising the important work being undertaken by the Law Commission to modernise the legislative framework for friendly societies. We have engaged with the Law Commission as it has developed its final report and draft bill Opens in a new window. Should any legislative changes be made, the PRA stands ready to update its approach and guidance as necessary.
I hope that what I’ve shared today will highlight that a successful transfer is not simply about completing a transaction or changing an address. It’s about finding the right long-term home for a friendly society’s members.
I am grateful to Hannah-Kousar Rashid for preparing these remarks. I am also grateful to Abi Batchelor, Alex Tapp, Giles Woodruff, Nozipho Gazi, Robert Kipling, Robyn Dwyer, Sanjeev Chandran, and Wayne Snow for their support and comments.

The observations shared in this speech are based on a range of firms and transfers at different times. They are illustrative of the general approach taken. Some details may have been changed or combined from different transfers to ensure confidentiality. As such, the information included should not be considered attributable to any one firm or transfer.

Why oil refineries must evolve to survive

For the oil-refining industry, the energy transition is an existential challenge. While refineries are critical to national energy security, as the Middle East conflict and the Russia-Ukraine war have shown, declining global oil demand in future means that closures are inevitable.
Each of the world’s 700-plus refineries is unique in its capacity, crude slate, configuration, product yield and market access. All operate in a landscape shaped by macroeconomic, geopolitical and energy transition pressures, however, and that landscape is evolving.
Slowing population growth, electrification and improving fuel efficiency lead Wood Mackenzie to expect that global oil demand will peak in the early 2030s and decline gradually after that. All refiners face this market-driven destiny, although the exact pressures will vary by region.
There is no universal remedy that can bestow long-term resilience, but many refineries will be able to strengthen their position if they make the right choices. This edition of Horizons examines the options available and explains which type of refinery will be best placed to adapt to survive and even thrive in this changing environment.

All eyes on refining
The refining sector has its own distinct and complex fundamental drivers. Oil refining is, at its core, a conversion business. This means refining margins are mostly independent of oil prices, driven instead by the difference in price between oil products and crude oil, known as ‘crack spreads’. For refiners operating between these large commodity markets, where persistent investment drives competition, typical benchmark margins are relatively thin. However, the most competitive refiners, or those with structural advantages, outperform significantly.
The spotlight has been on refiners since the start of the Middle East conflict. Disruption to Middle Eastern oil supply has pushed benchmark refining margins to record highs, as constrained crude and oil product supply struggles to meet global demand. This strain has been exacerbated by damage to Russian refineries. The resulting energy shock has forced many countries to ban oil product exports, implement commercial curfews, close businesses or release strategic oil reserves.
Yet, the sector also faces major long-term structural and strategic challenges. To navigate these, refiners must adapt to evolving patterns of crude oil supply, product demand, increasing competition, and tighter environmental and sustainability targets.
The highly competitive nature of the sector means that long-run average refining margins are slim, and currently elevated margins will return to more modest levels when the Middle East conflict ends. Refining generates lower returns on capital than upstream, increasing the challenge that downstream companies face in accessing the capital needed to make critical investments for the future.
Figure 1: Crude price and refining margins are loosely connected Brent price vs global composite gross refining margin (US$/bbl, real)

Source: Wood Mackenzie Product Markets Service
A history of adaptation, resilience and innovation
The refining sector has always adapted to ever-changing market dynamics. Refineries were originally established by oil majors as a critical part of a vertically integrated supply chain that spanned well to wheels. The emergence of global commodity markets in the 1980s relegated refining to a low-margin sector suffering from over-capacity, as the oil shocks of the 1970s disrupted the trajectory of oil demand growth. Petrochemical integration was a source of value, with the supply of clean fuels becoming a ‘stay-in-business’ requirement. The construction wave of new refining capacity across the Middle East and Asia in the 2000s delivered national benefits broader than earning a commercial rate of return, namely, domestic energy resilience, a platform for further industrialisation and value capture along the supply chain.
The refining sector has had to constantly evolve with the needs of the market and policymakers. Those that have been bold and able to adapt to these ever-changing dynamics have grown into the successful oil majors, refining specialists and major national oil companies (NOCs) we know today.
Figure 2: The refining sector has evolved to meet market and policy needs

Expand

Competitive position is a key attribute for all refineries, measured by their net cash margin (NCM), the cash from refining operations after payment of feedstock, fixed and variable costs on a per-barrel-of-throughput basis. The following figure shows the global refining NCM profile for 2024 and 2025. New refineries target a first-quartile position to generate high cash flow, with major refinery upgrades aiming to move sites up the curve. These investments push other sites down the curve towards lower margins – refiners who do nothing are effectively on a downward escalator.
Figure 3: Refinery earnings vary widely, with few loss-making sites in 2024 and 2025Global NCM profile against cumulative refining capacity (kb/d)

Source: Wood Mackenzie Refinery Evaluation Model
Competitive advantage is secured through combinations of:

obtaining access to lower-cost crude oil (either through location or crude quality)
investing to build a complex configuration that can convert and upgrade lower-value crudes into higher-value transport fuels, petrochemicals and speciality products
locking in advantaged access to demand centres, where alternative sources of product supply involve costly import logistics
integrating with upstream or downstream operations, ranging from crude production to retail fuel sales, petrochemical supply and trading operations
ensuring low costs of energy, labour and emissions.

Many of these factors are location/country dependent and cannot be readily replicated by refineries in other regions. Scale is not included here, as it is established at the point of construction. Although it is a key driver of investment economics, its impact on NCM is limited to lowering fixed costs on a per-barrel basis.
The energy transition threatens the commercial viability of the refining sector in its current form. Declining demand for refined products means more sites will become loss-making, leading to closure unless they adapt. There is no adaptation silver bullet, however, due to the uneven pace of regional energy transition and the heterogeneity of the refining sector.

Regional and industrial characteristics
Each refinery is unique and most assets have been developed over time to meet the specific scale, needs and product focus of their relevant markets, available feedstocks and access to technology. Some refineries can trace their origins back more than a century. Most new-build assets over the past decade feature economies of scale, high complexity, petrochemical integration and high-efficiency, low-emission technologies. Differences in such features are the primary determinants of which assets will remain competitive as the energy transition applies pressure unevenly across products and geographies.

Refining archetypes
While all refineries are unique, they can be divided into five main archetypes, which serve as a useful lens for considering potential future adaptation strategies:

Large scale, high complexity. These are among the most competitive assets, benefitting from economies of scale and an ability to process a wide range of lower-quality crudes into the highest-value oil products, enabling them to push products successfully into export markets. Examples include major refineries on the US Gulf Coast, modern export-oriented refineries in the Middle East and the new Dangote refinery in Nigeria.
Complex chemical-integrated. Refineries that also have major petrochemical production facilities (such as stream cracking, aromatics or polymers) can shift output away from declining transport fuel markets and increase their margin. Examples include several medium-scale integrated refiners in Europe and Asia, and an increasing number of new, highly integrated mega-sites in China.
Coastal cracking. The most common refining type. They have some ability to upgrade crude to transport fuels, but lack full-complexity conversion of heavier products. Their coastal location gives them access to imported crudes and product distribution, but exposes them to international competition. Most refineries in OECD countries are configured in this way.
Small-scale speciality. Smaller-scale assets with production focused on high-value, niche products such as lubricants, bitumen, waxes and solvents. Their lack of scale and complexity is both a strength and a weakness; they do not compete in commodity markets and have less exposure to declining transport fuel demand. A small number of this type of asset already exists around the world.
Small scale, low complexity. Small assets with only the simplest refinery upgrading processes, typically only producing transport fuels. Their edge is often that they are the only supply source for a given product in a particular location, making them resilient to global shifts, but vulnerable to local disruption. Most of the refineries of this type have either already been upgraded to more complex types or closed due to lack of profitability. Examples include NOC-owned and operated assets in developing countries, which are often protected, so continue to operate despite incurring losses.

Refineries are most commonly described in terms of their crude distillation unit (CDU) capacity, a basic crude processing scale; complexity (on a scale of 1 to 25), which measures how much a refinery has invested in plant and equipment to upgrade crude into higher-value products, with a higher score reflecting more flexibility on crude quality and product yield; and NCM.

Refineries with a higher complexity are generally capable of achieving greater NCM, but other crude and location-specific factors also have a significant impact.
Figure 4: Refinery complexity is an important driver of NCM

Note: The chart excludes refineries with capacity lower than 150 kb/d.
Source: Wood Mackenzie Refinery Evaluation Model
Changes driving adaptation
Refined product demand is expected to peak at 108 mb/d in 2032 (from 105 mb/d in 2025) before declining. The pace of the energy transition will not be uniform, but rather driven by economics and policy, leading to regional differences. Generally, robust growth in electric vehicle uptake will hit gasoline demand hardest, while diesel/gasoil and jet/kerosene will remain comparatively resilient as heavy road transport and aviation lack a clear route to decarbonisation. Liquified petroleum gas (LPG) and naphtha will be supported by growing demand for petrochemical feedstocks. Demand for speciality products (such as lubricants, waxes, bitumen and sulphur) will remain largely independent of the energy transition, as bio-based alternatives do not yet exist at scale.
The energy transition requires decarbonisation of both a refinery’s operations and its product outputs. European refineries are more likely to invest in operational decarbonisation than Asian or Middle Eastern competitors due to national and European Union (EU)-level emissions policy. As carbon capture and green hydrogen adoption has yet to scale, reducing indirect end-use emissions may prove the more viable route: some sustainable aviation fuels already cut emissions by up to 80% compared with conventional jet fuel.
Against a backdrop of declining demand, diverging costs and uneven pressure from policymakers to decarbonise, new investments in capacity expansion are increasingly difficult to justify. The exception is where demand growth and security-of-supply concerns are still strong enough to override the economics; India alone is expected to host 40% of global capacity additions to 2030 as part of a broader push for self-reliance.
This, though, is capacity added locally into a global market in decline. The defining global feature of the next decade and beyond will be refinery rationalisation, with an estimated 20% of existing global capacity – those on the ‘down escalator’ (with falling or negative NCM) ‒ increasingly at risk of closure. Exposure to that risk varies sharply by archetype, reflecting how unevenly competitive advantages hold up under pressure. Refiners will, therefore, need to understand their relative market, policy and competitive exposure, and consider what strategies they may need to deploy.

Adapt or die
There is a range of adaptation strategies that can be deployed. Not all options may be viable for each refinery, and the high capital cost and future market uncertainty make some of these investments challenging. Refiners will need to make strategic decisions on the way forward in an uncertain world.
Figure 5: Potential refinery pathways and outcomes

Expand

Petrochemical integration
This is the primary means of offsetting declining road-fuel demand by shifting LPG and naphtha molecules into the production of olefins, aromatics and polymers. Petrochemical investments are more likely to be attractive at world scale while there is persistent demand growth, as the petrochemical market navigates its own cyclical nature and large-scale, competing investments. Asian and Middle Eastern exporters lead with large, heavily integrated facilities built with state backing.Smaller-scale simple and cracking configurations (for example, EU and US assets) are likely to lack the scale to be competitive here. Larger complex sites and new greenfield assets in advantaged locations (for example, in the Middle East and Asia) are the most likely candidates for major future chemicals integration.
Bio and circular conversion
This involves substituting crude oil with sustainable feedstocks (such as used cooking oil, pyrolysis or recycled plastic feedstocks, and second-generation ethanol) to produce higher-value/policy-mandated sustainable products, such as renewable diesel or sustainable aviation fuel. The technology is now well developed, and lower-level co-processing of these feedstocks has been incorporated into conventional refineries. There are also options to develop dedicated processing units or convert older/closed refinery processing units, but competition for limited volumes of quality renewable feedstocks will pose a challenge. This will largely apply to those refiners with greatest access to these premium markets (namely, EU coastal refineries). However, production could be developed by assets outside key consumer markets if they have access to renewable feedstocks and export finished products.
Carbon capture and storage (CCS)
CCS is essential to mitigating direct plant CO2 emissions, reducing emissions costs and maintaining a social licence to operate (in regions with relevant policy or societal pressure). It could become an existential retrofit for regions with high emission costs. Major investments have so far remained challenging, as the capital and operating costs of such facilities are high, the technology is relatively nascent, and the commercial case typically relies on government support. The cost-efficient deployment of capture technology and access to sequestration sites will remain a challenge.This option is most likely in Europe and the wider OECD region, whereas many Asian, Middle Eastern or developing-country facilities face no immediate pressure to deploy it.
Double down on conventional upgrading
Leaning into scale and complexity is the most intuitive way for refineries to improve their yield slate and product value, processing lower-cost feedstocks and benefitting from economies of scale. This will require significant capital investment in conventional refining processing to increase the crude processing and product upgrading capacity of the plant, increasing margins and economies of scale, but exposing the asset further to competitive export markets.
This option is most feasible for Middle Eastern/Asian refiners with access to capital, space to expand and access to export markets. A smaller number of well-positioned assets in other regions may also be able to achieve this, but all will need to be able to out-muscle competitors in key product export markets.
Capacity consolidation
This involves reducing crude processing capacity to fit product output into the local advantaged hinterland markets where they may have stronger pricing power and limited competitive pressure. This approach increases effective site complexity, as consolidated sites can selectively rationalise crude capacity and optimise their upgrading capabilities.This approach may be favoured by inland refiners in declining markets with costly logistics that make exports to coastal/international markets prohibitive (for example, refineries in OECD countries with declining domestic demand).
Focus on speciality products
Refineries can focus on low-volume, high-value non-transport products (such as lubricants, waxes, bitumen or niche petrochemicals) that will remain in demand and be largely insulated from the energy transition. This shift away from commodity fuel markets is often more of an art than a science, with success requiring highly advanced capabilities, including trading, marketing and distribution. Limited demand for these products will make this option challenging for many players. Such an approach may be favoured by smaller assets with limited scale and few alternatives. Owners with existing integration or experience in these speciality markets may be best placed.
Full value-chain integration
Integrated assets span upstream production, midstream infrastructure, retail distribution networks and trading capabilities. This approach has the potential to capture additional margin and secure offtake of production and renewable feedstocks, or place product into secure sales channels. This has been a common approach for many of the oil majors in the past, but divestments across the business have led to a more fractured and merchant system. This approach may become more relevant again in a post-peak-oil-demand world and is an increasingly common operating model for trading companies and major NOCs.
Diversification of the business
Refineries can move into adjacent sectors. This may be driven by a desire to manage longer-term exposure to pure refining-sector margins via investment in adjacent sectors, such as power supply, renewables, energy and product storage, gas/liquefied natural gas, ammonia, chemicals/derivatives, retail fuels and electric vehicle charging.This approach may be more applicable to independent refiners in declining markets that lack the scale or position to make larger or structural investments in their small or medium scale refineries.

A refinery’s afterlife
Fewer options exist for the weakest refining assets driven to closure by poor commercial performance or failure to adapt.

Terminal conversion. This is a pragmatic exit strategy when complex retrofits are not economically viable. Location is key to success: by leveraging market access, infrastructure and deep-water logistics, operators can preserve a vital foothold in the regional supply chain by repurposing existing oil and product storage tanks and marine facilities.
Conversion to other industrial use. Examples of this strategy include power generation as an energy park or the production of alternative fuels.
Closure and site remediation. If a refinery is unable to adapt or overcome the challenges of a rapidly tightening market, its inevitable outcome is site closure with land remediation, potentially at a significant cost.

Conclusion:A vision of future refining

World-class refineries of the future will be based around highly competitive assets located in integrated energy and product parks, producing fuels, liquid renewables, petrochemicals and speciality products. They will produce and deliver lower-carbon products through decarbonised operations and have the scale and complexity to compete internationally.
The broader ecosystem will contain ‘sector specialists’ and bio-sites that can monetise local competitive advantages, whether through advantaged feedstock availability, regulatory frameworks or state support. Refineries that are not first-quartile performers need to plan to pivot away from transport fuels and establish when this shift is to be made, as 2040 is only three to four turnaround cycles away.
While oil products remain the backbone of the global economy, refining will remain a strategically vital industry for several decades. However, evolving demand and operating standards mean that it will be necessary to adapt.
Not all refineries will be able to do so effectively, but many will survive and thrive, continuing to ensure the smooth functioning of the global economy.
Hope is not a strategy, so refiners need to continue to adapt, or die.

articles.title: The future of work: A more human transformation
articles.text:
Economics & markets

The future of work: A more human transformation

November 03, 2026

We live in an age of technological disruption. Increasingly capable technologies such as artificial intelligence can seem to set the stage for an apocalyptic future without jobs.

As Vanguard Global Chief Economist Joe Davis will discuss with Aneesh Raman at the New York Times DealBook Summit on November 18, the reality is more encouraging. Raman is chief economic opportunity officer at Microsoft and coauthor of the best-selling book Open to Work: How to Get Ahead in the Age of AI. Davis is the author of the best-selling Coming Into View: How AI and Other Megatrends Will Shape Your Investments.
Vanguard has been studying the future of work for nearly 10 years, since we began the research that culminated in our October 2018 paper Megatrends: The future of work. In that paper, we argued that technology automates tasks, not entire jobs. We concluded that as work shifts toward uniquely human activities, labor demand should persist. The challenge is equipping workers with the technological, creative, and emotional skills needed in an increasingly automated economy.

Algorithms and uniquely human tasks

Today, most occupations contain tasks complementary to AI. We're spending less time on repetitive, rules-based tasks that can be captured in an algorithm and more time on uniquely human tasks.
AI’s path combines three mechanisms of technological change. Automation brings efficiency gains as tasks shift from human to machine execution. Augmentation is when machines enhance human productivity. And transformation happens when general-purpose technologies fundamentally reorganize economic production.
History offers perspective on the timeline ahead. Electricity initially depressed productivity as factories and workers adapted. The surge came only after decades of reorganization. Digital computers emerged in the 1940s, but their impact accelerated only in the late 1980s and 1990s. AI appears positioned to unfold over an accelerated timeline.

The labor market paradox ahead

The vast majority of occupations will see their task compositions evolve as automation takes hold. New jobs requiring uniquely human capabilities will emerge. The workforce transformation underway is less about jobs vanishing and more about roles adapting. We’re heading toward a labor market paradox—more robots, but not enough people.
This competition between technology and demographics isn’t new. British economist Thomas Malthus predicted in 1798 that population growth would outpace food production. The Earth’s population grew from more than 800 million then to eight billion today while becoming richer and healthier. Technological progress has repeatedly defied such warnings. Preparing the workforce for jobs that demand more of us as humans and less of us as machines remains the critical challenge ahead.

articles.title: Democratic Midterm Wins Alter the Crypto and AI Landscape
articles.text:
Insights / Research / Democrats’ Sweeping Victory Alters Landscape for Crypto, AI

Written by:

Alex Thorn
Head of Firmwide Research

Topics

AI

Cryptocurrency

Regulation

research • November 06, 2026

Democrats’ Sweeping Victory Alters Landscape for Crypto, AI

This article originally appeared in Galaxy Research's weekly newsletter. Subscribe to get timely insights delivered to your inbox every Friday morning.WHAT HAPPENEDDemocrats won both the U.S. House and Senate by wide margins, guaranteeing divided government for the second half of President Trump’s second term. Democrats flipped seven Senate seats (with two still uncalled as of writing), 35 House seats, five governorships, and up to 12 state legislative chambers.Democrats likely secured the fourth-best midterm performance on the House side since 1986 with a projected +35 to 41 new seats from their prior 214, which is behind losses for the incumbent president’s party in 2010 (-64) and 1994 (-54), almost even with 2018 (-42), and ahead of 2006 (-30). On the Senate side, Democrats’ performance places it near the top of the last 10 midterms, with +7 vs. the incumbent president’s party beating all but 1986 and 1994 (both -8) and 2014 (-9). Ballotpedia qualifies the Senate gains as a “wave” though the House margin still falls short of the site’s standard for that language. This is only the third time since 1986 that the opposition party flipped both Congressional chambers in a midterm election.

The most notable Congressional loss for digital assets advocates came in Ohio, where Jon Husted (R), who had filled J.D. Vance’s vacated seat, lost to former Senator Sherrod Brown (D). Brown had previously been Chair of the Senate Banking Committee but was ousted in 2024 by Sen. Bernie Moreno (R), a former car dealership owner who founded a firm using blockchain technology to trace vehicle title ownership and who was heavily backed by crypto advocates in 2024. Crypto political action committees had reportedly spent $40m supporting Husted and $24m opposing Brown. Other key crypto advocate losses included Bryan Steil (R-WI), head of the House Financial Services digital assets subcommittee; Zach Nunn (R-IA); Ann Wagner (R-MO); Bill Huizenga (R-MI); and Mike Lawler (R-NY) (who conceded though the race has yet to be called by AP). At the time of writing, the Chairman of the House Financial Services Committee, French Hill (R-AR), was ahead by 4400 votes in a race that is still too close to call.Other digital assets supporters had better evenings, with Josh Gottheimer (D-NJ), Ritchie Torres (D-NY), and House Agriculture Chair GT Thompson (R-PA) all reelected. Senator Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY), a leading Democratic voice on crypto and the chair of the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, delivered a bigger-than-expected majority for the party in the Senate, possibly strengthening her standing in the caucus. Overall, Stand With Crypto counts 19 pro-crypto senators and 226 pro-crypto House members elected against eight anti-crypto senators and 106 anti-crypto House members. Industry critic Molly White’s tracker finds that in the 12 competitive races so far, the side backed by crypto and AI PACs lost nine, while the industry’s picks in safer races went 40 for 40.With the Senate and House flipping to Democrats, committee leadership will also flip. Senator Elizabeth Warren (D-MA) is likely to become Chair of Senate Banking, while Rep. Maxine Waters (D-CA) is again positioned to helm the House Financial Services Committee. Artificial intelligence advocates also faced setbacks, with the AI industry’s “biggest bet on a competitive general election race” going to Darline Graham in South Carolina, who lost to Annie Andrews. The data center fight was perhaps most consequential in Texas, where Democrats won every statewide office for the first time in three decades, though Republicans held control of the Texas Senate 19-12. Gina Hinojosa (D) defeated Gov. Greg Abbott (R) 53% to 46%, and Democrats also won lieutenant governor, attorney general, comptroller, and railroad commissioner. Markets performed well immediately following the election, with bitcoin rallying back above $80,000 and the S&P 500 and Nasdaq each gaining over 1% on Wednesday, but broader markets rolled over Thursday morning, with tech, AI, data center names, and crypto all trading lower. At the time of writing, S&P 500 was -3.7% and Nasdaq 100 -5.5% on the day, bitcoin was trading at $75,888, just above its 50-week moving average ($75,838), while ether was trading -6.8% at $2249. The dollar held mostly flat while gold and oil rose.

OUR TAKETuesday’s election result is already the biggest Senate loss for a president’s party since 2014, and the House is on track to be the fourth biggest midterm loss since 1986, or third if House gains top 2018’s 42 seats. A 260-seat Democratic House would be the biggest majority since 1991-93 when Democrats held 267. The House win is even more notable in 2026 given that in 1994 and 2010 the losing party held dozens of seats that leaned toward the other party, so there were plenty of easy pickups. Today’s House is much more sorted with fewer competitive districts. And the Democratic strength extended deep down the ballot, gaining five governorships giving them 21 trifectas (when one party holds the governorship and both chambers of the state legislature), the party’s most since 1992. In a post on X, Vice President JD Vance wrote that “the reason we lost is the war” in Iran, and offered four fixes for Republicans: ending the war, focusing on cost of living and inflation, putting America first, and changing the U.S. relationship with Israel. At a press conference, Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R-FL) called the election “close to an extinction-level event for Republicans in many parts of the country” and added that it was a rejection of Republicans in Washington. “This midterm, no question, was a rebuke of the president and the Congress,” he later told Fox News.Senator Jon Ossoff (D-GA) said in his victory speech that the Democratic victories were the “first sight of dawn” two years into Trump’s second term. Senator Ed Markey (D-MA), who himself beat Republican crypto advocate challenger John Deaton, posted on X about Big Tech executives, saying “they are going to need to plant new forests for all of the subpoenas.” Rep. Greg Casar, chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, called for AI CEOs to testify under oath. Politico reported that several major Washington law firms are hiring lawyers to help clients handle the new scrutiny. Incoming House Oversight Chair Robert Garcia warned Republicans to “lawyer up.” Fortune reported that Trump family businesses, including World Liberty Financial, would face additional scrutiny.The big question is the extent to which Democrats focus on investigations and backward-looking scrutiny versus demonstrating to the country that the party is ready to lead. Tyler Williams, former Counselor to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, told me on the Galaxy Brains podcast this week that Democrats will at some point need to demonstrate the capability to govern before heading into the 2028 election cycle. That need could moderate their more partisan instincts. Markets fell sharply Thursday on speculation that Democrats would increase scrutiny of AI, but another big story was AI’s setbacks in the states. No statewide data center measures were on the ballot this year. A proposed Ohio constitutional ban on data centers above 25 megawatt capacity failed to qualify, and a Massachusetts initiative is aiming for 2028. But local measures went overwhelmingly against data centers: of 41 on Tuesday’s ballot in 10 states, voters sided against data centers in 40. Twenty-seven of 28 restrictions passed, and all 13 measures that would have eased development failed. Ohio accounted for 21 of the 41, including 11 bans. The lone exception was the city of Harwood, North Dakota (population: 794). While Georgia had no ballot measure on data centers, Democrats won majority control of the Public Service Commission for the first time in decades, and the PSC approves Georgia Power’s build-out for large loads.The Democratic Party’s success in Texas was among the most surprising contributions to AI jitters, with markets rattled due to the state’s key position in the ongoing data center buildout. Hinojosa beat Abbott handily, and her campaign rhetoric was aggressive on the data center issue. But while some of her language was blunt, Hinojosa’s policy position on data centers appears to be more moderate: her moratorium plan is a pause pending the passage of some future legislation, not a permanent ban. And her agenda is mostly rules rather than an outright ban: requiring union labor, protecting water supplies, and ending the nondisclosure agreements that make projects hard to track. Like Abbott, Hinojosa has said she wants to make sure Texans don’t pay more for power because of data centers, and she wants to end tax subsidies that cost the state billions in sales tax revenue. The blue victory in Texas didn’t create the data center pause – Abbott has already instituted it. Hinojosa’s plan overlaps with Abbott’s on cost allocation and tax breaks but goes further on how long a pause would last and what conditions come after it. And if the GOP Senate blocks her bills, the condition she’s cited for lifting her pause never arrives unless she lifts it herself.The election results demonstrated a breakdown of President Trump’s coalition that will have implications across a range of policy matters, including many that we consider out of scope for our coverage. And while journalist Eleanor Terrett reported that House Democrats are discussing plans to expand Maxine Waters’ Crypto Investor Consumer Bill of Rights (her 2025 CLARITY amendment) into a broader crypto market structure bill, we previously wrote that we do not expect substantial movement in Congress on key digital assets legislation. In the absence of legislation, the Trump administration’s SEC, CFTC, and banking regulators have been clarifying the rules of the road for crypto under their statutory authorities, and they have two years left to complete that work. AI policy matters, however, could see more movement in the next Congress. Divided government tends to be okay for markets broadly, but there are big questions looming about AI governance, safety, and impact on labor. We don’t view those questions as inherently partisan, so let’s hope that the next Congress can make productive, thoughtful policy the priority for the American people.

articles.title: View from the markets: The earnings season has been good, but is it good enough? - BNP Paribas Asset Management - United States
articles.text:
By Daniel Morris, Chief Market Strategist

At first blush, there is little to complain about regarding the third-quarter earnings results so far (about half of the companies in the S&P 500 and MSCI Europe have reported). Compared to the third quarter in 2025, profits have risen by 26% for the S&P 500 and by 40%(!) for Europe, with double-digit figures for other major indices, based on data from FactSet (see Exhibit 1). This is well above historical norms.

The worry is that those values are not far off what was expected by analysts, and in one case it was below. Earnings have come in only 2% better than expected for the S&P 500. Typically, earnings surprises (how much better or worse results are versus consensus) run in the 3-4% range. Over the previous few quarters, they were even higher. This quarter few indices have matched that.

The chart shows clearly what the source of the disappointment has been: technology. The surprise for the Nasdaq 100 index is -3% and for emerging market (EM) tech stocks it is -8%. The disappointments in emerging markets were almost entirely driven by tech stocks; results for the other sectors were 1% better.

There are two questions: Are these disappointments surprising and how much do they matter?

Given not only how high expectations have been for technology stocks, and how rapidly the artificial intelligence theme is developing, it is not surprising that companies have reported results that are further off the mark than is typically the case.

Though there has been some disappointment in the short term (which will drive the short-term performance of the stock), the more important consideration for investors is the medium-term outlook (which will determine the stock’s medium-term path).

It is worth recalling that consensus estimates for Nasdaq 100 earnings growth in 2027 is 35% and for emerging market technology stocks it is 39%. Even if actual results are a few percentage points lower, and if valuations do not change significantly, indices would typically appreciate in line with earnings.

Sector drivers

It is not only the tech sector that has boosted EPS (earnings-per-share) growth rates. Higher energy prices have contributed to strong results for indices like MSCI Europe and Russell Value. Excluding the energy sector, earnings growth for MSCI Europe is a (still good) 17%. But even setting aside the gains from tech and higher oil prices, results across other sectors are robust. The automobile industry continues to be a drag on the consumer discretionary sector, but most of the others are seeing high single or double-digit earnings growth (see Exhibit 2).

Whether this broadening in earnings continues, or even accelerates, will partly depend on the rate of adoption of AI technologies. There is already significant anecdotal evidence of companies finding meaningful productivity improvements through AI. One example is insurance companies reducing their claims review times and credit losses by using micro-expression recognition technology.

Stories of CFOs becoming alarmed by high AI bills also suggests adoption is accelerating. This will be critical not only for the future rate of non-tech company earnings growth, but also for the hyperscalers, as they look for the return on their massive capital expenditure.

Performance data/data sources: FactSet, BNP Paribas AM, as of 30 October 2026, unless otherwise stated. Past performance should not be seen as a guide to future returns.
