articles.title: South Africa Leads Sub-Saharan Africa’s Crypto Growth
articles.text:
Summary
Everyday financial needs are driving Sub-Saharan Africa’s crypto growth. The region’s crypto economy grew 13.4% to $101 billion, making it the fastest-growing globally. Adoption is driven by individuals using crypto to manage finances and send money, alongside businesses looking to reduce cross-border payment costs and connect across markets.
South Africa and Nigeria lead the region, but follow different paths. Together, they account for more than three-quarters of regional crypto activity. South Africa’s crypto economy grew 52% to $39.3 billion, reinforcing its position as a regional hub for crypto activity and cross-border flows. Nigeria recorded $38.1 billion in crypto activity, as domestic exchanges supported a growing crypto services sector despite a 3% decline in its broader crypto economy.
Stablecoins, personal wallets, and business-oriented transactions are all central to adoption. Demand for these reflects demand for greater control over funds, access to dollar-denominated value, and practical solutions for everyday payments, savings, and business. Scaling these use cases will depend on continued investment, regulatory clarity, and stronger integration with existing financial and business infrastructure.

The 2026 Geography of Crypto Report

Reserve your copy
While Sub-Saharan Africa was the smallest crypto economy this year, it was also the fastest-growing: between July 1, 2025 and June 30, 2026, it grew 13.4% to reach $101 billion. South Africa was a key driver of this growth.Crypto adoption across the region is being fueled by a simple reality: many people and businesses still struggle to access affordable, reliable financial services. For individuals, crypto offers an alternative way to manage their finances and send money. For businesses, it can enable faster, more cost-effective cross-border payments and settlements.For the region, crypto’s appeal is about more than inventing new financial products or investment opportunities; it’s about helping to address everyday challenges.In other words, as Mercy Emmanuel, Stablecoin and Blockchain Commercial Lead at Nigerian fintech company Flutterwave, explains: “For African markets, the most commercially relevant innovations will be those that reduce friction in existing financial activities rather than those that introduce complexity simply for the sake of using blockchain technology.”South Africa and Nigeria dominate regional activity as growth diverges across smaller marketsSouth Africa and Nigeria dominate the regional picture, together accounting for more than three-quarters of total crypto activity in Sub-Saharan Africa.The two countries are following different trajectories, however. South Africa’s crypto economy reached $39.3 billion during the report period, growing 52% year-over-year despite the global bear market. Growth was broad-based, with increases across every category measured, led by cross-border peer-to-peer (P2P) stablecoin flows and service flows.Nigeria’s crypto economy was nearly as large, reaching $38.1 billion, but activity declined 3% year-over-year. Growth in overall service and centralized exchange (CEX) activity was outweighed by a 45% decline in decentralized exchange (DEX) activity and a 17% drop in cross-border P2P flows. Nigeria also placed third in our grassroots adoption index.More broadly, CEX and DEX activity played a significant role in shaping growth trajectories across regional markets. Ghana’s crypto economy grew 80% to $5.1 billion, driven by increases in both CEX and DEX activity, while Senegal saw activity surge 215% to $2.3 billion, fueled by strong CEX growth. In contrast, Ethiopia recorded an 8% decline to $3.7 billion, largely reflecting a drop in DEX activity. Together, these contrasting trajectories highlight the uneven pace of crypto adoption across the region. Smaller markets have significant room to grow and can gain ground quickly, but their activity may also be more volatile and sensitive to market and regulatory shifts that can either accelerate adoption or slow momentum.A third of Sub-Saharan Africa’s crypto economy lands in personal walletsOur research finds that personal wallets are playing an outsized role in Sub-Saharan Africa’s crypto economy, reflecting an adoption pattern in which individuals are central to how crypto is held and transferred.Personal wallets accounted for 32.3% of the value received across the region during the 2026 period — the highest share globally. This suggests that adoption in large part is shaped by users’ looking to manage their own funds, rather than relying on established exchanges or other intermediaries.Cross-border P2P transfers accounted for the bulk of this activity, representing 70.9% of the value received, compared with 18.5% from domestic P2P transactions and 10.7% from service to personal wallet transactions.Limited access to custodial services and regulatory uncertainty may help explain why users favor self-custody. For example, Nigeria had restrictions on banks serving crypto exchanges from 2021 to 2023, and has since had tensions with major international platforms. Such regulatory shifts can impact user preferences for self-custody, with users looking to avoid future uncertainty or market disruptions.Stablecoin activity surged more than sixfold across regionStablecoins are also rapidly defining Sub-Saharan Africa’s crypto market. Between 2022 and 2026, the value of stablecoins received through P2P channels grew more than sixfold, from $2.3 billion to $14.6 billion, while Bitcoin value received fell 60%, from $36 billion to $14.6 billion.This points to a practical use case for stablecoins across the region: allowing people and businesses to hold value in U.S. dollars and other currencies without having to open denominated bank accounts. In a region where local currencies fluctuate, access to foreign currency can be restricted, and cross-border transfers are costly and slow, stablecoins provide a way to receive payments, preserve dollar value, and move money.These use cases are increasingly drawing attention for the crypto economy. As Philip Kwaw Sebuabe, Head of the Virtual Assets Department at the Bank of Ghana, puts it: “Stablecoins are attracting interest beyond trading, particularly for cross-border payments, remittance settlement, and holding foreign-currency value.”Gillian Darko, Vice President of Strategy at Yellow Card, a stablecoin payments infrastructure company, shares this view, identifying stablecoins as the region’s biggest opportunity over the next year. She sees their potential to meet demand for more reliable payment systems and better connect payments with savings and investment.Cross-border transfers highlight stablecoin’s utility perhaps most directly. Stablecoin remittance value more than doubled year-over-year in the region, from $235 million to $492 million, while Bitcoin remittance value remained largely flat. Cross-border stablecoin transfer volumes also increased nearly fivefold, suggesting stronger growth in actual use, not just transaction value.This reflects the high regional demand for cross-border payment solutions. As Flutterwave’s Mercy Emmanuel explains, “Africa has significant demand for international financial connectivity, but payment flows remain fragmented across currencies, markets and financial institutions. Stablecoins provide an opportunity to improve how value moves between these systems.”In light of this, local-currency stablecoins are gaining attention. Rob Downes, Head of Digital Assets at the pan-African bank Absa Corporate and Investment Banking (CIB), points to “the growth in local fiat stablecoins” in the region — including experimentation in South Africa, Ghana, Kenya, and Tanzania. For instance, the Bank of Ghana is examining cedi-backed models that would allow stablecoins to facilitate settlement while beneficiaries receive cedis through bank accounts or mobile-money wallets, without needing to hold crypto themselves.Philip Kwaw Sebuabe also highlights a key advantage of stablecoins: their ability to facilitate the transfer of value outside conventional banking hours. Unlike traditional bank transfers, which are often constrained by business hours, weekends and public holidays, stablecoin transactions can be processed 24 hours a day, seven days a week. Such functionality is particularly valuable in international commerce, remittances and financial markets.These developments all point to two complementary roles for stablecoins: providing access to dollar-denominated value and improving payment options regionally.The successful integration of stablecoin offerings will depend largely on regulatory clarity. Various countries in the region have passed new stablecoin rules, including both Ghana and Kenya last year. These laws aim to bring greater clarity to the growing stablecoin market across the region to support broader implementation.Crypto corridors expand across region as businesses seek cheaper cross-border paymentsOur research saw rapid growth in intra-regional business-like payments, suggesting that crypto is playing an increasingly important role in cross-border business transfers across the region. Our measure captures payments to businesses from both individual consumers and other businesses.This growth comes amid persistent frictions in traditional cross-border business payments. Only a small share of intra-African payments are cleared within the continent, leading to high annual losses and regulatory barriers. Against this backdrop, crypto payment corridors connecting African businesses and consumers is an appealing alternative.The numbers are telling — with active intra-regional corridors nearly doubling during the report period, from 80 to 152 (with 95 of these recording flows in both directions). Additionally, total transaction volume more than tripled, from $34.3 million to $116.5 million. Average volume per corridor also increased from $429,000 to $766,000, pointing to both broader connectivity and deeper transaction activity across these routes.The significance of this is not simply that more crypto is moving between African markets, but that crypto payment channels may be helping connect businesses and consumers that conventional financial infrastructure is serving imperfectly.While there appears to be high demand for these crypto payment channels across the region, the ability for financial institutions and other key payment players to embrace crypto will define in large whether adoption can scale.Gillian Darko underscores the importance of banks in facilitating intra-African transfers, international payments, and remittances. Stablecoin payments in particular, she notes, must be integrated with existing banking systems to connect digital transactions with the broader financial infrastructure.North America leads crypto remittance flows into Sub-Saharan AfricaBeyond business-like payments, crypto is playing a growing role in remittances to Sub-Saharan Africa, where the high cost of traditional transfer services makes cheaper alternatives particularly valuable.Remittances is a key source of income for many people in the region, with remittances making upwards of one-fifth of GDP in countries such as The Gambia and Lesotho. In total, the region saw $41 billion in remittances inflows in 2025.Yet sending money to the region is also very expensive: the World Bank reported an average cost of 7.9% for a $200 transfer, the highest of any region globally. This is a prohibitely high cost when even modest savings on transfer fees can make a difference for recipients. This is where crypto is now playing a role, helping reduce costs, remove barriers, and speed up transfer times.Our research found Western nations accounted for the bulk of crypto-remittance inflows into Sub-Saharan Africa, reaching $888 million during the report period — a 36% increase year-over-year. The number of transfers grew even faster, rising 43% to more than one million transactions in 2026.North America, which has large diaspora communities from Nigeria, Ghana, and Ethiopia, dominated remittance inflows into the region at $645 million. Meanwhile, inflows from Australia and New Zealand recorded the fastest growth, with totals nearly tripling from $48 million in 2024 to $143 million in 2026. Western Europe grew, albeit more modestly, from $79 million to $100 millionThese figures point to the growing use of crypto for remittance inflows into Sub-Saharan Africa, with adoption expanding across multiple sending regions.There is also a potential for crypto to help diaspora communities beyond direct remittance payments. As Yellow Card’s Gillian Darko highlights, blockchain has the potential to open new channels for diaspora investment, which could help to improve financing and distribution while connecting regional businesses and assets to new sources of capital.Diaspora communities help shape crypto remittance patternsOur research also finds that diaspora size and characteristics can help shed light on where remittances into Sub-Saharan Africa are coming from.During the report period, North America and Australia sent more crypto remittances than population size alone would predict, while Western Europe sent considerably less. Western Europe is home to 64% of the Sub-Saharan Africa-born residents across the countries we analysed, yet the region accounted for just 10% of crypto remittances. France highlights this disparity: despite hosting nearly as many Sub-Saharan Africa-born residents as the U.S., it sent just $5.4 million to the region, compared with $223 million from the U.S.When you look at per-capita flows, Canada comes out on top. Canada recorded the highest outflow, rising from $586 to $736 per Sub-Saharan Africa-born resident, while the U.S. rose more modestly to $143. Meanwhile, Western Europe lagged far behind, rising from just $14.50 to $17.90 per resident — roughly one-sixteenth the level of these other markets, despite hosting a large share of the region’s diaspora.These differences may reflect a combination of economic and political conditions in sending countries, the financial circumstances of diaspora communities, and the maturity of local crypto markets. Economic opportunities and social welfare systems can influence how much people are able to send abroad, while the availability and mainstream adoption of crypto can shape whether it is used for remittances.This may help explain why the U.S. and Canada account for such a large share of crypto inflows to Sub-Saharan Africa, given both their sizable diaspora populations and well-established crypto markets. This suggests that in-country dynamics can impact crypto remittance flows, with the relationship between migration and crypto-based financial support depending heavily on these home-country contexts.How South Africa’s businesses are accepting cryptoOur research finds that South Africa hosts a robust crypto-fueled real world economy, one where consumers and businesses pay for goods and services with crypto.To measure this we looked at domestic business-like payments in South Africa: transfers between wallets for which the recipient’s transaction resembles that of a teller providing service. This is a broad spectrum: it runs from businesses that may be paying for long-term contacts in crypto, to consumers that scan a QR code to pay for their hamburger. We capped transfer size at $50,000 to eliminate outliers that could skew the data. This category includes bona fide businesses as well as P2P traders, and other vendors.We found that South Africa saw $8.34 billion in business-like transactions in the 2026 period, with each quarter seeing stronger totals than the last. In fact, Q2 of 2026 (the last quarter in our study period) saw over $1 billion more service-like transfers than Q3 of 2025 (the first quarter of our study period.These business-like payments grew faster even than South Africa’s booming institutional crypto sector, which saw $1.29 billion of inflows for the period.The robust growth in business-like payments came amid an expansion in the infrastructure South Africans need in order to pay for goods in crypto. In 2025, Scan to Pay, a popular pay-by-QR code service, and MoneyBadger, a cryptocurrency platform, rolled out a payments program where consumers can pay with BTC for everyday items. As of August 2026, the partnership had a retail footprint of nearly 700,000 store locations.Carel van Wyk, CEO of MoneyBadger, says South Africans are increasingly using crypto for everyday purchases, both in-store and online. The company’s analysis of Q2 2026 payments found that half were under $13 and 87% were below $60, while ecommerce accounted for 48% of total payment value. “Together with the repeat usage we observe, this shows that crypto is becoming part of customers’ everyday spending habits,” van Wyk notes.South Africa is the region’s crypto hubSouth Africa has historically been a major gateway for international investment in Africa: it is home to Africa’s largest stock market, has a robust banking footprint, an established industrial sector, and maintains strategic trade links across the region. All these ingredients foster capital flows for the entire continent’s real-world economy. Our research indicates that it is also serving as Africa’s conduit for international crypto.To assess whether crypto flows from South Africa to neighbouring countries mirror broader economic ties, we compared cross-border crypto payments with South Africa’s foreign direct investment (FDI) relationships, as South Africa has long been a major source of intra-regional FDI.The overlap between notable South African crypto and FDI inflows into Nigeria, Kenya, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Tanzania, Namibia, and Zimbabwe suggests that crypto flows may follow some of the same regional corridors as traditional investment, reflecting established business relationships and economic ties.​​But the overlap is uneven across countries. Botswana and Zambia attract relatively high levels of South African FDI but see lower crypto flows from South Africa, while Senegal and Cameroon show the opposite pattern. This suggests that crypto activity and South African investment are only partially aligned across the region.While crypto flows do not always mirror FDI patterns, their overlap across several key markets points to the possible role of South Africa as a regional hub for crypto related business and trade activity. This is also consistent with our findings that business-like payments are playing an increasingly important role in South Africa’s domestic crypto economy, pointing to crypto’s growing role in business activity at large.South Africa’s role as a regional crypto hub may soon change, however. In August, the National Treasury and the South African Reserve Bank (SARB) published a draft Crypto Asset Manual for Cross-Border activities that looks to bring crypto assets into the country’s capital flows management framework. The draft rules would mean individuals could move crypto offshore through authorized local providers only, and that companies would not be allowed to move crypto across the border in either direction. But amidst strong backlash, the SARB recently announced it is revising these draft rules, aiming to shift away from pre-approvals.In whatever form the final rules adopt, they will likely have implications for how individuals and businesses can move crypto to and from the country.Nigeria is outpacing the region on service adoption, with domestic exchanges driving growthNigeria, the region’s second largest crypto economy, is highly service-oriented. Substantial activity flows through cryptocurrency platforms and other services — Nigerian users sent $25.2 billion to crypto services during the report period. This was a 172% increase from just four years earlier, outpacing the region’s growth.Domestic exchanges drove nearly all of this increase, accounting for $4.13 billion, or 92% of the additional inflows. In total, domestic platforms received $6.22 billion, equivalent to half of Nigeria’s centralized exchange inflows. This marks a significant shift in market share, up from 27% in 2025 and just 7% in 2022.Nigeria’s restrictive stance toward international exchanges in recent years may help explain why domestic platforms are growing. In 2024, authorities temporarily restricted access to several international exchanges amid concerns over naira depreciation and crypto-driven exchange-rate volatility. While that action proved temporary, enduring disagreements between Nigerian regulators and international crypto exchanges have left Nigerians with fewer venues that support naira trading pairs, creating an opening for domestic growth.This shift toward a more structured regulatory environment was reinforced in July 2026, when Nigeria’s President signed an Executive Order on Virtual Asset Coordination, setting up a council chaired by the Central Bank to coordinate the country’s regulators. The new order aims to harmonize the regulation of virtual assets in the country, including stablecoins, including providing a controlled environment to test new virtual asset products and services. Looking ahead, Nigeria’s SEC has proposed new operating rules, and exchanges and custodians face higher capital requirements by June 2027.These developments could strengthen Nigeria’s domestic crypto ecosystem even more by giving local platforms a clearer regulatory framework and creating opportunities to expand their services. However, higher capital requirements and compliance costs may favor larger, well-funded firms, potentially reshaping competition in the market.Nigeria still dominated by peer-to-peer activity that is Bitcoin drivenOur research finds that P2P activity remains an important feature of Nigeria’s market as well, with Bitcoin playing a much larger role in smaller transfers than in the region as a whole or globally. This distinguishes Nigeria’s crypto economy not only in how users access services, but also in how they transact.Bitcoin accounted for 92% of Nigeria’s small domestic wallet transfers (below $10,000), or $923 million of $1 billion in the 2026 period, compared with 22% in the rest of Sub-Saharan Africa.These figures point to a market where Bitcoin plays an unusually prominent role in everyday, direct transfers, rather than stablecoins dominating as they do in many other markets.Overall, Nigeria’s crypto market combines a growing domestic exchange ecosystem with a distinctive reliance on Bitcoin for smaller P2P transfers. This suggests that, despite the expansion of formal services, crypto use in Nigeria remains shaped largely by demand for direct access and flexible transfers of value. Understanding this is important for assessing how Nigerians use crypto and how the market may evolve as domestic services and regulation mature.Building the next phase of growth in Sub-Saharan AfricaSub-Saharan Africa’s evolving crypto adoption patterns will be key to watch over the coming year. Just as South Africa’s crypto economy is increasingly shaped by business-like activity, Nigeria’s is defined by P2P activity and a preference for bitcoin. Across the region, demand for cross-border payments and settlement is driving adoption, including among financial institutions. And stablecoins are offering new ways to address fragmented payment systems and currency barriers.How these trends look in six or twelve months will depend on several factors, from institutional investment to consumer demand. Regulation, however, will be particularly decisive. Greater regulatory clarity could help accelerate adoption by giving businesses, investors, and financial institutions the confidence to engage with crypto. As Absa CIB’s Rob Downes notes, “it’s hard to look past regulation as the critical enabler across Africa” at the moment.The central question is whether growing investment in Sub-Saharan Africa’s crypto economy can translate into greater financial connectivity and more accessible financial services across the region. Ultimately, crypto’s long-term significance in the region will depend on its ability to continue delivering tangible benefits for individuals and businesses, moving beyond experimentation and investment to become a meaningful part of the region’s financial and business infrastructure.

Treasury Issuance and Dealer Balance Sheets
Jonathan Glicoes, Lubomir Petrasek, Zack Saravay, and Mary Tian
Primary dealers play an important role as intermediaries in Treasury securities and repo markets, and demand for their intermediation rises on issuance dates. Recent increases in Treasury issuance have raised questions about dealers' capacity to meet this increased demand. This note examines how dealers manage their balance sheets around issuance dates.

In summary, we find that primary dealers take up a sizeable but diminishing portion of Treasury securities issuance at auctions. On average, dealer balance sheets increase on issuance dates by 21 cents for every dollar of Treasury securities issued, and this effect tends to be larger during periods of Federal Reserve balance sheet runoff. About two-thirds of the increase in dealer balance sheets is due to increased demand from clients for Treasury securities financing and the remainder is due to increased Treasury securities inventories. The effects on dealer inventories typically dissipate in three to five days following issuance, but the effects on demand for Treasury financing appear more persistent, leaving a longer-lasting imprint on dealer balance sheets. Issuance reduces spare intermediation capacity at Treasury trading desks by bringing the desks closer to their internal risk limits, suggesting that higher Treasury issuance contributes to increased pressures on dealer balance sheets. Treasury buybacks offset the impact of issuance, reducing dealer inventories and internal risk limit usage at Treasury trading desks.

Role of dealers in primary Treasury securities markets

Primary dealers play an important role in primary Treasury securities markets. They are required to "bid on a pro-rata basis in all Treasury auctions at reasonably competitive prices."1 Although primary dealers' share of Treasury securities allocation at auctions has decreased over the past decade, they still take up about one-half of Treasury bill issuance and about one-fifth of the issuance of Treasury coupon securities (Figure 1). Not all of the auction take-up is absorbed on dealer balance sheets, as dealers pre-sell a large part of their allocation to clients in the when-issued market between the auction and the issuance date. Nevertheless, dealers continue to play a crucial role in auctions by placing bids on their own account as well as that of their customers. Dealers also provide repo financing for clients' Treasury positions, enabling their clients to take down a greater volume of issuance. Because of their central role, primary dealers' balance sheets are subject to large changes on Treasury issuance dates.

Figure 1. Percent of Treasury Security Auction Allocations by Investor Class

Note: SOMA allocations are excluded from the calculation. Key identifies in order from top to bottom.

Source: U.S. Department of the Treasury.

Response of dealer balance sheets to Treasury issuance

To understand the effects of Treasury auctions on dealers' balance sheets, we analyze how their Treasury positions and repo volumes change on days when Treasury securities are issued. On issuance dates, primary dealer balance sheets are likely to increase because of settlements of the securities awarded to primary dealers (unless they were presold between the auction and the settlement), and because of increased demand for financing of these securities and those purchased by clients.

Using data from Complex Institution Liquidity Monitoring Reports (FR 2052a), we measure the daily Treasury positions, dealer repo, and reverse repo (financing provided to clients) of the eight largest GSIB-affiliated dealers. We measure Treasury issuance using public auction data from Treasury Direct. We estimate a regression of daily changes in positions and financing on the daily amount of Treasury issuance, separating coupon securities from bills. We also control for quarter-ends using a dummy variable, since Treasury repo volumes often decrease on quarter-end dates due to window dressing. Finally, we control for the amount purchased under the Treasury's buyback program, in which it purchases coupon securities from primary dealers to achieve cash management goals or support market liquidity.2

As shown in Table 1, for every dollar of Treasury coupon securities issued, dealers' balance sheets increase by about 21 cents in total—positions increase by 8 cents and repo and reverse repo each increase by 13 cents. Dealers' positions and repo also increase in response to bill issuance, although the magnitude of the effect is smaller, as bills are typically distributed to clients quickly and do not tend to be financed in repo.3 Treasury buybacks cause a sharp decrease in dealers' positions, while their repo activity is not significantly affected.4 The results also show drops in dealers' balance sheets on quarter-ends, particularly for repo activity, consistent with window dressing activity or certain regulatory constraints.5

We also examine how dealers' sensitivity to Treasury issuance differed during the two recent periods of quantitative tightening (QT). During QT periods, demand for dealer Treasury intermediation and financing is likely to be bigger as clients end up holding more of the newly issued securities. In these regressions, we include two dummy variables for the QT1 period from October 2017 to July 2019 and for the QT2 period from June 2022 to the end of our sample in June 2025. We also interact these QT dummies with our Treasury issuance variables. The results, shown in Table 2, suggest that the effect of issuance on dealer balance sheets is often stronger during QT periods. In particular, dealers' positions increased by 3.3 cents more for each dollar of coupon issuance during QT1 than during non-QT periods. And dealers' repo and reverse repo each increased about 13 cents more for each dollar of coupon issuance during QT2 than during non-QT periods.6 The sensitivity of dealers' repo and reverse repo to bill issuance also appears to increase during QT periods, though by less than for coupons, as bills are less likely to be financed in repo.7

To better illustrate how dealers' sensitivity to issuance has varied over time, we calculate our baseline regression on a one-year rolling window. The coefficients for dealers' sensitivity to coupon issuance are plotted in Figure 2. This exercise confirms that dealers' balance sheets are more sensitive to issuance during periods of QT and shows that their repo volumes have been particularly sensitive during the QT2 period. This recent heightened sensitivity of repo is likely due to the increased takedown of issuance by investment funds, who borrow from dealers through repo to finance these securities. In particular, this period coincides with a pickup in relative value trading by hedge funds, which requires high amounts of leverage sourced through Treasury repo.

How persistent is the effect on dealer balance sheets?

We construct comprehensive measures of primary dealer flows for Treasury securities around auction and issuance dates using a combination of data from Government Securities Dealer Reports (FR 2004) and regulatory Treasury TRACE. The FR 2004-WI schedule provides information on when-issued transactions—forward transactions prior to issuance—engaged in by primary dealers, as well as their auction take-down and forward financing agreements, while TRACE provides comprehensive data for all secondary market Treasury transactions. Leveraging these two data sets together allows us to construct CUSIP-level measures of dealer net positioning around auction and issue dates.8

Figure 3 shows dealer-level mean activity in all issued CUSIPs from March 2016 to July 2025. The chart on the left (Panel A) is presented in event-time relative to the auction date, and the right chart (Panel B) provides a similar picture relative to the issuance date. The two charts demonstrate that primary dealers engage in substantial short selling across the maturity spectrum prior to receiving their allocation from the auction on day zero. By the issuance day, dealers pre-sell most of the auction take-up, so their net position on the issuance date is only a fraction of their auction allocation. Once their allocation is available, they continue to sell through their holdings, with a notably longer half-life (indicating greater retention) for the thirty-year tenor and shorter half-life for the ten- and twenty-year tenors, shown in Figure 4.9 Overall, these estimates suggest that dealers sell off almost all of the auction inventory within 3 to 5 days following the auction.10

Source: FR2004, TRACE and Treasury Direct.

Additional analysis using the FR 2052a data confirms that the effect of coupon issuance on dealers' long positions dissipates within roughly 3 days following issuance. However, the increase in their reverse repo on issuance dates is more persistent and still measurable during the week following the issuance, suggesting that dealers continue to finance newly issued securities for their clients. As shown in the previous section, dealers' reverse repo increases by more than their positions in response to issuance. Thus, much of the increase in dealers' balance sheets lasts beyond the days immediately following issuance.

How Treasury issuance affects dealer intermediation capacity

We examine whether an increase in Treasury issuance can lead to an increase in dealer balance-sheet constraints. Broadly speaking, two types of balance sheet constraints are most relevant for dealers' Treasury intermediation: (1) regulatory constraints, in particular the SLR, and (2) internal constraints on risk-taking, such as value at risk (VaR) limits at Treasury trading desks.

Figure 5. Supplementary Leverage Ratio

Source: FR Y−9C

Accessible version

The SLR is relevant for Treasury market intermediation as it has the potential to impose a high regulatory capital requirement for a relatively low-risk but high-volume activity. However, both Treasury and repo exposures enter the SLR denominator as the daily average over the entire quarter, and short-term fluctuations in dealer exposures around Treasury issuance dates are unlikely to have a meaningful impact on the quarterly average. Taking the average effect on primary dealer balance sheets of 21 cents for every dollar of Treasury coupon securities issued as a baseline, a quarterly auction volume of Treasury coupon securities of $1 trillion would in the aggregate increase dealer balance sheets by about $210 billion.11 Assuming the effect on dealer balance sheets takes 5 days following the auctions to unwind, the average effect over the quarter on dealer SLR exposure is about $17.5 billion. Assuming a 10-day duration of the balance sheet impact, in view of the greater persistence of repo financing, the average quarterly effect on the SLR denominator is about $35 billion. Even so, the increase in exposure appears small compared to the total headroom of primary dealers under the SLR, which exceeds $5 trillion.

Besides the immediate effects of Treasury issuance discussed in this note, the increase in the amount of Treasury securities outstanding is likely to have a longer-lasting effect on dealer balance sheets due to the increase in demands for dealer intermediation when there are more outstanding Treasury securities. These effects are discussed by Cochran et al. (2024) who find that under normal market conditions, the regulatory minimum SLR requirement would not be a binding constraint for dealer Treasury intermediation.

Analysis of VaR-based constraints
Dealer intermediation around issuance dates could also be constrained by internal risk limits, imposed by management at the trading desk level. The most widely used limit by Treasury trading desks is the maximum Value at Risk (VaR), which specifies the maximum level of trading portfolio risk a desk could carry, in terms of a model-calibrated potential loss in a tail event. Unlike the SLR which does not take risk into account, VaR is risk sensitive. As market conditions change, portfolio risks also change, pushing desks closer to or away from their VaR limits. Figure 6 shows the mean VaR usage, that is, the ratio of portfolio VaR to the VaR limit, across a sample of Treasury market-making desks at large GSIBs. Over the sample period, mean VaR usage was on average 35 percent, indicating that desks used about one-third of their headroom under their internal risk limits.

Figure 6. Mean VaR Usage for UST Market−Making Desks

Note: VaR usage, calculated at the desk level, is the ratio of a desk's VaR to its daily limit. The figure shows the mean VaR usage across a sample of large dealers' UST market−making desks. The projection is created by a regression over the last twelve months of available data, forecasted to the present.

Source: FR VV−1

Accessible version

We examine the historical relationship between Treasury bills and coupon issuance, Treasury coupon buybacks, and VaR usage. In particular, we regress levels of mean VaR usage for UST market-making desks at time t and (t+1) on the volume of Treasury bills and coupon issuance based on auction dates at time t and Treasury coupon buybacks at time t. In addition, we control for interest rate volatility (MOVE) and dealers' Treasury long positions. The regression is at a daily frequency with a sample period of January 2016 to June 2025.

Regression results are shown in Table 3. The results show that a $100 billion increase in Treasury issuance implies an increase in mean VaR usage of 2.5 percentage points (about one-third of a standard deviation) on the same day (column 1) and an increase in mean VaR usage of 2.2 percentage points the following day (column 4), suggesting an increase in dealers' risk limit constraints. The coefficients are statistically significant at the 1 percent level, with robust standard errors, after controlling for MOVE.

Column 2 shows that Treasury coupon buybacks reduce dealer balance sheet constraints with respect to VaR usage. A $1 billion increase in Treasury buybacks implies a decrease of 0.5 percentage points on the same day and a decrease of 0.4 percentage points the following day (column 5). These magnitudes control for MOVE and are in addition to effects of Treasury issuance.

In column 3, we add in long (settled) positions as a control.12 Not surprisingly, the magnitude of the effect of Treasury issuance decreases somewhat after adding in Treasury positions, since the two are strongly related. However, the coefficient remains statistically significant at the 1 percent level, implying a 1.2 percentage point increase in mean VaR usage for every $100 billion increase in Treasury issuance (column 3). Adding in long positions also notably increases the magnitude of the effect of Treasury buybacks – every $1 billion increase in buybacks implies a 1.3 percentage point decrease in VaR usage.

Though not shown, the results are similar and robust when we use issuance dates for Treasury bills and coupons issuance instead of auction dates.

Overall, these results show a significant effect of Treasury issuance on VaR usage, a risk-based constraint that dealers face at the trading-desk level that can limit their intermediation capacity in the Treasury market.13

Implications for increased Treasury issuance

We find that dealer balance sheets expand around Treasury issuance, as demand for dealer market-making and repo intermediation rises. Although the immediate increases in dealer positions are typically quite short-lived, persisting for about 3-5 days on average, they have a measurable impact on dealers' risk-based constraints, as measured by VaR. These constraints become more binding during periods of elevated market volatility. Moreover, the effects of Treasury issuance on demand for financing appear more persistent, leading to a more sustained increase in dealer balance sheets. Overall, our findings suggest that upcoming increases in Treasury issuance will contribute to increased pressures on dealer balance sheets, which warrant monitoring.

Who Is Consuming Chinese Tokens?

Laila Khawaja

Gavekal Technologies: Chips | 29 Oct 2026

An unverified claim that over half of China’s domestic tokens are used for video and micro drama generation has sparked a heated online debate. Critics contrast China’s supposed use of scarce compute resources for entertainment with an alleged US focus on coding and productivity. The controversy took place as Chinese AI video models lead global rankings and as Chinese micro dramas and video generation applications rapidly expand their global influence. While the underlying data remain unconfirmed, the debate reveals the potential disconnect between Beijing’s ambitions for economy-wide AI transformation and the commercial realities of Chinese AI companies.

articles.title: Is the US exorbitant privilege eroding? | Brookings
articles.text:
Commentary

Is the US exorbitant privilege eroding?

Robin Brooks

Robin Brooks

Senior Fellow
- Economic Studies

November 5, 2026

The U.S. Treasury Department building in Washington, D.C. Photo: Shutterstock / Sergey Novikov

8 min read

Bluesky Streamline Icon: https://streamlinehq.comBluesky

U.S. Treasury debt has been a cornerstone of global financial markets for many decades because it is the closest thing the world has to a safe asset that can be easily and cheaply traded. It is this unique status of Treasury debt that has given the U.S. an important component of its exorbitant privilege: the ability to issue debt more cheaply than its peers in other advanced economies. However, with no end in sight to budget deficits and U.S. public debt projected to rise out of control, markets have begun to charge a risk premium relative to the rest of the G10. This post shows what has been happening to the U.S. convenience yield—the yield markets are willing to forgo in order to hold Treasuries—and how this advantage has eroded over time. This erosion is not new—it has been playing out steadily over the past decade—but it does mean that the exorbitant privilege associated with Treasury debt is eroding. That could bring higher borrowing costs for the government in the years ahead and—potentially—a weaker dollar.
What are convenience yields?
The convenience yield of U.S. Treasuries is the yield that markets are willing to forgo to hold a safe and liquid asset. There are two principal ways to measure the “specialness” of U.S. Treasury debt, which underpins its convenience yield. The first is to compare Treasury yields to yields on other U.S. assets of comparable maturity, which is typically debt of AAA-rated companies, i.e., the most creditworthy firms, or interest rate swaps, which price the path of Fed policy out into the future (in addition to term premia). The second is to compare Treasury yields to yields on government bonds in other advanced economies and—adjusting for the fact that foreign yields are denominated in currencies other than the dollar—looking at the spread between the U.S. and a trade-weighted foreign average.
Both approaches to calculating the convenience yield are conceptually similar. They compare the yield on Treasuries to some other asset—domestic or foreign—that does not have the specialness of U.S. government debt. It is the evolution over time of the spread between Treasury yields and yields on other assets that provides information on whether the specialness of U.S. government debt is declining in a relative sense.
Both approaches show that the specialness of U.S. government debt has fallen over time. This is not a recent phenomenon. It has played out steadily over the past decade and has been linked in academic research to increased U.S. debt issuance, which is eroding the specialness of Treasury securities. Of course, because both measures are relative, a declining convenience yield could mean either a loss of specialness of U.S. government debt or an increase in the specialness of U.S. corporate or foreign government bonds against which it is being compared. However, the recent resurgence of debt worries in Europe makes the latter explanation less likely, at least for foreign government bonds.
This post lays out the second approach, which calculates how much U.S. Treasury yields are above or below foreign government bond yields of similar maturity after these are hedged back into U.S. dollars using foreign exchange (FX) forwards. According to this approach, the U.S. lost its ability to issue debt more cheaply than its peers nearly a decade ago. Indeed, the cost of U.S. debt was steadily rising relative to its peers until 2022, after which it has stabilized. The most obvious reason for this is that the fiscal picture abroad has weakened faster than for the U.S. because central banks around the world have been raising interest rates to combat high inflation.
The U.S. convenience yield versus the G10
Figure 1 shows the difference between the 10-year U.S. Treasury yield and a trade-weighted average 10-year yield on government bonds in Germany (DE), Japan (JP), the UK (GB), Canada (CA), Switzerland (CH), Sweden (SE), and Australia (AU). To make the yields comparable, 10-year currency forwards are used to hedge yields on these government bonds into dollars (what this calculation essentially does is to sell the foreign currency exposure implicit in foreign bond holdings forward so that there is no FX risk). This differential is thus purely in dollar terms and therefore a good proxy for how “special” markets think Treasury debt is compared to the rest of the G10. When this difference is positive, it means the 10-year Treasury yield is above its trade-weighted average, i.e., the U.S. pays more to borrow than its peers, even adjusting for currency risk. Rather than enjoying a convenience yield, markets are demanding a premium to hold U.S. debt. If the difference is negative, the U.S. is able to issue 10-year debt more cheaply than its peers after adjusting for currency denomination differences.

Figure 1

Bluesky Streamline Icon: https://streamlinehq.comBluesky

Figure 1 shows that the U.S. used to issue debt on average over 10 basis points more cheaply than the trade-weighted foreign average, but this convenience yield eroded steadily and turned positive in 2018, meaning the U.S. began to pay a premium over its G10 peers. This erosion continued until 2022, after which the premium the U.S. pays stabilized around 15 basis points. This is likely because the rise in global interest rates since COVID-19 has shone a light on the precarious state of public finances globally, with high-debt countries in Europe looking especially vulnerable. This is helping the U.S. look better on a relative basis, but—of course—this does not mean borrowing costs in an absolute sense are falling. They are rising, but they are rising elsewhere too.

Figure 2

Bluesky Streamline Icon: https://streamlinehq.comBluesky

Figure 2 shows the two building blocks in the convenience yield calculation. The black line is the straightforward 10-year yield differential, i.e., it is the 10-year Treasury yield minus its trade-weighted foreign counterpart. The red line is what 10-year currency forwards price in by covered interest parity for this rate differential. Since U.S. yields tend to be higher than the trade-weighted foreign average, this means currency forwards price in dollar depreciation to offset higher yields. The convenience yield—the blue line, which is the same as in Figure 1—is the difference between these two, i.e., it is—in effect—a violation of the covered interest parity condition.

Figure 3

Bluesky Streamline Icon: https://streamlinehq.comBluesky

Figure 3 compares the annual average for the convenience yield in Figures 1 and 2 to the difference between U.S. public debt and a trade-weighted average for the same set of foreign countries. Two points stand out. First, the trend erosion in the convenience yield matches the steady rise in U.S. debt relative to its G10 peers. Second, the recent stabilization of the U.S. convenience yield—or premium rather—does not line up with an ongoing rise in U.S. debt relative to its peers. This is likely because countries like France are experiencing fiscal stress at lower debt than the U.S., which is helping the U.S. look more attractive on a relative basis.
Conclusion
The U.S. lost its ability to issue debt more cheaply than its peers nearly a decade ago. Indeed, the cost of U.S. debt was steadily rising relative to its peers until 2022, after which it has stabilized. The most obvious reason for this is that the fiscal picture abroad has weakened faster than in the U.S., which now—in a relative sense—helps the U.S. But, of course, it has not restored the borrowing-cost advantage the U.S. once enjoyed.
The big question, which we will address in a follow-on post, is what all this means for the status of the dollar as a reserve currency. The ability of the U.S. to issue debt more cheaply than its peers and the status of the dollar are obviously linked. The best way to think about the two is to recognize that the erosion of the U.S. convenience yield is still a relatively contained and small phenomenon. That may explain why U.S. reserve currency status has been relatively robust through lots of policy volatility in recent years. At the end of the day, the changes in the U.S. convenience yield are still small, but they reflect a longstanding erosion of the special borrowing-cost advantage the U.S. has historically enjoyed in Treasury markets.

The Middle East conflict has tested ADNOC, Saudi Aramco and QatarEnergy, and the response is already redefining their business development agendas.
In the near term, all three NOCs are focused on restoring capacity and strengthening export resilience. Over the longer term, the conflict will reshape how they approach domestic resource access, partnerships and M&A, at home and abroad.
Interest in Middle East resources among IOCs and international NOCs will remain strong. Uncertain and volatile environments make low-cost barrels attractive, and the region has the lowest of the lot. However, elevated geopolitical risk may lead some international companies to become more selective about future exposure, pushing NOCs to widen their partnership pool to new entrants.
Drawing on research from Wood Mackenzie’s Corporate Strategy & Analytics Service (CSAS) , the full report explores how the conflict is reshaping the priorities of ADNOC, Saudi Aramco and QatarEnergy, and what this could mean for future partnerships and investment.
Fill in the form to download the full report, or read on for a preview of some of the key themes explored.
1. ADNOC is leading the recovery and raising its ambitions
ADNOC is leading the recovery. Freed from production caps, ADNOC is looking beyond its current oil capacity target while. the UAE is also targeting gas self-sufficiency by 2030.
How could ADNOC balance oil growth, gas self-sufficiency and international expansion? The full report sets out the trade-offs.
2. Aramco's gas push could open up the Kingdom’s upstream to international partners
As the world's largest and lowest-cost oil producer, Aramco has considerable financial and operational flexibility. But the demands on management are mounting: maintaining oil capacity, expanding domestic gas and diversifying its portfolio.
How could Aramco's growing gas ambitions reshape its strategy and create new opportunities for international partners? The report examines where those openings could emerge.
3. QatarEnergy faces its most complex partner decisions in years
QatarEnergy's North Field West Expansion and LNG repair programme may create new partnership opportunities. Exploration remains central to QatarEnergy's international strategy but should it also consider development-stage acquisitions?
What could this mean for QatarEnergy’s existing and future partnerships? Find out more in the full report.
4. The road ahead
The conflict has increased the number of competing priorities facing regional NOCs, with ADNOC, Aramco and QatarEnergy having to balance domestic priorities with their international ambitions.
Partner selection, more than capacity alone, is likely to separate the NOCs that emerge strongest. Download the full report for the complete analysis across upstream, gas and LNG.

articles.title: When the Index Falls 4%, the Real Story Is Underneath | Franklin Templeton
articles.text:
When the Index Falls 4%, the Real Story Is Underneath

Wall Street’s midterm post-election celebration lasted one session. US stocks plunged on Thursday as artificial intelligence (AI) and chip stocks sold off, erasing the gains from Wednesday’s rally. The S&P 500 fell about 4%, the Nasdaq Composite dropped 5.5% to close in correction territory, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average lost more than 1,800 points.

The fear gauge responded in kind. The VIX1 jumped more than 65% intraday, its biggest one-day surge in over two years.

More volatility is possible as many market participants find themselves in crowded trades and are offsides on their AI bets.

Dispersion on Display

By the close, 430 of the S&P 500’s 503 stocks had fallen, while 73 rose.2 Within that, the gap between the best and worst performers was enormous. Several chip names fell significantly in the session, while AppLovin gained more than 30% after its earnings report.

Dispersion is a reminder that index-level returns can hide a lot of movement underneath. Even after Thursday’s drop, the market remains up 9% year-to-date. Beneath that headline, many investors may not realize that dispersion—the difference in return between the top and bottom stock performers—has been wide.

Why It Matters for Taxable Investors

No investor wants losses, but volatility is inevitable, and days like yesterday can provide a silver lining by way of long-term tax assets. Tax-loss harvesting means selling a security that has declined to realize a capital loss, which can offset gains elsewhere in a portfolio at a later date. Wide dispersion creates more of these opportunities, even in a year when the overall market is up.

The catch is that sharp drawdowns can appear and reverse within days, so acting on them calls for a disciplined, systematic process rather than guesswork.

What This Looked Like in Practice

That dynamic played out in real time on Thursday. As the selloff unfolded, our Canvas accounts realized almost US$20 million in losses, tipping us over US$1 billion in realized losses for clients year-to-date.

The Takeaway

One day doesn’t make a trend, and volatility is rarely predictable. But it’s a useful reminder to look beneath the headline index, understand what you own and how concentrated it is, and use periods of turbulence to review portfolios and tax positions with a plan in mind.

articles.title: View from the markets: Financial market implications of the US midterm elections - BNP Paribas Asset Management - Corporate English
articles.text:
By Daniel Morris, Chief Market Strategist

As it turns out, this time the polls were right. If anything, they understated how well the Democratic Party would do across a range of elections. How significant, though, are the implications for US economic growth and asset prices?

One ‘parlour game’ that strategists play is to compare market returns after midterms, or when different parties control the presidency and the Congress. While perhaps entertaining, such analysis has little practical value as it assumes ‘all else being equal’ –that the only variable that is changing is the make-up of the government.

Needless to say, everything else is actually far from equal, from interest rates to GDP growth and inflation, which are far more significant factors for the markets.

In general, what happens in Washington has only a marginal impact on the economy and markets. The exception is when one party controls both the presidency and all of Congress (House of Representatives and Senate).

When that is the case, it is more likely legislation can be passed (such as Obamacare or the One Big Beautiful Bill) that is significant enough to impact, if not the whole economy, than at least particular sectors. When government is divided, the inevitable compromises required to pass legislation means the impact is often less.

This configuration of full, single-party control has recently tended to occur only at the beginning of presidencies, with mid-term elections then giving partial or total control to the opposition party.

Not only is the legislation passed of less impact when control is divided, there is generally less of it, as compromises generally are difficult to reach.

So, the view that investors had prior to the recent state and local elections should generally still prevail. Our view remains constructive on the outlook for equities as recent macroeconomic data continues to be positive. The third quarter earnings season results were good (if slightly disappointing), and the outlook over the next few quarters is still encouraging. Non-tech heavy indices (like the Russell Value) have tended to move steadily upwards.

The recent tech market sell-off is a continuation of what began in late June. The mid-terms have added an extra bit of uncertainty as investors worry whether data centre buildouts, on which a large of share of expected earnings growth is predicated, will be slowed by Democratic control of governorships and state legislatures.

We expect economic growth to continue more or less as before, regardless of what happens in Washington, which would point to medium-term gains in equities, but with potentially above-average volatility.

Data sources: Bloomberg, FactSet, BNP Paribas Asset Management as of 5 November 2026 (unless otherwise stated). Past performance should not be seen as a guide to future returns.

articles.title: Five Things Families Should Know About the FAFSA | Franklin Templeton
articles.text:
For families planning to fund college, completing the Free Application for Federal Student Aid (FAFSA) is an important step in understanding financial options available to them. While the FAFSA for the upcoming academic year typically becomes available on October 1, navigating the process involves more than simply completing a form. Understanding the requirements and planning ahead can make a meaningful difference. Here are five key things families should know as they navigate the financial aid process.

1. Income generally matters more than assets in determining aid

Colleges use the Student Aid Index (SAI) to help determine a student’s financial need and eligibility for federal student aid, including grants, loans and work-study programs. The SAI considers both a family’s income and assets, but the two are not weighted equally. In general, income has a greater impact on the calculation than assets. The SAI calculation generally considers four main factors: parent income, parent assets, student income, and student assets. The formula is driven primarily by income, while savings have a more modest impact. Under the federal aid formula, the assessment of parental income generally ranges from 22%–47%, while assessable parental assets may be counted at a rate of up to approximately 5.64%, depending on the family's circumstances. For students, 50% of income and 20% of assets may be counted. For this reason, parent-owned 529 plans are generally treated more favorably in the federal aid calculation established under the Uniform Gifts to Minors Act (UGMA) or Uniform Transfers to Minors Act (UTMA), which are typically considered student assets.

Source: SAI Formula, 2026-2027, Federal Student Aid, an Office of the U.S. Department of Education.

2. Grandparent-owned 529 plans are not considered as part of the aid calculation

Due to changes in the FAFSA process, distributions from grandparent-owned 529 savings plans are no longer treated as student income in the SAI calculation. This includes other non-parent-owned accounts as well. Historically, while a grandparent-owned 529 was not counted as a reportable asset on the FAFSA, distributions from the account could be treated as student income, potentially reducing eligibility for need-based financial aid in a subsequent academic year. Beginning with the 2024—25 FAFSA, this is no longer the case.

However, some colleges require families to complete the CSS Profile administered by the College Board, in addition to the FAFSA, when determining eligibility for institutional financial aid. The CSS-Profile may request information on non-parent-owned 529 accounts, and colleges may consider these accounts when calculating aid eligibility. Families should understand the requirements of each college to which a student is applying.

3. Complete the FAFSA as early as possible

Completing the FAFSA as early as possible may help families maximize their financial aid opportunities. While the application determines eligibility for federal aid, some state and institutional aid programs have their own deadlines and limited funding, making early submission particularly important. Families should check federal, state, and college-specific deadlines to avoid missing potential aid opportunities.

4. Don’t assume your income is too high to qualify

Even if a family believes its income is too high to qualify for financial aid, completing the FAFSA will still be worthwhile. There is no universal income cutoff for federal student aid eligibility. Eligibility depends on several factors such as the cost of attendance, which will vary among colleges. Completing the FAFSA may also be necessary to access certain state-based aid, institutional grants and scholarships, as well as federal student loans. Having a FAFSA on file can also be helpful if a family experiences a significant change in financial circumstances, such as a job loss or substantial reduction in income. In these situations, families can contact the college’s financial aid office to discuss their circumstances and determine whether an adjustment to their financial aid eligibility may be warranted. Lastly, some colleges require a completed FAFSA to be considered for merit-based scholarships or other forms of aid not based on financial need.

5. Not all financial aid is created equal

A financial aid package may include a combination of grants, work-study opportunities, and student loans, each of which affects a family’s college costs differently. Families should look beyond the total amount of aid offered and focus on how much represents free assistance versus borrowing. They should also consider other factors that affect the overall cost of an aid package, including interest rates and loan terms. For example, a financial aid package that includes student loans may be considerably more expensive today than a similar package offered several years ago, given the broad increase in interest rates.

Closing thoughts and action steps

Remember to file the FAFSA every year. Families must submit a new FAFSA for each academic year to be considered for federal student aid
Get organized before you begin. Gather relevant tax information, records of reportable assets, and other information to help completing the application easier.
Use available resources. Visit studentaid.gov to learn more about the FAFSA process and use the Federal Student Aid Estimator to get an early estimate of potential federal student aid eligibility.
Engage with college financial aid offices. If your family is comparing offers from several colleges, consider contacting financial aid offices directly to ask questions about an award, clarify available assistance, or discuss whether additional financial aid may be available. Some colleges may be willing to reconsider an offer based on competing awards or a change in family circumstances.

For more information on how 529 college savings plans may affect financial aid eligibility, check out our brochure, Saving for Education with 529s and the Effect on Financial Aid, for additional insights and planning considerations. Follow Bill Cass, CFP®, CPWA® Director of Wealth Planning

articles.title: Is Japan’s Repatriation Wave Starting?
articles.text:
Is Japan’s Repatriation Wave Starting?

Udith Sikand

Gavekal Research | 6 Nov 2026

It has long been one of the big questions hanging over global financial markets: at what point will Japanese portfolio investors decide the relative rewards of holding US$5trn in overseas assets no longer outweigh the risks, and begin to repatriate capital in earnest. Every so often, the expectation of increased repatriation flows is enough to trigger a nasty bout of global volatility, as it did in the summer of 2024.Since then, the rise in Japanese government bond yields has quietly changed the calculus for Japanese investors. So far it is more a trickle than a flood, but over the 12 months to September, Japanese investors repatriated a net ¥5.5trn of foreign portfolio assets. Now, the latest evolution of the Bank of Japan’s stance, apparent at its late-October policy meeting, may lend additional momentum to the incipient flow. If so, it could create a structural bid for the yen, one of the world’s most undervalued currencies.

articles.title: HSBC Funding the Future Survey - AI and the IPO window
articles.text:
Back to InsightsGlobal Investment ResearchData scienceHSBC Funding the Future Survey - AI and the IPO windowBy Shiva Joon, CFA, Data Scientist3 November 2026ArticleArticleShare via EmailShare on FacebookShare on LinkedInShare on TwitterThe tenth edition of our proprietary Funding the Future Survey finds that private market investors see stronger deal prices, but raising fresh funds remains tough. Their concerns about AI are also changing.Carried out by Survation, this survey captures the views of 217 global investors representing a significant portion of the private and public high-growth investment community. Survey participants represented AUM of USD3.6trn, of which cUSD1.5trn is attributed to VC and private equity (PE) investors. The fieldwork took place from 15 September to 12 October 2026.
Private investors are modestly more confident about the coming quarter than they were in July, with 48% expecting an increase in VC and PE activity, against 44%. The 12-month view has softened to 54% from 64%, though as the regional section shows, that fall is concentrated in Asia Pacific rather than spread across the market.54%Of private investors are confident about the coming 12 months, the lowest in the survey’s historyThe deals in front of investors look better than at any point in the survey's history. Some 51% report that recent financings in their universe have mostly been up rounds, the highest reading we have recorded, while only 3% report mostly down rounds, the lowest. On aggregate it would seem the repricing that defined 2022 and 2023 appears to have worked its way through. On closer inspection, however, AI deals are a big driver of this trend.
What has not recovered is the supply of new capital. Only 21% of private investors expect fundraising conditions to improve over the coming year, down from 34% in July, and the deterioration holds in every region we track. The share reporting that their dry powder has increased over the last twelve months has fallen to 23%, a series low. Investors are deploying faster than they are raising.75%Of private investors expect a US interest rate hikeThe macro backdrop has moved against them. Three quarters of private investors and 77% of listed investors now expect the next move in US interest rates to be a hike, having expected no change as recently as July. Market pricing has moved the same way in the past few months, so the survey is confirming the repricing. For private markets the consequences of the changing rate environment have become the single largest headwind investors name, cited by 87% against 66% in July, and expectations around ask/bid spreads have deteriorated almost as sharply.
AI remains the overwhelming answer to where private capital is going, named by 85% of private investors as the sector they expect to attract the most private-market investment over the coming quarter.
Some 56% now think a meaningful slowdown in AI infrastructure spending is likely within six to twelve months, up from 51%, with those calling it very likely rising to 20% from 11%. Asked where such a slowdown would be felt most, 55% now name data centre real estate and colocation providers, against 24% in July. Hyperscale cloud providers have fallen from 33% to 20%, and specialised AI compute and chip vendors from 25% to 15%. Four further survey responses point the same way: energy and power availability has risen to the second-largest potential upside for AI capex; anxiety about chip supply has eased; infrastructure and energy has overtaken technology as the expected growth area in private direct lending; and the energy transition has become the fastest-rising of the long-term themes we track.
Against all this, we think investors remain committed to the theme but are more willing to act on disappointment than they were earlier in the year. Some 29% would now cut AI exposure by a quarter if their named downside materialised, against 7% in July.85%Of private investors are planning to exit at least one portfolio company in the next twelve monthsExit intent is at a series high, with 85% of private investors planning to exit at least one portfolio company in the next twelve months. Trade sales remain the preferred route at 73%, but buyouts have fallen to 35% from 46%, consistent with a higher expected cost of leverage, while IPOs (initial public offerings) have risen to 35% and mergers to 31% from 17%.
What investors expect to list has shifted decisively towards AI, named by 63% against 36% in July. One long-standing finding from our survey has changed in this wave: the share of investors preferring their portfolio companies to list in the US has fallen to 57% from 79%, while the share stating a preference for an Asian listing has doubled to 18%, similar to those preferring EMEA (18%).Disclosure appendixThe following analyst(s), who is(are) primarily responsible for this document, certifies(y) that the opinion(s), views or forecasts expressed herein accurately reflect their personal view(s) and that no part of their compensation was, is or will be directly or indirectly related to the specific recommendation(s) or views contained in this research report: Shiva Joon, CFA
