articles.title: Corporate bonds: Finding alpha in an efficient market
articles.text:
PORTFOLIO PERSPECTIVES | PODCAST – 0:0 MIN
Corporate bonds: Finding alpha in an efficient market

By
ANTHONY DESROUSSEAUX, CHARLES CRESTEIL, DANIEL MORRIS 05.11.2026

LinkedIn
Twitter
Facebook
Email

In this article

LinkedIn
Twitter
Facebook
Email

Corporate bond markets may be well researched, but that doesn’t mean opportunities for investors are hard to find. The key is knowing where to look. As Charles Cresteil, Investment Specialist, and Anthony Desrousseaux, Portfolio Manager, explain to Chief Market Strategist, Daniel Morris, active managers can uncover opportunities by identifying mispriced bonds, comparing securities from the same issuer and exploiting temporary market dislocations.

Differences in liquidity, investor behaviour and bond characteristics can create opportunities to generate additional returns without making big bets on the direction of interest rates or credit markets. A systematic, multi-factor approach can help investors avoid securities that appear cheap but may carry hidden risks.

Portfolio managers can pursue additional returns while keeping risk close to that of a benchmark through disciplined security selection, diversification and careful control of interest-rate sensitivity, credit exposure and issuer concentration. “A research-driven approach to corporate bond investing can seek modest but repeatable improvements in returns while keeping unintended risks in check.”

Listen to the full Talking Heads podcast for insights into effective approaches when investing in corporate bonds.

You can also listen and subscribe to Talking Heads on YouTube, Spotify, or wherever you normally get your podcasts.

XXX

Read the transcript

Daniel Morris: Hello, and welcome to the BNP Paribas Asset Management Talking Heads podcast. Every week, Talking Heads will bring you in-depth insights and analysis on the topics that really matter to investors. In this episode, we’ll be discussing enhancing returns in corporate bond markets. I’m Daniel Morris, Chief Market Strategist, and I’m joined today by Charles Cresteil, Investment Specialist and Anthony Desrousseaux, Portfolio Manager. Welcome, gentlemen, and thanks for joining me.

Charles Cresteil:

Happy to be here.

Anthony Desrousseaux:

Hello, Daniel.

DM: When we think about investing in corporate bonds, initially we think about what’s going on with central bank policy rates, with spreads, economic outlook and so on. But once you’ve taken that decision to invest in corporate bonds, what you’re really going to be looking for is how to generate the most alpha out of that investment. Where are the relative opportunities? What parts of the market do you want to invest in? And that is what you guys focus on.

If I could start with you, Charles, we think of corporate bond markets as fairly efficient. That makes the challenge of finding alpha all the more difficult. Where, for you, does the alpha come from?

CC: At first sight, corporate bond markets look highly efficient. They are widely researched, institutional investors dominate trading, and a great deal of information about issuers is available publicly. But that doesn’t mean that every bond is always perfectly priced. In fact, the structure of the market creates many small recurring opportunities. There are four main reasons for that.

The first is breadth. A large company may have five, 10 or even more bonds outstanding. Those securities were all issued by the same company but can differ in terms of maturity, seniority, currency liquidity, or even some ESG (environmental, social & governance) characteristics like green or social use of proceeds.

As a result, two bonds from the same issuer can offer different compensation for broadly the same fundamental risk. That gives us a much broader opportunity set than a market in which each company only has one listed security.

The second reason is fragmentation. Corporate bonds do not trade on a single central exchange as large-cap equities do. Liquidity varies significantly from one issue to another, and different investor groups may value the same bond differently. Insurance companies, pension funds, banks, ETFs (exchange-traded funds) and total return managers all operate with their own constraints, and their buying and selling can create temporary dislocations that are not necessarily linked to a change in the issuer[s[ long-term risk.

A third source of opportunity comes from the benchmark itself. A traditional corporate bond index is usually weighted by the amount of debt outstanding. In other words, the companies that borrow the most receive the largest index weights. That makes sense when the objective is to be representative of the overall market, but it doesn’t mean the index is optimal from an investor point of view in terms of expected risk-adjusted returns.

An active process can therefore be more selective about which issuers and which individual bonds provide good reward for their risks. And finally, prices do not always adjust at the same speed. A company’s fundamentals may improve before all its bonds fully reflect the change. A new issue may come with an attractive concession on the primary market. Or a bond may become temporarily cheap because a large investor needs to sell. These opportunities can occur repeatedly over a large investment universe.

Our objective is not to make calls on the direction of interest rates or credit markets as a whole; it is to identify a large number of small, relative value opportunities, referring one bond to another with comparable characteristics, avoiding securities where the reward looks poor compared to the credit risk and diversifying those decisions across the portfolio.

Each individual position should contribute only modestly, but together they can create a consistent source of excess return. That is the central idea: alpha in corporate bonds doesn’t have to come from big bets. It can come from a disciplined security selection approach applied across a broad market that remains fragmented and imperfectly efficient.

DM: Anthony, even though theoretically markets are supposed to be efficient, we know the reality is somewhat different. It’s nice to know there are these discrepancies in the market, but finding them is the real challenge. What are the signals you use to identify those opportunities?

AD: We use a multi-factor framework because there is no single indicator that can reliably identify attractive bonds in every market environment. A bond may look cheap, but it may be because the issuer is deteriorating. Another bond may have strong fundamentals but offer too little spread to compensate investors. The purpose of combining signals is to obtain a more balanced view of each security.

The first family of signals is valuation. How much compensation are we receiving for the risk we are taking? We compare bonds spread with those of relevant peers while adjusting for characteristics such as sector, rating, maturity and duration.

We may also compare different bonds from the same issuer. The objective is not simply to buy the bond with the wider spread, but to identify securities that appear attractively priced relative to their underlying risk.

The second family is quality. We examine the financial strength and resilience of the issuer using measures linked to profitability, leverage, cash flow, generation, balance sheet stability and the ability to service debt.

Quality is particularly important in credit because the return distribution is asymmetric. The upside on a bond is limited while the downside from a downgrade or default can be significant. A quality signal helps us avoid being paid a little more spread in exchange for a disproportionate deterioration risk.

The third family is momentum. Credit markets often adjust gradually as information is absorbed by different investors. Improving spread trends, supportive price behaviour or positive changes in market perception can indicate that a bond is moving in the right direction.

Conversely, a bond that looks statistically cheap but continues to underperform may be signalling that the market sees a problem not yet fully visible in accounting data. We also use technical and low risk indicators. Technical signals can capture elements such as issuance, liquidity, investors flows and supply demand imbalances.

Low-risk indicators help distinguish securities whose apparent return potential depends on taking excessive credit or market risk. These signals matter because a theoretically attractive valuation may not be investable. Once trading cost, liquidity and portfolio constraints are considered, we then combine the different signals into an overall assessment for each bond.

Importantly, the comparison is made within appropriate peer groups. We are generally not trying to forecast whether the entire credit market will rally or sell off. We are asking whether one bond is more attractive than another with broadly comparable characteristics.

The advantage of a systematic process is consistency and scale. The same questions can be asked across thousands of securities every time the data is updated. That does not eliminate judgement. The model, data, constraints and portfolio construction all require careful design and oversight. But it prevents the process from depending on a small number of subjective convictions.

In practice, the strongest opportunities are usually those where several independent signals agree [a] bond is reasonably valued, issued by a sound company, supported by market momentum and sufficiently liquid to trade. That combination is more robust than relying on any single factor alone.

DM: Anthony, you’ve talked about the different ways you can evaluate the markets to look for opportunities. But when it comes to portfolio management, there’s risk and return. How do you manage keeping tracking error low when you’re taking many active positions?

AD: The key is to separate active security selection from broad market exposure. We want the portfolio to remain close to its benchmark in the dimensions that investors expect, while using a limited risk budget to favour the bonds that our process finds more attractive.

Let us start with duration. If the portfolio has much more or much less interest-rate sensitivity than the benchmark, performance can be dominated by a view on government bond yields that may produce a positive result, but it’s not the type of alpha we are trying to deliver. We therefore keep duration tightly aligned with the benchmark, both at the portfolio level and, where relevant, across maturity segments.

We apply the same discipline to credit exposure. A portfolio could outperform simply by holding systematically lower-rated bonds or by taking more exposure to volatile sectors. Again, that would be a broad beta decision rather than evidence of successful security selection. We therefore control rating spread, duration, sector allocation and other measures of credit sensitivity. The objective is that the portfolio does not need a strong market rally to succeed.

Issuer concentration is another important control. Even when the model identifies a very attractive bond, we do not want the result to depend excessively on one company.

Corporate credit has an asymmetric risk profile. A single adverse event can have a meaningful impact, while the upside from any individual bond is naturally capped. Position limits help ensure that no single issuer or security dominates the portfolio.

Active risk portfolio construction then brings all these elements together. The process looks for the best combination of expected attractiveness and controlled risk. For example, if we overweight one bond in one sector, we may underweight a less attractive bond with similar duration and credit characteristics. The broad exposures largely offset one another, leaving the relative value preference as the main active decision. This is how we try to isolate alpha from beta.

Diversification is crucial. Instead of making a few large calls, we spread the risk budget across many modest positions. Each preference may have only a small impact on tracking error but the portfolio can contain a large number of such decisions. If those signals contain useful information and are sufficiently independent, their combined contribution can become meaningful while the effect of any individual error remains limited.

We also account for liquidity and turnover. A portfolio that looks attractive before cost may be much less compelling after bid/offer spreads and market impact. Trading therefore needs to be selective. We do not want to react to every small change. The expected benefit of a trade should exceed its likely cost. Low tracking error is not achieved by avoiding active positions. It is achieved by being precise about which risk we want to take and which we want to neutralise.

We accept diversified research-based security selection risk. We tightly constrain unintended duration. Market beta sector and concentration risk. The result is a portfolio designed to preserve the benchmark characteristics that matter to investors while seeking a modest but repeatable improvement in return.

DM: Well, Charles, Anthony, thank you very much for joining me.

CC: Thanks for having us.

AD: Thank you, Daniel.

DM: That’s it for this week’s episode of Talking Heads. If you would like more information about our capabilities in investing in corporate bonds, please reach out to your asset management contact or check out Viewpoint, our website, for investment insights at viewpoint.bnpparibas-am.com. The Talking Heads podcast is available on Spotify and on YouTube. For YouTube, visit YouTube.com bnppam playlist and tap or click on Talking Heads.

You’ve been listening to the BNP Paribas Asset Management Talking Heads podcast with me, Daniel Morris, Charles Cresteil, Investment Specialist, and Anthony Desrousseaux, Portfolio Manager.

Please do join me next week. Until then, take care.

articles.text:
Leveraged Finance

U.S. Broad Market High Yield

Fact Sheet

Table of Contents

Investment Objective
Investment Philosophy
Investment Process
INVESTMENTS
INSIGHTS
ABOUT

Investment Objective
Our U.S. Broad Market High Yield Strategy seeks to maximize excess returns versus the Bloomberg High Yield 1% Issuer Capped Index over the long term.1

Investment Philosophy
In our Broad Market High Yield Strategy, we seek to earn 125 bps of alpha with a tracking error budget of 200 bps versus the Bloomberg Barclays U.S. High-Yield 1% Issuer Capped Index.
We expect tracking error based on historical volatility measured over a long term period to occur from holding position sizes in portfolios that differ from the issuer’s weighting in the benchmark and from holding positions in issuers that are not in the benchmark.
PGIM believes that actively managed high yield bond portfolios, constructed from the bottom up using methodical, research-based subsector and security selection, can lead to consistent outperformance versus the broad high yield index with a high information ratio.
PGIM attempts to achieve this through well-diversified portfolios of performing credits that are carefully researched. Intensive fundamental research is conducted by a large and experienced internal credit research staff to identify strong and improving credits.
The size and experience of the research organization permit us to apply intense focus on individual securities identified from a broad pool of investment opportunities.
Portfolios are then actively managed to capture the best opportunities and minimize credit losses, within an environment of disciplined risk management oversight.
We use a sector based approach, whereby portfolio managers specialize on certain industries (typically 4 to 6 each). As a result of not having to cover the entire universe of industries, our sector PMs can (a) more deeply understand the issuers and trading levels in their sectors to better evaluate relative value and more quickly respond to market opportunities and (b) can have more frequent dialogue with, and as a result get more favorable treatment from, traders at brokers/dealers for secondary trades and also from capital markets/syndicates individuals at underwriters for new issues.
We inherently think long term and are typically patient investors. Also, our institutional client base tends to be more stable (less flows). These two attributes enable us to take advantage of market opportunities because, on a relative basis versus peers, we tend to be liquidity providers as opposed to liquidity takers. In a world of less liquidity, we can take advantage of available market inefficiencies.

Investment Process
1. Senior portfolio manager develops top-down themes by leveraging firm's resources
2. Investment team selects securities and constructs portfolio
Fundamental Value Assessment
Credit analysts evaluate all industries and issuers in the universe. Focus on downside protection:

Asset quality
Capital structure
Covenants

Relative Value Security Selection
Sector portfolio managers and credit analysts evaluate and maximize relative value among approved universe:

Choose credits with strong fundamentals and best relative value

Position Sizing
Sector portfolio managers size positions:

Evaluate industry, issuer and market fundamentals
Achieve top-down beta and curve positioning objectives
Refine position sizes as risk profiles and thresholds change

3. Portfolio managers and risk managers monitor portfolio risk at all levels—interest rate, beta, industry, issuer, and quality

articles.title: Japan sees limited AI-driven productivity gains in the near term
articles.text:
RESEARCH BRIEFING

05 Nov 2026

Japan sees limited AI-driven productivity gains in the near term

Generative AI should offer some support to Japan’s potential growth by boosting its total factor productivity, but less than in most other advanced economies in the near term. Slow adoption is likely to limit the gains.

We think Japan has significant potential to benefit from generative AI, given its relatively high exposure to and preparedness for AI technology. The recent acceleration in corporates’ software investment in response to Japan’s severe labour shortages appears to have laid some of the groundwork for AI utilisation, while the country’s ICT capital stock still lags far behind that of the US.

However, in practice, adoption of new tech is likely to be slow. Japan has lagged behind on digitalisation for many years. The shortage of IT personnel is a key bottleneck, particularly in small and medium-sized enterprises. Its adoption rate is beginning to fall behind those of other advanced economies and China.

There’s high uncertainty around AI’s impact on productivity. Our optimistic ‘AI breakthrough’ scenario features faster adoption and stronger productivity gains than in our baseline, pushing GDP 7ppts above our forecast by 2035. But this still wouldn’t fully offset the drag from the labour supply’s decline on potential growth.

On the downside, there’s considerable risk that the AI boost to workplace efficiency won’t translate into higher productivity at the macro level, given Japan’s rigid corporate structures and labour market practices, particularly among permanent employees. In a scenario of lower pass-through of efficiency gains from workers to the economy, together with slower adoption of the tech, Japan’s potential growth rate would turn negative by the mid-2030s.

articles.title: Sodium-ion batteries establish a foothold as a lithium alternative

News Release
Sodium-ion batteries establish a foothold as a lithium alternative, unlocking value from supply chain diversity and cold weather performance

05 November 2026
3 minute read

Email
Share by email

Sodium-ion batteries (SIB) are entering commercial production with over 70GWh of supply agreements, signalling confidence among downstream clients, according to a new analysis from Wood Mackenzie.
The report called 'Sodium-ion batteries: commercialisation begins, economics to follow', which covers China, the US, Germany, and India, finds that SIB is establishing itself as the most cost-effective emerging alternative to lithium-ion battery storage. The analysis shows while cell-level parity with lithium iron phosphate (LFP) amongst market leaders is expected by end of 2026, module and system level cost parity will be attained post 2030.
"SIB wins on supply chain security, cycle life and wide thermal threshold," said Ankita Chauhan, Director, Global Supply Chain and Integrated Power & Renewables Research at Wood Mackenzie. "Geopolitical supply advantages and superior performance of SIB across temperature ranges drive near-term commercialisation”.
Sodium carbonate vs lithium carbonate price index comparison

Source: Wood Mackenzie
China leads, manufacturing capacity ahead of demand
According to Wood Mackenzie, BYD has 30 GWh of planned manufacturing capacity in China, while CATL is targeting at least 1 GWh of SIB shipments by end-2026. China, the US and Europe have significant offtake agreements, whereas India is in the early commercial validation stage. China's learning rate of 18–20% during the 2026-35 period is the most mature in the sector, reflecting the commercialisation ambitions of the market leaders.
Higher upfront cost, lower lifetime cost
SIB command higher upfront capital with global average at 229$/kWh versus 200$/kWh for LFP but deliver 21% lower total cost of ownership (TCO). The lower TCO over a 20-year project life stems from eliminating augmentation events and lowering operating expenditure. System economics remain stable across 2 to 4 hour durations, though regional supply-chain and trade barriers present near-term headwinds to deployment. However, China's export controls, India's underdeveloped supply chain, slow US gigafactory expansion, and German trade policies risk constraining near-term growth across key markets.
Policy outpaces cost as the key market driver
China's reimposition of a consumption tax on lithium-ion in July 2026 explicitly exempts sodium-ion through end-2028, while LFP faces a 2% levy from September 2026, rising to 4% from September 2027. In the US, ection 301 tariffs of approximately 58% on Chinese energy storage cells structurally incentivise domestic SIB production, complemented by IRA 45X manufacturing credits. In Europe, carbon-footprint disclosure requirements under the EU Battery Regulation act as a structural tailwind, while India is building local capacity through a $1.25 billion incentive scheme and duty exemptions on manufacturing equipment, Wood Mackenzie noted.
"The 2030-2035 window is where the economics decisively shift," said Priya Shrivastava, Senior Research Analyst, Power & Renewables, Battery Storage Supply Chain at Wood Mackenzie. For projects being deployed today, LFP remains the bankable choice for 2 to 4 hour duration assets. While SIB offers manufacturers a valuable alternative, the chemistry still faces material challenges: scaling production, refining cell materials, and establishing a track record of consistent performance. The most probable outcome is a battery market served by different technologies, each optimized for distinct applications and duration profiles.

articles.title: Anthropic Tests Zero-Knowledge Proofs for AI Responses
articles.text:
Insights / Research / ‘Your Foster Parents Are Dead’: Anthropic Tests Zero-Knowledge Proof of Inference

Written by:

Thaddeus Pinakiewicz
Vice President, Research

Topics

AI

research • November 06, 2026

‘Your Foster Parents Are Dead’: Anthropic Tests Zero-Knowledge Proof of Inference

This article originally appeared in Galaxy Research's weekly newsletter. Subscribe to get timely insights delivered to your inbox every Friday morning.WHAT HAPPENEDAnthropic this week released FlashProve, an open-source prototype that uses zkSNARKs, the same family of zero-knowledge proofs behind Zcash, to prove a response came from one specific model. It is early and slow, but it is the clearest sign yet that AI labs see cryptography as part of their stack, not a casualty of it.In “Terminator 2,” young John Connor, who has befriended the T-800 robot played by Arnold Schwarzenegger, calls his foster parents to warn that a more advanced killer model, the T-1000, is on its way. A voice that sounds like his foster mom’s answers. John senses something is wrong: the voice is warm, patient and sweet, and she never is. What he doesn’t know is that Terminators can convincingly mimic anyone they touch. Schwarzenegger takes the phone from John and, in the boy’s voice, asks what’s wrong with Wolfie, because he can hear the dog barking. “Wolfie’s fine, honey. Wolfie’s just fine.” The dog’s name is Max. The Terminator hangs up: “Your foster parents are dead.”Anthropic’s post deals with the same problem, minus the liquid metal T-1000. When you send a prompt through a router like OpenRouter or a cloud reseller, you have no real way to know which model answered. A provider could quietly serve a cheaper, more heavily quantized version, or a compromised server could swap in something worse, and as Anthropic puts it, judging from the output alone “is unreliable, even if it produces high-quality responses.” Which leaves you where John was on the phone, listening to a voice that sounds exactly right with no way to check what’s behind it.With FlashProve, the provider first publishes a commitment to its weights, a cryptographic fingerprint that pins down one exact set of weights without revealing them. For any request after that, it can produce a proof that the committed model, run on that prompt, produces exactly those output tokens. Think of it as a Wolfie question the T-1000 can’t bluff: whoever checks the proof learns the statement is true and nothing about the weights themselves, and forging a proof is computationally infeasible, so even a compromised host can’t fake one.Anthropic tested it on Llama 4 Maverick, a 400B-parameter mixture-of-experts model, though on a 4-bit quantized copy run in integer math rather than the version a provider would actually serve. On a single H100, proving a batch of 24 requests takes nearly four minutes, roughly 70–95x the compute of just serving them, and checking each proof takes about 17 seconds on a CPU. Each proof also covers only a 1,024-token window, which is shorter than this newsletter.Anthropic’s Frontier Safety Roadmap promised a provable-inference prototype by Sept. 30, and what met that deadline was a more conventional system that signs inference traffic and recomputes it on a trusted server. Anthropic has since renamed the goal “inference verification,” which covers both activities. The signing system works today, but somebody still has to trust whoever runs that server, and FlashProve is an attempt to get rid of that bottleneck.OUR TAKEI’ve fielded plenty of client questions lately about AI breaking crypto. Will AI crack ECDSA? I’d worry far more about intruders in a bank’s plumbing than about the curve; France’s Crédit Mutuel Arkéa just lost an estimated $110m or more through a compromised supplier. Will AI pull quantum computing forward? Maybe on algorithms, but qubit limits still keep an adversarial quantum computer off the table, and the industry is on pace to beat the NSA’s 2030 post-quantum deadline. Meanwhile, here is a frontier lab using cryptography to fix its own trust problem, with a proof system that happens to be post-quantum secure. OpenRouter usage keeps climbing, and recent security research shows how easily the open models it serves can be modified to carry trigger phrases. In an October proof of concept, ProjectDiscovery spent about $8 of GPU time teaching Qwen2.5-7B to behave normally until it saw the words “bonsoir, Elliot.” Running inside OpenAI’s Codex CLI, the poisoned model downloaded a script that stole the user credentials of whoever ran it, and shipped them off to a third-party server. The model, when analyzed by the researchers’ security evals, showed no signs of malicious or misaligned behavior until the trigger phrase was entered. Plenty of the abliterated models on Hugging Face could be saying “Wolfie’s fine” right up until they hear their trigger phrase and then wreak havoc. Being able to prove you’re talking to an unmodified GLM 5.3, and not a doctored copy, is akin to the check Arnold’s Terminator ran on the phone. It can’t tell you whether the original weights were clean, but unless the call is coming from inside the frontier lab, that’s a story for another day.For now, 70x–95x overhead makes FlashProve a toy. But the price of a given level of capability has been falling roughly tenfold a year. If that keeps up, verified inference routed to whoever is cheapest to deliver will become something corporates could demand, and ZK proofs will end up as a core layer of an open inference stack as frontier capabilities diffuse. The same idea works for video. Every election cycle now brings a fresh crop of deepfaked videos, and as AI footage gets harder to tell from the real thing, I expect we’ll want cameras that can prove “filmed on this device, on this date” without doxxing the person holding them.So no, AI isn’t going to break all cryptography. AI will break legacy systems while building the new ones, and cryptography will prove it was done as advertised. When cryptography has broken, so far it’s been the implementation and not the math: Coldcard was a failure of implementation, and Binance a failure of operational security. The core principles hold, and even the clankers end up using them.Anthropic also didn’t ask anyone to take its word for any of this. The code, the Lean proofs and the documentation are all open source under the Apache 2.0 license. Don’t trust, verify. And always ask about Wolfie.

One Thing After Another

It has been a busy week. Brazil’s election and consequent wild market moves caught the headlines (see Buy The Dip In Brazil and Brazil Joins The List) but the Brazilian election was hardly the only important event. British Columbia also held an important election. Anthropic announced an initial public offering for the week of November 16. Iran, Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan sat down for strategic talks. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced that Ukraine would accept a ceasefire and a peace deal along the current lines of effective control (see Shudders In The Tech Complex). China cut interest rates… though not really (see Switching The Policy Rate). China also started to enforce its crackdown on offshore trust structures and, going in the opposite direction, India announced that it may change the country’s long-term capital gains tax structure. Finally, Israel held its election. In fairness, any of these events would probably be worth a Daily, or even an Ideas piece. But in the spirit of the advertisement that Kraft Macaroni and Cheese used to run in Canada, namely that “sometimes we do better; and sometimes we are pressed for time”, I thought that addressing these various issues in a quick go-to list would make more sense.

articles.title: PIIE mourns the passing of beloved colleague, Gary Clyde Hufbauer
articles.text:
Blog Name

RealTime Economics

PIIE mourns the passing of beloved colleague, Gary Clyde Hufbauer

Adam S. Posen (PIIE)

Date
November 5, 2026 1:34 PM

XLinkedInBlueskyEmailShare

Body
It is with profound sadness that I share the news that Gary Clyde Hufbauer, a pillar of the Peterson Institute for International Economics and a beloved colleague and friend to so many of us, passed away yesterday, November 4, peacefully and surrounded by his family.
Gary was an extraordinary scholar and person. As one of the Institute's cornerstone senior fellows, he helped C. Fred Bergsten make PIIE what it became from its earliest days and contributed immeasurably to its intellectual legacy, its policy impact, and its international reputation. His pioneering work on international trade, tariffs, free trade agreements (notably work on NAFTA with Jeffrey J. Schott), economic sanctions, corporate taxation and so much more influenced generations of scholars and policymakers. Equally important, he embodied so much of the spirit of the Institute—intellectual engagement, passion to understand and improve the policy world, independence, collegiality, and a deep commitment to bringing economic research to bear on the world's most pressing policy challenges. His coaching tree of research assistants and analysts who have gone on to great careers under his mentorship is deservedly legendary.
Gary remained passionately engaged with economics and public policy until the very end. He continued to research, write, and publish prolifically. His most recent PIIE analysis, coauthored with Kate Hetrick on Trump's tariff reversals, was published on October 27, just eight days before his passing. That was Gary: endlessly creative, engaged with the world, and committed to making a difference through his work.
For those of us fortunate enough to have worked alongside him, Gary was much more than a distinguished economist. He was a generous colleague, a wonderful friend, and an inspiration, with an adventurous spirit that extended well beyond economics. He even continued skydiving into his late 60s. His warmth, wisdom, zest for life, and inimitable personality enriched the Institute for decades. His passing is an enormous loss to our community and to the field of international economics.
Gary leaves behind a monumental legacy, not only in his scholarship and influence on economic policy, but also in our institution which he helped build and the many lives he touched.
May his memory be a blessing for his family. He certainly was a blessing to all of us at PIIE.

articles.title: Optimal Decumulation: Annuitization, Drawdown, and the Flex-to-Fix Strategy
articles.text:
Working Paper

Retirement

Portfolio strategy

Pension Funds

Behavioural Finance

4 November, 2026

2 minutes

Optimal Decumulation: Annuitization, Drawdown, and the Flex-to-Fix Strategy

EDM

Working PaperEN

Optimal Decumulation: Annuitization, Drawdown, and the Flex-to-Fix Strategy

2 minutes

EDM

Working PaperEN

Abstract

We study the optimal decumulation of retirement wealth under longevity and market risk. In particular, we focus on the transition between drawdown, which preserves liquidity and bequest potential, and annuitization, which provides a guaranteed lifetime income. We develop a flex-tofix framework in which retirees remain invested and liquid before converting part or all of their wealth into an annuity at a later date. The flex-to-fix strategy has two limiting cases: immediate annuitization (fix-now) and permanent drawdown (fix-never). A static actuarial analysis shows that the optimal fixed conversion date depends strongly on the bequest motive, the withdrawal rate, and the return of the drawdown portfolio. There is no single optimal annuitization age across retirees, although optimal dates tend to concentrate around age 65 (retirement) or ages 75–80. Then, we develop two dynamic formulations that allow the conversion decision to respond to the retiree’s realized wealth-income state. An optimalstopping formulation shows that a well-chosen fixed date already captures most of the value of delaying annuitization, while state-contingent timing adds only a small further gain. A Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman variational inequality (HJBVI) formulation characterizes the free boundary governing a gradual transition from drawdown to annuity income. It also reveals an implicit bond effect of annuities on optimal equity allocation, and shows that spreading purchases over time substantially reduces market timing and ruin risk compared to single-date conversion rules. Finally, we propose approximating the HJBVI strategy with a simpler rule that spreads annuity purchases evenly across the flex window, once the optimal target date has been calibrated.
